rows.title: openIfChanged returns null and isCurrent() stays true after a flush when the only changes are doc-values updates
rows.summary: You open an NRT reader, update a doc-values field (or soft-delete through updateDocValues), and then call flush(), a no-op forceMerge(1), or open readers with writeAllDeletes=true. You expect DirectoryReader.openIfChanged(reader, writer) to return a reader that sees the change. Instead it returns null and reader.isCurrent() is true, so SearcherManager keeps the stale searcher, and hasUncommittedChanges() can also return false while updates are uncommitted.

rows.title: A MUST_NOT clause next to a scoring ToParentBlockJoinQuery is checked against child documents instead of parents, so excluded parents are returned, and the search throws when a parent/child block straddles a 4096-doc window
rows.summary: You index parent/child blocks and search BooleanQuery(MUST ToParentBlockJoinQuery(skill:java, parentsFilter, ScoreMode.Avg), MUST_NOT status:hidden), expecting only the parents that are not hidden, which is what count() of the same query and ScoreMode.None return. Instead, on main the hidden parent p2 comes back for Avg, Max, Min and Total ([p1, p2] instead of [p1]); a MUST_NOT clause that matches only child documents (MUST_NOT skill:java) removes both parents ([] instead of [p1, p2]); and in a 6,000-doc segment where a block straddles doc 4096 the search throws AssertionError in ReqExclBulkScorer$WindowBits.get with -ea and ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException (index -1) with -da. The cause is that since #16669 ReqExclBulkScorer folds the MUST_NOT matches of each 4096-doc window into a bit set that it passes to the required clause as acceptDocs, and the join's BlockJoinBulkScorer forwards that acceptDocs unchanged to its child scorer (ToParentBlockJoinQuery.java:541), so the exclusions are tested on child doc IDs, some of them below the window, and never on the parents it collects.
rows.area: join / block join (ToParentBlockJoinQuery.BlockJoinBulkScorer) x search / BooleanQuery MUST_NOT bulk scoring (ReqExclBulkScorer, #16669)

rows.title: Vector similarity queries report isCacheable() == true although their per-segment result depends on live docs, the search timeout and the filter, so a shared query cache serves one reader's or one search's result to another
rows.summary: You search with a vector similarity (threshold) query, for example FloatVectorSimilarityQuery, in a non-scoring context such as IndexSearcher#count or ConstantScoreQuery, with a query cache that several readers or searchers share (the IndexSearcher default in 9.10.0-10.6.0, 10.6.0 by reading). You expect every reader and every search to get the hits it gets without the cache. Instead the cache hands one reader's or one search's per-segment result to another: an older point-in-time reader misses a document that only a newer reader has deleted (99 hits instead of 100), a search without a timeout gets the empty result of an earlier timed-out search (0 instead of 100), and with a filter on an updated doc-values field a newer reader gets a document that no longer matches the filter (100 instead of 99).
rows.area: search / vector similarity queries and the query cache

rows.title: Doc-values-rewritten multi-term queries are invisible to QueryVisitor, so they escape the nested clause limit and the query-cache RAM budget
rows.summary: You run a query tree whose leaves are multi-term queries rewritten with MultiTermQuery.DOC_VALUES_REWRITE (or SortedSetDocValuesField/SortedDocValuesField.newSlowSetQuery) under IndexSearcher's maxClauseCount. You expect IndexSearcher.rewrite to count each such leaf toward the nested clause limit, and an LRUQueryCache to account for the terms a cached query holds. Instead MultiTermQueryDocValuesWrapper.visit calls visitor.getSubVisitor(FILTER, query) and throws the result away, so each leaf counts as 0: with maxClauseCount=8 a query with 10 such leaves raises no TooManyNestedClauses, and a cached 50,000-term TermInSetQuery that holds 966,712 bytes is accounted as 200 bytes; search results stay correct.
rows.area: search / multi-term queries
rows.affected: every release since 8.6.0, branch_10_6 and main [read]

rows.title: With index sorting and a parent field, deleting only a block's parent makes every later merge fail
rows.summary: You use index sorting with a parent field and document blocks, and delete only the parent document of a block. You expect later merges to work. Instead MultiSorter finds no parent for the orphaned child (nextSetBit returns NO_MORE_DOCS), every later merge of that segment throws (an EOFException with the default codec on a file-system directory, IndexOutOfBoundsException on ByteBuffersDirectory), the writer closes tragically and uncommitted documents are lost.

rows.title: HNSW merge-time graph reuse can leave the entry node with no neighbours, dropping kNN recall to zero
rows.summary: You delete a cluster of documents around the HNSW entry node and merge, for example with forceMerge(1), so the merge reuses and repairs the biggest segment's graph. You expect kNN recall to stay about the same. Instead the repair cannot reconnect an entry node that lost every neighbour, every search starts at that isolated node and returns only it (recall@10 0.906 to 0.000 in the repro), and CheckIndex reports no problem.

rows.title: StandardAnalyzer and the other JFlex-generated scanners (StandardTokenizer, UAX29URLEmailTokenizer, ClassicTokenizer, WikipediaTokenizer, HTMLStripCharFilter) silently index no tokens for a text value that ends in an unpaired high surrogate, such as a string cut inside an emoji; values longer than the scan buffer lose or split their last buffer window
rows.summary: You index a text field with StandardAnalyzer at default settings, and the value ends in an unpaired high surrogate, for example 'hello world' followed by U+D83D, which is what cutting a Java String inside an emoji, or decoding the JSON escape \ud83d, produces. You expect hello and world to be indexed and end() to report the input length as the final offset, as happens when the same lone surrogate sits mid-text and as Lucene 7.6.0 did. Instead the scanner's refill reads the whole text, looks one char ahead for the missing low surrogate, hits end of input and reports 'no new input', so the scanner ends the stream without scanning what it just read: no tokens, final offset 0, and the document does not match title:hello; values longer than the 255-char buffer lose or split their last window instead.

rows.title: Two field names that differ only in an unpaired surrogate are written to disk as the same U+FFFD name, so IndexWriter commits an index that DirectoryReader and a new IndexWriter refuse to open (on main also colliding field attribute keys and commit user-data keys)
rows.summary: You add a document with two field names that differ only in an unpaired surrogate, for example 'f\uD800' and 'f\uFFFD' (or two different lone surrogates in the same position), and commit; addDocument and commit return normally, as IndexWriter documents that malformed UTF-16 is silently replaced with U+FFFD, and you expect the committed index to open. Instead DataOutput#writeString writes both names as the same bytes ('f' + U+FFFD), so DirectoryReader.open and a new IndexWriter throw IllegalArgumentException 'duplicate field names: 0 and 1 have: f\uFFFD' for the whole index, and CheckIndex can only recover it by dropping the whole segment. On main the same happens for two colliding field attribute keys or commit user-data keys ('duplicate key'), and a lone-surrogate index-sort field name is stored in its U+FFFD form, so a new IndexWriter with the same sort is refused.

rows.title: IndexWriter.deleteDocuments(Query) and updateDocuments(Query, ...) rewrite the query separately on each segment, so reader-dependent queries (kNN, the default FuzzyQuery and other top-N term rewrites, CommonTermsQuery, MoreLikeThisQuery, score ranges) delete a set that depends on the segment layout and differs from what IndexSearcher.search returns
rows.summary: You call IndexWriter.deleteDocuments(query) (or updateDocuments(query, docs)) on an index with two or more segments and expect it to delete the documents IndexSearcher.search(query) returns, since the javadoc says it 'Deletes the document(s) matching any of the provided queries'. Instead the writer rewrites the query on a separate one-segment IndexSearcher for each segment, so top-k, top-N term expansion and index statistics are computed per segment: a kNN query with k=2 deletes up to 2 documents per segment (4 on two segments), a default FuzzyQuery deletes 60 documents where search finds 50, and MoreLikeThisQuery or a score-range predicate deletes none of the documents search returns. With the same documents committed in one segment before the delete, the delete equals the search result, so the segment layout alone decides what is deleted, and the result is permanent once committed.

rows.title: updateDocument racing commit() can leave two live documents for one key (a lost delete) and operations above the sequence number commit() returned in the commit point, because DocumentsWriterFlushControl.nextPendingFlush flushes a DWPT of the new delete queue during the running full flush
rows.summary: Several threads replace documents by key with updateDocument while another thread calls commit(); you expect every commit point to hold exactly one live document per key and only the operations up to the sequence number commit() returned. Instead, an indexing thread that has just seen 'no full flush running' in nextPendingFlush can, if the commit's full flush starts at that moment, flush a buffer that belongs after the commit inside it, so the commit contains newer operations and, when the delete half of an update misses the older document, two live documents for one key. With assertions enabled it often shows instead as a tragic AssertionError in DocumentsWriter.doFlush that closes the writer.

rows.title: The frozen-FieldType validation cache (#15886) keys a field on its first value's type, so for a field built from several field types a later document skips the per-field schema check (or is checked against stale state after a rejected addBatch), depending on value order, flushes and earlier operations
rows.summary: You index documents whose field id is a StringField plus a SortedDocValuesField, adding the StringField first, and then a document that has only the StringField. You expect IllegalArgumentException, as Lucene's per-field consistency rule (LUCENE-9334, MIGRATE.md) requires, as 9.0-10.4 do, and as main still does when the doc-values value comes first, the type is an unfrozen copy, or a flush comes in between. Instead the document is accepted, because the frozen-FieldType cache added in 10.5.0 (#15886) caches the first value's type after the union of all the document's values was validated and then skips the check for every later document whose first value has that type; on the same fast path the schema state is not rebuilt, so after a rejected addBatch a valid StringField + StoredField document fails with 'index options: expected DOCS, but it has NONE'.

rows.title: tryUpdateDocValue is overwritten by an earlier, still-buffered doc-values update
rows.summary: You update a doc-values field by term and, before that buffered update is resolved, call tryUpdateDocValue on the same document. You expect the later tryUpdateDocValue to win, as sequence numbers say. Instead it is applied in place with the next delete generation, the earlier term update resolves later and wins, and the wrong value (or a lost un-delete) is durable.

rows.title: IndexWriter.deleteDocuments with a kNN query runs on the writer's pooled segment reader, whose live docs miss the writer's own earlier deletes, and on the whole flushed segment including documents added later, so the query picks its k nearest among documents already deleted or added after the call and the acknowledged delete removes fewer documents than it should, often none (since 9.0.0)
rows.summary: You index 10 documents with vectors, delete the nearest one (d0) by its id term, commit, then call deleteDocuments(new KnnFloatVectorQuery(field, target, 1)) and expect it to delete the nearest remaining document, d1, which is what an NRT search at that point returns. Instead nothing more is deleted: IndexWriter runs delete queries on its internal pooled SegmentReader, whose live docs are not refreshed after deletes, so the kNN query still sees d0 as live and picks it again (also after an NRT reopen, or with both deletes in one session). Likewise, while the documents are still buffered, a document added after the kNN delete can take the top slot inside the flushed segment and is then cut by the delete's docID limit, so the delete removes nothing.

rows.title: IndexWriter.updateBinaryDocValue and updateDocValues(Term, BinaryDocValuesField) keep the caller's BytesRef without copying it, so documents still buffered in RAM get the bytes that BytesRef holds at the writer's next document or flush instead of the value passed to the call (every release since 4.8.0)
rows.summary: You call IndexWriter.updateBinaryDocValue(term, field, value), or updateDocValues(term, binaryDocValuesField), and afterwards reuse or change that BytesRef, for example one BytesRefBuilder scratch for a loop of updates or a BinaryDocValues.binaryValue() taken from another reader; each document should get the value it was passed. Documents in flushed segments do, but documents still buffered in RAM get whatever bytes the BytesRef holds when the writer next adds a document or flushes, so a loop over one scratch buffer gives every buffered target the last value. The wrong value is committed silently: no exception, CheckIndex is clean, and the outcome depends on whether the target document had already been flushed.

rows.title: A deleteDocuments or updateDocument(s) call with a term over 32,766 bytes is rejected but stays in IndexWriter's shared delete queue, so every later add and delete and the next commit, NRT reopen or close() fail until rollback() (regression in 9.9.0; up to 9.8.0 such a delete was a no-op)
rows.summary: You add a document, call deleteDocuments(new Term("id", t)) with t longer than 32,766 bytes, and commit. No indexed term can be that long, so you expect the delete to match nothing (as it did up to 9.8.0) or to be rejected, and the commit to contain the document. Instead the delete throws BytesRefHash.MaxBytesLengthExceededException after it was already queued and is never removed from the queue, so every later addDocument and delete throws the same exception and commit() fails (with assertions off an IllegalStateException 'Can't close queue unless all changes are applied', with -ea an AssertionError that closes the writer); the only clean way out is rollback().

rows.title: IndexSearcher#count hangs forever when Weight#count throws, for example on a query timeout, on a segment split into intra-segment partitions
rows.summary: You search with an executor and intra-segment partitions (IndexSearcher.slices(..., allowSegmentPartitions=true)) and call IndexSearcher#count, and the first partition of a segment to arrive throws from Weight#count, for example the ExitingReaderException of a stock ExitableDirectoryReader timeout. You expect the exception to propagate, as TaskExecutor#invokeAll promises. Instead TotalHitCountCollectorManager completes the segment's shared future only on success or CollectionTerminatedException, so the other partitions wait in an unbounded get() and the call never returns (with no test hooks, 124/200 and 176/200 calls hung on main, 44/50 on 10.5.2).
rows.area: search / concurrency

rows.title: IndexWriter.forceApply marks a re-resolving update packet finished outside the IndexWriter lock when its re-iteration matches no segment, so a merge that commits in that gap skips the packet's already-resolved doc-values updates and nobody applies them again: an acknowledged updateNumericDocValue/updateDocValues is lost and softUpdateDocument leaves two live versions of the document, also after commit (since 7.0.0)
rows.summary: You update a document's doc-values field (updateNumericDocValue, updateDocValues) or replace a document with softUpdateDocument while background merges run; IndexWriter returns a sequence number, so every later NRT reader and commit should show the change. If the update packet must re-resolve because a merge committed meanwhile and that merge's result was dropped as fully deleted, IndexWriter.forceApply finds no segment left, leaves the IndexWriter lock and only then marks the packet finished; a second merge that commits in that gap treats the packet as still running, skips its already-resolved update on the merged-away segment, and nobody applies it again. The update is silently lost (id 3 keeps value 30 instead of 7, also after commit and reopen), and with softUpdateDocument the old version is never soft-deleted, so two live versions of one document remain.
rows.area: index / IndexWriter frozen update packets vs. merge carry-over (forceApply, commitMergedDeletesAndUpdates, BufferedUpdatesStream)

rows.title: Merge doc-values carry-over (#16570) can lose an acknowledged update or close the writer on a duplicate delGen
rows.summary: While a merge runs, a document in a merging segment gets an older doc-values update that is still being applied and a newer update to the same segment and field that finishes first. You expect the newest value to win on the merged segment. Instead the merge gives the carried-over on-disk value a delGen at or above the in-flight packet's, so the older value silently wins and survives commit and reopen, or, with assertions on and equal gens, a duplicate-delGen assertion closes the writer and discards uncommitted changes.

rows.title: An un-delete through IndexWriter#tryUpdateDocValue during a merge of the document's segment returns success and is visible to NRT readers, but the merge commit silently drops the document
rows.summary: With a soft-deletes field, you soft-delete a document and later restore it with tryUpdateDocValue(reader, docID, <soft-deletes field = null>) while a merge of its segment is running. You expect what the javadoc promises: the segment has not been merged away, so the update succeeds and returns a sequence number > 0 and the document stays live (otherwise the call returns -1 and you retry). Instead the call does return > 0 and NRT readers show the document again, but the merge, which already treated it as deleted and left it out, commits without it, so the restored document disappears with no error and the next commit persists the loss.

You expect what the javadoc promises: the update succeeded (otherwise it would have returned -1), so a stays live through any later merge and is in the next commit. Instead the merge of a's segment that starts next, while the other thread's packet is still unfinished, does not write the un-delete to disk first, reads a as deleted and drops it, so the next commit no longer contains a (count(id:a) = 0) and nothing reports an error.

rows.title: An IOException late in a doc-values update write leaves IndexWriter open but inconsistent: published update files are never checkpointed and get deleted while still referenced, and a failed pooled-reader re-open silently drops the update
rows.summary: You update a doc-values field (updateNumericDocValue, updateBinaryDocValue, or a soft delete) and open an NRT reader, flush or commit, and the doc-values update write throws a non-tragic IOException after the new files were already published into the segment's SegmentCommitInfo (re-opening the writer's pooled segment reader fails, or a second segment's update write in the same batch fails); the writer stays open (isOpen() true, no tragic exception) and you keep using it. You expect the acknowledged update to reach the next NRT reader and commit, and every file the writer's SegmentInfos references to stay on disk, as in 6.x and as the since-deleted test testNoLostDeletesOrUpdates required. Instead the writer skips its IndexFileDeleter checkpoint and keeps a stale pooled reader whose pending update was already pruned: in releases (and on main with maxDocValuesOverlays=0) the next update rewrites the column from that stale reader and a later commit succeeds with the update reverted (doc 0 = 0 instead of 100, no exception), while with overlays (main's default) or on the partial-batch path the writer later deletes the published files and NRT opens or commits fail with NoSuchFileException. On main's default config the silent revert happens too when the next step is a merge of that segment, for example forceMerge(1): the merge reads the stale pooled reader, the published overlay files are no longer referenced, and the following commit succeeds with the old value and a clean CheckIndex.

rows.title: A non-tragic exception during an NRT reopen or commit full flush aborts the DWPTs other threads filled during that flush, silently losing acknowledged documents and updates while the writer stays open
rows.summary: One thread opens an NRT reader from the IndexWriter (or commits) while other threads keep indexing, and the reopen or commit fails after its flush with an ordinary, non-tragic exception, for example an I/O error while opening a segment file; the writer stays open and the other threads' updateDocument and addDocument calls returned normally with sequence numbers. You expect those changes in the next commit, whose sequence number covers them, and updateDocument to stay atomic. Instead Lucene discards the per-thread buffers that filled up and were parked during the failed full flush, so the added documents never reach the index, and the update keeps only its delete, so the updated document disappears entirely.
rows.area: index / DocumentsWriter full flush (DocumentsWriterFlushControl.abortFullFlushes, blockedFlushes) and the error paths of IndexWriter.getReader and prepareCommit

rows.title: An exception inside DocumentsWriterPerThread.prepareFlush is not tragic: IndexWriter stays open but drops the in-memory segment and the deletes and doc-values updates it had just frozen, so the next successful commit lacks acknowledged operations its sequence number covers
rows.summary: You buffer a document, a delete and doc-values updates in an IndexWriter, and commit() fails with an ordinary exception while the in-memory segment is being prepared for flushing (executed: ArithmeticException 'integer overflow' after about 2.2 million updateNumericDocValue calls on a 1 KB id); the writer stays open and reports no tragic exception. You expect either the writer to close itself, as it does for every other failure while flushing a segment, or the next successful commit (or close()) to contain every operation its returned sequence number covers. Instead the failed flush has already taken the buffered deletes and updates out of the shared delete queue and then drops them together with the in-memory segment, so the next commit silently lacks the buffered document, keeps the deleted document live and holds a stale doc-values value.
rows.area: index / DocumentsWriter flush failure handling (DocumentsWriter.doFlush, DocumentsWriterPerThread.prepareFlush, DocumentsWriterDeleteQueue.freezeGlobalBuffer)

rows.title: An Error (in practice an OutOfMemoryError) while an NRT reopen or commit that has no buffered documents freezes the buffered deletes and doc-values updates is replaced by IllegalStateException("Can't close queue unless all changes are applied") from the finally of DocumentsWriter.flushAllThreads, so IndexWriter stays open instead of closing itself and its next commit silently drops those acknowledged deletes and updates (with -ea an AssertionError replaces the Error; every release since 8.2.0)
rows.summary: You commit documents id:1 and id:2, call deleteDocuments(id:1) and updateNumericDocValue(id:2, dv, 22) (both return sequence numbers), and then open an NRT reader from the writer or call commit() with no documents buffered, and an OutOfMemoryError strikes while the writer freezes those two buffered changes; the IndexWriter javadoc says the writer closes itself after an Error, so you expect to see the Error and a closed writer (or, if the writer stays usable, a later commit that contains both changes). Instead the finally of DocumentsWriter.flushAllThreads closes the delete queue that the flush has already swapped out, and its close() throws IllegalStateException("Can't close queue unless all changes are applied"), which replaces the Error; IndexWriter does not treat that as tragic and stays open, the old queue with both changes is abandoned, and the next commit() returns -1 with id:1 still live and dv(id:2) still 2. With -ea an AssertionError ('Can not replace a full flush queue if the queue is not closed') replaces the Error instead, and since 10.0.0 it closes the writer.
rows.area: index / IndexWriter full flush (DocumentsWriter.flushAllThreads naked-delete freeze, DocumentsWriterDeleteQueue.close)

rows.title: If anything throws in IndexWriter.finishCommit after segments_N was renamed into place but before the commit checkpoint took the new commit's file references (an InfoStream exception, or an OutOfMemoryError at that point), the writer closes as tragic but its finalizer first releases those references, so files that only the new commit uses are deleted and the newest durable commit, and with it DirectoryReader.open and a new IndexWriter, fails until that segments_N is removed by hand (LUCENE-8217 dropped the LUCENE-5958 guard; every release since 7.4.0)
rows.summary: You call prepareCommit(), let a merge (here forceMerge(1)) retire the segments of the prepared commit, and then call commit(); right after commit() has renamed pending_segments_2 to segments_2, your InfoStream's next log call throws (an OutOfMemoryError at the same point does the same). IndexWriter correctly treats this as a tragedy and closes itself, and you expect the finished commit segments_2 to stay readable, as it does on 7.3.1. Instead finishCommit's try-with-resources finalizer releases the commit's file references before the commit checkpoint has taken its own, so the merged-away segment's files are deleted and DirectoryReader.open(dir) fails with CorruptSegmentInfoException '_1.si cannot be read' until segments_2 is deleted by hand.

rows.title: Exact PhraseQuery/MultiPhraseQuery: when the first query term occurs twice at one document position, the phrase freq exceeds the maxFreq()/impacts bound, so Scorer#getMaxScore is below score() and TOP_SCORES search drops the best hit
rows.summary: You index text with an analyzer that can put the first word of a phrase twice at one position (for example KeywordRepeatFilter plus a stemmer, or index-time synonyms queried through QueryBuilder) and run an exact phrase search with IndexSearcher#search(q, n); you expect the same top hits as scoring every match. ExactPhraseMatcher counts such a phrase occurrence once per copy of the first word, so the document's phrase freq is 2, but the bound it reports for skipping work (maxFreq() and the block impacts behind getMaxScore) is the smallest term freq, 1. Once more than 1000 hits are counted the searcher skips documents whose real score is competitive: in the repro search(q, 1) returns doc 0 although exhaustive scoring ranks doc 1100 first, with no error.

rows.summary: You search the fields title and body with MultiFieldQueryParser under AND_OPERATOR and expect what its class javadoc promises: every query term must appear, in any field, so adding a field never loses a document that QueryParser on one of those fields finds. Instead getFieldQuery takes clause i of each field's analyzed BooleanQuery as 'term position i' and requires every such group: with title tokenized on whitespace and body on letters, 'wi-fi router' becomes +(title:wi-fi body:wi) +(title:router body:fi) +(body:router), which misses a document titled 'wi-fi router' and matches one with title 'router' and body 'wi router' (released since 6.2.0, default settings since 7.0.0; since #16446 the single word 'wi-fi' loses the match too). Since #16446 (in 10.6.0), with autoGeneratePhraseQueries and the multi-word synonym 'guinea pig' -> 'cavy', 'guinea-pig' becomes +(body:"guinea pig") +(body:cavy), so even MultiFieldQueryParser over body alone finds nothing where QueryParser(body) finds the document.

rows.title: LatLon distance sort used as a later Sort key drops closer tied hits after 1024 bottom updates, because LatLonPointDistanceComparator keeps a stale bounding box when the bottom grows (every release since 6.1.0)
rows.summary: You search with Sort(cat INT, LatLonDocValuesField.newDistanceSort("loc", 0, 0)), so distance only breaks ties of cat, over 1026 documents: docs 0..1023 each have a smaller cat than the one before (so each becomes the new top hit) and lie about 1 km from the origin, and docs 1024 and 1025 share the smallest cat, with doc 1025 (about 1500 km away) closer than doc 1024 (about 2000 km). You expect doc 1025 as the top hit, because Sort says a later SortField breaks ties and the distance sort orders by ascending distance. You get doc 1024, with no error: after 1024 bottom updates the comparator rebuilds its competitive bounding box only on every 64th update, so it keeps the 1 km box built for the old bottom, and compareBottom rejects doc 1025 as outside that box without computing its distance.

rows.title: NRTSuggester returns too few or wrongly ranked suggestions in a segment with only a few deleted documents, because its deleted-document queue slack (long)(topN / liveDocsRatio) rounds back down to topN
rows.summary: You index suggestions with SuggestField, delete one document or update it (which deletes the old version), and ask SuggestIndexSearcher.suggest for the top n completions; you expect the top n live completions, because NRTSuggester enlarges its bounded search queue 'to account for the filtered out suggestions' of deleted documents. With few deletions that enlargement, (long)(topN / liveDocsRatio), rounds back down to topN (for one deletion in ten documents, (long)(1 / 0.9) = 1), so a deleted completion that takes a result slot is thrown away and nothing replaces it: with abc_0, the best of abc_0..abc_9 in one segment, deleted, suggest('abc_', 1) returns [] instead of [abc_1], and after updateDocument lowers the best entry's weight from 1000 to 1, suggest(num=1) returns that entry at weight 1 instead of the live entry at weight 999. Deleting more documents (5 of 10) gives the queue enough room and the same lookup works.
rows.area: suggest / document (NRT) suggester (NRTSuggester.getMaxTopNSearcherQueueSize via SuggestIndexSearcher and CompletionQuery; Util.TopNSearcher queue depth)

rows.title: A document block that IndexWriter rejects at a child (a documented, non-aborting IllegalArgumentException such as an immense term) leaves the block's already numbered documents in the in-memory segment as deleted documents with no parent after them, and the next accepted block's parent adopts them: ToParentBlockJoinQuery count() under every ScoreMode and ScoreMode.None searches return that parent although none of its live children matches (every release since 5.3.0)
rows.summary: You add a block [red child, a child with a term longer than MAX_TERM_LENGTH, parent], which IndexWriter rejects with its documented IllegalArgumentException, then add a second block [blue child, parent], commit, and count ToParentBlockJoinQuery(color:red, parents, ScoreMode.None). You expect 0, because addDocuments promises that a reader sees all or none of a block and the only red child was in the rejected block (you do get 0 when that block is never added). Instead count() returns 1: the rejected block's first two documents kept doc IDs 0 and 1 as deleted documents with no parent after them, and the join maps the deleted red child to the next parent, doc 3, which belongs to the accepted block.

rows.title: ThaiTokenizer and ThaiAnalyzer silently drop a number written directly after a period, '#' or currency sign (2567 in 'พ.ศ.2567', 1,500 in 'ราคา ฿1,500', 42 in 'page.42'), because a word segment is skipped whole when its first character is not a letter or digit
rows.summary: You index Thai text such as 'ประชุมวันที่ 1 ม.ค.2567' or 'ราคา ฿1,500' with the stock ThaiAnalyzer and expect the year 2567 or the amount 1,500 to be searchable, as they are when written 'พ.ศ. 2567' or 'ราคา 1,500 บาท'. Instead the number never reaches the index: the JDK word BreakIterator returns it together with its leading period or currency sign as one segment ('.2567', '฿1,500'), and ThaiTokenizer skips any segment whose first character is not a letter or digit, so the whole number is thrown away. A TermQuery for 2567 then finds 0 documents instead of 1, with no error.

rows.title: BrazilianStemmer step2 tests for the suffix 'ira' but removes 'ava', so -ira words (mentira, partirá) stay unstemmed and -ava verb forms (cantava, ficava) lose only the final 'a', and a search for one form misses the others (mentiras, cantavam, ficar)
rows.summary: You index Brazilian Portuguese text with the stock BrazilianAnalyzer; one document says 'mentiras' or 'eles cantavam', and a query says 'mentira' or 'cantava'. You expect each pair to share a stem (ment, cant), because step2 is documented to delete the verb suffix it finds in RV, the class's own rule list deletes both -ira and -ava, and Snowball Portuguese does the same. Instead the branch at BrazilianStemmer.java:958 tests 'ira' but removes 'ava', so -ira words keep the whole word (mentira stays mentira) and the class's correct 'ira' rule further down can never run, while no branch tests -ava at all, so cantava loses only its final 'a' (cantav); both queries find 0 hits.

rows.title: Classic QueryParser and MultiFieldQueryParser ignore an explicit phrase slop ("..."~N) when the phrase analyzes to a token graph (multi-word synonyms, WordDelimiterGraphFilter) or, for QueryParser, carries token boosts, and search with the default phraseSlop instead: fewer hits with the default slop 0, extra hits for an explicit ~0 when a larger default slop is set
rows.summary: You parse "guinea pig food"~1 with the classic QueryParser over an analyzer with a multi-word synonym 'guinea pig => cavy' and expect the documented proximity search, the words within one position of each other on every synonym path, as "pig food"~1 gives for a phrase without synonyms. Instead the parser analyzes the phrase with its default phraseSlop (0) and applies the explicit ~1 afterwards only to a top-level PhraseQuery or MultiPhraseQuery, so the BooleanQuery of per-path phrases that a token graph produces ('body:"cavy food" body:"guinea pig food"') and the BoostQuery that a token boost produces ('(body:"pig food")^2.0' for "pig|2.0 food"~1) keep slop 0, and 'my guinea pig dry food' is not found. The same root cause also over-matches: after setPhraseSlop(1), an explicit exact "guinea pig food"~0 is searched with slop 1 and returns extra documents; MultiFieldQueryParser has the graph defect in both directions but not the boost one, because its applySlop unwraps BoostQuery (since 9.6.0, #12196).

rows.title: Sequential DrillSideways skips the two-phase matches() check of the second-cheapest drill-down dimension on segments without deletions, so documents that fail that dimension but are in its approximation are returned as drill-down hits and counted in the facets (released since 5.3.0)
rows.summary: You run DrillSideways without an executor on a DrillDownQuery with two or more dimensions, one of which is a two-phase query such as a distance or range drill-down with a fast-match query or a PhraseQuery, and expect the hits to match every dimension and each dimension's sideways counts to cover the documents that match all the other dimensions. Instead, on a segment with no deleted documents, when that dimension is the second-cheapest by approximation cost and the base query is broad, DrillSidewaysScorer never calls its TwoPhaseIterator#matches(), because the condition 'acceptDocs == null || acceptDocs.get(docID) && (dc.twoPhase == null || dc.twoPhase.matches())' parses as 'acceptDocs == null || (get && matches)'. So every document in that dimension's approximation (inside the bounding box but outside the radius, the phrase words in another order) is treated as matching it, returned as a hit and counted in the facets, while concurrent DrillSideways and plain boolean queries on the same searcher give the correct sets.
rows.area: facet / DrillSideways (sequential DrillSidewaysScorer, drill-down-advance strategy, two-phase drill-down dimensions)

rows.title: Sequential DrillSideways lets a TOP_SCORES hit collector prune the shared base query, so drill-sideways facet counts silently miss matching documents
rows.summary: You run a sequential DrillSideways search (no executor) with a filter-style base query drilled down to color=red, and pass a TopScoreDocCollectorManager with a finite total-hits threshold (10 in the repro, or IndexSearcher's default 1000) as the hit collector through search(DrillDownQuery, CollectorManager, List). You expect the drill-sideways counts for color to include every document that matches the base query (75 in the repro), as the same search does with an exhaustive hit collector or with the concurrent DrillSideways. Instead the counts are silently too low (11, or 1001 instead of 2250 at threshold 1000): the base query is scored with the hit collector's TOP_SCORES mode and its scorer is handed to the hit collector, whose min-competitive-score updates make the shared base iteration skip documents that the sideways collectors then never see; the top hits are correct.

rows.title: ShingleFilter with unigrams on (its default) after a stop filter covers a hole at the start of the text only with a filler shingle whose position length jumps over the next word's position, while the filler-only unigram is suppressed, so the token graph is disconnected and QueryBuilder's graph analysis silently drops that word: 'the lord' becomes body:_ lord and misses a document 'lord' (since 6.4.0)
rows.summary: You analyse queries with ShingleFilter after a stop filter (ShingleAnalyzerWrapper over EnglishAnalyzer, or WhitespaceTokenizer, StopFilter and ShingleFilter with its defaults) and search for 'the lord' with QueryBuilder or the classic QueryParser; you expect the query to keep the word 'lord' that the analyzer emits, so a document 'lord' (or 'Lord of the Rings') is found, as it is with graph queries switched off. Instead the removed 'the' leaves a hole at the start, and ShingleFilter covers it only with the filler shingle '_ lord' (position 0, position length 2): the filler-only unigram that would reach position 1, where the unigram 'lord' starts, is never output, so the token graph is disconnected. QueryBuilder's graph analysis keeps only start-to-end paths, builds body:_ lord and finds nothing, with no error.

rows.summary: You write a RegexpQuery or RegExp whose character class starts a range with an escaped character, such as [\.-z]. You expect it to match the range from '.' to 'z', as in 10.1 and java.util.regex. Instead, since 10.2.0, it is parsed as the three characters '.', '-' and 'z', so the query silently matches different terms.

rows.title: ShapeField.encodeTriangle puts the wrong edge flag on the first edge when it flips a clockwise triangle, so LatLonShape and XYShape CONTAINS queries return wrong hits
rows.summary: You index a polygon with LatLonShape or XYShape and run a CONTAINS query that asks whether the polygon fully contains a box (or another query shape); you expect a match exactly when the box lies inside the polygon. When ShapeField.encodeTriangle turns one of the polygon's clockwise tessellation triangles counter-clockwise, it swaps two vertices but gives the new first edge the 'belongs to the polygon boundary' flag of the wrong old edge, so a real boundary edge can lose its flag and an internal diagonal can gain one. CONTAINS then silently says yes for boxes that stick out of the polygon (in one executed case a box 99.9998% outside it) and no for boxes well inside it.

rows.title: Polygon2D.intersectsLine/intersectsTriangle never test the query polygon's hole edges, so LatLonShape/XYShape INTERSECTS misses, and DISJOINT matches, a line or polygon whose vertices all lie in holes but which crosses the polygon between them
rows.summary: You index a line or polygon with LatLonShape or XYShape and search with a query polygon that has holes, for example a region with two lakes cut out; a line from one lake to the other crosses the land between them, so INTERSECTS should return it and DISJOINT should not. Polygon2D.intersectsLine/intersectsTriangle report an intersection only when a vertex of the indexed shape is inside the polygon (holes excluded) or one of its edges crosses the outer ring; they never test the hole edges, so when every vertex lies in a hole the shape counts as not intersecting. The query returns the wrong documents with no error (repro: the square [0,10]^2 with holes [1,3]x[4,6] and [7,9]x[4,6]; of the line (2,5)-(8,5), the box [2,8]x[4.5,5.5] and the point (5,5), INTERSECTS returns only the point and DISJOINT returns the line and the box).

rows.title: LatLonShape circle (distance) queries miss lines and polygons whose edge crosses the circle with no vertex inside, because Circle2D tests only the edge point closest to the centre in raw lon/lat degrees, not the point closest by haversine distance (DISJOINT matches them instead)
rows.summary: You index a two-point LatLonShape line from (lat 60.38, lon 9.8) to (lat 59.78, lon 10.4) and run LatLonShape.newDistanceQuery with INTERSECTS and a 10 km circle around (lat 60, lon 10). The line passes 8.95 km from the centre, so you expect 1 hit, and the circle's own contains() accepts a point of the line; you get 0 hits and no error, and DISJOINT matches the line instead. When neither end is inside, Circle2D tests only the point of the segment closest to the centre in raw lon/lat degrees (here 11.19 km away), not the point closest by haversine distance, so diagonal edges that cross the outer part of the circle are missed.

rows.title: Intervals.notContainedBy(small, or(B1, B2)) returns small intervals that lie inside B1 or B2, because the default disjunction rewrite turns it into an OR of per-clause filters
rows.summary: You index 'i love new york', 'york city is big' and 'york is here' and search notContainedBy(york, or(phrase(new, york), phrase(york, city))), meaning 'york that is not part of new york or york city'; you expect only the third document, which is what or(false, ...) and the nested form notContainedBy(notContainedBy(york, 'new york'), 'york city') return. Instead all three documents match: the default disjunction rewrite (LUCENE-8477) pulls the OR out of the excluded operand and builds or(NOT_CONTAINED_BY(york, 'new york'), NOT_CONTAINED_BY(york, 'york city')), which computes 'not inside B1 or not inside B2' where the javadoc promises 'not inside (B1 or B2)'. So adding a clause to the exclusion adds hits: notContainedBy(a, or(phrase(c, a), b)) matches 'c a' although notContainedBy(a, phrase(c, a)) does not.

rows.title: Intervals.atLeast stops early when the sub-iterator it just used runs out, so it loses minimal intervals and misses documents when nested; the same hand-over also lets a stale sub-iterator re-enter and return a non-minimal interval out of order
rows.summary: You index 'a b' and read the intervals of Intervals.atLeast(1, term a, term b), or search ordered(c, atLeast(1, a, b)) over 'a c b'; you expect [0,0] and [1,1], exactly what or(a, b) returns, and one hit. Instead atLeast returns only [0,0] and the ordered query finds nothing: when the sub-iterator just popped from atLeast's proximity queue has no further interval, nextInterval() does not pull a replacement from its background queue and ends, although the other source still has intervals. The same hand-over never advances waiting sub-iterators past the current start, so atLeast(1, b, phrase(a, b)) on 'a b b' returns [1,1] then [0,1] (out of order, and [0,1] contains [1,1]) and loses [2,2].

rows.title: NGramPhraseQuery matches documents its own PhraseQuery does not whenever adjacent gram positions do not come from adjacent text: multi-valued n-gram fields with a position increment gap below n (Lucene's default gap is 0), CJKAnalyzer text with a break between CJK runs (punctuation, a digit, a Latin word or a stop word), and NGramTokenizer pre-tokenizing through isTokenChar
rows.summary: You wrap the analyzer's phrase query in NGramPhraseQuery, which its javadoc presents as a PhraseQuery optimized for n-gram fields that you may use 'rather than PhraseQuery' (the introducing review said 'the same results will be returned, scoring will differ'), and expect the same matching documents. Instead the rewrite keeps only the first gram, every n-th gram and the last gram at their relative positions ("ab bc cd" becomes "ab ? cd"), which is only correct when grams n positions apart always come from one unbroken run of text, and nothing checks that. So a 2-gram field with the two values 'xab' and 'zcd' (default gap 0), CJKAnalyzer text such as '東京。新大学' or '東京6大学野球', and a whitespace-pre-tokenized 2-gram field holding 'xab zcd' or 'multi long' all match a phrase ('abcd', '東京大学', 'tion') that the PhraseQuery itself does not match.

rows.title: ToParentBlockJoinSortField treats a parent as having a missing child value whenever its block holds any document outside childFilter, even if every document has the sort field (regression in 10.5.0)
rows.summary: You index blocks with two kinds of non-parent documents, for example P1 = [type:a s=y n=40, type:b s=x n=7, parent P1] and P2 = [type:a s=d n=10, parent P2], and sort the parents of a ToParentBlockJoinQuery with new ToParentBlockJoinSortField("s", STRING, false, parents, childFilter type:a), expecting 'P2=d P1=y', which is what Lucene 10.4.0 returns. The cause is that ToParentDocValues decides whether some child lacks a value by comparing the number of childFilter documents that have a value with the number of all documents in the block, so any document outside childFilter, with or without the field, forces the missing value.

rows.title: Grouping with a within-group sort that equals Sort.RELEVANCE but is a different object (new Sort(), new Sort(SortField.FIELD_SCORE)) returns the wrong documents per group when results from slices or shards are merged, and since 10.5.0 a NaN GroupDocs.maxScore

Instead TopGroupsCollector tests 'withinGroupSort == Sort.RELEVANCE' (same object), so it collects each group with the field-sort collector, whose hits carry score NaN, while TopGroups.merge tests equals and merges those hits by their NaN scores. When results from 2 or more slices or shards are merged, each group's page then comes out slice by slice or shard by shard (the finder's test returns a score-1 document instead of the score-4 one), and since 10.5.0 the merged maxScore is NaN, on main even for a sequential GroupingSearch.

rows.title: Document suggester with skipDuplicates=true and an index-time synonym returns fewer than n distinct suggestions (n=2 drops one that n=3 returns), because Util.TopNSearcher drops its queue before the last result although acceptPartialPath can still reject that path, and NRTSuggester sizes the queue from entries per analyzed form, which ignores synonym graph paths
rows.summary: You index suggestions through a CompletionAnalyzer with an index-time synonym (b => xb, keeping the original, so 'a b' is indexed as 'a b' and 'a xb'), add a second suggestion 'a xc', and call SuggestIndexSearcher.suggest(prefix 'a', 2, skipDuplicates=true); you expect the two distinct suggestions [a b/10, a xc/3], which n=3 does return. Instead you get only [a b/10]: Util.TopNSearcher sets its queue to null for the last result when maxQueueDepth == topN, assuming the last path always completes, but the duplicate filter (acceptPartialPath) rejects that path when it reaches 'a xb', so the sibling arc that leads to 'a xc' is never queued and the search ends early (called directly, TopNSearcher even reports isComplete=true for such a search). NRTSuggester makes the queue that small because it counts entries sharing one analyzed form, not the analyzed paths per suggestion that its javadoc describes, so a synonym never enlarges it; with two synonyms (b => {xb, yb}) the duplicate paths fill the queue and both n=2 and n=3 lose a suggestion even with the shortcut removed.
rows.area: suggest / document suggester (NRTSuggester skipDuplicates, queue sizing) and util / FST (Util.TopNSearcher)

rows.title: RegexCompletionQuery lets '.' and negated character classes match the document suggester's internal end byte (0x00), so a suggestion one character shorter than the pattern is returned ('foo.' returns foo as well as food, 'foo..' returns food)
rows.summary: You run a RegexCompletionQuery, which 'takes a regular expression as the prefix of the query term', over the suggestions foo (weight 5), food (1) and fox (2), and expect 'foo.' and 'foo[^x]' to return only food (the only suggestion with a matching four-character prefix) and 'foo..' to return nothing (no suggestion has five characters). Instead 'foo.' and 'foo[^x]' return [foo, food] with foo ranked first, and 'foo..' returns [food]. The document suggester stores every suggestion in its FST as the analyzed text followed by an internal end byte 0x00 and dedup bytes, and RegexCompletionQuery hands the regex automaton, whose '.' and negated classes include U+0000, to the FST intersection unchanged, so the pattern runs past the end of the suggestion into these internal bytes.
rows.area: suggest / document (NRT) suggester (RegexCompletionQuery automaton intersected with the NRTSuggester FST, including the internal END and dedup bytes; also inside ContextQuery)

rows.title: BlendedInfixSuggester loses a distinct suggestion when a duplicate entry arrives while its result set is full: boundedTreeAdd evicts the lowest result before TreeSet.add rejects the duplicate, so lookup returns num-1 suggestions, or a lower-ranked fetched suggestion in place of a higher-ranked one
rows.summary: You build a BlendedInfixSuggester with its default settings (POSITION_LINEAR, numFactor 10) from {the lake:1000, lake:950, lake:950, my lake:920} and call lookup("lake", false, 2); blending gives lake 950, the lake 900 and my lake 828, num=3 returns [lake/950, the lake/900, my lake/828], so you expect [lake/950, the lake/900]. Instead you get [lake/950, my lake/828], and without 'my lake' only [lake/950]. When the bounded result set is full, boundedTreeAdd (BlendedInfixSuggester.java:294-306) removes the lowest result with pollFirst() before it calls results.add(result), and that add does nothing for the second 'lake' because LookUpComparator (:383-407) already holds an equal element, so 'the lake' is lost and a later, lower-ranked hit takes its slot.

rows.title: ContextQuery gives an exact context's boost to any longer indexed context that starts with it (exact 'red' boosts a suggestion indexed under 'redwood') when that longer context is matched through a shorter prefix context or addAllContexts(), so document-suggester hits get wrong scores and a wrong order

rows.title: RescoreTopNQuery lets deleted documents take top-n slots, and IndexSearcher#count counts them

Instead a deleted document whose rescore value ranks in the top n takes one of the n slots, so the search returns fewer than n hits (n=2: [2] instead of [2, 1]) while IndexSearcher#count still reports 2; the deleted document itself is never returned.

rows.title: RescoreTopNQuery builds its inner Weight with ScoreMode.COMPLETE_NO_SCORES, so a values source that needs scores (DoubleValuesSource.SCORES, an expression using _score) reads 0 instead of the inner query's score

Instead RescoreTopNQuery runs the inner query in a mode that produces no scores, so the source reads 0 for every match and the result is doc 0 with score 0.0 (the first match by doc id); for a kNN inner query the scores are right until the query cache caches the inner query, and from then on (the 5th identical search with the usage-tracking policy) they read 0 too.

rows.title: RescoreTopNQuery passes negative DoubleValuesSource values through as negative scores, so a top-k BooleanQuery that ORs it with another clause silently returns no hits
rows.summary: You index 10 documents with a numeric doc-values field v = -2..-11 and run BooleanQuery(SHOULD RescoreTopNQuery(MatchAllDocsQuery, DoubleValuesSource.fromLongField("v"), 1), SHOULD MatchAllDocsQuery) with searcher.search(q, 10), expecting all 10 documents, since each one matches the MatchAllDocsQuery clause and count(q) is 10. Instead it returns 0 hits and totalHits 0. RescoreTopNQuery copies the raw value -2 into the score, although Lucene requires non-negative scores (LUCENE-7996) and FunctionScoreQuery maps negative values to 0, so the clause reports a max score of -2, the two clauses' max scores sum to -1, below the initial minimum competitive score of 0, and MaxScoreBulkScorer skips the whole window as if no document could compete.

rows.title: ScorerUtil.minRequiredScore (new in 10.3.0, #14827) never terminates when the remaining clauses' max score is negative at a minimum competitive score of 0, so with assertions disabled a top-k BooleanQuery with a negative-scoring SHOULD clause spins forever in MaxScoreBulkScorer, the infinite loop that LUCENE-10428 had turned into an exception
rows.summary: You run IndexSearcher.search(q, 10) on a 3-document index, where q ORs a clause that scores every document -1 and reports -1 as its max score with a MatchAllDocsQuery, and expect it to return the 3 documents or throw, as 10.2.2 does and as Lucene has promised since LUCENE-10428 (9.1.0: 'Queries with a misbehaving score function may no longer cause infinite loops in their parent BooleanQuery'). With assertions disabled it never returns: MaxScoreBulkScorer treats the -1 clause as non-essential at the initial minimum competitive score 0 and calls ScorerUtil.minRequiredScore(-1.0, 0f, 2), whose loop starts at 1.0 and subtracts Math.ulp(0f) = 1.4e-45, a step that is lost in double arithmetic, so its exit test never changes. The same happens without custom code through RescoreTopNQuery over negative values, and IndexSearcher#setTimeout does not stop it.

rows.title: SynonymQuery, MultiPhraseQuery, CombinedFieldQuery and SpanOrQuery ask IndexSearcher#termStats only about terms that occur in the local reader, so an override that supplies distributed (whole-collection) statistics is never asked about a query term that occurs only on other shards, and documents on those shards score differently than in the whole collection (since 8.3.0, LUCENE-8921)

You expect each document to get the score it gets when you search the whole collection, as TermQuery and PhraseQuery do. rows.title: IndriDirichletSimilarity produces negative scores, and since 10.3.0 a top-k TermQuery search under it silently returns no hits, because BatchScoreBulkScorer passes a hit to the collector only if its score is at least the initial minimum competitive score of 0

rows.title: SweetSpotSimilarity with a length plateau (setLengthNormFactors with min >= 2) breaks Similarity's norm-monotonicity contract, so default top-k search silently misses the best hits

Below the plateau a 2-term field scores lower than a 10-term field although its norm is smaller, which breaks the rule that a greater norm never scores higher; the postings writer relies on that rule, keeps only the short field's (freq, norm) pair for the block, advertises a block maximum of 0.471, and top-k search skips the block.

rows.title: CombinedFieldQuery computes its max score as score(+Infinity, 1), which is NaN under AxiomaticF2LOG/F2EXP, so top-k pruning silently drops the best hits

CombinedFieldScorer reports score(Float.POSITIVE_INFINITY, 1) as its max score, although SimScorer#score requires a finite freq and documents score(Float.MAX_VALUE, 1) as the bound; for the F2 similarities that is Inf/Inf = NaN, and MaxScoreBulkScorer, for which NaN is never below the minimum competitive score, then makes the other clause required. Documents that match only the CombinedFieldQuery are skipped: in a 3000-document index the default search returns doc 0 (score 2.1975672) as the top hit instead of doc 2000 (6.383921), and the upstream oracle CheckHits.checkTopScores fails.

rows.title: IndriAndQuery returns documents that match none of its clauses when a clause uses two-phase iteration (PhraseQuery, doc-values range queries), because IndriDisjunctionScorer iterates the clauses' approximations and never calls TwoPhaseIterator.matches()
rows.summary: You build an IndriAndQuery from SHOULD clauses, for example the phrase "a b" plus the term c, or a doc-values range n in [1, 10] plus the term c, and expect the documents that match at least one clause, as its javadoc ('matches documents matching combinations of subqueries') says. IndriDisjunctionScorer walks the approximations of its two-phase clauses and never runs their exact matches() check; a segment where only one clause has a scorer is exact, so the same document can be rejected in one segment and returned in another.

rows.title: LogOddsFusionQuery returns the raw clause score in segments where only one clause has a scorer, so identical documents score differently depending on their segment and explain() disagrees with the score

Instead, in a segment where only one clause has a scorer, the query hands back that clause's own scorer unchanged, so documents there get the raw clause score: in the repro two documents with identical content score 0.6386912 and 0.5532073, while explain() reports 0.6386912 for both.

rows.title: Monitor with RegexpQueryHandler silently misses matching RegexpQuery queries, because the handler indexes each one under a fragment of its pattern text (for example 'cat|dog', 'colou' or '?mail') that matching terms do not contain

rows.title: Monitor with RegexpQueryHandler silently misses regexp matches on any short token that contains a supplementary character (an emoji, a CJK Extension B ideograph, a Gothic or Adlam letter), because SuffixingNGramTokenFilter emits no ngrams for that token
rows.summary: You build a Monitor whose presearcher uses RegexpQueryHandler, register the query /hel.*/ and match a document whose text is 'hello😀' (WhitespaceAnalyzer, one token). Instead SuffixingNGramTokenFilter, which should emit every substring of the token with the suffix 'XX' so that the query's index term 'helXX' is found, starts its gram size at the token's UTF-16 length (7) but checks it against the token's code-point count (6), gives up on the token without emitting a single ngram, and the query is silently never run.

rows.title: Monitor.match running while Monitor.register re-registers the same query id can silently miss that query, because register puts the new version's cache entries into the live cache map before the new index documents are committed and the query index searcher is refreshed

rows.title: TermStates#get hands a lazily looked-up TermState to the other partitions of the same segment without safe publication, so under intra-segment concurrency a partition can read docFreq or file pointers still at 0 and a non-scoring term or phrase query silently misses matches (executed on aarch64)
rows.summary: You search with an IndexSearcher that splits one segment into several partitions (the documented intra-segment concurrency) and count a non-scoring PhraseQuery, expecting the same count as a sequential search (500). Instead, on aarch64 about once per 10^5 to 10^6 searches the count is 437, 438 or 375 with no error: all partitions share one lazily filled TermStates, and TermStates#get stores each freshly cloned TermState into a plain array slot that the other partitions read with plain loads, so a partition can see the object before its fields (docFreq 0, sometimes a zero docStartFP or posStartFP) and gets an empty or garbage postings list for its doc range. Publishing the slot with a release store and reading it with acquire loads removes the failure in every test (0 in 1.2M end-to-end searches, 0 in 122.9M root-cause lookups).

rows.title: Merging segments of an index sorted by a FLOAT or DOUBLE field misplaces a NaN whose sign bit is set, so the merged segment violates its declared index sort (CheckIndex at level 2 or higher reports it) and sorted searches that terminate early on the index sort return wrong top hits
rows.summary: You configure IndexWriterConfig#setIndexSort with a FLOAT (or DOUBLE) SortField over a FloatDocValuesField (DoubleDocValuesField), index a document whose value is a NaN with the sign bit set, for example the run-time negation of a NaN, and expect every flushed and merged segment to follow the sort, in which Float.compare puts every NaN after +Infinity. Flush gets this right, but a merge orders documents by NumericUtils.sortableFloatBits of the raw stored bits, which ranks that NaN below -Infinity, so the merged segment follows neither order: segments {3, 1, NaN} and {2, 0.5} sorted descending merge to [2.0, 0.5, NaN, 3.0, 1.0]. CheckIndex at level 2 or higher reports the segment as unsorted, and a top-1 search sorted by the index sort returns 2.0 instead of NaN, and 2.0 instead of 3.0 for a query that does not match the NaN document.
rows.area: index / index sorting at merge time (IndexSorter.FloatSorter/DoubleSorter merge keys, MultiSorter) -> search / TopFieldCollector index-sort early termination

rows.title: FieldExistsQuery#count undercounts documents whose norms-free text field analyzes to no tokens but still has a doc value, so IndexSearcher#count is too low
rows.summary: You index a text field with norms turned off together with a doc-values field of the same name, some document's text analyzes to no tokens (for example an empty string), and you call IndexSearcher#count(new FieldExistsQuery(field)). You expect the count to equal the number of documents the query returns, because the query matches every document that has a doc value. Instead, on a segment without deletions, Weight#count returns Terms#getDocCount, which counts only documents with at least one term, so the count is 1 for 2 hits, or 0 for 1 hit when no document in the segment has a term.

rows.title: With a soft-deletes field configured, an IndexWriter opened from a near-real-time reader's IndexCommit (IndexWriterConfig#setIndexCommit) counts the reader's deletions again, so its next commit can drop a segment that still has live documents, write a commit that cannot be opened, or turn a soft delete into a hard delete (since 7.4.0)

You expect the new writer to start from the reader's point in time and commit every document, with the soft delete still soft. Instead it counts each deletion the reader sees again (a committed soft delete three times, an uncommitted hard delete twice), so its next commit drops a 3-document segment that has 2 live documents, writes a 2-document commit that DirectoryReader.open rejects with 'invalid deletion count: 3 vs maxDoc=2', or hard-deletes the soft-deleted document, and a later forceMerge can silently attach one document's terms to another document's stored fields.

rows.title: An IndexWriter opened from a leaf-sorted reader's IndexCommit pairs each segment with the segment reader at the same leaf position, so deleteDocuments(term) deletes another segment's documents and the commit persists that silently

You expect the index to keep only b, as it does when the reader has no sorter or when the same commit is taken from DirectoryReader.listCommits. Instead the writer deletes b and keeps a: ReaderPool pairs segmentInfos.info(i) (segment order) with reader.leaves().get(i) (sorted order) by position, so each segment's pooled reader carries the other segment's documents, the delete matches a's data but is recorded under _1, and the commit writes _1's live docs, with CheckIndex clean.

rows.title: Multi-dimensional PointInSetQuery skips segments that contain matching points, because its segment early exit uses the lexicographically first and last set points as per-dimension bounds
rows.summary: You subclass PointInSetQuery for a 2-D point field, as Lucene's own tests do, and search for the set {(0,1), (1,0)} in an index whose segment holds one document at (1,0). You expect that document to match, as it does for the one-point set {(1,0)}. Instead, since 10.3.0 the query keeps the first and last set points in sorted order, (0,1) and (1,0), as if they were the set's per-dimension minimum and maximum, concludes from dimension 1 (1 is above the segment's maximum 0) that the segment cannot match, and skips it, so count() is 0 with no error; adding a point to a set can thus remove hits.

rows.title: A FLOAT or DOUBLE sort on a NUMERIC doc-values field with a skip index and no points silently returns wrong or missing top hits when values have the sign bit set (negative values, or -0.0 with a tie-break sort): skipper pruning compares sortable-encoded bounds with the raw IEEE-bit block min/max
rows.summary: You store float or double values as raw IEEE bits in a single-valued NUMERIC doc-values field with a skip index and no points (for example NumericDocValuesField.indexedField("f", Float.floatToRawIntBits(v)), the layout of Lucene's own skip-index sort test) and sort on it with SortField.Type.FLOAT or DOUBLE. You expect the same hits as on the same values without a skip index, lowest value first. Instead, with 10,000 docs holding 0, -1, ..., -9999 and a TermQuery that matches all of them, the ascending top 3 is [-8191, -8190, -8189] instead of [-9999, -9998, -9997] and a descending searchAfter(-9000) returns no hits, because the pruning compares bounds in NumericUtils sortable order with skipper block min/max in raw-bit order, and the two orders disagree for values with the sign bit set.

rows.title: Doc-values exact and range queries silently miss or add documents on a skip-indexed field that holds raw float/double bits and that the index is sorted by as FLOAT or DOUBLE: SortedNumericDocValuesRangeQuery's index-sort shortcut checks the sort field's name but not its type
rows.summary: You index the floats -1f and -2f as raw bits in a skip-indexed doc-values field (FloatDocValuesField.indexedField("f", Float.floatToRawIntBits(v))), sort the index by that field with new SortField("f", SortField.Type.FLOAT), and count the documents matching NumericDocValuesField.newSlowExactQuery("f", Float.floatToRawIntBits(-1f)). You expect 1, which is what you get without the index sort or without the skip index. You get 0: the query's index-sort shortcut computes one contiguous doc-ID range as if the documents were in the order of their stored longs, but the FLOAT sort puts -2f (raw -1073741824) before -1f (raw -1082130432), the reverse of the long order, and the shortcut never checks the sort type.
rows.area: search / doc-values range queries, index-sort shortcut (SortedNumericDocValuesRangeQuery.canUsePrimarySortShortcut, SortedSkipperScorerSupplier)

rows.title: IndexSortSortedNumericDocValuesRangeQuery casts its long bounds to int on an INT index sort, so Long.MIN_VALUE / Long.MAX_VALUE open ends (or any bound outside the int range) silently return wrong hits and counts
rows.summary: You sort the index by SortField("f", SortField.Type.INT), index the values -5, 3 and 20 in a NumericDocValuesField, and search new IndexSortSortedNumericDocValuesRangeQuery("f", Long.MIN_VALUE, 10, fallback), where the fallback is NumericDocValuesField.newSlowRangeQuery("f", Long.MIN_VALUE, 10) (f <= 10, written with the open-end convention that the fallback documents). You expect the 2 documents the fallback returns, as the class javadoc requires. You get 1: the doc-values binary search narrows the bound with (int) Long.MIN_VALUE, which is 0, so -5 is missed; (int) Long.MAX_VALUE is -1 in the same way, and the 4-byte points path has the same cast.
rows.area: search / IndexSortSortedNumericDocValuesRangeQuery (index-sort range shortcut: INT sort comparator path and 4-byte points path)

rows.title: BinaryPoint.newExactQuery and the one-dimensional newRangeQuery keep the caller's byte[] as the query bounds (BinaryPoint.pack returns the caller's array for one dimension), while the same factory packs a private copy for two or more dimensions, so a caller that refills its buffer silently changes queries it already built
rows.summary: You write a one-dimensional binary key into a scratch byte[], build BinaryPoint.newExactQuery(field, scratch), write the next key into the same array, build a second query and OR the two; you expect each query to match the key it was built for, as BinaryPoint's two-dimension range queries and its one-value newSetQuery do. Instead both queries now mean the second key (they compare equal and print the same bounds) and the OR finds 1 document instead of 2; likewise a one-dimensional newRangeQuery whose lo/hi arrays the caller overwrites afterwards matches 0 documents instead of the range it was built for. BinaryPoint.pack returns new BytesRef(point[0]), a wrapper over the caller's array, when there is one dimension, and PointRangeQuery stores that array as its bounds, so matching, equals, hashCode and toString read whatever the caller's array holds at the time.
rows.area: document / point query factories (BinaryPoint, PointRangeQuery)

rows.title: kNN and vector-similarity searches that hit the IndexSearcher timeout before collecting any hit return 0 hits with IndexSearcher.timedOut() == false, so the timed-out search looks like a search without matches
rows.summary: You set a timeout with IndexSearcher#setTimeout and run a kNN query (KnnFloatVectorQuery or KnnByteVectorQuery) or an approximate FloatVectorSimilarityQuery/ByteVectorSimilarityQuery, and the timeout fires before the vector search has found its first hit. You expect what a TermQuery gives under the same timeout: 0 hits with IndexSearcher#timedOut() == true, the documented signal ('Returns true if any search hit the timeout') that the answer is incomplete. Instead the search returns 0 hits, TotalHits '0 hits' (EQUAL_TO) and timedOut() == false, so the timed-out search cannot be told apart from a search that has no matches; IndexSearcher#count of a kNN query behaves the same way.
rows.area: search / IndexSearcher timeout reporting for vector queries (AbstractKnnVectorQuery rewrite, AbstractVectorSimilarityQuery scorerSupplier)

rows.title: JoinUtil term joins (TermsQuery, TermsIncludingScoreQuery) compare equal on the from searcher's reader-context id instead of the collected terms, so after a join whose from-side search hit IndexSearcher#setTimeout, a shared query cache serves the partial join's hits to later requests that did not time out
rows.summary: You run a JoinUtil term join on an IndexSearcher with setTimeout, the deadline passes while the join collects its from-side terms, and later requests build the same join on the same reader without any timeout, all sharing one query cache (the IndexSearcher default in 9.3.0-10.6.0). You expect every later request to get the complete join's hits, as it does without the cache. Instead the partial join compares equal to the complete one, because TermsQuery and TermsIncludingScoreQuery compare the from searcher's reader-context id rather than the collected terms, so the cache hands the later requests the partial join's hits (0 instead of 1 in the repro, 50 of 12,000 with the 10.6.0 defaults) while their timedOut() is false.
rows.area: join / JoinUtil term joins (query identity) and the query cache under IndexSearcher#setTimeout

rows.title: Closing a FilterCodecReader runs the wrapped reader's close hook directly (in.doClose() instead of in.close()), so a DirectoryReader that still uses that segment silently finds 0 hits, and its own close later releases the segment a second time and throws
rows.summary: You wrap a segment of an open DirectoryReader in a FilterCodecReader (for example to pass it to IndexWriter.addIndexes), take the usual extra reference with incRef(), and close the wrapper, expecting the DirectoryReader to keep working, because the IndexReader javadoc says a reader 'will not really be closed until decRef has been called for all outstanding references' and FilterLeafReader behaves exactly that way. Instead FilterCodecReader.doClose() calls the wrapped reader's internal close hook (in.doClose()) rather than releasing a reference (in.close()), so the segment's files are closed while the DirectoryReader still uses it: a TermQuery that matched 1 document now finds 0 with no error, reading stored fields throws AlreadyClosedException, and closing the DirectoryReader later releases the same resources a second time and throws.

rows.title: Since 10.4.0 Lucene opens indexes created by Lucene 8 once Lucene 9 has rewritten every segment, but without Lucene 9's field-consistency leniency for them (LUCENE-10518), so FieldExistsQuery returns documents that lack the doc value (or throws) and IndexWriter refuses the index
rows.summary: You have an index first created by Lucene 8 that Lucene 9 later rewrote completely (every live segment is 9.x), in which a field is indexed in every document but has a doc value in only some (Lucene 9 allowed that only for such 8.x-created indexes), and you open it with Lucene 10.4.0 or later, which accepts it since #14607. You expect FieldExistsQuery on that field to return only the documents with the doc value, as Lucene 9.12.3 does and Lucene 9's own TestFieldExistsQuery#testOldIndices asserts, and IndexWriter to open whatever DirectoryReader.open accepts. Instead, once the documents share a segment FieldExistsQuery silently rewrites to MatchAllDocsQuery and also returns the document without the doc value (hits [d1, d2] instead of [d1], count 2 instead of 1), while they sit in separate segments it throws IllegalStateException, and IndexWriter and FieldInfos.getMergedFieldInfos throw IllegalArgumentException 'cannot change field "my_field" from doc values type=BINARY to inconsistent doc values type=NONE'.

rows.title: PointRangeQuery rewrites a range that covers every indexed point to FieldExistsQuery without checking that each leaf has points, so on a MultiReader whose other index stores the field without points it also matches (or, under MUST_NOT, drops) documents that have no point
rows.summary: You open a MultiReader over two separately built indexes, one whose document has field p only as a doc value (5000, no point) and one whose document has LongField p=100, and count LongPoint.newRangeQuery("p", 0, 1000); you expect 1, which is what each index gives on its own (0 + 1) and what 10.2.2 returns. You get 2 with no error: since 10.3.0 (#14609) PointRangeQuery.rewrite sees that the reader-wide point range [100, 100] lies inside the query and, because every leaf has doc values, norms or vectors for p, replaces the query with FieldExistsQuery(p), which also matches the document that has no point. Under a MUST_NOT clause the same rewrite drops that document instead.
rows.area: core / search: PointRangeQuery.rewrite (GITHUB#14609 full-coverage rewrite to FieldExistsQuery, new in 10.3.0) on composite readers

rows.title: SlowCompositeCodecReaderWrapper's merged vector iterator numbers ordinals by position and ignores each input's own index(), so addIndexes of two or more SortingCodecReader inputs through a reordering merge policy writes vectors onto the wrong documents
rows.summary: You re-sort two or more segments with SortingCodecReader and pass them to one IndexWriter.addIndexes(CodecReader...) call on a writer that has no index sort but uses a merge policy that reorders addIndexes merges, such as BPReorderingMergePolicy (an identity OneMerge#reorder is enough), and you expect every document to keep the vector it was indexed with, as it does without the reorder. Instead the merged view that IndexWriter builds for the reorder (SlowCompositeCodecReaderWrapper) numbers vectors by iteration position, while each SortingCodecReader input reports and reads vectors by its original ordinal, so in each input the k-th document in sorted order is written with the vector at original ordinal k. Nothing throws, with or without assertions, CheckIndex reports the new index clean, and kNN search then scores documents by other documents' vectors, in an executed probe including the vector of a document deleted before the call.
rows.area: index / addIndexes reorder path: SlowCompositeCodecReaderWrapper merged vector values (MergedDocIterator) over SortingCodecReader inputs

rows.title: Merging into a Lucene104 scalar-quantized FLOAT32 vector field that does not use COSINE centers the merge source's own vector arrays in place, so IndexWriter.addIndexes changes a source that keeps its arrays (MemoryIndex, FloatVectorValues.fromFloats) and can store wrong full-precision vectors or wrong quantized codes
rows.summary: You index a FLOAT32 field with Lucene104ScalarQuantizedVectorsFormat and EUCLIDEAN, DOT_PRODUCT or MAXIMUM_INNER_PRODUCT by calling IndexWriter.addIndexes(SlowCodecReaderWrapper.wrap(...)) on a MemoryIndex, or on a FilterLeafReader that serves new vectors from your own list through FloatVectorValues.fromFloats, and you expect the merge only to read its source, as it does for COSINE fields and for the older Lucene99 scalar-quantized formats. Instead the quantizer subtracts the merged centroid from the source's own arrays: afterwards the MemoryIndex vector {1,2,3,4} reads back as {0,0,0,0} when it is the only vector, and as {1.5,0.75,-2,1.5} when merged together with a second source holding {-2,0.5,7,1}, a second addIndexes of it stores that centered vector as the full-precision vector, and your list holds centered vectors. When two documents share one float[] in a single addIndexes, the second is quantized from the already-centered array, so it scores 0.160 against 0.066 for its identical copies (exact 0.066) and ranks first.
rows.area: codecs / quantized vector formats merge (Lucene104 scalar-quantized, Lucene102 binary-quantized) with index / addIndexes through SlowCodecReaderWrapper and memory / MemoryIndex

rows.title: Classic QueryParser with the default splitOnWhitespace=false: since #16446 an AND/OR that directly follows a token the analyzer drops (such as a stopword) binds to the whole preceding run of plain terms instead of the last term, so typing the stopword changes which documents match (regression new in 10.6.0, also on main and branch_10_6)
rows.summary: You parse 'apple banana the AND cherry' with the classic QueryParser at its default settings and an analyzer that drops 'the', and expect the same query as for 'apple banana AND cherry', namely body:apple +body:banana +body:cherry, which is what Lucene 10.5.2 returns and what main returns with splitOnWhitespace=true. On main you get +(body:apple body:banana) +body:cherry, so a document containing only 'apple cherry' now matches; with the AND default operator, 'apple banana the OR cherry' becomes (+body:apple +body:banana) body:cherry instead of +body:apple body:banana body:cherry, so a document with only 'cherry' matches and one with only 'apple' no longer does. The cause is #16446, which now adds the analysed run 'apple banana' as one clause: the stopword yields no clause, so the following conjunction's 'make the preceding clause required (or optional)' step in addClause changes the whole run instead of 'banana'.
rows.area: queryparser / classic QueryParser and MultiFieldQueryParser (QueryParser.jj MultiTerm run grouping, QueryParserBase.addClause conjunction step)
