rows.title: Sort.getPrimarySortField (new in 10.6.0, #16424) skips an index-sort field that the reader's FieldInfos do not list, or whose skip index holds a single value, even when that field still orders the documents (a FilterLeafReader hides it but keeps the index sort, or a BinarySortField derives its key from other fields), so doc-values range queries on the next sort field, LongField.newRangeQuery included, return wrong hits or throw
rows.summary: You sort an index by two fields, say (c, f), and then either read it through a FilterLeafReader that hides c from FieldInfos but, like every FilterLeafReader by default, still reports the index sort (c, f) in getMetaData(), or sort by a BinarySortField subclass whose key is derived from another doc-values field, as its javadoc allows; a doc-values range query on f should still match exactly the documents whose f is in the range, as it does on 10.5.2. On main and 10.6.0, Sort.getPrimarySortField (added by #16424) finds no FieldInfo for c (or for the BinarySortField's own name), concludes that sorting by it 'has no effect', and returns f as the primary sort, so the range queries' index-sort shortcuts binary-search a segment that is not ordered by f. The result: most ranges miss matching documents and some return documents outside the range (43 of 55 ranges wrong in an independent test; f:[1 TO 3] returns 0 hits instead of 2), and LongField.newRangeQuery can throw IllegalArgumentException 'minDoc must be < maxDoc'.

rows.title: With doc-values overlays (on by default on main), a second advanceExact on the same document does not restart a multi-valued SORTED_NUMERIC column's values, so SortedNumericSortField sorts return the wrong top hits (or throw)
rows.summary: You index three documents with a multi-valued SortedNumericDocValuesField m = {50,60}, {10,90}, {30,40}, set doc 2 to the single value 70 with IndexWriter.updateSortedNumericDocValue (default IndexWriterConfig on main), and sort all documents by new SortedNumericSortField("m", LONG), which keys each document by its minimum value. You expect doc 1 first (minimum 10), which is what you get with overlays disabled. You get doc 2: the overlay view ignores a second advanceExact on the document it already sits on, so when the collector reads doc 1 again its value cursor continues at 90 instead of restarting at 10, and with a MAX sort the cursor can run past the end of the column and throw.

rows.title: ThaiTokenizer with a user dictionary silently drops the vowel or tone marks that follow a dictionary word ending inside a character cluster (with {แม่น}, 'แม่น้ำ' (river) is tokenized as just [แม่น] (accurate)), because the match is accepted at a non-boundary and the remainder, which now starts with a mark, is skipped
rows.summary: You configure ThaiTokenizer with a user dictionary that contains an ordinary short word such as แม่น ('accurate') or ผล ('result') and expect it to change only where words split. Instead, when the dictionary word is followed in the text by a combining vowel or tone mark, as in แม่น้ำ ('river') or ผลิต ('produce'), the tokenizer cuts the character cluster and throws the mark away: แม่น้ำ becomes the single token แม่น, and ผลิต becomes [ผล, ต]. Because queries are analyzed the same way, a search for แม่น้ำ also matches documents that only contain แม่น, with no error.

rows.title: StableTflSimilarity scores SynonymQuery and CombinedFieldQuery with the length of a placeholder term string ('synonym pseudo-term', 19 code points, or 'pseudo_term', 11), not the length of the query terms
rows.summary: You set StableTflSimilarity on the searcher, whose javadoc derives a term's rarity from the length |t| of the query term, and you search with a SynonymQuery (for example the one QueryBuilder builds when a synonym filter stacks 'dog' and 'dogs' at one position) or with a CombinedFieldQuery. You expect the real query terms' length to be used, so that SynonymQuery{ab, cd} on a document that contains 'ab' once scores like TermQuery(ab), and a one-field CombinedFieldQuery scores like a TermQuery on a copy field. Instead both queries hand the similarity a fixed placeholder term ('synonym pseudo-term', 19 code points; 'pseudo_term', 11 code points), so every synonym group is scored as an almost maximally rare 19-character term and every combined-field term as an 11-character one: SynonymQuery{ab, cd} scores 1.4050181 instead of 1.3490043, and in 200-token documents the group {dog, dogs} scores 2.13x TermQuery(dog) and outranks a document that matches 'elephant'.

rows.title: SynonymQuery with a repeated term adds that term's totalTermFreq once per copy, so the pseudo-term statistics it gives the Similarity can exceed the field's sumTotalTermFreq (AssertionError in SimilarityBase with -ea, scores from impossible statistics with -da)

Instead SynonymWeight takes the largest docFreq of the terms but adds the repeated term's totalTermFreq once per copy: on a field with the documents 'a' and 'a a b' (sumTotalTermFreq 4), SynonymQuery(a, a) passes totalTermFreq 6. With assertions enabled every SimilarityBase similarity throws AssertionError from fillBasicStats when the Weight is built; with assertions disabled they score from impossible statistics, for example LM Dirichlet uses a collection probability P(t|C) of 1.17 for SynonymQuery(x, x, x) where TermQuery(x) uses 0.5.

rows.title: BlendedTermQuery blends shard-local statistics in rewrite() and passes the blended values to IndexSearcher#termStats, so an override that returns per-term distributed statistics undoes the blend and the blended terms no longer score alike (known: elastic/elasticsearch#42957 and #9884, partial overlap) (released)

Instead BlendedTermQuery.rewrite blends the shard's own statistics (df = max, ttf = sum) and TermQuery passes those blended values as the docFreq/totalTermFreq arguments of termStats, which the override turns back into per-term values: 'apple' scores 0.630 and 'pear' 0.131.

rows.title: Merges through BPReorderingMergePolicy with BpVectorReorderer break document blocks even when a parent field is configured
rows.summary: You index documents in blocks (children followed by their parent) with IndexWriterConfig#setParentField, and use BPReorderingMergePolicy with a BpVectorReorderer over a float vector field. You expect merges to keep every block together with its parent last, because IndexWriter only lets a merge reorder documents when the parent field identifies the blocks, and setParentField promises that IndexWriter does not alter the order of a block. Instead BpVectorReorderer moves each document on its own and puts every document without a vector after all documents with one, so the merged segment's blocks are silently scrambled and ToParentBlockJoinQuery joins children to the wrong parent (59 of 60 children in one run), with no exception and with assertions on or off.
rows.area: misc / BP merge-time reordering

rows.title: BpVectorReorderer's in-place command-line reorder commits an empty or partial index over the original when reordering fails
rows.summary: You run BpVectorReorderer's command line (main(path, field), which calls reorderIndexDirectory) to renumber the documents of an existing index in place, and expect that if the reorder fails you get the exception and the index still holds all its documents. Instead, when computing a doc map or addIndexes throws (for example the documented NotEnoughRAMException), the try-with-resources around the OpenMode.CREATE IndexWriter closes it, close() commits by default, and the new commit holds only the segments rewritten before the failure, while the original commit and its files are deleted. A 10-document index ends with 0 documents, and through main() with default options an index created by Lucene 9.x or 10.x, or one with a soft-deletes or parent field, is wiped to 0 documents.
rows.area: misc / index: BpVectorReorderer command line (main -> reorderIndexDirectory, an in-place rewrite through an OpenMode.CREATE IndexWriter and addIndexes)

rows.title: FunctionScoreQuery's block-max bound multiplies by the wrapped query's no-score max score (0 for a TermQuery), so a BooleanQuery that contains it can drop the true top hits
rows.summary: You index a popularity field with a skip index (NumericDocValuesField.indexedField("popularity", v)) and search BooleanQuery(SHOULD FunctionScoreQuery(TermQuery(body:a), DoubleValuesSource.fromLongField("popularity")), SHOULD TermQuery(body:b)) for the top hit, expecting the same hit as an exhaustive search, because the function query scores each matching document by its popularity value. Instead, with 5,000 documents that all match body:a, where only doc 4999 has popularity 100 (all others 1) and only doc 0 matches body:b, TOP_SCORES and the plain IndexSearcher.search(q, 1) return doc 0 (score 4.69) instead of doc 4999 (score 100). The cause is that the scorer's getMaxScore returns innerMaxScore * valueMaxScore * boost, where innerMaxScore is the max score of the wrapped TermQuery, which FunctionScoreQuery itself weighted without scores (so it reports 0), although score() is value * boost and never reads the wrapped score; every block therefore reports a bound of 0, and MaxScoreBulkScorer stops scoring documents that only the function clause makes competitive.
rows.area: queries / FunctionScoreQuery block-max pruning (#16431)

rows.title: TermStates#equals compares only docFreq, so BooleanQuery still merges blended or fuzzy TermQuery clauses whose totalTermFreq differs, and similarities that read totalTermFreq then score them wrongly (the part of the #10309 fix, #12354, that was left out; main only)
rows.summary: You OR two fuzzy queries, FuzzyQuery('aaaab', 1) and FuzzyQuery('baaaa', 1), which both expand to the indexed term 'aaaa', and search with LMDirichletSimilarity; you expect each document to score the sum of the two clause scores, as it does under BM25 and as #12354 ('Do not merge term queries with different docFreq', the fix of #10309) set out to restore. Instead the blended rewrite gives both TermQuery(t:aaaa) clauses the same docFreq (the max, 3) but different totalTermFreq (the sum, 4 and 8); TermStates#equals compares only docFreq, so BooleanQuery merges them into (t:aaaa)^1.5 with the first clause's statistics, and docs 0-2 score 0.0011983 instead of 0.00059916, while the same query with the clauses swapped (equal per BooleanQuery#equals) scores them 0.0.
rows.area: search / TermQuery equality and BooleanQuery clause de-duplication (blended and fuzzy TermStates)

rows.title: A reopened reader returns the doc values of a discarded writer session or commit when a later writer session reuses the same doc-values generation number
rows.summary: You keep a reader open while a writer session updates doc values and then ends without committing (rollback(), or close() with commitOnClose=false), or while a writer opened on an older commit with setIndexCommit discards the newer commit; a later writer session updates doc values of the same segment and commits, and you reopen the old reader with DirectoryReader.openIfChanged. You expect the reopened reader to show the latest commit, as a fresh DirectoryReader.open on that commit does ('If the IndexCommit differs from what the provided reader is searching, open and return a new reader'). Instead it silently returns the discarded values (for example 99 11 instead of 10 300), because the later session wrote different files under the same doc-values generation number and the reopen reuses the old reader's doc-values producer for that number.
rows.area: index / DirectoryReader reopen with doc-values updates (generation numbers reused across writer sessions)

rows.title: If tryDeleteDocument removes a segment's last live document and closing that segment's pooled reader throws, IndexWriter stays open but never counts the change, so NRT readers hide the document while commit() and close() keep it
rows.summary: You call tryDeleteDocument on the only live document of a segment, and closing that segment's pooled reader inside IndexWriter throws an IOException; the writer stays open and you keep using it. You expect what the writer serves to its NRT readers to be what commit() persists, and hasUncommittedChanges() to report the pending change. Instead the segment is already gone from the writer's SegmentInfos but checkpoint() and changed() were skipped, so new NRT readers no longer show the document while hasUncommittedChanges() is false, commit() returns -1 and, after close(), the committed index still contains the document.
rows.area: index / IndexWriter tryDeleteDocument (dropDeletedSegment, change accounting)

rows.title: If closing a pooled segment reader throws inside IndexWriter.deleteAll, the segments are already cleared but the change is never counted: the writer stays open and its NRT readers show an empty index, yet hasUncommittedChanges() is false and commit() and close() keep every document, until a later unrelated commit silently applies the failed deleteAll
rows.summary: You commit two documents, open and close an NRT reader (so the writer keeps pooled segment readers), and call deleteAll(); closing one of the pooled readers throws (for example a core ClosedListener your cache registered throws its declared IOException, or closing a file fails), so deleteAll() throws an IOException and the writer stays open. You expect the writer to stay self-consistent: what its NRT readers show is what commit() persists, and hasUncommittedChanges() reports the pending change. Instead deleteAll has already removed every segment but skipped counting the change, so new NRT readers show 0 documents while hasUncommittedChanges() is false, commit() returns -1 and writes nothing, close() keeps both documents on disk, and the next unrelated addDocument plus commit silently applies the deleteAll that failed.
rows.area: index / IndexWriter deleteAll (change accounting on the exception path, ReaderPool.dropAll)

rows.title: IndexWriter.deleteAll misses a segment flush that another thread is already running, so documents added before deleteAll survive it and are committed
rows.summary: Several threads index into one IndexWriter, and one of them is in the middle of writing its full in-memory buffer out as a new segment when another thread calls deleteAll(). You expect deleteAll to drop every buffered document and every segment, like opening a new IndexWriter with OpenMode.CREATE, so the next commit is empty: every document was added with a smaller sequence number than deleteAll's, and some of those addDocument calls had already returned before deleteAll was called. Instead deleteAll returns without waiting for that segment to be published, the flushing thread then adds it to the freshly cleared index, and its documents survive deleteAll into the commit, still carrying the old field schema.
rows.area: index / IndexWriter deleteAll versus a concurrent segment flush (DocumentsWriter.lockAndAbortAll, flush-ticket queue)

rows.title: A deleteAll() that overlaps addIndexes clears the incoming fields from the writer's field schema, but addIndexes still publishes its segment, so a later document can give such a field another doc-values type and the committed index can no longer be opened by an IndexWriter
rows.summary: One thread imports an index with IndexWriter.addIndexes while another thread calls deleteAll() on the same writer. You expect the outcome of one of the two orders: either the imported documents are deleted, or they stay and their fields keep their doc-values types, and in both cases the committed index opens again in a new IndexWriter. Instead deleteAll can clear the imported fields from the writer's schema while addIndexes still publishes the imported segment, so a later document can give an imported field another doc-values type, the commit succeeds, and the next new IndexWriter on that index throws IllegalArgumentException ('cannot change field "f" from doc values type=NUMERIC to inconsistent doc values type=SORTED').

rows.title: IndexWriter.deleteAll can deadlock with a concurrent flush publish and a concurrent tryDeleteDocument or addIndexes, because DocumentsWriter.lockAndAbortAll waits for the flush-ticket purge lock while holding the DocumentsWriter monitor
rows.summary: Three threads share one IndexWriter: one adds documents and its addDocument() flushes and publishes the new segment, one calls tryDeleteDocument() on an NRT reader (or addIndexes()), and one calls deleteAll(). You expect all three calls to return, because IndexWriter is documented as completely thread safe for concurrent calls of any of its methods. Instead they can deadlock for good: deleteAll() holds the DocumentsWriter monitor (in lockAndAbortAll) and waits for the flush-ticket purge lock, the publishing thread holds that purge lock and waits for the IndexWriter monitor (publishFlushedSegment), and tryDeleteDocument() (or addIndexes()) holds the IndexWriter monitor and waits for the DocumentsWriter monitor to get a sequence number (getNextSequenceNumber).
rows.area: index / IndexWriter deleteAll (IndexWriter-DocumentsWriter lock order)

rows.title: A doc-values update racing IndexWriter.deleteAll() can be queued after deleteAll has cleared its field from the writer's field schema; applying it then makes every commit, NRT reopen and close() fail (a tragic close with assertions on), or, if a document added in between gives the field another doc-values type, commits a segment whose field cannot be read
rows.summary: One thread calls deleteAll() on an IndexWriter while another thread updates a doc-values field with updateDocValues, updateNumericDocValue or softUpdateDocument. You expect the update either to be dropped with everything else (if it came first) or to apply to the documents indexed after deleteAll, as on a fresh writer. Instead, when the update checked its field before deleteAll cleared the writer's field schema and is queued just after, the writer can no longer commit, refresh or close (NullPointerException with assertions off, a tragic AssertionError with them on), and when a document added in between gives the field another doc-values type, the commit succeeds but writes a segment whose field cannot be read.
rows.area: index / IndexWriter doc-values updates vs deleteAll (writer-wide field schema, FieldInfos.FieldNumbers)

rows.title: After addDocument fails with a non-tragic exception while an in-memory segment copies its backlog of buffered deletes and doc-values updates, the segment's next document resets its delete slice past the operations that were never applied, so IndexWriter stays open and the next successful commit silently lacks an acknowledged delete of a buffered document
rows.summary: You add a document to an IndexWriter, then send a long run of doc-values updates (executed: 2.2 million updateNumericDocValue calls selected by one 1 KB term) and delete the buffered document; the next addDocument fails with ArithmeticException 'integer overflow' while the in-memory segment copies that backlog into its own buffer, and the writer stays open with no tragic exception. You expect either the writer to close itself or the next successful commit, whose sequence number is above the delete's, to reflect the delete. Instead the following addDocument finds no new deletes and resets the segment's delete slice past the operations the failed copy never reached, so the commit succeeds and the deleted document is still in the index.

rows.title: If the IndexWriter InfoStream throws a RuntimeException while a flushed segment is being published, IndexWriter drops that already written segment (and, for some log lines, the deletes and doc-values updates on its flush ticket) but stays open, so the next successful commit silently lacks acknowledged documents its sequence number covers (every release since 4.0.0)
rows.summary: You enable IndexWriter's InfoStream, add a document and commit, and the logging call for one of the 'publish' lines of that commit throws an unchecked exception (executed: a java.util.logging Handler behind Lucene's JavaLoggingInfoStream that fails once); commit() throws, and the writer stays open with no tragic exception. You expect either the writer to close itself, as it does when the segment flush itself fails or a published delete packet fails to apply, or the next successful commit to contain every operation its returned sequence number covers. Instead the segment was already fully written and its flush ticket is removed from the queue whether or not it was published, so the segment never joins the index: the retried commit returns seqNo 5, above the addDocument's seqNo 2, yet the committed index has 0 documents.

rows.title: If commit() fails with an InfoStream exception after the pending segments file is synced, the commit's file references are released twice, so a later rollback() (or close() with commitOnClose=false) deletes files of the last commit and the index can no longer be opened
rows.summary: You enable an InfoStream on an IndexWriter, commit one document, add a second one and call commit() again, and the InfoStream throws a RuntimeException on the 'done all syncs' message that Lucene logs after it has written and fsynced pending_segments_2; commit() fails without closing the writer, so you call rollback(), whose javadoc says the index will then be as it was when commit() was last called. Instead, startCommit has kept the half-finished commit as its pending commit while prepareCommitInternal's catch has already released that commit's file references, and rollback() releases them a second time, so the file deleter removes _0.cfe, _0.cfs and _0.si, which segments_1 still needs. DirectoryReader.open(dir) then fails with CorruptSegmentInfoException (NoSuchFileException _0.si), close() with commitOnClose=false does the same, and with -ea rollback() throws AssertionError 'RefCount is 0 pre-decrement' instead.
rows.area: index / IndexWriter commit failure handling (IndexWriter.startCommit, prepareCommitInternal and rollback; IndexFileDeleter reference counts)

rows.title: IndexWriter.addIndexes(CodecReader...) opens its merged segment with an estimated merge size of -1 ('unknown'), which NRTCachingDirectory reads as a tiny merge, so the whole merged segment is cached in heap past maxMergeSizeMB until the next commit, and a large addIndexes can end in OutOfMemoryError with a tragic writer close (every release since 3.2.0; before 5.0.0 through addIndexes(IndexReader...))
rows.summary: You wrap your directory in NRTCachingDirectory with maxMergeSizeMB 1.0 and call IndexWriter.addIndexes(CodecReader...) with the segments of an index of about 2 MB. You expect the merged segment to be written to the wrapped directory, because NRTCachingDirectory caches only flushes and merges whose estimated size is at most maxMergeSizeMB and, since LUCENE-9115, no files of unknown size. Instead IndexWriter opens every output of that merge with a merge size of -1, NRTCachingDirectory compares -1 with its limits and admits it, so all 2.1 MB stay in the heap cache until the next commit; with more data than free heap the merge fails with OutOfMemoryError and the writer closes.

rows.title: Copying a ParallelLeafReader into an index (IndexWriter.addIndexes over SlowCodecReaderWrapper, or a merge whose OneMerge.wrapForMerge returns one) silently stores a later sub-reader's stored fields under another field's name: ParallelLeafReader.storedFields() lets each sub-reader visit with its own FieldInfo numbers while getFieldInfos() renumbers the fields, and StoredFieldsWriter.MergeVisitor skips its remap-by-name step when the numbers look aligned
rows.summary: You build two indexes in lockstep, as ParallelLeafReader requires (index A stores title='Lucene in Action', index B stores price='42'), wrap them in a ParallelLeafReader, which itself returns both fields correctly, and copy it into a new index with IndexWriter.addIndexes(SlowCodecReaderWrapper.wrap(reader)), expecting the copy to hold title and price. Instead the copy holds title='Lucene in Action' and title='42' and no price field, with no error and a clean CheckIndex: storedFields() lets B report price with B's own field number 0, the parallel reader's getFieldInfos() numbers price 1, and because the target's merged numbers equal the parallel reader's, the stored-fields merge skips its remap-by-name step and writes the value under number 0, which is title. A merge whose OneMerge.wrapForMerge adds a parallel index with stored fields behind each segment goes wrong the same way (a 'summary' value stored as a second 'id').
rows.area: core / index (ParallelLeafReader stored fields x StoredFieldsWriter.MergeVisitor, on addIndexes and wrapForMerge copies)

rows.title: SmartChineseAnalyzer and ThaiTokenizer lose a supplementary character (an emoji, a CJK Extension B ideograph) that straddles their 1024-char buffer in text with no line break, because SegmentingTokenizerBase.refill cuts the surrogate pair in half: smartcn indexes two U+FFFD halves and ThaiTokenizer drops the character
rows.summary: You index a Chinese paragraph of more than 1024 chars with no line break through the stock SmartChineseAnalyzer, and it contains an emoji or a rare ideograph such as U+20000; you expect that character to be searchable wherever it falls, as it is one position earlier or later. Instead, when its first UTF-16 half is the last char of the tokenizer's 1024-char buffer, SegmentingTokenizerBase cuts the pair in two: smartcn emits the halves U+D840 and U+DC00 as two terms, which the index stores as U+FFFD, and ThaiTokenizer drops the character. A TermQuery for U+20000 then finds 0 documents instead of 1, with no error.

rows.title: SmartChineseAnalyzer silently drops letters and letter-numbers as if they were punctuation, among them the Chinese zero U+3007 (二〇〇八年 -> 二, 八, 年) and the Roman numerals Ⅰ-Ⅻ (第Ⅲ章 and 第Ⅳ章 analyze identically), because Utility.getCharType classifies four whole Unicode blocks as DELIMITER
rows.summary: You index Chinese text with the stock SmartChineseAnalyzer, whose javadoc says its default stop list is 'simply a list of punctuation', so you expect only punctuation to disappear. Instead Utility.getCharType returns DELIMITER for four whole code-unit ranges (0x0021-0x00BB, 0x2010-0x2642, 0x3001-0x301E, 0xFE30-0xFF63) that also hold 248 letters and letter-numbers, among them U+3007 〇 and the Roman numerals Ⅰ-Ⅻ; each one becomes ',' and the stop list removes it. So 二〇〇八年 ('2008') analyzes to [二, 八, 年], 第Ⅲ章 and 第Ⅳ章 ('chapter III', 'chapter IV') give the same terms and positions, and the phrase query for 第Ⅲ章 matches both documents (2 hits, 1 expected), with no error.

rows.title: UkrainianMorfologikAnalyzer overrides neither normalize() nor initReaderForNormalization, so prefix, wildcard, regexp, range and fuzzy terms from the query parsers skip its lower-casing and its apostrophe, stress-mark, soft-hyphen and ґ mapping and miss words spelled exactly as in the document
rows.summary: You index Ukrainian text with UkrainianMorfologikAnalyzer, which maps typographic apostrophes to ', removes stress marks and soft hyphens, maps ґ to г and lower-cases every token before lemmatizing, so the document 'м’ясо Lucene' is stored as the terms м'ясо and lucene. A prefix, wildcard, regexp, range or fuzzy query built by a query parser sends its term through Analyzer.normalize, documented to return 'the representation that it would have in the index', but this analyzer overrides neither normalize(String, TokenStream) nor initReaderForNormalization, so normalize returns the text unchanged. As a result 'м’яс*', 'Luc*', 'Luce?e' and '[Lucene TO Lucene]' find nothing while "м'яс*" and 'luc*' find the document, and normalize("Lucene") returns 'Lucene' although the index holds 'lucene'.

rows.title: CustomAnalyzer.normalize skips the token filters inside a when()/whenTerm() block or a ProtectedTermFilterFactory (ConditionalTokenFilterFactory has no normalize()), so query-parser range, fuzzy, prefix, wildcard and regexp terms are not lower-cased or folded like the indexed term and silently miss documents
rows.summary: You build a CustomAnalyzer whose lowercase filter sits inside a conditional block (withTokenizer("whitespace").whenTerm(t -> t.length() > 2).addTokenFilter("lowercase").endwhen(), or a ProtectedTermFilterFactory wrapping lowercase as in that factory's javadoc), index 'Lucene' (stored as the term 'lucene') and search with the classic QueryParser range [Lucene TO Lucene]. You expect Analyzer.normalize("f", "Lucene") to return 'lucene', 'the representation that it would have in the index', and the query to find the document, as both do for the same chain without the condition. Instead normalize returns 'Lucene' unchanged and the query finds 0 documents with no error, and Apa*, Apach?, APACHE~1 and /Apa.*/ miss 'Apache' the same way, because ConditionalTokenFilterFactory overrides create() but not normalize(), so CustomAnalyzer.normalize never reaches the normalize() of the wrapped filters.

rows.title: ICUCollationKeyAnalyzer does not override attributeFactory(String), so Analyzer.normalize returns the plain UTF-8 bytes instead of the ICU collation key, and classic QueryParser range queries on an ICU collation-key field match the wrong documents
rows.summary: You index the values a, b, c, d and e in a TextField analyzed with new ICUCollationKeyAnalyzer(Collator.getInstance(ULocale.ROOT)) and parse "[b TO d]" with the classic QueryParser on the same analyzer; you expect the 3 documents b, c and d, which is what the java.text twin CollationKeyAnalyzer gives. You get 0: the parser builds both range bounds with Analyzer.normalize, which takes its term attribute from attributeFactory(fieldName), and ICUCollationKeyAnalyzer gives its collation attribute factory only to its KeywordTokenizer and does not override attributeFactory, so normalize("b") is the UTF-8 byte [62] while the index holds the ICU collation key [2d 1 5 1 5 0]. With other inputs the same range both misses documents inside it and matches documents outside it.
rows.area: analysis-icu / collation (ICUCollationKeyAnalyzer vs Analyzer#normalize; classic QueryParser range bounds)

rows.title: JapaneseKatakanaUppercaseFilterFactory and JapaneseHiraganaUppercaseFilterFactory do not override normalize(), so CustomAnalyzer.normalize leaves small kana unmapped and query-parser prefix, wildcard, regexp, fuzzy and range terms that contain them silently miss the indexed documents
rows.summary: You build a CustomAnalyzer with the kuromoji small-kana filters (withTokenizer("keyword").addTokenFilter("japaneseKatakanaUppercase").addTokenFilter("japaneseHiraganaUppercase")), and indexing キャットちょっと stores the term キヤツトちよつと. You expect Analyzer.normalize("f", "キャットちょっと") to return キヤツトちよつと, 'the representation that it would have in the index', as it does for the similar cjkWidth filter. Instead it returns the input unchanged, because both factories override create() but not normalize() and CustomAnalyzer.normalize only chains each factory's normalize(), so query-parser multi-term terms keep their small kana and silently miss: a document キャット is found by the term query キャット but not by the prefix query キャ* or the range [キャット TO キャット].

rows.title: BrazilianStemmer throws away the result of its "logias" -> "log" rule, so plural -logias nouns stay unstemmed and stop matching their singular
rows.summary: You index Brazilian Portuguese text with the stock BrazilianAnalyzer (or BrazilianStemFilter), one document says 'metodologia' and a query says 'metodologias'; you expect both words to stem to 'metodolog' and match, as the stemmer's own rule table says ('logias' in R2 is replaced by 'log', exactly like the singular 'logia'). Instead step1 calls replaceSuffix(CT, "logias", "log") without assigning the result and still returns true, which also makes stem() skip step2 and step4, so the plural is indexed as the whole word 'metodologias' and the search finds 0 hits. Long -logias plurals such as metodologias, antropologias, terminologias, epistemologias, fenomenologias and odontologias are hit; shorter ones such as tecnologias, ideologias and biologias are not, because the rule does not fire for them and step2 stems them.
rows.area: analysis-common / Brazilian Portuguese stemmer (BrazilianStemmer.step1; BrazilianStemFilter, BrazilianAnalyzer and the 'brazilianStem' factory)

rows.title: QueryAutoStopWordAnalyzer inherits its delegate's reuse strategy although its analysis chain differs per field, so with a stock delegate (GLOBAL_REUSE_STRATEGY) the chain built for the first field a thread analyses is reused for every other field: one field's stop words drop another field's query terms and a field's own stop words are kept (since 4.5.0)
rows.summary: You wrap a stock analyzer such as StandardAnalyzer in QueryAutoStopWordAnalyzer, which computes a separate set of very common words (stop words) for each field from the index, and use that one analyzer for queries on several fields. You expect each field to lose only its own stop words, as the class's per-field design and its upstream test testNoFieldNamePollution say ('Filter should not prevent stopwords in one field being used in another'). Instead the analyzer reuses the analysis chain it built for the first field it analysed on the thread, so a word that is common in one field is removed from queries on another field (MultiFieldQueryParser parses 'boring' to an empty query instead of variedField:boring), and in the other order a field's own stop words stay in.

rows.title: HTMLStripCharFilter (since 10.5.0) treats a start tag whose name only begins with script, style or br (<scripts>, <style-guide>, <stylesheet>, <brand>) as a script, style or br tag, so it silently drops all text after it up to the next </script> or </style> (often to the end of the value) and misapplies escapedTags to such names
rows.summary:
You strip '<scripts>hello</scripts> world' (or '<style-guide>hello</style-guide> world') with HTMLStripCharFilter and expect '
hello
 world', which is what Lucene 10.4.0 gives and what main gives for the same shape with any other name, such as '<scrapes>'. Since 10.5.0 the output is empty: the start-tag rules for script and style no longer require a delimiter after the name, so the longer name is taken for a <script> or <style> tag and everything up to the next literal </script> or </style>, here the end of the input, is dropped (for '<stylesheet>hello</stylesheet> world' a StandardTokenizer after the filter emits no token at all). With escapedTags={brand}, '<brand>Acme</brand>' likewise comes out as '
Acme</brand>' instead of unchanged.

rows.title: HTMLStripCharFilter drops the visible text after a tag when a quoted attribute value ends with whitespace, a name and '=' (title="a b=", alt="x y ="): the scanner re-reads the value's closing quote as the opening quote of a new attribute value, so the tag runs on to the next quote of the same kind; the GITHUB#15754 fix (#15756) covers only the shape without whitespace
rows.summary:
You strip '

one

two

three

' with HTMLStripCharFilter and expect the words 'one two three', as the GITHUB#15754 fix (#15756, 10.5.0) now gives for title="ab=". Instead only 'three' comes out: the scanner may treat the value's opening quote as plain tag text, then read ' b=' plus the value's closing quote as the start of a new quoted value, which runs to the next double quote in the document, so the tag swallows 'one two' and that text is never indexed. No error is raised, and the #15754 input itself is handled correctly on main.

rows.title: HTMLStripCharFilter drops an unclosed '<name' or '</name' when the input ends right after the name, but outputs the same text when any character follows it, so 'a < b' indexes only 'a'
rows.summary: You run 'price a < b' through HTMLStripCharFilter and StandardTokenizer and expect [price, a, b], which is what you get for 'price a < b ' (one trailing space) or 'price a < b c'. Instead you get [price, a]: when the input ends right after '<' [whitespace] Name or '</' Name with no '>', the end-of-input handler throws the pending text away, while anywhere else the same unclosed construct is output as text, as the upstream tests require for '<ahref=http:..' at end of input. A TermQuery for 'b' therefore misses the document; other shapes are 'a<b' -> 'a', 'x <p' -> 'x ', 'a </b' -> 'a ' and 'if a < b.' -> 'if a ' ('.' is a name character).

rows.title: WikipediaTokenizer silently drops letters and digits from plain text that Unicode 3.0 already had (µ in '5 µm', ª/º in '1ª'/'2º', fullwidth digits and letters, ligatures such as ﬁ, Yi syllables, Arabic presentation forms; 2,083 BMP code points that ClassicTokenizer keeps) because its LETTER and DIGIT macros are hard-coded 2008 range lists
rows.summary: You tokenize ordinary plain text with WikipediaTokenizer, for example '5 µm', '1ª edición 2º piso', '２０２６ year', 'ﬁle' or the Yi text 'ꀀꀁ', and expect every letter and digit to end up in a token, as it does with ClassicTokenizer (whose grammar is also pinned to Unicode 3.0) and StandardTokenizer. Instead WikipediaTokenizer skips these characters without an error: '5 µm' gives [5, m], '1ª 2º' gives [1, 2], 'ﬁle' gives [le], and '２０２６', 'ＡＢＣ' and 'ꀀꀁ' give no token; an exhaustive check of the BMP finds 2,083 letters and digits that ClassicTokenizer keeps and WikipediaTokenizer drops. The cause is the grammar: ALPHANUM is built from LETTER and DIGIT macros that are fixed range lists copied in 2008 (WikipediaTokenizerImpl.jflex:154, :156), which miss U+00AA, U+00B5, U+00BA and every letter or digit from U+2000 up to the halfwidth forms outside the CJ and Korean ranges, so these characters fall into the '[^]' ignore rule (:216); StandardTokenizer had the same lists and replaced them with [:letter:]/[:digit:] in 2.4 (LUCENE-1126), but the WikipediaTokenizer copy was never updated.
rows.area: analysis-common / wikipedia: WikipediaTokenizer (JFlex grammar character classes, WikipediaTokenizerImpl.jflex LETTER/DIGIT macros)

rows.title: WordDelimiterGraphFilter with IGNORE_KEYWORDS moves the position hole of a swallowed delimiter-only token (a standalone '/', '-' or '&') to after the next keyword token, so exact phrases across the keyword miss or over-match (released since 7.4.0)
rows.summary: You analyze 'lucene / solr rocks' with a whitespace tokenizer, a keyword marker that marks 'solr', and WordDelimiterGraphFilter(GENERATE_WORD_PARTS | IGNORE_KEYWORDS), and expect the hole left by the swallowed '/' to stay in front of 'solr' (position increments {1, 2, 1}), exactly as when 'solr' is not a keyword, is marked without IGNORE_KEYWORDS, or is a protected word. Instead the keyword branch returns 'solr' before the pending increment is applied, so 'solr' gets 1 and 'rocks' gets 2 ({1, 1, 2}); with the same analyzer at index and query time the exact phrase "solr rocks" finds 0 of the 1 matching documents, and the phrase "lucene solr" matches the document 'lucene / solr', which the chain without the keyword mark does not.

rows.title: ShingleFilter with minShingleSize >= 3 ends the token stream early when a hole (for example a removed stop word) is near the end, so the last word(s) are never output as unigrams and are missing from the index ('a cup of tea' loses 'tea'; 'the cat' yields no token at all)
rows.summary: You index 'a cup of tea' with WhitespaceTokenizer, StopFilter{a, of, the} and ShingleFilter(min 3, max 3) with unigrams on (the default), and expect every real word to be indexed as a unigram, because the javadoc says unigrams 'are always output, regardless of whether any shingles are available' and that the unigram option 'is independent of the min shingle size'. Instead, when the window starts with the filler left by the removed stop word, incrementToken() skips the all-filler unigram, finds fewer than minShingleSize positions left for a shingle and returns false, which ends the stream although 'tea' is still in its window: 'tea' is never indexed and TermQuery(tea) finds 0 documents. With min 4 up to two trailing words are lost, a value such as 'the cat' yields no token at all, and nothing throws, with assertions on or off.
rows.area: analysis-common / shingle (ShingleFilter, ShingleFilterFactory, ShingleAnalyzerWrapper)

rows.title: FixedShingleFilter takes the gap before each token of a graph route from that token's stream position increment, so tokens stacked right after a hole (a removed stop word followed by a preserved original, a stemmed variant or a synonym) get shingles that skip the filler ('at café' for 'at the café') while the correct ones ('at _ café') are missing, and a token after a multi-position token gets a filler it should not have ('login _' instead of 'login page'); released since 8.0.0
rows.summary: You run 'coffee at the café' through WhitespaceTokenizer, StopFilter{the}, ASCIIFoldingFilter(preserveOriginal=true) and FixedShingleFilter(2), and expect the filler that stands for the removed 'the' in every shingle that crosses it, as the folded 'cafe' gets it ('at _'), because the class javadoc says the filter 'handles position increments > 1 by inserting filler tokens' and 'will output stacked shingles' for stacked tokens. Instead the original 'café', stacked behind 'cafe' with position increment 0, is joined straight to 'at': you get [coffee at, at _, at café], at size 3 'coffee at café' appears and 'at _ café' is missing, and on a canned stream a(+1) b(+2) c(+0) swapping only the stream order of the two stacked tokens changes the output from [a _, a c] to [a _, a b]. The same misreading gives 'login _' instead of 'login page' after a two-position token 'login' over 'log' plus a removed 'in', and nothing throws, with assertions on or off.

rows.title: JapaneseTokenizer with the default discardPunctuation=true drops the dictionary nouns （株） （有） （社） （財） whole, Han letter included, because it tests only the token's first character for punctuation (known: #10430 / LUCENE-9390) (released)
rows.summary: You tokenize 東芝（株） with JapaneseTokenizer (default discardPunctuation=true) and expect [東芝, （株）], because only punctuation tokens are to be dropped and （株） is a dictionary noun. Instead you get [東芝]: the tokenizer discards any token whose first character is punctuation, so the noun and its Han letter 株 vanish; the same happens to （有）, （社） and （財） in all three modes.

rows.title: JapaneseNumberFilter and KoreanNumberFilter emit a composed number on the attribute state of the token after it, so the number takes that token's part of speech, reading, position increment and position length (車は三台 with は removed by a StopFilter gives 3 +1 名詞-接尾-助数詞 instead of 3 +2 名詞-数) (known: #10130, Japanese part of speech) (released since 6.0.0 / 8.2.0)
rows.summary: You add JapaneseNumberFilter (or KoreanNumberFilter) to an analysis chain and expect a composed number such as 3 (from 三) to keep the attributes of the numerals it replaces: the javadoc says its part of speech and reading come from 'the last token used to compose the normalized number', and as a replacement it should sit at the position of its first numeral. Instead the filter reads one token past the number to find its end, captures that look-ahead token's state and overwrites only the term and offsets, so in 車は三台 with は removed by a StopFilter the number comes out as '3 +1 名詞-接尾-助数詞' (the increment and part of speech of 台) instead of '3 +2 名詞-数'. No error is raised; a part-of-speech stop filter after it then drops numbers that are followed by a particle or a space (the case reported in #10130), and a hole in front of the number disappears, so phrase queries over it can miss.
rows.area: analysis / kuromoji and nori number filters (JapaneseNumberFilter, KoreanNumberFilter: attribute state of the composed number token)

rows.title: Nori: user-dictionary nouns still use the context ids of mecab-ko-dic 2.0.3 after Lucene 10.0 moved to mecab-ko-dic 2.1.1, so the particle after a user noun gets the wrong part of speech (학교가: 가 becomes the verb 'go'; 학생이: 이 becomes the copula) and KoreanAnalyzer indexes spurious terms such as 가 and 이
rows.summary: You add a noun such as 학교 ('school') to a nori user dictionary, or a new word such as 깃허브, and analyze '학교가' or '깃허브가 있다' with KoreanTokenizer or KoreanAnalyzer, and expect the noun to connect to the following particle like a plain common noun (NNG) with the same final syllable, which is what the constants' own comments say ('NNG left', 'NNG right with hangul and a coda on the last char', '... no coda') and what 9.x does. Instead the four hard-coded user-noun context ids are still the numbers of mecab-ko-dic 2.0.3, while 10.0.0 switched the bundled dictionary to mecab-ko-dic 2.1.1, in which those numbers name other contexts (the coda flag is inverted and the left id is a 'state change' noun subclass), so the subject particle 가 is analyzed as the verb 가 'go' (VV) and 이 as the copula (VCP) or a complement particle, and KoreanAnalyzer indexes [학교, 가] instead of [학교] and [깃허브, 가, 있] instead of [깃허브, 있]. Setting the constants to the 2.1.1 ids (LEFT_ID 1780, RIGHT_ID 3532, RIGHT_ID_T 3534, RIGHT_ID_F 3533) restores the analysis the bundled dictionary gives the same noun.
rows.area: analysis / nori KoreanTokenizer user dictionary (UserDictionary right ids, UserMorphData left id vs the bundled mecab-ko-dic-2.1.1 connection costs)

rows.title: OpenNLPLemmatizerFilter silently drops keyword-marked tokens that end a sentence (and every token but the first of a sentence made only of keyword tokens), because since 9.5.0 it ends a sentence once it has used all lemmas, and keyword tokens get no lemma
rows.summary: You analyze text with OpenNLPTokenizer, OpenNLPPOSFilter, a keyword marker that protects some words (for example KeywordMarkerFilter with the pattern 'evening') and OpenNLPLemmatizerFilter, and expect the protected words to pass through unlemmatized, which is what the filter's KeywordAttribute handling is for. Instead 'They sent him running in the evening' becomes [they, send, he, run, in, the]: the protected last word is gone, and when every word of a sentence is protected only its first word survives ([They]). The filter ends a sentence once it has emitted one lemma per non-keyword token (OpenNLPLemmatizerFilter.java:64, a 9.5.0 change from #11734), so the keyword tokens after the last non-keyword token are thrown away.

rows.title: JapaneseTokenizer with discardPunctuation=true (the default, and the only setting JapaneseAnalyzer uses) still emits the punctuation-only segments of a user-dictionary entry, so an entry that segments a dotted name (レオナルド・ダ・ヴィンチ as レオナルド ・ ダ ・ ヴィンチ) indexes '・' terms that take positions, and phrase queries for parts of the name such as "ダ・ヴィンチ" stop matching (since 3.6.0)
rows.summary: You give JapaneseTokenizer (or the stock JapaneseAnalyzer) a user dictionary with the well-formed entry 'レオナルド・ダ・ヴィンチ,レオナルド ・ ダ ・ ヴィンチ,レオナルド ・ ダ ・ ヴィンチ,カスタム名詞' and keep discardPunctuation=true, whose javadoc says 'true if punctuation tokens should be dropped from the output'; you expect [レオナルド, ダ, ヴィンチ], which is what the tokenizer gives for the same text without the entry. Instead it emits [レオナルド, ・, ダ, ・, ヴィンチ], exactly as with discardPunctuation=false, because the code that expands a user entry into its segments (ViterbiNBest.backtrace, and registerNode for n-best output) never checks for punctuation, while the other token paths do. The kept dots take positions, so for a one-document index 'レオナルド・ダ・ヴィンチの絵' the phrase queries "ダ・ヴィンチ", "ダ ヴィンチ" and "レオナルド ダ ヴィンチ" find the document without the entry and miss it with the entry, with no error.
rows.area: analysis-kuromoji / JapaneseTokenizer user-dictionary output (ViterbiNBest backtrace USER branch and the n-best registerNode copy) vs discardPunctuation

rows.title: Kuromoji UserDictionary loads entries whose whitespace makes the stored segment lengths disagree with the surface form (a half-width space inside the surface, a tab between segments, a space after a comma), so JapaneseTokenizer later emits a term that starts with a space and drops the entry's last character, throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException, or emits an empty token
rows.summary: You add the entry 'ソニー ミュージック,ソニー ミュージック,ソニー ミュージック,カスタム名詞' (a name written with a half-width space) to a Kuromoji user dictionary and expect it either to be rejected when the dictionary loads, as LUCENE-8933 promises for segmentations that do not match the surface form ('This change avoids unexpected runtime exceptions or behaviours', MIGRATE.md), or to give tokens that cover ソニー ミュージック. Instead it loads, and JapaneseTokenizer emits ソニー[0,3) and ' ミュージッ'[3,9): one term starts with a space and the final ク is in no token, because the load-time check compares the two columns with all whitespace removed, while the stored segment lengths come from splitting the segmentation on ' ' only and the dictionary key keeps its whitespace. Two related entry shapes also load: a tab between segments (日本<TAB>経済 新聞) makes incrementToken throw ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException 'arraycopy: last source index 7 out of bounds for char[6]', the exact LUCENE-8933 symptom, and a space after each comma gives an empty token [0,0) (an AssertionError with -ea).
rows.area: analysis / kuromoji user dictionary (ja.dict.UserDictionary entry validation; USER-token expansion in ViterbiNBest and JapaneseTokenizer.incrementToken)

rows.title: HyphenationTree.hyphenate does not shift its added start and end points past leading characters that are in none of the grammar's character classes, so HyphenationCompoundWordTokenFilter misses the subwords of tokens such as 3zimmerwohnung or "zimmerwohnung (the same word with a trailing quote decomposes)
rows.summary: You index text through HyphenationCompoundWordTokenFilter with a hyphenation grammar and the dictionary {zimmer, wohnung}, and expect '3zimmerwohnung' (one StandardTokenizer token) or '"zimmerwohnung' (WhitespaceTokenizer) to add the subwords zimmer and wohnung, as 'zimmerwohnung' and 'zimmerwohnung"' (trailing quote) do. Instead no subword is added: HyphenationTree.hyphenate skips the leading characters that are in no character class and shifts its inner hyphenation points past them, but it adds the start and end points unshifted (0 and the letter count), so '3zimmerwohnung' gets [0, 7, 13] instead of [1, 7, 14] and every candidate slice either starts on the '3' or loses the final letter. With two or more such characters the points are not even ascending ('!!abcde' gives [0, 6, 5]), and nothing throws.
rows.area: analysis-common / compound (HyphenationTree, HyphenationCompoundWordTokenFilter)

rows.title: Hyphenation grammars whose TernaryTree key array grows past 65,535 chars load without error but silently lose or corrupt patterns, because TernaryTree stores key-array offsets in 16-bit chars (the Norwegian OFFO grammars the Lucene docs point to: nb/nn 1,158 of 27,448 patterns wrong, 1.2 no.xml 309 of 26,017)
rows.summary: You load a well-formed FOP-format hyphenation grammar with HyphenationCompoundWordTokenFilter.getHyphenationTree (or HyphenationTree.loadPatterns, or the factory's hyphenator file) and expect findPattern to return every pattern's values afterwards, or an exception if the grammar does not fit. For a grammar whose stored key tails pass 65,535 chars, such as the Norwegian nb.xml from the OFFO download the Lucene docs link to (27,448 patterns, 52,404 nodes), loading succeeds but 1,158 patterns return wrong values (1,111 are not found at all), and with the OFFO 1.2 Norwegian grammar real words such as 'forfatter' are hyphenated and decompounded differently. The cause: TernaryTree keeps the offset of each key tail in its key array in a 16-bit char (lo[p] = (char) kv.alloc(len + 1), TernaryTree.java:151, and (char) k in compact() at :408/:410) without a range check, so past 65,535 the offset wraps and the new tail is written over an earlier one; grammars past 65,535 nodes fail with StackOverflowError instead, which Apache FOP's open FOP-2569 reports, a related but different defect.
rows.area: analysis-common / compound hyphenation (TernaryTree insert and compact via HyphenationTree.loadPatterns and HyphenationCompoundWordTokenFilter)

rows.title: UAX29URLEmailTokenizer ends a URL token at the first $ + ! * ' ( ) or , in the URL path, although both RFCs its grammar cites allow these characters there, so URLs such as https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Python_(programming_language) or http://example.com/a+b/c are split
rows.summary: You run text such as 'see https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Python_(programming_language) now' or 'http://example.com/a+b/c' through UAX29URLEmailTokenizer, whose javadoc says URLs are 'tokenized according to the relevant RFCs', and expect each URL as one <URL> token, because RFC 3986 (sub-delims are allowed in path segments) and RFC 1738 (its 'safe' and 'extra' characters are allowed in hsegment and fsegment) both allow $ + ! * ' ( ) and , in a path. Instead the <URL> token stops right before the first such character ('https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Python_', then 'programming_language' as a word; 'http://example.com/a', then 'b' and 'c'), because the grammar's two path-segment rules use RFC 3986's narrow 'unreserved' set inside rules shaped after RFC 1738, so these characters are rejected under either RFC. The same characters in the query, fragment or userinfo stay inside the URL token, and nothing reports an error.
rows.area: analysis / UAX29URLEmailTokenizer JFlex URL rules (path segments of http(s), scheme-less, ftp and file URLs; analysis-common)

rows.title: SimplePatternTokenizer and SimplePatternSplitTokenizer stop scanning when a non-matching lookahead reaches the end of the input, so later tokens are dropped (or later separators ignored)
rows.summary: You tokenize 'say "hello world' with SimplePatternTokenizer and the pattern "[^"]*"|[a-z]+ (a quoted string or a word) and expect [say, hello, world], because the javadoc says the longest match at each start point is the next token and the class otherwise skips one character and tries again (PatternTokenizer with the same regex gives these three tokens). Instead you get only [say]: the lookahead from the unclosed quote runs to the end of the input without ever matching, and that end-of-input branch ends tokenization instead of retrying at the next character, so 'hello' and 'world' are never indexed (minimal case: abc|b on 'ab' gives [] instead of [b]). SimplePatternSplitTokenizer has the same branch and emits the whole rest as one token: separator <[^>]*>|[ ]+ on 'x < y' gives [x, '< y'] instead of String.split's [x, <, y]; nothing throws.
rows.area: analysis / pattern tokenizers (analysis-common: SimplePatternTokenizer, SimplePatternSplitTokenizer and their simplePattern / simplePatternSplit factories)

rows.title: ICUTokenizer silently drops Korean words when a Hangul syllable is followed by a combining mark, soft hyphen, ZWNJ, ZWJ or U+FEFF: the Hangul rules of Default.rbbi do not attach the trailing Extend/Format character, so the segment gets rule status 0 and is skipped as a non-word (U+D55C U+AD6D U+00AD U+C5B4 keeps only U+C5B4; since 4.7.0, LUCENE-4381)
rows.summary: You tokenize the Korean word U+D55C U+AD6D U+C5B4 ('Korean language') with the default ICUTokenizer, once as is, once with an invisible soft hyphen (U+00AD) after its second syllable and once with a combining mark after each syllable, and expect the word to be indexed every time, because ICUTokenizer 'Breaks text into words according to UAX #29' (ICUTokenizer.java:31), whose rule WB4 attaches Extend and Format characters to the preceding letter, and StandardTokenizer indeed keeps U+D55C U+AD6D U+00AD U+C5B4 as one <HANGUL> token. Instead, the two Hangul rules of Default.rbbi (:127 '$HangulSyllable {200};', :191 '$HangulSyllable $HangulSyllable {200};') have no trailing $ExFm*, unlike every other rule of their group, so the generic status-0 rule (:122) gives the longer match, the segment ending in that character gets rule status 0, and ICUTokenizer skips every status-0 segment as a non-word (:209-214): U+D55C U+AD6D U+00AD U+C5B4 yields only U+C5B4, and U+D55C U+0336 U+AD6D U+0336 U+C5B4 U+0336 (strikethrough), U+D55C U+AD6D U+C5B4 U+FEFF and the Middle Korean tone-marked U+B098 U+302E U+B78F U+302E yield no token at all, silently. Lucene 4.6.1 kept all of these words; the gap came with the ICU 52.1 rule import in 4.7.0 (LUCENE-4381) and is in every release since.
rows.area: analysis-icu / segmentation (ICUTokenizer with DefaultICUTokenizerConfig; break rules Default.rbbi -> Default.brk)

rows.title: SmartChineseAnalyzer indexes whitespace characters as terms: VERTICAL TAB, FORM FEED, OGHAM SPACE MARK and the eleven spaces U+2000-U+200A (EN QUAD to HAIR SPACE, among them EN, EM and THIN SPACE) each become a one-character term, because Utility.getCharType classifies them OTHER instead of SPACE_LIKE
rows.summary: You index text with the stock SmartChineseAnalyzer, whose segmenter has a character class for 'Characters that act as a space' (CharType.SPACE_LIKE) and skips those characters, so you expect any space to separate words without a trace, as an ordinary space, a tab or the ideographic space U+3000 does. Instead Utility.getCharType knows only those five, and VERTICAL TAB, FORM FEED, OGHAM SPACE MARK and U+2000-U+200A fall through to OTHER and are each indexed as a one-character term: 'hello<THIN SPACE>world' gives [hello, U+2009, world], a TermQuery for U+2009 alone finds the document, and '中<U+2009>国' gives [中, U+2009, 国] where '中 国' gives [中国]. So the exact phrase "hello world" matches only 3 of 7 documents that differ only in the separator (space, tab and U+3000 match; FORM FEED, U+1680, EM SPACE and THIN SPACE miss), and HTML indented with    gets two whitespace terms, with no error.
rows.area: analysis-smartcn / HHMM segmenter character classes (Utility.getCharType SPACE_LIKE test -> HHMMSegmenter OTHER branch -> one-character STRING term; SmartChineseAnalyzer and HMMChineseTokenizer)

rows.title: Japanese completion suggester (JapaneseCompletionAnalyzer / JapaneseCompletionFilter): words with a small tsu before shi, chi or tsu (雑誌, 決して, マッチ, 三つ) are never suggested for their Hepburn or input-method spellings zasshi, kesshite, macchi/matchi, mittsu, because romaji_map.txt maps ッシ only to 'ssi', ッチ only to 'tti' and ッツ only to 'ttu', while the base rows シ/チ/ツ list shi/chi/tsu and the neighbouring rows ッシャ and ッチャ do double the consonant ('ssha', 'ccha')
rows.summary: You index 雑誌 ('magazine'), マッチ ('match') and 三つ ('three') in a document suggester with JapaneseCompletionAnalyzer, whose javadoc lists modified Hepburn among the supported romanizations, and expect typing 'zasshi', 'macchi' or 'mittsu' to suggest them, just as 'issho' suggests 一緒 and 'maccha' suggests 抹茶. Instead nothing is suggested: the bundled romaji_map.txt gives the small-tsu rows ッシ, ッチ and ッツ only the spellings 'ssi', 'tti' and 'ttu', although the base rows シ, チ, ツ list shi, chi, tsu and the neighbouring rows ッシャ and ッチャ list 'ssha' and 'ccha'. Only the Kunrei spellings (zassi, matti, mittu) find these words.
rows.area: analysis / kuromoji completion romanization (romaji_map.txt read by KatakanaRomanizer; JapaneseCompletionFilter, JapaneseCompletionAnalyzer)

rows.title: Two antipodal COSINE vectors make the OSQ centroid zero, so flush or merge fails and the writer closes
rows.summary: With the scalar-quantized (OSQ) vectors format and COSINE, you index vectors whose normalized sum is exactly zero, such as {1,0} and {-1,0}, into one segment. You expect flush and merge to work. Instead normalizing the zero centroid throws 'Cannot normalize a zero-length vector', the writer closes tragically with its buffered documents lost, and merges stay blocked.
rows.area: codecs / vectors

rows.title: Since 9.12.0 the default postings writer stores the byte length of a level-1 block's competitive impacts in a signed short, so with a custom Similarity whose norms do not fit in a byte, a term with 8,192 or more postings in one segment (4,096 before 10.4) can need more than 32,767 bytes: flush fails an assertion with -ea, and with -da the segment is written but that term's postings then throw when read or are read back wrong
rows.summary: You index with the default codec and a custom Similarity whose norm is the field length (or another value that does not fit in a byte), and one term appears in 8,192 documents of a segment with growing frequencies, for example through Lucene's DelimitedTermFrequencyTokenFilter. You expect the term's postings to read back exactly as indexed. Instead the writer stores the length of the level-1 skip block's impact list, which here exceeds 32,767 bytes, in a signed short: with assertions on, flush fails; with assertions off, the segment is written and reading the term's postings throws 'numBytes must be >= 0', or, with wider norms, decodes wrong data (doc 0 with freq 1,602,871,807 instead of 1,000, and most documents missing).
rows.area: codecs / postings writer and reader (Lucene104 level-1 skip data, ImpactLength; the same field in the Lucene912, Lucene101 and Lucene103 formats)

rows.title: When a dense LongColumn's values cursor throws during addBatch, the NUMERIC/SORTED_NUMERIC doc values it already delivered stay buffered with no document, so later documents of that field in the same segment are stored with another document's value
rows.summary: You index a dense LongColumn as NUMERIC or SORTED_NUMERIC doc values with IndexWriter#addBatch, its values cursor throws part-way (for example after 255 earlier documents, a 2-document batch whose cursor fails on its 2nd value), and you keep adding documents to the same writer. You expect what Lucene's own recovery test asserts: the exception propagates, the batch's documents are deleted, and a document added afterwards with value 42 reads back 42. Instead the values the cursor delivered before the throw stay in the doc-values buffer with no document attached, so the good document reads back -1 (a value of the rejected batch) and every later document of that field in the segment is shifted by the same number of values, which survives commit, reopen and forceMerge(1) while CheckIndex finds nothing wrong.
rows.area: index / columnar addBatch doc values (dense NUMERIC and SORTED_NUMERIC writers)

rows.title: When IndexWriter#addBatch fails part-way through a dense points column, the point bytes it already copied stay in the points buffer, so documents added later to the same in-memory segment are silently indexed with the rejected batch's point values
rows.summary: You add a batch with IndexWriter#addBatch whose dense points column (a LongColumn, or a BinaryColumn with point dimensions) has more values than fit in one 4 KiB chunk, and the batch fails after the first chunk, because Lucene's own length check rejects a value of the wrong width or because your cursor throws; Lucene rejects the batch with a non-aborting exception, the writer stays open, and you keep indexing. You expect the rejected batch to leave no trace, as Lucene promises for non-aborting exceptions and as its own ThrowMidBatchRecovers tests assert, so a document you add next with IntPoint p=7 matches p == 7. Instead the dense path had already copied the first chunk's point bytes into the field's buffer without recording doc IDs for them, so the next document is paired with the rejected batch's first value (the only live document, added with p=7, matches p == 1000 instead), every later point of that field in the segment is shifted, CheckIndex stays clean and the wrong values survive merges.
rows.area: index / columnar addBatch (dense points, PointValuesWriter)

rows.title: An addBatch that registers a new term-vector field but frames no rows leaves a segment whose FieldInfos declare term vectors with no term-vector files, so the committed index cannot be opened
rows.summary: You add a document, then call IndexWriter#addBatch with a column batch that declares a new text field with term vectors but adds no row: the batch is empty, or it is rejected with IllegalArgumentException because a later column conflicts with the existing schema, or its column cursor throws before the first row. You expect the earlier document to commit and the index to open, as it does when the same rejection happens through addDocument. Instead the segment's FieldInfos say the field has term vectors but no term-vector files were written, so DirectoryReader.open on the commit throws CorruptIndexException ('No sub-file with id .tvd found in compound file'), or, with the default IndexWriterConfig, commit() itself throws.
rows.area: index / columnar addBatch (term vectors)

rows.title: A SORTED_SET DictionaryColumn tuple that addBatch rejects (out-of-range ordinal, or ordValue() throws) leaves an empty document in the doc-values buffer, so the next flush fails and closes the IndexWriter, or with -da commits a segment whose field cannot be read
rows.summary: You add a batch with IndexWriter#addBatch whose SORTED_SET DictionaryColumn gives the first value of some document an ordinal outside the dictionary (or whose cursor throws while returning that ordinal); Lucene rejects the batch with an IllegalArgumentException, the writer stays open with no tragic exception, and you keep indexing. You expect the rejected batch to leave no trace, as Lucene promises for non-aborting exceptions (the batch's documents are marked deleted and the index stays consistent), so a later document with two SORTED_SET values commits and reads back normally. Instead the doc-values writer had already opened the rejected document before it checked the ordinal and records it with zero values, so the next commit fails (AssertionError with -ea, ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException with -da), closes the writer and loses all uncommitted documents, or, with -da and some value layouts, succeeds but writes a segment whose field throws NullPointerException when opened or fails CheckIndex.
rows.area: index / columnar addBatch (DictionaryColumn SORTED_SET doc values, SortedSetDocValuesWriter)

rows.title: PersistentSnapshotDeletionPolicy adopts a broken newest save file on load and deletes the good older one, so an OS crash, power loss or process kill while snapshot() or release() writes its save file silently drops every earlier persisted snapshot, and IndexWriter then deletes the snapshotted commits
rows.summary: You use PersistentSnapshotDeletionPolicy to protect a commit (for example for a backup): snapshot() returns, which its javadoc says means the snapshot is persisted, and later the machine crashes, loses power or the process is killed while another snapshot() or release() call is writing the next save file snapshots_N. You expect that after a restart the policy still holds the earlier snapshot (persist() keeps the previous save file until the new one is fsynced, so there is a good file to fall back on). Instead loadPriorSnapshots() takes its state from the newest, empty or truncated save file even though reading it threw, deletes the good older save file, and reports no snapshots, with no exception or log, so the next IndexWriter deletes the snapshotted commit (in the repro: snapshot count 0, segments_1 deleted, only commit 2 left).
rows.area: index / deletion policies (PersistentSnapshotDeletionPolicy save-file loading, crash recovery)

rows.title: IndexSplitter.split writes each copied segment into the destination commit without its doc-values update metadata, so on main the copy silently reads wrong doc values, and in every release since 4.6.0 the first IndexWriter opened on the copy deletes the copied update files and the copy can no longer be opened
rows.summary: You update a doc value in a segment (updateNumericDocValue, updateBinaryDocValue, or a soft delete), commit, and copy that segment to a new index with IndexSplitter.split, expecting the copy to hold the same documents and values and to stay a normal index. Instead split() copies all of the segment's files but writes a destination commit that records only the segment's generation numbers, not its per-commit field-infos files, doc-values update files or (on main) doc-values overlays. So on main the copy reads an updated field from its newest sparse update alone (price 10,999,12,13 reads as none,999,none,none), and in every release since 4.6.0 the first IndexWriter opened on the copy deletes the copied update files as unreferenced, after which the copy cannot be opened (NoSuchFileException: _0_1.fnm).
rows.area: misc / index tools (IndexSplitter.split) over core / index: SegmentCommitInfo per-commit doc-values update state

rows.title: ReindexingEnrichedDirectoryTaxonomyWriter.reindexWithNewOrdinalData rebuilds only the last committed taxonomy, so categories added since that commit are dropped and their ordinals are later reused for other categories
rows.summary: You index a document with the category Author/Bob through a ReindexingEnrichedDirectoryTaxonomyWriter after its last commit, then call reindexWithNewOrdinalData to refresh the per-category data, whose javadoc promises 'The ordinals themselves will be preserved, so the caller does not need to update references to them in the main index'. Instead the method rebuilds the taxonomy from a reader of the last commit, so Author/Bob disappears (the writer's getSize() drops from 4 to 3) and its ordinal 3 goes to the next new category, Author/Carol. After both indexes are committed, the main index's Bob document is counted as Carol (Alice=1 Carol=1 instead of Alice=1 Bob=1) with no error; on a taxonomy that was never committed the call throws IndexNotFoundException.
rows.area: facet / taxonomy (ReindexingEnrichedDirectoryTaxonomyWriter.reindexWithNewOrdinalData)

rows.title: PerFieldPostingsFormat merge leaves stale inherited format attributes on a field that has no postings left after a segment written by a non-per-field postings codec (for example SimpleTextCodec), so the merged segment cannot be opened
rows.summary: You index a field with a per-field postings codec (for example a Lucene104Codec subclass that maps the field to its own postings format), then, in a writer session whose codec's postings format is not per-field (SimpleTextCodec or a custom codec), delete every document that has the field and force-merge, and then go back to the per-field codec and merge again. You expect the committed index to open, because every call returned normally. Instead the merged segment still records the field's old format name and suffix although the merge wrote no files for that group, so DirectoryReader.open and CheckIndex fail with CorruptIndexException caused by a missing <segment>_<format>_<suffix>.psm (for example _4_FST50_0.psm).

rows.title: BPIndexReorderer assumes every segment ends with a parent document: once a segment ends with child documents that have no parent after them, each BP reordering merge in which that segment comes last throws and closes the IndexWriter
rows.summary: You index document blocks with IndexWriterConfig#setParentField, merge through BPReorderingMergePolicy with a BPIndexReorderer, and a segment ends up ending with child documents that have no parent after them, for example because you deleted or updated only the parent of its last block and a merge dropped it, or because IndexWriter rejected a block at one of its children (with the documented IllegalArgumentException) just before a flush. You expect later merges to work: IndexWriter accepted every call, CheckIndex calls the index clean and a plain merge of the same segment succeeds. Instead BPIndexReorderer, which assumes the merged view ends with a parent, runs past the end of its arrays in the next reordering merge in which that segment comes last (ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException with assertions off, AssertionError with them on), and IndexWriter closes with a tragic exception, loses uncommitted changes and fails the same way after every reopen.

rows.title: A document block rejected at a child can be flushed as a fully deleted segment without the parent field; if the merge policy keeps it (SoftDeletesRetentionMergePolicy can), merges that combine it only with segments without multi-document blocks throw 'expected parent doc field ... across all segments' and close IndexWriter, again after every reopen
rows.summary: You set IndexWriterConfig#setParentField (no index sort) and a merge policy that keeps fully deleted segments, such as SoftDeletesRetentionMergePolicy, and IndexWriter rejects a document block at a child with a documented non-aborting exception (for example a term longer than MAX_TERM_LENGTH) while that block is the only content of its in-memory segment, for example the first thing indexed after a commit. You expect the rejection to leave a consistent index that keeps merging, as the addDocument javadoc promises ('if an Exception is hit ... the index will be consistent'). Instead the block is flushed as a fully deleted segment whose FieldInfos have no parent field (IndexWriter registers the parent field only when it reaches a block's last document), the merge policy keeps it, and every merge that combines it only with segments holding no multi-document block throws IllegalStateException 'expected parent doc field to be "_parent " across all segments but found a segment with different field "null"' and closes IndexWriter, also after the index is reopened, until forceMergeDeletes removes the segment.

rows.title: With a soft-deletes field configured, IndexWriter's merge assumes OneMerge#wrapForMerge only revives documents: for each merged segment without hard deletes, every live document that a merge wrapper hides (which the javadoc allows) lowers the new segment's soft-delete count by one, so the merge throws 'invalid softDelCount=-1' when nothing is revived, and under SoftDeletesRetentionMergePolicy commits a too-low count (numDocs and IndexSearcher#count over-count, CheckIndex rejects it, later merges of it throw); regression since 7.7.0 (LUCENE-8569)
rows.summary: You set IndexWriterConfig#setSoftDeletesField and a merge policy whose OneMerge#wrapForMerge hides expired documents (its javadoc says a wrapper may 'add/remove fields or documents'), index two segments without hard deletes, and call forceMerge(1); you expect the merge to drop the expired document and succeed, as the same merge does without a soft-deletes field, or with one when the segment happens to hold a hard delete. Instead IndexWriter derives the carried-over soft deletes as getSoftDelCount() - wrappedReader.numDeletedDocs(), which counts each hidden live document as a dropped soft delete, so the count comes out -1 and the merge throws IllegalArgumentException 'invalid softDelCount=-1 (maxDoc=2)'. With SoftDeletesRetentionMergePolicy on top (one retained soft-deleted document) the merge silently commits softDelCount=0, so numDocs and IndexSearcher#count report 3 where 2 documents are live, CheckIndex reports 'actual soft deletes: 1 but expected: 0', and after the retention window the next merge of that segment throws 'invalid softDelCount=-1 (maxDoc=3)'.

rows.title: CachingCollector and CachingCollectorManager report isCached() true (no overflow) but hold only the hits their wrapped first-pass collector let through (TOP_SCORES pruning, early leaf termination, skipped leaves), so replay() silently feeds the second pass fewer matches than re-running the query

Instead the cache holds only the hits the first-pass collector let through: TopScoreDocCollectorManager(10, 1000), the IndexSearcher#search(Query, int) default, prunes non-competitive hits (even when the score-caching variant tells the searcher it needs COMPLETE), an index-order TopFieldCollector stops each segment early, and TotalHitCountCollector skips whole segments it can count from index statistics. In the repro, replaying into a hit counter sees 1001, 2 and 0 of 5000 matching documents, with no error.

rows.title: RandomSamplingFacetsCollector.createManager samples the hits twice when a search has more than one slice: the reduce reads each slice's already-sampled getMatchingDocs() as its original hits, so the sample is far too small and every amortized facet count is biased low (regression from #13542, 10.0.0 onward)
rows.summary: You count facets on a sample of a large result set with RandomSamplingFacetsCollector.createManager(sampleSize, seed) on an IndexSearcher that has an executor, and expect what a one-slice search gives: about sampleSize sampled hits, taken at the rate sampleSize / totalHits that getSamplingRate() reports, so that amortizeFacetCounts estimates the real counts. Instead, with two or more slices the reduce fills the reduced collector's original hits from FacetsCollectorManager.reduceMatchingDocs, which calls each slice collector's getMatchingDocs(), the accessor RandomSamplingFacetsCollector overrides to return that slice's sample; the reduced collector then samples those samples again. The sample shrinks to about sampleSize^2 x numSlices / totalHits and every amortized count is low by the per-slice ratio, with no error: 2 segments of 1,024 matching docs with sampleSize 128 and one slice per segment give 16 sampled hits and an amortized count of 256 instead of 128 and 2,048, and default slicing on 2 segments of 262,144 docs with sampleSize 4,096 gives 64 sampled hits and 8,192 instead of 4,096 and 524,288.

rows.title: Multi-valued range facet counts drop matches when a document's values do not arrive in ascending order (custom MultiLongValuesSource/MultiDoubleValuesSource, or raw-bit doubles with two or more negative values): LongRangeCounter.addMultiValued assumes sorted values
rows.summary: You compute range facet counts over a multi-valued source, for example the distances from the user to each of a document's locations computed by your own MultiDoubleValuesSource, or doubles stored as raw bits in a SortedNumeric field and read with fromDoubleField or the DoubleRangeFacetCounts(String, ...) constructor. You expect each range to count every document that has at least one value in it, which is exactly what the range's own drill-down query finds. Instead, when a document's values arrive in descending order (a custom source in its natural order, or raw-bit doubles whenever the document has two or more negative values), the counter skips every later value that sorts below an interval it already counted for that document, so a document with distances {3.0, 0.5} is missing from '< 1 km' and '< 2 km'.

rows.title: RandomSamplingFacetsCollector samples one hit per (int) (1 / samplingRate) hits but amortizes by the untruncated samplingRate, so amortized facet counts are up to 2x too high (1999 hits with sampleSize 1000: every hit is sampled, yet every count is doubled)
rows.summary: You sample facet counts with RandomSamplingFacetsCollector and sampleSize 1000 on a query with 1999 hits, call amortizeFacetCounts to scale the sampled counts back up, and expect estimates of the true counts; here the sample happens to contain every hit, so the right answer is the exact counts 667/666/666. Instead you get 1333/1331/1331 and a dimension total of 3996 for 1999 hits, with no error: the collector computes samplingRate = 1000 / 1999 = 0.50025 but samples one hit per bin of (int) (1 / samplingRate) = 1 hit, and it amortizes, and reports through getSamplingRate(), with the untruncated rate. In general the counts are too high by totalHits / (sampleSize * binSize), between 1 and 2, worst just below twice the sample size.

rows.title: TaxonomyFacetFloatAssociations with a DoubleValuesSource reports a too-high LabelAndValue.count for every label that has matching documents below it in a hierarchical dimension, because FloatTaxonomyFacets rolls the counts up again at every ancestor level (values are right; every release since 9.11.0)
