Instead getTopChildren and getAllChildren report a (9.0) with count 4, because FloatTaxonomyFacets#updateValueFromRollup first calls super.updateValueFromRollup, which rolls up the counts of the whole sub-tree, and then its own rollup(childOrdinal), which calls updateValueFromRollup again for every descendant, so the sub-tree counts are added once more at each ancestor level. Values and leaf counts are right; only LabelAndValue.count of labels with descendants is inflated, and the deeper the tree, the larger the overcount.

rows.title: LongRangeGroupSelector and DoubleRangeGroupSelector load their per-segment values only in setScorer, so grouping with score-less caching returns wrong groups (8.6.0-10.5.2) or throws NullPointerException (10.6.0 by reading, and main), and DistinctValuesCollector with a range value selector always throws NullPointerException
rows.summary: You group a two-segment index (prices 5, 15, 25 | 35, 45, 55) into price ranges with GroupingSearch and new LongRangeGroupSelector(price, new LongRangeFactory(0, 20, 60)), sort by a field, and turn on the documented second-pass cache without scores, setCaching(100, false); you expect the same groups as without the cache: LongRange(0, 20) -> docs 0, 1, LongRange(20, 40) -> 2, 3, LongRange(40, 60) -> 4, 5. Instead every release from 8.6.0 to 10.5.2 returns LongRange(0, 20) -> none, LongRange(20, 40) -> 0, 3 and LongRange(40, 60) -> 1, 2, 4, 5 with no error (the first segment's documents are grouped by the second segment's prices), 10.6.0 (by reading) and main throw NullPointerException, and DistinctValuesCollector with a range selector as its value selector throws NullPointerException in every version; DoubleRangeGroupSelector behaves the same. The cause is that both range selectors fetch their per-segment values only in setScorer(), while the score-less cache replay and DistinctValuesCollector's per-group collector call setNextReader and advanceTo on the selector but never setScorer.

rows.title: Taxonomy Facets#getTopDims returns another dimension's children, childCount and value under a multi-valued dimension's name, because replacing the bottom of the top-dims queue updates dim and value but not dimOrd (released since 9.2.0)

rows.title: DiversifiedTopDocsCollector and its manager put every document without a key into key 0's group, so a keyless document uses up key 0's maxHitsPerKey quota and real key-0 hits are silently dropped from the top hits

rows.title: DoubleDocValuesStats and SortedDoubleDocValuesStats (lucene/misc) start max at Double.MIN_VALUE, the smallest positive double, so max() returns 4.9E-324 instead of the real maximum whenever every collected value is <= 0 (and min() returns Double.MAX_VALUE when every value is +Infinity)
rows.summary: You collect statistics for a double doc-values field with DocValuesStats.DoubleDocValuesStats (or SortedDoubleDocValuesStats) and expect max() to be the largest collected value; the javadoc calls it 'the maximum value of the field' and leaves it undefined only when count() is zero. If every collected value is zero or negative, max() returns 4.9E-324 instead: max starts at Double.MIN_VALUE, which is the smallest positive double, not the most negative one, and no value <= 0 ever beats it, so for {-5, -3, -4} you get count 3 and min -5.0 but max 4.9E-324. The same mix-up on the other side makes min() return Double.MAX_VALUE when every value is +Infinity; the long variants start at Long.MAX_VALUE / Long.MIN_VALUE and are correct.

rows.title: SortedDoubleDocValuesStats (lucene/misc) reads core DoubleField values as raw IEEE bits, so negative values give a silently wrong min, sum and mean (DoubleField -5.0 and 3.0 give min -0.8749999999999999)

rows.title: SimpleNaiveBayesDocumentClassifier applies a documented 'field^boost' (e.g. 'title^10') only on its first call: it writes the stripped field name back into the caller's textFieldNames array, so every later classification silently returns the unboosted result (released since 6.0.0)

rows.title: BooleanPerceptronClassifier with batchSize > 1 can silently lose the weight updates of misclassified training documents: the weight FST is rebuilt only when a misclassified document sits at a multiple of batchSize and never after the last batch, and updates inside a batch are computed from the last FST build and overwrite each other, so the trained model is wrong (released since 5.0.0)
rows.summary: You index two training documents labelled false, 'bb' and 'aa aa', train BooleanPerceptronClassifier with bias 1.5 and batchSize 2, and expect assignClass('aa aa') = false, which is what batchSize 1 gives on the same data and what both an online and a mini-batch perceptron give. Instead it returns true (score 0.81): the update for the misclassified 'aa aa' (batch position 1) is written only to the pending weight map, because the FST that holds the weights is rebuilt only when a misclassified document sits at a position that is a multiple of batchSize, and the constructor ends by clearing that map without a final rebuild. Updates inside a batch are also computed from the last FST build and overwrite each other, so with batchSize 10 and three training documents 'aa' labelled false only the first update is applied and the model still answers true.

rows.title: SimpleNaiveBayesClassifier applies its documented training query only to the per-word counts: the class prior and the likelihood denominators are computed over the whole index, so labelled documents outside the training set can decide the class (released since 4.6.0; same pattern in SimpleNaiveBayesDocumentClassifier and CachingNaiveBayesClassifier)
rows.summary: You index four training documents marked split:train (fruit: 'apple', 'pear', 'plum'; vehicle: 'car') and ten more vehicle documents marked split:other, build SimpleNaiveBayesClassifier with the training query split:train and classify 'apple', expecting what the same classifier trained on an index holding only the four training documents answers: fruit (0.811), with prior P(fruit) = 3/4. Instead it answers vehicle (P(fruit) = 0.445), and for an empty input, which only the prior decides, it gives P(fruit) = 3/14, the whole-index share. The query is ANDed only into the per-word counts (getWordFreqForClass); the prior (docFreq(class) / Terms.getDocCount()) and the likelihood denominator (average unique terms per document x docFreq(class) + that document count) ignore it, because countDocsWithClass applies the query only in a getDocCount() == -1 fallback that current codecs never take.

rows.title: BooleanPerceptronClassifier adds its term weights to its FST in Java String (UTF-16) order instead of the UTF-8 byte order the FST requires, so a text field with a term starting with a supplementary character (such as an emoji) and a term starting with a character in U+E000..U+FFFF (such as a fullwidth letter) makes training throw AssertionError with -ea and, with -da, silently loses term weights (in some term layouts all of them) or throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException (released since 5.0.0)
rows.summary: You index two documents, 'P P P' labelled true and 'N' labelled false, where P is U+F900 (a CJK compatibility ideograph) and N is U+1D400 (mathematical bold capital A), train BooleanPerceptronClassifier with the default bias (the average term frequency, here 2), and expect assignClass(P) = (true, 0.393), which is what the same corpus gives with ASCII terms or with ordinary CJK ideographs. Instead the constructor throws AssertionError 'inputs are added out of order lastInput=[f0 9d 90 80] vs input=[ef a4 80]' with -ea, and with -da assignClass(P) returns (false, 0.632) because P's weight can no longer be found in the FST. The classifier keeps its weights in a ConcurrentSkipListMap<String, Double>, whose String order (UTF-16 code units) puts U+1D400 (D835 DC00) before U+F900, and adds their UTF-8 encodings in that order to an FSTCompiler that requires UTF-8 byte order (EF before F0) and checks it only with an assert.

rows.title: Sandbox SortedNumericDocValuesMultiRangeQuery classifies each clause by the sign of 'lower - upper', which overflows, so a legal half-open clause such as [Long.MIN_VALUE, 10] or [-5, Long.MAX_VALUE] given together with another clause is silently dropped as if it were reversed (values 5 and 150 with the clauses [Long.MIN_VALUE, 10] and [100, 200] count 1, not 2); since 10.3.0

Instead the count is 1 and the query prints f:[100..200]: building the query sorts out reversed clauses by the sign of 'lower - upper', and Long.MIN_VALUE - 10 overflows to a large positive number, so the legal clause is thrown away as if it were reversed. Every clause wider than 2^63 is lost the same way, while one clause alone takes a different code path and is right.

rows.title: Geo3DPoint distance queries with a radius below about 1 km silently return wrong results in both directions: each document's decoded point lies a few millimetres off the planet surface and is tested against a circle plane nearly tangent to the surface, so a 10 m query misses documents at its own centre and matches documents about 100 m away
rows.summary: You index locations as Geo3DPoint on the default WGS84 model and run Geo3DPoint.newDistanceQuery with a small radius, say 10 m, expecting the points within 10 m (the javadoc allows up to 0.5% error). Instead the query misses about half of the points inside the radius, even a document located exactly at the query centre, and returns points about 100 m away, while LatLonPoint gives the right answer on the same data. The cause is that each document's stored x/y/z is decoded to a point a few millimetres off the planet surface, and that point is tested against the circle's cutting plane, which for a small circle meets the surface at a grazing angle and turns millimetres into 100-190 m.

rows.title: On WGS84, geo3d path end caps are shifted toward the equator, so Geo3DPoint.newPathQuery and Geo3DDocValuesField.newPathSort miss documents just beyond a poleward path end (sort value +Infinity) and match documents tens of km beyond an equatorward end
rows.summary: You run Geo3DPoint.newPathQuery (or Geo3DDocValuesField.newPathSort) on WGS84 with a north-south path, for example from (44N,20E) to (45N,20E), and expect it to match the points within pathWidthMeters of the path, with round end caps of that radius around the first and last points, as it does on PlanetModel.SPHERE. Instead both end caps are shifted about 21 km toward the equator: with pathWidthMeters 20000 the query misses documents 12 and 16 km beyond the north end (sort value +Infinity), and with pathWidthMeters 1000 it matches documents 10 to 40 km south of the first point (sort values 10006 to 40034 m). The end-cap plane (GeoStandardPath.CutoffSingleCircleSegmentEndpoint, built by CircleSegmentEndpoint through the two segment corners with its normal inside the origin-containing cutoff plane) points along the end point's geocentric direction, which on an ellipsoid is not the surface normal there, so the cap circle is centred equatorward of the end point.

rows.title: Geo3D distance sorts read a document's doc values twice in any segment where some document has two or more points, so top-N and searchAfter results come back in the wrong order with another document's distance as the sort value (even a filtered-out or deleted document's), or the search throws EOFException (every release since 7.0.0)
rows.summary: You index documents with Geo3DDocValuesField, at least one of them with two or more points (the javadoc allows this and says the closest one is used), and ask for the top 2 hits sorted by Geo3DDocValuesField.newDistanceSort; you expect the head of the full sorted order, each hit carrying its own closest distance. Instead the top 2 come back in the wrong order and a hit reports the distance of the next document, because the comparator reads the document's values once in compareBottom (or compareTop) and again in copy without re-positioning the SortedNumericDocValues iterator, which its javadoc forbids ('Do not call this more than docValueCount times'), so the second read takes the following document's values or runs past the end of the data and throws EOFException. The same happens with searchAfter paging and all seven Geo3D sort factories, and because document order decides which value is read, a hit can report the distance of a document that a filter, a live-docs wrapper or a delete hides from the search.

rows.title: Geo3D distance, path and outside-distance sorts (Geo3DDocValuesField) drop hits under IndexSearcher.searchAfter: compareTop compares the cursor, which is in meters, with the document's distance in planet units, so on WGS84 every page after the first loses all finite-distance hits (released since 6.1.0)

With six documents 3 to 8 degrees north of the origin and page size 2, page 2 should be [2, 3, 4, 5] and is []; on PlanetModel.SPHERE, where meters and planet units coincide, the same paging is correct.

rows.title: Intervals.ordered(X, X) with two equal sub-sources that span several positions lets the two copies of X overlap, so ordered(phrase(a, a), phrase(a, a)) matches 'a a a' and ordered(unordered(a, b), unordered(a, b)) matches 'a b a' (one b), while the same query with an equivalent but unequal second source finds nothing
rows.summary: You ask for two occurrences of X in order with Intervals.ordered(X, X), for example X = unordered(a, b) ('a near b', twice) or X = phrase(a, a), and expect the usual ordered rule that the sub-intervals do not overlap (the fn:ordered documentation says 'Source intervals must not overlap'). Instead, because the two arguments are equal, OrderedIntervalsSource.build merges them into a RepeatingIntervalsSource, which joins consecutive intervals of a single sub-iterator without checking that they are disjoint, so ordered(unordered(a, b), unordered(a, b)) matches 'a b a', which has only one b, and ordered(phrase(a, a), phrase(a, a)) matches 'a a a'. The same query with an equivalent but unequal second source, ordered(X, or(X, a term that occurs nowhere)), correctly finds nothing, and so did Lucene 8.4.1.

rows.title: RepeatingIntervalsSource's iterator computes width() with the sign inverted (start - end + 1 per repeated sub-interval), so when Intervals.ordered/unordered repeat a sub-source wider than one position (for example the same phrase twice) gaps() is over-reported, maxgaps drops real matches and Weight#matches disagrees with the scorer
rows.summary: You search with an interval query that repeats a multi-word piece, for example maxgaps(0, ordered(phrase(new, york), phrase(new, york))) on the text 'new york new york', and expect a match because the two phrases sit back to back with no gap. Instead it finds nothing: Lucene turns equal sub-sources into a RepeatingIntervalsSource whose iterator adds start - end + 1 instead of end - start + 1 for each copy, so width() is 0 instead of 4, gaps() is 4 instead of 0, and maxgaps rejects the interval. The Matches path of the same class uses the right formula, so Weight#matches returns a match for the very document the scorer rejected; repeats of single words are unaffected because their start equals their end.

rows.title: Intervals.unordered/ordered given the same disjunction twice merge it into one repeated source that the gap-sensitive disjunction rewrite does not look into (RepeatingIntervalsSource.pullUpDisjunctions returns itself), so maxgaps(0, unordered(X, X)) with X = or(b, phrase(c, b)) misses 'c b c b', and maxgaps or phrase over ordered(X, X) miss the same way

Instead, because the two arguments are equal, Lucene merges them into one RepeatingIntervalsSource whose pullUpDisjunctions() returns only itself, so the rewrite never runs, the longer 'c b' alternative is minimized away inside X, and the query returns no hits. maxgaps(0, ordered(X, X)) and phrase(a, ordered(X, X)) miss in the same way, and so does Intervals.analyzedText for the query text 'york york' with a synonym york -> 'new york' (unordered, maxGaps 0) on the document 'new york new york'.

rows.title: A nested Intervals.ordered(a, a) or unordered(a, a) passes its inner gap up to its parent, so maxgaps(0, ordered(ordered(a, a), a)) misses 'a x a a' while maxgaps(0, ordered(ordered(a, b), a)) matches 'a x b a'
rows.summary: You nest a repeated pair inside another interval operator, for example ordered(ordered(a, a), a), and filter it with maxgaps(0, ...): the IntervalIterator#gaps javadoc counts only the gaps between the parent's immediate sub-intervals, so 'a x a a' (sub-intervals [0,2] and [3,3]) should match, just as maxgaps(0, ordered(ordered(a, b), a)) matches 'a x b a'. Instead, because the two arguments of the inner ordered(a, a) are equal, Lucene builds it as a RepeatingIntervalsSource whose width() is the sum of its two copies (2) rather than its span (3), so the parent counts the inner 'x' as its own gap (gaps 1) and maxgaps(0) silently drops the document. The same happens for ordered(unordered(a, a), b), unordered(ordered(a, a), b) and ordered(x, ordered(a, a)), while wrapping the inner pair in a no-op filter such as maxwidth(100, ...) brings the hit back.

rows.title: Geo3DDocValuesField.newDistanceSort and newOutsideDistanceSort with a maximum radius below about 10 km test each document's 21-bit decoded point, which lies metres off the planet surface, against the circle's nearly tangent plane: about half the documents inside the circle, even at its centre, get distance +Infinity and sort last, documents up to about 8 km away get finite distances, and inside documents get outside distances of up to the radius instead of 0.0
rows.summary: You store locations with Geo3DDocValuesField on the default WGS84 model and sort hits with Geo3DDocValuesField.newDistanceSort(field, lat, lon, 1000, WGS84), expecting ascending distance from the centre with the distance in metres (and, with newOutsideDistanceSort, 0.0 for points inside the circle). Instead about half of the documents inside the 1 km radius, even ones 10 m from the centre, get +Infinity and sort last as if they had no location, some documents 2-3 km away get finite distances and sort ahead of them, and inside documents get outside distances of up to 988 m, while LatLonDocValuesField's distance sort orders the same points correctly. The cause: each doc value decodes to a point up to about 4.5 m off the planet surface, and the comparators pass that point unprojected to the circle's membership test, a single plane that for a 1 km circle lies only about 8 cm below the surface at the centre, so the decode error, not the distance, decides in or out.

rows.title: LatLonDocValuesField.newSlowGeometryQuery with CONTAINS and two or more Point geometries matches documents that hold only some of the query points, while its documented IndexOrDocValuesQuery partner LatLonPoint.newGeometryQuery requires all of them
rows.summary: You index points with LatLonPoint and LatLonDocValuesField and ask for the documents that contain both P1 and P2 (CONTAINS with two Point geometries); a document that holds only P1 must not match, and LatLonPoint.newGeometryQuery, which builds one MUST clause per query point, indeed matches none. LatLonDocValuesField.newSlowGeometryQuery, which its javadoc says to pair with that query in an IndexOrDocValuesQuery (whose two queries 'must match the same documents'), accepts a document as soon as any one of its points equals any one query point, so it computes an OR instead of an AND. In the repro (1000 one-point documents, half at P1 and half at P2) the points query returns 0 hits, the doc-values query returns all 1000, and 'id:7 AND IndexOrDocValuesQuery(points, docValues)' returns document 7, with no error.

rows.title: XY distance sort used as a later Sort key drops closer tied hits, because XYPointDistanceComparator.setBottom keeps an old, too-small bounding box when the bottom grows (a missing-value bottom of +Infinity, or growth after 1024 bottom updates)
rows.summary: You sort three documents, (cat b, distance 1), (cat a, no location) and (cat a, distance 3), with Sort(new SortField("cat", STRING), XYDocValuesField.newDistanceSort("loc", 0, 0)) and ask for the top 1; you expect the (a, 3) document, because ties on cat are broken by ascending distance and a missing location counts as +Infinity and sorts last. Instead you get the (a, no location) document: when it becomes the queue bottom, setBottom skips rebuilding the comparator's bounding box because +Infinity is not below Float.MAX_VALUE, so the box built for the earlier bottom at distance 1 stays, and compareBottom rejects the (a, 3) document as outside it. The same stale box arises after 1024 bottom updates, when only every 64th update rebuilds it and the bottom grows on another one; a nearest-first distance sort is not affected because its bottom only shrinks.
rows.area: core / document: XY distance sort (XYDocValuesField.newDistanceSort, XYPointDistanceComparator)

rows.title: NumberRangePrefixTreeStrategy with setPointsOnly(true): an Intersects query for a date or number unit coarser than full precision (a year, month, day, ...) matches no documents
rows.summary: You index full-precision dates such as 2014-10-23T21:22:33.159 with a NumberRangePrefixTreeStrategy over DateRangePrefixTree on which you called setPointsOnly(true), and search makeQuery(new SpatialArgs(SpatialOperation.Intersects, tree.parseShape("2014-10"))). You expect the documents from October 2014, because each point lies inside that month, IsWithin with the same shape and the same query with pointsOnly=false find them, and the LUCENE-7845 CHANGES entry describes this pointsOnly TermQuery shortcut as an optimization for 'a simple date interval (e.g. 1 month)'. Instead RecursivePrefixTreeStrategy.makeGridShapeIntersectsQuery builds a TermQuery on the month's token plus the leaf byte, a term that pointsOnly indexing at full precision, the normal path, never writes (each point stores every coarser level only as a non-leaf prefix term), so the query matches nothing; the same happens for a year, day, hour, minute or second and for a range that normalizes to one unit.

rows.title: Geo3dRectangleShape.getCrossesDateLine() tests whether a box spans longitude 0 instead of whether it crosses the dateline, so PointVectorStrategy and BBoxStrategy return wrong hits for Geo3d boxes and circles at the dateline or the prime meridian
rows.summary: You use the Geo3d spatial context (Geo3dSpatialContextFactory) with PointVectorStrategy or BBoxStrategy and query or index a box that crosses the dateline, such as rect(170, -170, -10, 10), or one that spans longitude 0, such as rect(-10, 10, -10, 10). You expect getCrossesDateLine() to follow the spatial4j Rectangle contract (true exactly when the box crosses the -180/180 meridian, that is minX > maxX, as spatial4j's RectangleImpl and this class's own getWidth() assume), so a point at longitude 175 is found inside 170..-170 and an indexed box -10..10 does not match a query box at 100..110. Instead Geo3dRectangleShape.getCrossesDateLine() returns getMaxX() > 0 && getMinX() < 0 ('spans longitude 0'), which is false for 170..-170 and true for -10..10: PointVectorStrategy searches the empty range 170..-170 and returns 0 hits (also for circle(180, 0, 5)), and BBoxStrategy stores xdl=F for the dateline box and misses it (0 hits instead of 1), but stores xdl=T for -10..10, reads it as [-10, 180] plus [-180, 10] and matches it against 100..110 (1 hit instead of 0).

rows.title: Geo3dShape.relate(Rectangle) swaps WITHIN and CONTAINS when the rectangle is not a Geo3d shape (such as ctx.getWorldBounds() or a PackedQuadPrefixTree cell), so IsWithin/Contains on stored shapes give the opposite answer and RecursivePrefixTreeStrategy over PackedQuadPrefixTree returns documents far outside the query shape (regression in 7.1.0)
rows.summary: You use the Geo3d spatial context and relate a Geo3d shape to a spatial4j rectangle that the Geo3d shape factory did not build, for example a 10-degree circle against the context's own ctx.getWorldBounds(), or run a SerializedDVStrategy IsWithin(ctx.getWorldBounds()) query over that circle, and expect WITHIN (the circle lies inside the world) and one hit. Instead relate() returns CONTAINS and the query matches nothing, while Contains(world bounds) matches the circle: Geo3dShape.relate(Rectangle) asks spatial3d how this shape relates to the rectangle but then applies the mapping written for the opposite question (how the other shape relates to this one), so the two nested answers come out swapped, whereas the same box built by the Geo3d factory relates correctly. Lucene builds such rectangles itself, so RecursivePrefixTreeStrategy over PackedQuadPrefixTree, whose cells are plain spatial4j rectangles, treats a cell that contains a small query circle as lying inside the circle and returns every document in that cell, for example a point at (100.3, 37.7) for a half-degree circle at (1, 1).

rows.title: Geo3dShapeFactory.pointXYZ(x, y, z) and the Geo3d builders' pointXYZ read longitude, latitude and a third value as geocentric Cartesian x, y, z, so 3-coordinate points, lines and multi-points land somewhere else (pointXYZ(30, 10, 0) becomes lon 18.43, lat 0) and polygons with z = 0 are rejected as 'all points are coplanar' (since 7.1.0)
rows.summary: You use the Geo3d spatial context and build a point from longitude 30, latitude 10 and an elevation of 0, with ShapeFactory.pointXYZ(30, 10, 0) or by reading the GeoJSON position [30, 10, 0], and expect the point (30, 10), which is what spatial4j's own factory returns and what its contract implies (pointXYZ is pointXY plus a third dimension that an implementation may ignore or reject). Instead you get longitude 18.43, latitude 0: Geo3dShapeFactory.pointXYZ and the builders' shared Geo3dPointBuilder.pointXYZ hand the three numbers to spatial3d's new GeoPoint(x, y, z), which reads them as a geocentric Cartesian vector, so points, lines and multi-points built this way silently land elsewhere (a multi-point relates DISJOINT to its own vertex) and a polygon whose vertices all have z = 0 is rejected with InvalidShapeException 'Invalid polygon, all points are coplanar'. The reviewer of the original change had noted that these x, y, z are longitude, latitude and a user-defined value, 'not geo-centric coordinates', but the code was committed unchanged in 2017.

rows.title: LatLonShape/XYShape newSlowDocValuesBoxQuery reports Weight#isCacheable() == true although it reads the shape from binary doc values, so after an in-place doc-values update the query cache keeps returning the old matches

You expect the reopened searcher to stop matching that document, because a query that reads doc values must report itself not cacheable once those doc values have been updated (SegmentCacheable). Instead its Weight#isCacheable stays true (inherited from SpatialQuery#queryIsCacheable, which always returns true), the segment keeps its core cache key, and the cache keeps serving the pre-update result (5 hits instead of 4 in the repro) until the segment is merged away or the entry is evicted.

rows.title: For a sloppy PhraseQuery with a repeated term (for example "very very"~1), Weight#matches reports an end position and end offset past the match, at a later occurrence of the repeated term that repeat-collision resolution has already advanced to, so Matches-based highlighting (the default UnifiedHighlighter) marks too much text

Lucene reports positions 0-3, 'very very good very', because after finding the match the sloppy matcher moves the second 'very' on to the later occurrence to resolve a collision between the two copies of the term, and endPosition()/endOffset() are read only afterwards, from that moved state. The reported span is not the window of any valid match (positions 0 and 3 are two moves apart, the slop is 1); the hit itself and its score are correct.

rows.summary: You keep a keyword field as doc values only, filter on it with SortedSetDocValuesField.newSlowSetQuery or a PrefixQuery with DOC_VALUES_REWRITE (DocValuesRewriteMethod says it 'can be used to perform these queries against an unindexed docvalues field'), and expect Weight#matches to return non-null Matches (MATCH_WITH_NO_TERMS) for every hit, as its javadoc promises for DocValues queries and as newSlowExactQuery on the same field does. Instead matches() looks the matched terms up in the field's postings, which do not exist, so it returns null for every hit; for +body:fruit #tags:(banana) the UnifiedHighlighter with default settings returns 'a ripe fruit in a basket' with no highlighted term, while the same query with newSlowRangeQuery as the filter highlights 'fruit'. As a MUST_NOT clause the same null makes Weight#matches non-null for documents the clause excludes; hits, counts and scores stay correct.
rows.area: core / search: MultiTermQuery rewrite methods (DocValuesRewriteMethod, DOC_VALUES_REWRITE) and the Matches API (Weight#matches)

rows.title: FastVectorHighlighter drops a match at a position that holds stacked tokens (index-time synonyms, stems) when the token that sorts first there starts a query phrase that does not continue: FieldPhraseList tries only the first stacked token with any query-map entry, so dogs OR "dog house" on 'my dogs' (synonym dog stacked on dogs) highlights nothing (a LUCENE-5538 regression, 4.7.1 on)
rows.summary: You index 'my dogs' with an index-time synonym filter that stacks 'dog' on 'dogs' (term vectors with positions and offsets), search dogs OR "dog house", which matches through dogs (Weight#matches reports offsets 3-7), and call FastVectorHighlighter.getBestFragment, expecting 'my dogs', which the TermQuery alone gives. Instead you get null, with no error. FieldPhraseList starts a candidate with the first token at that position that has any entry in the query's phrase map ('dog', which sorts first and only starts the phrase "dog house"), finds that the phrase does not continue, adds nothing and never tries 'dogs' at the same position; Lucene 4.7.0 highlights this correctly, and the LUCENE-5538 fix in 4.7.1 introduced the loop.
rows.area: highlighter / vectorhighlight FieldPhraseList and FieldTermStack (FastVectorHighlighter phrase search over stacked tokens)

rows.title: Classic Highlighter turns the position holes of an exact PhraseQuery or MultiPhraseQuery (for example from removed stop words) into SpanNearQuery slop, so it highlights nearby pairs that do not match and can miss the occurrence that does
rows.summary: You index 'rock roll rock and roll' with a stop-word analyzer, search for the phrase "rock and roll" (QueryParser and QueryBuilder make it rock at position 0 and roll at position 2, slop 0, and Weight#matches reports the only match at positions 2-4), and highlight the hit with Highlighter and QueryScorer, expecting 'rock roll rock and roll'. Instead you get 'rock roll rock and roll', and on 'rock roll roll', which matches only as the first rock plus the last roll, you get 'rock roll roll', with the matching last word unmarked. WeightedSpanTermExtractor turns the phrase's one hole into slop 1 of an ordered SpanNearQuery, which accepts 0 or 1 words between the terms instead of exactly 1 and keeps only the shortest span per start; MultiPhraseQuery has the same conversion, and the UnifiedHighlighter with weight matches turned off reaches it through PhraseHelper.
rows.area: highlighter / original Highlighter, QueryScorer and WeightedSpanTermExtractor (phrase-to-span conversion)

rows.title: Default UnifiedHighlighter (WEIGHT_MATCHES) rewrites the query again on its own per-leaf or one-document reader, so statistics-dependent queries such as CommonTermsQuery lose their highlights
rows.summary: You search with CommonTermsQuery(SHOULD, MUST, 0.5) over 'the' (in 5 of 6 documents) and 'fox' (2 of 6), which the searcher rewrites to +fox the, and highlight the hit 'quick brown fox' with a default UnifiedHighlighter built on that same searcher. You expect 'quick brown fox', which the highlighter returns with WEIGHT_MATCHES off and the legacy Highlighter and FastVectorHighlighter also give. Instead the snippet has no mark, because FieldOffsetStrategy rewrites the query again on the hit's own segment or a one-document view of it, where 'the' counts as rare and becomes required (+the +fox), so the hit no longer matches; the result changes with segment layout alone, and MoreLikeThisQuery with its default minDocFreq rewrites there to an empty query, so its hits are never highlighted.
rows.area: highlighter / UnifiedHighlighter WEIGHT_MATCHES path (FieldOffsetStrategy) with statistics-dependent query rewrites (CommonTermsQuery, MoreLikeThisQuery)

rows.title: Since 10.3.0, a field-sorted top-n search whose query fully matches a segment without deletions (MatchAllDocsQuery, a range covering the segment) no longer skips non-competitive documents: the comparator's initial all-docs competitive iterator reports a run to maxDoc through UpdateableDocIdSetIterator.docIDRunEnd, so DenseConjunctionBulkScorer hands the whole segment to the collector in one collectRange call (performance regression; results correct)
rows.summary: You run a top-10 search sorted on a LONG field with points (or a STRING field with a terms index, or a LONG field with a skip index) with MatchAllDocsQuery over one 100,000-doc segment that has no deletions. You expect Lucene to skip non-competitive documents, as 10.2.2 does for this exact search (about 1,000-1,750 docs collected) and as a TermQuery matching the same docs still does on main (about 8,200). Instead main and every release since 10.3.0 collect all 100,000 docs, because the comparator's competitive iterator starts as all docs and since #14532 reports a run up to maxDoc, so DenseConjunctionBulkScorer collects the whole segment in one collectRange call before the comparator narrows the iterator; the top hits are still correct, only the pruning is lost.
rows.area: search / sorting (TopFieldCollector competitive iterator x DenseConjunctionBulkScorer collectRange shortcut)

rows.title: smartcn: the double-hashing step of BigramDictionary (AbstractDictionary.hash2, an operator-precedence slip) is 0 for some Chinese word + ASCII or Latin-1 punctuation pairs, so each such bigram lookup re-reads one slot 402,136 times (about 0.7 ms instead of about 0.1 us) and SmartChineseAnalyzer analyzes ordinary prose 2-7x slower and text dense in such pairs 67x-174x slower, with unchanged tokens
rows.summary: You analyze Chinese text written with ASCII punctuation, for example '我们要发展经济和文化,加强法律,增加资金,继续努力,共同进步.', with the default SmartChineseAnalyzer; its bigram dictionary is an open-addressing hash table with double hashing, so you expect each bigram frequency lookup to take a handful of probes and the text to cost about as much as the same sentence with full-width punctuation, which gives the same tokens. Instead AbstractDictionary.hash2 computes ((33h + d) & 0xFF) and then ((33h + d) >> 8), because '+' binds tighter than '&' and '>>' (AbstractDictionary.java:195-196), so the probe step is always in [0, 288] and is 0 for some keys whose last char is below U+0100, such as '对@,' or '文化@,'; when such a key's home slot holds another bigram, BigramDictionary.getBigramItemIndex (BigramDictionary.java:213-233) re-reads that same slot until i reaches PRIME_BIGRAM_LENGTH = 402,137 and then returns 'not found'. The tokens stay correct, but that sentence repeated 100 times takes about 220 ms of CPU instead of about 2.6 ms (85x on main), and 1x with a one-line guard.
rows.area: analysis-smartcn / HHMM segmenter bigram dictionary (BigramDictionary.getBigramItemIndex, AbstractDictionary.hash2; reached through SmartChineseAnalyzer and HMMChineseTokenizer)

You expect 0 hits, which is what the inner query alone returns. Instead the search throws an AssertionError with assertions enabled, or ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException 'Index 0 out of bounds for length 0' without them, because rewrite() hands its empty top-n list to a helper that reads the first entry; the kNN query's own rewrite checks for this case and returns MatchNoDocsQuery.

rows.title: SortRescorer (and Expression#getRescorer) never rewrites its Sort against the searcher, unlike IndexSearcher#search(Query, int, Sort): sorts that need a rewrite throw, and a legacy query() function sort silently uses the default Similarity
rows.summary: You rescore the top hits with new SortRescorer(sort) or expression.getRescorer(bindings) and expect the same order and sort values that IndexSearcher#search(query, n, sort) gives for the same Sort on the same searcher, because DoubleValuesSource tells clients to rewrite against the searcher and IndexSearcher does that for sorted searches. Instead SortRescorer builds its collector from the Sort as given (SortRescorer.java:48-49): for a sort on new QueryValueSource(q, 0).asDoubleValuesSource() on a ClassicSimilarity searcher the hits come back in BM25 order with BM25 values (doc0=0.1468, doc1=0.1246 instead of doc1=1.0, doc0=0.894), and ValueSource sort fields or fromQuery sorts throw. Passing sort.rewrite(searcher) inside rescore() fixes every case.
rows.area: search / rescoring (SortRescorer; expressions ExpressionRescorer inherits it)

A DoubleValuesSource.fromQuery sort throws 'This DoubleValuesSource must be rewritten' from both helpers, and a ValueSource#getSortField sort throws 'SortField needs to be rewritten'.

rows.title: GroupingSearch#search never rewrites its group sort or within-group sort against the searcher, unlike IndexSearcher#search(Query, int, Sort): sorts that need a rewrite throw, and a legacy query() function sort silently orders groups, group documents and group heads with the default Similarity

Rewriting both Sorts against the searcher at the start of groupByFieldOrFunction and groupByDocBlock fixes every case.

rows.title: A kNN query built with a null KnnSearchStrategy, documented as 'the default strategy will be used', throws NullPointerException when a seeded HNSW search runs (SeededKnnVectorQuery, or the optimistic re-entry pass when a segment is re-entered)
rows.summary: You build a kNN query with an explicit null search strategy, for example new KnnFloatVectorQuery(field, target, k, null, null), whose javadoc says 'If null, the default strategy will be used', and run it wrapped in SeededKnnVectorQuery, or as a plain query on a multi-segment index where the optimistic second pass re-enters a segment. You expect the same hits as with KnnSearchStrategy.Hnsw.DEFAULT. Instead Lucene wraps the null in KnnSearchStrategy.Seeded for the seeded HNSW walk, and Seeded.nextVectorsBlock() calls originalStrategy.nextVectorsBlock() without a null check, so the search throws 'NullPointerException: Cannot invoke KnnSearchStrategy.nextVectorsBlock() because this.originalStrategy is null' (KnnSearchStrategy.java:169) and returns nothing.
rows.area: search / kNN query layer (KnnSearchStrategy.Seeded, optimistic re-entry pass, SeededKnnVectorQuery)

rows.title: JoinUtil's numeric join on Float or Double throws 'values are out of order' when the from side has two or more distinct negative values
rows.summary: You build JoinUtil.createJoinQuery("fromF", false, "toF", Float.class, fromQuery, searcher, ScoreMode.None) where the from documents store -1 and -2 in a FloatDocValuesField and the to documents index FloatPoint -1, -2 and 3, and expect a query that matches the two to documents with -1 and -2, because the javadoc lists Float and Double as supported numeric types with no sign restriction. Instead createJoinQuery throws IllegalArgumentException 'values are out of order: saw [40 7f ff ff] before [3f ff ff ff]' (that is, -1 before -2; releases before 10.4.0 show an UnsupportedOperationException raised while that message is built), and Double and every scoring ScoreMode fail the same way. The cause is that JoinUtil sorts the collected Float/Double join values as raw IEEE bits in signed-long order, which for negative numbers is the reverse of numeric order, and streams them in that order into PointInSetQuery / PointInSetIncludingScoreQuery, which require strictly ascending points.
rows.area: join / JoinUtil numeric (point-based) query-time join

rows.title: UnifiedHighlighter throws MaxBytesLengthExceededException when a TermInSetQuery's toString() is longer than 32766 bytes (for example 886 UUID-like ids), because PassageScorer groups match labels in a BytesRefHash
rows.summary: You search with a TermInSetQuery of 886 UUID-shaped ids (or 4,000 short terms) on a field indexed with offsets, get the hit, and call the default UnifiedHighlighter's highlight() on that field, expecting the snippet with the matching id in <b>, as the equivalent ConstantScoreQuery over a SHOULD BooleanQuery of the same ids gives. Instead highlight() throws BytesRefHash$MaxBytesLengthExceededException 'bytes can be at most 32766 in length; got 32786' from PassageScorer.score. For a multi-term set query the highlighter labels each match with the query's whole toString(), which lists every term, and PassageScorer groups those labels in a BytesRefHash, which rejects entries over 32766 bytes; 885 ids (a 32,749-byte toString()) still work.
rows.area: highlighter / UnifiedHighlighter passage scoring (PassageScorer match labels)

rows.title: Weight#matches of Intervals.atLeast, or iterating the Matches it returns, throws IllegalStateException (AssertionError with -ea) for a matching document once an Intervals.or(...) source has run out of intervals, so default UnifiedHighlighter highlighting of such a query fails
rows.summary: You index 'a c b a' and ask Weight#matches, or the default UnifiedHighlighter, for Intervals.atLeast(2, term a, term b, or(term c, term d)); you expect the positions [0,1] [1,2] [2,3] that the query's own interval iterator returns and that the control atLeast(2, a, b, c) gives, and the snippet 'a c b a'. Instead iterating the Matches throws IllegalStateException (AssertionError with -ea) from DisjunctionIntervalIterator.currentOrd and the whole highlight call fails, also for the query text 'fn:atLeast(2 a b fn:or(c d))': atLeast's match callback asks every source for its sub-matches, including the or() source that has no interval left and that atLeast has already dropped. For some documents Weight#matches itself throws (atLeast(2, or(c, d), b, phrase(a, b)) on 'c a b').

rows.title: UnifiedHighlighter's re-analysis offset strategies decode every extracted query term as UTF-8, so a binary term (for example a binary StringField id reached with requireFieldMatch=false) makes highlighting throw
rows.summary: You build UnifiedHighlighter.builder(null, analyzer).withFieldMatcher(f -> true) (the documented requireFieldMatch=false switch) and call highlightWithoutSearcher("body", query, "hello world", 1) with query = SHOULD id: + SHOULD body:hello, and expect "hello world", because binary terms are documented Lucene input (StringField's BytesRef constructor), the id term can never occur in analyzed text, the byte-based POSTINGS and TERM_VECTORS offset sources do not throw on such a term, and the classic Highlighter and the default field matcher highlight the same query. Instead the call throws: the default MemoryIndexOffsetStrategy passes the raw term bytes to Automata.makeStringUnion, which is documented to take UTF-8 and throws IllegalArgumentException 'Invalid UTF8 header byte: 0x9f', and TokenStreamOffsetStrategy (withPassageRelevancyOverSpeed(false)) calls BytesRef.utf8ToString, which throws AssertionError with -ea and ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException with -da. The same happens through highlight() on a stored text field without offsets, and on a field with offsets when the query also has a prefix clause on it.

rows.title: Default UnifiedHighlighter (WEIGHT_MATCHES) rebuilds the query's Weight on its own single-leaf searcher, so JoinUtil global-ordinals joins throw IllegalStateException and ParentChildrenBlockJoinQuery reads its top-level parent id as a segment-local id

rows.title: DateRecognizerFilterFactory gives every filter it creates the same java.text.DateFormat, so an analyzer built from it throws NumberFormatException or ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException when several threads analyse text at the same time
rows.summary: You build an analyzer with CustomAnalyzer from a whitespace tokenizer and the dateRecognizer filter (datePattern=yyyy-MM-dd, locale=en-US) and analyse text such as '2024-01-15 foo 1999-12-31' from four threads at once, as IndexWriter does with its indexing threads. You expect every thread to get the same date tokens as a single-threaded run, because Analyzer gives each thread its own set of token stream components. Instead some analyses throw NumberFormatException ('multiple points', 'For input string: ""') or ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException, because DateRecognizerFilterFactory creates one java.text.DateFormat, which is not thread-safe, and create() passes that same instance to the filter of every thread.

rows.title: SimplePatternTokenizer's String constructors do not determinize the regexp (and ignore determinizeWorkLimit), so valid patterns such as ab|ac or http|https throw 'please determinize the incoming automaton first'
rows.summary: You build a tokenizer with new SimplePatternTokenizer("ab|ac") (or the three-argument String constructor with a determinizeWorkLimit) and expect a working tokenizer for any valid RegExp, as the constructors' javadoc ('See RegExp for the accepted syntax'), the sibling SimplePatternSplitTokenizer and both factories give you. Instead the constructor throws IllegalArgumentException('please determinize the incoming automaton first'): it passes new RegExp(regexp).toAutomaton() unchanged to the Automaton constructor, which rejects non-deterministic automata, and since Lucene 10.0 (LUCENE-10010) RegExp no longer determinizes its result. The determinizeWorkLimit argument is never used.

rows.title: SortedSetDocValues faceting throws NullPointerException from getTopChildren/getAllChildren for a dimension that is configured hierarchical but has no document in the reader, instead of returning null as the Facets javadoc says (regression since 9.3.0)

rows.title: FreeTextSuggester.lookup throws AssertionError (-ea) or NullPointerException (-da) when a word the analyzer removed (a stop word) comes right before the key's last word, because it reads the count of the filler-only context '_', which the n-gram model never stores (lookup('the w') with the default constructor and EnglishAnalyzer)

rows.title: ComplexPhraseQueryParser: a fuzzy word inside a phrase ("big cat~") throws IllegalArgumentException 'Unknown query type ... ConstantScoreQuery' at search time when the field holds a short term within the edit distance (here 'a') among the top expansions, and so does an interior ^0, because a zero-boost clause rewrites to BoostQuery(ConstantScoreQuery) and the span conversion unwraps only BoostQuery
rows.summary: You index 'big cat' and 'a', parse "big cat~" with ComplexPhraseQueryParser (a fuzzy word inside a phrase is the syntax its class javadoc and upstream tests use) and count the hits, expecting 1. Instead IndexSearcher.count throws IllegalArgumentException 'Unknown query type:org.apache.lucene.search.ConstantScoreQuery': the fuzzy expansion 'a' (2 edits from 'cat', length 1) gets boost 0, BoostQuery.rewrite turns a zero-boost clause into BoostQuery(ConstantScoreQuery(q), 0), and the span conversion strips only BoostQuery, so it meets a ConstantScoreQuery and rejects it. rows.title: kNN and vector-similarity query constructors keep the caller's query-vector array instead of copying it, so a caller that refills that buffer before the query runs silently changes which documents the query matches and what it is equal to
rows.summary: You decode a query embedding into a scratch float[], build new KnnFloatVectorQuery(field, scratch, k), decode the next embedding into the same array, build a second query and OR the two; you expect each query to search the vector it was built from, as TermQuery does when built from a reused BytesRef. Instead both queries now search the second vector and compare equal, so the OR returns 1 hit instead of 2 (the neighbour of the first vector is lost); the same holds for KnnByteVectorQuery, KnnFloat16VectorQuery, the three vector-similarity queries and the join DiversifyingChildren*KnnVectorQuery classes. The constructors store the caller's array itself (VectorUtil.checkFinite returns its argument) and search, equals and hashCode all read it, although getTargetCopy() returns a copy precisely so that callers cannot reach that array.
rows.area: search / vector queries (KnnFloat/Byte/Float16VectorQuery, Float/Byte/Float16VectorSimilarityQuery; join DiversifyingChildren*KnnVectorQuery)

rows.title: MemoryIndex stores binaryValue() instead of IndexableField.storedValue(), so stored StringField/KeywordField values built from a String and stored IntField/LongField/FloatField/DoubleField values come back as binary bytes (Document.get and numericValue() return null), and a StoredField built from a StoredFieldDataInput is dropped (released since 9.6.0)
rows.summary: You build a MemoryIndex from a document with StringField("id", "doc-1", Store.YES), a KeywordField(String, Store.YES) or an IntField("count", 5, Store.YES) and read it back through storedFields().document(0), expecting the same stored values IndexWriter returns, since MemoryIndex has supported stored fields since 9.5.0 (#11999). Instead MemoryIndex stores the field's binaryValue() rather than its storedValue(): the String comes back as its UTF-8 bytes, so Document.get("id") returns null, and the numbers come back as their sortable point bytes (IntField 5 as [80 00 00 05]), so numericValue() returns null. A StoredField built from a StoredFieldDataInput is not stored at all; the BytesRef constructors and plain StoredField values are unaffected.
rows.area: memory / MemoryIndex stored fields

rows.title: IndexingChain.invertTerm adds 2 to the field length for each single-term (InvertableType.BINARY) value, so untokenized DOCS_AND_FREQS fields with norms get double the norm and a lower BM25 score
rows.summary: You index one value in an untokenized field whose FieldType has DOCS_AND_FREQS and norms enabled, once through a plain Field (TokenStream inversion) and once through the single-term path (a Field subclass whose invertableType() returns BINARY, or an IndexWriter#addBatch BinaryColumn or DictionaryColumn). You expect the same field length and norm, 1 per value, because FieldInvertState#getLength is the 'total number of terms in this field' and a BINARY value is documented as a single value with term frequency one. Instead IndexingChain.invertTerm adds 2 to the length for every value, so the norm is 2 (2k for k values) and the BM25 score of the identical document drops (0.082873434 to 0.058813408 in the repro), while the postings still record freq 1 per value.
rows.area: index / indexing chain (single-term BINARY inversion, norms)

rows.title: MemoryIndex ignores TermFrequencyAttribute, so FeatureField values and custom term frequencies are indexed as frequency 1 and their postings frequencies, term statistics, norms and scores differ from IndexWriter's (Lucene Monitor's single-document matching included)
rows.summary: You add a document with FeatureField("features", "pagerank", 10f), or a tokenized DOCS_AND_FREQS field whose TokenStream sets TermFrequencyAttribute (for example DelimitedTermFrequencyTokenFilter on 'a|7'), to a MemoryIndex and expect its postings, statistics and scores to equal those of the same document in a one-document IndexWriter index, as they do for ordinary fields. Instead MemoryIndex.storeTerms never reads the attribute and counts every token as frequency 1: FeatureField.newLinearQuery scores 4.5918E-41 instead of 10.0, newSaturationQuery with the pivot 10 scores exactly 0.0 (MemoryIndex.search's 'no match' value) for a document that matches, and a term with custom frequency 7 reports freq 1, sumTotalTermFreq 1 and a lower BM25 score. Lucene Monitor inherits it (since 8.6.0): the same FeatureField document scores 10.0 in a two-document batch (IndexWriter path) and 4.5918E-41 when matched alone (MemoryIndex path).

rows.title: MemoryIndex drops the final position increment of each value of a multi-valued field (and the gaps after leading values with no tokens), so phrase and other position queries disagree with IndexWriter, including Lucene Monitor's single-document matching
rows.summary: You add a document whose text field has two values, 'quick the' and 'fox', to a MemoryIndex with an analyzer that removes the stop word 'the', and expect the positions of a one-document IndexWriter index: IndexWriter keeps the hole the removed trailing 'the' leaves (TokenStream.end() reports it as a final position increment), so 'fox' is at position 2 and the phrase "quick fox" does not match. MemoryIndex.storeTerms never adds that final increment, puts 'fox' at position 1 and matches the phrase; the reverse also happens (the input of upstream's TestIndexWriter#testStopwordsPosIncHole matches a phrase on IndexWriter but not on MemoryIndex), and values that produce no tokens before the first token skip the position and offset gaps ([the | quick fox] with gap 100: IndexWriter quick at position 101, offsets 4-9; MemoryIndex position 0, offsets 0-5). Lucene Monitor inherits it: a stored phrase query matches the document when it is matched alone (MemoryIndex path) but not when the same document is in a two-document batch (IndexWriter path).

rows.title: An unfrozen MemoryIndex does not reset its lazily built per-field state when more values are added to a field after a read, so later searches miss the new terms or points, throw ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException, return unsorted SORTED_NUMERIC values or score with stale norms
rows.summary: You add a value to a field of a MemoryIndex that is not frozen, search it, add more values to the same field, and search again; you expect the second search to see everything, like a MemoryIndex built from the same adds, because freeze() is the only documented point after which no data may be added and adding the same field several times is supported. Instead the field keeps the read state that the first read built lazily and nothing ever resets (the sorted term ids, the point min/max and 1D order, the sorted doc values, the cached norm): a term or IntPoint added later is silently not found (for example IntPoint p=2, search, p=1: newExactQuery(p, 1) no longer matches), SORTED_NUMERIC values come back as 2, 1, the score uses the old norm, or the search throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException from the corrupted term dictionary (an AssertionError under -ea for some inputs).
rows.area: memory / MemoryIndex lazy per-field read state (sorted terms, points and doc-values preparation, norms)

rows.title: MemoryIndex keeps a SORTED or BINARY doc value as a shallow BytesRef clone of the caller's bytes, so if the caller later overwrites its byte array the value the MemoryIndex reports silently changes (regression of LUCENE-10405, since 9.1.0)

It reports "tan", with no error: since 9.1.0 MemoryIndex stores BINARY and SORTED doc values as BytesRef.clone(), which BytesRef documents as a shallow copy that shares the caller's byte array. SORTED_SET values, indexed terms, points and vectors are still copied into the MemoryIndex's own storage.

rows.title: MemoryIndex takes omitNorms from the first instance of a field name, so a doc-values or stored-only instance added first gives an omitNorms text or keyword field norms and different scores than IndexWriter
rows.summary: You put a document into a MemoryIndex in which a SortedDocValuesField (or a NumericDocValuesField or a StoredField) named title comes before Field("title", "quick brown fox") with a type that omits norms, and expect what IndexWriter gives for the same document: no norms for title and the score of a field without norms. Instead MemoryIndex builds the field's FieldInfo from the first instance, whose type reports omitNorms=false, so title gets norms and TermQuery title:fox scores 0.13076457 instead of IndexWriter's 0.1798013; with the text field first, MemoryIndex agrees with IndexWriter. The same happens for a multi-valued StringField with a SortedSetDocValuesField before each value, and in the mirror order (a non-indexed type with omitNorms=true before a text field with norms) MemoryIndex drops the norms instead.

rows.title: StoredFieldDataInput(ByteArrayDataInput) takes the input's end position as its length, so a ByteArrayDataInput that does not start at position 0 (a slice at a non-zero offset, or a partly read input) silently stores extra trailing bytes, or makes addDocument fail and close IndexWriter
rows.summary: You add new StoredField(name, new StoredFieldDataInput(new ByteArrayDataInput(bytes, offset, len))) and expect the stored value to be exactly those len bytes, because the record's length is documented as 'the length of the data input'. The convenience constructor copies ByteArrayDataInput.length(), which is the end position offset + len, so for an 8-byte slice at offset 4 of a 16-byte array the document stores 12 bytes, the slice plus the next 4, with no error. If fewer bytes than the offset follow the slice, the stored fields writer reads past the array, addDocument throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException and IndexWriter closes itself.
rows.area: index / stored fields (StoredFieldDataInput: DataInput-backed StoredField values, #14213)

rows.title: JoinUtil's single-valued term and numeric joins treat a 'from' document without a join value as if it had the empty term or the number 0, so they also return the 'to' document whose key is empty or 0 and add the value-less documents' scores to it (since 4.0.0)
rows.summary: You join orders to customers with JoinUtil.createJoinQuery("customer", false, "id", fromQuery, searcher, scoreMode), or the numeric overload with Integer.class, where fromQuery matches two orders and only one of them has a customer key, and expect only that order's customer back, because the javadoc returns the to-documents that 'have the same terms' as the matching from-documents. Instead the order without a key is collected as if its key were the empty term (term join) or 0 (numeric join), so the customer whose id is "" or 0 is returned too, in every ScoreMode, and a real customer 0 also gets the key-less order's score (Max 5.0 instead of 1.0). The same call with multipleValuesPerDocument=true on the same single-valued field, and the global-ordinals join, return the correct answer.

rows.title: JoinUtil's numeric join reads a DoubleField or FloatField from field as raw IEEE bits, so a join on a negative value silently misses its matches
rows.summary: You index one from document with DoubleField("from", -5.0) and one to document with DoubleField("to", -5.0), and count JoinUtil.createJoinQuery("from", true, "to", Double.class, new MatchAllDocsQuery(), fromSearcher, ScoreMode.None) on the to index; you expect 1, because the javadoc lists floats and doubles and allows SORTED_NUMERIC from fields, which is what DoubleField writes. You get 0 with no error: DoubleField stores NumericUtils.doubleToSortableLong(-5.0), but JoinUtil's multi-valued Float/Double path decodes the stored long as raw IEEE bits (Double.longBitsToDouble, Float.intBitsToFloat), so the join looks up -0.8749999999999999 instead of -5.0. Positive values are unaffected because their sortable and raw bits are the same, and FloatField fails the same way.
rows.area: join / JoinUtil numeric (point-based) query-time join: multi-valued Float/Double decode of core DoubleField/FloatField doc values

rows.title: A scoring JoinUtil term join re-sorts its shared BytesRefHash on every non-scoring createWeight, so one join query used by a scoring search and a count() at the same time silently returns too few hits (known: #13018 / open PR #13019, partial overlap) (released since 10.5.0)
rows.summary: You build one join query with JoinUtil.createJoinQuery(..., ScoreMode.Max) and, as the IndexSearcher thread-safety and Query-reuse javadoc allow, run searcher.search(join, n) in one thread while another thread runs searcher.count(join); every scoring search should return all 20,000 joined documents. Instead each count() builds a TermsQuery whose constructor sorts the join's BytesRefHash again in place, rewriting the ids array that the scoring search iterates as its ords, so the scoring search silently returns fewer documents (18,120 to 19,023 of 20,000 in the recorded runs).
rows.area: join / JoinUtil term join (TermsIncludingScoreQuery, TermsQuery)

rows.title: JoinUtil numeric score joins (PointInSetIncludingScoreQuery, ScoreMode Max, Min, Avg or Total) ignore the boost, so BoostQuery, boosted BooleanQuery clauses and BooleanQuery's folding of duplicate clauses leave their scores unchanged; the part of GITHUB#12388 that was left out
rows.summary: You build a numeric query-time join with JoinUtil.createJoinQuery("fromId", false, "toId", Integer.class, fromQuery, searcher, ScoreMode.Max) (or Min, Avg, Total), wrap it in BoostQuery(join, 10), and expect each to-document's score to be 10 times its join score, as BoostQuery documents ('the produced scores will be boosted by boost'), as the string-field join over the same documents does, and as GITHUB#12388 ('JoinUtil queries were ignoring boosts', 9.8.0) made every other JoinUtil join do. Instead the PointInSetIncludingScoreQuery that JoinUtil returns never reads the boost passed to createWeight and its scorer returns the raw join score, so BoostQuery(join, 10) scores 0.13076457 instead of 1.3076458, and BooleanQuery[SHOULD join, SHOULD join], which Lucene rewrites to one clause with boost 2, scores 1x instead of 2x. rows.title: SpanNotQuery with a negative post (or dist) drops every include span that follows the last exclude span in a document, because NO_MORE_POSITIONS - post overflows int

Nested as spanNear([spanNot(a, b, 0, -1), c], 0, true), the document no longer matches at all (count 0 instead of 1).

rows.title: Closing a clone or full-length slice of a multi-chunk MMapDirectory input nulls the MemorySegment[] it shares with the original and other clones, which then fail with NullPointerException
rows.summary: You open a file with MMapDirectory that is larger than one mmap chunk, make a clone (or a slice that covers the whole file), close that clone and keep reading the original; you expect the original and the other clones to be unaffected, as they are for single-chunk files, for partial slices, for other directories and on 10.0.0. Instead the clone shares the original's array of memory segments and close() fills that array with nulls, so the original's next access to another chunk throws NullPointerException, from then on the never-closed original reports AlreadyClosedException, and closing it afterwards leaves its arena and the file mapping open. You expect the next read to re-read the failed region or to throw again. Instead, since 8.6.0 refill() has already marked the buffer as holding the new region before readInternal failed, so the next reads silently return up to one buffer of bytes from the previous region (or zeros), and one transient failure while opening a healthy index makes DirectoryReader.open report it as corrupt.

rows.title: JapaneseCompletionFilter expands a reading into every combination of romaji spellings with no bound, so 24-32 kana (for example 32 x "ン", or 32 x "し" in QUERY mode) throw OutOfMemoryError inside one incrementToken() call

rows.title: SimpleQueryParser drops the '+', '|', quote or '(' typed directly after a phrase slop, so "a b"~2+c parses as phrase OR c and "a b"~2|c (default operator AND) as phrase AND c
rows.summary: You parse "a b"~2+c with SimpleQueryParser and expect what its javadoc defines, the near query AND c, just as "a b"~2 +c and "a b"+c parse. Instead the parser skips the character right after the slop digits, so the '+' is lost and you get phrase OR c (on an index with the documents 'a b' and 'c' it matches 2 documents instead of 0); the same happens to '|' ("a b"~2|c becomes AND under default MUST), to a quote ("a b"~2"c d" becomes the phrase OR c OR d) and to '(' ("a b"~2(c+d) loses its group). The cause is an off-by-one in consumePhrase: parseFuzziness already stops on the delimiter that ends the slop, and the unconditional '++state.index' that was written to step over the closing quote then skips that delimiter.

rows.title: StandardQueryParser with setMultiFields normalizes field-less prefix and wildcard terms with field null, before the multi-field expansion, so per-field analyzers are ignored for them (and a PerFieldAnalyzerWrapper over Map.of throws NullPointerException)

rows.title: SpanContainingQuery and SpanWithinQuery miss documents and spans when the little query's spans end out of order (for example a SpanOrQuery of a longer near clause and a shorter clause that can occur inside it): their single forward pass tests only the current little span (containing) or never goes back to a big span it skipped (within), so a later, shorter little span inside a big span is never tried

Instead both return nothing, because the little spans arrive sorted by start as [0,3) and then [1,2) (their ends go down, which the Spans contract allows), and each query's single forward pass gives up after testing only the longer little span [0,3): containing moves on to the next big span, within moves the big iterator past [0,2) and never comes back. The same happens in a sentence-scoped search for '(apple NEAR/5 pie) OR cake' on 'bos apple cake eos bos pie eos' (the 'cake' sentence is missed only because 'apple ... pie' crosses into the next sentence), so adding a word to a document or an OR alternative to the query can remove a hit; nothing extra is ever returned.

rows.title: AnalyzingSuggester and FuzzySuggester count skipped duplicate copies of a surface form toward maxSurfaceFormsPerAnalyzedForm, so distinct lower-weighted surface forms are silently dropped
rows.summary: You build an AnalyzingSuggester or FuzzySuggester from entries in which one text repeats, for example 256 documents with 'Apple iPhone' and one with 'apple iphone', which a lowercasing analyzer maps to the same analyzed form, and you expect both surface forms back, because maxSurfaceFormsPerAnalyzedForm (default 256) is documented as the 'maximum number of surface forms to keep for a single analyzed form' and repeated copies are documented as removed. build() increments its per-analyzed-form counter and applies the limit before it checks whether the surface form was already seen, so every skipped copy still uses up a slot: lookup('apple ip') returns only [Apple iPhone], and with a limit of 2 the entries a/10, a/5, A/3 give [a/10] instead of [a/10, A/3]. rows.title: Util.TopNSearcher returns a queued final output without calling acceptResult, so FreeTextSuggester spends a top-N slot on a word it already predicted and drops a better suggestion

rows.title: ConcatenateGraphFilter without a token separator (and so CompletionAnalyzer with preserveSep=false) silently drops a concatenated path around a position hole, because Automaton.addEpsilon copies from a dest state that its own first addTransition sorts and reduces in place (AssertionError with -ea)

With assertions disabled you get only 'playwho', so a suggestion reached through the synonym (prefix 'playth') is silently missing; with -ea the filter throws an AssertionError in Automaton.getNextTransition. The cause is Automaton.addEpsilon: it copies the transitions of a state that is still being built, and its own first addTransition to the other state sorts and shrinks that state in place mid-copy, so some transitions are copied twice and others never.

rows.title: With an INT index sort, merges order documents by the full 64-bit doc value while flush, sorted search and CheckIndex use its low 32 bits, so merging a value outside the int range writes a segment that violates its declared index sort (CheckIndex at level 2 or higher rejects it) and sorted searches that terminate early on the index sort return wrong top hits (a regression in 8.2.0)

CheckIndex (level 2 or higher) then reports 'segment has indexSort=<int: "s"> but docID=1 sorts after docID=2' and a top-1 search sorted by the index sort returns b instead of a, while before the merge the same index is clean and returns a.

rows.title: FloatVectorSimilarityQuery and ByteVectorSimilarityQuery with traversalSimilarity == resultSimilarity (the 3- and 4-argument constructors: the plain ones in 9.10.0-10.4.0, the deprecated Explicit classes in 10.5.2 and 10.6.x, removed on main and branch_11x by #16965) silently drop documents whose similarity is exactly resultSimilarity, because the collector's minCompetitiveSimilarity() rises to the inclusive threshold and every searcher treats an equal score as not competitive

Once a hit at the threshold is collected, ExplicitVectorSimilarityCollector.minCompetitiveSimilarity() = min(traversalSimilarity, maxSimilarity) equals the inclusive result threshold, and both the exhaustive scan (a 64-vector batch is collected only if its best score > minCompetitiveSimilarity()) and the graph search (score >= nextUp(minCompetitiveSimilarity())) treat an equal score as not competitive; the one-line fix returns min(nextDown(traversalSimilarity), maxSimilarity).

rows.title: Reordering merges (BPReorderingMergePolicy) silently break document blocks written before Lucene 9.9, because IndexWriter's reorder guard reads the unrecorded LeafMetaData#hasBlocks flag as 'no blocks'
rows.summary: You have an index with document blocks (children followed by their parent, added with IndexWriter#addDocuments) that was written by Lucene 9.8 or earlier, open it with a current Lucene, and force-merge it through BPReorderingMergePolicy. You expect the merge to leave the blocks alone, because since 9.11 IndexWriter lets a merge reorder documents only when there are no blocks or a parent field identifies them, and such an old index cannot have a parent field. Instead the guard trusts LeafMetaData#hasBlocks, which was never recorded before 9.9 and reads false for those segments, so the reorderer renumbers the documents one by one and interleaves the blocks, with no exception and a clean CheckIndex, while the same documents written by 9.9.2 are left intact.

rows.title: A binary doc-values update whose term matches many documents copies its value once per matched document into one int-sized buffer when it is applied, so at 2^31 bytes in one segment (about 2^30 for the first update of a field in a packet) commit throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException (AssertionError with -ea) and IndexWriter closes itself, losing the update and every uncommitted document (every release since 4.8.0)

Instead, applying the update appends a full copy of the value for every matched document to one int-addressed BytesRefBuilder, which overflows at 2^31 bytes: commit throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException (with -ea, AssertionError 'size must be positive (got -2147483648): likely integer overflow?'), IndexWriter treats it as a tragic event and closes itself, and both the update and the extra uncommitted document are gone. On 7.7.0 and later a lone update fails at half that size (1,100 documents x 1 MiB) because of the linked bug that applies the first update of a field twice, and ordinary value sizes suffice too (530,000 documents x 4 KiB).

rows.title: While a document sits buffered in an idle in-memory segment, IndexWriter keeps every later delete and doc-values update reachable, uncounted by ramBytesUsed() and never released by the RAM buffer, so a delete-only or update-only stream grows the heap until OutOfMemoryError (default config, since 4.0.0)
rows.summary: You add a document to an IndexWriter with the default config and then, without a commit, NRT reopen or flush(), send a long stream of deleteDocuments(Term) or doc-values update calls, and expect the heap held by those buffered deletes to stay around the RAM buffer, because the writer applies and drops them each time they reach it, as it does when nothing is buffered. Instead the in-memory segment that holds the one document keeps a pointer into the shared delete queue that moves only when that segment indexes again or is flushed, so every later delete stays reachable after it was applied. IndexWriter.ramBytesUsed() does not count it, nothing flushes that segment, and the heap grows with every call until OutOfMemoryError. The same happens without any delete-only run when two threads indexed at once and then one thread keeps calling updateDocument: the second in-memory segment stays idle and pins every later delete term until the active segment fills the RAM buffer and is flushed.

rows.title: ParallelCompositeReader picks a field's owner separately in each segment, so when two parallel indexes share a field, the later index's values show through in segments where the earlier index has no document with that field, and hits change after a merge

rows.title: ICUTokenizer loses a supplementary character (an emoji, a CJK Extension B ideograph) whose surrogate pair straddles the end of its 4096-char read chunk in text with no whitespace, because refill() cuts the pair in half
rows.summary: You index a long Chinese paragraph with no spaces or line breaks through the stock ICUTokenizer, and it contains an emoji or a rare ideograph such as U+20000; you expect that character to be a token wherever it falls, as it is one position earlier or later. Instead, when its first UTF-16 half is the last char of the tokenizer's 4096-char read chunk, refill() gives the word breaker a chunk that ends in a lone high surrogate and starts the next chunk with the lone low surrogate; both halves get rule status 0 and are skipped, so the character is in no token. A TermQuery for it finds 0 documents instead of 1, with no error.

rows.title: ArabicStemmer removes at most one prefix, so after it strips the conjunction waw it never strips the article that follows (wa+bi-al-, wa+li-l-, wa+ka-al-, wa+fa-al-), unlike the light10 algorithm ArabicAnalyzer documents
rows.summary: You index Arabic text with the stock ArabicAnalyzer, whose javadoc says it implements light stemming 'as specified by' the light10 paper; that paper removes a leading waw ('and') first and then a definite article, so 'وبالكتاب' ('and with the book') should stem to 'كتاب' ('book'), like 'الكتاب' and 'بالكتاب'. Instead ArabicStemmer.stemPrefix scans one list (the six articles, then waw) and returns after the first match, so once it has removed the waw it never tries the articles: 'وبالكتاب' becomes 'بالكتاب' and 'وللطلاب' becomes 'للطلاب'. A TermQuery for the analyzed form of 'الكتاب' then finds 0 of 1 documents that contain only 'وبالكتاب', with no error.

rows.title: HindiAnalyzer runs HindiNormalizationFilter before HindiStemFilter, so the 20 of HindiStemmer's 67 suffix rules that are spelled with a long vowel or candrabindu (-ती -tī, -ाती -ātī, -ेगी -egī, -ोगी -ogī, -ूंगा -ūṁgā, -ाई -āī, -नी -nī, ...) can never fire, and feminine and future verb forms keep part of their suffix: 'खाती' (khātī) is indexed as 'खात' (khāt) while 'खाता' (khātā) and 'खाते' (khāte) give 'खा' (khā)
rows.summary: You index Hindi text with the stock HindiAnalyzer; one document says 'वह रोज़ खाती है' (vah roz khātī hai, 'she eats every day') and a query says 'खाता' (khātā, the masculine form of 'eats'). You expect both forms to stem to 'खा' (khā), because HindiStemmer implements Ramanathan and Rao's light stemmer, whose suffix list contains -ती (-tī), and Lucene's own TestHindiStemmer pins खाती (khātī) -> खा next to खाता -> खा. Instead HindiAnalyzer runs HindiNormalizationFilter first, which folds the long vowel signs ी (ī) and ू (ū), the long vowels आ (ā), ई (ī) and ऊ (ū) and the candrabindu ँ (m̐) to their short or plain forms, so the 20 suffix rules spelled with those characters can never match: 'खाती' is indexed as 'खात' (khāt) and the query finds nothing, with no error.

rows.title: TeluguAnalyzer folds the long vowel sign ో (ō) to ొ (o) before TeluguStemFilter runs, so TeluguStemmer's locative '-లో' (-lō) rule can never fire, and 'నగరంలో' (nagaramlō, 'in the city') is indexed as 'నగరంల' (nagaramla) instead of 'నగరం' (nagaram)
rows.summary: You index Telugu text with the stock TeluguAnalyzer; a document says 'నగరంలో' (nagaramlō, 'in the city') and a query says 'నగరం' (nagaram, 'city'). rows.title: BengaliNormalizer's khio rule tests U+09BF (vowel sign I) instead of U+09B7 (SSA), so the common conjunct ক্ষ (KA+HASANTA+SSA) is never folded to KHA / KA+KHA as the rule comment and the cited paper say, and the malformed KA+HASANTA+VOWEL SIGN I is folded instead

Its normalizer has a rule labelled 'Khio (Ka + Hoshonto + Murdorno Sh)' and says it implements a cited paper, which folds the conjunct ক্ষ (KA+HASANTA+SSA) to খ (KHA) at the start of a word and to কখ (KA+KHA) elsewhere, so ক্ষমা should normalize to খমা. Instead the rule's condition compares the third character with U+09BF (BENGALI VOWEL SIGN I) instead of U+09B7 (BENGALI LETTER SSA), one hex digit off, so the rule never fires on real text: ক্ষমা becomes ক্সমা and পরীক্ষা becomes পরিক্সা (only the separate 'All sh' rule applies, SSA to SA), while the malformed sequence KA+HASANTA+VOWEL SIGN I is folded instead (ক্িমা becomes খমা), with no error.

rows.title: BengaliNormalizer's medial-visarga rule copies the next character before that character is folded, so SHA, SSA, NNA (and the other one-to-one folded letters) survive after a visarga and those spellings stop matching the SA/NA spelling the same normalizer conflates everywhere else
rows.summary: You index or query Bengali text with the stock BengaliAnalyzer or BengaliNormalizationFilter. Its normalizer folds SHA (শ) and SSA (ষ) to SA (স) everywhere and turns a medial visarga (ঃ) into a copy of the next letter (gemination), so নিঃশব্দ ('silent'), নিঃষব্দ and নিঃসব্দ should all become নিসসব্দ (SA SA), just as the class's other gemination rule turns বিশ্ব into বিসস in an upstream test. Instead the visarga branch copies the next character before the loop has folded it and never revisits the copy, so নিঃশব্দ becomes নিশসব্দ (SHA SA) and নিঃষব্দ becomes নিষসব্দ (SSA SA): the three spellings give three different terms, and a document written with one of them is not found by a query written with another, with no error.

rows.title: StandardTokenizer (StandardAnalyzer's tokenizer) and UAX29URLEmailTokenizer misapply the UAX #29 Hebrew quote rules WB7a-WB7c next to other word characters: a Hebrew letter + ASCII apostrophe swallows a following digit or underscore (BET'2 is one term), an ASCII apostrophe after a Hebrew letter that ends a mid-word chain is dropped (HE.SHIN' -> HE.SHIN), and a word with an ASCII quotation mark between Hebrew letters is split when it also contains a mid-word '.', ':' or quote (ALEF.TSADI"LAMED, TAV"ALEF.BET)
rows.summary: You index Hebrew text with the stock StandardAnalyzer, whose StandardTokenizer says it implements the UAX #29 word-break rules, among them WB7a-WB7c, which keep an ASCII apostrophe after a Hebrew letter (BET') and an ASCII quotation mark between two Hebrew letters (TAV"ALEF) inside a word, and you expect them to combine with the other rules as the annex and ICU do: BET'2 gives [BET', 2], HE.SHIN' gives [HE.SHIN'], and TAV"ALEF.BET and ALEF.TSADI"LAMED are single words. Instead the grammar writes 'Hebrew letter + quote' as a separate piece that may be glued to any following piece but cannot continue a letter chain, so BET'2 becomes one term (a search for 2 misses the document), HE.SHIN' loses the apostrophe, and the quoted words are split into [TAV"ALEF, BET] and [ALEF.TSADI, LAMED]. StandardTokenizer and UAX29URLEmailTokenizer behave the same, with no error.
