rows.title: WikipediaTokenizer silently drops Chinese and Japanese text inside wiki markup (links, categories, headings, bold/italics, templates, citations, external-link labels): its grammar has a CJ token rule only for plain text, and every markup state matches ALPHANUM only
rows.summary: You tokenize Chinese or Japanese wiki text with WikipediaTokenizer, for example '[[日本]]', '[[Category:日本]]', '== 日本 ==' or "x '''東京''' y", and expect the text inside the markup to become tokens, as it does for Latin and Korean text in the same markup ('[[Japan]]', '[[한국]]') and for Chinese/Japanese plain text ('日本' gives 日|<CJ> and 本|<CJ>). Instead every Chinese/Japanese character inside markup is skipped without an error: '[[日本]]', '[[Category:日本]]', '== 日本 ==' and '<ref>日本</ref>' give no token at all, '[http://example.org 日本]' gives only the URL, and "x '''東京''' y" gives x and y, with y typed bold. The cause is the grammar: its only CJ token rule is for plain text (WikipediaTokenizerImpl.jflex:201), while all nine markup lexical states have a token rule for ALPHANUM only and ignore every other character (:219-309), and the CJ character class is disjoint from ALPHANUM.
rows.area: analysis-common / wikipedia: WikipediaTokenizer (JFlex grammar lexical states, WikipediaTokenizerImpl.jflex)

rows.title: JapaneseNumberFilter and KoreanNumberFilter, meeting a stacked token after two or more numerals, drop the numerals after the first and keep the first one's text in the number buffer, where it is prepended to the next number (十一石二鳥と五 ends in 15 instead of 5) (known: #11398 / #11397, offsets only) (released since 6.0.0 / 8.2.0)
rows.summary: You run 十一石二鳥と五 through JapaneseTokenizer (search mode, compounds kept, the configuration of the upstream TestJapaneseNumberFilter) and JapaneseNumberFilter, and expect the separate number 五 at the end to normalize to 5, since stacked tokens are documented to be left untouched. Instead the filter re-emits 十, drops 一, keeps 十 in its number buffer and later emits 十 + 五 = 15; KoreanNumberFilter has the same code.

rows.title: JapaneseNumberFilter and KoreanNumberFilter honour KeywordAttribute only on the token that starts a number, so a keyword-protected numeral word directly after a numeral token is merged into the number and normalized (三 + protected 京一 gives 30000000000000001, the name 오경일 with 경일 protected gives 50000000000000001) (released since 6.0.0 / 8.2.0)
rows.summary: You put SetKeywordMarkerFilter in front of JapaneseNumberFilter (or KoreanNumberFilter) to protect a word made of numeral characters, as the class javadoc suggests for the name 京一, and expect that word to come out unchanged wherever it occurs. That works when the word starts a number (田中京一 gives 田中, 京一, the upstream testName), but the filter checks the keyword flag only on the first token of a number and accepts every following numeral token without looking at it, so a protected word right after a numeral is appended to the number: 社員の三京一 gives the single token 30000000000000001 (offsets 3-6) instead of 3 and 京一, and the Korean name 오경일 (tokens 오 / 경일, 경일 protected) gives 50000000000000001. No error is raised; a TermQuery for the protected word then misses the document (executed).
rows.area: analysis / kuromoji and nori number filters (JapaneseNumberFilter, KoreanNumberFilter: KeywordAttribute inside a number composition)

rows.title: TeeSinkTokenFilter: a sink never clears attributes that only its own filter chain adds (SinkTokenStream.incrementToken() calls restoreState() without clearAttributes()), so a keyword marker or StemmerOverrideFilter before a stemmer on a sink silently leaves every token after the first protected word unstemmed

Instead it gets [the, quick, foxes, jumped]: the sink replays each token with restoreState() but never calls clearAttributes(), and the KeywordAttribute that only the sink's chain added is not in the tee's captured states, so once 'quick' is marked as a keyword every later token stays marked and is not stemmed. Nothing is thrown; a query for stemmed:fox finds nothing.

rows.title: Nori UserDictionary picks a user noun's right context id (last syllable with a final consonant, without one, or not Hangul) from the last character of the whole entry line instead of the noun, so a trailing space or an inline comment ('학교 # memo') changes how the word after the noun is analysed
rows.summary: You load a nori user dictionary whose line for the noun 학교 ('school') ends with a space, or carries an inline comment as in '학교 # memo' (the parser deletes '#' to the end of the line but keeps the space before it), and expect the same analysis as with the plain line '학교', because the parser splits the line on whitespace and gets the same noun with no segmentation. Instead UserDictionary.java:94 takes the noun's right context id, which tells the tokenizer whether the noun's last syllable ends in a consonant, from the last character of the whole line, here the space, so the noun gets the generic id and the word after it is analysed differently: on 9.12.3 '학교이' gives 이/VCP with '학교' but 이/J with '학교 ', and KoreanAnalyzer turns '학교가방을 샀다' into [학교][가방][사] with '학교' but [학교][방][사] with '학교 ', losing the term 가방 ('bag'). The two line forms disagree in every release from 7.4.0 to 10.6.0 (10.6.0 by reading) and on main (main: '학교이' gives 이/JKS vs 이/VCP, '사람이나' gives [사람] vs [사람][이]), and a shorter segmentation such as '세종시 세종' takes the id from 종 (final consonant) instead of 시 (none) in the same way.
rows.area: analysis / nori UserDictionary (right context id of user nouns, used by the Viterbi connection costs)

rows.title: ICUFoldingFilter folds the Tajik/Abkhaz letter CHE WITH DESCENDER (ҷ U+04B7, Ҷ U+04B6) to the different letter ABKHASIAN CHE (ҽ U+04BD) instead of to CHE (ч U+0447), so Tajik text is not found by the same words typed with plain ч
rows.summary: You index Tajik text such as 'Ҷумҳурии Тоҷикистон' with ICUFoldingFilter, whose javadoc lists 'Diacritic removal (including stroke, hook, descender)', and expect the same words typed without the Tajik letters, 'Чумхурии Точикистон', to find it, as they do for ҳ, қ and the other WITH DESCENDER letters. Instead the hand-copied line '04B7>04BC' in DiacriticFolding.txt maps CHE WITH DESCENDER to ABKHASIAN CHE, so ҷ and Ҷ are indexed as ҽ while the query's ч stays ч, and the query gets 0 hits. In Abkhaz, which uses ҷ, ҽ and ҿ as three separate letters, all three fold to ҽ and match each other.

rows.title: SoraniNormalizer checks for a word-final HEH before it removes trailing directional marks, so a word ending in HEH followed by RLM, LRM or ALM keeps HEH (U+0647) instead of becoming AE (U+06D5) as the class javadoc says
rows.summary: You analyze Sorani Kurdish text with the stock SoraniAnalyzer or SoraniNormalizationFilter. The normalizer's javadoc says a word-final HEH (U+0647) is converted to AE (U+06D5) and that formatting characters such as directional controls are removed, so خانه ('house') followed by an invisible right-to-left mark should normalize like خانه itself, to خانە. Instead the HEH rule asks 'is this the last character?' while the trailing mark is still in the buffer, and the mark is deleted only later in the same pass, so خانه+RLM (and +LRM, +ALM) becomes خانه with a plain HEH and no longer matches خانە, with no error.

rows.title: COSINE vectors whose float32 squared norm underflows pass validation and give Inf/NaN scores or poison OSQ segments
rows.summary: You index, or query with, a non-zero COSINE float vector whose float32 squared norm is 0 or subnormal. You expect it to be rejected like an all-zero vector or to score sensibly. Instead it is accepted: on the default codec it scores +Inf/NaN, a NaN batch maximum hides 64 neighbouring documents and CheckIndex falsely fails; on OSQ one such vector makes the segment centroid NaN, so kNN returns 0 hits and every merge fails.
rows.area: codecs / vectors
rows.affected: 9.0.0 to 10.5.2 (33 releases) and main [exec]; the 0-hit searches and the CheckIndex failure from 10.4.0, the quantized merge failure from 10.2.0

rows.title: When IndexWriter#addBatch rejects a vector part-way through a DENSE vector column, the core HNSW and scalar-quantized vectors writers fall out of step with a flat field writer that keeps the default addDenseValues (new in #16734): the next commit closes the IndexWriter, or with assertions off commits a corrupt HNSW graph or misaligned COSINE quantization state
rows.summary: You index vectors with IndexWriter#addBatch and a DENSE VectorColumn into an HNSW or scalar-quantized format whose per-field flat storage is your own FlatFieldVectorsWriter (plugged in through the public Lucene99FlatVectorsWriter strategyFactory constructor, without overriding addDenseValues), and Lucene rejects the third vector of a 3-document batch (NaN, or a zero vector with COSINE). You expect what the addDenseValues javadoc and Lucene's own recovery test promise: the batch's documents are deleted, the writer stays open and consistent, and the next commit writes a readable, searchable segment. Instead the flat writer has kept the batch's first two vectors while the HNSW wrapper added no graph nodes for them (and the scalar-quantized wrapper no centroid sums or COSINE magnitudes), so with assertions on the next commit fails ('Level 0 expects to have all nodes', or an assertion in the quantizer) and closes the writer, losing every uncommitted document, and with assertions off it commits an HNSW graph that cannot be read back (EOFException, CheckIndex at level 2 or more fails, a kNN query for a document's own vector returns another document), or the COSINE quantized writer throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException at commit or commits NaN codes so that kNN finds no document of the segment.
rows.area: codecs / vectors writers (Lucene99HnswVectorsWriter and Lucene104ScalarQuantizedVectorsWriter field writers over a flat field writer; columnar addBatch DENSE vector bulk path)

rows.title: DirectoryTaxonomyWriter gives an existing category a second ordinal after an addCategory call fails with an IOException while the writer opens its near-real-time reader, because the cache stays marked complete or the reader stays stale
rows.summary: You index facet categories with a default DirectoryTaxonomyWriter; one addCategory call throws an IOException because the writer could not open its near-real-time reader (for example on the call whose new category makes the 4000-entry cache evict), and you keep using the writer, as IndexWriter allows after a non-fatal exception. You expect a later addCategory of a category that is already in the taxonomy to return its existing ordinal, as TaxonomyWriter.addCategory promises. Instead the writer still trusts its cache as complete (or its old reader), indexes the category again and returns a new ordinal (l0: 4001 instead of 1; a retried 'new': 14 instead of 13), and commit() persists one label under two ordinals, so its facet counts are split between them.
rows.area: facet / taxonomy writer (DirectoryTaxonomyWriter.addCategory exception safety: cacheIsComplete and reader-manager freshness after a failed near-real-time reader open)

rows.title: DirectoryTaxonomyWriter.replaceTaxonomy is not failure-atomic: if addIndexes throws, the taxonomy is already emptied but the writer keeps its old ordinal counter and cache, so later addCategory calls and the next commit or close() store an empty or broken taxonomy
rows.summary: You call replaceTaxonomy on a DirectoryTaxonomyWriter to swap in a rebuilt taxonomy, the call throws (in the repro an IOException while a file of a valid, closed source is read, or IndexNotFoundException because the source holds no index), and the application then closes the writer as usual or keeps using it. You expect the failed call to leave the taxonomy that the writer and its last commit describe, so that addCategory returns 'its existing ordinal' for an existing category (TaxonomyWriter.java:53) and the root keeps ordinal 0. Instead replaceTaxonomy has already emptied the internal index with deleteAll() while the writer keeps its old ordinal counter, cache and parent arrays: close() commits a taxonomy of size 0 (expected 4), a kept-open writer returns ordinal 2 for dim/a although the commit no longer has it and stores a new label with ordinal 4 at docID 0, and over a main index that still refers to the old ordinals the facet counts a=2 b=1 x=1 y=1 come out as x=3 y=2.
rows.area: facet / taxonomy writer (DirectoryTaxonomyWriter.replaceTaxonomy failure path: deleteAll before addIndexes, writer state reset only on success)

rows.title: UpgradeIndexMergePolicy rewrites the old segments its delegate declines with its own plain OneMerge, which a wrapping delegate never sees, so IndexUpgrader (or UpgradeIndexMergePolicy) with a SoftDeletesRetentionMergePolicy inside silently purges the soft-deleted documents the retention policy must keep
rows.summary: You configure soft deletes with SoftDeletesRetentionMergePolicy("soft", MatchAllDocsQuery::new, new TieredMergePolicy()), which must keep every soft-deleted document, and upgrade a one-segment index written by Lucene 10.5.2 (10 visible plus 3 soft-deleted documents) with new IndexUpgrader(dir, thatConfig, false).upgrade(). You expect the segment to be rewritten in the current format with all 13 documents, exactly as happens when the same index has two old segments. Instead TieredMergePolicy treats the lone segment as already merged, UpgradeIndexMergePolicy rewrites it with its own 'merge remaining ones into new segment' OneMerge that the retention policy never wraps, and the 3 retained documents are purged with no error (maxDoc 13 -> 10; partial retention queries lose their documents the same way).

rows.title: SoftDeletesRetentionMergePolicy.keepFullyDeletedSegment ignores the wrapped policy when its retention query has a non-null scorer with no hits, so a fully soft-deleted segment that the wrapped policy keeps (for example the soft-deleted documents an inner SoftDeletesRetentionMergePolicy retains) is dropped at commit
rows.summary: You wrap one SoftDeletesRetentionMergePolicy (retention query 'keep everything') in a second one whose retention query is LongPoint seq:[3 TO 4], index two documents with seq 1 and 10, soft-delete both through updateDocValues and commit; you expect both soft-deleted documents to stay in the index (maxDoc 2), as they do with the inner policy alone, because the outer policy asks the wrapped policy whenever its own query matches nothing. Instead the commit drops the segment (maxDoc 0): keepFullyDeletedSegment asks the wrapped policy only when the query's scorer is null, and a range that lies between the segment's values gives a non-null scorer with no hits, for which it answers 'do not keep' by itself. A range outside the segment's values (null scorer) keeps the documents, so two queries that both match nothing give opposite answers.
rows.area: index / merge policies (SoftDeletesRetentionMergePolicy: keeping fully deleted segments)

rows.title: DirectoryTaxonomyWriter gives every later category a wrong ordinal after IndexWriter rejects one enriched ordinal document: the rejected document keeps its docID but the writer's ordinal counter does not advance
rows.summary: An application adds its own fields to taxonomy ordinal documents with ReindexingEnrichedDirectoryTaxonomyWriter (or an enrichOrdinalDocument override), IndexWriter rejects one category's field (for example a term over 32766 bytes or a vector of a different dimension), addCategory throws IllegalArgumentException, and the application skips that category and keeps going. You expect only that category to be missing and every later addCategory to return the category's ordinal, the one a taxonomy reader reports for it, with an existing category keeping its ordinal (TaxonomyWriter.addCategory). Instead IndexWriter keeps the rejected document as a deleted document that still uses up a docID while the writer's ordinal counter does not move, so every later category gets an ordinal one below its docID: readers resolve it to the previous category (even the rejected label), facet counts land under the wrong labels or throw ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException or CorruptIndexException, and a reopened writer returns 3 instead of 2 for a category that already exists.

rows.title: ReindexingEnrichedDirectoryTaxonomyWriter.reindexWithNewOrdinalData is not failure-atomic: when the ordinal-data appender throws part-way, the taxonomy has already been deleted and only partly re-added, and a following close() commits it, so main-index ordinals lose their labels or are handed to other categories
rows.summary: You call reindexWithNewOrdinalData on a ReindexingEnrichedDirectoryTaxonomyWriter with a new ordinal-data appender, the appender throws for one category (in the repro an IllegalStateException on d/b; an appender that reads the last label component throws on the root category, which reaches the appender only during a reindex), and the application then closes the writer as usual. You expect the method's promise 'The ordinals themselves will be preserved, so the caller does not need to update references to them in the main index' to hold, or at least the last committed taxonomy to survive the failed call. Instead the method has already deleted the whole taxonomy and re-added only the categories before the failing one, and close() commits that: the taxonomy shrinks from 5 to 3 categories, d/b and d/c resolve to -1 while main-index documents still carry their ordinals 3 and 4, and if the writer is kept in use new categories take those ordinals, so facet counts a=2 b=1 w=1 z=1 come out as w=3 z=2 with no error (other layouts make FastTaxonomyFacetCounts throw ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException).

rows.title: addIndexes(CodecReader) from a reader whose term vectors list a field with zero terms writes a term-vector chunk that the default codec cannot read back, and every later merge that re-encodes the segment closes the IndexWriter
rows.summary: You copy an index with IndexWriter.addIndexes(CodecReader...) through a reader that removes some terms consistently from the postings and the term vectors (CheckIndex at its strictest level accepts this reader), so one document's term-vector field is left with zero terms. You expect the new segment to read back and merge like any other, as the postings do (the postings writer simply drops the emptied field). Instead the default term-vector format writes per-field AvgCharsPerTerm floats that its own reader does not expect, so when the emptied field stores offsets the other documents of the chunk throw 'offset 0 is invalid' on read, and because the reader lists the emptied field but returns null for it, the next merge that re-encodes the segment fails with 'Wrong number of values added' and closes the IndexWriter, on every retry.

rows.title: With an index sort, a document whose sort field is indexed without doc values (for example only as a StringField) is accepted by addDocument, and the next flush throws IllegalStateException and closes the IndexWriter, losing every uncommitted document (since 8.6.0)
rows.summary: You configure an index sort on a field, for example new Sort(new SortField("sort", SortField.Type.STRING)), and add a document that carries that field only as a StringField, without the SortedDocValuesField that sorting reads, before any committed document has the field. You expect addDocument to reject the document up front, as it has rejected a doc-values field of the wrong type since LUCENE-8441 (7.5.0), or the field to count as missing. Instead addDocument accepts it, and the next flush or commit throws IllegalStateException 'unexpected docvalues type NONE for field 'sort' (expected=SORTED). Re-index with correct docvalues type.' and closes the IndexWriter, so every document added since the last commit is lost.

rows.title: Mixing SuggestField and ContextSuggestField under one field name is accepted by addDocument and rejected only when the completion postings are written at flush or merge, where the IllegalArgumentException is tragic: the IndexWriter closes and loses every uncommitted document, and two cleanly committed segments of the two types make every merge that combines them close the writer again, also in a new writer (released since 5.3.0)
rows.summary: You index a SuggestField document and a ContextSuggestField document under the same field name; addDocument accepts both, and the suggest module's design (LUCENE-6459) says such a mix is rejected with an IllegalArgumentException, so you expect an input error that leaves the writer and your other documents alone. Instead the type is compared only in CompletionFieldsConsumer while postings are written, so the IllegalArgumentException 'single field name has mixed types' fires inside flush or merge, where IndexWriter treats every exception as tragic: the writer closes and drops every uncommitted document. If the two types landed in different segments, both commit cleanly, but every merge that combines them closes the writer, also in any new writer, until you delete all documents of one type.
rows.area: suggest / document suggester (CompletionFieldsConsumer type check at flush and merge; core flush and merge abort paths)

rows.title: IndexWriter accepts doc-values updates of a field that a custom index-sort key reads (such as a BinarySortField subclass that derives its key from another doc-values field), so the segment keeps its old order while still declaring the index sort: CheckIndex rejects it, sorted searches that terminate early return wrong top hits, and merges carry the disorder forward
rows.summary: You configure an index sort with a BinarySortField subclass whose key is derived from another doc-values field (sort by the numeric field price, ties broken by the binary field sku, declared on sku), index a(5), b(7), c(8), and then change c's price to 1 with updateNumericDocValue; you expect the writer either to reject the update, as it rejects an update of sku itself ('cannot update docvalues field involved in the index sort'), or to keep the segment sorted. Instead the update is accepted, the segment stays in the order a, b, c while still declaring the sort, CheckIndex reports 'segment has indexSort=<binary: "sku"> but docID=1 sorts after docID=2', and a top-1 search sorted by the index sort returns a instead of c because it stops at the first non-competitive document. The cause is that IndexWriterConfig#setIndexSort protects only the SortField#getField names, while a custom index sort may read any field.

rows.title: addIndexes(CodecReader...) takes the reserved document count and the new segment's soft-delete count from the readers before OneMerge#wrapForMerge, so a merge whose wrapper removes documents over-reserves documents and, with soft deletes, commits a wrong soft-delete count that can drop live documents or corrupt a later merge (since 9.9.0)
rows.summary: You install a merge policy whose findMerges(CodecReader...) returns a OneMerge whose wrapForMerge removes documents (its javadoc allows this: 'add/remove fields or documents'), for example to drop soft-deleted or expired documents while importing, and call IndexWriter.addIndexes(CodecReader...); you expect the writer to account for the documents the merge actually wrote, as the regular merge path does. Instead addIndexes reserves the live-document count of the unwrapped readers, so getPendingNumDocs stays too high for the rest of the writer session, and with soft deletes it stores the unwrapped readers' soft-delete count in the new segment, so DocStats.numDocs under-counts and CheckIndex (level 2 and up) reports 'actual soft deletes: 0 but expected: 1'. With assertions off, later operations then build on that wrong count: a live document can vanish from the committed index, and a later ordinary forceMerge can merge two documents into one doc ID (a search for one returns the other) or fail with CorruptIndexException.
rows.area: index / IndexWriter addIndexes(CodecReader...) accounting (reserveDocs, addIndexesReaderMerge soft-delete count) x MergePolicy#findMerges(CodecReader...) / OneMerge#wrapForMerge

rows.title: Range facet counters add every hit the fastMatchQuery rejects to FacetResult.value, so the dimension total is too high and depends on the segment layout
rows.summary: You build a range facet counter (LongRangeFacetCounts or DoubleRangeFacetCounts on a single-valued field or values source, or a range-on-range counter) with a fastMatchQuery that removes only hits outside every range, which is what it is for, and read FacetResult.value. You expect the same dimension total as without the fastMatchQuery: the number of hits that fall into at least one range. Instead each segment adds all of its hits up front but subtracts only the documents the fastMatchQuery let through, so the hits it rejected stay in the total (3 instead of 1 in the minimal repro, while the range count is 1), and the same documents and query give 3 in one segment and 1 in two.
rows.area: facet / range and range-on-range facet counts (FacetResult.value with a fastMatchQuery)

rows.title: Taxonomy facets: for a sub-path of a single-valued hierarchical dimension, FacetResult.value from getTopChildren/getAllChildren is the sum of the children, so documents labeled at the sub-path itself are left out, while getSpecificValue, drill-down and SortedSetDocValues faceting count them
rows.summary: You index two documents with taxonomy facets in a dimension configured only with setHierarchical("Publish Date", true): one labeled Publish Date/2010 and one labeled Publish Date/2010/10. Both documents have a value for the path Publish Date/2010 (a DrillDownQuery on it matches 2 and getSpecificValue("Publish Date", "2010") returns 2), so FacetResult.value of getTopChildren(10, "Publish Date", "2010") and getAllChildren("Publish Date", "2010") should be 2, as its javadoc ('Total number of documents containing a value for this path') and SortedSetDocValues faceting with the same config say. FastTaxonomyFacetCounts returns 1 for both: for a single-valued dimension it adds up the path's immediate children and never uses the path's own rolled-up count, so the document labeled at 2010 itself is left out.

rows.title: Grouping collectors never ask for scores on behalf of their group selector, so DoubleRangeGroupSelector or LongRangeGroupSelector over a score-dependent source (e.g. DoubleValuesSource.SCORES) groups every hit by the placeholder score of a non-scoring search (0 in every repro) when no sort or reducer needs scores, or when AllGroups/AllGroupHeads runs alone (since 8.6.0)
rows.summary: You group hits into score ranges, for example with new DoubleRangeGroupSelector(DoubleValuesSource.SCORES, new DoubleRangeFactory(0, 1, 10)), and sort the groups by a field, expecting each hit in the range of its own score, which is what the same search returns with the default relevance group sort (three ranges, [1,2) = {0, 3}, [2,3) = {1}, [3,4) = {2, 4}, in the repro). Instead GroupingSearch returns one empty group [0,1) (LongRangeGroupSelector: LongRange(0, 1)), and AllGroupsCollectorManager on its own reports one range instead of three, because the grouping collectors take their ScoreMode only from their sorts or reducer, so the query runs without scores and the selector, which reads the collector's Scorable through DoubleValuesSource.fromScorer, sees the placeholder score 0 for every hit. GroupSelector has no way to say that it needs scores; a GroupSelector#needsScores() hook (true for the range selectors when their source needs scores), ORed into the four collectors' score modes, fixes it.
rows.area: grouping / GroupSelector score needs (FirstPass, SecondPass/TopGroups, AllGroups, AllGroupHeads collector score modes)

rows.title: Grouping by a function such as sum(a,b) puts documents without a value into several null groups, one per partial value, because the function value fillers keep the partial value when exists is false (AssertionError with -ea; second-pass NullPointerException since 10.4.0)
rows.summary: You index two documents with a float doc-values field a = 5 and a = 7 and no field b, and group all documents with GroupingSearch by the function sum(a, b). You expect one null group holding both documents, because sum(a, b) does not exist for either of them and the grouping javadocs put documents without a group value 'in a null group'. You get two groups that both read as null, one per partial sum, because FloatDocValues' value filler stores the partial sum as the value of a MutableValueFloat whose exists flag is false, against MutableValueFloat's documented rule that a missing value must be 0; with -ea the search throws AssertionError in MutableValueFloat.hashCode, and since 10.4.0 a group limit of 1 makes the second pass throw NullPointerException.

rows.title: Grouping by if() or def() puts a document for which the function has no value into the real 0.0 group instead of the null group, because the default FunctionValues value filler never sets MutableValue.exists (def() since 4.0.0, if() since 5.0.0)
rows.summary: You index two documents, one with the numeric doc-values field x = 0 and one without x, and group all documents with GroupingSearch by the function if(1, x, x), which returns x and reports exists() == false exactly when x is missing. You expect two groups, one for x = 0 and a null group for the document without x, which is what grouping by x itself gives and what the grouping javadoc ('instead of putting them in a null group') describes. You get one group, 0.0 with exists() == true, holding both documents, because IfFunction and DefFunction inherit the default FunctionValues value filler, which writes floatVal(doc) = 0 and never sets MutableValue.exists, so the flag keeps its initial value true.

rows.title: SortedSetDocValues faceting builds its facet tree from the byte order of the encoded paths, so a label or dimension name that equals a sibling's name followed by a character below U+001F (TAB, CR, LF, or the U+001E that FacetsConfig writes when it escapes U+001E/U+001F) moves a label's children under that sibling, or drops a whole dimension or one of its labels
rows.summary: You index hierarchical SortedSetDocValues facets, for example cat/shoes/red in one document and cat/'shoes<TAB>' (an untrimmed input) in another, and expect getTopChildren(10, 'cat', 'shoes') to return red=1, as taxonomy faceting does for the same labels. Instead it returns null and the leaf 'shoes<TAB>' reports red=1: the encoded paths sort by byte, a character below the path delimiter U+001F places 'shoes<TAB>' between 'shoes' and 'shoes U+001F red', and the reader state infers parent, child and sibling links only from the order of consecutive ordinals. The same happens for a label that contains U+001F or U+001E (FacetsConfig escapes both with U+001E), and dimension names such as 'd' next to 'd<TAB>' make dimension d disappear or, for a flat multiValued + requireDimCount dimension, lose one label, all with no error.
rows.area: facet / SortedSetDocValues faceting (DefaultSortedSetDocValuesReaderState: the per-dimension DimTree and OrdRange built from the field's ordinals in term order, shared by SortedSetDocValuesFacetCounts and ConcurrentSortedSetDocValuesFacetCounts)

rows.title: FacetsConfig writes the bare dimension term of a flat multiValued + requireDimCount SortedSetDocValues dimension without escaping it, so a dimension name containing U+001F or U+001E is read back as a different path: the dimension loses one label and reports that label's count as its own, a phantom dimension appears, a name with two U+001F makes facet-state construction throw for the whole field, and (-ea) a name ending in U+001E throws AssertionError
rows.summary: You index three documents under a flat SortedSetDocValues facet dimension named 'color<U+001F>code', configured multiValued and requireDimCount, with labels {x, y}, {x} and {z}, and expect getTopChildren to return value=3 with x=2, y=1, z=1, as taxonomy faceting does for the same name. Instead it returns value=2 with only y=1 and z=1, and getAllDims also shows a phantom dimension 'color' with label 'code'. FacetsConfig escapes U+001F/U+001E in every facet term except this one bare dimension term (FacetsConfig.java:494), while the reader decodes every term as if it were escaped, so the raw term is read back as a different path.

rows.title: DirectoryTaxonomyWriter indexes a facet label that contains an unpaired surrogate a second time, under a new ordinal, once its writer cache has been filled from the taxonomy index, because the cache compares the label's Java string while the index stores its UTF-8 term with the surrogate replaced by U+FFFD; the taxonomy then holds two categories with one path and facet counts for that value are split
rows.summary: You add a facet value with an unpaired surrogate, for example FacetField("dim", "x\uD83D") built from a string cut inside an emoji, in one writer session and the same value again in a later session, with the default DirectoryTaxonomyWriter; you expect the existing ordinal back, as TaxonomyWriter.addCategory promises, and one facet entry with count 2. Instead, once the second session has filled its cache from the index (after 11 new categories by default), the cached key is the stored form "x\uFFFD", the original string misses, the writer trusts its now complete cache and indexes the label again (ordinal 14 instead of 2), so the facet result shows x\uFFFD (1) twice. The duplicate stays in the taxonomy for good; within one fresh session the writer likewise gives "x\uD83D" and "x\uFFFD" ordinals 2 and 3, although the taxonomy reader resolves both to 2.

rows.title: RandomSamplingFacetsCollector.amortizeFacetCounts caps each amortized label count at the docFreq of the label's drill-down term, so with a non-default FacetsConfig DrillDownTermsIndexing (NONE on any dimension, or FULL_PATH_ONLY / DIMENSION_AND_FULL_PATH on a hierarchical dimension) it silently returns 0, or a value below the true count
rows.summary: You sample facet counts with RandomSamplingFacetsCollector on a dimension whose FacetsConfig skips drill-down terms (DrillDownTermsIndexing NONE, or FULL_PATH_ONLY / DIMENSION_AND_FULL_PATH on a hierarchical dimension), call amortizeFacetCounts to scale the sampled counts up to estimates of the full counts, and expect what the default indexing gives: about sampled / samplingRate per label, capped by the label's real count. Instead each label is capped at reader.docFreq of its drill-down term, which these modes do not index at all (docFreq 0) or index only for the documents whose full path is that label, so a label seen 15 times in a 10% sample comes back as 0 and a label on 1000 documents comes back as 500. Nothing fails, and in the same FacetResult the amortized dimension total (for example 1000) no longer matches its children (all 0).
rows.area: facet / sampling (RandomSamplingFacetsCollector.amortizeFacetCounts x FacetsConfig drill-down term indexing)

rows.title: DrillDownQuery.clone() shares the per-dimension BooleanQuery.Builder objects with the original, so adding a value to a dimension both copies already constrain changes what the other copy matches (released since 4.7.0)
rows.summary: You build a DrillDownQuery that restricts color=red, call clone(), and add color=blue to the clone (or to the original), expecting the copy you did not touch to keep matching only red, as clone() and the upstream testClone imply. Instead both copies match red OR blue: the clone shares each dimension's internal BooleanQuery.Builder with its source, and add() on an existing dimension appends a SHOULD clause to that shared builder in place. Since 9.0 a copy that was already searched keeps a cached snapshot and shows the leaked value only after its own dimension changes again (then 3 hits where 2 are correct), and the two copies stay equals() with the same hashCode while they match different documents.
rows.area: facet / DrillDownQuery (clone() and the per-dimension BooleanQuery.Builder state)

rows.title: PositiveScoresOnlyCollector inherits its wrapped collector's scoreMode() and setWeight(), so a wrapped sort-by-field TopFieldCollector or TotalHitCountCollector silently gets the wrong hits or count instead of exactly the hits that score > 0 (score-mode leg since 5.1.0, count leg since 9.3.0)
rows.summary: You wrap a collector in PositiveScoresOnlyCollector, whose javadoc says it 'makes sure only documents with scores > 0 are collected' and which Collector's overview says 'wraps any other Collector', and expect the wrapped collector to see exactly the matches that score > 0: in the repro 6 hits for the TermQuery g:y with a TopFieldCollector sorted by a field, and counts 0 for (f:x)^0 and 6 for (g:y)^2 OR (f:x)^0 with a TotalHitCountCollector. Instead the sort-by-field collector receives 0 hits and the counter reports 12 for both queries, because PositiveScoresOnlyCollector, which reads scorer.score() itself, inherits two FilterCollector hooks: scoreMode() reports the wrapped collector's no-score mode, so the search builds scorers without scores and the > 0 test reads placeholder values (0 for TermQuery, so real hits are dropped; a constant positive value for FunctionScoreQuery over MatchAllDocsQuery, so zero-score hits get through), and setWeight() hands the wrapped TotalHitCountCollector the Weight, so it counts whole segments with Weight#count and never goes through the filter. Overriding scoreMode() to return COMPLETE when the wrapped collector needs no scores, and passing on a Weight whose count() returns -1 (or not forwarding setWeight at all), fixes both.
rows.area: core / search collectors (PositiveScoresOnlyCollector; FilterCollector scoreMode and setWeight forwarding; TotalHitCountCollector Weight#count shortcut)

rows.title: ValueSource#asLongValuesSource() always reports needsScores() false although it feeds the passed scores to the wrapped ValueSource, so a sort on a score-dependent ValueSource (for example a function over ValueSource.fromDoubleValuesSource(DoubleValuesSource.SCORES)) runs without scores and silently returns sort values not computed from the real score (all 0 in the two-document repro) and hits in doc-id order (since 6.4.0)
rows.summary: You build a ValueSource that depends on the score, new LinearFloatFunction(ValueSource.fromDoubleValuesSource(DoubleValuesSource.SCORES), 1000f, 0f) (1000 x score), expose it with asLongValuesSource() and sort a TermQuery's hits on its getSortField(true); you expect the hits in score order with sort values 1000 x score ([doc1=132, doc0=68]), because LongValuesSource#needsScores is documented as 'Return true if document scores are needed to calculate values' and asDoubleValuesSource() of the same ValueSource answers true. Instead the long bridge (ValueSource.WrappedLongValuesSource) answers needsScores() false (ValueSource.java:156) although its getValues hands the passed scores to the wrapped source under the 'scorer' context key (:130-131); LongValuesSortField forwards that false to Sort.needsScores(), so the search collects without scores and every hit gets sort value 0, in doc-id order ([doc0=0, doc1=0]), with no exception.
rows.area: queries / function queries (ValueSource to LongValuesSource bridge: ValueSource#asLongValuesSource, WrappedLongValuesSource.needsScores, consumed by LongValuesSource#getSortField)

rows.title: DocValuesStatsCollectorManager merges LongDocValuesStats and SortedLongDocValuesStats (lucene/misc) through their wrapping long sum(), so on a searcher with an executor mean(), variance() and stdev() are silently wrong (for example about 8x too small, or negative) once a slice's long sum or the reduce's running long sum passes Long.MAX_VALUE, as 6 epoch-nanosecond timestamps do, while the same search without an executor is exact
rows.summary: You index ordinary large long values, for example 24 epoch-nanosecond timestamps in 6 segments, compute LongDocValuesStats (or SortedLongDocValuesStats) with DocValuesStatsCollectorManager exactly as its class javadoc shows on new IndexSearcher(reader, executor), and expect mean() = 1.7616096115E18, 'the mean of all values of the field' and the value the same search without an executor returns, because merge() promises 'the combined statistics of both segments as if they had been collected together'. Instead mean() is 2.243809386908707E17 (about 8x too small; other slicings give a negative mean) and variance() and stdev() are wrong too, because merge() recomputes the combined mean as (sum + otherSum) / count from long sums that have wrapped past Long.MAX_VALUE, while serial collection keeps a running mean that never reads the sum. Only sum() is documented as possibly overflowing; count(), min() and max() stay right.

rows.title: KNearestNeighborClassifier, KNearestFuzzyClassifier, KNearestNeighborDocumentClassifier and BooleanPerceptronClassifier add their documented training filter query (and the class-field restriction) as scoring Occur.MUST clauses, so a training query that filters out nothing changes the k-NN class scores and can flip the assigned class, the nearest neighbours or the learned perceptron model (released since 4.6.0)
rows.summary: You index three labelled documents ('aa bb' as Y, 'aa' as X, 'aa' as X), build KNearestNeighborClassifier with k = 3 once with no training query and once with MatchAllDocsQuery (the parameter is documented as 'a Query to eventually filter the docs used for training the classifier', and this one removes nothing), and expect the same answer for 'aa bb bb'. Instead the answer flips from Y (class scores Y 0.333, X 0.309) to X (X 0.417, Y 0.333), because the training query and the class-field WildcardQuery are added as scoring Occur.MUST clauses, so their scores are added to every neighbour's MoreLikeThis score before each vote is weighted by score / maxScore; a training query whose score differs between documents, such as TermQuery(split:train) on a text field every document has, even replaces the nearest neighbour (k = 1: 'aa', class X, becomes 'aa bb', class Y). KNearestFuzzyClassifier and KNearestNeighborDocumentClassifier return different class scores in the same way, and BooleanPerceptronClassifier, which trains in the score order of the same kind of query, learns a different model ('aa' answers true instead of false).
rows.area: classification / k-NN classifiers and BooleanPerceptronClassifier (training query)

rows.title: KNearestFuzzyClassifier ignores its documented 'field^boost' syntax: an entry such as 'title^10' in textFieldNames is looked up as a literal field name, so that field contributes nothing, and with a single boosted field assignClass returns null
rows.summary: You build a KNearestFuzzyClassifier with a text field written as 'text^2' or 'title^10', as its constructor javadoc says you may, and expect the same classes as with the plain field name (with that field weighted more). Instead the entry is used verbatim as the name of a field called 'text^2', which does not exist, so that field adds no terms to the query: with one text field assignClass returns null and getClasses an empty list, and with several fields the boosted one is silently ignored. The sibling KNearestNeighborClassifier, whose javadoc has the same sentence, parses the boost and classifies normally.

rows.title: DatasetSplitter.split can silently leave a whole labelled class out of all three output indexes when some documents have no class value, and throws NullPointerException, leaving the output writers locked, when a segment has no class field
rows.summary: You split an index with DatasetSplitter.split(reader, train, test, cv, analyzer, false, "cls"), where one segment holds d0 without a class value, d1 of class a and d2 of class b. You expect every live document in one of the three new indexes, and every class present, which is what the grouping by class was added for (LUCENE-7196). Instead d2, and with it all of class b, is in none of the outputs: split asks GroupingSearch for as many groups as there are class values, but the documents without a value form one more (null) group that takes one of those slots; and if a segment has no class field at all, split throws NullPointerException from terms(classFieldName).size() before its try block, so its three IndexWriters are never closed.

rows.title: BM25NBClassifier scores a class that has no live, training-query-matching document as if it had probability 1 (log prior 0 and log-likelihood 0), so with few classes it outranks the trained classes and is assigned although it has no training data (released since 7.0.0)
rows.summary: You index four training documents labelled fruit ('apple banana', 'apple pear') or vehicle ('car truck', 'car bus') plus one document labelled heldout that your training query split:train excludes, build BM25NBClassifier with that query and classify 'apple', expecting fruit, which is what the classifier answers when the heldout document is absent. Instead assignClass returns heldout (getClasses: heldout 0.568, fruit 0.273, vehicle 0.159), and the same happens with no training query when every document of a label is deleted but its segment is not yet merged ('apple' -> gone 0.681). BM25NBClassifier makes every term of the class field a candidate class (MultiTerms.getTerms), and for a class with no live, query-matching document both of its searches find no hit, so calculateLogPrior falls back to 0 and getTermProbForClass to 1 (log 0): the class scores exactly 0, while each trained class sums log(top BM25 score) over the prior and every input token, which is negative whenever those scores are below 1.
rows.area: classification / BM25NBClassifier (assignClass and getClasses)

rows.title: DatasetSplitter puts at most about half of each class into the test index, whatever testRatio is
rows.summary: You split an index with new DatasetSplitter(0.8, 0).split(...) to put 80% of the documents into the test index. You expect about 8 of every 10 documents of each class in the test index, as crossValidationRatio 0.8 gives 8 of 10 in the cross-validation index. Instead the test index gets only 5 of 10 and training gets the other 5, because the loop lets a document into the test index only when its running counter b is even (DatasetSplitter.java:153, 'if (b % 2 == 0 && tc < testSize)'), so at most every other document can be a test document, with no error.

rows.title: LatLonPoint#nearest reports an EQUAL_TO TotalHits that counts deleted documents
rows.summary: You index documents with a LatLonPoint field, delete or update some of them, and call LatLonPoint.nearest(searcher, field, lat, lon, n) with n larger than the index. You expect TopFieldDocs.totalHits, which is labelled TotalHits.Relation.EQUAL_TO (exact), to count only documents that can be hits, here the hits returned. Instead the total is the per-segment sum of PointValues#getDocCount, an index statistic that still counts deleted documents, so 3 documents with one deleted return 2 hits but report exactly '3 hits', more than reader.numDocs().

rows.title: Geo3D distance and path sorts (Geo3DDocValuesField.newDistanceSort, newPathSort) skip the secondary SortField for hits outside the shape's bounding box once the queue bottom is +Infinity, so top-N keeps the earliest out-of-radius documents in doc order instead of the first N of the sorted order (released since 6.1.0)
rows.summary: You sort a query with Sort(Geo3DDocValuesField.newDistanceSort(field, lat, lon, maxRadiusMeters, planet), secondary SortField) and expect search(q, n, sort) to return the first n hits of the sorted order: every hit outside the radius reports distance +Infinity (like a document without the field), so the secondary field should order them. Instead, five documents at latitude 60 sorted around (0,0) with a 1,000 km radius and a secondary 'tie' key descending give top 2 = [1, 0] although the full order is [4, 3, 2, 1, 0] (WGS84; the same on SPHERE with a 0.2 planet-radius circle; with a sixth document missing the field, [5, 1] instead of [5, 4]), and newPathSort does the same. The cause: once the queue bottom is +Infinity, compareBottom rejects (-1) every later document whose points lie outside the shape's bounding box instead of reporting a tie (0), so the secondary SortField is never consulted.
rows.area: spatial3d / Geo3D distance sort comparator (Geo3DPointDistanceComparator.compareBottom bounds shortcut; Geo3DDocValuesField.newDistanceSort and newPathSort)

rows.title: Intervals.before(source, reference) treats a source interval at position 0 as before a reference interval that also starts at position 0, so for example before(york, york) matches the one-word document 'york'
rows.summary: You search with Intervals.before(source, reference), for example before(term new, phrase(new, york)) on the text 'new york', or before(term york, term york) on the one-word text 'york'. You expect no match, because the javadoc says before 'Returns intervals from the source that appear before intervals from the reference' and nothing comes before the first word. Instead both documents match: before() is built from a helper that places a pseudo-interval one position before each reference match, and for a reference at position 0 the helper clamps that position to 0 instead of producing nothing, so a source at position 0 counts as 'before' it; prepend one unrelated word and the same text correctly stops matching.

rows.title: Intervals.ordered(a, a) and Intervals.unordered(a, a) report minExtent() 1, so the default disjunction rewrite under phrase/maxgaps leaves or(ordered(a, a), a) unsplit and phrase(x, or(ordered(a, a), a), c) misses 'x a a c'
rows.summary: You search with Intervals.phrase(x, Intervals.or(Intervals.ordered(a, a), a), c), meaning 'x, then either a a or a, then c', on the text 'x a a c' and expect a hit, because phrase(x, ordered(a, a), c) alone matches it and Intervals.or is documented to rewrite itself under gap-sensitive parents so that alternatives of different lengths are not lost. Instead it finds nothing: ordered(a, a) and unordered(a, a) are built as a RepeatingIntervalsSource whose minExtent() returns the minExtent of a single 'a' (1) instead of 2, the rewrite assumes that only single-position sources report 1 and so keeps or(ordered(a, a), a) as one OR, and inside that OR the interval of 'a a' contains the interval of a single 'a' and is minimized away. The same query with two different words, phrase(x, or(ordered(a, b), a), c) on 'x a b c', matches as expected.
rows.area: queries / intervals (RepeatingIntervalsSource.minExtent for ordered/unordered of equal sub-sources; Disjunctions rewrite under phrase/maxgaps)

rows.title: The intervals disjunction rewrite looks only one level into an or(), so an or() inside a maxwidth, fixField or extend wrapper (or inside an ordered()) that is itself one alternative of another or() is never split, and phrase, maxgaps or containedBy miss hits: phrase(x, or(maxwidth(5, or("b c", b)), y), d) misses 'x b c d', which phrase(x, maxwidth(5, or("b c", b)), d) matches
rows.summary: You build phrase(x, or(W, y), d) with W = maxwidth(5, or(phrase(b, c), b)) and expect the hit on 'x b c d' that phrase(x, W, d) finds, because Intervals.or 'Automatically rewrites if wrapped by an interval source that is sensitive to internal gaps' and adding an alternative y that occurs in no document cannot remove a match. Instead the rewrite (Disjunctions.splitDisjunctions) asks the outer or() for its alternatives only one level deep, so W reaches the phrase whole (here grouped with y into one minimizing or(), because W's shortest match is one position), the inner or() drops the interval 'b c' in favour of the 'b' it contains, and the query returns no hits. The same happens with fixField(g, or(...)) or extend(or(...), 0, 0) in place of maxwidth, with containedBy or maxgaps as the parent, and with an ordered() alternative whose own or() has alternatives of different lengths.
rows.area: queries / intervals (gap-sensitive disjunction rewrite of LUCENE-8477: Disjunctions.splitDisjunctions and Disjunctions.pullUp vs an alternative of an or() that has disjunctions of its own: maxwidth, extend, fixField, ordered)

rows.title: Spatial heatmap: HeatmapFacetCounter gives non-zero counts to cells outside a non-rectangular input shape when documents are indexed with coarse leaf cells, although the javadoc says those cells are always 0
rows.summary: You index non-point shapes (rectangles, polygons) with the default RecursivePrefixTreeStrategy and ask PrefixTreeStrategy.calcFacets (HeatmapFacetCounter) for a heatmap with a circle or another non-rectangular input shape; the javadoc says the grid covers the input's bounding rectangle and that 'the non-intersecting cells will all be 0'. Instead, a document whose shape was indexed as a leaf cell coarser than the heatmap level has its count added to every heatmap cell under that leaf, including cells that do not intersect the input shape at all, because the code that spreads these coarse ('ancestor') counts never checks the cells against the input shape; point documents and rectangular inputs come out right. In the minimal repro (the setup of Lucene's own testQueryCircle plus one square document), 8 cells that are disjoint from the circle report 1 instead of 0, with no error.

rows.title: Geo3dShapeFactory passes a line string's buffer distance to spatial3d's GeoPathFactory, which takes radians, without the degrees-to-radians conversion its circle() applies, so in the Geo3d spatial context a line buffered by 1 degree is 1 radian (57.3 degrees) wide and buffers above about 1.57 throw
rows.summary: You use the Geo3d spatial context, build a line from (0,0) to (10,0) with buffer(1), and expect a corridor reaching 1 degree from the line, because spatial4j distances are in the units of x and y (degrees in a geo context) and spatial4j's standard geo context and the same factory's 1-degree circle both say a point at (5, 20) is DISJOINT. Instead the line CONTAINS that point and its bounding box is about [-57.3, 67.3] x [-57.3, 57.3]: Geo3dLineStringBuilder.build hands the buffer straight to GeoPathFactory.makeGeoPath, whose width is an angle in radians, while the factory's circle() and Geo3dRectangleShape.getBuffered convert degrees with DEGREES_TO_RADIANS. The same happens when the Geo3d context reads spatial4j's polyshape string for a 1-degree buffered line, and every buffer above about 1.5708 is rejected with 'Cutoff angle out of bounds', so a buffer of 2 degrees cannot be built at all.
rows.area: spatial-extras / spatial4j bridge to spatial3d (Geo3dShapeFactory line-string builder, Geo3dLineStringBuilder.build), reached through the public LineStringBuilder API, the deprecated lineString(List, double), multi-line builders and the Geo3d context's polyshape reader (and the GeoJSON reader when its optional parser is present)

rows.title: PointVectorStrategy's distance value source gives a document without a point the distance 180 * multiplier even in a non-geo (Cartesian) SpatialContext, so an ascending distance sort lists it before real documents farther than 180 units and makeRecipDistanceValueSource scores it as if it were 180 units away (the other strategies that implement makeDistanceValueSource use Double.MAX_VALUE there; regression in 7.0.0 from LUCENE-7737)
rows.summary: You index points with PointVectorStrategy in a non-geo SpatialContext (for example world bounds -1000..1000), add a document without a point, and sort a query by makeDistanceValueSource(point).getSortField(false), expecting the point-less document last, as BBoxStrategy, SerializedDVStrategy and the prefix-tree strategies do: in a non-geo context they give it Double.MAX_VALUE, the rule LUCENE-4208 set for all strategies ('180 if geo, Double.MAX_VALUE otherwise'). Instead it gets distance 180.0, so with a document at (500, 0) and the query point (0, 0) the ascending order is none,far instead of far,none, and makeRecipDistanceValueSource over the query box -1000..1000 scores it 0.440 against 0.220 for a real document 500 units away. The cause: vector/DistanceValueSource sets nullValue = 180 * multiplier with no isGeo() branch; the branch was dropped in the 7.0 port from ValueSource to DoubleValuesSource (LUCENE-7737).

rows.title: QueryBitSetProducer caches each segment's bit set under the segment core key without asking Weight#isCacheable, so a reused ToParentBlockJoinSortField child filter keeps its old child selection after an in-place doc-values update and a reopen that shares the core: parents sort 'B A' instead of 'A B', with no error; since 5.3.0
rows.summary: You sort parent documents with ToParentBlockJoinSortField by the lowest price among in-stock children, using new QueryBitSetProducer(NumericDocValuesField.newSlowExactQuery("stock", 1)) as the child filter, then put one child back in stock with IndexWriter#updateNumericDocValue, commit and reopen with DirectoryReader.openIfChanged. You expect the reopened searcher to sort by the new selection ('A B': A's cheapest in-stock child now costs 1, B's costs 5), because the child filter defines which children take part and a query that reads updated doc values is not cacheable (SegmentCacheable). Instead QueryBitSetProducer returns the bit set it cached for the old reader under the segment core key, which an in-place doc-values update does not change, and never asks the Weight whether the result may be cached, so the parents still sort 'B A'; a fresh producer or a newly opened reader gives 'A B'.
rows.area: join / QueryBitSetProducer per-segment cache (the childFilter of ToParentBlockJoinSortField) and the SegmentCacheable contract

rows.title: LongRange/DoubleRange#getQuery(fastMatchQuery, valueSource) reports its Weight as cacheable without asking the fast-match query, so after an in-place doc-values update the query cache keeps returning the old matches
rows.summary: You build a range filter or drill-down with LongRange or DoubleRange#getQuery(fastMatchQuery, valueSource) whose fast-match query reads a doc-values field (for example NumericDocValuesField.newSlowExactQuery("inStock", 1)), run it through a query cache, then change that field for one document in place with IndexWriter#updateNumericDocValue and reopen the reader. You expect the reopened searcher to use the new value, because a query that depends on updated doc values must report itself not cacheable (SegmentCacheable), and the fast-match query alone does. Instead the range query's Weight#isCacheable asks only the value source, the segment keeps its core cache key, and the cache keeps serving the pre-update result (5 hits instead of 4 in the repro) until the segment is merged away or the entry is evicted.
rows.area: facet / range drill-down queries (LongRange and DoubleRange ValueSourceQuery and MultiValueSourceQuery) and the query cache

rows.title: LateInteractionFloatValuesSource#isCacheable always returns true although it reads the multi-vectors from binary doc values, so after an in-place update of a LateInteractionField the query cache keeps returning the old matches of a FunctionMatchQuery or DoubleRange query over it

You expect the reopened searcher to stop matching that document, because a source that reads doc values must report itself not cacheable once those doc values have been updated (SegmentCacheable). rows.title: Classic Highlighter counts the unused positions before a MultiPhraseQuery's first position as gaps, so a phrase that starts at position 1 or later (a leading stop word plus a synonym) is highlighted with extra slop and non-matching pairs get marked
rows.summary: You search for the quoted phrase "the dogs bark" with an analyzer that removes the stop word 'the' and adds the synonym dog for dogs (QueryParser and QueryBuilder build a MultiPhraseQuery [dogs|dog] at position 1, bark at position 2, slop 0), and highlight the text 'dogs often bark but my dogs bark' with Highlighter and QueryScorer, expecting 'dogs often bark but my dogs bark' (Weight#matches reports only positions 5-6, and the same query starting at position 0, or a PhraseQuery at positions 1 and 2, is highlighted that way). Instead you get 'dogs often bark but my dogs bark', with no error. WeightedSpanTermExtractor counts every empty slot from index 0 up to the last position as a position gap, including the unused slot 0 below the first position, so the phrase becomes an ordered SpanNearQuery with slop 1 instead of 0 (one extra unit per leading slot, also for sloppy phrases), while its PhraseQuery branch measures gaps from the first position.

rows.title: UnifiedHighlighter re-analysis under the default WEIGHT_MATCHES flag builds its MemoryIndex without payloads, so payload-checking queries get missing or extra highlights or make highlight() throw IllegalArgumentException
rows.summary: You index a field whose tokens carry payloads as a plain TextField (no offsets), search with SpanPayloadCheckQuery or with IntervalQuery(Intervals.term(term, payloadFilter)), which matches the document, and highlight the hit with the UnifiedHighlighter on its default flags. You expect the snippet the highlighter gives with offsets in postings or with WEIGHT_MATCHES off, 'both terms. only terms.' for a check on the second 'terms'. Instead re-analysis builds its one-document MemoryIndex without payloads (MemoryIndexOffsetStrategy stores payloads only when the span PhraseHelper is position-sensitive, and WEIGHT_MATCHES replaces that helper with PhraseHelper.NONE), so Weight#matches on that copy finds nothing and the snippet is 'both terms. only terms.', while the interval query makes highlight() throw IllegalArgumentException 'Cannot create a payload-filtered iterator over field body because it has no indexed payloads'.

rows.title: ParentsChildrenBlockJoinQuery's Weight#matches ignores the join and returns Matches for documents the query does not match (parent documents, children of non-matching parents, children over childLimitPerParent), so as a MUST_NOT clause it strips the Matches and highlights of real hits, and Lucene Monitor's HighlightsMatch matcher reports the wrong documents
rows.summary: You index parent/child blocks, build a ParentsChildrenBlockJoinQuery (children that match childQuery and whose parent matches parentQuery, at most childLimitPerParent per parent) and ask its Weight for Matches, directly, inside a BooleanQuery, through the default UnifiedHighlighter or through Lucene Monitor, and you expect non-null Matches exactly for the join's hits, as Weight#matches documents ('or null if the document does not match the parent query'). Instead matches() returns the union of the parent query's and the child query's Matches on the same document without checking the join, so it is non-null for the parent document itself, for children of parents that do not match and for children over the limit (in the finder's test the only hit is doc 0, but docs 0, 1, 2 and 3 get Matches). Searches stay correct, but a query such as +text:size -join loses the Matches and highlights of its real hits, and Monitor's HighlightsMatch matcher reports documents the stored query does not match.

rows.title: SpanWithinQuery's Weight#matches reports the contained (little) span's positions but the enclosing (big) span's offsets and sub-matches, so Matches-based highlighting (the default UnifiedHighlighter, MatchRegionRetriever) marks the enclosing terms and a field with offsets highlights differently from the same text indexed with positions only
rows.summary: You index 'ab ac bc' in a field with offsets and ask Weight#matches for SpanWithinQuery(big = SpanNear([ab, bc], slop 1, in order), little = ac); you expect one match, 'ac' at position 1 with offsets [3,5) and sub-matches only inside it, which is what the equivalent Intervals.containedBy(ac, ordered(ab, bc)) reports. Instead the match says positions [1,1] but offsets [0,8) and lists ab@0 and bc@2 as sub-matches, because the offsets and sub-matches come from Spans#collect, which for SpanWithinQuery also collects the enclosing span. So the default UnifiedHighlighter marks 'ab ac bc' instead of 'ab ac bc', and MatchRegionRetriever returns [0,8) on a field with offsets but [3,5) on the same text indexed with positions only; hits and scores are unaffected.
rows.area: queries / span queries Matches API (SpanWeight#matches takes offsets and sub-matches from ContainSpans#collect for SpanWithinQuery; seen through the UnifiedHighlighter and MatchRegionRetriever)

rows.title: Intervals.atLeast Matches report offsets and sub-matches from a source the minimisation loop already dropped, so highlighting marks tokens outside the match
rows.summary: You index 'the quick' with 'fast' stacked on 'quick' as an index-time synonym (position increment 0, offsets [4,9)) and ask Weight#matches for Intervals.atLeast(2, the, quick, fast); you expect its only minimal interval, positions [1,1] (quick and fast), with offsets [4,9), and for the text 'the quick fox' the default UnifiedHighlighter snippet 'the quick fox'. Instead the match keeps positions [1,1] but reports startOffset 0 (offsets [0,9)) and a sub-match for 'the' at position 2147483647 (NO_MORE_INTERVALS), so the highlighter returns 'the quick fox'. The minimisation loop in nextInterval() popped 'the' as its lead in an earlier round and then returned through its in-loop exit without clearing it, and getCurrentIterators() still adds that lead to the offsets and sub-matches.

rows.title: A repeated multi-term interval source such as Intervals.ordered(prefix(caf), prefix(caf)) returns non-null Weight#matches, and the default UnifiedHighlighter marks the word, for a document it does not match when the field indexes two matching terms at one position (the one-word text 'café' with ASCIIFoldingFilter preserveOriginal), because MultiTermIntervalsSource.matches reports one entry per expanded term at a position while intervals() reports the position once; since 8.5.0
rows.summary: You index the one-word text 'café' with WhitespaceTokenizer + ASCIIFoldingFilter(preserveOriginal=true), which puts 'café' and 'cafe' at position 0, and run IntervalQuery("f", Intervals.ordered(prefix("caf"), prefix("caf"))), that is two words starting with 'caf'. Search agrees that the document does not match (count 0), so Weight#matches must return null, as its javadoc says and as the same query written with Intervals.or(term("cafe"), term("café")) does. Instead Weight#matches returns a match at [0,0]: MultiTermIntervalsSource.matches merges the two expanded terms with MatchesUtils.disjunction, which lists position 0 once per term while intervals() lists it once, and the repeated source counts the two entries as two occurrences, so the default UnifiedHighlighter marks 'café' in 'café bar' for a hit of 'bar OR ordered(caf*, caf*)' that matched only through 'bar'.

rows.title: IndriQuery.visit reports the whole query as a leaf and never visits its clauses, so QueryVisitor.termCollector, UnifiedHighlighter term extraction, IndexSearcher's cumulative clause limit and RamUsageEstimator.sizeOf all ignore an IndriAndQuery's clauses
rows.summary: You build an IndriAndQuery of ordinary TermQuery clauses, for example f:a and f:b, and inspect it with a QueryVisitor, as term extraction, highlighting, IndexSearcher's clause-count check and the query RAM estimate do. You expect the visitor to reach both clauses, as it does for a BooleanQuery over the same clauses, because Query#visit is documented to 'recurse through the query tree, visiting any child queries'. Instead IndriQuery.visit only calls visitor.visitLeaf(this), so termCollector returns [], with maxClauseCount=4 a 51-clause IndriAndQuery and BooleanQuery(IndriAndQuery(3), IndriAndQuery(3)) both run while the same nesting of BooleanQuery clauses throws TooManyClauses, and RamUsageEstimator.sizeOf gives 1,024 bytes for 1,000 clauses against 1,169,024 for the BooleanQuery.

rows.title: MatchRegionRetriever's default OffsetsFromTokens strategy ignores QueryVisitor#consumeTermsMatching, so prefix, wildcard, regexp, term-range and multi-term TermInSetQuery matches on fields without positions get no hit regions
rows.summary: You index a stored field without positions (one document 'foo bar', IndexOptions DOCS_AND_FREQS, or a StringField), run a PrefixQuery('ba') that matches it, and ask MatchRegionRetriever (or MatchHighlighter) with its default strategies for the hit regions; you expect the region [4,7) for 'bar', which a TermQuery('bar') on the same field, a FuzzyQuery('baz'~1) and the same PrefixQuery on a field with positions all give. Instead the field gets no hit regions at all ({}), although the document is a hit and Weight#matches reports a match on that field. The default strategy for such fields, OffsetsFromTokens, collects the query's terms only through QueryVisitor#consumeTerms, while constant-score multi-term queries report theirs through consumeTermsMatching, so its term set stays empty and no re-analysed token is kept.

rows.title: Since #16669 (10.6.0 and main), ReqExclBulkScorer no longer skips long runs of excluded doc IDs: for +R -X it scores the required clause in every 4096-doc window, even windows X fully excludes, so R's iterator steps through all of its matches inside X's runs (10,001 moves for 1,000 hits in a 10,000-doc segment, where 10.0.0-10.5.2 need 1,001; performance regression, results correct)
rows.summary: You search +R -grp:old, where R matches every document and grp:old matches one run of consecutive doc IDs covering 9,000 of the 10,000 documents of a segment. You expect Lucene to jump over the excluded run, as 10.3.0 to 10.5.2 do in one docIDRunEnd step (on every release from 10.0.0 to 10.5.2 the required clause's iterator moves 1,001 times for the 1,000 hits). Instead, since #16669 ReqExclBulkScorer loads the exclusion into a bit mask per 4096-doc window and always runs the required clause over every window, even windows the exclusion covers completely, so the iterator moves 10,001 times; the 1,000 hits are still right, only the work now grows with the length of the excluded run.

rows.title: Since #16857 (upstream main and branch_11x, unreleased), a numeric field-sorted search reads a later segment's whole competitive points range before the scorer is set: TopFieldLeafCollector's constructor calls setHitsThresholdReached() while NumericComparator's iteratorCost is still its -1 'no scorer yet' value, so the 8x selectivity check never rejects (1,001 point doc IDs read where releases read 0; performance regression, results correct)
rows.summary: You run searcher.search(new TermQuery(new Term("brand", "lux")), 10, new Sort(new SortField("price", SortField.Type.LONG))) over two segments: the first has 1,001 hits, so the default 1,000-hit threshold is crossed there, and in the second the query matches one document that cannot compete. You expect the second segment not to read its points, because the comparator builds its competitive iterator from points only when that cuts the query's own cost at least 8x; 645d4fe, 10.6.0, 10.5.2 and 9.12.3 read 0 point doc IDs there. Instead, since #16857 the new leaf collector tells the comparator about the threshold before setScorer(), while its cost is still the -1 'no scorer yet' value (so the 8x limit becomes 2^61-1), and it intersects the whole competitive range, 1,001 doc IDs; the top 10 is still right, only the work is wasted.

rows.title: A relevance-first TopFieldCollector (Sort.RELEVANCE or Sort(FIELD_SCORE, tiebreak)) never sets the minimum competitive score when totalHitsThreshold is crossed, so skipping starts only if a later hit is competitive, and the search can score every match (performance regression since 8.7.0; results correct)
rows.summary: You run IndexSearcher#search(query, 10, Sort.RELEVANCE), or a searchAfter page sorted by Sort(SortField.FIELD_SCORE, tiebreak), on a query with many matches, and expect it to start skipping non-competitive documents once 1,000 hits are counted, as search(query, 10) does and as LUCENE-8507 made relevance-first TopFieldCollector do from 8.0.0 to 8.6.3. Instead TopFieldCollector.countHit flips totalHitsRelation to GREATER_THAN_OR_EQUAL_TO on the hit that crosses the threshold, before thresholdCheck's EQUAL_TO-guarded updateMinCompetitiveScore call runs, so that call can never take effect and the minimum competitive score is set only when a later hit is competitive; with the best documents first, the relevance-sorted search scores all 10,011 matches where search(query, 10) stops at 1,024, with the same top 10. This is a regression from LUCENE-9449 (8.7.0); results are always correct.
rows.area: search / sorting (TopFieldCollector, relevance-first sort: minimum competitive score at the totalHitsThreshold crossing)

rows.title: DoubleValuesSourceRescorer.rescore passes null scores to a DoubleValuesSource whose needsScores() is true, so rescoring with DoubleValuesSource.SCORES, an expression that reads _score or a FunctionScoreQuery.boostByValue source throws (AssertionError with -ea; NullPointerException or a misleading 'Unrecognized variable (_score)' RuntimeException with -da), while explain() on the same input returns normally

rows.title: A facet dimension set to DrillDownTermsIndexing.NONE that shares its index field ($facets by default) with term-indexing dimensions makes FacetsConfig emit two schemas for that field, so since 9.0.0 IndexWriter rejects documents of one kind once a document of the other kind is indexed, and after a commit until the index is cleared or rebuilt
rows.summary: You call config.setDrillDownTermsIndexing("rating", NONE), leave every dimension in the default index field $facets, and index one document with only FacetField("rating", "5") and then one with FacetField("author", "Bob"); you expect both to be indexed, as they are on Lucene 8.9 to 8.11 and as they are when rating gets its own index field. FacetsConfig.build gives the first document a doc-values-only $facets (NONE adds no drill-down terms) and the second a $facets with drill-down terms, and since 9.0 Lucene requires one schema per field, so the second addDocument throws IllegalArgumentException 'Inconsistency of field data structures across documents for field [$facets] of doc [1]. index options: expected 'NONE', but it has 'DOCS'' (with taxonomy facets the reverse order fails the same way). After a commit, a new IndexWriter keeps rejecting documents of the other kind ('cannot change field "$facets" from index options=NONE to inconsistent index options=DOCS') until the index is cleared or rebuilt.

rows.title: CompletionScorer silently ignores the BulkScorer [min, max) window instead of rejecting it, so a CompletionQuery run through IndexSearcher#search with a timeout (even one that never fires) or with intra-segment partitions returns repeated suggestions and drops others
rows.summary: You run a CompletionQuery through IndexSearcher#search with a TopSuggestDocsCollector (for example suggestSearcher.search(query, collector)) on a searcher that has a timeout set, even one that never fires, or that splits a segment into intra-segment partitions. You expect the same top suggestions as SuggestIndexSearcher#suggest, or a loud error if this path is unsupported, because BulkScorer#score must score only the documents in [min, max) and a timeout that never fires must not change results. Instead CompletionScorer runs its whole-segment top-N lookup again on every window or partition, so the top suggestions come back several times and lower ones are dropped (500 suggestions, n=5: [499, 499, 498, 498, 497] instead of [499, 498, 497, 496, 495]; one suggestion returned 5 times; partitions: [499 x5]), while the total says EQUAL_TO and timedOut() is false.

rows.title: KnnVectorValues.fromDISI's advance() leaves index() stale, so on Lucene 10 sparse byte vectors in segments written by Lucene 9.4 read back as zeros or as another document's vector
rows.summary: You open, on Lucene 10, an index whose segment was written by Lucene 9.4.2 with a byte vector field that only some documents have, move the field's iterator to a document with advance(doc) and read vectorValue(iterator.index()), which is what ByteKnnVectorFieldSource does, and expect that document's own vector, because DocIndexIterator.index() is documented as the ordinal of the current document and DocIdSetIterator.advance() must behave like repeated nextDoc() calls. Instead every document that has a vector reads as all zeros: the iterator that KnnVectorValues.fromDISI builds, which this one reader returns, counts the ordinal only in nextDoc(), and its advance() moves to the document without moving the ordinal, so index() stays at -1 (the reader then hands back its never-filled buffer); after earlier nextDoc() calls, index() is an earlier document's ordinal and the read returns that document's vector. Lucene 9.x reads the same index correctly; the defect came with the 10.0 vector-values API change #13779.
rows.area: index / vector values iteration (KnnVectorValues.fromDISI) with backward-codecs / Lucene 9.4 sparse byte vector reader

rows.title: ShapeDocValues.relate() rewinds to position 0 of the backing array instead of to the BytesRef's offset, so a LatLonShape or XYShape doc value built from a BytesRef slice (offset != 0) silently relates wrongly to queries
rows.summary: You build a LatLonShape or XYShape doc value from a BytesRef that points into the middle of a larger byte array (offset != 0), for example with LatLonShape.createLatLonShapeDocValues(BytesRef) or as a MemoryIndex field, and expect relate() and the doc-values shape queries to answer exactly as for the same bytes at offset 0. rows.title: MatchingFacetSetsCounts decodes the facet-set binary doc value from position 0 of BytesRef.bytes instead of BytesRef.offset, so a value that a reader returns as a slice of a larger array is counted from the wrong bytes (silently wrong facet-set counts, or NegativeArraySizeException / ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException)
rows.summary: You count facet sets with MatchingFacetSetsCounts over a reader that hands back a document's facet-set binary doc value as a BytesRef slice of a larger array (offset != 0), for example a MemoryIndex holding a value that was packed into a shared buffer, and expect the same counts as for a compact copy of the same bytes. Instead count() reads the dimension count from bytes[0] and the dimension values from bytes[4..length) of the backing array, ignoring the offset, so the document is counted under whatever bytes start that array: a document whose set is (3,4), stored right after an encoding of (1,2), is counted as (1,2)=1 and (3,4)=0, with no error. When the leading bytes do not decode to a sane dimension count, the MatchingFacetSetsCounts constructor throws NegativeArraySizeException or ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException instead, while the same value indexed through IndexWriter with the default codec is counted correctly.
