rows.title: JoinUtil's single-valued term join forgets a from-document that scored exactly 0, so ScoreMode.Min and ScoreMode.Avg give too-high, order-dependent scores
rows.summary: You build JoinUtil.createJoinQuery("join", false, "ref", fromQuery, searcher, ScoreMode.Min) where two from-documents share the join value x and fromQuery scores them 0 and 2 (one matches only a FILTER clause), and expect the to-document with ref x to score min(0, 2) = 0, or (0 + 2) / 2 = 1 with ScoreMode.Avg, because the ScoreMode javadoc says 'the min of all child scores' and 'the average of all child scores' and the multi-valued join returns exactly that on the same documents. Instead both modes return 2: the single-valued collector uses an accumulated score of exactly 0 to mean 'this join value has not been seen yet', so after a from-document that scored 0, the next from-document with the same value overwrites the stored minimum (Min) or restarts the sum and count (Avg). Which documents match does not change; only scores and ranking are wrong, and they depend on collection order (scores [0, 2] go wrong, [2, 0] come out right).

rows.title: QueryBuilder drops every token boost (BoostAttribute) from a quoted phrase as soon as one of its words has a single-word synonym, so typed word|weight boosts and weighted-synonym weights are silently ignored there, while plain phrases, graph phrases and unquoted queries keep them
rows.summary: You give a phrase a token boost, for example "fast|0.5 car" through DelimitedBoostTokenFilter, or use weighted synonyms such as 'cat, kitty|0.5', and expect the quoted phrase to keep the boost the way QueryBuilder's other paths do: "fast|0.5 tiger" becomes (body:"fast tiger")^0.5, and a multi-word weighted synonym gives one boosted phrase per path. But as soon as one word of the phrase has a single-word synonym ('car, automobile'), QueryBuilder builds a MultiPhraseQuery in analyzeMultiPhrase, which never reads BoostAttribute: "fast|0.5 car" becomes the unboosted body:"fast (automobile car)" (score 0.2615 instead of 0.1308), and the quoted "cat food" scores 'kitty food' the same as 'cat food' (0.7130 both), although the unquoted query ranks it lower. The matching documents are unchanged; only scores and ranking are wrong, and there is no error.
rows.area: core / util QueryBuilder phrase building with token boosts (analyzeMultiPhrase; BoostAttribute from DelimitedBoostTokenFilter and weighted synonyms; reached through the classic, multi-field and simple query parsers)

rows.title: QueryBuilder counts a removed leading stop word as a position, so a quoted phrase such as "the dogs", whose one remaining word carries a same-position synonym or variant, becomes a one-position MultiPhraseQuery instead of the SynonymQuery that "dogs" gives, and is scored differently (since 6.0.0)
rows.summary: You analyze query text with stop-word removal and a same-position synonym (dogs -> dog) and call createPhraseQuery(field, "the dogs"), or type the quoted phrase "the dogs" into the classic QueryParser. You expect the SynonymQuery(dogs, dog) that "dogs" and "dogs the" give, because the remaining terms sit at one position and QueryBuilder generates phrases only 'when terms occur at more than one position'; you get the one-position MultiPhraseQuery field:"(dogs dog)", which rewrites to a plain disjunction of the two terms. The same documents match, but BM25 scores them differently (doc 'dogs' rises from 0.2774 to 0.7135 and no longer ties with doc 'dog'), because createFieldQuery adds up position increments, so the hole left by 'the' counts as a second position.

rows.title: Surround query parser ignores a ^ weight written directly on the operand of a field prefix (title: lucene^3, title: body: lucene^3, body: or(a, b)^2), because FieldsQuery builds its operand with makeLuceneQueryFieldNoBoost
rows.summary: You parse the surround query or(title: lucene^3, body: lucene), whose parser documents 'boosting (via ^)', and expect the title match to count three times, exactly like the same weight on the parenthesised field query or((title: lucene)^3, body: lucene). Instead the weight is kept on the parsed term (toString shows title:lucene^3.0), but FieldsQuery.makeLuceneQueryNoBoost builds its operand with makeLuceneQueryFieldNoBoost, so no BoostQuery is created: the title document scores 0.13076457 instead of 0.39229375, no more than the body-only match, which the weight was meant to outrank. Every weight on the direct operand of a field prefix is dropped (a term, an OR, a distance query, with one field or several); only scores and ranking change, never which documents match.
rows.area: queryparser / surround (FieldsQuery field prefixes and ^ weights)

rows.title: Lucene Monitor's ScoringMatch and ExplainingMatch score a registered DisjunctionMaxQuery with a tie-breaker below 1 as the sum of its matching disjuncts instead of max + tieBreaker * others
rows.summary: You register a DisjunctionMaxQuery such as (title:apple | body:apple) with tie-breaker 0 in a Monitor and match a document that has apple in both fields with ScoringMatch or ExplainingMatch, expecting the score the query itself gives that document: the best field's score plus tie times the others, which is what IndexSearcher returns (0.1798013 in an independent test). Instead the Monitor reports the sum of both field scores (0.3105659), because the default QueryDecomposer splits the DisjunctionMaxQuery into one query per disjunct and the scoring matchers add up the scores of the parts. In the 'albino elephant' example of DisjunctionMaxQuery's own javadoc, this makes the document with 'albino' in both fields tie with the document that matches both words, which the query is designed to rank higher.
rows.area: monitor / query decomposition and match scoring (QueryDecomposer DisjunctionMaxQuery split, ScoringMatch/ExplainingMatch resolve)

rows.title: XML query parser ignores the text inside CDATA sections: DOMUtils.getText has no CDATA_SECTION_NODE case, so <TermsQuery fieldName="f">a <![CDATA[b]]></TermsQuery> parses to f:a only and a CDATA-only LikeThisQuery silently matches nothing (every release since 1.9)
rows.summary: You parse an XML query whose text is partly or wholly a CDATA section, for example <TermsQuery fieldName="f">a <![CDATA[b]]></TermsQuery>, with Lucene's XML query parser. XML defines a CDATA section as ordinary character data, and the shipped DTD declares TermsQuery as (#PCDATA) whose 'Child text is analyzed', so you expect the same query as for the plain text 'a b', (f:a f:b). Instead DOMUtils.getText skips CDATA section nodes and you get (f:a): mixed text silently loses the CDATA words, a CDATA-only LikeThisQuery matches nothing, and the other CDATA-only elements throw ParserException.
rows.area: queryparser / xml (DOMUtils.getText, the text reader of every text-taking builder; CoreParser)

rows.title: Surround query parser keeps the escaping backslashes inside a quoted term, so "a\"b" searches for a\"b instead of a"b and "c:\\temp dir" searches for c:\\temp dir instead of c:\temp dir
rows.summary: You parse a surround query with a quoted term that escapes a double quote or a backslash, such as "a\"b" or "c:\\temp dir", and run it on a field that holds the untokenized value a"b or c:\temp dir. You expect a match, because the grammar comment on the QUOTED token says 'escape quoted quote or backslash by backslash' and the lexer accepts a backslash inside quotes only as such an escape. Instead the parser strips only the outer quotes, so SrndTermQuery searches for a\"b and c:\\temp dir with the backslashes kept: 0 hits, or a silent match on a different document that holds that escaped text, and no surround syntax matches those terms exactly.
rows.area: queryparser / surround (QueryParser.jj QUOTED token and SimpleTerm production, SrndTermQuery)

rows.title: Flexible StandardQueryParser: term literals inside fn: interval functions keep their escape backslashes, so fn:or(a\:b) searches for the text a\:b instead of the term a:b
rows.summary: You parse fn:or(a\:b) (or fn:ordered(a\:b c), fn:fuzzyTerm(a\:b 0), fn:or("a\"b")) with StandardQueryParser and expect it to find the documents that hold a:b (or a"b), because the parser's javadoc says 'any character can be quoted with a backslash' and the same escaped literal outside fn: is parsed as the term a:b. Instead the IntervalText and IntervalFuzzyTerm grammar productions pass the raw token text, backslashes included, to AnalyzedText and FuzzyTerm, so the interval query searches for the text a\:b. With WhitespaceAnalyzer it misses the a:b document and matches a document that holds a\:b; with StandardAnalyzer it becomes BLOCK(a,b) and matches 'a b c'; no error is raised.

rows.title: ComplexPhraseQueryParser: a quoted phrase that is only one parenthesized group is read as a sequence of positions, so "(john OR jonathan)" matches only the sequence 'john jonathan' and "(jo* -john)" matches documents whose only jo* term is john
rows.summary: You parse "(john OR jonathan)" or "(jo* -john)" with ComplexPhraseQueryParser and search; inside a complex phrase a bracketed group is one position with alternatives (class javadoc example "(john jon jonathan~) peters*", upstream tests "(john OR johathon) smith" and "(jo* -john) smith") and one-element phrases are supported, so you expect the documents that contain john or jonathan, or a jo* term other than john. Instead the classic grammar drops parentheses around the whole input (QueryParser.jj:289-293 and :311), so the second pass gets the same BooleanQuery as for "john OR jonathan", and ComplexPhraseQuery.rewrite makes each member a consecutive position: "(john OR jonathan)" becomes spanNear([john, jonathan], 0, true) and matches only documents that contain the sequence 'john jonathan', and "(jo* -john)" becomes spanNot(spanOr(jo*), spanNear([spanOr(jo*), john])) and also matches 'john smith', whose only jo* term is john.
rows.area: queryparser / complexPhrase: ComplexPhraseQueryParser (ComplexPhraseQuery.parsePhraseElements second-pass parse, read by ComplexPhraseQuery.rewrite)

rows.title: FSTCompletionLookup sorts weights as unsigned bytes, so negative weights get the highest buckets and are suggested before positive ones
rows.summary: You build an FSTCompletionLookup from two suggestions, apple with weight 10 and apricot with weight -10, and ask lookup("ap", true, 2) for the best completions first. You expect apple first, because the class javadoc says buckets come from 'sorting the input by weight', InputIterator says 'higher numbers mean better suggestions', and encodeWeight accepts every int. Instead you get [apricot/5, apple/0], with no error: build() sorts the weights by their unsigned big-endian bytes, where every negative int (first byte 0x80 or above) comes after every non-negative int, so all negative weights land in the highest buckets and are suggested first.
rows.area: suggest / FST completion suggester (FSTCompletionLookup.build weight bucketing)

rows.title: FuzzyCompletionQuery with unicodeAware=true compares the query's code points with the UTF-8 bytes of the matched suggestion, so its prefix-similarity boost stops at the first non-ASCII letter and exact prefixes lose their boost advantage over typos
rows.summary: You build a FuzzyCompletionQuery with unicodeAware=true, the documented option that measures the query 'in Unicode code points (actual letters) instead of bytes', and expect a suggestion that shares more leading letters with the typed prefix to get a larger boost, exactly as for ASCII text. Instead FuzzyCompletionWeight.setNextMatch compares the query's code points with the UTF-8 byte labels of the matched suggestion, so the count stops at the first non-ASCII letter: for the query 'aéc' over aécd (weight 3) and the typo axcd (weight 4) both get boost 1 and the exact prefix ranks second, [axcd/4.0, aécd/3.0], while the same data in ASCII ('abc' over abcd and axcd) gives [abcd/6.0, axcd/4.0]; for an all-CJK or all-Cyrillic query every suggestion gets boost 0, so the exact prefix only ties with typos and the weight alone decides. Only scores and ranking are wrong (the suggestions found are right), for the plain query and inside a ContextQuery.
rows.area: suggest / document (NRT) suggester (FuzzyCompletionQuery: FuzzyCompletionWeight.setNextMatch prefix-similarity boost in unicodeAware mode, also inside ContextQuery)

rows.title: FSTCompletionLookup ignores exactMatchFirst=false for by-weight lookups after build() and load(), so an exact match is always ranked first
rows.summary: You build an FSTCompletionLookup(dir, "fst", 10, false) from star (weight 1), star wars (100) and start (50) and ask lookup("star", true, 3) for the most popular completions first. You expect [star wars/6, start/3, star/0], because the constructor javadoc says that with exactMatchFirst=false exact matches 'appear in the order of discretized weight and alphabetical within the bucket'. Instead you get [star/0, star wars/6, start/3], with no error, after build() and equally after store() and load(): both paths create the internal by-weight FSTCompletion with its exact-first default, and the flag reaches only the alphabetical completion, where it changes nothing.

rows.title: MinHashFilter with hashSetSize >= 2 drops one of the kept lowest hash values when a token repeats while its (hash, bucket) set is full, so the min-hash signature depends on token repeats and order instead of only on the token set ('b a a' keeps 1 of 2 values; 'c a c b' and 'c a b c' give different signatures)
rows.summary: You analyse 'b a a' with MinHashFilter(hashCount 1, bucketCount 1, hashSetSize 2) and expect the same two min hashes as for 'b a', because the filter keeps 'the N lowest values' of the tokens' hashes (MinHashFilter.java:38-40; hashSetSize is 'the no. of min hashes to keep') and the lowest values of a token set do not change when a token repeats. Instead, FixedSizeTreeSet.add removes the full set's largest value (pollLast) before TreeSet.add finds that the repeated value is already there, so 'b a a' gives one value; a later new token, however large its hash, then fills the free slot ('c a c b' keeps the hashes of c and b, not the true lowest two, c and a), and the same tokens in another order ('c a b c') give yet another signature. In the javadoc's '1 hash and keep the 100 lowest values' setting with 5-word shingles, a 150-word text read twice has the same shingle set as the text read once but a signature of 99 values that misses one of the 100 lowest.
rows.area: analysis-common / minhash (MinHashFilter.FixedSizeTreeSet bottom-k set; MinHashFilterFactory 'minHash')

rows.title: Word2VecModel: a term added twice silently shifts the vector of every later term, so Word2VecSynonymFilter returns synonyms computed from other terms' vectors
rows.summary: You build a Word2VecModel in which one term appears twice, through the public addTermAndVector or by loading a Deeplearning4j-format zip with Dl4jModelReader or Word2VecSynonymFilterFactory, and you expect every term to keep its own vector, as the class javadoc ('containing the vectors for each word in dictionary') and the upstream test of vectorValue(term) say. addTermAndVector stores each entry at the next array slot but ignores that BytesRefHash.add gives no new id to a term it already holds, while vectorValue(term) looks the vector up by that id, so after the first repeat every later distinct term reads the slot of the term before it. For the model [a(1,0), a(1,0), b(0,1), c(-1,0)] vectorValue(b) returns a's vector and vectorValue(c) returns b's, and with the model [car, car, auto, banana, fruit] and the factory defaults 'banana' is expanded with the neighbours of 'auto' ([auto, car, car]) instead of [fruit], with no error or warning.

rows.title: DirectIOIndexInput.fill moves filePos to the next block, and clears the buffer, before its EOF check and before the channel read succeeds, so after a read that threw, a legal seek or the next read on the same input returns bytes of another file position or a spurious EOFException (since 9.0.0)
rows.summary: You read a file through the misc DirectIODirectory, one read on an input throws (an EOFException because it asked for more bytes than are left, or an IOException from a transient storage error), and you then seek back to a legal position, or simply read again, on the same input. You expect the bytes at the file pointer, or another exception (after the same read-past-EOF sequences MMapDirectory returns the right bytes). Instead fill() had already moved its window position (filePos) to the next block, and on the read path cleared the buffer, before it threw, so the next reads silently return bytes of a different position of the same file (or throw EOFException at a legal position) while getFilePointer() reports the requested one.

rows.title: AnalyzingInfixSuggester.build() can commit and then throw, and its catch block leaves writer == null, so refresh() becomes a no-op: the old suggestions stay served while the directory holds the build that threw, and the next add()/update() or a reopen silently switches to it (default settings, since 9.2.0)
rows.summary: You rebuild an AnalyzingInfixSuggester with default settings, build() throws an IOException, you call refresh() and keep using the instance, and you expect it to serve what its index holds, so that a later add() adds exactly one suggestion. Instead build() has already committed the new index (closeIndexWriterOnBuild defaults to true) before it opens the SearcherManager on it; when that open fails, the catch block rolls back (which cannot undo the commit), sets writer = null and keeps the old SearcherManager, so refresh() is a no-op, lookups serve the old suggestions ([old apple]) while the directory holds the failed build ([new avocado]), and after the next add() lookups return [another apricot, new avocado], with the old suggestion gone. A second trigger needs no I/O fault: build() first closes, and so commits, a writer that holds an add() or update() not yet refreshed, and if the rebuild's input then throws, refresh() never shows that committed change.
rows.area: suggest / analyzing infix suggester (AnalyzingInfixSuggester.build() failure path; inherited unchanged by BlendedInfixSuggester)

rows.title: LogMergePolicy.findMerges wraps 'start + mergeFactor' when mergeFactor is Integer.MAX_VALUE (or within about the segment count of it), which setMergeFactor accepts, so commit and flush throw once two size levels exist (every release since 2.3.0)
rows.summary: You configure LogDocMergePolicy (or LogByteSizeMergePolicy) with setMergeFactor(Integer.MAX_VALUE), which the setter accepts (it rejects only values below 2, and its javadoc recommends large values for batch indexing), bulk-load one large segment, add one document and commit, and expect the commit to succeed with no merge, as it does with Integer.MAX_VALUE - 1. Instead findMerges computes the end of each merge window as 'int end = start + mergeFactor', which wraps negative for every size level that does not start at segment 0, and its minimum-size packing step then calls levels.get(-2147483648), so commit() throws IndexOutOfBoundsException (OutOfMemoryError 'Requested array size exceeds VM limit' before 10.2.0). Every later commit and flush of new documents fails the same way until the factor is lowered; on main a 20,000,000-document segment followed by a 1-document flush is enough.
rows.area: index / merge policy (LogMergePolicy.findMerges level window; LogDocMergePolicy, LogByteSizeMergePolicy)

rows.title: kNN vector queries size each segment's result heap from the requested k, not from what the segment can return, so k = Integer.MAX_VALUE throws IllegalArgumentException and k = 2^28 runs out of a 2 GiB heap on a 3-document index (core KnnFloat/KnnByteVectorQuery without a filter: regression in 9.10.0; join DiversifyingChildren*KnnVectorQuery: since 9.8.0)
rows.summary: You run a KnnFloatVectorQuery with a k larger than the index, for example k = Integer.MAX_VALUE to mean 'all vectors', and expect every vector back, as k = 1000 over 3 vectors gives, and as 9.9.2 gives for any k. Instead each segment's collector is built with a heap sized from k (k + 1 longs on a single-segment index) before the segment's vector count is looked at: k = Integer.MAX_VALUE throws IllegalArgumentException('initialCapacity must be > 0 and < 2147483630; got: 2147483647') from TernaryLongHeap, and k = 2^28 over a 3-document index throws OutOfMemoryError with a 2 GiB heap. Lucene used to cap k at the segment's vector count ('bound k by total number of vectors to prevent oversizing data structures'); a search speed-up change dropped that cap in 9.10.0, and the join DiversifyingChildren*KnnVectorQuery never had it.
rows.area: search / kNN vector queries (per-segment collector sizing: AbstractKnnVectorQuery, TopKnnCollectorManager, TopKnnCollector; join DiversifyingNearestChildrenKnnCollectorManager)

rows.title: SortRescorer and Expression#getRescorer size their sort collector by topN instead of by the number of first-pass hits, so a topN far above the hit count (such as Integer.MAX_VALUE for 're-sort them all') throws (OutOfMemoryError on main, IllegalArgumentException in current releases) or allocates memory in proportion to topN, while QueryRescorer and DoubleValuesSourceRescorer return the hits
rows.summary: You run a first-pass search that returns 5 hits and re-sort them with new SortRescorer(sort).rescore(searcher, firstPass, Integer.MAX_VALUE), meaning 're-sort all of them'; you expect the 5 hits back in sort order, as topN = 5 or 10 give and as QueryRescorer and DoubleValuesSourceRescorer give for any topN. Instead the call throws OutOfMemoryError 'Requested array size exceeds VM limit' on main (IllegalArgumentException 'maxSize must be >= 0 and < 2147483631' in 10.x and 9.x), because SortRescorer sizes its TopFieldCollector, which pre-allocates its arrays, by topN instead of by the number of hits it was given. Smaller large values succeed but cost memory in proportion to topN (about 120 MB for 4 hits at topN = 10^7), and Expression#getRescorer inherits the same code.

rows.title: TieredMergePolicy.setMaxMergedSegmentMB(0), a value the setter accepts, makes commit(), close() and forceMergeDeletes() throw once a segment has enough deletes: the doFindMerges candidate loop never admits a segment, so the merge candidate is empty (AssertionError with -ea, IndexOutOfBoundsException with -da); a regression since 7.5.0

Instead the candidate loop in doFindMerges requires 'bytesThisMerge < maxMergedSegmentBytes', which is 0 < 0 before the first segment is added, so no segment is ever admitted and the candidate list stays empty. 'assert candidate.size() > 0' then fails with -ea, and candidate.get(0) throws IndexOutOfBoundsException ('Index 0 out of bounds for length 0') with -da, out of the writer call.

rows.title: A negative cache limit (GroupingSearch.setCaching(-1, ..) / setCachingInMB(-1.0, ..), CachingCollector.create(.., -1), CachingCollectorManager) is accepted and caches nothing, yet isCached() stays true, so replay() delivers no documents and grouped search silently returns groups with no documents and totalHitCount 0 (since 9.8.0; from 5.0.0 to 9.7.0 replay threw instead)
rows.summary: You enable caching for a grouped search (or wrap a first-pass collector in CachingCollector or CachingCollectorManager) with a negative limit, for example setCaching(-1, true) meant as 'no limit', and expect either an IllegalArgumentException or the documented fallback for a cache over its limit: isCached() false and the query re-run. Instead the limit is accepted and nothing is cached (a negative count is the collector's own internal 'purged' marker), but isCached() stays true, so replay() delivers none of the collected documents and GroupingSearch returns its top groups with no documents and totalHitCount 0 instead of 20 in the repro, with no error. From 5.0.0 to 9.7.0 the same input failed at replay with an AssertionError (-ea) or IndexOutOfBoundsException (-da).

rows.title: QueryNodeProcessorPipeline's listIterator()/subList() views, and replaceAll / Collections.replaceAll built on them, put processors on the pipeline without its QueryConfigHandler, so the flexible query parser silently skips point, boost and default phrase slop handling or throws NullPointerException
rows.summary: You customise a flexible query parser pipeline, for example StandardQueryParser's, by inserting or replacing a processor through the pipeline's java.util.List API: pipeline.listIterator() then add or set, subList(..).set, pipeline.replaceAll or Collections.replaceAll. You expect the processor to receive the pipeline's QueryConfigHandler, as it does with add(k, p) or set(k, p), because the class says it 'takes care of setting this QueryConfigHandler on all processor on pipeline'. Instead those paths write through the private ArrayList's own views and leave the processor with a null handler, so a replaced PointQueryNodeProcessor turns n:5 into a TermQuery that finds 0 of 1 matching documents, a replaced BoostQueryNodeProcessor drops field boosts, and most other stock processors throw NullPointerException at parse.
rows.area: queryparser / flexible core: QueryNodeProcessorPipeline (java.util.List views and default methods)

rows.title: Tessellator bridges a hole whose left-most vertex touches an outer-ring edge to a vertex off that edge, so LatLonShape and XYShape index the hole (in some shapes also area outside the polygon) as part of the shape, or reject a valid polygon
rows.summary: You index a polygon whose hole touches the outer boundary at one corner, which the Tessellator javadoc allows ('Holes may only touch at one vertex'), for example the outer ring (2,0) (1,1) (0,2) (3,3) with the hole (1,1) (1,2) (2,2), and you expect a point inside the hole not to match. To cut the polygon into triangles Lucene first joins the hole to the outer ring with a bridge; when the hole's left-most corner lies on an outer edge, Tessellator.fetchHoleBridge links it to the vertex before that edge instead of the edge's own endpoint, so the bridge runs across the hole. The triangles then cover the hole and an INTERSECTS query for a point in it matches the document with no error, or, for other shapes such as a hole corner touching the middle of an outer edge, the valid polygon is rejected with 'Unable to Tessellate shape'.
rows.area: geo / Tessellator hole elimination (polygon indexing for LatLonShape and XYShape)

rows.title: Tessellator: after a hole that touches the outer ring at one vertex is merged, the leftover copies of that vertex make a later hole's bridge cross the first hole, so LatLonShape and XYShape index a valid two-hole polygon with triangles that cover a hole, or reject it (regression from #15211, in 10.4.0 and 9.12.3)
rows.summary: You index a valid polygon with two holes, where hole A touches the outer ring at one corner (the Tessellator javadoc allows 'Holes may only touch at one vertex') and hole B touches nothing, for example the outer ring (0,0) (2,5) (0,10) (10,10) (10,0) with hole A (2,5) (5,6) (4,8) and hole B (6,5) (8,4) (8,6), and you expect a point inside hole A not to match. The triangles then cover hole A, and an INTERSECTS query for a point in it matches the document with no error, while with checkSelfIntersections=true the same valid polygon is rejected with 'Polygon self-intersection'.

rows.title: Tessellator bridges a later hole across an earlier hole when the earlier hole touches the outer ring at a vertex where an outer edge and a hole edge are collinear: after filterPoints drops the straight-run copy of that vertex, fetchHoleBridge breaks an equal-x ray tie at it by ring order, so LatLonShape and XYShape match points inside the hole (depends on the outer ring's start vertex)
rows.summary: You index a valid polygon with LatLonShape or XYShape whose clockwise outer ring (2,3) (2,5) (4,4) (5,0) (0,0) has a counter-clockwise hole A (2,3) (1,1) (2,1), which touches the ring only at V=(2,3) where the outer edge (2,5)-(2,3) and the hole edge (2,3)-(2,1) lie on the line x = 2, and a second hole B (3,3) (4,2) (4,3) that touches nothing, and you expect the triangles to cover the polygon minus both holes (area 12.5). After hole A is merged at V, the filterPoints pass that eliminateHoles runs after every hole (Tessellator.java:347) drops the copy of V on that straight run; hole B's leftward ray from (3,3) then hits two edges exactly at V, and fetchHoleBridge keeps whichever comes first in ring order (the strict 'x > qx' at :549), so with the ring written from (2,3) hole B is bridged to (0,0) straight across hole A. The triangles then cover hole A (total area 16.0), the point (1.75,1.5) inside hole A matches INTERSECTS and misses DISJOINT, and the strict path rejects the polygon as self-intersecting; the other four ring starts are exact on main (on 8.2.0-9.12.2 and 10.0.0-10.3.2 the failing start is (2,5) instead).

rows.title: Tessellator flags a hole bridge that lies inside a longer outer-ring edge as an internal edge, so LatLonShape and XYShape CONTAINS queries match boxes that stick out of a valid polygon whose two holes touch the same outer edge
rows.summary: You index a valid polygon whose two holes each touch the same straight outer edge at one point, for example the triangle (0,0) (7,12) (12,0) with the holes (2,0) (5,1) (3,3) and (5,0) (8,1) (6,3), both touching the bottom edge y = 0, and you expect a CONTAINS box query to match only boxes that lie inside the polygon. While joining the second hole to the ring, Tessellator.eliminateHole draws a bridge from (5,0) to (2,0) that runs along the outer edge but marks it as an internal edge, because it only compares the bridge with the ring edges next to its two ends, so the indexed triangle loses its 'belongs to the polygon' flag on that piece of the boundary. LatLonShape and XYShape CONTAINS queries then match the box x [3,4], y [-0.5,0.3], which sticks out below the polygon, with no error, on every release executed since 8.4.0.

rows.title: Tessellator covers a hole of a valid polygon when two holes and the outer ring meet at one vertex and an outer edge continues straight into a hole edge there: the filterPoints call after each hole merge drops the copy of that vertex the next hole needs, so LatLonShape and XYShape match points inside the hole (since 8.2.0)
rows.summary: You index a valid polygon with LatLonShape or XYShape whose outer ring and two holes meet only at one vertex P, with an outer edge running straight into a hole edge through P, for example POLYGON((2 6, 2 7, 4 0, 0 0, 2 6), (2 6, 3 1, 3 2, 2 6), (2 6, 1 1, 2 1, 2 6)), and expect the triangles to cover the polygon minus both holes. After hole B (2,6) (1,1) (2,1) is merged at P, the filterPoints call that Tessellator.eliminateHoles runs after every hole (Tessellator.java:347) removes the copy of P that lies on the straight line (2,7)-(2,6)-(2,1); hole A, whose left-most vertex is P, is then merged at the only remaining copy of P, in the wrong wedge, and ear clipping emits triangles over hole B (twice the tessellation area is 25 instead of 20). A point inside hole B such as (1.8, 2) then matches an INTERSECTS point query and a box inside hole B is not DISJOINT; on 9.12.3, 10.4.0 and later this happens only when the outer ring is written starting at P, on 8.2.0 to 9.12.2 and 10.0.0 to 10.3.2 for every ring start tested.

rows.title: XYShape point queries can miss a polygon at one of its own vertices: Component2D.pointInTriangle rejects the second vertex (b) of a clockwise triangle, and ShapeField.encodeTriangle makes XY triangles counter-clockwise only on their sortable-int encodings, so a stored triangle can decode clockwise; an INTERSECTS point query at that vertex misses the polygon and DISJOINT returns it (since 8.5.0)
rows.summary: You index the clockwise triangle (0,1) (1,2) (3,3) as an XYPolygon with XYShape.createIndexableFields and run XYShape.newPointQuery at each of its corners; you expect every corner to match the polygon (INTERSECTS) and none to be DISJOINT from it, as happens for the same triangle moved by (8,8) and for every point of its edges. Instead the INTERSECTS query at (1,2) finds nothing and the DISJOINT query at (1,2) returns the document: ShapeField.encodeTriangle checks the winding on the sortable-int encodings of the floats, which are ordered like the floats but not evenly spaced, so the stored triangle decodes clockwise, and Component2D.pointInTriangle reports the second vertex of a clockwise triangle as outside. The same happens with projected metre-like coordinates, for example at vertex (518885,4395432) of a hexagon whose x range crosses 2^19.
rows.area: geo / XYShape point queries (Component2D.pointInTriangle; ShapeField.encodeTriangle orientation for XY)

rows.title: Tessellator rejects a valid polygon whose holes touch nothing, depending on the outer ring's start vertex, when an earlier hole's bridge continues an outer edge: isLocallyInside treats the resulting straight angle as never inside, so fetchHoleBridge cannot switch to the only correct copy of the bridge end (regression in 8.2.0)
rows.summary: You index a valid polygon with two holes that touch nothing, for example the clockwise outer ring (4,5) (5,1) (0,0) (1,1) with the counter-clockwise holes (2,2) (4,3) (3,3) and (3,2) (3,1) (4,1), and you expect XYShape or LatLonShape.createIndexableFields to return its triangles whichever vertex the outer ring starts at. The first hole is joined to the ring by a bridge from (2,2) to (1,1) that continues the outer edge (0,0)-(1,1) in a straight line; the second hole's bridge search then lands on (1,1), and the only copy of (1,1) whose angle contains that hole has a straight angle, which Tessellator.isLocallyInside always rejects ('area == 0 -> return false'). When the outer ring starts at (5,1) or (0,0) the search keeps the other copy, the bridge crosses the ring and indexing throws 'Unable to Tessellate shape. Possible malformed shape detected.', while the starts (4,5) and (1,1) give the exact area 9; 8.1.1 accepts every start, 8.2.0 to main reject two of them.

rows.title: Tessellator: when three or more holes meet at one vertex P, maybeMergeHoleWithSharedVertices joins the hole whose left-most vertex is P to the first copy of P in ring order (since #15700) even when the hole lies outside that copy's wedge, so LatLonShape and XYShape reject a valid polygon with 'Unable to Tessellate shape' depending on the order of its holes; upstream's own LUCENE-9400 test polygon is rejected in 3 of its 6 hole orders (regression in 10.4.0)
rows.summary: You index a valid polygon whose three holes meet only at one corner P, for example the triangle (0,0) (7,12) (12,2) with the holes A (8,8) (6,7) (7,6), B (9,3) (10,4) (7,6) and C (6,6) (6,4) (7,4) (7,6), which all touch at P=(7,6) (the Tessellator javadoc allows 'Holes may only touch at one vertex'), and you expect XYShape.createIndexableFields or LatLonShape.createIndexableFields to return its triangles, as 10.3.x does for every hole order. Since #15700 (first released in 10.4.0), once the first holes are joined at P the ring holds several copies of P, each bounding a different wedge around P, and when hole B (whose left-most vertex is P) is joined, the Tessellator takes the first copy of P in ring order, through an index comparison that depends on the input order of the holes, without checking that B lies in that copy's wedge. For the hole orders ABC, ACB and BAC this picks a wrong copy and both calls throw IllegalArgumentException 'Unable to Tessellate shape', and upstream's own LUCENE-9400 regression polygon (TestTessellator.testComplexPolygon41) is likewise rejected in 3 of its 6 hole orders.

rows.title: Tessellator rejects a valid polygon whose holes touch the outer ring and each other at single vertices with 'Unable to Tessellate shape', because #15739 made the reflex-vertex test in isLocallyInside inclusive ('<= 0'): a regression in 10.5.0 (10.4.0 accepts the polygon)
rows.summary: You index a valid polygon with holes, for example an L-shaped outer ring (0,0) (0,12) (4,12) (4,4) (12,4) (12,0) with three small triangular holes that touch the ring and each other only at single shared corners, which the Tessellator javadoc allows ('Holes may only touch at one vertex'), and you expect XYShape.createIndexableFields or LatLonShape.createIndexableFields to return its triangles, as 10.4.0 does. Instead, since #15739 (first released in 10.5.0), both calls throw IllegalArgumentException 'Unable to Tessellate shape. Possible malformed shape detected.', so the document cannot be indexed, although every proper subset of the holes tessellates. The cause is that #15739 changed the reflex-vertex branch of Tessellator.isLocallyInside from '< 0' to '<= 0', which accepts a candidate exactly collinear with a neighbouring edge; reverting that comparison fixes this polygon but breaks the #15731 polygon #15739 was written for, so a correct fix has to be more selective.

rows.title: GeoUtils.lineCrossesLineWithBoundary treats collinear segments that do not overlap as crossing and EdgeTree.crossesTriangle lets such pairs through, so LatLonShape/XYShape polygon and line INTERSECTS queries match disjoint shapes and DISJOINT queries drop them
rows.summary: You index a polygon with LatLonShape or XYShape and search with a polygon or line using INTERSECTS (or DISJOINT); you expect a match only when the two shapes share at least one point. When one of the indexed shape's triangles has an edge on exactly the same straight line as a query edge, but further along that line so the two segments do not overlap, and the triangle's third corner reaches back over the query edge, Lucene reports a crossing: GeoUtils.lineCrossesLineWithBoundary answers true for any two collinear segments, and EdgeTree.crossesTriangle only pre-filters by the triangle's bounding box. INTERSECTS then returns the disjoint document and DISJOINT drops it, with no error (repro: query square [0,2]x[0,2] and indexed triangle (3,0),(4,0),(1.5,4), separated by the line x + 0.375y = 3; a box query over the same square answers correctly).

rows.title: Polygon2D.containsLine/containsTriangle accept a segment or triangle whose vertices lie on the boundary of a non-convex polygon even when it passes outside between them, so LatLonShape/XYShape WITHIN queries return false positives
rows.summary: You index a line or polygon whose corner points lie exactly on the boundary of a non-convex (dented) query polygon, for example a road between two corners of a district, and search for shapes WITHIN that polygon; you expect only shapes that lie inside it. Polygon2D.containsLine/containsTriangle accept a segment or triangle when every vertex is contained, with boundary points counting as inside, and no polygon edge crosses it strictly; that shortcut is only valid for convex polygons, so a segment that cuts across a dent between two boundary points, or a triangle that fills the dent and whose interior lies outside, is reported as contained. The WITHIN query returns those documents with no error (repro: for the polygon (0,0),(4,0),(4,4),(2,1),(0,4), WITHIN returns the indexed segment (0,4)-(4,4) and the indexed notch triangle (0,4),(4,4),(2,1) although (2,4) and (2,3) are outside the polygon).
rows.area: geo / shape queries (Polygon2D containsLine/containsTriangle, LatLonShape and XYShape WITHIN)

rows.title: LatLonShape/XYShape CONTAINS with a query polygon that has holes returns indexed shapes that do not contain it, because Polygon2D.withinTriangle never tests the query's hole edges
rows.summary: You index polygons with LatLonShape or XYShape and ask which of them CONTAIN a query polygon that has holes, for example a region with two lakes cut out; an indexed polygon whose own hole runs across the land between the two lakes does not cover that land, so it must not match. Polygon2D.withinTriangle rejects an indexed triangle only when one of its vertices is inside the query or one of its real (original-shape) edges crosses the query's outer ring; it never tests the query's hole edges, so an edge that starts and ends inside query holes and crosses the land between them goes unnoticed and the shape is returned as CONTAINS, with no error. Repro: query = the square [0,10]^2 with holes [1,3]x[4,6] and [7,9]x[4,6]; doc 0 = the square [-1,11]^2 with a hole [2,8]x[4.5,5.5] (it does not cover the query point (5,5)), doc 1 = the same square without a hole; CONTAINS returns [0, 1] instead of [1] for XYShape and LatLonShape, while a point query at (5,5) correctly returns only doc 1.

rows.title: Lat/lon distance queries can drop a point whose distance equals the radius and match a point one ulp beyond it, because GeoUtils.distanceQuerySortKey does not return the largest sort key within the radius (every release since 6.1.0)
rows.summary: You index points with LatLonPoint (or LatLonDocValuesField or LatLonShape) and run a distance query whose radius is exactly a point's distance from the center as Lucene computes it (SloppyMath.haversinMeters, the same value a distance sort or LatLonPoint.nearest reports), and expect that point to match, because the query matches 'points within the specified distance' and Lucene's own test oracle is haversinMeters(center, point) <= radius; with the radius one ulp smaller you expect it not to match. Instead the point is often missing in the first case and often still matches in the second (each in roughly a fifth to a third of random cases, depending on the points): for example, two points that both the distance sort and haversinMeters put 8154434.476304402 m apart are not matched by any of the three distance queries with exactly that radius. The cause is GeoUtils.distanceQuerySortKey, which turns the radius into a sort-key threshold by binary search: it returns the first key it meets whose distance equals the radius, not the largest such key, so a point on a larger key of the same distance fails 'key <= threshold', and when no key has exactly that distance it returns the smallest key whose distance exceeds the radius.
rows.area: core / geo distance queries (GeoUtils.distanceQuerySortKey, shared by LatLonPoint, LatLonDocValuesField and LatLonShape circle queries)

rows.title: XYShape circle queries miss lines and polygons that enter the circle only near its extreme x or y, and can report CONTAINS for a polygon the circle sticks out of, when the centre coordinate is large relative to the radius, because XYRectangle.fromPointDistance rounds the circle's bounding box inward
rows.summary: You index an XYShape line that passes just inside a circle and search with XYShape.newDistanceQuery (INTERSECTS) for an XYCircle whose centre coordinate is large compared with the radius, for example centre (2^23, 2^23+1), radius 1.3 and the segment (2^23+1, 2^23)-(2^23+2, 2^23+3), which passes 1.265 from the centre, expecting the hit you get for the same shapes moved exactly to the origin. Instead INTERSECTS finds nothing and DISJOINT matches the document, because XYRectangle.fromPointDistance builds the circle's bounding box as x + nextUp(r) in float, which rounds to nearest (2^23 + 1.3 becomes 2^23 + 1), and since 8.6.0 Circle2D's Cartesian contains() rejects every point outside that too-small box before its exact distance test, including the segment's closest point to the centre. The same box makes CONTAINS report that a polygon contains a circle that sticks out of it.
rows.area: geo / XYShape circle queries (XYRectangle.fromPointDistance, Circle2D.CartesianDistance)

rows.title: On WGS84 and other non-spherical planet models, the outside distance from a point to a geo3d circle smaller than about 50 km is +Infinity in most directions (GeoCircle.computeOutsideDistance with the ARC or LINEAR style, and so Geo3DDocValuesField.newOutsideDistanceSort, which then sorts valid documents as if they had no value), because Plane.arcDistance and Plane.linearDistance look for the edge on the line where the circle's plane meets a plane through the origin, the plane normal and the point, and on an ellipsoid that line misses a small circle
rows.summary: You build a 1 km circle on the default WGS84 planet model (GeoCircleFactory.makeGeoCircle, or Geo3DDocValuesField.newOutsideDistanceSort with maxRadiusMeters 1000) and ask for the outside distance of points 3 km from the centre, expecting about 2 km in every direction (0.0 inside, distance to the edge outside). Instead computeOutsideDistance returns +Infinity at 10 of 12 bearings (only due north and due south are right), and the sort gives most documents outside the circle +Infinity, the value the javadoc reserves for documents missing the field, so they sort last. The cause: Plane.arcDistance and Plane.linearDistance look for the nearest edge point on the line where the circle's plane meets a plane through the origin, the plane normal and the point; on a sphere that line passes through the circle's centre, but on an ellipsoid the circle plane's normal is tilted, the line passes about 21 km from the circle at latitude 40, and for a smaller circle it finds no edge point at all, so the minimum keeps its +Infinity start value.

rows.title: GeoStandardPath outside distance measures end caps (and one-point paths) to the end point instead of the cap edge, so values are too large by up to the path half-width and Geo3DDocValuesField.newOutsidePathSort misorders documents
rows.summary: You build a path with a width (GeoPathFactory.makeGeoPath, or the pathWidthMeters of Geo3DDocValuesField.newOutsidePathSort) and ask for the outside distance of a point beyond one of its ends, expecting 'the distance from a point to the closest outside edge' (GeoOutsideDistance), which is how the same path measures points beside its segments and how GeoCircle measures a circle. Instead you get the distance to the path's end point, i.e. the gap plus up to the half-width: on the unit sphere a point 0.001 rad beyond the end of a path of half-width 0.01 gets 0.011, a one-point path reports 0.011 where the same-size GeoCircle reports 0.001, the value jumps from 0 to about the half-width as a point crosses the end cap's edge, and on WGS84 the outside-path sort ranks a document 1 km beyond the end of a path of half-width 5 km (5992 m) after one 3 km beside it (3067 m). The cause is BaseSegmentEndpoint.outsideDistance, which every endpoint with a width inherits: it measures to the end point itself, which is the edge only for a zero-width path.
rows.area: spatial3d / geom path outside distance (GeoStandardPath segment endpoints; Geo3DDocValuesField.newOutsidePathSort)

rows.title: Geo3D outside distance to a lat/lon box that reaches a pole (GeoNorthRectangle / GeoSouthRectangle) ignores the pole, so Geo3DDocValuesField.newOutsideBoxSort gives documents beyond the pole the distance to a far corner (39.88 instead of 10 degrees for the box lat 60..90 x lon -10..10 and the point (80, 180)) and sorts them after nearer documents
rows.summary: You sort documents by their outside distance from a lat/lon box that reaches the North Pole, for example latitude 60..90 x longitude -10..10, with Geo3DDocValuesField.newOutsideBoxSort. A document at (80, 180) is only 10 degrees (about 1,112 km) from that box, because the box contains the pole, so it should sort before a document at (35, 0), which is 25 degrees south of the box. Instead GeoNorthRectangle.outsideDistance never considers the pole, where both side edges of the box end, and returns the distance to a far corner (39.88 degrees on the sphere; 4,434,716 m against 2,779,879 m in the WGS84 sort), so the nearer document sorts last; GeoSouthRectangle has the mirror bug at the South Pole.

rows.title: Geo3d reports two shapes that touch at a single point as nested (WITHIN/CONTAINS) instead of overlapping when the touch point is a circle's one sampled edge point, so IsWithin and Contains spatial queries (SerializedDVStrategy, CompositeSpatialStrategy) return circles that lie mostly outside the query shape
rows.summary: You create a circle and a box (or a second circle) that touch at exactly one point, for example with the Geo3d spatial context a 20-degree circle centred at latitude 55 and a box whose southern edge is latitude 75, and expect relate() to report INTERSECTS (shapes that share a point intersect, and spatial3d may only weaken WITHIN to OVERLAPS, never the reverse). Instead it reports WITHIN or CONTAINS, as if one shape were inside the other: GeoBaseAreaShape.getRelationship infers nesting from sampled edge points plus a plane-intersection test, a standard circle has a single edge point, and when that point lies on the other shape's boundary the 1e-12 membership test counts it as inside while Plane.intersects' one-solution test misses the touch. So SerializedDVStrategy's IsWithin(box) returns the circle although its centre is 20 degrees outside the box, while radius 19.9 or 20.1 degrees gives the correct DISJOINT or INTERSECTS.

rows.title: GeoBBox.expand clamps a widened longitude bound at +-180 degrees instead of wrapping it across the antimeridian, so expanded geo3d boxes (and Geo3dRectangleShape.getBuffered / WKT BUFFER(ENVELOPE(...)) in a Geo3D spatial context) miss the part beyond the dateline
rows.summary: You take a geo3d box whose east edge is near the dateline, for example longitudes [2.5, 3.0] radians, and call expand(0.3), or in a Geo3D spatial context you search 'Intersects(BUFFER(ENVELOPE(172, 178, 4, -4), 4))'. You expect each bound to move out by the angle, so the box now crosses the dateline and reaches -2.983 radians (-178 degrees), as the same code already does for a box that crosses the dateline and as spatial4j's own geo rectangle buffer does. Instead expand passes the unwrapped bound 3.3 to GeoBBoxFactory.makeGeoBBox, which clamps it to PI, so the box stops at 180 degrees and a document at (-179.5, 1) is not found (0 hits instead of 1); the west edge and all 13 GeoBBox classes with a longitude range behave the same way.

rows.title: GeoDegenerateLatitudeZone.isWithin compares z with sin(latitude) at a 1e-10 tolerance instead of using its own planet-model plane, so a zero-height geo3d box spanning all longitudes rejects the points on its own latitude on WGS84 and, on any planet model, can report CONTAINS for areas just below it, which makes Geo3D prefix-tree searches match points tens of degrees away
rows.summary: You build a geo3d box whose top and bottom latitude are equal and which spans all longitudes, for example GeoBBoxFactory.makeGeoBBox(WGS84, 0.5, 0.5, -PI, PI), and expect it to contain exactly the points on that latitude, as the same line over [-179, 179] degrees does. Its isWithin compares a point's z with sin(latitude), the unit-sphere value, with a 1e-10 tolerance, instead of the planet-model plane that the class builds and uses everywhere else, so on WGS84 it rejects every point on its own latitude (and accepts a parallel about 1.2 km away). On any planet model, including the default sphere of the Geo3D spatial context, the 100x looser tolerance makes getRelationship report that the line CONTAINS a rectangle just below it, so a prefix-tree Intersects query for rect(-180, 180, 45.000000001, 45.000000001) matched 4 points at latitudes 10, 10, 30 and 44 degrees, while the [-179, 179] control matched none.

rows.title: GeoExactCircle.computeOutsideDistance never measures the slice end points where two of its approximation slices meet, so a point outside whose nearest edge point is such a joint gets +Infinity or the distance to the far side of the circle: on WGS84 every point due north or due south of the centre, at any radius; on the sphere a point 0.001 rad due west of a 1e-4 rad exact circle gets 0.0012
rows.summary: You build an exact circle on the default WGS84 planet model (GeoCircleFactory.makeExactGeoCircle, centre latitude 0.3 and longitude 0.2, radius 0.1 rad, about 637 km, accuracy 1e-6) and ask computeOutsideDistance for a point 0.11 rad due north of the centre, expecting 'the distance from a point to the closest outside edge' (GeoOutsideDistance), about 0.0096. Instead you get +Infinity, and the same for every point due north or due south at any distance; on the unit sphere a point 0.001 rad due west of a 1e-4 rad exact circle gets 0.0012, the distance to the far side of the circle. The cause: GeoExactCircle.outsideDistance takes the minimum of each slice's plane distance bounded to that slice's sector and never measures the slice end points, so when the nearest edge point is a joint between two slices, the point's foot on each neighbouring plane falls just outside its sector, both return +Infinity, and the minimum is +Infinity or a foot on the far side.

rows.title: geo.Rectangle checks minLat <= maxLat only with an assert, so a lat/lon box with swapped latitudes (new Rectangle, LatLonShape.newBoxQuery, a WKT ENVELOPE) throws a bare AssertionError with -ea and is silently accepted with -da, where LatLonShape box queries then return hits that match no region; the Cartesian twin XYRectangle throws IllegalArgumentException for the same mistake
rows.summary: You build a lat/lon box with the minimum and maximum latitude swapped, for example LatLonShape.newBoxQuery(field, INTERSECTS, 10, 5, 0, 1) or the WKT text ENVELOPE(0, 1, 5, 10), and expect an IllegalArgumentException, as XYRectangle gives for the same mistake and as Rectangle itself gives for an out-of-range latitude. Rectangle's constructor checks the order only with 'assert maxLat >= minLat', so with assertions enabled you get a bare AssertionError, and with assertions disabled the inverted box is accepted. The shape query then matches only shapes that cross both latitude lines (INTERSECTS) or the complement of those (DISJOINT), which is neither the empty result that LatLonPoint.newBoxQuery gives for the same box nor the result of the swapped box.

Instead the query is accepted, because the XYShapeQuery constructor has validated nothing since LUCENE-9194 (8.5.0) folded the old XY line query into it. rows.title: LatLonPoint.newGeometryQuery with QueryRelation.CONTAINS returns a query that matches nothing instead of the documented IllegalArgumentException when the geometry array is empty or holds a null (LatLonDocValuesField.newSlowGeometryQuery does the same for a null element), because the CONTAINS shortcut runs before any argument check (since 8.8.0, LUCENE-9641)
rows.summary: You call LatLonPoint.newGeometryQuery("f", QueryRelation.CONTAINS) with no geometries (an empty array), or with an array that holds a null, and expect the IllegalArgumentException its javadoc promises ('if latLonGeometries is null, empty or contain a null'), which INTERSECTS and WITHIN and the doc-values twin LatLonDocValuesField.newSlowGeometryQuery("f", CONTAINS) throw for the empty array ('geometries must not be empty'). Instead you get a query that matches no document: a ConstantScoreQuery over an empty BooleanQuery for the empty array, and MatchNoDocsQuery('Contains LatLonPoint.newGeometryQuery with non-point geometries') for a null element, which newSlowGeometryQuery also returns for a null element. The CONTAINS shortcut runs before any argument check: its loop never runs for an empty array, and a null element fails 'instanceof Point' and lands in the branch meant for valid non-point geometries.

rows.title: Geo3DPoint.newDistanceQuery accepts a negative radius (for example -1 m) instead of throwing the IllegalArgumentException its javadoc promises, and silently builds the radius-0 query, while LatLonPoint.newDistanceQuery rejects the same radius
rows.summary: You call Geo3DPoint.newDistanceQuery("f", PlanetModel.WGS84, 0, 0, -1) with a negative radius, for example a computed radius that went below zero, and expect the IllegalArgumentException its javadoc promises (radiusMeters 'must be non-negative and finite'; '@throws IllegalArgumentException if ... radius is invalid'), which LatLonPoint.newDistanceQuery throws for the same value ("radiusMeters: '-1.0' is invalid"). rows.title: QuadPrefixTree/PackedQuadPrefixTree with non-power-of-two world bounds put a point that lies on a grid line into a cell whose shape excludes it, so Intersects misses the document (deep trees throw InvalidShapeException)
rows.summary: You index a point with RecursivePrefixTreeStrategy over a QuadPrefixTree (or PackedQuadPrefixTree) in a non-geo SpatialContext whose world bounds are not powers of two, such as Web Mercator's +/-pi*6378137, and the point lies exactly on a grid line (for example longitude 45 degrees projected, at y = 0) or on the world's east edge. You expect Intersects with that same point, or with a box whose edge passes through it, to find the document, because getCell is documented to return 'the cell containing point p' and the query error may only inflate a shape, never shrink it. Instead getCell chooses the cell by comparing the point with mid-points accumulated one way while QuadCell.makeShape rebuilds that cell's edges another way, the two floating-point results differ by one ulp, so the indexed cell's shape ends just short of the point, the query treats it as disjoint and returns 0 hits (and with the 50-level factory default a query for a point on the world's top edge throws InvalidShapeException).

rows.title: S2PrefixTree: a Contains query whose shape is a point P misses a document indexed with that same point P when P lies on an S2 cell edge (the equator, an S2 face edge, (0,0)), because the query side follows every child cell that touches P while indexing puts P in one cell per level
rows.summary: You index a document with point P through RecursivePrefixTreeStrategy over S2PrefixTree in the Geo3d spatial context and search with SpatialOperation.Contains and the same point P, expecting the document, because Contains is documented as the OGC 'Covers' predicate and its evaluate(P, P) is true, RecursivePrefixTreeStrategy builds a ContainsPrefixTreeQuery for it, a point query is resolved at full precision, and the geohash and quad trees do return the document. When P lies exactly on an S2 cell edge, for example Point(10, 0) on the equator, Contains finds 0 documents while Intersects finds 1. Indexing puts P in one cell per level (S2PrefixTree.getTreeCellIterator, from S2CellId.fromLatLng), but at query time S2PrefixTreeCell.getNextLevelCells has no point case and returns every child cell that touches P (2 on an edge, 4 at (0,0)), and ContainsPrefixTreeQuery requires the document to be in all of them.

rows.title: PackedQuadPrefixTree in a geo context indexes a point at longitude +180 under the -180 edge cell, but point queries look in the +180 edge cell, so RPT and CompositeSpatialStrategy Intersects/Contains with that same point miss the document
rows.summary: You index a point at longitude +180, for example Pt(180, 10), with RecursivePrefixTreeStrategy over PackedQuadPrefixTree(SpatialContext.GEO, 8) and query Intersects or Contains with that same point; the document must match, since a point intersects and contains itself and the prefix-tree approximation may only add matches (SpatialArgs: the error 'should not shrink' the shape). Instead the query returns 0 hits, and so does CompositeSpatialStrategy's Intersects: indexing keeps the first cell in Z order whose rectangle relate()s to the point, and a geo rectangle treats +180 as -180, so the point is stored in the cells at the -180 edge, while the point query's cell lookup (PackedQuadPrefixTree.getCell, a mid-point walk since LUCENE-8755 in 8.3.0) sends x=+180 to the cells at the +180 edge. The same point at -180, QuadPrefixTree, and a rectangle query touching +180 still find the document.

rows.title: PointVectorStrategy misses a point at longitude +180 or -180 when a rectangle query that does not cross the dateline has its edge on that meridian with the other sign (-180 vs +180)

Instead a point stored at x=+180 is missed by a box whose west edge is -180 (Pt(180,0) with rect(-180,-170,-10,10): 0 hits, oracle 1), and a point at x=-180 by a box whose east edge is +180 (Pt(-180,0) with rect(170,180,-10,10)). BBoxStrategy and both prefix-tree strategies in the same module return the hit; PointVectorStrategy.makeWithin filters x with one plain DoublePoint range [minX, maxX] for every non-crossing box, so +180 and -180 are different values to it.

rows.title: BBoxStrategy and PointVectorStrategy miss a shape on a query edge at 0 when the shape's coordinate and the edge are zeros of opposite sign (-0.0 vs +0.0), so BBoxStrategy finds a point Intersecting a rectangle but not Within it
rows.summary: You index a point stored at longitude -0.0 (for example parsed from 'POINT(-0 5)') with BBoxStrategy and PointVectorStrategy and query the rectangle Rect(minX=0.0, maxX=10, minY=0, maxY=10); you expect the point to match Intersects and IsWithin in both strategies, because SpatialOperation.evaluate says it lies on the rectangle's west edge (spatial4j compares coordinates as primitives, so -0.0 == 0.0). Instead BBoxStrategy finds it for Intersects but not for IsWithin, and PointVectorStrategy finds it for neither, with no error. Both strategies pass the rectangle's 0.0 edge unchanged as an inclusive DoublePoint range bound, and DoublePoint orders -0.0 below +0.0; BBoxStrategy's Intersects uses only exclusive bounds, which it moves with Math.nextUp/Math.nextDown, and those give the same result for both zeros.

rows.title: LatLon distance sort from a pole origin: the competitive bounding box (7 cm margin) rejects documents that tie with the queue bottom near the opposite pole, so the secondary SortField is skipped and top-N and searchAfter results are wrong
rows.summary: You index two points about 45 cm from the north pole with LatLonDocValuesField and sort with Sort(LatLonDocValuesField.newDistanceSort("p", -90, 146.5868...), new SortField("tie", INT)); both documents report the same distance (2.0015113815150492E7 m) and search(n=2) correctly returns [1, 0], the tie broken by "tie". You expect search(n=1) to return that head, doc 1, and one-hit searchAfter pages to return [1, 0]. Instead search(n=1) returns doc 0 and the pages return only doc 0: once doc 0 is the queue bottom, the comparator's pruning box (radius = the bottom's sloppy distance + 7 cm) leaves out doc 1, whose exact distance near the antipode exceeds that sloppy distance by more than 7 cm, so compareBottom returns -1 instead of 0 without computing doc 1's equal key and the secondary sort never runs.

rows.title: LatLonShape WITHIN a circle that crosses the dateline matches a line or polygon whose vertices lie inside the circle on both sides of the dateline, although Lucene runs its edges through longitude 0, far outside the circle: Circle2D.containsLine/containsTriangle test only the vertices
rows.summary: You index a two-point LatLonShape line from (lat 0, lon -179.5) to (lat 0, lon 179.5); Lucene runs its edge straight through (0, 0), so the document matches INTERSECTS a 100 km circle around (0, 0). A WITHIN query with a 100 km circle around (0, 180), 20,000 km from that point, should then return 0 hits, but it returns 1 with no error. Circle2D treats a circle that crosses the dateline as two longitude pieces, and containsLine/containsTriangle accept a shape once every vertex lies in either piece, never checking that the edges between them stay inside.

rows.title: ShapeDocValues getCentroid() returns (0, 0), far outside the shape's own bounding box, when the shape's total encoded length or area is zero (a line whose points coincide after encoding, or a polygon thinner than one encoding step)
rows.summary: You build a doc-values shape with LatLonShape.createDocValueField or XYShape.createDocValueField and ask for its centroid; you expect getCentroid(), documented as 'the centroid location for the geometry', to be a point of the shape, inside the bounding box that the same object returns. For a line whose points coincide after encoding (new Line({40, 40}, {-70, -70}), or two points closer than one encoding step) or a polygon thinner than one encoding step, Lucene returns Point(0.0, 0.0) instead, 7,500 km or more from the shape in these examples: the centroid is weighted by length or area, and when the total weight is zero the code skips the division and keeps the zero numerator. The other public factory, createDocValueField(name, createIndexableFields(name, line)), returns the real point for the same line.

rows.title: LatLonShapeDocValues and XYShapeDocValues getEncodedMinX/MinY/MaxX/MaxY return a tree node's box instead of the shape's bounding box after a relate() call that descends the shape's tree, because the getters read the reader's reusable scratch box
rows.summary: You build a LatLonShapeDocValues (or XYShapeDocValues) from a shape's doc-value bytes, call relate() with a query box, and then read getEncodedMinX/MinY/MaxX/MaxY, which are documented as 'the shape's bounding box'; you expect the same four values as before the relate() call. Instead, when the query box crosses the shape's box so that relate() walks down the shape's tree, the getters afterwards return the box of the last tree node visited: for the points (0,0), (10,10), (20,20) and a small box around (0,0), relate() correctly answers CELL_CROSSES_QUERY but getEncodedMaxX() then returns 0 instead of encodeLongitude(20) = 238609294, with no error. The getters read the reader's single reusable scratch box, which relate() overwrites for every node it visits, while getBoundingBox() of the same object, computed once in the constructor, stays correct.

rows.title: Tessellator.cureLocalIntersections adds each triangle it cuts off twice, so LatLonShape and XYShape index that triangle twice and the shape doc-values centroid counts its area twice
rows.summary: You index a polygon with LatLonShape or XYShape (createIndexableFields or createDocValueField) and expect each triangle of its tessellation to be stored once. When the Tessellator's cure step (cureLocalIntersections) cuts off a triangle to repair a small local self-intersection, it appends that same triangle twice (two identical tessellation.add calls at Tessellator.java:890 and :892, left by LUCENE-8620 in 8.3.0), so the shape carries one extra indexed triangle, ShapeDocValuesField.numberOfTerms is one too high and getCentroid() counts that triangle's area twice; query results do not change. On its own the cure step fires only for self-crossing rings, which the javadoc excludes but the default checkSelfIntersections=false path accepts (for example POLYGON((6 3, 0 6, 4 0, 3 4, 5 1, 3 2, 6 3)), duplicated on every release from 8.3.0), and a valid polygon reaches it only when it already hits LFV-210 (a hole touching the shell), whose fix removes it.
rows.area: geo / Tessellator cure step (polygon indexing for LatLonShape and XYShape, shape doc values)

rows.title: Tessellator self-intersection check misses crossings in polygons with more than 80 points, so LatLonShape/XYShape.createIndexableFields with checkSelfIntersections=true accept and index a self-crossing polygon
rows.summary: You index the self-crossing ring (x y) 5 2, 3 2, 6 0, 9 9, 7 5, 1 1 with XYShape.createIndexableFields("f", polygon, true), written with 74 extra points on its straight edge from (5,2) to (3,2), so 81 points in all. You expect the IllegalArgumentException 'Polygon self-intersection at ...' that the same call throws for the 7-point and the 80-point forms of the same ring, because the javadoc says that with checkSelfIntersections the validity of the polygon is checked. Instead the call returns triangle fields and the self-crossing polygon is indexed: above 80 points the Tessellator runs the check on its z-order (Morton) path, which never uses the two edges at the start vertex as primary edges and finds other edges only when their start vertex lies in the primary edge's bounding box, so it does not compare every pair of edges.

rows.title: With checkSelfIntersections=true, XYShape and LatLonShape accept a ring whose horizontal or vertical edges overlap each other, but reject the same ring rotated by 45 degrees: the bounding-box prefilter in Tessellator.checkIntersectionPoint returns before the overlap test for collinear axis-parallel edges
rows.summary: You index a polygon with XYShape.createIndexableFields(name, polygon, true), asking Lucene to check that it is valid, and its ring runs back over part of itself along a horizontal line: (4,4) (1,1) (4,1) (2,0) (0,1) (2,1), whose edges (1,1)-(4,1) and (0,1)-(2,1) overlap on y = 1 for x from 1 to 2. You expect the IllegalArgumentException 'Polygon ring self-intersection', which is exactly what the same ring rotated by 45 degrees gets. Instead the ring is accepted and indexed as if the check were off, because checkIntersectionPoint's bounding-box prefilter skips every edge pair whose boxes only touch, and two collinear horizontal (or vertical) edges always have boxes that only touch, so the overlap test behind the prefilter is never reached for them; LatLonShape behaves the same.

rows.title: Geo3dRectangleShape.reset(minX, maxX, minY, maxY) replaces the wrapped spatial3d box but keeps the old minX/maxX/minY/maxY, so with the Geo3d spatial context BBoxStrategy shape values report a stale box for every document and BBoxStrategy overlap-ratio relevance scores are wrong
rows.summary: You use the Geo3d spatial context (Geo3dSpatialContextFactory) with BBoxStrategy and read each document's box with makeShapeValueSource() or rank by makeOverlapRatioValueSource(queryBox, ...), or you call reset(10, 20, 30, 40) on a Geo3d rectangle yourself. You expect reset to replace the whole rectangle (the spatial4j Rectangle.reset javadoc: 'Resets the state of this shape given the arguments'; spatial4j's own RectangleImpl.reset assigns all four bounds), so getMinX()..getMaxY() return 10, 20, 30, 40, the shape values return each document's indexed box, and a document box equal to the query scores 1.0, as it does with the default SpatialContext.GEO. Instead Geo3dRectangleShape.reset rebuilds only the wrapped GeoBBox and clears the center and bounding-box caches, never assigning the four fields that getMinX()..getMaxY(), getWidth(), getHeight() and getCrossesDateLine() read: the rectangle equals rect(10, 20, 30, 40) but reports its previous bounds, BBoxValueSource (which creates one rect(0, 0, 0, 0) per segment and resets it for each document) reports (0, 0, 0, 0) for every document, and the self-overlap score is 0.0.

rows.title: SpatialStrategy.makeRecipDistanceValueSource takes zScaling from half the corner-to-corner great-circle distance of the query's bounding box, which goes the short way round the globe once a geo box is wider than 180 degrees of longitude, so edge scores fall far below the documented ~0.1 (0.0082 for rect(-170,170,-10,10), 0.0028 for a 5S-5N band of all longitudes; released since 4.0.0)
rows.summary: You score a geo spatial query with makeRecipDistanceValueSource, whose javadoc says zScaling is one tenth of the distance from the centre to the farthest edge, so scores run from 1 at the centre down to about 0.1 at the furthest edge. For a box wider than 180 degrees of longitude the method instead takes half the great-circle distance between the box's two opposite corners, and that distance goes the short way round the globe: for rect(-170,170,-10,10) zScaling is 1.41 instead of 17.0, and the edge point (170,0) scores 0.0082 instead of about 0.091 (for the band rect(-180,180,-5,5), 0.0028). Nothing fails; distance is over-weighted, so with FunctionScoreQuery.boostByValue a hit with inner score 10 at 170 degrees ranks below a hit with inner score 1 at 10 degrees on the band query, the reverse of the documented scaling.

rows.title: BBoxStrategy's overlap-ratio relevance (BBoxOverlapRatioValueSource) undercounts the overlap of two dateline-crossing boxes that intersect in two longitude pieces, so the score is too low
rows.summary: You index a dateline-crossing rectangle with BBoxStrategy in the default geo context and score it with makeOverlapRatioValueSource and a query rectangle that also crosses the dateline, and you expect the documented score intersectionArea/queryArea*p + intersectionArea/targetArea*(1-p), where intersectionArea is 'the area of the intersection between the query and target envelopes'. When the two boxes wrap far enough round the globe that they overlap twice, once across the dateline and once on the far side (query rect(10,-170,-10,10) and document rect(170,20,-10,10) share 170..-170 across the dateline, 20 degrees, and 10..20, 10 degrees), the score counts only the piece across the dateline: 0.10317460317460317 instead of 0.15476190476190477 at p = 0.5. The both-cross branch computes the width as right - left + 360, which is only that piece, while the branch for one crossing box already adds up both pieces.

rows.title: DirectSpellChecker with a non-default StringDistance prunes candidates by comparing the metric's score with FuzzyTermsEnum boosts, so better candidates are never inspected (regression since 7.0)
rows.summary: You give DirectSpellChecker a metric such as LevenshteinDistance or JaroWinklerDistance and expect what setDistance documents: candidates drawn from the term dictionary by Damerau-Levenshtein (the internal similarity), then ranked by your metric. Since 7.0 the code stores your metric's score in ScoreTerm.boost, a field documented as the internal similarity, and then skips later candidates and tells FuzzyTermsEnum to lower its edit distance by comparing their internal similarity with that number, which is on a different scale, so better terms are never looked at. With default settings, the index {lucen, lucena, lucenb, lucenc, lucend, lucenes} and the query 'lucene', LevenshteinDistance returns 'lucen' (0.833) instead of 'lucenes' (0.857), and with maxInspections=1 and the index {lucen, lucenes} all three shipped metrics return 'lucen' although 'lucenes' scores higher under the internal similarity and under each metric.
rows.area: suggest / spell checking (DirectSpellChecker.suggestSimilar with a non-default StringDistance; FuzzyTermsEnum competitive-boost pruning)

rows.title: SpellChecker.indexDictionary de-duplicates against its cached searcher instead of the index its new IndexWriter writes, so a rebuild with OpenMode.CREATE silently drops every word of the new dictionary that the old spell index already had (and after a failed searcher reopen, later calls drop words or index them twice)

You expect the spell index to hold apple and cherry. Instead it holds only cherry: the new writer starts from an empty index, but indexDictionary skips every word that its cached searcher of the old index still contains, so apple is silently dropped; the same stale check makes a call after a failed searcher reopen drop words (after clearIndex()) or index them twice (on a retry).

rows.title: RussianAnalyzer does not remove its default stop words when they are written with ё (её, ещё, всё, неё, чём): its StopFilter runs before the stemmer folds ё to е, although the bundled stop list says ё is translated to е
rows.summary: You analyze Russian text with the stock RussianAnalyzer. Its default stop list, the bundled Snowball russian_stop.txt, says in its header that 'letter ё is translated to е', so it lists её, ещё, всё, неё and чём only as ее, еще, все, нее and чем, and since 9.0 the same analyzer without stop words maps the ё and е spellings of every word that reaches its stemmer to one term. But the StopFilter runs before the only step that folds ё to е (the Snowball RussianStemmer), so the е spellings are removed while the ё spellings pass the StopFilter and are indexed as е, ещ, все, не and чем: 'Он все еще читает книгу' gives [чита, книг] but 'Он всё ещё читает книгу' gives [все, ещ, чита, книг], with no error.

rows.title: TeluguAnalyzer runs its StopFilter after Indic and Telugu normalization, but its default stop list is not normalized, so 13 of the 43 single-word default stop words (for example కూడా, 'also') are never removed
rows.summary: You analyze Telugu text with the stock new TeluguAnalyzer(), whose default stop list (te/stopwords.txt) holds common function words such as కూడా ('also') that the analyzer should drop. The analyzer normalizes every token before its StopFilter and folds long vowel signs to short ones (ూ to ు, ీ to ి, ే to ె, ో to ొ), but the list holds only the unnormalized spellings, so the StopFilter sees కుడా and never matches the entry కూడా. As a result 13 of the 43 single-word default stop words are never removed and are indexed and searched as ordinary terms, while the Hindi analyzer, which has the same chain, ships the normalized forms in its list and removes all of its stop words.

rows.title: BengaliAnalyzer never removes 13 of its 116 default stop words (e.g. কারণ, শুধু, মধ্যে, অন্য) because its StopFilter runs after Indic/Bengali normalization while the bundled stopwords.txt has only unnormalized spellings
rows.summary: You index Bengali text with the stock BengaliAnalyzer, whose constructor javadoc says it uses the default stop words from its bundled stopwords.txt, so a listed word such as কারণ ('because') should produce no token. But the analyzer runs IndicNormalizationFilter and BengaliNormalizationFilter before its StopFilter, and they rewrite letters (শ and ষ to স, ণ to ন, ঙ to ং, the ্য sign is dropped), while the bundled list holds only the original spellings, unlike the Hindi list in the same module, which also carries the normalized forms. So 13 of the 116 default stop words never match and are indexed and searched as ordinary terms (কারণ becomes কারন, শুধু becomes সুধু, অন্য becomes অন), with no error.

rows.title: QueryAutoStopWordAnalyzer's percentage constructors compute the stop-word threshold from numDocs() (live documents) but compare it with docFreq(), which still counts deleted documents, so after updateDocument terms below the configured percentage become stop words and are silently dropped from queries (since 2.4.0)
rows.summary: You index three documents whose body fields are 'w', 'x' and 'y', re-index each one unchanged with updateDocument (the deleted copies are not merged away yet), open a reader and build new QueryAutoStopWordAnalyzer(analyzer, reader) with its default 40% threshold; you expect no stop words, because the javadoc makes a term a stop word only when it is in more than maxPercentDocs 'of index documents', and each term is in 1 of the 3 live documents and in 2 of the 6 documents that count the deleted copies (33% either way). Instead getStopWords("body") returns [w, x, y] and the analyzer drops 'w' from a query: the percentage constructor computes the threshold from live documents only, (int) (numDocs() * 0.4f) = 1 (QueryAutoStopWordAnalyzer.java:113), but compares it with TermsEnum.docFreq() = 2 (:140), which still counts the deleted copies, so the 'percentage' it tests is 67% here and can exceed 100%.

rows.title: SoraniAnalyzer, LatvianAnalyzer and GalicianAnalyzer load the '#' comment lines of their bundled stopwords.txt as stop words: 60 of the 122 entries of SoraniAnalyzer.getDefaultStopSet(), 9 of 170 for Latvian (including a bare '#') and 1 of 161 for Galician are comment text
