rows.title: WordDelimiterGraphFilterFactory's types option (and the deprecated WordDelimiterFilterFactory's) refills the whole Latin-1 type table from getType() instead of the filter's default table, so any rule, even one that restates a character's own type, silently changes how 8 other characters (¹ ² ³ ¼ ½ ¾ ª º) are tokenized
rows.summary: You give WordDelimiterGraphFilterFactory a types file with one rule for a character that is not in your text (for example '$ => DIGIT', or even '- => SUBWORD_DELIM', which '-' already is) and expect every other character to keep the type it has without the option. Instead parseTypes fills all 256 Latin-1 entries from WordDelimiterIterator.getType() (the Unicode general category), while the table the filter uses without the option is built from Character.isLowerCase/isUpperCase/isDigit; the two disagree on exactly 8 characters, so 'm² x³ 1½ ¼' analyzes to [m, ², x, ³, 1½, ¼] instead of [m, x, 1] and 'ªB' is no longer split. Nothing reports an error; a small change that seeds the Latin-1 entries from the default table fixes both factories.

rows.title: Word2VecSynonymProvider returns maxSynonymsPerTerm + 1 synonyms when the query term is not among its own k+1 HNSW hits (tied vectors or an approximate-search miss), so Word2VecSynonymFilter emits one synonym more than the documented maximum
rows.summary: You configure Word2VecSynonymFilter with maxSynonymsPerTerm=k, whose javadoc calls it the 'maximum number of result returned by the synonym search', so you expect at most k synonyms per token. Word2VecSynonymProvider.getSynonyms searches the HNSW graph for k+1 neighbours on the assumption that the query term is always its own nearest neighbour, drops only the query term and never caps the result, so when the term is not among the hits it returns all k+1. With three terms that share one vector and k=1, getSynonyms(c) returns [a, b] and the filter emits 2 SYNONYM tokens; with 4000 distinct clustered vectors and the factory defaults, 4 terms get 6 synonyms because the approximate search with a beam of 6 does not reach the query term itself, although it is its own strict nearest neighbour by a margin of more than 0.03.

rows.title: SpellChecker.indexDictionary checks for already-indexed words only against the spell index as it was before the call, so a word that one dictionary repeats is indexed once per occurrence and suggestSimilar returns it several times, pushing distinct suggestions out
rows.summary: You index a word list into SpellChecker with one indexDictionary call, and the list contains a word twice, for example a PlainTextDictionary with the lines relieve, relieve, receive. You expect each word to be indexed once, as indexDictionary already ensures for words that were in the spell index before the call, so suggestSimilar("recieve", 2) returns [relieve, receive]. Instead the duplicate check looks only at the spell index as it was before the call, so the repeated word is indexed twice and suggestSimilar returns [relieve, relieve], pushing receive out; the same words split over two calls are de-duplicated correctly.

rows.title: SpellChecker.suggestSimilar with SuggestWordFrequencyComparator drops more frequent suggestions: once the queue is full it raises the accuracy cutoff to the score of the least frequent queued word, which is a valid bound only for a score-first order (since 3.1, LUCENE-2479)
rows.summary: You build an index-based SpellChecker with the shipped SuggestWordFrequencyComparator ('Frequency first, then score') and ask for suggestions restricted to a field, expecting the most frequent qualifying words among the retrieved candidates. Once the queue holds numSug words, suggestSimilar raises its accuracy cutoff to the score of the queue's head, which under this comparator is the least frequent queued word, so a later candidate that is more frequent but scores slightly lower is rejected before its frequency is even read. With 'receive' in 50 documents and one-edit neighbours such as 'relieve', 'reprieve' and 'retrieve' in one document each, suggestSimilar('recieve', 1, reader, field, SUGGEST_WHEN_NOT_IN_INDEX) returns [relieve] instead of receive (numSug 1-3 all leave it out; numSug 4 ranks it first).

rows.title: WordBreakSpellChecker.suggestWordBreaks drops better suggestions when maxChanges >= 3: the full-queue early return added in 9.12.0 (GITHUB#12100) assumes a breadth-first order that the depth-first recursion does not follow
rows.summary: You index some words and call WordBreakSpellChecker.suggestWordBreaks with setMaxChanges(3) or more, and you expect the maxSuggestions splits of the term that rank best by Lucene's own order (fewest breaks, then highest frequency). Instead, once an earlier branch of the search has filled the queue, a later branch returns before it looks for its own splits, so a better split can be missing: with the index {a, ab, b, c, d, e}, the term 'abcde', maxChanges=4 and maxSuggestions=1 the method returns [a b c d e] (4 breaks) instead of [ab c d e] (3 breaks), while asking for 2 suggestions returns both in the right order. No error is raised, raising maxChanges from 3 to 4 makes the answer worse, and 9.11.1 returns the right split.

rows.title: DirectSpellChecker.suggestSimilar computes its candidate budget numSug * maxInspections in int: with setMaxInspections(Integer.MAX_VALUE) ('inspect everything') and any even numSug the budget wraps to -numSug, so the call throws NullPointerException or silently returns no suggestions
rows.summary: You tell DirectSpellChecker to inspect as many candidates as it likes with setMaxInspections(Integer.MAX_VALUE) and ask suggestSimilar for 2 suggestions; you expect the best suggestions, at least as good as with a budget of 1000. Instead the internal budget numSug * maxInspections overflows int to -2: if the word has a one-edit neighbour the call throws NullPointerException, and if its only neighbours are two edits away it returns an empty array with no error. The outcome flips with the parity of numSug (1 and 3 work, 2 and 4 fail), and the one-line fix is to compute the budget in long and cap it at Integer.MAX_VALUE.
rows.area: suggest / spell checking (DirectSpellChecker.suggestSimilar candidate budget numSug * maxInspections)

rows.title: Document suggester: NRTSuggester computes topN = num * prefixPaths.size() in int, so when the product passes Integer.MAX_VALUE it wraps and SuggestIndexSearcher.suggest can silently return no suggestions or a truncated list (10^6 contexts in a segment: num 2147 returns 2147 suggestions, num 2148 returns none)
rows.summary: You index suggestions with ContextSuggestField, one context each, so that one segment holds 10^6 distinct contexts, and call SuggestIndexSearcher.suggest(query, num, false) with a ContextQuery over a PrefixCompletionQuery that matches every context (no contexts added, which ContextQuery documents as 'suggest across all contexts', or a shared context prefix via addContext(prefix, boost, false)); you expect the top num completions, and num = 2147 does return 2147. With num = 2148 you get no suggestions and no error: NRTSuggester.lookup computes topN = num * prefixPaths.size() in int (NRTSuggester.java:142), 2148 x 10^6 wraps to -2146967296, and Util.TopNSearcher's loop 'while (results.size() < topN)' never runs. When the product wraps to a small positive value the list is silently cut to that many (3000 contexts and num = 1431656 return 704 of 3000), and a RegexCompletionQuery or FuzzyCompletionQuery with many matching prefixes behaves the same (1000 regex prefixes and num = 2147484 return none).

rows.title: MoreLikeThis keeps the lowest-scoring selected terms when the query reaches the boolean clause limit, so the truncated query silently drops the most interesting terms (regression since 4.10.0)
rows.summary: You let MoreLikeThis select more terms than the global boolean clause limit, for example setMaxQueryTerms(2000) on a long text under the default limit of 1024, and call like(...). You expect the query, which createQuery deliberately truncates to the clause limit instead of failing, to keep the 1024 most interesting (highest tf*idf) of the selected terms, as it did up to 4.9.1. Instead createQuery pops its queue lowest score first and stops at the first TooManyClauses, so the query holds the 1024 lowest-scoring selected terms and none of the best ones (in the repro, 0 of the 76 top words survive).

rows.title: WordBreakSpellChecker.suggestWordCombinations still applies minSuggestionFrequency under SUGGEST_MORE_POPULAR, although the setter says it does not apply in that mode (suggestWordBreaks follows the setter), so valid combined words are silently dropped
rows.summary: You configure a WordBreakSpellChecker with setMinSuggestionFrequency(2), whose javadoc says the minimum is 'Not applicable when used with SUGGEST_MORE_POPULAR', and ask suggestWordCombinations for SUGGEST_MORE_POPULAR suggestions; you expect every indexed combined word that is at least as frequent as its most popular part, which is the method's own MORE_POPULAR rule and what suggestWordBreaks does with the same setting. Instead the minimum still filters combinations: with sun, flower and sunflower in one document (docFreq 1 each), suggestWordCombinations([f:sun, f:flower], 5, reader, SUGGEST_MORE_POPULAR) returns no suggestion instead of sunflower. The cause is the check combinedTermFreq >= minSuggestionFrequency (WordBreakSpellChecker.java:208), which runs after the MORE_POPULAR rule in every mode.

rows.title: Hunspell spell-checker: CHECKCOMPOUNDTRIPLE misses an x|xx triple letter (one letter before the boundary, two after) at the second and later boundaries of a compound, so words such as operabareeel (opera + bare|eel) are accepted (absolute break position compared with the tail's relative length)
rows.summary: You load a Hunspell dictionary with CHECKCOMPOUNDTRIPLE, which hunspell(5) defines as 'Forbid compounding, if compound word contains triple repeating letters (e.g. foo|ox or xo|oof)', and expect Hunspell.spell to reject a compound with a triple letter at any boundary, as C Hunspell 1.3.2 and 1.7.2 do and as Lucene's own checkcompoundtriple fixture requires for bareeel (bare|eel). Instead Lucene rejects bareeel but accepts operabareeel, barebareeel and foobareeel (opera, bare or foo + bare|eel), and with the public Swedish dictionary (sv_SE) it accepts sommarmusikradiooomskuren while it rejects musikradiooomskuren. The cause: Hunspell.mayBreakIntoCompounds receives an absolute break position (the tail's offset in the word plus the relative break) but tests 'breakPos < length - 1' against the tail's relative length, so at the second and later boundaries the x|xx half of the check is skipped whenever the absolute break position is at least the tail length minus 1, while the xx|x half ('breakPos > offset + 1') is offset-aware and still works.
rows.area: analysis / hunspell (Hunspell.spell compound checking)

rows.title: Hunspell spell() skips the per-entry checks on COMPOUNDRULE compound parts, so it accepts compounds that C Hunspell rejects: a KEEPCASE first part in capitalized or upper case, a FORCEUCASE last part in lower case, and a NEEDAFFIX or FORBIDDENWORD entry as a first or middle part
rows.summary: You load a Hunspell dictionary that joins foo/G and bar/H by 'COMPOUNDRULE GH', give foo or bar one of the per-entry flags KEEPCASE, FORCEUCASE, NEEDAFFIX or FORBIDDENWORD, call Hunspell.spell, and expect the answer C Hunspell 1.3.2 and 1.7.2 give (and Lucene itself gives when the same parts are joined by COMPOUNDFLAG): Foobar and FOOBAR rejected when foo is KEEPCASE, foobar rejected when bar is FORCEUCASE, and foobar rejected when foo is a NEEDAFFIX virtual stem or a FORBIDDENWORD entry. Instead spell() returns true in all four cases, with and without -ea, in every release since 8.9.0; on the public Swedish dictionary sv_SE it accepts lower-case rule compounds such as tolvkronorsgatan that the dictionary's FORCEUCASE flag and C Hunspell reject. The cause: checkCompoundRules takes every non-final part as a raw dictionary.lookupWord result, without the NEEDAFFIX, FORBIDDENWORD, COMPOUNDFORBIDFLAG and first-part case (KEEPCASE) filters, and checkLastCompoundPart never applies the FORCEUCASE check (hasForceUCaseProblem) that the COMPOUNDFLAG path uses.

rows.title: Hunspell Dictionary with FLAG UTF-8 and an 8-bit SET other than ISO8859-1 silently merges UTF-8 flags that share a lead byte, so spell() and the stemmer accept forms the dictionary forbids (some SET values fail to load instead)
rows.summary: You load a Hunspell dictionary whose affix file says FLAG UTF-8 (flags are UTF-8 characters) and SET ISO8859-2, KOI8-R, microsoft-cp1251 or another 8-bit encoding except ISO8859-1, with two suffix classes whose flags are, say, U+00E1 and U+00E2, and expect what C Hunspell 1.3.2 and 1.7.2 do on the same bytes: a word that carries only the first flag takes only the first suffix. Instead Lucene reads the flags from text already decoded with the SET charset, so each 2-byte flag becomes two characters and an affix rule keeps only the first one, the shared lead byte: both classes merge, spell() accepts the forbidden forms (kote, lasa in the repro) and the stemmer returns kot for kote, with no error. Only no SET, SET ISO8859-1 and SET UTF-8 work; ISO8859-14 merges too (its decoder reports ISO-8859-1 as its charset, and the re-encode turns remapped flag bytes into '?'), and with ISO8859-3, -6 or -8 the load throws UnmappableCharacterException because a flag byte is unassigned in that charset.

rows.title: Stempel: running Optimizer or Optimizer2 on an already merge-reduced trie silently corrupts it, because Optimizer.optimize remaps references to rows it has not placed yet to row 0
rows.summary: You build a stempel table with the Compile tool and a method string that has two merge passes (for example '-M22' or '-0ME22'), or you call reduce(new Optimizer2()) (or Optimizer) on a table that a merge pass already reduced, such as a loaded table; Optimizer2's javadoc says its row joining keeps the stemmer able to 'recognize words for which the original trie was built', so the training words should keep their stems, as they do after one pass. Instead the second pass silently corrupts the trie: two Optimizer2 passes over the one-word trie {aab -> Da} lose its only entry, Compile '-22' stems every training form of a small table to null and '-M22' leaves every form unstemmed (while '-2' and '-M2' are correct), and one more Optimizer2 pass over the bundled Polish table changes 8,356 of 21,147 keys whose whole path is stored. The cause is Optimizer.optimize (inherited by Optimizer2): it walks the rows from the highest index down and remaps every child reference through a remap[] array that is still 0 for rows it has not placed yet, which is only correct when every child has a higher index than its parent; a freshly built trie has that property, but the output of a merge pass does not (shared rows, self-loops, pre-order renumbering).

rows.title: Stempel's Row.store writes the count of all cells but skips the empty ones, so a stemmer table reduced with Gener (Compile method letter G) fails to load with EOFException or loads misaligned and gives wrong stems
rows.summary: You compile a stemmer table with the stempel Compile tool using a method string that contains G (Gener, the reduction that drops infrequent commands), or reduce a trie with Gener and store it, and expect StempelStemmer.load to read the table back and stem like the trie that was stored. Instead Row.store writes the number of all cells of a row and then skips the empty cells (no command and no reference) that Gener leaves behind, so Row(DataInput) reads too many cell records and runs into the next row: usually load fails with java.io.EOFException (Compile -0ME2G, -0M2G and -0MEG on an 11-lemma Polish table, -EG on a 20-line table, the bundled table reduced with Gener, which then has 38,322 empty cells), and sometimes the table loads without error but answers wrongly (Compile G on a 4-line dictionary: for 'walked' the expected patch is Db and the loaded table gives null). Writing getCells(), the existing count of the non-empty cells, fixes it in one line and changes no byte of any table without empty cells, such as the bundled table and every table compiled without G.
rows.area: analysis/stempel / egothor stemmer table serialization (Row.store vs Row(DataInput); Gener, Compile 'G', StempelStemmer.load)

rows.title: Hunspell spell-checker: a CHECKCOMPOUNDPATTERN simplified compound form (the optional replacement field) after the first compound part is checked from the start of the whole word, so valid compounds such as dampfschiffahrt (dampf + schiff|fahrt with 'ff f ff') are rejected and some words (schiffschiffahrt, or auu with 'u u u') make spell()/suggest() throw StackOverflowError (expandReplacement returns offset 0 over an array that still holds the earlier parts)
rows.summary: You load a Hunspell dictionary whose CHECKCOMPOUNDPATTERN rule has a replacement, which hunspell(5) documents as 'The optional replacement parameter allows simplified compound form' (for example 'CHECKCOMPOUNDPATTERN ff f ff' from the Hunspell ChangeLog, for pre-reform German Schiffahrt = Schiff + Fahrt), and expect Hunspell.spell to accept the simplified form wherever it occurs in a compound, as native Hunspell 1.3.2 and 1.7.2 do for dampfschiffahrt, donaudampfschiffahrt, barfozar and barfur, and to return true or false for every word. Instead Lucene accepts schiffahrt but rejects dampfschiffahrt and donaudampfschiffahrt (and barfozar, barfur and barbozan on the content of its own checkcompoundpattern2/3 fixtures), and spell()/suggest() throw StackOverflowError for schiffschiffahrt, for 'auu' with the one-word dictionary au and 'CHECKCOMPOUNDPATTERN u u u', and for words of native Hunspell's own checkcompoundpattern4 (Telugu sandhi) fixture. The cause: CheckCompoundPattern.expandReplacement builds the expanded word from the start of the whole word (word.chars[0 .. word.offset + breakPos], which keeps the earlier compound parts for the FORCEUCASE check) but returns it as a CharsRef with offset 0, while its callers index it relative to the current part, so at the second and later boundaries the stem lookup starts at the beginning of the word and the remaining tail never gets shorter.
rows.area: analysis / hunspell (Hunspell.spell and suggest compound checking, CHECKCOMPOUNDPATTERN replacements)

rows.title: Hunspell: a bracket or dot affix condition with fewer character patterns than the strip is checked against the wrong end of the strip (a suffix rule at the strip's start, a prefix rule at its end), so the rule never applies when it should, or always applies when it should not
rows.summary: You load a Hunspell dictionary with the suffix rule 'SFX A abc d [c]' (strip abc, add d, condition [c]) on the root xabc and expect the condition to be tested where Hunspell lines it up, at the end of the root, which for a condition shorter than the strip is the end of the strip: xd should be a correct word with stem xabc and 'SFX A abc e [a]' should never apply, as C Hunspell 1.3.2 answers and as Lucene itself answers when the same condition is written as the literal c. Instead Lucene rejects xd and accepts xe as a form of xabc, and the prefix rules 'PFX B abc d [a]' and 'PFX B abc e [c]' on the root abcx are reversed the same way (dx rejected, ex accepted); spell, getRoots and HunspellStemFilter give these wrong verdicts and stems with no error. The cause is AffixCondition.compile: for a condition with [ ] or . and no more character patterns than the strip, it decides the rule once at load by matching the strip against 'kind == PREFIX ? ".*" + condition : condition + ".*"', which tests the strip's start for SFX and its end for PFX, the two templates swapped between the kinds.
rows.area: analysis / hunspell (affix conditions: Dictionary loading, Hunspell.spell/getRoots, Stemmer and HunspellStemFilter)

rows.title: Hunspell COMPLEXPREFIXES accepts a second prefix after an inner prefix rule whose continuation class does not allow it: with 'PFX A 0 re', 'PFX C 0 un', 'PFX C 0 dis/A' and foo/C, spell("reunfoo") is true and HunspellStemFilter stems reunfoo to foo, although only dis, not un, allows re (a regression since 9.5.0)
rows.summary: You load a hunspell dictionary that sets COMPLEXPREFIXES (twofold prefix stripping) with the outer prefix 'PFX A 0 re', an inner prefix class C with two rules, 'un' without a continuation class and 'dis/A', and the root foo/C, and expect what hunspell(5), C Hunspell 1.3.2 and 1.7.2 and Lucene up to 9.4.2 do: re may only precede dis, so redisfoo is a word and reunfoo is not, just as Lucene still checks the mirror-image twofold suffixes rule by rule. Instead spell("reunfoo") is true, getRoots("reunfoo") is [foo] and HunspellStemFilter turns the token reunfoo into foo, because since 9.5.0 Stemmer.isAffixCompatible returns true for any prefix stripped after another prefix (Stemmer.java:541, 566) and the only remaining gate is the dictionary-wide check that some prefix rule carries the flag A (Dictionary.isSecondStagePrefix).

rows.title: Hunspell getAllWordForms, generateAllSimpleWords and compress return words that spell() rejects: the sanity check canStemToOriginal accepts any affix path that strips a form back to the stem text, so with 'NEEDAFFIX X', 'SFX A 0 s/XB', an unrelated 'SFX C 0 s' and foo/A, getAllWordForms("foo") returns foos
rows.summary: You load a Hunspell dictionary with 'NEEDAFFIX X', 'SFX A 0 s/XB' (so foos needs one more suffix), 'SFX B 0 en' and an unrelated class 'SFX C 0 s', with the entries foo/A and bar/C, and call Hunspell.getAllWordForms("foo"). You expect [foo, foosen]: spell() rejects foos (C Hunspell 1.7.2 does too), and the generator's check canStemToOriginal is documented to keep only forms that are 'accepted by the spell-checker and analyzed to be the form of the original dictionary entry'. Instead you get [foo, foos, foosen], because canStemToOriginal accepts as soon as any affix-stripping path gives back the stem text, here class C, which foo does not even have, and ignores which affixes were stripped (WordFormGenerator.java:211); generateAllSimpleWords leaks the same words, and compress([kat, kater, katern]) suggests kat/PQ, which does not accept kater.
rows.area: analysis / hunspell (WordFormGenerator: canStemToOriginal, getAllWordForms, generateAllSimpleWords, compress)

rows.title: Hunspell: the part of an affix condition that overlaps the strip is checked with java.util.regex without escaping the dash, so a bracket such as [a-c] there means the range a..c instead of the set {a, -, c} that hunspell(5) defines, and the rule is applied or dropped wrongly
rows.summary: You load a Hunspell dictionary with the rules 'SFX A b x [a-c]' and 'SFX A b y [^a-c]' on the root ab and expect [a-c] to mean what hunspell(5) says, the set {a, -, c} ('Dash hasn't got special meaning'), so the first rule never applies (ab ends in b) and the second one does: C Hunspell 1.3.2 and 1.7.2 reject ax and accept ay. Instead Lucene's Hunspell.spell accepts ax and rejects ay (likewise xa and ya for the PFX twins on ba), and HunspellStemFilter stems ax to ab and leaves ay unstemmed. AffixCondition.compile decides the part of a condition that overlaps the strip once, at load time, with String.matches (java.util.regex) on the raw condition text, which reads [a-c] as a range, while the part checked against the stem goes through escapeDash; a reversed pseudo-range such as [c-a] even makes java.util.regex throw, and the rule is silently turned into 'never applies'.
rows.area: analysis / hunspell (AffixCondition: affix conditions used by Hunspell.spell/suggest and by stemming through Stemmer/HunspellStemFilter)

rows.title: Hunspell spell() accepts two-word flag-based compounds (COMPOUNDFLAG or COMPOUNDBEGIN/END) when COMPOUNDWORDMAX is 1 (or 0, which the parser clamps to 1), because the word-count check skips the first compound part
rows.summary: You load a Hunspell dictionary with 'COMPOUNDFLAG C', 'COMPOUNDMIN 1', 'COMPOUNDWORDMAX 1' and the words foo/C and bar/C, call Hunspell.spell("foobar"), and expect false: hunspell(5) defines COMPOUNDWORDMAX as the maximum word count in a compound, and C Hunspell 1.3.2 and 1.7.2 reject foobar. Instead Lucene returns true, with and without -ea; COMPOUNDWORDMAX 0, which the parser clamps to 1, behaves the same, while with COMPOUNDWORDMAX 2 Lucene correctly accepts foobar and rejects foobarfoo. The cause: checkCompounds counts parts only when a previous part exists ('prev != null && prev.index > compoundMax - 2'), so the first part is never counted and checkCompoundsAfter accepts first part + last part at any limit; the original LUCENE-9699 check, which did enforce a limit of 1, was lost in a 2021 refactoring (LUCENE-9729).
rows.area: analysis / hunspell (Hunspell.spell compound checking, COMPOUNDWORDMAX)

rows.title: Hunspell getAllWordForms, generateAllSimpleWords and compress never generate a suffix that only a prefix's continuation class allows: with ampere/U and 'PFX U 0 kilo/S', spell() accepts amperes and kiloamperes, but getAllWordForms("ampere") returns only [ampere, kiloampere]
rows.summary: You load a Hunspell dictionary in which a prefix rule's continuation class allows a suffix, for example 'PFX U 0 kilo/S' and 'SFX S 0 s' with the entry ampere/U, and ask Hunspell.getAllWordForms("ampere") for all forms of that entry. You expect ampere, amperes, kiloampere and kiloamperes: Lucene's own spell() accepts all four and analyzeSimpleWord() analyses each one as a form of ampere/U, as C Hunspell 1.7.2 also does. Instead you get only [ampere, kiloampere], because WordFormGenerator applies suffixes only from the entry's own flags and then forbids any suffix once a prefix has been applied (WordFormGenerator.java:378); generateAllSimpleWords misses the same words, and compress() suggests an unneeded flag (for work/P with 'PFX P 0 re/S', compress([work, rework, reworks]) proposes work/PS, which also adds the unrequested word works).
rows.area: analysis / hunspell (WordFormGenerator: getAllWordForms, generateAllSimpleWords, compress)

rows.title: A reordered addIndexes(CodecReader...) silently drops the stored fields and term vectors of the first document after an empty (maxDoc 0) input reader: SlowCompositeCodecReaderWrapper.docIdToReaderId keeps an Arrays.binarySearch hit on a repeated doc start and reads that document from the empty reader
rows.summary: You call IndexWriter.addIndexes(CodecReader...) with a 3-document reader, an empty reader (maxDoc() == 0) and a 2-document reader on a writer whose merge policy reorders the merge, such as BPReorderingMergePolicy or any OneMerge#reorder that returns a DocMap (the identity is enough), and you expect all 5 documents to keep their stored fields and term vectors, as they do with the same call without reordering. Instead the merged view that IndexWriter builds for the reorder (SlowCompositeCodecReaderWrapper) has doc starts [0, 3, 3, 5], Arrays.binarySearch finds start 3 at the empty reader's index, and docIdToReaderId keeps that exact hit, so merged doc 3 (the first document of the third reader) is read as doc 0 of the empty reader. The new segment is written without any error under -ea and -da: that document is still found by its id term and keeps its doc values, but its stored fields and term vectors are gone.
rows.area: index / addIndexes reorder path: SlowCompositeCodecReaderWrapper doc-ID-to-reader lookup (stored fields, term vectors), reached through misc BPReorderingMergePolicy or any OneMerge#reorder

rows.title: Index-sorted IndexWriter.addIndexes(CodecReader...) with an empty (maxDoc 0) input reader silently writes a corrupt segment: MultiSorter gives the empty reader's nonexistent doc 0 a merged doc id, so the postings of later documents point one document too far
rows.summary: You sort an IndexWriter by a long field k and call addIndexes(CodecReader...) with the single segment of a sorted 2-document index {a k=1, c k=2} followed by an empty reader that advertises the same sort (SortingCodecReader.wrap(SlowCodecReaderWrapper.wrap(new ParallelLeafReader()), sort)), and you expect a 2-document segment in which a TermQuery on id:a returns the document that stores a, as it does without an index sort or with the empty reader listed first. Instead MultiSorter.sort also queues a cursor at doc 0 for the empty reader, whose nonexistent doc 0 (missing sort value 0) is popped first and takes merged doc id 0, so a and c are mapped to 1 and 2 while the new segment has maxDoc 2. With assertions disabled addIndexes and commit succeed, but id:a returns the document that stores c and the posting of id:c points at doc 2 (>= maxDoc 2), which only CheckIndex at level 2 or higher reports.
rows.area: index / index sorting at merge: MultiSorter doc maps, reached through IndexWriter.addIndexes(CodecReader...)

rows.title: MemoryIndex returns term vectors for fields whose FieldInfo says storeTermVector=false (a regression of LUCENE-6402 since 6.5.0), so its reader fails CheckIndex and IndexWriter.addIndexes(SlowCodecReaderWrapper.wrap(reader)) writes a segment that CheckIndex rejects
rows.summary: You build a MemoryIndex with MemoryIndex.fromDocument from a document whose body field stores term vectors and whose title is a plain TextField, copy its reader into an index with IndexWriter.addIndexes(SlowCodecReaderWrapper.wrap(reader)), and expect a clean index, as when the same document is added with IndexWriter.addDocument. Instead the copy succeeds and CheckIndex (level 2 or higher) reports the new segment broken, 'docID=0 has term vectors for field=title but FieldInfo has storeTermVector=false', because the MemoryIndex reader returns term vectors for every field with terms while, since 6.5.0, its FieldInfo takes storeTermVector from the field type. The bad segment survives merges with natively added documents, and the MemoryIndex reader itself already fails TestUtil.checkReader, even for a document that has only a plain TextField.

rows.title: Monitor's QueryDecomposer ignores minimumNumberShouldMatch=1 when a BooleanQuery has one required clause and no usable SHOULD clause, so Monitor.match reports queries that match nothing
rows.summary: You register with the Monitor a BooleanQuery that has one required clause and minimumNumberShouldMatch=1 but no SHOULD clause that can match, for example 'topic AND at least one of [list]' built from an empty list, (+text:alpha)~1. Core Lucene defines this query to match nothing (BooleanQuery.rewrite returns MatchNoDocsQuery and IndexSearcher counts 0 hits), so you expect the Monitor never to report it. Instead the default QueryDecomposer keeps such a query whole only when minimumNumberShouldMatch > 1 and otherwise replaces it by its lone required clause (plus its MUST_NOT exclusions), which the Monitor runs as the final matcher, so Monitor.match reports the query for every document containing alpha, for example 'alpha beta'.
rows.area: monitor / query decomposition (QueryDecomposer.decomposeBoolean)

rows.title: Monitor's QueryDecomposer turns a BooleanQuery whose only required clause is a single FILTER clause into that clause as a scoring query, so ScoringMatch and ExplainingMatch report a positive score for a query (or query part) that scores 0, and twice the true score when such a query is nested in a disjunction
rows.summary: You register with the Monitor a BooleanQuery whose only required clause is a FILTER clause, for example '#body:apple' or '(#body:apple) body:banana', and ask for scores with ScoringMatch or ExplainingMatch; since FILTER clauses 'do not participate in scoring', you expect the score IndexSearcher gives the same query: 0 for '#body:apple' and 0.13076457 for the nested query on the document 'apple banana'. Instead the default QueryDecomposer treats the FILTER clause like a MUST clause and replaces the query by that clause as a plain scoring query, so ExplainingMatch and ScoringMatch report 0.13076457 for '#body:apple' (0.26152915 for '(#body:apple)^2') and 0.26152915, twice the true score, for the nested query. Matching is correct; only the reported scores and explanations are wrong.
rows.area: monitor / query decomposition (QueryDecomposer.decomposeBoolean; ScoringMatch, ExplainingMatch)

rows.title: QueryTimeListener.timingMatcher never finishes the matcher it wraps, so wrapping ParallelMatcher or PartitionMatcher makes Monitor.match silently return no matches and no errors (since 8.2.0)
rows.summary: You register a TermQuery f:a in a Monitor and match the document 'a b' with QueryTimeListener.timingMatcher(ParallelMatcher.factory(executor, QueryMatch.SIMPLE_MATCHER, 2), listener). You expect the 1 match that ParallelMatcher.factory alone reports, plus a timing callback per query. Instead getMatchCount() is 0 and getErrors() is empty: the wrapper forwards matchQuery() to the inner matcher, but its doFinish() only copies the inner matcher's match lists and never calls the inner finish(), and ParallelMatcher and PartitionMatcher collect their matches (and errors) only in that finish step.
rows.area: monitor / matcher composition (QueryTimeListener.timingMatcher wrapper around CandidateMatcher; ParallelMatcher, PartitionMatcher)

rows.title: ConcurrentQueryLoader with queueSize < threads never loads any query: each worker's batch size queueSize / threads is 0, so queries added before close() are silently dropped and adding more than queueSize queries blocks forever
rows.summary: You create new ConcurrentQueryLoader(monitor, 2, 1), add one query and close the loader, the add-then-close pattern of the class javadoc. You expect the query to be registered (monitor.getQueryCount() == 1), as it is with (1, 1) or (2, 2). Instead each of the two workers gets a batch size of queueSize / threads = 1 / 2 = 0, so no worker ever takes anything off the queue: close() returns normally with no error and getQueryCount() is 0 (and with more than queueSize queries add() would block forever).
rows.area: monitor / ConcurrentQueryLoader (bulk loading of queries into a Monitor)

rows.title: A read-only Monitor's purgeCache() returns without refreshing when another refresh is running, so a query committed before the call can stay invisible after it returns
rows.summary: You open a read-only Monitor over a query index that a writable Monitor updates, register and commit a new query with the writer, and call purgeCache() on the read-only Monitor, whose javadoc says read-only users 'MUST call it when you want new changes'. You expect the new query to match once the call returns. Instead, if another refresh of the same Monitor (its own background refresh, or another thread's purgeCache()) is already running and has read the older commit, purgeCache() calls the non-blocking SearcherManager.maybeRefresh(), which returns false at once, drops that result and still notifies the onPurge listeners; the running refresh then installs the older commit, so the new query is still unmatched after both have returned, until some later refresh.
rows.area: monitor / read-only query index (ReadonlyQueryIndex.purgeCache refresh)

rows.title: Monitor.purgeCache after a register whose commit or post-commit refresh failed with an I/O error rebuilds the query cache from the stale searcher and drops that query, although IndexWriter still publishes it at the next commit: getQueryIds()/getQuery() then list the query but match() never reports it until the Monitor is reopened (since 8.2.0)
rows.summary: You register q1 = f:apple on a Monitor with a persistent query index and the index's commit fails once with an IOException (here a single Directory.sync failure), so register() throws; then purgeCache() runs (explicitly, or as the default background purge) and a later register(q2) succeeds. You expect the Monitor to agree with itself: IndexWriter kept q1's document and publishes it with q2's commit, so a query that getQueryIds() and getQuery("q1") report as stored should match a document containing 'apple'. Instead match() never reports q1, because purgeCache rebuilt the query cache by scanning the searcher that the failed commit left stale, dropped q1's cache entry and never adds it back; only closing and reopening the Monitor, or registering q1 again, makes it match.

rows.title: Lucene Monitor's QueryDecomposer collects a query's parts in a Set, so a sub-query that occurs more than once in a registered query (a repeated SHOULD or MUST clause, or a term shared by two nested disjunctions) is scored once by ScoringMatch and ExplainingMatch instead of once per occurrence
rows.summary: You register a query such as '(red apple) (green apple)' or 'apple apple' in a Monitor and match the document 'red green apple' with ScoringMatch or ExplainingMatch, expecting the score the query itself gives that document, which is what IndexSearcher returns, because BooleanQuery counts a repeated clause at every occurrence (0.5230583 and 0.26152915). Instead the Monitor reports 0.39229372 and 0.13076457: the default QueryDecomposer collects the query's parts in a Set, which keeps equal parts once, and the scoring matchers add up the scores of the distinct parts, so the shared 'apple' is counted once. Which queries match is not affected; only the scores and explanations of such queries are too low.
rows.area: monitor / query decomposition and match scoring (QueryDecomposer Set<Query> parts, ScoringMatch/ExplainingMatch resolve)

rows.title: Monitor HighlightsMatch drops a hit when another hit has the same positions but different offsets (for example shingles or multi-word synonyms), because HighlightsMatch.Hit.compareTo ignores offsets
rows.summary: You register a query such as wi OR "wi fi" (or the prefix query wi*, or guinea OR cavy with a 'guinea pig => cavy' synonym rule) in a Monitor whose analyzer stacks tokens at one position, match a document with HighlightsMatch.MATCHER, and expect both hits that Weight#matches reports: for 'wi fi' with ShingleFilter(2,2) and unigrams these are 0(0)->0(2) for 'wi' and 0(0)->0(5) for 'wi fi'. Instead HighlightsMatch keeps only one of them and getHitCount() is 1, because Hit.compareTo compares start and end positions only and the hits are kept in TreeSets, which treat compareTo == 0 as a duplicate, although Hit's own equals (a record over all four fields) says the two hits differ. Which hit survives depends on clause order, and the same root cause makes getHits(field).contains(...) ignore offsets and lets HighlightsMatch.equals return true for two objects whose hashCodes differ.
rows.area: monitor / HighlightsMatch hit set (Hit.compareTo used as TreeSet identity)

rows.title: WordDelimiterGraphFilter catenates non-adjacent subwords and gives catenations a too-long position length when a catenation run starts with a subword typed ALPHA|DIGIT (any supplementary character such as an emoji, or a character mapped to ALPHANUM in a types table), so graph phrase queries can match documents that lack a subword (released since 6.5.0)
rows.summary: You run WordDelimiterGraphFilter with CATENATE_WORDS or CATENATE_NUMBERS on a token such as 'U+20000-ab-12' (a supplementary character at the start) or '@x-ab-12' with '@' mapped to ALPHANUM, and expect catenations only of adjacent subwords of one kind, each placed over exactly the parts it contains, as the ASCII control 'x-ab-12' gets (xab at [0,2), no number catenation). Instead, because such a subword is typed ALPHA|DIGIT and a run started by it is never ended by a subword it does not absorb, the filter emits catenations of non-adjacent parts ('U+20000 12', '@x12', 'U+20000abcd' across '12') and catenations whose position length also covers the skipped part ('U+20000ab' at [0,3), over '12'). At search time QueryBuilder turns that graph into a phrase query with a bare-term alternative, so the phrase 'U+20000hot-sale-50' also matches a document 'U+20000hot-sale-49' (executed).

rows.title: ThaiCharFilter tests its multi-character rules (double Sara E, decomposed Sara Am, tone mark before an above/below vowel) on the raw look-ahead characters, before its own zero-width removal and deduplication have run on them, so a zero-width character or a repeated tone mark inside such a pattern leaves the anomaly in the output and the default ThaiAnalyzer merges the word with its neighbours
rows.summary: You index Thai text with the default ThaiAnalyzer, which runs ThaiCharFilter before the tokenizer, and expect a word typed with two of the typos the filter documents fixing (ที่ with its tone mark typed twice and before the vowel, ท่่ี, or แมว written as two Sara E with an invisible zero-width joiner between them) to be indexed like the clean word, because the filter's javadoc says it removes zero-width characters, deduplicates repeated tone marks, reorders a tone mark typed before an above/below vowel, joins double Sara E and recomposes decomposed Sara Am precisely so that the BreakIterator does not merge adjacent words. ThaiCharFilter makes one pass and tests its multi-character patterns against the raw next characters, while zero-width removal and deduplication act only on the character at the front of its buffer, after the earlier character has already been emitted, so the output still holds the tone-before-vowel, double Sara E or decomposed Sara Am sequence (ท่ี, เเมว, ทํา), which a second pass of the same filter would clean. The BreakIterator then merges words: ฉันทำงานท่่ีบ้าน is indexed as [ฉัน, ทำ, งาน, ที่บ้าน] instead of [ฉัน, ทำ, งาน, บ้าน], ฉันรักเ + ZWJ + เมวมาก as [ฉัน, รักแมวมาก], and a TermQuery for บ้าน or แมว finds 0 documents.

rows.title: ThaiNormalizer looks for a decomposed Sara Am before it converts Lakkhangyao or removes an extra tone mark, so its output can still be the decomposed form (Nikhahit + tone + Sara Aa), and the default ThaiAnalyzer indexes น้ำ ('water') typed with two tone marks inside a decomposed Sara Am as a different term
rows.summary: You index Thai text with the default ThaiAnalyzer (or ThaiNormalizationFilter) in which the word น้ำ ('water') is typed with a decomposed Sara Am and an extra tone mark inside it, น + Nikhahit + Mai Ek + Mai Tho + Sara Aa, and you expect the term น้ำ, because ThaiNormalizer documents that it recomposes Nikhahit + tone + Sara Aa into Sara Am and (per its code comment and upstream test) keeps the last of two different tone marks. ThaiNormalizer tests for the decomposed Sara Am in one forward pass over the raw characters, before it converts a following Lakkhangyao and before its last step removes the extra or repeated tone mark, and it never checks again, so the output is นํ้า (U+0E19 U+0E4D U+0E49 U+0E32), still the decomposed form; a query for น้ำ misses the document, while a second normalize() call, or the same two tone marks typed in the other order, gives น้ำ. When the token filter runs without ThaiCharFilter, ท + Nikhahit + Lakkhangyao likewise gives ทํา instead of ทำ, and a doubled tone mark inside the decomposed form gives นํ้า.
rows.area: analysis-common / Thai (ThaiNormalizer.normalize rule order; ThaiNormalizationFilter, the 'thaiNormalization' factory and the default ThaiAnalyzer as consumers; new in 10.6.0)

rows.title: OpenNLP POS, chunker and lemmatizer filters emit no token for a whole field value when an earlier filter removes every token of its first sentence, because SentenceAttributeExtractor starts at sentence index 0 and reads a first token from sentence 1 as an empty sentence, which the filters take as the end of the stream
rows.summary: You build an OpenNLP chain that removes some tokens before a sentence-aware filter, for example tokenizer -> POS tagger -> TypeTokenFilter keeping only nouns -> lemmatizer, and analyze 'He did not come back. They sent him running in the evening.', expecting the lemmatized nouns of the second sentence, [they, evening], as you get for that sentence alone. Instead the whole value yields no token: SentenceAttributeExtractor starts with currSentence = 0, so when the first token it receives already belongs to sentence 1 it returns an empty first sentence, and the POS, chunker and lemmatizer filters all treat an empty sentence as the end of the stream. A fully removed sentence in the middle of the text is handled correctly; only the first one is not.

rows.title: CJKBigramFilter never applies the position increment of its CJK input tokens to the bigrams and unigrams it builds from them, so the hole that a StopFilter (or any token-removing filter) placed before it leaves in front of CJK text disappears and an exact phrase matches across the removed word, while a non-CJK token behind the same hole keeps it; since 3.6.0
rows.summary: You build an analyzer StandardTokenizer > StopFilter(['the']) > CJKBigramFilter and analyze 'foo the 東京'. You expect [foo +1, 東京 +2]: the removed 'the' leaves a one-position hole, as it does for 'foo the bar', which the same chain turns into [foo +1, bar +2], so that the phrase 'foo 東京' does not match. Instead CJKBigramFilter builds the bigram 東京 from a cleared attribute state and never copies the position increment of the CJK input token, so the stream is [foo +1, 東京 +1] and, with this analyzer at index and query time, the phrase 'foo 東京' matches the document 'foo the 東京' (the phrase 'foo bar' does not match 'foo the bar').

rows.title: JapaneseTokenizer n-best output (nBestCost > 0) with the default discardPunctuation=true gives a dictionary word that spans a discarded punctuation character (アイワ・コーポ) a position length one too long, so its path in the token graph skips the next word and a QueryBuilder query for アイワ・コーポ東京支店 makes 東京 optional
rows.summary: You enable n-best output on JapaneseTokenizer (for example setNBestCost(2000)), keep the default discardPunctuation=true, analyze アイワ・コーポ東京支店 (a company name followed by 'Tokyo branch'), and expect a valid token graph in which the dictionary word アイワ・コーポ ends where 東京 starts, as it does with discardPunctuation=false. Instead ViterbiNBest.fixupPendingList counts the dropped ・ as an extra position, so アイワ・コーポ gets position length 3 instead of 2 and ends where 東京 ends, which breaks the analysis package rule that tokens with the same end position must have the same end offset. QueryBuilder then builds +((+アイワ +コーポ +東京) アイワ・コーポ) +支店 for an all-words query, and that query also matches a document about the Osaka branch (アイワ・コーポの大阪支店), which has no 東京.

rows.title: WordDelimiterGraphFilter drops the hole of a swallowed last token (a punctuation-only token such as the '--' in 'foo --', or a token whose parts the flags all switch off) and any stop-word hole that token carries, because it has no end() override, so the final position increment is 0 and the next value of a multi-valued field starts too early (released since 6.5.0)
rows.summary: You analyse 'foo --' (or 'foo the --' behind a StopFilter) with a whitespace tokenizer and WordDelimiterGraphFilter at its default flags, and expect the swallowed punctuation-only token to leave a hole that end() reports as a final position increment of 1 (2 with the stop word), as the filter does mid-stream ('foo -- bar' puts bar at +2, which upstream tests assert) and as StopFilter does for 'foo the'. Instead the filter keeps that hole in an internal accumulator that only a later emitted token applies and has no end() override, so the final increment is 0. In a multi-valued field with the default gap 0 the next value 'bar' then lands at position 1 instead of 2: PhraseQuery(foo, bar) matches the values 'foo --' | 'bar' while the StopFilter control 'foo the' | 'bar' does not, and the phrase QueryBuilder builds for 'foo -- bar' matches the single value 'foo -- bar' but not the two values (both executed).

rows.title: NGramTokenFilter and EdgeNGramTokenFilter end() overwrite the input's final position increment instead of adding to it, so a trailing hole (such as a removed trailing stop word) is lost and the next value of a multi-valued field starts too early (released since 7.4.0)
rows.summary: You analyse 'abc the' with a whitespace tokenizer, StopFilter and then NGramTokenFilter(3,3) or EdgeNGramTokenFilter(1,3); StopFilter reports the removed trailing 'the' as a final position increment of 1 in end(), and because the n-gram filter drops nothing here you expect end() to still report 1. Instead both filters call super.end() and then replace that value with only the increments of tokens they dropped themselves, so end() reports 0 ('abc x the' gives 1 instead of 2) and the trailing hole is lost. In a multi-valued field with Lucene's default gap 0, the second value 'def' of ['abc the', 'def'] is then indexed at position 1 instead of 2, and PhraseQuery('abc','def') matches the document (1 hit) where the same chain without the n-gram filter gives 0 hits (executed).
rows.area: analysis / common n-gram token filters (NGramTokenFilter, EdgeNGramTokenFilter: final position increment in end())

rows.title: ConditionalTokenFilter (ProtectedTermFilter, CustomAnalyzer when()/whenTerm()) reports a final position increment of 0 when the last token went through the wrapped filters, so a trailing hole from upstream (such as a removed trailing stop word) is lost and the next value of a multi-valued field starts one position too early (since 7.4.0)
rows.summary: You analyse 'abc the' with WhitespaceTokenizer, a StopFilter that removes 'the', and a ProtectedTermFilter that wraps a LowerCaseFilter (or the CustomAnalyzer equivalent whenTerm(...).addTokenFilter("lowercase").endwhen()), and expect end() to report the removed stop word as a final position increment of 1, as the same chain does without the condition and as the class itself does when the last token is protected ('x the' gives 1). Instead it reports 0 whenever the last token went through the wrapped filter, although LowerCaseFilter never touches positions: end() keeps the wrapped chain's end state, and the internal wrapper that feeds that chain resets the increment to 0. In a multi-valued field ['abc the', 'def'] with the default gap 0, 'def' is then indexed at position 1 instead of 2, so the PhraseQuery "abc def" matches the document (1 hit) where the plain chain gives 0 (executed).

rows.title: ConcatenatingTokenStream loses a source's trailing position increment (for example a removed stop word) when the next source produces no tokens, so later tokens are indexed too close and phrase queries over-match
rows.summary: You build one field from several token streams with ConcatenatingTokenStream, for example the values 'alpha the', '' and 'beta', each run through a StopFilter that removes 'the'. You expect the hole left by the removed 'the' to survive, as it does when no empty value sits in between and as IndexWriter keeps it for the same values in a multi-valued field, because LUCENE-8650 (7.7.0) made the class carry each source's final position increment over to the next token. Instead each exhausted source overwrites the pending increment instead of adding to it, and end() reports only the last source's own increment, so a source with no tokens erases the hole: 'beta' is indexed directly after 'alpha', the exact phrase "alpha beta" matches this document but not the single value 'alpha the beta', and with an empty last source end() reports 0 instead of 1.
rows.area: analysis / common miscellaneous (ConcatenatingTokenStream#incrementToken and #end: carry-over of child final position increments)

rows.title: ConcatenateGraphFilter treats a custom tokenSeparator as its internal one-byte separator label: an ASCII separator is doubled wherever it already occurs inside a token ('e-mail' becomes 'e--mail'), and a non-ASCII separator fails an assertion with -ea or is written as one truncated byte with -da (U+2013 becomes U+0013, U+00B7 a lone 0xB7 byte, i.e. invalid UTF-8)
rows.summary: You join tokens with ConcatenateGraphFilter (or the concatenateGraph factory) and a custom tokenSeparator, and expect what the javadoc says, every token joined with that separator: the single token 'e-mail' stays 'e-mail', 'e-mail' and 'x' joined with '-' give 'e-mail-x', and 'new' and 'york' joined with U+2013 give the UTF-8 bytes of new, U+2013, york. Instead the filter passes the custom separator to an escaper written for its internal one-byte label U+001F, so every occurrence of an ASCII separator inside a token is doubled ('e--mail', 'e--mail-x', and 'new york' for a keyword token with a space separator). A non-ASCII separator fails the escaper's assertion with -ea and, with -da, is cut to its low byte: U+2013 gives 'new' U+0013 'york', and U+00B7 gives the invalid UTF-8 term [6e 65 77 b7 79 6f 72 6b].

rows.title: ContextSuggestField accepts contexts that contain U+001E or U+001F although its javadoc promises an IllegalArgumentException for reserved characters; the completion analysis then drops U+001E (a suggestion indexed under context 'a<U+001E>b' is stored as, returned for and labelled with the exact context 'ab') and doubles U+001F (context 'a<U+001F>b' never matches its own exact query and is reported as 'a<U+001F><U+001F>b')
rows.summary: You index one suggestion under context 'ab' and another under context 'a<U+001E>b' with ContextSuggestField, and expect an IllegalArgumentException, because the constructor javadoc says it throws one 'if value or contexts contains any reserved characters' and U+001E and U+001F are exactly the characters that SuggestField and CompletionQuery reject as reserved (or, at the least, a context that round-trips). Instead both documents are indexed: ContextQuery.addContext("ab") returns both and reports both with context 'ab', addContext("a<U+001E>b") returns nothing, and a context 'a<U+001F>b' is also accepted, its exact query returns nothing and addAllContexts() reports it as 'a<U+001F><U+001F>b'. The cause: ContextSuggestField.validate checks a context only for U+001D (CONTEXT_SEPARATOR); the context then goes through ConcatenateGraphFilter, which turns a U+001E byte into an epsilon and escapes U+001F by doubling it, while ContextQuery builds its automaton from the raw characters, so the index side and the query side disagree.

rows.title: AnalyzingSuggester and FuzzySuggester do not escape the 0x00 byte that ends each analyzed form, so a U+0000 in a suggestion or key makes them return the same suggestion twice, lose the EXACT_FIRST exact match, or return entries that do not start with the key
rows.summary: You build an AnalyzingSuggester (or a FuzzySuggester) with its default constructor and KeywordAnalyzer from two entries, 'cat' with weight 1 and 'cat\u0000\u0000s' with weight 5, and call lookup('cat', 5); you expect each entry once with the exact match 'cat' first, which is what you get when the second entry uses U+0001 instead of U+0000. Instead you get [cat/1, cat\u0000\u0000s/5, cat/1]: the suggester stores each entry as its analyzed bytes, then a 0x00 end marker, then a dedup byte, without escaping a 0x00 that belongs to the text, so the stored input of 'cat' is a prefix of the stored input of 'cat\u0000\u0000s', and the FST top-N search returns 'cat' a second time through a path that skips the suggester's duplicate filter. The same collision makes lookup('foo\u0000') return 'foo' and lets a longer U+0000-extended entry take the EXACT_FIRST exact-match slot.

rows.title: FreeTextSuggester.build() resets its unigram token total before it reads the input, so a rebuild that throws (an empty dictionary, an IOException from the input, or build()'s own separator-byte rejection) leaves the previous model scored against a zero or partial total: unigram suggestions get wrong scores (every one Long.MAX_VALUE, i.e. 1.0, when the total is 0), a backed-off unigram outranks the real bigram predictions, and store() persists it
rows.summary: You build a FreeTextSuggester (bigram model) from {foo bar baz, foo bar, foo bee, fun}, so lookup('f') scores foo 3/8 and fun 1/8 and lookup('foo b') ranks 'foo bar' (2/3) and 'foo bee' (1/3) above the backed-off unigram baz (0.4 x 1/8); then you rebuild the same instance from an empty dictionary, or one whose next() throws IOException, catch the exception and keep using it. You expect the previous model to be untouched, as its FST and getCount() are, because build() publishes those only after success. Instead build() has already set the unigram token total to 0, so foo and fun both score Long.MAX_VALUE (1.0), baz jumps to first place at 1.0 ahead of both real bigram predictions, and store() writes the zero total so a reloaded copy is damaged the same way.

rows.title: AnalyzingSuggester and FuzzySuggester take the new input's payload flag before build() can fail, so after a failed rebuild (or during a rebuild) lookups decode the previous FST in the wrong payload format: the payload glued to the suggestion text, or the suggestion returned as the payload
rows.summary: You build an AnalyzingSuggester (or FuzzySuggester) from input with payloads, for example 'foo' with weight 10 and payload 'p1', then rebuild the same instance from a dictionary without payloads whose input throws an IOException partway through, and you expect lookups to keep returning the previous build ('foo', payload 'p1') or nothing. Instead lookup('fo') returns the text 'foo<U+001F>p1' with payload null, because build() stores the new input's payload flag at its start (AnalyzingSuggester.java:394) but replaces the FST only at its end (:589-590), so the old FST is read with the new flag; in the opposite direction (old build without payloads, failed rebuild with payloads) lookups return empty text with 'foo' as the payload, or trip the suggester's own assertion with -ea. A lookup made while such a rebuild is still reading its input sees the same mixture, and store() writes it to disk, so load() brings it back.

rows.title: Suggest Lookup.load() assigns its count and model fields while it is still reading the stream, so a load that throws (a stored copy cut short, a read failure, or FreeTextSuggester rejecting a model saved with other settings) leaves a mix of the previous and the new model: TSTLookup serves part of the new tree and some lookups throw NullPointerException, AnalyzingSuggester/FuzzySuggester can decode the new FST with the old payload flag, FreeTextSuggester scores the old FST with the new token total, and FST/WFSTCompletionLookup report the new count over the old FST
rows.summary: You build a TSTLookup from {aa, ab, ba, bb, cア}, then call load() with a stored copy of another model that is cut short or whose stream throws IOException part-way, and catch the exception. You expect the lookup to hold either its previous data or no data, but it reports the new model's getCount() and serves part of the new tree, and some lookups throw NullPointerException; the same happens when you load into a newly constructed TSTLookup. The other Lookups do the same in their own way, because each load() assigns count and model fields one after another as it reads: AnalyzingSuggester/FuzzySuggester can decode the new FST with the old payload flag (payload glued to the key), FreeTextSuggester scores the old FST with the new token total and changes getCount() even when it rejects a complete model saved with other grams/separator settings, and FST/WFSTCompletionLookup report the new count over the old FST.

rows.title: CachingNaiveBayesClassifier and SimpleNaiveBayesDocumentClassifier offer and assign the empty class term '', which SimpleNaiveBayesClassifier and BM25NBClassifier skip, so the Naive Bayes classifiers disagree on the same index
rows.summary: You index training documents where some carry an empty class value (for example StringField("cat", "") for unlabelled rows) and build SimpleNaiveBayesClassifier, CachingNaiveBayesClassifier and SimpleNaiveBayesDocumentClassifier on the same reader, expecting the two subclasses to offer the same classes as their parent, which (like BM25NBClassifier) skips the empty class term with 'if (next.length > 0)'. Instead the caching and document classifiers list '' as a class: getClasses('car') gives ['', 'fruit', 'vehicle'] against the parent's ['fruit', 'vehicle'], and with two empty-class 'car bus' documents both assign '' to 'car bus' where the parent assigns 'vehicle'. Their class loops (CachingNaiveBayesClassifier.reInitCache and SimpleNaiveBayesDocumentClassifier.assignNormClasses) lack the parent's length check; whether the fix adds it there or removes it from the parent and BM25NBClassifier is open.
rows.area: classification / Naive Bayes classifiers (CachingNaiveBayesClassifier, SimpleNaiveBayesDocumentClassifier vs SimpleNaiveBayesClassifier, BM25NBClassifier)

rows.title: ProtectedTermFilterFactory does not pass its luceneMatchVersion to the filters it builds from wrappedFilters, so since 10.5 a wrapped truncate with prefixLength under a pinned pre-10.5 version truncates by code points instead of the legacy UTF-16 chars
rows.summary: You configure ProtectedTermFilterFactory with wrappedFilters=truncate and truncate.prefixLength=4 and pin luceneMatchVersion to 10.4.0 (in the factory args, or through CustomAnalyzer.withDefaultMatchVersion), on Lucene 10.5 or later. You expect the wrapped truncate to keep the legacy behaviour that the pinned version selects for back-compat, the first 4 UTF-16 chars, as an unwrapped truncate and the equivalent when()/endwhen() form do under the same version. Instead populateInnerFilters builds the wrapped factory from the 'truncate.*' arguments only, so it runs at Version.LATEST and keeps 4 code points: the token 'ab😀😀cd' becomes 'ab😀😀' instead of 'ab😀', with no error.
rows.area: analysis / common miscellaneous (ProtectedTermFilterFactory#populateInnerFilters: wrappedFilters factory construction; symptom in TruncateTokenFilterFactory prefixLength)

rows.title: Since 9.0 the utr30.nrm build passes gennorm2 its inputs sorted by file name, so the standard NFKC data overrides Lucene's own UTR#30 folding tables and ICUFoldingFilter turns spacing accents such as ´ ¨ ¯ ¸ into a space inside the term instead of removing them, while ` and ^ are still removed
rows.summary: You normalize a keyword field with ICUFoldingFilter and index 'O´Brien' (an acute accent used as an apostrophe); you expect the term 'obrien', because Lucene's own folding table DiacriticFolding.txt deletes U+00B4 along with the other spacing diacritics, as every release up to 8.11.x did and as the filter still does for ` and ^. Since 9.0.0 the term is 'o brien': a 2021 build change (LUCENE-9900) started passing the data files to the gennorm2 compiler sorted by file name, which puts the standard NFKC files last, and in gennorm2 a later file overrides an earlier one, so ´ ¨ ¯ ¸ ˘ ˜ and other spacing accents now become a space and 236 modifier letters fold to their base letter instead of being removed. The change was meant only to make regeneration incremental and its review assumed the order did not matter; 292 entries of Lucene's tables are now dead, and 271 code points fold differently.
rows.area: analysis / icu (ICUFoldingFilter UTR#30 folding data: the gennorm2 input order of the utr30.nrm regeneration step in lucene/analysis/icu/build.gradle, and the shipped utr30.nrm)

rows.title: ICUTransformFilterFactory accepts direction="Forward" or "FORWARD" without error (it validates the value case-insensitively) but then builds the reverse transliterator, so every token is silently transformed the wrong way (regression of LUCENE-4877, since 4.3.0)
rows.summary: You build an ICUTransformFilterFactory with id=Cyrillic-Latin and direction="Forward", which the factory accepts because it checks direction case-insensitively, and analyze 'Российская Федерация'. You expect the forward Cyrillic-Latin transliteration [Rossijskaâ, Federaciâ], as with direction="forward". You get the Cyrillic tokens back unchanged, with no error: the validation hands back the caller's own spelling, the factory then tests "forward".equals(direction), and every accepted spelling other than exact lower-case 'forward' builds the reverse (Latin-Cyrillic) transliterator.

rows.title: SynonymGraphFilterFactory and SynonymFilterFactory keep a UTF-8 byte order mark at the start of a synonyms file, so the file's first rule silently stops working and a commented-out first line that contains a comma becomes a live rule
rows.summary: You configure SynonymGraphFilterFactory (or SynonymFilterFactory) with a synonyms file that an editor saved as UTF-8 with a byte order mark (bytes EF BB BF) and expect the same rules as from the file without the mark, because Lucene's shared resource-line loader skips a leading BOM for the word-list factories that read through it (WordlistLoader.getLines, 'skip initial bom marker', SOLR-1865) and the synonym factory itself skipped it until 3.4.0. Instead the factory decodes the file with its own UTF-8 reader and SolrSynonymParser keeps U+FEFF glued to the first line: with the first rule 'foo, bar' the text 'foo' is no longer expanded (and 'bar' gains the invisible synonym '\uFEFFfoo'), a first rule 'baz => qux' never fires, and a first line '#couch, sofa' is no longer a comment, so 'sofa' expands to '\uFEFF#couch'. In WordNet format the fixed-column synset id (substring(2, 11)) is shifted by one character, so the first word ends up in a synset of its own; nothing reports an error.
rows.area: analysis-common / synonym file loading (SynonymGraphFilterFactory and the deprecated SynonymFilterFactory loadSynonyms -> SolrSynonymParser, WordnetSynonymParser)

rows.title: Kuromoji and Nori UserDictionary.open keep a leading UTF-8 byte order mark, so Nori silently drops the first user-dictionary entry and Kuromoji refuses to load the file
rows.summary: You give KoreanTokenizerFactory or JapaneseTokenizerFactory a user dictionary file that an editor saved as UTF-8 with a byte order mark (bytes EF BB BF), and expect the same dictionary as from the file without the mark, because Lucene's shared resource-line loader skips a leading BOM for the other file-based analysis factories (WordlistLoader.getLines, 'skip initial bom marker', SOLR-1865). Instead both factories decode the file themselves and pass it to UserDictionary.open, which keeps the invisible U+FEFF on line 1: in Nori the first entry becomes '\uFEFF세종시', which no text contains, so 세종시 is segmented [세, 종시] instead of the user's [세종, 시] with no error. Kuromoji (9.0.0 and later) rejects the file with 'Illegal user dictionary entry \uFEFF関西国際空港 - the concatenated segmentation (関西国際空港) does not match the surface form (\uFEFF関西国際空港)', and when line 1 is a '#' comment or blank it throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException 'Index 1 out of bounds for length 1', because the BOM hides the comment from its 'skip empty lines or comment lines' check.
rows.area: analysis-kuromoji + analysis-nori / user dictionary loading (UserDictionary.open, reached through the JapaneseTokenizerFactory / KoreanTokenizerFactory userDictionary argument)

rows.title: FileDictionary(InputStream) and PlainTextDictionary(Path/InputStream) decode the file as UTF-8 themselves but keep a leading byte order mark, so the file's first entry carries an invisible U+FEFF: prefix suggesters never suggest it and SpellChecker.exist() does not find it
rows.summary: You build a suggester or a spell checker from a UTF-8 text file whose first line is 'foo<TAB>5' (or just 'foo') but which an editor saved with a byte order mark (the bytes EF BB BF), passing it to FileDictionary(InputStream) or PlainTextDictionary(Path or InputStream), whose javadoc says 'NOTE: content is treated as UTF-8', and you expect the same entries as from the same file without the mark, because the mark is only an encoding signature and Lucene's own line loaders skip it (WordlistLoader.getLines, SOLR-1865; hunspell, LUCENE-5505). Instead these constructors decode the bytes with Java's UTF-8 decoder, which returns the mark as the character U+FEFF, and nothing removes it, so the first entry becomes '\uFEFFfoo': WFSTCompletionLookup, FSTCompletionLookup and TSTLookup return nothing for lookup("fo"), AnalyzingSuggester returns '\uFEFFfoo', and a SpellChecker reports exist("foo") = false. No error is raised and only the first line is affected.
rows.area: suggest / text-file dictionaries (FileDictionary feeding Lookup.build, PlainTextDictionary feeding SpellChecker.indexDictionary)

rows.title: With format="snowball", StopFilterFactory, KeepWordFilterFactory, CommonGramsFilterFactory and SuggestStopFilterFactory keep a leading UTF-8 byte order mark glued to the first word of the words file, so that word silently stops matching, while the default "wordset" format of the same factories strips the mark
rows.summary: You configure StopFilterFactory (or KeepWordFilterFactory, CommonGramsFilterFactory, CommonGramsQueryFilterFactory or SuggestStopFilterFactory) with format="snowball" and a UTF-8 words file that begins with a byte order mark, and expect the same words that the default "wordset" format reads from such a file, because that format skips a leading BOM (WordlistLoader.getLines, 'skip initial bom marker', a rule recorded in SOLR-1865). Instead the snowball loader keeps the invisible U+FEFF glued to the first word, so the set holds "\uFEFFthe" instead of "the" (getStopWords() = [a, \uFEFFthe, an]): StopFilter no longer removes 'the', KeepWordFilter drops the tokens of the first keep word, CommonGrams does not treat it as common, and a BOM before a comment or blank first line adds a stray "\uFEFF" entry. No error is raised.

rows.title: ICUTokenizerFactory keeps the UTF-8 byte order mark at the start of a custom per-script rule file (rulefiles) as rule text, so the file either fails with a misleading ICU syntax error or loads without error and the tokenizer then emits no tokens for that script (every release since 4.1.0)
rows.summary: You configure ICUTokenizerFactory with rulefiles="Latn:latin.rbbi" and a rule file saved as UTF-8 with a byte order mark (BOM), as editors such as Windows Notepad often write and as ICU's own rule-file compiler genbrk accepts (it strips the BOM, and its man page recommends one), and expect the same tokens as with the same file without the BOM. Instead ICUTokenizerFactory.parseRules decodes the BOM to U+FEFF and passes it to ICU's RuleBasedBreakIterator(String) as rule text: a file that starts with the rule '.+ {200};' (alone or after '#' comment lines) compiles with U+FEFF as a literal prefix of that rule, so 'ab cd' gives no tokens at all instead of ['ab cd'], and a file that starts with a comment and '!!forward;' (the shape of Lucene's Latin-break-only-on-whitespace.rbbi) fails with 'IllegalArgumentException: Error 66052 at line 2 column 1'. Nothing on disk is corrupted, but in the silent case all text of the tailored script disappears from the analyzed output with no error.
rows.area: analysis / ICU (ICUTokenizerFactory per-script rule files: rulefiles, parseRules)

rows.title: Stempel's Trie.reduce with Gener or Lift rewrites the cells of the trie it is given, so reducing PolishAnalyzer.getDefaultTable(), documented as unmodifiable, silently changes the stems of every later PolishAnalyzer and StempelPolishStemFilterFactory in the JVM
rows.summary: You call reduce(new Gener()) or reduce(new Lift(..)) on a stempel Trie, for example on PolishAnalyzer.getDefaultTable(), which is documented as 'an unmodifiable instance of the default stemmer table', and expect what Trie.reduce's javadoc says, 'the newly reduced Trie', with the input left as it was (Optimizer and Optimizer2 behave so). Instead Lift.optimize and Gener.optimize take the input's own row list and rewrite its cells in place (Lift moves commands up a level and clears references, Gener drops infrequent commands and references) before copying them into the result, so the input answers differently afterwards: after PolishAnalyzer.getDefaultTable().reduce(new Gener()) every new PolishAnalyzer stems 'książkami rzekami pracowali' to [książk, rzekami, pracowali] instead of [książek, rzekść, pracować], and a one-key trie {aa -> Da} reduced with Lift(false) starts to answer getLastOnPath('a') = Da instead of nothing. Copying the rows before the rewrite fixes it; upstream TestStemmer, which reduces one trie five times, then needs a fresh trie per reduction.
rows.area: analysis/stempel / egothor stemmer trie reductions (Trie.reduce with Lift and Gener; the shared PolishAnalyzer.getDefaultTable() table)

rows.title: DelimitedPayloadTokenFilterFactory creates one instance of a custom PayloadEncoder class and hands it to every filter it creates, so all threads using the analyzer share it, and nothing documents that a custom encoder must be thread-safe: an encoder that reuses its BytesRef silently stores other documents' payloads during ordinary concurrent indexing, and one whose payloads vary in length makes the next flush throw and the IndexWriter close itself
rows.summary: You configure DelimitedPayloadTokenFilterFactory with your own PayloadEncoder class whose encode() reuses one BytesRef, which is correct inside any single token stream because PayloadAttributeImpl deep-copies payloads, and you index from four threads; you expect every document to keep its own payload, as it does when each filter gets its own encoder through the public constructor. Instead the factory creates the encoder once in inform() and passes that one instance to every filter in create(), so the per-thread analyzer components share it and another thread's encode() overwrites a payload before the indexer reads it: on main, 384 to 7,153 of 20,000 documents end up with another document's payload, with no exception. PayloadEncoder, the factory and the analysis-factory javadocs say nothing about the encoder being shared or needing to be thread-safe, while the sibling PhoneticFilterFactory creates its class-loaded encoder per filter for exactly this reason.
rows.area: analysis / analysis-common payloads (DelimitedPayloadTokenFilterFactory, PayloadEncoder, DelimitedPayloadTokenFilter)

rows.title: Kuromoji's romaji reading (ToStringUtil.getRomanization, used by JapaneseReadingFormFilter with useRomaji=true) writes the small tsu ッ as a doubled consonant only before the k, s, t and p rows and silently drops it before any other kana, so loanwords with ッ before g, z/j, d, b or h/f lose it: バッグ 'bag' and バグ 'bug' both become 'bagu', ベッド becomes 'bedo'
rows.summary: You analyze Japanese text with JapaneseTokenizer and JapaneseReadingFormFilter(useRomaji=true), whose romanizer is documented as 'Romanize katakana with modified hepburn', and expect the small tsu ッ to double the next consonant, as the method already does for キット -> 'kitto' and マッチ -> 'matchi'. Instead the 'ッ' case appends a consonant only for the カ, サ, タ and パ rows and appends nothing otherwise, so バッグ 'bag' becomes 'bagu', the same term as バグ 'bug', ベッド becomes 'bedo' and スタッフ becomes 'sutafu'. Distinct words then match each other, and a romaji query 'baggu' finds no document that contains バッグ.
rows.area: analysis / kuromoji romanization (ToStringUtil.getRomanization; JapaneseReadingFormFilter romaji mode)

rows.title: Kuromoji's completion table romaji_map.txt has no rows for チェ, イェ, ツァ/ツィ/ツェ/ツォ, ディ/デュ and ウォ, although it has rows for their siblings (チャ/チュ/チョ, シェ/ジェ, ッイェ, ティ/テュ, ウィ/ウェ), so raw-romaji prefixes such as 'che', 'ye' and 'tsa' suggest nothing for words like チェック, イェール and ツァー
rows.summary: You index ordinary loanwords such as チェック, イェール, ツァー, ディスク or ウォッカ with JapaneseCompletionAnalyzer and expect a user who types the usual romaji, che(kku), ye or tsa (or the IME keystrokes dhi, dhu, who), to get them as suggestions, because the analyzer lists (modified) Hepburn, Kunrei-shiki and Wapuro romanization as supported and its table already has these spellings for the sibling kana: シェ she, ジェ je, チャ cha, ティ thi, テュ thu, ウィ wi, ウェ we and even the doubled form ッイェ yye. Instead romaji_map.txt has no row for チェ, イェ, ツァ, ツィ, ツェ, ツォ, ディ, デュ or ウォ, so KatakanaRomanizer splits each into its base kana plus a small vowel (チ+ェ -> tixe/chixe, イ+ェ -> ixe, ツ+ァ -> tuxa/tsuxa, デ+ィ -> dexi, ウ+ォ -> uxo) and these raw-romaji queries suggest nothing. Queries typed in kana, including partly composed ones such as ちぇっk, still match, because the index and query sides use the same fallback.
rows.area: analysis / kuromoji (JapaneseCompletionFilter and JapaneseCompletionAnalyzer romanization data: the bundled table romaji_map.txt that KatakanaRomanizer reads)

rows.title: Kuromoji's completion table romaji_map.txt has three typo rows: the ッヘ row uses a hiragana へ (U+3078) in its key, so katakana ッヘ is romanized 'xtuhe' instead of 'hhe' and a word like ヨッヘン is not suggested for 'yohhen', and the ッスォ and ッドゥ rows carry the copied spellings 'suxo' and 'ddoxi'
rows.summary: You index the katakana name ヨッヘン with JapaneseCompletionAnalyzer and type its romaji 'yohhen' into a suggester, and expect the name to be suggested, just as ヨッハン is suggested for 'yohhan'. Instead nothing is suggested: the table row meant for ッヘ, 'ッへ,hhe' (romaji_map.txt line 219), has the look-alike HIRAGANA LETTER HE (U+3078) in its key, and romanize() only ever receives katakana or a-z, so the row can never match and ッヘ falls back to 'ッ'->'xtu' plus 'ヘ'->'he' (indexed as 'yoxtuhen'). The same table gives ッスォ the undoubled spelling 'suxo' (line 281, the spelling of スォ) and ッドゥ the spelling 'ddoxi' (line 289, copied from ッドィ) instead of 'ssuxo' and 'ddoxu'; a three-character table edit fixes all three.
rows.area: analysis / kuromoji (JapaneseCompletionFilter and JapaneseCompletionAnalyzer romanization table romaji_map.txt, read by KatakanaRomanizer)

rows.title: JapaneseIterationMarkCharFilter expands the unvoiced kana iteration mark ゝ/ヽ after the na-row, the small tsu and the handakuten kana (な に ぬ ね の, っ, ぱ ぴ ぷ ぺ and their katakana forms) to a different kana, so なゝめ becomes などめ instead of ななめ (のゝしる becomes のねしる, ぱゝ becomes ぱば), because kana that have no voiced form are stored as self-mappings in the voicing table and the 'is voiced' check reads every self-mapping as voiced
rows.summary: You put JapaneseIterationMarkCharFilter in front of an analyzer and index なゝめ, the older spelling of ななめ ('diagonal'), and expect the filter to replace the iteration mark ゝ with the repeated kana, as its javadoc promises ('normalizes ... iteration marks to their expanded form'). Instead it emits などめ, so the index holds a different word and a search for ななめ finds nothing; the same happens for 19 more kana (のゝ becomes のね, ぱゝ becomes ぱば, っゝ becomes っぢ, and the katakana forms with ヽ). The filter decides whether the preceding kana is voiced by checking whether it maps to itself in its voicing table, but the kana that have no voiced form (っ, な..の, ぱ ぴ ぷ ぺ) are stored there as self-mappings too, so it strips a dakuten they never had and emits the preceding code point.

rows.title: ASCIIFoldingFilter folds the ligature ﬆ (U+FB06) to 'st' but has no entry for its sibling ﬅ (U+FB05 LATIN SMALL LIGATURE LONG S T, NFKD 'st'), so 'faﬅ' is indexed unchanged and the ASCII query 'fast' does not find it
rows.summary: You fold text with ASCIIFoldingFilter, whose javadoc says it converts characters 'into their ASCII equivalents, if one exists' and lists the Alphabetic Presentation Forms block, and you search in plain ASCII. You expect 'faﬅ' (with the long-s-t ligature U+FB05, whose NFKD is 'st') to be indexed as 'fast', just as 'faﬆ' (U+FB06) and 'faſt' (long s U+017F) are; instead the table has cases for U+FB00-FB04 and U+FB06 but none for U+FB05, so the character passes through unchanged, the term stays 'faﬅ' and the query 'fast' finds nothing. The fix is one case label (U+FB05 added to the U+FB06 'st' group) plus the matching row of the generated testAllFoldings array.
