rows.title: ICUFoldingFilter removes the hook, stroke or descender from older Cyrillic letters such as ҧ (U+04A7) but from none of the 24 letters of that kind added in Unicode 4.1-7.0, such as its modern Abkhaz counterpart ԥ (U+0525), so the two spellings of a word give different terms
rows.summary: You index Abkhaz text in the older spelling 'аҧсуа' with ICUFoldingFilter, whose javadoc lists 'Diacritic removal (including stroke, hook, descender)' and which folds ҧ (U+04A7) to п, and you expect the modern spelling 'аԥсуа', written with ԥ (U+0525, the modern-orthography counterpart of U+04A7), to find it. Instead the hand-copied Cyrillic table in DiacriticFolding.txt, taken from the 2004 UTR#30 draft data for Unicode 4.0 and never extended, has no line for ԥ or for any of the other 23 hook, stroke or descender letters added in Unicode 4.1-7.0 (ӷ ӻ ӽ ӿ ԓ ԡ ԣ ꚋ ԧ ԩ ԯ and the capitals), so they are only case-folded and keep the mark, and the query finds 0 documents. All 48 older letters of the same kind lose the mark (46 fold to their base letter; ҷ/Ҷ fold to a wrong letter, the separate bug LFV-855).

rows.title: SpanishPluralStemmer's special-case list has the singular 'contrarreloj' where the plural 'contrarrelojes' belongs, so the singular is cut to 'contrarrel', the plural stems to 'contrarreloje', and the two forms never match
rows.summary: You stem Spanish text with SpanishPluralStemFilter, which CHANGES describes as 'precise stemming of Spanish plurals', and expect the plural 'contrarrelojes' to reduce to 'contrarreloj' and the singular 'contrarreloj' to stay as it is, as 'relojes' -> 'reloj' and 'bojes' -> 'boj' do. Instead the singular becomes 'contrarrel' and the plural 'contrarreloje', so a document containing 'contrarrelojes' is not found by the query 'contrarreloj'. The cause is one entry of the hand-written special-case list (SpanishPluralStemmer.java:163): the 12 other entries are plurals in -es whose last two letters stem() removes (:173, 'return len - 2'), but this entry is the singular, and the missing plural falls through to the generic 'remove the final s' rule (:222-224).

rows.title: TeluguNormalizer composes ఒ + ౌ (U+0C12 LETTER O + U+0C4C VOWEL SIGN AU) into AU (U+0C14) but never applies its own AU -> OO fold to the result, so in a chain without IndicNormalizationFilter in front the two spellings of AU normalize to different terms
rows.summary: You analyze Telugu text with TeluguNormalizationFilter (or the 'teluguNormalization' factory) without IndicNormalizationFilter in front of it, as in the factory javadoc example. The normalizer folds the letter AU (ఔ, U+0C14) to OO (ఓ, U+0C13), a rule the upstream test pins, and it also recognizes the two-character spelling ఒ + ౌ (U+0C12 U+0C4C) as AU, so both spellings of a word such as ఔషధం ('medicine') should give the same term. Instead the composition writes AU at a position that the single left-to-right pass never visits again, so ఒౌషధం keeps AU (term ఔషధం) while ఔషధం becomes ఓషధం, and the two spellings silently stop matching each other.
rows.area: analysis-common / Telugu normalizer (TeluguNormalizer.normalize; TeluguNormalizationFilter and the 'teluguNormalization' factory)

rows.title: JapaneseTokenizer and KoreanTokenizer cut an unknown word at the 1024-char cap (MAX_UNKNOWN_WORD_LENGTH) even in the middle of a surrogate pair, so a supplementary character (an emoji, a CJK Extension B ideograph) at char 1023 of a long same-class run is emitted as two unpaired surrogate halves and indexed as U+FFFD
rows.summary: You analyze a long run of text that kuromoji or nori treat as one unknown word, for example 1,200 chars of Thai without spaces through the 'japanese' tokenizer, or 400 x (U+1F441 U+FE0F) emoji through the default KoreanAnalyzer, and the run holds an emoji or a rare ideograph such as U+20000; you expect every term to consist of whole characters, as it does when that character sits one position earlier or later. Instead both tokenizers stop the unknown word at exactly 1024 UTF-16 chars without checking for a surrogate pair, so when the character's first half is char 1023, term 0 ends in a lone high surrogate and term 1 starts with the lone low surrogate. The index silently stores both halves as U+FFFD, and in the unigram modes a TermQuery for the character finds 0 documents instead of 1.
rows.area: analysis / kuromoji and nori Viterbi unknown-word length cap (JapaneseTokenizer and the 'japanese' factory; KoreanTokenizer, KoreanAnalyzer and the 'korean' factory)

rows.title: JapaneseTokenizer and KoreanTokenizer with discardPunctuation=true (the default) keep punctuation and symbols outside the BMP (U+10100, U+1E95E, emoji such as U+1F600) as tokens, because isPunctuation classifies a single UTF-16 unit (the high surrogate), while BMP characters of the same general category are dropped (released since 3.6.0 and 7.4.0)
rows.summary: You tokenize '日本 😀 日本' or '한국 𐄀 한국' (U+1F600, U+10100) with JapaneseTokenizer or KoreanTokenizer and discardPunctuation=true, the default, and expect [日本, 日本] and [한국, 한국], because the javadoc says punctuation tokens are dropped and both tokenizers drop every BMP character of the same Unicode general category (Po U+3001, So U+2605, Sm U+2207). Instead the supplementary character is kept as a token ([日本, 😀, 日本], [한국, 𐄀, 한국]): isPunctuation(char) calls Character.getType on the high surrogate alone, whose type is SURROGATE, so the discard test at the token start never sees the real category. No error is raised; the default KoreanAnalyzer indexes the extra token, and the default JapaneseAnalyzer removes it only later, through its part-of-speech stop filter, which leaves a position gap.

rows.title: SimplePatternTokenizer and SimplePatternSplitTokenizer join an unpaired high surrogate with the character after it, so a following space no longer separates two words and a following letter is lost
rows.summary: You tokenize 'a' U+D83D ' b' (an unpaired high surrogate, as left by cutting a string inside an emoji, then a space and 'b') with SimplePatternTokenizer('[^ ]+') or SimplePatternSplitTokenizer('[ ]+') and expect two tokens, 'a'+U+D83D [0,2) and 'b' [3,4): that is what String.split("[ ]+"), PatternTokenizer and WhitespaceTokenizer give, and what the tokenizers' own automaton accepts under CharacterRunAutomaton.run. Instead both emit one token 'a'+U+D83D+' b' [0,4), because nextCodePoint() pairs the high surrogate with whatever unit follows it without checking for a low surrogate, so the space becomes part of the made-up code point U+11820 and stops being a separator; with a letters-only pattern the next letter is lost the same way (SimplePatternTokenizer('[a-z]+') on U+D83D 'ab' gives 'b' [2,3) instead of 'ab' [1,3)), and nothing throws.
rows.area: analysis / pattern tokenizers (analysis-common: SimplePatternTokenizer, SimplePatternSplitTokenizer and their simplePattern / simplePatternSplit factories)

rows.title: ICUTokenizer with myanmarAsWords=false silently drops the Myanmar modifier letters U+A9E6 and U+AA70 (Shan and Khamti reduplication, as in 'ကꧦ'), and Common-script letters such as MICRO SIGN that fall into a Myanmar run, because MyanmarSyllable.rbbi gives a token status only to syllables and numbers
rows.summary: You tokenize Myanmar-script text with ICUTokenizer in syllable mode (new DefaultICUTokenizerConfig(true, false), or ICUTokenizerFactory with myanmarAsWords="false"), whose only documented effect is that Myanmar text 'will be tokenized as syllables', and expect every letter to end up in some token, as in the default mode, where 'ကꧦ' (KA + U+A9E6 MYANMAR MODIFIER LETTER SHAN REDUPLICATION) gives [ကꧦ] and 'ကꩰ' (KA + U+AA70 MYANMAR MODIFIER LETTER KHAMTI REDUPLICATION) gives [ကꩰ]. Instead syllable mode gives [က] for both, a mark on its own gives no token, and 'ကောင်း µm' gives [ကောင်း, m] (the space and µ are Common script, so the script iterator keeps them in the Myanmar run), all without an error. The cause is the rule file: MyanmarSyllable.rbbi gives a non-zero rule status only to syllables built on a consonant, consonant placeholder or independent vowel ({200}) and to numbers ({100}), and ICUTokenizer skips every segment with status 0.
rows.area: analysis / ICU (DefaultICUTokenizerConfig syllable rules MyanmarSyllable.rbbi / MyanmarSyllable.brk, used for Myanmar text when myanmarAsWords=false; ICUTokenizerFactory 'icu' with myanmarAsWords="false")

rows.title: UAX29URLEmailTokenizer does not emit an ftp URL with no path ('ftp://host') as one URL token, although its http rule and RFC 1738 make the path optional
rows.summary: You run text such as 'get it from ftp://ftp.example.com today' or 'ftp://localhost' through UAX29URLEmailTokenizer, whose javadoc says URLs are 'tokenized according to the relevant RFCs', and expect each ftp URL as one <URL> token, because RFC 1738 (section 3.2.2: 'The whole url-path may be omitted, including the "/" delimiting it') and RFC 3986 (an empty path after an authority) allow it, and the same tokenizer already keeps 'http://localhost' whole. Instead it emits 'ftp' as <ALPHANUM> followed by the rest on its own ('ftp.example.com' as <URL>, 'localhost' as <ALPHANUM>, '192.0.2.10' as <NUM>, '//anonymous@ftp.example.org' as <EMAIL>), because the grammar's FTPurl rule makes the '/'-led FTPorFILEpath mandatory while the http rule beside it makes its path optional. With a trailing slash ('ftp://ftp.example.com/') the URL is one token, and nothing reports an error.
rows.area: analysis / UAX29URLEmailTokenizer JFlex URL rules (FTPurl production; analysis-common)

rows.title: CSVUtil.parse decodes every quoted field except the last one of the line, so a quoted last field (for example the part-of-speech of a kuromoji user-dictionary entry) keeps its quote characters
rows.summary: You parse a CSV line whose last field is quoted, for example CSVUtil.parse("x," + CSVUtil.quoteEscape("To be, or not to be")), or load a kuromoji user dictionary written with every field quoted, and expect the quoted value to be decoded the same way as in any other position, as parse does for every field followed by a comma. Instead the last field comes back raw, enclosing quotes and doubled inner quotes included: parse("\"a,b\",\"c,d\"") returns [a,b, "c,d"], and the dictionary line "abcd","a b cd","foo1 foo2 foo3","bar" yields tokens whose part-of-speech is "bar" with the quotes. The cause is one line: parse passes each comma-terminated field through unQuoteUnEscape (CSVUtil.java:56) but adds the final field as sb.toString() (:65).

rows.title: CSVUtil.parse keeps the enclosing quotes of a field that holds both a comma and a double quote, so it does not decode CSVUtil.quoteEscape output
rows.summary: You encode a value that holds both a comma and a double quote with CSVUtil.quoteEscape, which doubles the quotes and wraps the value in quotes (the exact output Lucene's own TestCSVUtil.testQuoteEscapeQuotesAndComma expects), put it before another field in a CSV line, and expect CSVUtil.parse to give the value back, as it does for values with only a comma or only a quote. Instead parse unescapes the inner quotes but keeps the enclosing ones: the value a "b", c is encoded as "a ""b"", c" and parse returns "a "b", c" with the outer quotes still on it. The cause is the unquote regex ^"([^"]+)"$ (CSVUtil.java:29), which strips enclosing quotes only from a field that has no quote inside.

rows.title: Kuromoji's DictionaryBuilder silently accepts a reading or pronunciation of 128 or more chars and stores its length in 7 bits, so the built system dictionary returns an empty or truncated reading and a garbage pronunciation (a too-long base form, by contrast, is rejected)
rows.summary: You build a custom kuromoji system dictionary with DictionaryBuilder from an IPADIC-format CSV that has a row whose reading is 128 katakana chars long (or, more naturally, a 64-char proper noun with a 136-char reading), and you expect either an IllegalArgumentException at build time, as the builder throws for a stored base form of 16 or more chars that its compact format cannot hold, or the reading back unchanged. Instead the build succeeds, because putEntry writes each length as (byte) (length << 1 | kanaFlag) with no check, so the stored length is the real length mod 128: getReading and JapaneseTokenizer's ReadingAttribute return "" for the 128-char reading and only the first 8 chars of the 136-char one, a 128-char pronunciation comes back empty, a pronunciation stored after a wrapped reading is decoded from the reading's own bytes (a 4-char pronunciation came back as the single char U+0304), and JapaneseReadingFormFilter indexes the empty or truncated reading as the term.
rows.area: analysis / kuromoji system dictionary builder (ja.dict.TokenInfoDictionaryEntryWriter reading and pronunciation length bytes; TokenInfoMorphData decoding; custom dictionaries built with DictionaryBuilder)

rows.title: Nori's DictionaryBuilder checks that rows sharing a left context id have the same part of speech only with a Java assert, so with assertions off a custom system dictionary silently gives those words the part of speech of another row and KoreanPartOfSpeechStopFilter drops or keeps them wrongly
rows.summary: You compile a custom nori system dictionary with DictionaryBuilder from MeCab-format rows in which the noun 가 (NNG) and the particle 는 (JX) share left context id 1, and expect the builder either to reject the source (the compiled format keeps only one part of speech per left id, and kuromoji's builder throws 'Multiple entries found for leftID' for the same case) or each word to keep its own part of speech. Instead, with assertions off, the builder overwrites the single slot for left id 1 with the part of speech of the row it writes last, because the only check is an assert (TokenInfoDictionaryEntryWriter.java:100): 가 then reports left POS JX, and KoreanTokenizer followed by KoreanPartOfSpeechStopFilter with DEFAULT_STOP_TAGS returns no token instead of [가]. With -ea the build fails with a bare AssertionError rather than an IllegalArgumentException that names the problem.

rows.title: Nori's DictionaryBuilder rejects a left context id of 8192 or more but silently accepts such a right context id, which does not round-trip through the compiled format, so the compiled dictionary returns a wrapped right id (changing segmentation) or makes KoreanTokenizer throw IndexOutOfBoundsException
rows.summary: You compile a custom nori system dictionary with DictionaryBuilder from MeCab-format sources in which a lexicon row (or an unk.def row) has right context id 16385, with a matrix.def that declares 16386 right ids, and expect the row either to be rejected, as a left id of 8192 is ('leftId >= 8192'), or to read back as 16385. Instead the builder accepts it and packs the id into a 14-bit field without any check (TokenInfoDictionaryEntryWriter.java:137), so Dictionary.getRightId returns 1 and KoreanTokenizer uses the connection costs of right id 1: in the repro '가나다' is split [가나, 다] instead of [가, 나다]. A right id in [8192, 16383] decodes to about 1.07 billion, and tokenizing any text that contains the word throws IndexOutOfBoundsException from ConnectionCosts.get.

rows.title: SimplePatternTokenizer and SimplePatternSplitTokenizer restart a failed match one UTF-16 unit after a supplementary start character, so they can emit tokens that start or end inside a surrogate pair
rows.summary: You tokenize 'E x', where E is an emoji such as U+1F525, with SimplePatternTokenizer and the pattern E[a-z]+|[^E ]+ (E followed by letters, or a run of characters other than E and space) and expect the single token 'x' [3,4): the attempt at E dies at the space, and the tokenizer, which steps its automaton over code points, should move on to the next code point (PatternTokenizer and java.util.regex give exactly [x]). Instead it also emits a token made of E's lone low surrogate U+DD25 at offsets [1,2), which the index stores as U+FFFD, because the failed-attempt branch pushes back all but one UTF-16 unit and so restarts in the middle of the pair. SimplePatternSplitTokenizer has the same step: separator Ea|[^Ea ]+ on 'Eb' yields the lone high surrogate [0,1) instead of the token 'E' [0,2), and with separator [^a-zE]+|E! the text 'abEcd' becomes 'ab' plus a lone high surrogate, then 'cd', instead of the one token 'abEcd'; nothing throws.
rows.area: analysis / pattern tokenizers (analysis-common: SimplePatternTokenizer, SimplePatternSplitTokenizer and their simplePattern / simplePatternSplit factories)

rows.title: IrishLowerCaseFilter lower-cases one UTF-16 unit at a time, so IrishAnalyzer leaves upper-case letters outside the BMP (Adlam, Osage, Deseret and others) unchanged
rows.summary: You index text with IrishAnalyzer (or put IrishLowerCaseFilter in a chain), whose filter is documented to 'normalise token text to lower case', and expect a capitalised word to match its lower-case form, as it does with LowerCaseFilter. For letters outside the BMP it does not: the Adlam capital U+1E900 stays U+1E900 instead of becoming U+1E922 (the Deseret capital U+10400 likewise stays, also after n-eclipsis), so a document holding the Adlam word U+1E900 U+1E923 is not found by U+1E922 U+1E923 (0 hits instead of 1). The loop at IrishLowerCaseFilter.java:55 passes one UTF-16 char to Character.toLowerCase, which returns a surrogate unit unchanged; BMP letters in the same token are lower-cased and nothing is thrown.
rows.area: analysis-common / ga (IrishLowerCaseFilter and IrishAnalyzer case mapping)

rows.title: DoubleMetaphoneFilter drops the alternate (secondary) code of a token whose text already equals its primary code, so 'JR' gets only JR while 'jr' gets JR and AR
rows.summary: You run text through DoubleMetaphoneFilter, documented as 'supporting secondary codes', and expect the token 'JR' to get the same codes as 'jr', because the encoder is case-insensitive and gives both the primary code JR and the alternate code AR. Instead, when a token's text already equals its own primary code, the filter keeps the token as the primary but never emits the alternate: 'jr' gives JR and AR, 'JR' gives only JR, in both inject modes and at every maxCodeLength where the token equals its code. A document containing 'JR' is then missed by a query that matches only through AR (executed: TermQuery AR matches the document 'jr' but not the document 'JR'), while matches through the primary code still work.

rows.title: CapitalizationFilter treats a second delimiter in a row ('. ', a double space) or a delimiter at the start of the token as the first character of the next word, so that word is not capitalized and misses keep, okPrefix and minWordLength ('dr. jekyll' -> 'Dr. jekyll', 'new york' -> 'New york', ' hello' -> ' hello')

Instead you get 'Dr. jekyll' and 'New york': after the delimiter that ends a word the loop skips the next character, so a second delimiter becomes the first character of the next word, the filter 'capitalizes' that delimiter and lower-cases the real first letter, and a keep word such as 'USA' after two spaces becomes 'usa'. With the default settings a token that starts with a space or a period (' hello world', '.net') keeps its first word lower case, and nothing throws.

rows.title: CapitalizationFilter changes case one UTF-16 char at a time, so cased letters outside the BMP (Adlam, Osage, Deseret and five other scripts) are neither capitalized nor lower-cased, while BMP letters in the same token are
rows.summary: You add CapitalizationFilter, documented to 'make the first letter capital and the rest lower case', and give it a word in a cased script outside the BMP, for example the Adlam word U+1E922 U+1E923 (two small letters), and expect U+1E900 U+1E923 (capital first letter). Instead every supplementary letter keeps its case: U+1E922 U+1E923 comes out unchanged, U+1E900 U+1E901 is not lower-cased to U+1E900 U+1E923, and 'aB' followed by the Osage capital U+104B0 gives 'Ab' + U+104B0, because processWord applies Character.toUpperCase(char) and toLowerCase(char) to single UTF-16 units and a surrogate unit maps to itself. BMP letters in the same token are mapped, nothing is thrown, and the onlyFirstWord and keep-word forceFirstLetter paths behave the same way.
rows.area: analysis-common / miscellaneous (CapitalizationFilter case mapping)

rows.title: SoraniNormalizer tests for format characters one UTF-16 char at a time, so format characters outside the BMP (U+E0001, the tag characters U+E0020..U+E007F, U+1BCA0..U+1BCA3, U+1D173..U+1D17A and others) are kept in the term, while BMP ones such as RLM and LRM are removed
rows.summary: You analyze Sorani Kurdish text with the stock SoraniAnalyzer or SoraniNormalizationFilter. The normalizer's javadoc says formatting characters are removed, and it does remove BMP ones such as the right-to-left mark, so کورد + X + ستان should become کوردستان for any invisible format character X. Instead it calls Character.getType on one UTF-16 char at a time, so a format character outside the BMP (for example U+E0001 or a tag character), which Java stores as two surrogate chars, is never recognized: it stays in the term, and the word no longer matches the same word without it, with no error.
rows.area: analysis-common / Sorani normalizer (SoraniNormalizer.normalize; SoraniNormalizationFilter, SoraniAnalyzer and the 'soraniNormalization' factory)

rows.title: LuceneLevenshteinDistance.getDistance returns 0 for two empty strings and max(n, m) (for example 3.0) when one string is empty, instead of a similarity score (a 2011 regression from LUCENE-3662)
rows.summary: LuceneLevenshteinDistance is documented as a similarity (StringDistance: 1 means identical, 0 maximally different) that is 'consistent' with FuzzyTermsEnum, and for two non-empty strings it returns 1 - distance / min(length). When a string is empty it instead returns a raw edit distance: 0 for getDistance("", "") and max(n, m) for one empty side, so getDistance("", "abc") = 3.0, three times the score of identical strings. Through DirectSpellChecker set up with new LuceneLevenshteinDistance(), minPrefix 0 and minQueryLength 1, an indexed empty term is suggested for the query "a" with score 1.0, while the default internal scoring filters it out.
rows.area: suggest / spell checking (LuceneLevenshteinDistance.getDistance, the StringDistance class behind DirectSpellChecker.INTERNAL_LEVENSHTEIN)

rows.title: Operations.isTotal returns true for a deterministic automaton that can reach a dead state, so an AutomatonQuery can match every term
rows.summary: You call Operations.isTotal, or build an AutomatonQuery, on a deterministic automaton that rejects some strings and has a reachable dead state, such as a complete DFA with an explicit sink state built by hand. You expect false, as Lucene 9.12.0 returns. Instead, since 10.0.0, isTotal checks only live states, so a transition into the dead state counts as coverage and it returns true; CompiledAutomaton then compiles the query to AUTOMATON_TYPE.ALL, and in the repro an AutomatonQuery matched 3 documents instead of 2.
rows.area: util / automaton

rows.title: Classic QueryParser and flexible StandardQueryParser: a TAB, LF, CR or U+3000 next to a range bound inside [..] or {..} becomes part of the bound, because RANGE_GOOP excludes only U+0020 although both grammars declare these characters as whitespace and skip them in the Range state; such ranges fail to parse or, when the character touches a bracket, silently change their bounds
rows.summary: You parse 'date:[20200101<TAB>TO<TAB>20201231]' or the multi-line 'date:[<LF>20200101 TO 20201231<LF>]' with the classic or the flexible standard query parser; both grammars declare TAB, LF, CR and U+3000 as whitespace and skip it inside ranges too, so you expect the same query as with spaces. Instead the range-bound token RANGE_GOOP, which excludes only U+0020 and the closing brackets, swallows any of these characters that touches a bound: the first query throws ParseException ('Was expecting: "TO"'), and the second parses without error into a TermRangeQuery whose bounds are '<LF>20200101' and '20201231<LF>', so it also matches 20191231 (4 hits instead of 3). In the same way 'date:{20200101 TO 20201231<TAB>}' admits its own exclusive endpoint, and a leading U+3000 makes the range match nothing.
rows.area: queryparser / classic and flexible standard grammars (Range lexical state, RANGE_GOOP token)

rows.title: Flexible StandardQueryParser narrows out-of-range int literals with intValue(), so i:[2147483648 TO *] matches every document with the field
rows.summary: You parse a point query whose literal lies outside the field's int range, such as i:[2147483648 TO *], i>=2147483648 or i:2147483648, with the flexible StandardQueryParser and an Integer PointsConfig. You expect no match, because no int value reaches that bound. Instead PointRangeQueryNodeProcessor and PointQueryNodeProcessor narrow the parsed number with Number.intValue(), which wraps it, so the range queries match all 5 documents of the repro and i:2147483648 matches the Integer.MIN_VALUE document.

rows.title: DateTools strings stop sorting by date and stop round-tripping outside years AD 1..9999: the 'yyyy' year-of-era pattern drops the BC era (2 BC sorts after AD 1 and parses back as AD 2; 1 BC and AD 1 give the same string) and gives years after 9999 a fifth digit (10000 sorts before 2026, and stringToTime throws ParseException on DateTools' own output)
rows.summary: You convert a date before AD 1 or after 9999 with DateTools.timeToString (or dateToString) and expect what the class javadoc promises: strings whose lexicographic order is date order, which stringToTime turns back into the same time. Instead the SimpleDateFormat pattern 'yyyy...' prints the year of era with no era and at least four digits: 2 BC-01-01 becomes "00020101", which sorts after AD 1's "00010101" and parses back as AD 2-01-01 (at YEAR resolution 1 BC and AD 1 both give "0001"), and 10000-01-01 becomes "100000101", which sorts before "20260101" and makes stringToTime throw ParseException, because the parser is chosen by string length. Range queries, prefix queries and sorts on such terms therefore return wrong results with no error.
rows.area: core / document (DateTools date-to-string term encoding: timeToString/dateToString and stringToTime/stringToDate)

rows.title: QueryParser.setTimeZone (and StandardQueryParser.setTimeZone) is used only to round the inclusive end of a date range to 23:59:59.999; both dates are still parsed in the JVM default time zone, so with a non-default zone d:[6/1/2005 TO 6/4/2005] covers a shifted window and exclusive ranges ignore the setting
rows.summary: You give the query parser a time zone with setTimeZone (plus setLocale and setDateResolution) and parse d:[6/1/2005 TO 6/4/2005], expecting what the QueryParser javadoc promises, a range 'between 2005-06-01 and 2005-06-04', read in that zone: June 1 00:00 to June 4 23:59:59.999 there. Instead both dates are parsed by a DateFormat that still uses the JVM default zone, and only the rounding of the inclusive end to 23:59:59.999 uses the configured zone, so the window starts at midnight in the JVM zone and ends at the end of the configured-zone day that contains the JVM-zone midnight of June 4: with the JVM on UTC and the parser on New York the June 4 New York documents are silently lost (and May 31 from 20:00 matches), with the JVM on UTC and the parser on Tokyo the first nine hours of June 1 are lost. Exclusive ranges such as {6/1/2005 TO 6/4/2005} ignore the configured zone entirely, and the classic and the flexible parser behave the same.
rows.area: queryparser / classic and flexible date ranges (QueryParserBase.getRangeQuery, TermRangeQueryNodeProcessor; setTimeZone and ConfigurationKeys.TIMEZONE)

rows.title: Flexible StandardQueryParser ignores setFuzzyMinSim for a fuzzy term without a number: 'term~' always gets FuzzyQuery.defaultMaxEdits (2 edits) whatever the configured value, while the classic QueryParser honours the same setting
rows.summary: You configure the flexible StandardQueryParser with setFuzzyMinSim(1f), which the shared CommonQueryParserConfiguration interface documents as 'Set the minimum similarity for fuzzy queries' and which the classic QueryParser applies to a fuzzy term without a number, then parse 'lucene~' and expect FuzzyQuery lucene~1 (at most one edit). Instead you get lucene~2, which also matches 'lucxna' (two edits), although getFuzzyMinSim() returns 1.0: the grammar (StandardSyntaxParser.jj FuzzyOp) fills in FuzzyQuery.defaultMaxEdits for a bare '~', and FuzzyQueryNodeProcessor copies the configured value onto the node only when its similarity is unset (below 0), which the grammar never produces. So the setter only changes what its getter returns; the sibling setFuzzyPrefixLength, stored in the same FuzzyConfig, is applied.
rows.area: queryparser / flexible standard parser fuzzy configuration (StandardSyntaxParser FuzzyOp, FuzzyQueryNodeProcessor, StandardQueryParser#setFuzzyMinSim / FuzzyConfig)

rows.title: DateTools.stringToDate and stringToTime parse with a lenient SimpleDateFormat and ignore trailing text, so a string of a supported length that is not in the yyyyMMdd... format ("2024123X", the ISO date "2019-12-31", month 13) silently returns another date instead of the documented ParseException (since 1.9)
rows.summary: You call DateTools.stringToDate (or stringToTime) on a string that is not in DateTools' yyyyMMdd... format, for example "2024123X" or the ISO date "2019-12-31", and expect the ParseException that both methods document ('if dateString is not in the expected format') and already give for a wrong length or an unreadable start such as "aaaa". Instead, because the string has one of the seven supported lengths, it goes to a lenient SimpleDateFormat through DateFormat.parse(String), which ignores trailing text and rolls impossible fields over, so a different date comes back with no error: "2024123X" gives 2024-12-03T00:00:00Z, "2019-12-31" gives 2018-10-31T17:00:00Z and "20041301" (month 13) gives 2005-01-01T00:00:00Z.
rows.area: core / document (DateTools string-to-date decoding: stringToDate and stringToTime)

rows.title: DateTools.round returns a time near Long.MAX_VALUE (AD 292278994) for Long.MIN_VALUE, and for times before the first resolution-unit boundary above it, instead of rounding down: the rounded-down time lies below the long range and the lenient Calendar arithmetic silently wraps
rows.summary: You call DateTools.round(Long.MIN_VALUE, Resolution.DAY), for example to align the open lower bound of a date range with day-rounded indexed values, and expect a time no later than the input, as the javadoc promises ('the date with all values more precise than resolution set to 0 or 1'). Instead you get 9223372036794351616, a time in AD 292278994 just below Long.MAX_VALUE, with no error: the start of that day lies below Long.MIN_VALUE, and the lenient GregorianCalendar that round() uses wraps around in its long arithmetic. YEAR, MONTH, HOUR, MINUTE and SECOND wrap the same way for inputs before the first unit boundary above Long.MIN_VALUE, and round(Date, Resolution) delegates, so it wraps too.
rows.area: core / document (DateTools resolution limiting: round(long, Resolution) and round(Date, Resolution))

rows.title: The phrase matchers add a document position and a query position offset in int: with an offset near 2^31 an exact PhraseQuery or MultiPhraseQuery loops forever inside one document (IndexSearcher#setTimeout does not stop it) and a sloppy one returns false hits
rows.summary: You build a PhraseQuery with term a at position 0 and term b at position Integer.MAX_VALUE (the builder accepts it, because it only checks that positions are >= 0 and in order) and count it on a one-document index whose text is 'x a b'. You expect 0 hits, because no indexed position can be that far from a. Instead the exact matcher adds a's document position 1 and b's offset Integer.MAX_VALUE in int, the sum wraps to a negative number, both of its advance steps then leave its state unchanged, and IndexSearcher#count never returns, even with a 1 s IndexSearcher#setTimeout; with slop 1 the same kind of overflow makes the sloppy matcher return the document 'b x x a' as a hit.
rows.area: search / phrase matching (ExactPhraseMatcher, SloppyPhraseMatcher and PhrasePositions position arithmetic; PhraseQuery.Builder and MultiPhraseQuery.Builder accept the positions)

rows.title: Highlighter with the default QueryScorer returns no fragment for a matching PhraseQuery or MultiPhraseQuery that has a position hole (for example a removed stop word) and a slop within the number of holes of Integer.MAX_VALUE: WeightedSpanTermExtractor converts it to a SpanNearQuery with the plain int sum slop + positionGaps, which wraps to about Integer.MIN_VALUE, so the span query matches nothing
rows.summary: You analyse 'the quick brown fox jumps' with a stop-word analyzer, search for the phrase "quick the fox" with slop Integer.MAX_VALUE (for example from the user text "quick the fox"~3000000000, which the classic QueryParser turns into "quick ? fox"~2147483647; the query matches), and highlight the hit with Highlighter and QueryScorer, expecting 'the quick brown fox jumps', which slop Integer.MAX_VALUE - 1 or the same phrase without the hole gives. Instead getBestFragment returns null, with no error: WeightedSpanTermExtractor rewrites the phrase as new SpanNearQuery(clauses, slop + positionGaps, inorder) with a plain int sum, the removed stop word counts as one position gap, the sum wraps to -2147483648, and a span query with that slop accepts no match, so no term is marked. MultiPhraseQuery has the same sum, and the UnifiedHighlighter with weight matches turned off reaches it through PhraseHelper and returns the passage with no highlight.
rows.area: highlighter / original Highlighter, QueryScorer and WeightedSpanTermExtractor (phrase-to-span conversion)

rows.title: FastVectorHighlighter with fragCharSize = Integer.MAX_VALUE (or any value above Integer.MAX_VALUE - spanStart) returns the whole field with only the first match highlighted: BaseFragListBuilder computes spanStart + fragCharSize in int, the sum wraps negative, and every later match is silently dropped (SimpleFragListBuilder, the default, and WeightedFragListBuilder)
rows.summary: You index the field 'aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa foo bbb foo ccc foo ddd' with term vectors (positions and offsets), search foo, and call FastVectorHighlighter.getBestFragments with fragCharSize = Integer.MAX_VALUE to get the whole field, expecting 'aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa foo bbb foo ccc foo ddd', which fragCharSize 1000 or Integer.MAX_VALUE - 100 gives. Instead you get 'aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa foo bbb foo ccc foo ddd', with no error: BaseFragListBuilder.createFieldFragList computes the fragment end as spanStart + fragCharSize in int, where spanStart is the first match's start minus the 6-char margin (15 here), so the sum wraps negative and the fragment closes at the end of the first match. The fragment is then re-centred to [0, Integer.MAX_VALUE), which covers the whole field, and every later match is discarded.
rows.area: highlighter / vectorhighlight BaseFragListBuilder (FastVectorHighlighter, SimpleFragListBuilder, WeightedFragListBuilder)

rows.title: Classic Highlighter: SimpleFragmenter and SimpleSpanFragmenter move their fragment boundary only one fragment size per break, so after a long token or a long gap between tokens (a run of spaces, stripped markup) every following word becomes its own fragment and getBestFragment can return just the highlighted word (every release since 1.9)

You expect the words after that stretch to be grouped into fragments of about fragmentSize characters again, so that the best fragment for 'gamma' is 'alpha beta gamma', as it is without the long token. Instead isNewFragment moves its boundary only one fragment size per break, so the boundary stays behind the text, every following word starts its own fragment until it catches up, and getBestFragment returns just ' gamma' (SimpleSpanFragmenter behaves the same).

rows.title: Classic Highlighter's SimpleSpanFragmenter splits a short phrase match across two fragments because its position counter lags the real token positions: the Highlighter never shows it the first token or tokens that overlap the previous one, so the phrase is recognised one or more words late and getBestFragment can return only half of it
rows.summary: You highlight 'Lucene is a search library written in Java' with the classic Highlighter, a QueryScorer for PhraseQuery 'search library', the default StandardAnalyzer and SimpleSpanFragmenter(scorer, 20), whose javadoc says it 'breaks text up into same-size fragments but does not split up Spans', and expect the 14-character phrase to stay in one fragment. Instead the fragments are 'Lucene is a search' | ' library written in Java' and getBestFragment returns 'Lucene is a search'; the same cut happens at the default fragment size 100 whenever the size threshold falls at the phrase's second word, and after a leading stop word or a word split by WordDelimiterGraphFilter the lag grows to two positions, so even three-word phrases are cut. The fragmenter counts positions only from the tokens the Highlighter shows it, and the Highlighter never shows it the first token or tokens that overlap the previous one, so it recognises the phrase one or more words late.

rows.title: Classic Highlighter's SimpleSpanFragmenter.start() does not reset waitForPos, so a Highlighter reused for the next text (or for the same text again) keeps suppressing fragment boundaries after a phrase match that ended the previous text: one oversized fragment, then one-word fragments and a different best fragment, depending on what was highlighted before

Hits and scores are unaffected; only the snippet layout changes, and it depends on what the same Highlighter highlighted before.

rows.title: UnifiedHighlighter's no-match summary of a multi-valued field counts the internal U+0000 value separator as a passage, so the summary contains a NUL character and shows one value or sentence fewer than requested
rows.summary: You store two values in one field ('First value.' and 'Second value.'), run a query that matches the document but not that field, and ask the UnifiedHighlighter for 2 passages; you expect the documented default summary, the first 2 sentences from the field (for example 'First value.... Second value.', the way the highlight path joins values). Instead you get 'First value.\u0000': the highlighter joins the values with an internal U+0000 separator, its SplittingBreakIterator reports a boundary on both sides of that character, and FieldHighlighter.getSummaryPassagesNoHighlight turns the 1-character gap into a passage, so the NUL is returned and takes the second value's slot (3 passages give 'First value.\u0000Second value.'). With an empty first value even 1 passage returns just '\u0000'.

rows.title: FastVectorHighlighter: its default SimpleBoundaryScanner can cut a fragment between the two halves of a supplementary character (an emoji, a CJK Extension B ideograph) when no boundary char lies within 20 chars of the cut, so the snippet starts with a lone low surrogate or ends with a lone high surrogate (every release with FastVectorHighlighter, 2.9 to 10.6.0)
rows.summary: You store the text 40 x U+1F600 (an emoji, two UTF-16 chars each) + ' foo' in a field with term vectors (positions and offsets), search f:foo and call new FastVectorHighlighter().getBestFragment(fieldQuery, reader, 0, "f", 100), expecting a snippet made of whole characters. Instead you get '\uDE00' + 23 x U+1F600 + ' foo': the fragment is centred on the match in UTF-16 units, its start (offset 33) falls between the two halves of the 17th emoji, and SimpleBoundaryScanner, finding none of its boundary chars within 20 chars, keeps that raw offset, so the snippet starts with a lone low surrogate; the fragment end has the same fallback and can end in a lone high surrogate. rows.title: Classic Highlighter: QueryScorer weights a term that several clauses name by clause order (the last term clause wins, the first span or phrase clause wins) instead of using the highest weight, so two equal() queries whose clauses differ only in order pick different best fragments (the classic-Highlighter sibling of #15434)
rows.summary: You highlight a text with the classic Highlighter and QueryScorer using two BooleanQuery objects that are equal() and differ only in clause order: (f:alpha)^5 (f:beta)^3 f:alpha and f:alpha (f:beta)^3 (f:alpha)^5. You expect the same best fragment for both, the one with alpha, because alpha's highest weight 5 beats beta's 3 (the rule that QueryScorer's own WeightedSpanTerm[] constructor, QueryTermScorer and, since #15434, the FastVectorHighlighter follow). Instead WeightedSpanTermExtractor keeps the weight of the term clause it visits last (and of the first span or phrase clause), so alpha gets weight 1 for the first query and its best fragment is the one with beta (' beta' for the repro's text 'alpha beta'), with no error.

rows.title: FastVectorHighlighter matchedFields: the merging constructor WeightedPhraseInfo(Collection) drops the term infos of the first merged match (while it keeps that match's boost and offsets), so WeightedFragListBuilder underweights a passage matched in several matched fields and can return the wrong best fragment (since 4.6.0)
rows.summary: You index one document whose fields a and b both hold 'running fast xx xx xx swim slow' (stored, with term vectors, positions and offsets) and highlight field a with FastVectorHighlighter.getBestFragments(..., matchedFields = {a, b}, 20, 1, new WeightedFragListBuilder(), new ScoreOrderFragmentsBuilder(), ...) for a:"running fast" OR b:fast OR a:"swim slow". You expect the passage that a:"running fast" and b:fast both match to be weighed with the term infos of both matches, as the merging constructor's comment ('merge the boosts and termInfos') and WeightedFieldFragList's sum-of-distinct-IDF-weights formula say, so the best fragment is 'running fast xx xx xx' (weight 2.13 against 0.87). Instead the merged match keeps the summed boost and both offsets but only the second match's term infos ('running' is lost), the passage weighs 0.61, and the best fragment returned is 'xx swim slow', with no error.

rows.title: GradientFormatter and SpanGradientFormatter reverse the colour gradient on every channel where the min colour is larger than the max colour, so with the javadoc's own white-to-black example the top-scoring term is drawn white
rows.summary: You build new GradientFormatter(maxScore, "#FFFFFF", "#000000", null, null), the javadoc's own example (white for a score of zero, black for maxScore and above), and highlight a term whose score is maxScore, expecting it to be drawn black. Instead it is drawn white (<font color="#FFFFFF">) and weaker terms get darker colours, because getColorVal always runs from the numerically smaller channel value to the larger one, whatever order the min and max colours were given in. The same happens on every colour channel where min > max, in GradientFormatter and in SpanGradientFormatter, which inherits the method.

rows.title: Classic Highlighter's SimpleSpanFragmenter splits a phrase match across fragments when two phrases overlap, when a longer phrase shares a shorter one's start (the result then depends on clause order), or when the phrase starts on stacked synonyms: it protects only the first span that starts at the current position, skips the span lookup while it waits for a span to end, and never sees a span that starts on a token the Highlighter does not show it
rows.summary: You highlight a text with the classic Highlighter, a QueryScorer and SimpleSpanFragmenter, whose javadoc says it 'breaks text up into same-size fragments but does not split up Spans', for a query with two overlapping phrases ('new york' OR 'york city hall'), two phrases that share a start ('new york' OR 'new york city hall'), or a phrase whose words get synonyms stacked on them by SynonymGraphFilter, and you expect every phrase match shorter than the fragment size to stay inside one fragment. Instead the fragmenter cuts inside the longer phrase ('The museum is near New York City' | ' Hall and the park', 'We flew to New York City' | ' Hall last week', 'I left my big laptop' | ' bag on the train'), so getBestFragment can return only part of the phrase, and in the same-start case listing the longer phrase first in the BooleanQuery makes the phrase come out whole. Hits, scores and which words are highlighted are correct; only the fragment boundaries are wrong.

rows.title: UnifiedHighlighter.highlightWithoutSearcher returns the text with no highlights under its default flags (WEIGHT_MATCHES) when the query also has a required or filter clause on another field
rows.summary: You build a UnifiedHighlighter without a searcher (builderWithoutSearcher, default flags) and call highlightWithoutSearcher("body", query, "a b c", 1) with +title:x +body:a or +body:a #year:[2000 TO 2030], expecting 'a b c', which highlight() gives for the same text on an indexed one-document copy, which the same call gives with withWeightMatches(false), and which 8.x gave by default. Instead it returns 'a b c' with no mark: under WEIGHT_MATCHES the whole query's Weight#matches runs on a MemoryIndex that holds only the highlighted field, where the other-field clause cannot match, so Matches is null ('doc doesn't match') and the highlighter falls back to the unmarked summary. The searcher path answers other-field clauses from the real index (OverlaySingleDocTermsLeafReader); the no-searcher branch has no such view, so a clause it cannot evaluate is treated as false.

rows.title: UnifiedHighlighter cuts a stored value at maxLength UTF-16 units even between the two halves of a supplementary character (an emoji, a CJK Extension B ideograph), so the snippet can end in an unpaired high surrogate, for example 'Hello \uD83D'
rows.summary: You store the value 'Hello U+1F600 world' (the emoji takes UTF-16 indexes 6 and 7), search for hello and highlight the hit with UnifiedHighlighter.builder(searcher, analyzer).withMaxLength(7), and expect a snippet made of whole characters, 'Hello ', just as maxLength 6 gives 'Hello ' and maxLength 8 gives the whole emoji. Instead LimitedStoredFieldVisitor keeps exactly 7 UTF-16 units, so the content and the snippet end with the first half of the emoji, 'Hello \uD83D', which String.getBytes(UTF_8) turns into 'Hello ?' and a strict UTF-8 encoder rejects. The same happens at the default maxLength 10,000 when a value's 10,000th unit is the first half of a supplementary character, and for a later value of a multi-valued field at its per-value budget.
rows.area: highlighter / UnifiedHighlighter stored-value loading (LimitedStoredFieldVisitor maxLength cut)

rows.title: UnifiedHighlighter.highlightWithoutSearcher ignores maxLength (the default 10,000 included): it analyzes and highlights the whole supplied text, although getMaxLength and Builder.withMaxLength document that content is truncated to maxLength before highlighting
rows.summary: You build a UnifiedHighlighter without a searcher (builderWithoutSearcher, optionally withMaxLength(20)) and call highlightWithoutSearcher on a text longer than maxLength, expecting the text to be cut to its first maxLength chars before highlighting, as getMaxLength ('Content will be truncated to this size before highlighting') and withMaxLength document and as the searcher entry points do. Instead the whole text is analyzed and highlighted: with maxLength 20, the 48-char text 'Alpha beta gamma. Delta epsilon. Lucene is here.' gives 'Lucene is here.' (its only match is at offset 33) where the searcher path returns 'Alpha beta gamma. ', and with the default maxLength of 10,000 a match at char 10,541 of a 10,560-char text is highlighted. The only truncation lives in the stored-field loader (LimitedStoredFieldVisitor), which this entry point never calls, although the re-analysis strategy it uses relies on it ('content is already truncated to maxLength').
rows.area: highlighter / UnifiedHighlighter (highlightWithoutSearcher entry point, maxLength option)

rows.title: CustomSeparatorBreakIterator is off by one next to the separator: following(p) skips the break right after a separator at p, preceding(p) returns p itself, a leading separator is not a break and a trailing one makes next() return the end twice, so UnifiedHighlighter passages built on it start or end one segment off
rows.summary: You give the UnifiedHighlighter a CustomSeparatorBreakIterator('.'), alone or inside LengthGoalBreakIterator, and expect passages to start and end at the breaks its own next() reports, just after each '.'. Instead following() and preceding() are off by one next to the separator: on 'Aa bb. Cc dd. Ee ff' (breaks 0, 6, 13, 19) following(5) returns 13 instead of 6 and preceding(13) returns 13 instead of 6, so a min-length-6 summary is 'Aa bb. Cc dd.' instead of 'Aa bb.' and the phrase 'dd ee' is shown as 'dd. Ee ff' instead of ' Cc dd. Ee ff'. Nothing throws and the match is still highlighted; only the snippet boundary moves by one segment.

rows.title: OpenNLPSentenceBreakIterator.next(n) returns DONE instead of the end of the text when the n-th boundary is the last one, so next(1) differs from next() and a caller that steps with next(n) until DONE loses the final sentence group
rows.summary: You set a text on an OpenNLPSentenceBreakIterator and call next(n) to jump n sentence boundaries, expecting the n-th boundary, as java.text.BreakIterator#next(int) promises ('Returns the nth boundary from the current boundary') and as n calls of next() give. When that boundary is the end of the text, next(n) returns DONE (-1) instead: with the model-free NLPSentenceDetectorOp on 'Whole text is one sentence.', next() from first() returns 27 but next(1) returns -1, and on the module's three-sentence test text (boundaries 0, 31, 59, 102) next(3) from first() returns -1 instead of 102 while next(2) correctly returns 59. The iterator is still moved to the end, so only the returned value is wrong; code that steps with next(n) until DONE loses the final sentence group.
rows.area: analysis / opennlp OpenNLPSentenceBreakIterator (java.text.BreakIterator implementation, next(int))

rows.title: OpenNLPSentenceBreakIterator on text that starts with whitespace: a backward walk with previous() returns a non-boundary and then throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException, and following() at an offset inside the leading whitespace throws StackOverflowError, because setText keeps the sentence detector's whitespace-trimmed first sentence start while first() and next() use the text's begin index
rows.summary: You create an OpenNLPSentenceBreakIterator, give it a text that starts with whitespace, for example ' Sentence number 1 has 6 words. Sentence number 2, 5 words.', and walk it backward with last()/previous() (the reverse loop shown in the BreakIterator javadoc), expecting the forward boundaries [0, 33, 60] in reverse order and then DONE. Instead previous() returns 2, which is not a boundary, and the next previous() throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException (Index -1); following(0) on a one-sentence text with leading whitespace recurses until StackOverflowError. The OpenNLP sentence detector trims whitespace from its spans and setText stores those starts unchanged, so the first stored sentence start lies after the begin index that first() and next() treat as the first boundary.
rows.area: analysis-opennlp / OpenNLPSentenceBreakIterator (public java.text.BreakIterator over OpenNLP sentence spans: setText, previous, following, moveToSentenceAt)

rows.title: CachingCollector (and CachingCollectorManager) never calls LeafCollector#finish on the collector it wraps, nor on the second-pass collector when it replays cached scores, so finish-dependent collectors such as FacetsCollector silently report no hits
rows.summary: You wrap a FacetsCollector, or any collector that does its per-segment work in LeafCollector#finish, in a CachingCollector or CachingCollectorManager so you can run the query once and replay the hits later, or you replay a score-caching cache into such a collector, and you expect the same facet counts as a plain IndexSearcher search. Instead the collector reports no hits: CachingCollector's per-leaf wrapper overrides finish() for its own bookkeeping and never passes the call on, and the score-caching replay never calls finish() at all, although the no-score replay does. In the repro a query that matches 20 documents gives 0 matching docs, with no error unless assertions are enabled.
rows.area: search / CachingCollector first pass and score-caching replay (CachingCollector, CachingCollectorManager)

rows.title: SecondPassGroupingCollector and GroupReducer never call LeafCollector#finish on the per-group leaf collectors, so a custom GroupReducer whose collector does its per-segment work in finish (for example a stock FacetsCollector per group) silently sees no documents
rows.summary: You write a GroupReducer that gives each group its own FacetsCollector (or any collector that compiles a segment's results in LeafCollector#finish), run it through SecondPassGroupingCollector, and expect each group's collector to see the documents of its group, as GroupReducer's javadoc says and as a plain IndexSearcher search would give. Instead every group's FacetsCollector reports no documents, with no error: GroupReducer.setNextReader replaces each group's leaf collector on every segment without calling finish() on the previous one, GroupReducer has no finish hook, and SecondPassGroupingCollector does not override finish(), so IndexSearcher's per-leaf finish() reaches only the outer collector. In the repro 5 documents in 2 segments are routed to groups a (3) and b (2), yet both groups report 0 hits; with assertions enabled FacetsCollector throws AssertionError on the second segment instead.
rows.area: grouping / GroupReducer and SecondPassGroupingCollector (second-pass per-group collectors)

rows.title: GroupReducer lets one group's CollectionTerminatedException escape SecondPassGroupingCollector, so IndexSearcher ends the whole segment and every other group silently misses its remaining documents in that segment
rows.summary: You write a GroupReducer whose per-group collector needs only the first documents of its group in a segment (for example a stock TopFieldCollector in index order with a hit threshold of 1, which then throws CollectionTerminatedException, as collectors may), run it through SecondPassGroupingCollector, and expect every group's collector still to see the documents of its own group, as GroupReducer's javadoc says and as MultiCollector does for its children. Instead GroupReducer.collect does not catch the exception, SecondPassGroupingCollector passes it on, and IndexSearcher ends the segment for the whole second pass, so all the other groups silently miss their remaining documents in that segment. In the repro one segment holds docs 0-2 in group a and docs 3-4 in group b: group a's collector stops on doc 1, group b reports no hit instead of doc 3, and the second pass counts 2 of 5 documents.

rows.title: The flat scalar-quantized vectors format (Lucene104ScalarQuantizedVectorsFormat) accepts BYTE vector fields but its byte search is a no-op, so unfiltered byte kNN and byte similarity queries return no hits
rows.summary: You index a BYTE vector field with Lucene104ScalarQuantizedVectorsFormat, a registered stand-alone flat (brute-force) format that accepts BYTE fields without error and searches its FLOAT32 and FLOAT16 fields by scoring every vector, and expect a byte kNN query to return the k nearest documents. Instead the reader hands byte searches to the raw flat reader, whose search method does nothing, so an unfiltered KnnByteVectorQuery returns 0 hits and ByteVectorSimilarityQuery.Adaptive with threshold 0 matches 0 of 10 documents, with no error. The same kNN query with a term filter that matches every document returns the exact top 3, because the filtered path falls back to exact search when the reader returns too few hits.

rows.title: Grouping LongRangeFactory and DoubleRangeFactory give the last range below max the full width, so its reported group bounds run past max and overlap the range for values >= max
rows.summary: You group documents with new LongRangeFactory(10, 10, 25), meaning buckets 10 wide starting at 10 and everything at or above 25 in one bucket, and expect what the javadoc says: [10, 20), a shorter final bucket [20, 25), and [25, MAX). Instead the value 22 is labelled LongRange(20, 30) while 27 is labelled LongRange(25, MAX), so the two reported ranges overlap; each group holds the right documents, but a range query built from the label [20, 30), the way Lucene's own selector tests rebuild a group, also returns the document with value 27 from the other group. DoubleRangeFactory behaves the same, because both getRange methods set the bucket's upper bound to its lower bound + width and never cap it at max.

rows.title: Grouping DoubleRangeFactory picks a value's bucket and computes that bucket's bounds with separately rounded arithmetic, so with a decimal width such as 0.1 the returned range can exclude the value and adjacent ranges leave gaps or overlap (DoubleRangeFactory(0, 0.1, 10).getRange(0.6) = DoubleRange(0.5, 0.6))
rows.summary: You group documents by a double field with new DoubleRangeFactory(0, 0.1, 10), buckets 0.1 wide, and expect each group's DoubleRange label to contain the values grouped under it, because DoubleRange is documented as [min, max). Instead the value 0.6 is grouped under DoubleRange(0.5, 0.6), which excludes 0.6, and 1.7 under DoubleRange(1.7000000000000002, 1.8000000000000003); 27 of the 100 values 0.0, 0.1, ..., 9.9 lie outside their own label, adjacent labels leave gaps (no label contains 0.6) or overlap, and a range query built from a label misses or picks up documents (values 0.55, 0.6, 0.65 form a group DoubleRange(0.5, 0.6) of 2 documents whose label matches 1). The cause is that getRange picks the bucket with Math.floor((value - min) / width) but computes its bounds separately as min + bucket * width and then that + width, and the three roundings disagree near boundaries; group membership itself stays consistent.

rows.title: Grouping DoubleRangeFactory gives the below-min group the lower bound Double.MIN_VALUE (4.9E-324, the smallest positive double) instead of the most negative value, so that group's DoubleRange label does not contain its own members
rows.summary: You group documents by a double field with new DoubleRangeFactory(-10, 5, 10), meaning buckets 5 wide from -10 to 10 and every value below -10 in one bucket, and expect the bucket returned for -20 to be a [min, max) range that contains -20, the way LongRangeFactory returns [Long.MIN_VALUE, -10). Instead DoubleRangeFactory returns DoubleRange(4.9E-324, -10.0): it uses Double.MIN_VALUE as the lower end, and Double.MIN_VALUE is the smallest positive double, not the most negative one, so the range is inverted and holds none of its members (with min > 0 it leaves out 0.0 and every negative member). Each group still holds the right documents, but its reported bounds are wrong, and a range query built from them, the way Lucene's own selector tests rebuild a group, finds none or only some of the group's documents.

rows.title: DoubleRange and FloatRange accept the bounds [0.0, -0.0] and store them inverted, so range queries silently miss such documents and contradict each other (WITHIN [0,0] but not INTERSECTS [0,0])
rows.summary: You index a DoubleRange or FloatRange with min 0.0 and max -0.0 (Java's negative zero, numerically equal to 0.0); the constructor accepts it, as it accepts [0.0, 0.0], so you expect queries to treat it as the point zero, or else an IllegalArgumentException like the one thrown for every other min > max pair. Instead Lucene stores the bounds in its sort order, where -0.0 is below 0.0, so the stored range is inverted: the document matches newWithinQuery [0,0] and newIntersectsQuery [-1,1] but not newIntersectsQuery [0,0] or newIntersectsQuery of its own bounds. The same happens with the doc-values slow intersects query and range-on-range facet counts, and a query with bounds [0.0, -0.0] misses a document [0.0, 0.0] that newContainsQuery with the same bounds matches.

rows.title: DoubleRangeFacetCounts orders -0.0 below +0.0 while DoubleRange.accept and getQuery treat the two zeros as equal: a document holding a zero of the opposite sign at an inclusive zero bound (for example -0.0 in [0, 1]) is matched by the range's own drill-down but not counted, and the accepted range [+0.0, -0.0] makes counting throw

You expect the count to include every document the range accepts, because DoubleRange.accept and the range's own drill-down query getQuery() compare with primitive >= and <=, treat -0.0 as equal to 0.0, and match those documents. Instead the counter converts bounds and values with NumericUtils.doubleToSortableLong, where -0.0 sorts below +0.0, so those documents are silently left out of the count (likewise +0.0 at an inclusive -0.0 upper bound), and the range [+0.0, -0.0], which the DoubleRange constructor accepts, makes DoubleRangeFacetCounts throw IllegalArgumentException 'matches nothing'.

rows.title: Facet DoubleRange, range-on-range DoubleRange and DimRange.fromDoubles/fromFloats do not exclude an exclusive bound that is an infinity: the empty ranges (+Inf, +Inf] and [-Inf, -Inf) are accepted and match the +Infinity / -Infinity documents instead of matching nothing
rows.summary: You build a facet range with an exclusive bound that is an infinity, for example new DoubleRange("> +Inf", Double.POSITIVE_INFINITY, false, Double.POSITIVE_INFINITY, true), meaning 'value > +Infinity', or the mirror [-Inf, -Inf) 'value < -Infinity'. No double is greater than +Infinity, so you expect a range that matches nothing, rejected with IllegalArgumentException 'matches nothing' as the class does for other empty ranges and as LongRange and DimRange.fromLongs do for an exclusive Long.MAX_VALUE bound. Instead the constructor makes the bound inclusive with Math.nextUp (or Math.nextAfter / Math.nextDown for the max), which leaves an infinity unchanged, so the range becomes [+Inf, +Inf]: DoubleRangeFacetCounts counts and the drill-down query matches every +Infinity document, and the copies in rangeonrange.DoubleRange and DimRange.fromDoubles/fromFloats count the same documents.

rows.title: Facet-set DimRange.fromDoubles/fromFloats (and range-on-range DoubleRange) make an exclusive bound inclusive with Math.nextUp/Math.nextDown, which skip the other signed zero, so a facet set holding -0.0 is counted by neither of the adjacent ranges [-1, 0) and [0, 1]
rows.summary: You index one document with a DoubleFacetSet holding -0.0 and count it with two RangeFacetSetMatchers, DimRange.fromDoubles(-1, true, 0, false) and DimRange.fromDoubles(0, true, 1, true), which split [-1, 1] at zero; you expect the two counts to add up to 1, because -0.0 belongs to [-1, 0) if the zeros are ordered as Double.compare orders them (the sortable order the matcher compares in) and to [0, 1] if they compare equal. Instead both counts are 0, with no error, while a covering [-1, 1] range counts the document: fromDoubles turns the exclusive max 0 into Math.nextDown(+0.0) = -Double.MIN_VALUE, which in sortable order lies below -0.0, so -0.0 falls between the two ranges. fromFloats, the mirror case (+0.0 against [-1, -0.0] and (-0.0, 1], where Math.nextUp(-0.0) skips +0.0) and range-on-range DoubleRange behave the same way.

rows.title: FunctionRangeQuery on a string field (BytesRefFieldSource / SortedSetFieldSource) compares term ordinals as float, so in a segment with more than 2^24 distinct values of the field it also matches values just outside the range bounds
rows.summary: You run FunctionRangeQuery(new BytesRefFieldSource("f"), "016777217", null, true, true) as a filter on a segment whose SORTED field f has more than 2^24 distinct values, and expect only documents whose value is at least "016777217". The document holding "016777216" matches too, with no error: getRangeScorer turns the string bounds into exact int ordinals but then compares each document's ordinal as a float, and above 2^24 neighbouring ordinals round to the same float. Only values within one float step of a bound are wrongly added; no in-range document is lost.

rows.title: DoubleDocValuesStats and SortedDoubleDocValuesStats (lucene/misc) return mean() = NaN instead of +/-Infinity when any value is collected after an infinite value, so the mean of {+Infinity, 1.0} is NaN while the mean of {1.0, +Infinity} is +Infinity
rows.summary: You collect statistics for a double doc-values field with DocValuesStats.DoubleDocValuesStats (or SortedDoubleDocValuesStats) and expect mean(), documented as 'the mean of all values of the field', to be +Infinity for the values {+Infinity, 1.0}: that is sum()/count(), and it is what java.util.DoubleSummaryStatistics, the oracle of the upstream test, returns. Instead mean() is NaN, because the running update mean += (val - mean) / count computes Infinity - Infinity as soon as the running mean is infinite and another value arrives; {+Infinity, +Infinity} also gives NaN, while sum() and max() report +Infinity. The answer depends on document order ({1.0, +Infinity} gives +Infinity) and, since 10.5.0, on the searcher: with an executor and one segment per slice, DocValuesStatsCollectorManager rebuilds the mean from the sums and returns +Infinity.

rows.title: TrecJudge counts every qrels grade other than the literal string "0" as relevant, so negative TREC grades (such as -2 for spam pages in TREC Web track qrels) are judged relevant and inflate the relevant-document count, precision, AP and MRR
rows.summary: You evaluate search quality with QueryDriver or QualityBenchmark and a TREC qrels file read by TrecJudge, expecting a document to count as relevant only when its grade is 1 or more, as trec_eval counts it. TrecJudge instead treats every grade token except the exact string "0" as relevant, so documents graded -2 (spam or useless, in TREC Web track qrels) or -1 count as relevant: a junk page graded -2 that ranks above the only relevant page gives 2 relevant documents, P@1 1.0 and AP 1.0, where trec_eval gives 1, 0 and 0.5. There is no error or warning.

rows.title: SubmissionReport writes scores of 1000 or more with a grouping comma ("1,200.5000") into the TREC run file that QueryDriver documents as the submission file for trec_eval, so trec_eval reads such a score as 1.0 and ranks those hits wrongly
rows.summary: You evaluate search quality with lucene/benchmark's SubmissionReport, for example through QueryDriver, whose usage text calls the output the 'submission file for trec_eval', and expect the score column of each TREC run line (qid Q0 docno rank score tag) to be a plain number. SubmissionReport formats scores with NumberFormat.getInstance(Locale.ROOT) and never turns grouping off, so a hit scoring 1200.5 is written as '1,200.5000'. trec_eval reads that column with C atof(), which stops at the comma and returns 1.0, and then re-sorts the run by the parsed score, so a run [1200.5, 900.25] is evaluated as [900.25, 1.0], with the top hit moved down, and the reported metrics are silently wrong.

rows.title: QualityStats.average(stats).getPrecisionAt(n) is not the mean per-query precision at n when n is above the mean result count: the mean that average() stored is replaced by a second extrapolation (mean P@10 0.4 instead of 0.6)
rows.summary: You evaluate search quality with QualityBenchmark, average the per-query results with QualityStats.average(stats) and ask the average for its precision at 10, expecting the mean of the per-query P@10 values (which, like trec_eval's P_10, already count missing ranks as non-relevant). If the queries returned different numbers of results and their mean is below 10, getPrecisionAt(10) ignores the correct mean that average() stored and extrapolates again from the precision at the mean result count: with setMaxResults(10), a query whose 10 hits are all relevant (P@10 = 1.0) and a query whose only 2 hits are relevant (P@10 = 0.2) give 0.4 instead of 0.6. There is no error, and the printed SUMMARY never shows the affected cutoffs.

rows.title: Float taxonomy facets: if one child label aggregates to NaN, getTopChildren can return a lower-valued label in place of a higher one (a=5, b=NaN, c=10 gives top-1 [a]), because TopOrdAndFloatQueue compares values with < and >; a regression in 9.11.0 from #12966
rows.summary: You aggregate a float weight per taxonomy label (FloatAssociationFacetField, or a DoubleValuesSource such as the expression clicks / impressions) and call getTopChildren(k), documented to return 'the topN child labels'. If one label's value is NaN (a=5, b=NaN, c=10), getTopChildren(1) returns [a (5.0)] although c=10 outranks a, and getTopChildren(2) returns [b (NaN), c (10.0)], so the top-1 is not even in the top-2, whatever rank NaN should get. TopOrdAndFloatQueue.OrdAndFloat#lessThan compares with < and > and otherwise falls back to the ordinal, so NaN ties with every value, the order is not transitive and the heap keeps the wrong labels; #12966 (9.11.0) let NaN-valued labels into this queue and, in the same change, ordered dims with the NaN-safe Float.compare.

rows.title: MutableValueFloat and MutableValueDouble equals() compare with ==, so a NaN value is not equal to itself and grouping by a float or double function puts NaN documents into empty groups (4.0.0 to 10.5.2) or throws IllegalArgumentException (main and, by reading, 10.6.0)
rows.summary: You group search hits by a float or double function, for example new DoubleFieldSource("v") or a 0/0 division, and some documents have the value NaN; you expect them to form one NaN group, because MutableValueDouble's own hashCode (doubleToLongBits) and compareTo (Double.compare) treat every NaN as one value. Instead equalsSameType compares with ==, under which NaN is not even equal to itself, so on releases up to 10.5.2 every NaN document becomes its own group, each such group comes back with 0 documents and the NaN documents drop out of the grouped hit count. On main and, by reading, 10.6.0 the same search fails with IllegalArgumentException 'group values differ across shards', because the result merge compares the NaN group value with itself.

rows.title: Taxonomy Facets#getAllDims sorts float-valued dims with a NaN-unsafe < / > comparator, so one dim whose value is NaN puts the other dims out of value order, breaks the documented rule that getTopDims equals the first entries of getAllDims, and with 32 or more dims can make getAllDims throw 'Comparison method violates its general contract!' (released since 4.7.0)
rows.summary: You aggregate float values per taxonomy dim (FloatAssociationFacetField weights or a DoubleValuesSource) and call getAllDims, documented to sort dims by value, and getTopDims, documented to return the same as the first entries of getAllDims. If one dim's value is NaN (dims a=1, b=NaN, c=2), getAllDims can return [a=1.0, b=NaN, c=2.0], with a ahead of c, while getTopDims(1, 10) returns [b=NaN]; with 32 or more dims, getAllDims can instead throw IllegalArgumentException 'Comparison method violates its general contract!' from List.sort. The getAllDims comparator compares doubleValue() with > in both directions and falls back to the dim name, so NaN ties with every value and the order is not transitive, while getTopDims has used the NaN-safe Float.compare (valueComparator) since #12966 (9.11.0).
rows.area: facet / taxonomy facets (TaxonomyFacets#getAllDims ordering of float-valued dims: float association and value-source facets)

rows.title: Geo3D circles with a radius between about 2e-5 m and 20 cm take the inside of their cut plane from the sign of rounding noise, so Geo3DPoint.newDistanceQuery with such a radius can match every point document on the planet
rows.summary: You build a Geo3D distance query with a very small radius, for example Geo3DPoint.newDistanceQuery with 1.24 cm, and expect it to match only points near the centre, or to be rejected as too small. The circle's cut plane passes within about r^2/2 of the circle's centre (here about 2e-18), far below double rounding, and SidedPlane takes the plane's inside from the sign of evaluate(center), which at that size is rounding noise. When the noise has the wrong sign the circle is the whole planet minus a speck (below about 1 mm, minus a patch of up to a few hundred metres near the centre), and the query silently returns every indexed point outside it: in the repro, all 3 documents thousands of kilometres away.
rows.area: spatial3d / geom circles (GeoStandardCircle cut plane and SidedPlane sidedness, behind Geo3DPoint.newDistanceQuery and GeoCircleFactory.makeGeoCircle)

rows.title: A sloppy PhraseQuery in which two different terms each repeat (for example "a b a b"~1) misses documents of a segment, exact-phrase matches included, when the segment's first candidate document has two of those terms stacked at one position, because SloppyPhraseMatcher builds its repetition groups once, from that document, by position instead of by term
rows.summary: You index text into a field whose analysis can put two words at one position (for example an index-time synonym) and search with a sloppy phrase such as "a b a b"~1, in which two different words each repeat; you expect every document within the slop, and certainly every document that holds the exact phrase, to match, whatever other documents share its segment. SloppyPhraseMatcher works out which phrase positions repeat each other only once per segment, on the first candidate document, and groups them by equal position in that document rather than by term, so when that document has a and b stacked at one position both words land in one group and the matcher then asks for more occurrences than exist. That document and later documents of the segment are missed with no error: in the two-document repro the plain document 'a b a b' matches with slop 0 but not with slop 1, while the same document indexed alone matches with slop 1.
rows.area: search / phrase queries (SloppyPhraseMatcher repetition groups: gatherRptGroups, non-multi-term branch)

rows.title: A sloppy PhraseQuery or MultiPhraseQuery with two entries at one position that a third entry pulls into the same repetition group misses documents its exact (slop 0) form matches, and for MultiPhraseQuery one unchanged query matches on some evaluations and misses on others, because SloppyPhraseMatcher checks its 'same offset is not a repetition' rule only pairwise and breaks equal-offset ties in HashSet order
rows.summary: You build a sloppy phrase query by hand with two entries at the same position, for example PhraseQuery a@0 a@1 a@1 (the second 'a' added twice at position 1), and expect slop 1 to match everything slop 0 matches and the query to give the same answer every time it runs. SloppyPhraseMatcher's rule that two entries from one query position are not repetitions of each other is checked only pairwise, so a third entry (a@0) pulls both into one repetition group and the matcher then forces them onto different document positions: the document 'a a' matches with slop 0 but not with slop 1 to 4. For MultiPhraseQuery the same collision is resolved in HashSet iteration order, because groups are sorted by offset only, so the one immutable query (a|b)@0 b@2 a@2 ~2 on one unchanged reader matches the document a@0, a@1 with b@1 stacked, a@2 in about half of 200 evaluations and misses it in the rest, with no error.
rows.area: search / phrase queries (SloppyPhraseMatcher repetition groups: gatherRptGroups same-offset exclusion, collide, advanceRepeatGroups, sortRptGroups tie order)

rows.title: IndexSearcher#count on a two-term disjunction over-counts, even above maxDoc, when the searcher timeout fires while the intersection is counted
rows.summary: You set a timeout with IndexSearcher#setTimeout and call IndexSearcher#count on a query like `a OR b`, where term b matches far fewer documents than term a, on an index without deletions. When the timeout fires you expect a partial count, at most the number of matching documents, which is what every other count and collect path returns under the same timeout (and what this path returned up to 9.9.2). Instead count() returns count(a) + count(b) minus a cut-short count of `a AND b`, which is too high (1041 for a 1000-document index with 955 matches when the deadline has already passed) and gets smaller, not larger, when the timeout fires later; timedOut() is true.
rows.area: search / IndexSearcher#count (two-clause term-disjunction shortcut, GITHUB#13036) under IndexSearcher#setTimeout

rows.title: A multi-segment kNN query's optimistic second pass, when cut short by the IndexSearcher timeout, replaces the hits a complete first pass already found, so a later timeout can return fewer or farther hits than an earlier one, down to 0 hits
rows.summary: You set a timeout with IndexSearcher#setTimeout and run a kNN query on an index with several segments; Lucene searches every segment once and, if that first pass completed, searches the segments that supplied the best hits a second time to improve the answer. You expect a timeout to give you the partial results found so far ('Return partial results only when timeout is met', AbstractKnnVectorQuery.java:296), so hits that the complete first pass already found are kept. Instead, when the timeout fires during the second pass, each re-entered segment's cut-short second-pass result (usually empty) replaces its first-pass hits, so the query keeps fewer or farther hits than a slightly earlier timeout would have given, down to 0 hits (IndexSearcher#count goes 6 -> 0 when one more timeout check is allowed).
rows.area: search / kNN query rewrite (AbstractKnnVectorQuery optimistic re-entry pass) under the IndexSearcher timeout

rows.title: SingletonSortedSetDocValues.intoBitSet does not refresh its cached ordinal, so nextOrd() returns an earlier document's ordinal and DocValuesRangeIterator.forOrdinalRange can return extra hits on single-valued segments
rows.summary: You take the SortedSetDocValues of a segment whose documents have at most one value each (DocValues.getSortedSet and LeafReader#getSortedSetDocValues then return a single-valued wrapper), call intoBitSet(upTo, ...), and read nextOrd() for the document the iterator now sits on; or you pass that view to DocValuesRangeIterator.forOrdinalRange on a skip-indexed field and load the matches in bulk. You expect nextOrd() to describe the current document, as after the nextDoc() loop that the intoBitSet javadoc says it behaves exactly like, and the range iterator to mark only documents whose value is in range. Instead the wrapper's intoBitSet moves the inner iterator without refreshing its cached ordinal, so with two documents a and b nextOrd() on doc 1 returns a's ordinal, and forOrdinalRange for [b, b] also marks doc 8192, whose value is a.
rows.area: index / doc values (single-valued SortedSetDocValues view, DocValuesRangeIterator)
