rows.title: Sparse multi-valued SortedNumericDocValues#rangeIntoBitSet (default codec), called after advanceExact(d) returned false, judges doc d by a neighbouring document's values (or throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException)
rows.summary: On a default-codec index with docs {0: [1,3], 1: no value, 2: [5,7]} in a multi-valued numeric doc-values field, you call advanceExact(1) on the field's SortedNumericDocValues (it returns false) and then rangeIntoBitSet(1, 3, 1, 3, bits, 0) on the same iterator. You expect no bit, because neither doc 1 nor doc 2 has a value in [1, 3], and that is what the method's documented per-document default returns from the same state. Instead the codec's override evaluates doc 1 with doc 0's values and marks it (in a DENSE block it uses the next valued document's values), and when no earlier document has values ({0: no value, 1: [1,3], 2: [5,7]}, advanceExact(0) then rangeIntoBitSet(0, 3, 1, 3, ...)) it throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException: Index -1.

rows.title: MultiDocValues norms view (also the merged reader passed to MergePolicy.OneMerge#reorder): advance(target) returns a document before target when target's segment has no norms for the field, so queries over that view can return duplicate or non-matching hits
rows.summary: You read the norms of a multi-segment index as one merged iterator (MultiDocValues.getNormValues(reader, "body"), or LeafReader#getNormValues on the merged reader that IndexWriter hands to a custom OneMerge#reorder), where doc 0's segment has the text field "body", docs 1-2 sit in a segment without it and doc 3's segment has it again, and call advance(1) on a fresh iterator. You expect 3, the first document at or after the target that has a norm, as the DocIdSetIterator#advance contract says and as the merged numeric doc-values view of the same index returns. Instead advance(1) returns 0, a document before the target, because advance() falls back to nextDoc() before it records which segment comes next, so nextDoc() restarts from the first segment; queries over that view inherit the backward step (FieldExistsQuery with intra-segment partitions returns [0, 0, 0, 3] instead of [0, 3], and a conjunction can return a document that fails one of its FILTER clauses).
rows.area: index / MultiDocValues merged norms view (also the merged reader passed to MergePolicy.OneMerge#reorder)

rows.title: SortedDocValues#ordinalRangeIntoBitSet's default implementation, called after advanceExact(d) returned false, reads ordValue() for doc d, which has no value, so it marks d using a neighbouring document's ordinal (or throws EOFException)
rows.summary: On a default-codec index with docs {0: 'a', 1: no value, 2: 'b'} in a SORTED doc-values field, you call advanceExact(1) on the field's SortedDocValues (it returns false) and then ordinalRangeIntoBitSet(1, 3, ord(a), ord(a), bits, 0) on the same iterator. You expect no bit, because neither doc 1 nor doc 2 has the value 'a', and that is what the per-document advanceExact/ordValue evaluation the javadoc describes returns. Instead the default starts at docID() == 1, calls ordValue() there (which the API calls illegal after a false advanceExact), gets doc 0's ordinal and marks doc 1; with {0: no value, 1: 'a', 2: 'b'} and advanceExact(0), the same call throws RuntimeException(EOFException).

rows.title: SlowCodecReaderWrapper's KnnVectorsReader.getVectorCount (new in 10.6.0) returns the vector count of the SegmentReader under every FilterLeafReader/FilterCodecReader layer instead of the wrapped view's, so it disagrees with get*VectorValues(field).size() of the same reader (6 instead of 3 for a view that exposes 3 of 6 vectors), and it throws NullPointerException for a vector field that the view adds
rows.summary: You wrap a FilterLeafReader that exposes only some of a segment's vectors (in the repro the 3 even documents of 6) with SlowCodecReaderWrapper.wrap, as callers of IndexWriter.addIndexes do, and ask the resulting reader's KnnVectorsReader for getVectorCount(fieldInfo); you expect 3, because the javadoc says it 'has the same meaning as get*VectorValues(field).size()' and the same reader's getFloatVectorValues and getByteVectorValues return 3 vectors. Instead it returns 6, the stored count of the SegmentReader under the filter, because the wrapper strips every FilterLeafReader and FilterCodecReader layer before it asks; a custom vectors format sees the same 6 for the 3 vectors it merges during addIndexes. For a view that adds a vector field to a segment without vectors, the call throws NullPointerException instead of returning the count (the javadoc documents only IllegalArgumentException).

rows.title: BlockTreeOrds TermsEnum: seekExact(term, termState) right after seekExact(ord) marks the enum positioned over an incomplete frame stack, so a later seekExact returns false for an existing term and seekCeil/next() throw or return made-up terms
rows.summary: You index a field with BlockTreeOrdsPostingsFormat (here 26 terms a00..a24 and b in one segment, default block sizes), position a TermsEnum with seekExact(0), take its termState() and call seekExact(term(), state) on the same enum, which the TermsEnum javadoc allows and which leaves it on a00. You expect a later seekExact("b") to return true, seekCeil("b") to return FOUND and next() after a24 to return "b", as they do without the extra TermState call and with every other terms dictionary. Instead seekExact("b") returns false, seekCeil("b") throws EOFException (or, in a segment whose terms file is larger than about 7 KB, returns NOT_FOUND with a made-up term) and next() after a24 throws, because seekExact(ord) loads only the target block and deliberately leaves the enum unpositioned, while the TermState seek's 'already on this term' shortcut marks it positioned anyway, so the next call reuses parent frames that were never loaded.

rows.title: MultiTermsEnum.next() after a successful seekExact re-seeks every sub-reader with the BytesRef that one sub's own term() returned, and MemoryIndex's terms enum overwrites that BytesRef during its binary search, so a merged terms enum over MemoryIndex readers skips a term, repeats one or goes back to an earlier one; since 4.1.0
rows.summary: You put two MemoryIndex readers, each holding the terms a, b, c, d and e in field f, into a MultiReader, take MultiTerms.getTerms(reader, "f").iterator(), call seekExact("a"), which returns true, and then next(). You expect "b", as the TermsEnum contract ('Each term in the enumeration is greater than the one before it') and upstream TestTermsEnum require, but you get "c". After seekExact the merged enum keeps the second sub's own term() BytesRef as its current term and next() re-seeks every sub with it; MemoryIndex's seekCeil binary-searches by writing each probe term into that same BytesRef, so it overwrites the target with the middle term, finds it equal and stops there.

rows.title: MemoryIndex's StoredFields.document offers the visitor fields that have no stored value and asks needsField only once per field name instead of once per stored value, so LazyDocument fails with ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException or silently loses values, and per-value NO/STOP decisions are ignored
rows.summary: You add a document with an indexed-only field body (TextField, Store.NO) and a stored field tag with two values t1, t2 to a MemoryIndex and read it through storedFields().document(0, visitor), with a visitor that records its needsField calls or with LazyDocument's lazy-loading pattern from TestLazyDocument, expecting what an IndexWriter index gives for the same document: one needsField(tag) per stored value, never a question about body, and the lazy values tag=t1, tag=t2. Instead MemoryIndex asks about body, which has no stored value, asks about tag only once and then delivers both values on that single YES, because its loop calls needsField once per field name before it checks whether the field has stored values. So LazyDocument's lazy body field throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException when read and tag=t2 is silently missing (with -ea LazyDocument's own inverted assertion, LFV-697, throws instead), and a visitor that wants only the first value of tag gets both.

rows.title: IndriAndQuery accepts MUST, FILTER and MUST_NOT clauses without complaint but ignores them when matching (it always matches the union of all clauses), while its explain does read MUST/FILTER, so it explains some of its own hits as non-matches
rows.summary: You build an IndriAndQuery from BooleanClauses with Occur values other than SHOULD, for example [MUST f:a, FILTER acl:x] or [SHOULD f:a, MUST_NOT f:secret], which the public constructor accepts, and run it. You expect either the meaning that BooleanClause.Occur documents (the same clauses in a BooleanQuery give {0, 2} and {0, 1}) or a rejection, and in any case an explain that agrees with the hits. Instead IndriAndWeight builds one disjunction over all clauses whatever their Occur, so MUST and FILTER clauses do not restrict ({0, 1, 2, 3}), a MUST_NOT clause adds the very documents it names ({0, 1, 2}; a lone MUST_NOT clause returns exactly them), and IndriAndWeight.explain, which does treat MUST/FILTER clauses as required, explains such hits as non-matches.

rows.title: Calling docIDRunEnd() on a two-phase disjunction's approximation between matches() and score() corrupts DisjunctionScorer's list of verified matches, so score() and getChildren() include a clause that does not match the current document, or never return (since 10.2.0)

You expect score() to return 0.06880058, the f:c score a fresh scorer gives, because docIDRunEnd() is documented not to affect the iterator; you get 0.59193045 with no error, because the phrase, which does not match doc 0, is added in. docIDRunEnd() walks the lead heap's topList(), which rewrites the same DisiWrapper.next links that matches() used to build the list of verified matches, and if the phrase also matches doc 0 the list becomes a cycle and score() never returns.

With the Panama provider doc 12 is set, with no error under -ea or -da. PanamaDocValuesRangeSupport.rangeIntoBitSet has no empty-range guard: loopBound = fromDoc + LONG_SPECIES.loopBound(toDoc - fromDoc) rounds the negative length down to a multiple of the lane count and lands below toDoc, the SIMD loop is skipped, and the scalar tail tests and sets the docs in [loopBound, toDoc) that were never requested (for [10, 5) with 4 lanes: docs 2, 3 and 4).

rows.title: NRTCachingDirectory.sync creates a commit's cached segment files in the underlying directory after the commit's directory fsync, so an OS crash right after the segments_N rename can leave a newest commit whose files are missing and an index that will not open
rows.summary: You index through NRTCachingDirectory (for example new NRTCachingDirectory(FSDirectory.open(path), 5.0, 60.0), the class javadoc's own example), call IndexWriter.commit(), and the machine crashes during that commit. You expect what Lucene's commit protocol and LUCENE-8048 are built for: after the crash the index opens to the previous commit or to the new one, because SegmentInfos.prepareCommit fsyncs the directory before the commit is published by renaming pending_segments_N to segments_N. Instead the newly flushed segment files are still in NRTCachingDirectory's RAM cache at that directory fsync; NRTCachingDirectory.sync creates them on disk only afterwards and fsyncs their bytes but never the directory, so the rename can become durable before the new files' names do, and in that crash state every open fails (CorruptSegmentInfoException: segment info file _1.si cannot be read), while the same steps on a plain FSDirectory open fine.
rows.area: store / NRTCachingDirectory (commit durability: IndexWriter.startCommit, SegmentInfos.prepareCommit/finishCommit)

rows.title: If Directory.rename(pending_segments_N, segments_N) throws after it took effect, the failed commit leaves the new segments_N in the index (SegmentInfos.finishCommit deletes only pending_segments_N), and IndexWriter then deletes files that this newest segments_N references, so DirectoryReader.open and a new IndexWriter fail until the file is removed by hand (every release since 5.0.0; the rename-branch residual of LUCENE-9477)
rows.summary: You commit through a Directory whose rename(pending_segments_2, segments_2) creates segments_2 and then throws an IOException; commit() throws, the writer stays open (the failure is not tragic), and you expect the index to still be the last good commit segments_1, which is what LUCENE-9477 made Lucene do when the directory sync right after the rename fails. Instead SegmentInfos.finishCommit deletes only pending_segments_2, so segments_2 stays in the directory unknown to the writer; as soon as a merge removes the segments it references (a merge that finishes during the commit's fsync, or any merge before the writer is closed or rolled back) the writer deletes their files, and DirectoryReader.open, and after a restart a new IndexWriter, fail with CorruptSegmentInfoException '_1.si cannot be read' although segments_1 and its files are intact. Without a merge, rollback() or close() deletes the failed commit's files before the stray segments_2 with no directory fsync in between, so a process kill or OS crash in that window leaves the same unopenable index.
rows.area: index / commit protocol failure cleanup (SegmentInfos.finishCommit, IndexWriter.finishCommit and rollback)

rows.title: If closing the temporary reader of a doc-values update write throws, the segment's fieldInfosGen keeps pointing at a .fnm file the cleanup just deleted, so every later commit and NRT open fails until rollback()
rows.summary: You update a doc-values field (for example with updateNumericDocValue) of a document whose segment is being merged, so the update is carried over to the merged segment, and the next commit writes it through a temporary reader whose close() throws an IOException; the commit fails and the writer stays open. You expect a second commit, once the fault is gone, to write the update, which is what the cleanup code itself prepares for ('so that a 2nd attempt to write will write to a new file'). Instead the segment's fieldInfosGen was already advanced to the new _N_<gen>.fnm, which the cleanup then deleted, so every later commit and NRT reader open fails on that missing file until rollback(), which throws away everything since the last commit.

rows.title: When releasing IndexWriter's old pooled segment reader throws (a reader-closed listener on an NRT leaf), the writer keeps the closed reader in its pool, so every later NRT open fails with AlreadyClosedException
rows.summary: You register a reader-closed listener on a segment of an NRT reader opened from an IndexWriter, close that reader, and later the writer refreshes its own pooled reader of that segment (for example after a delete, when the merge policy asks for the segment's latest reader); the listener throws while the writer releases the old reader. You expect that exception once and a writer that keeps working, because the old reader is closed either way and the new reader is already built. Instead the writer throws the new reader away and keeps the now closed old one in its pool, so every later DirectoryReader.open(writer) throws AlreadyClosedException ('SegmentCoreReaders is already closed') and the next delete plus flush closes the writer as tragic.
rows.area: index / IndexWriter reader pool (ReadersAndUpdates pooled-reader refresh through getLatestReader)

You expect r2, and any reader later opened from it, to keep working: openIfChanged(r2, newer commit) should return a usable reader of that commit, just as a fresh open of the commit does. Instead SegmentDocValues closed the producer before removing it from its cache and RefCount put the reference back when the close threw, so the reopened reader is handed the closed producer and its first doc-values read throws AlreadyClosedException ('Already closed.').

rows.title: DirectoryTaxonomyWriter counts a new ordinal in getSize() before it stores that ordinal's parent, so a concurrent getParent(getSize() - 1) returns 0 (the root) instead of the real parent, or throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException

rows.title: ThaiRepeatFilter (new in 10.6.0) emits the repeats of a word ending in the Thai repetition mark Maiyamok (U+0E46) before the tokens stacked on that word (a KeywordRepeatFilter copy, a synonym, a TypeAsSynonymFilter type token), so the stacked token moves one position later with a start offset that goes backwards and IndexWriter rejects the document

rows.title: Loading some well-formed hyphenation grammars (e.g. the current TeX Afrikaans patterns) throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException, because TernaryTree.insert(char[], int, char) sizes its node arrays with strlen(key) instead of strlen(key, start)
rows.summary: You load a well-formed FOP-format hyphenation grammar with HyphenationCompoundWordTokenFilter.getHyphenationTree (or HyphenationTree.loadPatterns, or the factory's hyphenator file) and expect it to load, as the TernaryTree javadoc's 'room for about 65000 nodes' suggests. For some grammars, for example the current TeX Afrikaans patterns or the repro's 1,310 random 4-8-letter patterns, loading instead throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException: Index 2048 out of bounds for length 2048 from TernaryTree.insert, called by compact() during trimToSize(). The cause: insert(char[] key, int start, char val) reserves room for strlen(key) + 1 nodes counted from index 0 instead of from start, and its only caller with start > 0, compact(), passes a key array whose index 0 is an empty string, so it reserves one node and a multi-node insert that crosses the 2048-node block boundary writes past the arrays; with strlen(key, start), the bound the String overload already uses, every failing grammar loads with all values right.
rows.area: analysis-common / compound hyphenation (TernaryTree.compact via HyphenationTree.loadPatterns and HyphenationCompoundWordTokenFilter)

rows.title: Hunspell Dictionary can fail to load with 'Too many collisions' when its entry count is a multiple of 961, because WordStorage takes the raw String.hashCode() modulo the table size (for example the en_US dictionary plus a 300-word custom list)
rows.summary: You load a Hunspell dictionary, for example the stock en_US dictionary plus a custom list of 300 words through HunspellStemFilterFactory's documented dictionary="en_US.dic,custom.dic" pattern, and expect it to load as it does with 299 or 301 custom words. Instead the Dictionary constructor throws RuntimeException 'Too many collisions. Try a larger Dictionary#hashFactor (now 1.0). If this doesn't help, please report this to dev@lucene.apache.org', so the analyzer cannot be built. WordStorage puts every word into slot Math.abs(String.hashCode() % tableSize) with tableSize = entry count x hashFactor (default 1.0); when that size is a multiple of 961 = 31*31, the slot of a short word depends almost only on its last two letters (31^2 divides every earlier term of the unmixed radix-31 hash), so short words with a common ending (six-letter '-er' words in en_US) pile into a few slots and one exceeds the hard limit of 20 entries.
rows.area: analysis-common / hunspell WordStorage (dictionary word hash table)

rows.title: WordDelimiterGraphFilterFactory (and the deprecated WordDelimiterFilterFactory) throw a java.util.NoSuchElementException with no message from inform() when the 'types' file holds no rule (empty, only comment or blank lines, or a sole '# => ...' rule that the loader drops as a comment), because parseTypes calls TreeMap.lastKey() on the empty rule map

rows.summary: You load a Hunspell dictionary whose affix file says SET ISO8859-10 (Latin-6, Nordic), a value the hunspell(5) man page lists among the possible SET values, or says ISO8859-14 (Latin-8, Celtic) spelled ISO-8859-14 or iso8859-14, and expect it to load: C Hunspell lower-cases the SET value and drops non-alphanumerics before its table lookup, and in Lucene every other listed ISO-8859 part loads in its hyphenated and lower-case spellings (ISO-8859-2, iso8859-2, ...). rows.title: TSTLookup recurses once per ternary-tree level in add/build, store, load and ramBytesUsed, so a deep tree (short keys added in sorted order, or one suggestion thousands of characters long) throws StackOverflowError, often only when the lookup is stored or loaded (every release since 3.3.0)
rows.summary: You add the 20,992 CJK Unified Ideographs to a TSTLookup in code-point order, or build one from a single suggestion of 20,000 characters, and expect to store it, load it back and ask its size, as Lookup.store and Lookup.load promise (they document failure only as a false return or an IOException) and as WFSTCompletionLookup does with the same 20,000-character suggestion. Instead add(), get() and lookup() work, but store(), load() and ramBytesUsed() throw StackOverflowError on the JVM's default thread stack, and for the long suggestion build() itself overflows, because TSTAutocomplete.insert, TSTLookup.writeRecursively and readRecursively and TernaryTreeNode.sizeInBytes each use one Java stack frame per tree level. Adding keys in sorted order turns each level's lo/hi links into a chain (that sorted insertion unbalances this tree was noted by its author, Ankul Garg, on SOLR-1316 in 2009, as a speed concern), so the tree gets about as deep as the number of distinct first characters, and every character of a key adds one more level even in build().
rows.area: suggest / ternary search tree suggester (TSTLookup add, build, store, load and ramBytesUsed; TSTAutocomplete.insert; TernaryTreeNode.sizeInBytes)

rows.title: FileDictionary treats its fieldDelimiter as a regular expression, so a delimiter such as '|', '.', '+' or '$' makes a valid suggestion file fail to load or silently mis-parse

(or LongRange#getQuery with the source's toLongValuesSource() view) and run it on an IndexSearcher, and expect it to match the documents whose query score falls in the range, as FunctionMatchQuery does with the same source, because core says Queries that use a DoubleValuesSource call rewrite() in createWeight. Instead the search throws UnsupportedOperationException 'This DoubleValuesSource must be rewritten': the range query hands the source to getValues without ever rewriting it against the searcher. With a legacy QueryValueSource view on a searcher that uses ClassicSimilarity the same omission is silent: the source scores with a fresh default-Similarity searcher, and the range [top score, top score] matches 0 documents where FunctionMatchQuery matches 3.
rows.area: facet / range drill-down and filter queries (DoubleRange/LongRange.ValueSourceQuery)

rows.title: ValueSource#asDoubleValuesSource and #asLongValuesSource never call createWeight, so a ValueSource that keeps per-query state in its context (ttf, sttf, or a user ValueSource) fails with NullPointerException through FunctionScoreQuery, its explain, or a LongValuesSource sort
rows.summary: You expose a ValueSource as a DoubleValuesSource with asDoubleValuesSource() and score with it through FunctionScoreQuery (for example FunctionScoreQuery.boostByValue, the documented replacement for the removed BoostedQuery), or sort by asLongValuesSource().getSortField(), and expect the per-document values the same ValueSource gives through FunctionQuery or its own getSortField (3 for ttf(text, test) in the repro). Instead the bridge builds a fresh context in getValues and explain and calls in.getValues without ever calling in.createWeight, so ttf and sttf, which compute their statistic in createWeight and return context.get(this) from getValues, throw NullPointerException ('this.val$fv' is null at ValueSource.java:210 or :144), and a user ValueSource that stores per-query state in createWeight, as the ValueSource javadoc describes, finds its context entry missing. FunctionQuery, FunctionRangeQuery and ValueSource#getSortField all call createWeight first, and the bridge's rewrite(searcher) already holds the searcher such a call needs.
rows.area: queries / function queries (ValueSource to DoubleValuesSource/LongValuesSource bridge: asDoubleValuesSource, asLongValuesSource)

rows.title: RangeMapFloatFunction (map()) never calls createWeight on its target and default value sources, so a target or default that keeps per-query state in the context (ttf, sttf, or a user ValueSource) fails with NullPointerException
rows.summary: You build map(x, 0, 2, ttf(text, test)) as new RangeMapFloatFunction(source, 0, 2, new TotalTermFreqValueSource(...), null) and score it with FunctionQuery, expecting every document whose x lies in [0, 2] to get the target's value (3 in the repro, the score FunctionQuery(ttf) gives on its own). Instead the search throws NullPointerException ('this.val$targets' is null at RangeMapFloatFunction.java:84); sttf as the default fails the same way (:85), and a user ValueSource that stores a per-query statistic in createWeight, as the ValueSource javadoc describes, finds its context entry missing. The cause: RangeMapFloatFunction.createWeight forwards only to source, while getValues also asks target and default for their values on the same context, whereas every other composite ValueSource forwards createWeight to all of its children.
rows.area: queries / function queries (RangeMapFloatFunction, map(): createWeight propagation to sub-ValueSources)

rows.title: IndriAndQuery does not rewrite its clauses, so a PrefixQuery, WildcardQuery, FuzzyQuery or other rewrite-only clause makes search, count and explain throw UnsupportedOperationException
rows.summary: You build an IndriAndQuery from ordinary clauses, for example a TermQuery and the PrefixQuery f:ban*, and search with it. You expect the documents the clauses match, as with the same IndriAndQuery built from clauses that IndexSearcher.rewrite has already rewritten. Instead the search throws UnsupportedOperationException 'Query f:ban* does not implement createWeight', because IndriAndQuery keeps the default rewrite (it returns itself) and IndriAndWeight creates a Weight for each clause exactly as given, which only primitive queries support.
rows.area: search / IndriAndQuery (composite query clause rewriting)

Instead Weight#matches throws UnsupportedOperationException for every matching document (ordered, unordered, maxgaps, atLeast), and highlighting throws for those and also for phrase, containing and containedBy, because the payload-filtered term's match iterator throws from getQuery(), which MatchesIterator#getQuery says returns a TermQuery for the current match; search and count still return the right hits.

rows.title: Multi-term interval sources (Intervals.prefix, wildcard, regexp, fuzzyTerm, range, multiterm) skip the has-positions check that Intervals.term performs, so positional interval queries over them on a field indexed without positions silently return wrong hits (usually none) instead of throwing the documented exception
rows.summary: You index 'alpha beta' into a field with IndexOptions.DOCS_AND_FREQS (no positions) and search IntervalQuery("body", Intervals.ordered(Intervals.prefix("alph"), Intervals.prefix("bet"))). You expect IllegalArgumentException ('... because it has no indexed positions'), because the IndexOptions javadoc says positional queries on such a field throw and the same query written with Intervals.term("alpha") and Intervals.term("beta") does throw. Instead MultiTermIntervalsSource never checks Terms#hasPositions(), runs the interval logic on the position -1 that the postings return, and silently reports 0 hits (1 of 2 on a MultiReader that also holds a positioned copy of the document); wildcard, regexp, fuzzyTerm, range and multiterm leaves behave the same way.
rows.area: queries / intervals (MultiTermIntervalsSource behind Intervals.prefix, wildcard, regexp, range, fuzzyTerm and multiterm; IntervalQuery search and Weight#matches)

rows.title: Sandbox HistogramCollectorManager fails the whole search with ArithmeticException when one segment lists a skip-indexed field but no document in it has a value (an empty DocValuesSkipper), because the dense leaf collector's '<= 1024' bucket-span check passes for the empty skipper's inverted bounds (10.2.0 through 10.6.0 and main)
rows.summary: You index two documents with the default codec, one without the field and one with NumericDocValuesField.indexedField("f", 50) (a doc-values skip index, as HistogramCollectorManager's javadoc recommends), delete the second, call forceMerge(1), and run IndexSearcher.search(MatchAllDocsQuery.INSTANCE, new HistogramCollectorManager("f", 10)). You expect an empty histogram, which is what the same index returns without a skip index and what the collector does for a segment that lacks the field. Instead the search throws ArithmeticException 'integer overflow': the merged segment still lists f, its skipper is empty (docCount() 0, minValue() Long.MAX_VALUE, maxValue() Long.MIN_VALUE, a state core writes and CheckIndex accepts), so the bucket span floorDiv(max, 10) - floorDiv(min, 10) is negative, passes the one-sided '<= 1024' check in HistogramCollector.getLeafCollector, and the dense HistogramLeafCollector's new int[Math.toIntExact(span + 1)] throws.
rows.area: sandbox / facets: plain histograms (HistogramCollector's skip-index dense leaf collector, single-valued NUMERIC or SORTED_NUMERIC field)

rows.title: NearestFuzzyQuery (used by KNearestFuzzyClassifier) computes idf from reader.numDocs() (live documents) and reader.docFreq() (which still counts deleted documents), so when deleted documents that are not yet merged away make up most of the index the idf is negative and rewrite throws 'boost must be a positive float' (released since 8.0.0)
rows.summary: You index 6 documents containing 'apple' (class fruit), delete 5 of them under NoMergePolicy (or soft-delete them and keep them with SoftDeletesRetentionMergePolicy), and then search NearestFuzzyQuery('apple') or call KNearestFuzzyClassifier.assignClass('apple'), expecting the one live document and the class fruit. Instead both throw IllegalArgumentException 'boost must be a positive float, got -0.25276297'. NearestFuzzyQuery computes idf = ln((numDocs+1)/(docFreq+1)) + 1 from reader.numDocs(), which counts only live documents, and reader.docFreq(), which still counts the 5 deleted copies, so idf = ln(2/7) + 1 < 0, and since LUCENE-7996 (8.0.0) BoostQuery rejects the resulting negative boost.
rows.area: classification / NearestFuzzyQuery (KNearestFuzzyClassifier)

rows.title: Sandbox numeric multi-range doc-values query whose clauses are all reversed (lower > upper) throws NoSuchElementException at search time instead of matching nothing (SortedNumericStabbingBuilder("f").add(3, 1).add(9, 7) on an index where f has a value); since 10.3.0
rows.summary: You index one document whose field f holds 5 (SortedNumericDocValuesField) and count new DocValuesMultiRangeQuery.SortedNumericStabbingBuilder("f").add(3, 1).add(9, 7).build(), a union of two empty ranges (lower > upper); you expect 0 hits, because the query drops reversed ranges on purpose and the same builder returns no hits for no range or for one reversed range. Instead IndexSearcher.count throws java.util.NoSuchElementException: once every clause is dropped the query's clause set is empty (it prints f:[]), and MultiRangeWeight.scorerSupplier reads its first element (sortedClauses.getFirst()) with no empty check.

rows.title: MoreLikeThis with setBoost(true) divides every term's score by the lowest selected score, so a selected term that scores 0 (a TFIDFSimilarity whose idf is 0, such as the textbook log(N/df) for a term in every document) makes like() throw 'boost must be a positive float, got NaN' (8.0 and later) or build NaN and Infinity boosts (4.10 to 7.x)
rows.summary: You enable boosting on MoreLikeThis (setBoost(true)) with a custom TFIDFSimilarity whose idf is 0 for a term that is in every document, as the textbook idf log(N/df) is, and call like(...) on text that contains that term and a rarer one. You expect a query with finite, non-negative boosts: the same call works with setBoost(false), and BoostQuery accepts a boost of 0. Instead createQuery divides each term's score by the first score popped from its ascending queue, which is the lowest selected score (0 here), so the zero-score term's boost is 0/0 = NaN and like() throws IllegalArgumentException 'boost must be a positive float, got NaN' on 8.0 and later, or builds the query with NaN and Infinity boosts on 4.10 to 7.x.
rows.area: queries / MoreLikeThis boosted query construction (MoreLikeThis.createQuery boost normalisation)

rows.title: AnalyzingInfixSuggester.ensureOpen() publishes its new IndexWriter before the SearcherManager opened on it and does not undo that when the manager cannot be opened, so refresh() refreshes the manager over build()'s closed writer and throws AlreadyClosedException
rows.summary: You build an AnalyzingInfixSuggester with the default closeIndexWriterOnBuild=true, add() a suggestion and call refresh(), and you expect the addition to become visible, as the add()/update() javadoc says, or at worst refresh() to be the no-op its own comment describes. The first add() after build() runs ensureOpen(), which assigns the writer field before it installs the SearcherManager opened on that writer, and refresh() (no lock) reads writer != null as 'the current manager is live', so in that gap it refreshes build()'s old manager, whose writer is closed, and throws AlreadyClosedException 'this IndexWriter is closed'. The gap is transient when refresh() runs on another thread during that first add() (or, contested, during a rebuild), and permanent after one IOException while ensureOpen() opens the manager: writer stays set, no later add() repairs it, and every refresh() fails until build() or a reopen.

rows.title: Monitor.match can throw NullPointerException while queries are being registered (or while a read-only Monitor refreshes), because QueryIndex keeps its per-reader term filters in a plain HashMap that the searcher refresh and reader-close listeners modify while match threads read it without a lock
rows.summary: You share one Monitor between threads: some threads call Monitor.match on documents while another registers new queries, and each register commits and opens a new query-index searcher, which the Monitor's design for searches during commits allows. You expect every match of a valid document to return its matching queries. Instead, when the internal map from searcher to term filter (a plain java.util.HashMap) grows, a concurrent match can look up its own searcher's entry and get null, and Monitor.match throws NullPointerException from TermFilteredPresearcher.buildQuery; the read-only Monitor fails the same way while its refresh runs.
rows.area: monitor / QueryIndex term-filter map (searcher refresh vs concurrent match, writable and read-only Monitor)

rows.title: AnalyzingSuggester and FuzzySuggester check a payload-enabled surface form for the reserved byte U+001F in bytes[0, length) of the backing array instead of in the BytesRef slice [offset, offset + length), so a valid slice is rejected with IllegalArgumentException and a slice that contains U+001F is accepted and later mis-split
rows.summary: You build an AnalyzingSuggester or FuzzySuggester with payloads from your own InputIterator whose surface forms are BytesRef slices of a larger byte array, for example "ab" at offset 1 of {0x1F, 'a', 'b'}, and expect it to behave exactly as for compact copies of the same bytes. Instead build() looks for the reserved separator U+001F in bytes[0, length) of the backing array, ignoring the slice's offset, while two lines later it writes the real slice: the valid slice "ab" is rejected with IllegalArgumentException 'surface form cannot contain unit separator character U+001F', and "a<U+001F>b" at offset 3 of {'x','x','x','a',0x1F,'b'}, whose compact copy is rejected, is accepted. The accepted entry is then split at the wrong place: without EXACT_FIRST, lookup("a") returns key "a" with payload "b<U+001F>p" instead of payload "p"; with the default EXACT_FIRST it returns nothing for that entry with -da and throws AssertionError with -ea.
rows.area: suggest / analyzing suggester (AnalyzingSuggester.build payload check, inherited by FuzzySuggester)

rows.title: FreeTextSuggester.build accepts a token that contains the separator byte whenever the shingled term stays within the gram limit, although its javadoc promises an IllegalArgumentException; later lookups whose last complete word occurs only inside that token throw AssertionError (-ea) or NullPointerException (-da)
rows.summary: You build a FreeTextSuggester with the default bigram model and separator U+001E over the single entry 'foo\u001ebar' (the upstream test input 'foo\u001ebar baz' without its neighbour 'baz'), using an analyzer that keeps it as one token such as UnicodeWhitespaceAnalyzer, and expect build() to throw IllegalArgumentException, as the constructor javadoc promises and as it does for 'foo\u001ebar baz'. Instead build() succeeds, because it only rejects an indexed shingle whose separator count implies more than grams words, so the token is stored as if it were the bigram (foo, bar) with no unigram 'foo'. A later lookup('foo ') then fails inside the suggester with AssertionError at FreeTextSuggester.java:576 (-ea) or NullPointerException in decodeWeight (-da), and lookup('f') returns the token itself with a wrong score.
rows.area: suggest / FreeTextSuggester (n-gram model joined with an in-band separator byte; build-side separator check)

rows.title: AnalyzingSuggester and FuzzySuggester getCount() counts analyzed paths instead of entries when the analyzer produces a token graph (synonyms, word-delimiter graphs), and store()/load() persist the inflated count
rows.summary: You build an AnalyzingSuggester or FuzzySuggester from the two entries 'fast car' and 'red car' with an analyzer whose synonym rule maps fast to {fast, quick}, and you expect getCount() to return 2, because Lookup#getCount is documented as 'the number of entries the lookup was built with'. It returns 3: build() increments its counter once for every analyzed path of an entry ('fast car' and 'quick car' here), not once per entry, so each entry counts as often as its token graph has paths (8 for the single entry 'wifi wifi wifi' with one stacked synonym), and store() and load() keep the inflated number. Lookups are correct, and analyzers that produce no token graph give the right count.
rows.area: suggest / analyzing suggester (AnalyzingSuggester.build and getCount, inherited by FuzzySuggester)

rows.title: SegmentOrder.fromSort(numeric sort).reorder(reader) throws NullPointerException when a leaf's getCoreCacheHelper() returns null, which LeafReader documents as legal (ParallelCompositeReader over two or more readers, SortingCodecReader or MemoryIndex leaves, content-altering FilterLeafReaders)
rows.summary: You call SegmentOrder.fromSort(new Sort(new SortField("f", SortField.Type.LONG, true))).reorder(reader) to visit the segments with the highest f values first, on a reader whose leaves do not support caching, for example a ParallelCompositeReader over two DirectoryReaders with two segments each. You expect a re-ordered view, because reorder() accepts any IndexReader and LeafReader#getCoreCacheHelper documents null as a legal return value ('not suited for caching') that other consumers such as LRUQueryCache and QueryBitSetProducer simply skip. Instead reorder() throws NullPointerException at SegmentOrder.java:137, where the leaf comparator's memo calls reader.getCoreCacheHelper().getKey() without a null check.

rows.title: A SegmentOrder built by SegmentOrder.fromSort(numeric Sort) sorts the leaves of every reorder() call with one shared comparator whose per-segment memo is an unsynchronized HashMap, so two threads calling reorder() on the same SegmentOrder at the same time can throw NullPointerException (Map.get returns null and is unboxed) (since 10.4.0)
rows.summary: You build one SegmentOrder with SegmentOrder.fromSort(new Sort(new SortField("f", SortField.Type.LONG, true))) and share it between searches, as you would a Sort or a Query, so two threads call order.reorder(reader) on the same freshly opened reader at the same time. You expect each call to return a re-ordered view: the strategy is built from an immutable Sort, its API exposes no state, and its javadoc says nothing about threads. Instead every reorder() of that strategy sorts the leaves with one comparator whose per-segment memo is a plain HashMap filled with containsKey/put/get and no lock, so a concurrent put or resize can make Map.get return null and reorder() throws NullPointerException 'Cannot invoke "java.lang.Long.longValue()" because the return value of "java.util.Map.get(Object)" is null' at SegmentOrder.java:141.

rows.title: UnifiedHighlighter with maxPassages = Integer.MAX_VALUE throws a message-less IllegalArgumentException for every document that has a match (FieldHighlighter sizes its passage queue with Math.min(64, maxPassages + 1), which wraps)
rows.summary: You ask the UnifiedHighlighter for at most Integer.MAX_VALUE passages, meaning 'no limit', and expect the same snippet that 1000 or Integer.MAX_VALUE - 1 gives (or, if the value is not allowed, an IllegalArgumentException that says so). Instead, for every document that has a match, FieldHighlighter.highlightOffsetsEnums sizes its passage queue with Math.min(64, maxPassages + 1); the + 1 wraps to Integer.MIN_VALUE, Math.min returns it, and the java.util.PriorityQueue constructor throws an IllegalArgumentException with no message. With per-field counts such as {1, MAX_VALUE} the field that asked for one passage loses its snippet too, because the whole call throws.

rows.title: GroupingSearch with groupLimit or groupDocsLimit = Integer.MAX_VALUE ('all remaining groups/documents') throws NegativeArraySizeException, OutOfMemoryError or an IllegalArgumentException naming -2147483648, because it does not cap the limits at maxDoc as IndexSearcher.search does and its collectors add offset + limit in int (every release since 4.0.0)
rows.summary: You call GroupingSearch.search(searcher, query, 0, Integer.MAX_VALUE) or setGroupDocsLimit(Integer.MAX_VALUE) to get every group, or every document of each group, and expect the same TopGroups as with a limit of maxDoc, the way IndexSearcher.search(query, Integer.MAX_VALUE) returns every hit. Instead the search throws: with offset 0 a NegativeArraySizeException -2147483648, an OutOfMemoryError 'Requested array size exceeds VM limit' or a queue-size IllegalArgumentException, and with offset 1 an IllegalArgumentException such as 'topNGroups must be >= 1 (got -2147483648)' or 'numHits must be > 0'. GroupingSearch hands the limits on uncapped to collectors that add offset + limit in int and pre-size their queues by the limit; nothing is ever returned wrong.

rows.title: AnalyzingInfixSuggester, WFSTCompletionLookup and FreeTextSuggester allocate storage for num results before they know how many suggestions match, so lookup(key, false, Integer.MAX_VALUE) on an 8-entry suggester throws instead of returning the 8 suggestions, and a large num allocates memory in proportion to num
rows.summary: You build an AnalyzingInfixSuggester, WFSTCompletionLookup or FreeTextSuggester from 8 entries that start with 'luc' and call lookup("luc", false, Integer.MAX_VALUE) to get every suggestion; num is documented as the 'maximum number of results to return', so you expect the 8 suggestions that num = 1000 returns, which is what TSTLookup and FSTCompletionLookup give for the same call. Instead each of the three sizes its result storage by num before it knows how many entries match (AnalyzingInfixSuggester builds a TopFieldCollectorManager of num slots that, unlike IndexSearcher.search, it never caps at maxDoc; the other two call new ArrayList<>(num)), so the call throws OutOfMemoryError 'Requested array size exceeds VM limit' (on 9.12.3, 10.5.2 and the 10.6 RC, AnalyzingInfixSuggester throws IllegalArgumentException 'maxSize must be >= 0 and < 2147483631' instead). A smaller but still large num succeeds and allocates memory in proportion to num rather than to the matches: 114 MiB per lookup for AnalyzingInfixSuggester and 38 MiB for the other two at num = 10^7.
rows.area: suggest / Lookup.lookup result sizing (AnalyzingInfixSuggester, WFSTCompletionLookup, FreeTextSuggester)

rows.title: NGramTokenizer and EdgeNGramTokenizer accept maxGram = Integer.MAX_VALUE, but their int buffer sizing wraps to a 1022-char read buffer and leaves the 16-char default term buffer, so the first text of 17 or more chars throws (ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException up to 1021 chars, an unrelated IllegalArgumentException from 1022)
rows.summary: You build EdgeNGramTokenizer(1, Integer.MAX_VALUE) (or NGramTokenizer, or a factory with maxGramSize=2147483647) to mean 'all n-grams, no upper limit', and you expect the same tokens as with maxGram = text length, or else a clear IllegalArgumentException from the constructor, which validates maxGram and accepts it. Instead init computes the buffer sizes 2 * maxGram + 1024 and 2 * maxGram in int, which wrap to 1022 and -2, so the tokenizer gets a 1022-char read buffer and keeps its 16-char default term buffer. Texts of up to 16 chars come out right, but the first text of 17 or more chars throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException 'Index 16 out of bounds for length 16' from incrementToken (from 1022 chars, an IllegalArgumentException about a buffer size the caller never passed).

rows.title: RescoreTopNQuery and LatLonPoint.nearest size their priority queue from the caller's n, not from what the index can return, so n = Integer.MAX_VALUE ('all') throws IllegalArgumentException and a large n throws OutOfMemoryError, even on an index of a few documents
rows.summary: You search with new RescoreTopNQuery(query, source, Integer.MAX_VALUE), or call LatLonPoint.nearest(searcher, field, lat, lon, Integer.MAX_VALUE), to get every candidate, and expect them all back, as n = 1000 (or 100) gives on a 9-document index and as nearest's documented equivalent, a MatchAllDocsQuery search sorted by distance, gives for Integer.MAX_VALUE. Instead both build a priority queue of n + 1 slots before looking at the index: Integer.MAX_VALUE throws IllegalArgumentException('maxSize must be >= 0 and < 2147483631') from inside the search, and a large n below that throws OutOfMemoryError (n = 3*10^8 under a 1 GB heap). IndexSearcher.search has capped the same request at maxDoc since LUCENE-2119, as Michael McCandless proposed there; the analogous fix caps RescoreTopNQuery's queue at maxDoc and nearest's at the number of indexed points (not maxDoc, because nearest returns a multi-valued document once per point).

rows.title: matchhighlight PassageSelector sizes its passage queue by maxPassages before it looks at any match, so maxPassages = Integer.MAX_VALUE ('all passages') throws IllegalArgumentException and a large maxPassages allocates maxPassages + 1 queue slots per call, even for a text with two matches
rows.summary: You call PassageSelector.pickBest on a short text with two matches (or MatchHighlighter with FieldValueHighlighters.highlighted) and pass maxPassages = Integer.MAX_VALUE to mean 'all passages', and you expect the same two passages that maxPassages = 10 returns, because maxPassages only caps the result (the method clamps its result to it) and there can never be more passages than matches. rows.title: TermInSetQuery#visit gives QueryVisitor an automaton supplier that throws IllegalArgumentException when any term is longer than 1000 bytes, so UnifiedHighlighter without WEIGHT_MATCHES fails on such a query
rows.summary: You search with a TermInSetQuery of the two terms 'short' and a 1001-byte term on a field indexed with offsets, get the hit, and highlight it with a UnifiedHighlighter built with withWeightMatches(false), expecting 'a short text', which is what the documented equivalent (a ConstantScoreQuery over a BooleanQuery of SHOULD TermQuery clauses) gives. Instead highlight() throws IllegalArgumentException 'This builder doesn't allow terms that are larger than 1000 UTF-8 bytes', and any QueryVisitor that asks the query for its automaton gets the same exception. For more than one term TermInSetQuery#visit hands visitors a supplier that builds Automata.makeBinaryStringUnion over all terms, and that builder rejects terms longer than Automata.MAX_STRING_UNION_TERM_LENGTH (1000 bytes, a guard for its recursive construction), although the query itself accepts such terms and searches with them.

rows.title: SpellChecker.suggestSimilar computes its hit budget 10 * numSug in int, so numSug = Integer.MAX_VALUE ('all suggestions'), 214748365 and every other count whose product wraps to <= 0 throw IllegalArgumentException 'numHits must be > 0' instead of returning the suggestions, and counts whose product wraps to a small positive value silently return fewer suggestions
rows.summary: You build an n-gram spell index with SpellChecker and call suggestSimilar(word, Integer.MAX_VALUE) to get all suggestions; you expect the same 9 suggestions that numSug 1000 returns on a 10-word dictionary. Instead SpellChecker multiplies numSug by 10 in int to size its search, the product wraps to -10, and the search throws IllegalArgumentException 'numHits must be > 0; please use TotalHitCountCollectorManager ...', naming a parameter the caller never passed; the same happens for half of all counts from 214,748,365 up, and in the blocks between (for example 429,496,730, whose product wraps to 4) the call silently returns fewer suggestions after allocating a queue of numSug slots. The fix is two lines: compute the budget in long and saturate it at Integer.MAX_VALUE, and size the queue by min(numSug, hits.length).

rows.title: BlendedInfixSuggester.lookup computes num * numFactor in int, so a large num wraps: num = Integer.MAX_VALUE throws IllegalArgumentException 'numHits must be > 0', some values throw NoSuchElementException, and specific values silently return fewer suggestions than exist
rows.summary: You build a BlendedInfixSuggester with its defaults (numFactor 10) from 8 entries that match 'luc' and call lookup("luc", false, Integer.MAX_VALUE) to get all suggestions; num is documented as the 'maximum number of results to return', so you expect the same 8 suggestions that num = 1000 returns. Instead the over-fetch count num * numFactor is computed in int (BlendedInfixSuggester.java:199) and wraps: a negative product throws IllegalArgumentException 'numHits must be > 0; please use TotalHitCountCollector ...' (num = Integer.MAX_VALUE or 214748365), a product below numFactor leaves room for 0 results and throws NoSuchElementException (num = 429496730), and a small positive product silently cuts the list (num = 429496731 returns only [lucas]; with numFactor 1000 already num = 4294969 does). So the number of suggestions can go down as num goes up.

rows.title: TermVectorLeafReader.getMetaData() always throws IllegalArgumentException ('minVersion must be set when createdVersionMajor is >= 7'), so a TermVectorLeafReader cannot be searched with a Sort, wrapped in a ParallelLeafReader or copied with addIndexes
rows.summary: You build a TermVectorLeafReader over one document's term vectors (new TermVectorLeafReader(field, terms), the public helper that 'wraps a Terms with a LeafReader') and use it like any other LeafReader, expecting getMetaData() to return metadata with no index sort, as MemoryIndex's in-memory reader does. Instead getMetaData() throws IllegalArgumentException('minVersion must be set when createdVersionMajor is >= 7') on every call, because it passes minVersion=null together with createdVersionMajor=Version.LATEST.major, a combination the LeafMetaData constructor rejects. So a field-sorted search (even with Sort.RELEVANCE), new ParallelLeafReader(reader) and addIndexes(SlowCodecReaderWrapper.wrap(reader)) all fail; a plain relevance search without a Sort works.
rows.area: highlighter / TermVectorLeafReader (LeafReader over one document's term vectors; LeafMetaData invariant)

rows.title: Stempel's base Reduce.optimize passes its new, empty row list to removeGaps instead of the trie's rows, so every Trie.reduce(new Reduce()) call throws IndexOutOfBoundsException
rows.summary: You reduce a stempel stemmer table with the base class of the egothor reductions, for example trie.reduce(new Reduce()), and expect what its javadoc promises: 'Optimize (remove holes in the rows) the given Trie and return the restructured Trie', a trie that still gives the same stems. Instead every call throws IndexOutOfBoundsException ('Index 0 out of bounds for length 0'), even for a one-word trie or the bundled Polish table. The cause is one wrong argument at Reduce.java:83: optimize passes its freshly created, empty list 'rows' to removeGaps as the list to read from, instead of 'orows' (the trie's own rows), which the sibling reductions Lift and Gener pass to the same helper.

rows.title: QualityQuery.compareTo is not a total order when numeric and non-numeric topic ids are mixed (ints compared as numbers, everything else as strings), so TrecTopicsReader and Trec1MQReader.readQueries, and with them QueryDriver, can throw IllegalArgumentException 'Comparison method violates its general contract!'
rows.summary: You read a TREC topics file with TrecTopicsReader or Trec1MQReader (as QueryDriver does) whose ids are mostly numbers but include a few sub-topic ids such as 1a or 10.1, or a few digit-only ids larger than Integer.MAX_VALUE, and expect the topics back sorted by id, as the readers' '// sort result array (by ID)' comment says. Instead QualityQuery.compareTo compares two int ids as numbers and every other pair as strings, which forms cycles (2 < 100 as numbers, 100 < 1a and 1a < 2 as strings), so Arrays.sort can throw IllegalArgumentException 'Comparison method violates its general contract!' (the repro: ids 1..111 plus 1a, 20a, 64a and 99a, each listed after its parent); when the sort does not detect the cycle, the topics come back in an order that depends on the file order. Separately, the int branch returns n - nOther, which overflows for extreme ids such as 2147483647 vs -1 (this needs a negative id).
rows.area: benchmark / search-quality package (QualityQuery, TREC topic readers)

rows.title: addIndexes of a SortingCodecReader (including the reader that BPIndexReorderer.reorder returns) into a writer that uses BPReorderingMergePolicy with BpVectorReorderer throws UnsupportedOperationException, because SortingCodecReader's vector views do not support copy()
rows.summary: You pass a SortingCodecReader, for example the reader that BPIndexReorderer.reorder returns or SortingCodecReader.wrap(reader, docMap, null), to IndexWriter#addIndexes on a writer whose merge policy is BPReorderingMergePolicy with a BpVectorReorderer, and expect the documents to be added and reordered, as they are for plain segment readers and as the same policy does with the postings BPIndexReorderer. Instead addIndexes throws UnsupportedOperationException and adds nothing: the policy reorders addIndexes as a forced merge, BpVectorReorderer's per-thread state calls copy() on the input's float vector values, and SortingCodecReader's vector views throw from copy() (with several such readers in one call the throw comes through SlowCompositeCodecReaderWrapper's merged copy()). Making copy() work is not enough on its own: BpVectorReorderer then treats the sorting view's ordinals as doc order, so the reordering is silently applied in the wrong doc space.
rows.area: misc / index: BpVectorReorderer merge-time reordering (BPReorderingMergePolicy) over core / index: SortingCodecReader vector views

rows.title: DatasetSplitter.split in its all-fields mode (fieldNames omitted) throws at the first document with a stored binary field, because it copies the bytes into an indexed, tokenized TextField-type field that Field rejects
rows.summary: You split an index into training, test and cross-validation indexes with DatasetSplitter.split and leave fieldNames out, which the javadoc documents as 'all [fields] should be used', and a document of the source index has a stored binary field such as new StoredField("payload", new byte[] {1, 2, 3}). You expect the split to succeed and keep the bytes; createNewDoc even has a branch written for binary values. Instead split() throws an IOException wrapping IllegalArgumentException 'cannot set a BytesRef value on a tokenized field', because every copied field gets the indexed, tokenized type TextField.TYPE_STORED and the core Field constructor refuses a BytesRef value on such a type, so no split of such an index is possible in that mode.

rows.title: ToParentBlockJoinSortField on a STRING field with max-child selection and childMissingValue=STRING_LAST throws IndexOutOfBoundsException when a parent has children both with and without the field
rows.summary: You sort parent documents by a string field of their children, descending, with new ToParentBlockJoinSortField("s", STRING, reverse=true, null, SortField.STRING_LAST, parents, children) (or the 8-argument form with reverseChildren=true), and expect the search to return the parents with children that lack the field sorted as missing-last, because the javadoc lists STRING_LAST as a legal child missing value that 'participates in the min/max selection among siblings'. Instead, as soon as the search collects a parent that has one child with the field and another child without it, it throws IndexOutOfBoundsException from the doc-values terms dictionary (Lucene90DocValuesProducer$TermsDict.seekExact via ToParentDocValues$SortedDVs.lookupOrd), with -ea and -da. The cause is that the block-join wrapper reports 'a missing child, sorted last, won the max' as the ordinal Integer.MAX_VALUE, and the string comparator TermOrdValComparator treats every ordinal other than -1 as a real one and looks it up.

rows.title: A float vector field routed to HnswBitVectorsFormat is rejected inside an aborting step of the indexing chain, so the one rejected document closes the IndexWriter and rolls back every document added since the last commit
rows.summary: You use HnswBitVectorsFormat, which accepts only byte vectors, and by mistake add a document with a float vector field (KnnFloatVectorField) that is new to the index. You expect addDocument to reject that one document with IllegalArgumentException and the writer to stay open, as the format's own test TestHnswBitVectorsFormat#testFloatVectorFails expects the exception and as happens for the same codec's dimension limit and for a vector dimension mismatch. Instead the check sits in KnnVectorsWriter#addField, which IndexingChain calls after registering the field and treats as an aborting step, so the exception also becomes the writer's tragic exception: IndexWriter closes itself, the next call throws AlreadyClosedException, and the documents added since the last commit are gone (the repro ends with 1 committed document instead of 3).
rows.area: codecs / HnswBitVectorsFormat x index / IndexingChain aborting-exception classification

rows.title: A document rejected for a custom TermFrequencyAttribute on a field with term-vector positions or offsets, postings positions or DOCS-only postings is rejected inside an aborting step of the indexing chain, so it closes the IndexWriter and rolls back every change since the last commit
rows.summary: You index a document whose analysis chain sets a custom term frequency (TermFrequencyAttribute, for example DelimitedTermFrequencyTokenFilter with a token like 'red|2') on a field that also stores term-vector positions or offsets, indexes postings positions (a default TextField), or is DOCS-only and repeats the term. You expect addDocument to reject only that document with its usual IllegalArgumentException or IllegalStateException and the writer to stay open, as it does for the neighbouring offset checks and for the duplicate-term check that #15584 made non-aborting. Instead the four checks run inside termsHashPerField.add, which IndexingChain treats as aborting, so the rejection also becomes the writer's tragic exception: IndexWriter closes itself, the next call throws AlreadyClosedException, and everything since the last commit is lost (the repro ends with 1 committed document instead of 3).

rows.title: A term repeated in one document of a DOCS_AND_CUSTOM_FREQS field closes IndexWriter, instead of skipping the document, when the term is a non-UTF-8 binary term such as the single byte 0xC3: the duplicate-term rejection builds its message with utf8ToString, which throws (since 10.5.0)
rows.summary: You index binary terms into a field with IndexOptions.DOCS_AND_CUSTOM_FREQS, which allows each term only once per document, and one document repeats a term that is not valid UTF-8, for example new BytesRef(new byte[] {(byte) 0xC3}) added twice as an untokenized Field. You expect addDocument to reject only that document with the non-aborting IllegalArgumentException 'Document update skipped due to duplicate termdoc term' and the writer to stay open, as happens for an ASCII or valid UTF-8 term and as the upstream test TestCustomTermFreq.testRepeatedTerms asserts. Instead TermsHashPerField.add builds the rejection message with termBytes.utf8ToString(), which throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException for these bytes; the indexing chain treats that as an aborting failure, so IndexWriter closes itself and every uncommitted document is lost.

rows.title: Field.storedValue() handles a String but no other CharSequence, so a stored field built from a StringBuilder, CharsRef or other CharSequence through the public StoredField(String, CharSequence, FieldType) or Field(String, CharSequence, IndexableFieldType) constructor makes IndexWriter.addDocument throw IllegalStateException 'Cannot store value of type ...' (regression in 9.6.0 from #12116)
rows.summary: You add a document holding new StoredField("f", new StringBuilder("x"), StoredField.TYPE) to an IndexWriter; you expect the value to be stored and read back as "x", since the public constructor takes a CharSequence and Lucene 7.7.0 to 9.5.x did exactly that. Instead addDocument throws IllegalStateException 'Cannot store value of type class java.lang.StringBuilder', because Field.storedValue(), added in 9.6.0 by #12116, has a text branch for String only and sends every other CharSequence to its error branch. The same happens for a Field with a stored type such as TextField.TYPE_STORED over a StringBuilder or CharsRef; only that document is rejected, and value.toString() works around it.

rows.title: IndexWriter#addBatch rejects an untokenized BinaryColumn or DictionaryColumn whose FieldType indexes positions or term-vector positions, which addDocument with the same Field type accepts: the column adapter always takes the single-term InvertableType.BINARY path for untokenized values, so the row pass throws 'Fields that are tokenized or index proximity data must produce a non-null TokenStream' after ColumnValidation accepted the type (since 10.5.0)

Instead addBatch throws IllegalArgumentException 'Fields that are tokenized or index proximity data must produce a non-null TokenStream, but f did not' in its row pass, after ColumnValidation accepted the type. The internal BinaryColumnAdapter picks the single-term InvertableType.BINARY path from tokenized() alone and returns no TokenStream, and IndexingChain.invertTerm allows BINARY only without proximity data, whereas Field always wraps an untokenized value in a one-token stream.

rows.title: When an AttributeFactory throws while IndexWriter adds TermFrequencyAttribute, FieldInvertState keeps the previous stream's attribute handles, so later accepted documents of that field are indexed with the wrong positions and offsets until the next flush
rows.summary: You add a document whose field value is your own TokenStream ending in two removed stop words ('x the the' through StopFilter), then a document whose analysis fails because your analyzer's AttributeFactory throws when IndexWriter asks for TermFrequencyAttribute, then the plain-text document 'a b' through the same analyzer with the factory working again. You expect the failed document to be dropped and 'a b' to be indexed at positions 0 and 1, as it is without the failure. Instead 'a b' is accepted at positions 1 and 3 and PhraseQuery f:"a b" finds nothing, with no error, because FieldInvertState.setAttributeSource recorded the analyzer's reused stream as cached before it fetched that stream's attributes, so every later document of the field keeps reading the first stream's position increment (frozen at 2) until the next flush.

rows.title: KnnFloatVectorField(String, float[], FieldType) accepts an empty vector when the FieldType has no vector attributes (vector dimension 0, as new FieldType() gives), although its javadoc promises IllegalArgumentException for an empty vector; if the document is indexed, the field is registered as a field without vectors (the KnnByteVectorField twin has the same gap; every release since 9.0.0)
rows.summary: You build new KnnFloatVectorField("v", new float[0], new FieldType()) and expect the IllegalArgumentException that this constructor's javadoc promises when 'the vector is empty' (the convenience constructors throw 'cannot index an empty vector' for the same vector). Instead the field is built without error: the constructor's only length check compares vector.length with fieldType.vectorDimension(), and a FieldType without vector attributes has dimension 0, so 0 == 0 passes. If the document is indexed, v is registered as a field with no vectors (not indexed, no doc values, not stored), and later real vectors for v in that index are refused by the per-field schema check.

rows.title: Hunspell COMPLEXPREFIXES: after removing the second prefix the Stemmer keeps removing prefixes, so words with three prefixes are accepted and a zero-length prefix recurses until StackOverflowError (also in HunspellStemFilter, where it closes the IndexWriter)
rows.summary: You load a hunspell dictionary that sets COMPLEXPREFIXES (twofold prefix stripping, meant for morphologically complex right-to-left languages) and chains prefixes through continuation classes, and expect at most two prefixes per word, as hunspell(5), C Hunspell and Lucene up to 9.4.2 do. Instead, after removing the second prefix the Stemmer goes on removing prefixes: with prefixes a, b, c chained on root x, the three-prefix word cbax is accepted by spell() and stemmed to x, and with a zero-length prefix that only passes on a flag (PFX A 0 0/B), the same prefix is removed again and again without shortening the word, so spell("bbx"), getRoots("bx") and HunspellStemFilter throw StackOverflowError. Inside IndexWriter.addDocument that Error closes the writer, and every later addDocument throws AlreadyClosedException.
rows.area: analysis / hunspell (Stemmer affix removal)

rows.title: Geo3DPoint.newPolygonQuery turns a degenerate polygon (for example three vertices on the equator) into an empty GeoCompositePolygon that is meant to match nothing, but every search with the query throws NullPointerException; Geo3DPoint.newShapeQuery with an empty GeoCompositePolygon fails the same way
rows.summary: You build Geo3DPoint.newPolygonQuery from an org.apache.lucene.geo.Polygon that Polygon accepts but whose vertices all lie on one great circle, for example lat {0,0,0,0} and lon {0,1,2,0}, and expect a query that matches nothing: Geo3DUtil.fromPolygon recognizes the polygon as degenerate ('// Polygon is degenerate') and deliberately replaces it with an empty GeoCompositePolygon. Instead every search with the query throws NullPointerException ('Cannot invoke Double.doubleValue() because the return value of XYZBounds.getMinimumX() is null'), because the empty shape adds nothing to its XYZBounds and the PointInShapeIntersectVisitor constructor unboxes the null bounds. Geo3DPoint.newShapeQuery with an empty GeoCompositePolygon fails the same way, while LatLonPoint.newPolygonQuery returns 0 hits for the same Polygon and newLargePolygonQuery rejects it with IllegalArgumentException when the query is built.

rows.title: With maxConn = 1, a merge that reuses an HNSW graph with a deleted vector never finishes: InitializedHnswGraphBuilder.rebalanceGraph adds one full graph level per pass until OutOfMemoryError
rows.summary: You index vectors with an HNSW format configured with maxConn = 1, a value the format accepts (1 to 512), delete or update one document and call forceMerge(1) (or let a natural merge run), and you expect the merge to finish, as it does in about a second with maxConn = 2 or 16. Instead the merge reuses the old graph, repairs it and calls rebalanceGraph, whose level loop stops only when size * (1/M)^level drops to 0: for M = 1 that target stays at the full size on every level and every node is promoted, so each pass adds one more complete graph level, without end. forceMerge never returns and the heap grows until OutOfMemoryError, which closes the IndexWriter (10.5.x has no abort check in the loop; main and 10.6.0 poll it, so rollback() can stop it).

rows.title: With beamWidth = 1, which the HNSW formats accept, every HnswGraphBuilder sizes its level-0 merge queue min(beamWidth / 2, M * 3) = 0 and throws, so building any HNSW graph fails and a merge closes the IndexWriter (since 10.2.0)
rows.summary: You configure a vector field with an HNSW format and beamWidth = 1, the smallest value the format and the graph builder accept ('beamWidth must be positive'), index vectors and merge, and you expect it to work as it did up to 10.1.0, only with a poorer graph. Instead every HnswGraphBuilder constructor sizes its level-0 merge candidate queue as Math.min(beamWidth / 2, M * 3), which integer division makes 0, and the heap rejects capacity 0 ('initialCapacity must be > 0 ... got: 0'), so no HNSW graph can be built at all. Small segments still flush without a graph, then the first merge that needs one throws and closes the IndexWriter, and the vector document that would push a segment past the graph threshold is rejected.

rows.summary: You build a codec with, for example, new Lucene99HnswVectorsFormat(16, 100, 0, executor), that is zero merge workers plus a merge executor. The constructor already rejects maxConn or beamWidth <= 0 and one worker with an executor, so you expect it to reject 0 as well (or to merge serially, as it does without an executor). Instead it accepts the value, indexing works, and the first merge that builds an HNSW graph throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException (NegativeArraySizeException for -1) inside HnswConcurrentMergeBuilder, whose worker array is sized by that count, and the IndexWriter closes itself with that exception.

rows.title: UniformSplit postings formats fail to flush or merge a field when deltaNumLines > targetNumBlockLines/3, a setting validateSettings accepts
rows.summary: You build a UniformSplit (or SharedTermsUniformSplit) postings format with targetNumBlockLines=4 and deltaNumLines=2, which the constructor accepts because its documented rule is only 0 <= delta < target, and commit a field with 3 terms. You expect the commit to succeed and the blocks to hold target +- delta lines. Instead the flush throws (AssertionError 'blockLines size: 3' with assertions on, IndexOutOfBoundsException 'Index -1 out of bounds for length 3' with them off) and the IndexWriter closes, because the code that splits a field's last block assumes its look-back window of 2*delta lines starts at line 1 or later, which is false whenever 3*delta > target and the last block has between target-delta+1 and 2*delta lines.

rows.title: DirectIODirectory accepts a mergeBufferSize that is not a multiple of the file system block size, and then every direct-I/O read fails, so merges hit a tragic exception; a size below the block size can also give a zero-capacity write buffer (BufferOverflowException, or writeBytes making no progress)
rows.summary: You create DirectIODirectory(FSDirectory, mergeBufferSize, minBytesDirect) with a mergeBufferSize that is not a multiple of the file system block size (for example 100000, or 4 * 4096 + 100, on a 4 KiB-block file system) and expect merges to read and write through direct I/O as usual, because the constructor documents the value only as 'Size of buffer to use for merging' and accepts any int. Instead every fresh top-level DirectIOIndexInput fails on its first read with IllegalArgumentException 'Negative position' or IOException 'Channel position ... is not a multiple of the block size', so a merge that reads through direct I/O fails while opening its segment readers and IndexWriter closes on a tragic exception (the index on disk stays intact, but the error sometimes surfaces as CorruptIndexException); with a size below the block size, some fresh outputs throw BufferOverflowException on the first writeByte and writeBytes on such an output loops without progress. The cause is that the direct buffers are aligned slices whose capacity is always a block multiple (and can be 0), while DirectIOIndexInput starts its file position at -mergeBufferSize and then advances it by the buffer's capacity, so the first read lands at -(mergeBufferSize mod blockSize) or at blockSize - (mergeBufferSize mod blockSize).
rows.area: misc / store DirectIODirectory (direct-I/O merge buffers)

rows.title: ByteWritesTrackingDirectoryWrapper(dir, true) gives every temp output it tracks the name 'ByteTrackingIndexOutput{<file>}' from IndexOutput#getName() instead of the file name, so the default stored-fields writer cannot reopen or delete its temp files and every merge (and the first flush of an index-sorted writer) fails with NoSuchFileException (since 9.5.0)
rows.summary: You wrap a directory in ByteWritesTrackingDirectoryWrapper(dir, true) to count flushed and merged bytes including temporary files, commit two one-document segments with the default codec and call forceMerge(1); you expect one merged segment with two documents, as with trackTempOutput=false, because Directory#createTempOutput says the temp file name is 'accessible via IndexOutput#getName()'. Instead the wrapper's temp outputs report getName() = 'ByteTrackingIndexOutput{_2_Lucene90FieldsIndex-doc_ids_4.tmp}' (ByteTrackingIndexOutput.java:33), and the stored-fields index writer, which reopens and deletes its temp files by getName(), fails the merge with NoSuchFileException at FieldsIndexWriter.finish. Every merge fails this way, and with an index sort the first flush fails too and closes the writer.

rows.title: Lucene90CompressingTermVectorsFormat documents and validates its last argument, blockSize, as a chunk count (>= 1), but the writer uses it as a DirectMonotonic block shift limited to [2, 22], so values such as 1024 or 1 are accepted and the first flush with term vectors throws and closes the IndexWriter (since 8.5.0)
rows.summary: You build a custom codec whose term vectors format is new Lucene90CompressingTermVectorsFormat(..., blockSize) and, as its javadoc says ('the number of chunks to store in an index block'), pass a chunk count such as 1024; the constructor accepts it, since it rejects only values below 1. You expect a format that writes and reads term vectors, or an IllegalArgumentException from the constructor, as the stored-fields twin Lucene90CompressingStoredFieldsFormat gives for the same argument. Instead the value goes unchanged to the writer, which uses it as a DirectMonotonicWriter block shift, so addDocument succeeds and the first flush with term vectors (here DirectoryReader.open(writer) or commit) throws 'blockShift must be in [2-22], got 1024' and closes the IndexWriter; blockSize 1, the constructor's own minimum, fails the same way.

rows.title: A kNN query whose filter iterates a BitSetIterator over a bit set shorter than the segment's maxDoc throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException (AssertionError with -ea) instead of returning the filtered hits, because AcceptDocs reuses that set as the accept bits without checking its length (since 9.3.0)
rows.summary: You run a KnnFloatVectorQuery with a custom filter whose scorer iterates a BitSetIterator over a FixedBitSet sized to its own matches (10 bits for docs 0..9) on a 100-document segment with no deletions, where every document has a vector. You expect the top k vectors among the filter's matches (here doc 9, with k = 1), as with the same filter backed by a maxDoc-sized set. Instead AcceptDocs.createBitSet hands the filter's 10-bit set unchanged to the HNSW reader as the accept bits (its other branches build maxDoc bits, and its fromLiveDocs entry point rejects bits whose length is not maxDoc), the reader tests it for every vector ordinal, and the search throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException (AssertionError 'index=10, numBits=10' with -ea) from FixedBitSet.get.

rows.title: SeededKnnVectorQuery built with its public seed-Weight constructor makes IndexSearcher.search throw IllegalArgumentException (or EOFException on a DENSE block) when a seed hit has no vector, because MappedDISI advances the vector iterator to a doc at or before its current one and the entry-point count includes seeds without a vector (since 10.3.0)
rows.summary: You index 2,000 documents with a float vector on the even ones only, build a seed Weight with IndexSearcher.createWeight for a term query that matches doc 1997 (no vector) and doc 1998 (the last vector doc), and search new SeededKnnVectorQuery(new KnnFloatVectorQuery("v", q, 2), seed, seedWeight) for 2 hits. You expect 2 hits, which SeededKnnVectorQuery.fromFloatQuery returns for the same seed, and the class javadoc only says the format may ignore a seed. Instead search throws IllegalArgumentException 'The number of entry points provided is less than the number of entry points requested': the caller's Weight skips the FieldExistsQuery filter that the internal path adds, MappedDISI maps doc 1997 to vector doc 1998 and then calls advance(1998) on an iterator already at 1998 (undefined for a DocIdSetIterator), which runs it off the end, while the entry-point count still counts both seeds.

rows.title: PatienceKnnVectorQuery over a SeededKnnVectorQuery stores a searcher-specific seed Weight in its own field during rewrite, so every search changes the query's equals/hashCode, and searching one query object concurrently on two different readers fails
rows.summary: You build PatienceKnnVectorQuery.fromSeededQuery(SeededKnnVectorQuery.fromFloatQuery(knnQuery, seedQuery)) and search it with IndexSearcher. You expect the query object to be unchanged by the search (Weight javadoc: 'searching does not modify a Query, so that a Query instance can be reused'), so it can be compared, cached and reused, including by several threads on different readers. Instead rewrite stores a new SeededKnnVectorQuery holding a seed Weight built for the current searcher in the query's own delegate field: after one search the query's hashCode has changed and it no longer equals an identical unsearched query, and when two searches of the same object on different readers overlap, the first one runs the other searcher's seed Weight on its later segments and fails with 'AssertionError: The top-reader used to create Weight is not the same as the current reader's top-reader' (-ea) or 'ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException: Index 1 out of bounds for length 1' at TermStates.get (-da).
