rows.title: FunctionQuery, FunctionRangeQuery and ValueSource sort fields share one non-thread-safe context map across the slices of an executor search, and scale() (ScaleFloatFunction) writes to it during the search, so when that write grows the map the search throws NullPointerException or silently returns different scores
rows.summary: You search with a FunctionQuery (or FunctionRangeQuery, or a sort by ValueSource.getSortField) whose function uses scale() together with about twenty context-storing sources such as query(), on an IndexSearcher built with an executor, and expect the same hits and scores as on a searcher without one, because IndexSearcher is documented as completely thread safe. Instead all slices share the Weight's one IdentityHashMap context (documented 'non-threadsafe'), ScaleFloatFunction.getValues puts its min/max entry into it from the slice threads, and when that put resizes the map other slices miss entries such as "searcher". The search then throws NullPointerException, or, on a searcher with a non-default Similarity, QueryValueSource silently rebuilds its weight with the default Similarity and the scores and top hits change.

rows.title: IndexSearcher.explain throws NullPointerException (AssertionError with -ea) for a span query inside a BooleanQuery that Lucene weights without scores (a FILTER or MUST_NOT clause, or the query of a FunctionScoreQuery whose source does not need scores), because BooleanWeight.explain calls score() on scorers built with COMPLETE_NO_SCORES
rows.summary: You search with a BooleanQuery such as '+body:quick -(spanNear([body:brown, body:fox], 0, true) body:dog)', which ComplexPhraseQueryParser builds from 'quick AND NOT ("brown fox" OR dog)', and call IndexSearcher.explain to see why a document matched or not; you expect an Explanation. Instead explain throws NullPointerException (AssertionError with -ea): Lucene builds the weight of a FILTER or MUST_NOT clause, or of the query inside a FunctionScoreQuery whose source does not read scores, without scores, but BooleanWeight.explain still asks that weight's scorers for score(), and a span scorer built without scores has no similarity scorer. Search results are correct and only explain fails, but Monitor's ExplainingMatch reports such a query as an error and loses its match.

rows.title: ParentsChildrenBlockJoinQuery throws IllegalStateException ('does not support intraSegment concurrency') when a scorer is requested twice for the same leaf, so IndexSearcher.explain of a BooleanQuery that contains it fails, even on a plain single-threaded searcher
rows.summary: You search with a BooleanQuery that combines a ParentsChildrenBlockJoinQuery with another clause and call IndexSearcher.explain on a hit, and you expect an explanation, because the Weight#scorer and Weight#scorerSupplier javadoc say a scorer (supplier) for the same LeafReaderContext may be requested multiple times as part of a single search call. Instead explain throws IllegalStateException 'ParentsChildrenBlockJoinQuery does not support intraSegment concurrency. Context ... was already seen.': the join query's Weight records every leaf it has built a scorer supplier for and refuses a second request, and BooleanWeight#explain makes exactly that second request (the join clause's own explain pulls a scorer, then BooleanWeight pulls its scorer for the same leaf to compute the score). The search itself returns the right hits; explain fails for every document that the BooleanQuery matches, including documents matched only by the other clause.
rows.area: join / block join (ParentsChildrenBlockJoinQuery: ParentsChildrenBlockJoinWeight#scorerSupplier intra-segment guard)

rows.title: Vector-similarity threshold queries (Float/Byte/Float16VectorSimilarityQuery at the default decay) explain every document whose exact similarity clears the threshold as a match, but return only what the approximate graph search collected, so explain calls documents the query does not return matches; inside a BooleanQuery or FunctionScoreQuery that explain then reports another document's score, fails an assertion or throws NullPointerException
rows.summary: You run a FloatVectorSimilarityQuery.Adaptive (or the Byte or Float16 variant) with the default decay and call IndexSearcher.explain for a document, and you expect explain to agree with the hits, as the kNN queries do: a document the query does not return is explained as a non-match. Instead explain applies the exact threshold test, so a document above the threshold that the approximate graph search did not collect is explained as '... = Score above threshold' although it is not a hit, and Weight.matches() of the same Weight returns null for it. Wrapped in a BooleanQuery, explain of such a non-hit returns a match with the next hit's score (-da), fails 'assert advanced == doc' (-ea) or throws NullPointerException when the segment has no vector hits, FunctionScoreQuery's explain throws the same NullPointerException, and the hits of a hybrid 'term OR vector' query can be explained with a vector contribution that is not in their score.
rows.area: core / search: vector-similarity queries (AbstractVectorSimilarityQuery Weight.explain vs scorerSupplier), with consequences in BooleanWeight.explain and FunctionScoreQuery.explain

rows.title: IndriAndWeight.explain does not check that its scorer landed on the requested document, so a document that matches no clause is explained as a match with another document's score, or explain throws (EOFException or IndexOutOfBoundsException from a norms read past the clause scorer's last match; AssertionError with -ea)
rows.summary: You search with an IndriAndQuery of SHOULD clauses, for example IndriAndQuery(SHOULD f:a), and call IndexSearcher.explain for a document that contains none of the clause terms and is not a hit. You expect a no-match explanation (isMatch false), as TermQuery and a BooleanQuery over the same clauses give. Instead IndriAndWeight.explain advances its scorer to the document, checks the result only with 'assert advanced == doc', and returns Explanation.match(scorer.score(), ...) for wherever the scorer landed: a match carrying the next hit's score, or, past the last match, an EOFException or IndexOutOfBoundsException from a norms read (AssertionError with -ea).
rows.area: search / IndriAndQuery (IndriAndWeight.explain)

rows.title: SpanPayloadCheckQuery.toString() and IndexSearcher.explain() throw NullPointerException when payloadToMatch contains a null entry, although the matcher accepts null as 'no payload at this position' and the query searches and counts correctly (since 5.4.0, LUCENE-6716)

You expect toString() to print the query and IndexSearcher.explain() to explain the hit. Both throw NullPointerException ('Cannot read field "bytes" because "termText" is null'), because toString() hands every entry, null included, to Term.toString(BytesRef), and explain builds its description from the query string.

rows.title: MultiPhraseQuery.Builder does not validate an empty Term[]: it throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException at the first position but accepts one at later positions, and toString() of the accepted query then throws, which also breaks explain and the 'indexed without position data' error
rows.summary: You build a phrase with MultiPhraseQuery.Builder and pass an empty Term[] for one position, for example the terms of a prefix expansion that found nothing (the class javadoc's 'microsoft app*' recipe); add(Term[]) documents the array as a disjunction, so you expect an empty position to match nothing, or the Builder to reject it with IllegalArgumentException. At the first position Builder.add throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException (it reads terms[0].field(), MultiPhraseQuery.java:127), while at any later position the array is accepted and search correctly returns 0 hits, but toString() throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException (terms[0].text(), :345). So logging the query fails, IndexSearcher.explain throws for a BooleanQuery or IndriAndQuery that holds it (BooleanWeight.java:99 and :103, IndriAndWeight.java:88), and on a field indexed without positions the documented IllegalStateException becomes that exception, because its message prints the query (:255-262).

rows.title: ConjunctionUtils.createConjunction sorts the caller's list of TwoPhaseIterators in place, so an immutable list such as List.of(a, b) whose match costs are not in ascending order throws UnsupportedOperationException, and a LinkedList throws IllegalArgumentException (since 9.0.0)
rows.summary: You combine two TwoPhaseIterators with the public ConjunctionUtils.createConjunction(List.of(a.approximation(), b.approximation()), List.of(a, b)), where a has matchCost 100 and b has matchCost 1. You expect a conjunction iterator over their common documents, which is what you get when the same list happens to be in ascending cost order: the javadoc describes both arguments only as lists 'to combine', and the method copies its first list before sorting it. Instead it throws UnsupportedOperationException, because the private ConjunctionTwoPhaseIterator constructor sorts the caller's second list in place by matchCost (CollectionUtil.timSort) before copying it; a LinkedList makes the same call throw IllegalArgumentException 'CollectionUtil can only sort random access lists in-place.' in any order, and a mutable ArrayList comes back reordered.

rows.title: CachingCollector#replay (and CachingCollectorManager#replay) lets a CollectionTerminatedException from the second-pass collector escape to the caller instead of ending only that leaf as IndexSearcher does, so replaying into an early-terminating collector, such as a TopFieldCollector sorted by the index sort, throws
rows.summary: You run a query once through a CachingCollector (or CachingCollectorManager) and then replay the cached hits into a second-pass collector, expecting the same result as running that collector through IndexSearcher. When the second-pass collector stops a segment early by throwing CollectionTerminatedException, which is how LeafCollector#collect documents early termination and what a stock TopFieldCollector sorted by the index sort does once a segment has more than 1000 hits, IndexSearcher simply moves on to the next segment, but replay lets the exception escape to the caller, without a stack trace. Catching it around replay is no workaround: the later segments are never replayed, so in the repro the top 10 come back as [1000..1009] instead of [0..9].
rows.area: search / CachingCollector replay (CachingCollector, CachingCollectorManager)

rows.title: GroupingSearch.setCaching(n, false) and setCachingInMB(mb, false) throw NullPointerException with the default within-group sort or the default includeMaxScore, because the score-less cache is replayed into a second pass that needs scores
rows.summary: You turn on GroupingSearch's documented second-pass cache without cached scores, new GroupingSearch("g").setCaching(10, false), and run an ordinary grouped search over two documents in groups A and B; you expect the same groups as without the cache, because the javadoc presents the cache as an optimisation that the second pass replays. Instead search() throws NullPointerException ('Cannot invoke Scorable.score() because this.scorer is null'): GroupingSearch builds the cache with the caller's cacheScores flag but replays it into a second pass that it builds itself from its defaults (within-group sort Sort.RELEVANCE, includeMaxScore=true), and both need scores, while a score-less replay never sets a Scorer. Whether a search fails depends on the hit count: when the hits overflow the cache, the cache is dropped, the query is re-run and the search succeeds.
rows.area: grouping / GroupingSearch second-pass cache (score-less CachingCollector / CachingCollectorManager replay into the TopGroups second pass)

rows.title: A rejected document leaves its doc-values skip index type in the field's per-document schema state, so later valid documents with that field are rejected until the in-memory segment is flushed
rows.summary: You index a document in which field f carries a skip-indexed doc-values field (for example SortedDocValuesField.indexedField, new in 10.0), IndexWriter correctly rejects it with IllegalArgumentException because f is already indexed without doc values (or because another field of that document is invalid), and you keep adding documents that have f without doc values. You expect only the bad document to be rejected, as for any non-aborting exception, and the next valid documents to be accepted, as they are when the rejected document used doc values without a skip index. Instead every later document with f and no doc values in the same in-memory segment is rejected ("doc values skip index type: expected 'NONE', but it has 'RANGE'", or "field 'f' cannot have docValuesSkipIndexType=RANGE with doc values type NONE") until the next flush, because IndexingChain.FieldSchema.reset() clears the per-document doc-values type but not the skip index type, so the rejected document's RANGE is left behind.
rows.area: index / IndexingChain per-field schema validation (FieldSchema)

rows.title: IndexWriter#addBatch marks the frozen FieldType of an earlier rejected document as validated, so later documents with that type skip the per-field schema check (a wrong-dimension vector is stored truncated)
rows.summary: You add a document whose 8-dimensional KnnFloatVectorField (built from one shared frozen FieldType) does not match the field's 4 dimensions, and Lucene correctly rejects it; you then index an IndexWriter#addBatch with a 4-dimensional vector column for the same field and add the same kind of 8-dimensional document again. You expect the same IllegalArgumentException, because Lucene requires a field to keep the same data structures in every document and checks each document against them. Instead the batch marks the rejected document's FieldType as already validated, so until the next flush every document with that FieldType instance skips the check: the 8-dimensional vector is accepted and stored as its first 4 values (CheckIndex clean), and a SORTED value for a NUMERIC doc-values field fails with ClassCastException instead of the schema error.
rows.area: index / IndexingChain per-field schema validation (frozen-FieldType cache) x columnar addBatch

rows.title: LatLonPoint.newDistanceFeatureQuery can skip a competitive document under top-k pruning: computeMaxDistance returns the lower end of its 1 m binary search, and the pruning box built from that radius adds only a 7 cm pad
rows.summary: You index points with LatLonPoint plus LatLonDocValuesField and run searcher.search(LatLonPoint.newDistanceFeatureQuery("loc", 1, 0, 0, 1000), 1), expecting the closest document, because Scorable#setMinCompetitiveScore lets a scorer skip only documents that score below the threshold and Lucene's own TestLatLonPointDistanceFeatureQuery asserts that pruned (TOP_SCORES) and unpruned (COMPLETE) top-k agree for this query. Instead, once a document 999.999 m due north (score 0.50000024) fills the queue, a document 999.803 m due north (score 0.5000492) is never visited and the farther one is returned. The scorer turns the threshold into a radius with a binary search that stops when the interval is 1 m wide and keeps the lower end (999.729 m, although every distance up to 999.999 m still competes), and the box it then searches adds only 7 cm to that radius, so competitive documents just beyond the box edge are dropped.
rows.area: core / document: LatLonPoint distance feature query (dynamic pruning through setMinCompetitiveScore)

rows.title: IndriDisjunctionScorer.getMaxScore always returns 0 although IndriAndScorer scores the weighted mean of its IndriScorer clauses, so when a clause scores above 0, top-k search prunes the IndriAndQuery and returns the wrong top hit
rows.summary: You put an IndriAndQuery whose two clauses are your own IndriScorer-based queries (each scores 100 on the last of 10,000 documents and 0 elsewhere, and reports a max score of 100) into a BooleanQuery as a SHOULD clause next to MatchAllDocsQuery, and ask IndexSearcher.search(q, 1) for the best hit; you expect the last document, which an exhaustive search ranks first with score 101.0, because Scorer.getMaxScore must bound every score. Instead top-k search returns doc 0 (score 1.0), with no error, under -ea and -da. IndriDisjunctionScorer.getMaxScore, which IndriAndScorer inherits, always returns 0 while IndriAndScorer scores the boost-weighted mean of its IndriScorer clauses (100 here), so once the minimum competitive score is above the summed max-score bounds of the two BooleanQuery clauses (0 + 1.0), MaxScoreBulkScorer skips the rest of the segment unscored, the last document included. An earlier 20,000-document repro (one clause scoring 100 on the last document, the other 0, next to the term query f:t) fails the same way: doc 0 (score 1.1e-5) instead of the last document (score 50.00001).
rows.area: search / IndriAndQuery (IndriDisjunctionScorer.getMaxScore, the max-score bound that top-k pruning reads)

rows.title: FunctionScoreQuery scores negative values as 0, but its block-max bound stays negative, so top-k search skips competitive documents
rows.summary: You index a numeric doc-values field with a skip index (NumericDocValuesField.indexedField("delta", v)) and search BooleanQuery(SHOULD FunctionScoreQuery(MatchAllDocsQuery, DoubleValuesSource.fromLongField("delta")), SHOULD TermQuery(body:b)) for the top hit, expecting the same hit as an exhaustive search, because FunctionScoreQuery documents that a negative value simply scores 0 (MIGRATE.md, LUCENE-7996). Instead, with 5,000 documents where doc 0 has delta 1, all others have -1000, and only doc 4999 matches body:b, TOP_SCORES and the plain IndexSearcher.search(q, 1) return doc 0 (score 1.0) instead of doc 4999. The cause is that the scorer's getMaxScore returns innerMaxScore * valueMaxScore * boost without the clamp at 0 that score() applies, so a block of negative values reports a bound of -1000 for documents that all score 0, and MaxScoreBulkScorer skips windows that hold competitive documents.

rows.title: DoubleValuesSource.fromDoubleField/fromFloatField declare their raw IEEE-bit decoders INCREASING, so on a skip-indexed raw-bits field one NaN makes a block's score bound NaN (FunctionScoreQuery under TOP_SCORES then silently drops the true top hit) and all-negative blocks get inverted bounds
rows.summary: You index doubles as raw IEEE bits in a NUMERIC doc-values field with a skip index (NumericDocValuesField.indexedField('rating', Double.doubleToRawLongBits(v))) and search BooleanQuery(SHOULD FunctionScoreQuery(MatchAllDocsQuery, DoubleValuesSource.fromDoubleField('rating')), SHOULD TermQuery) for the top hit, expecting the same top hit as an exhaustive search (a NaN value simply scores 0, as upstream TestFunctionScoreQuery#testNaN expects). Instead, with 5,000 docs valued 0.5, one NaN at doc 4500 and 50.0 at doc 4999, TOP_SCORES returns doc 1 (score 4.19) instead of doc 4999 (score 50). The cause is that fromDoubleField declares Double::longBitsToDouble INCREASING, so a block's maximum is read as the decoded largest raw long: NaN's raw bits are above every number's, giving a NaN bound, and negative values are in reverse raw order, so a block holding {-1.0, -2.0} reports getMaxScore -2.0 and getMinScore -1.0.

rows.title: DoubleValues.withDefault's getMaxScore returns the wrapped source's bound, which does not cover missingValue, so a FunctionScoreQuery over such a source can silently drop the true top hit under TOP_SCORES
rows.summary: You write a DoubleValuesSource that returns DoubleValues.withDefault(DoubleValuesSource.fromLongField("price").getValues(ctx, scores), 100) over a price field indexed with a skip index (NumericDocValuesField.indexedField), and search BooleanQuery(SHOULD FunctionScoreQuery(MatchAllDocsQuery, thatSource), SHOULD TermQuery(tag:t)) for the top hit, expecting the document without a price (which scores the default 100) to win, as it does in an exhaustive search. Instead, with 12,288 documents (prices i % 10, doc 0 = 50, doc 9000 without a price), the plain IndexSearcher.search(q, 1) returns doc 0 (score 50.0018) instead of doc 9000 (score 100). The cause is that withDefault.getMaxScore returns the wrapped source's bound, the skip-index block maximum, which counts only documents that have a value (9 in doc 9000's block), although withDefault itself produces missingValue (100) for documents without one, so pruning skips the block that holds the true top hit.

rows.title: DoubleValuesSource rounds the skip-index block bound to the nearest float, so with a boost FunctionScoreQuery's max score can be one ulp below a real score and top-k search returns the wrong top hit
rows.summary: You index a long counter with the doc-values skip index (NumericDocValuesField.indexedField('count', v)) and search BooleanQuery(SHOULD BoostQuery(FunctionScoreQuery(MatchAllDocsQuery, DoubleValuesSource.fromLongField('count')), 1.5f), SHOULD TermQuery(body:b)), expecting the same top hit as an exhaustive search. Instead, with 5,000 docs where doc 0 holds 2^24 and doc 4999 holds 2^24 + 1, the pruned search (TOP_SCORES, which plain IndexSearcher.search(q, 1) also uses) returns doc 0 (score 25165824) instead of doc 4999 (score 25165826). The cause is that the block bound is the decoded block maximum cast to the nearest float (2^24 + 1 becomes 2^24) and FunctionScoreQuery multiplies that rounded float by the boost, so the block's bound (25165824) is one float step below the score it must cover and the block is skipped; ordinary doubles do the same (0.065 with boost 1.1 scores 0.0715 under a bound of 0.071499996).

rows.title: On main, a 9.x/10.x int7/int4 scalar-quantized segment whose vectors are all identical (stored quantiles equal) is decoded with the min == max widening that #14049 added, not the quantizer that wrote it, so its vectors read 127 (int7) or 15 (int4) units lower in every dimension and exact matches score about 0 and rank last (unreleased, 11.0 only)
rows.summary: You index a field with the Lucene99 HNSW scalar-quantized format (int7, EUCLIDEAN) on 10.3.2 or 9.12.3, one segment holds only documents whose vector is [1,1,1,1], so the writer stores the quantiles (1, 1) and every code 0; you then open the unchanged index on main and search for [1,1,1,1]. Every release reader tested (9.9.2 to 10.6.0) decodes code 0 as 1.0, as the ScalarQuantizer formula for the stored quantiles says, and ranks those exact matches first with score 1.0. On main the reader rebuilds the quantizer through the min == max widening added by #14049, decodes those vectors as [-126,-126,-126,-126], and the exact matches score 1.5e-5 and rank last behind a document with half the similarity; int4 fields decode 15 units low, and DOT_PRODUCT and COSINE exact matches score 0.0.

rows.title: LMDirichletSimilarity accepts mu = 0, but then every document scores 0: log(1 + tf/(mu*P)) + log(mu/(dl+mu)) becomes +Infinity + -Infinity = NaN, and the 'score > 0' clamp turns NaN into 0
rows.summary: You configure LMDirichletSimilarity with mu = 0, which both constructors accept ('must be a non-negative finite value') and which upstream's TestLMDirichletSimilarity uses as its 'minimum value'. You expect documents that contain the query term more often than the collection model predicts to get a positive score and be ranked, as they are for every mu > 0 down to Float.MIN_VALUE, where the score already equals its finite mu -> 0 limit log(tf/(dl*P)). Instead score() computes log(1 + tf/0) + log(0/dl) = +Infinity + -Infinity = NaN, the 'score > 0 ? score : 0' clamp returns 0.0, and every hit scores 0.0, so the best match can come back last; explain() shows 'Infinity = term weight' and '-Infinity = document norm' under a 0.0 total.
rows.area: search / similarities (LMDirichletSimilarity)

rows.title: SweetSpotSimilarity.hyperbolicTf returns max instead of about min for frequencies far below xoffset, because its NaN fallback is right only for the Math.pow overflow above the midpoint, so a hyperbolic-tf subclass is not monotone in freq and ranks a document with one occurrence above one with hundreds
rows.summary: You subclass SweetSpotSimilarity so that tf() returns hyperbolicTf(freq), as its javadoc suggests, call setHyperbolicTfFactors(0, 2, 10, 400) and search, expecting the documented curve min+(max-min)/2*(tanh((freq-xoffset)*ln(base))+1): a tf near min (0) for frequencies far below the midpoint 400, rising to max (2) above it. Instead hyperbolicTf returns the maximum 2.0 for every frequency from 1 to 91 and drops to 0.0 at 92, so a document that contains the term once outranks an equally long one that contains it 400 times. Far below the midpoint Math.pow(base, xoffset - freq) overflows to Infinity (once xoffset - freq exceeds about 308 at base 10, about 2705 at the default base 1.3), the ratio becomes NaN, and the guard 'return Float.isNaN(result) ? max : result', which is right only for the overflow above the midpoint, returns max.
rows.area: misc / similarities (SweetSpotSimilarity hyperbolicTf helper)

rows.title: FeatureField.newSigmoidQuery (and the IntervalQuery sigmoid) return NaN scores when pivot^exp overflows or underflows a double, for pivot and exp values the factories accept
rows.summary: You rank documents with FeatureField.newSigmoidQuery (or IntervalQuery's pivot-and-exponent constructor) and pick a steep exponent with a large or tiny pivot, values the factory accepts because it only requires both to be positive and finite. You expect the documented score weight * S^exp / (S^exp + pivot^exp), a number between 0 and weight that equals weight/2 at S = pivot. Instead SigmoidFunction precomputes pivot^exp as a double, which becomes +Infinity or 0 for such parameters, so scores come out as Inf/Inf or 0/0 = NaN: with pivot 2^20 and exponent 60 every document scores NaN; since 10.2.0 NaN hits rank ahead of correctly scored ones, so the best document can come last, and on 9.x (assertions off) TopDocs even returns placeholder hits with doc id 2147483647.
rows.area: document / FeatureField sigmoid scoring (FeatureField.SigmoidFunction behind newSigmoidQuery; the same arithmetic is copied in queries / intervals IntervalScoreFunction.SigmoidFunction behind the 4-argument IntervalQuery constructor)

rows.title: FeatureField saturation and sigmoid queries and IntervalQuery scoring compute w*(1 - k/(S+k)) instead of the documented w*S/(S+k) (and the same rewrite for the sigmoid), so documents whose value is far below the pivot score exactly 0.0 or tie with documents that have different values
rows.summary: You rank with FeatureField.newSaturationQuery, whose javadoc says it 'will score documents as weight * S / (S + pivot)' (newSigmoidQuery and IntervalQuery's scoring state the same kind of formula), a value that is positive and grows with S, so a document with a smaller feature value should score lower but above 0. The code instead computes weight * (1 - pivot / (S + pivot)) (and 1 - k^a / (S^a + k^a) for the sigmoid) so that rounding cannot make scores decrease, and when S is far below the pivot the sum S + pivot rounds to almost exactly the pivot and the subtraction cancels. With pivot 1000 a document with S = 1e-5 scores exactly 0.0 while explain() prints 'computed as w * S / (S + k)', with the library's default pivot 199 adjacent pairs of distinct stored values tie, and IntervalQuery gives intervals 1,000,000 and 1,030,000 positions wide the same score and a 2^25-wide interval 0.0.
rows.area: document / FeatureField score functions (SaturationFunction and SigmoidFunction behind newSaturationQuery and newSigmoidQuery); queries / intervals IntervalScoreFunction (IntervalQuery's default saturation scoring and its pivot and pivot-plus-exponent constructors)

rows.title: IndriDirichletSimilarity accepts a negative, NaN or infinite mu without the IllegalArgumentException that LMDirichletSimilarity and NormalizationH3 throw for the same Dirichlet mu, so the bad setting shows up only as +Infinity or NaN scores and explanations (every release since 8.9.0)
rows.summary: You build new IndriDirichletSimilarity(-1f), or pass a NaN or infinite mu to any of its three mu constructors, and expect an IllegalArgumentException, as new LMDirichletSimilarity(-1f) and new NormalizationH3(-1f) throw ('illegal mu value: -1.0, must be a non-negative finite value') for the same Dirichlet smoothing parameter. Instead the constructor only stores the value, so the mistake surfaces later and silently: score() = log((freq + mu*P) / (docLen + mu)) becomes +Infinity at mu = -1 for a one-term document such as 'a' next to 'a b', and NaN for every document at a NaN or infinite mu, and explain() reports the same values.

rows.title: PerFieldSimilarityWrapper does not forward Similarity#computeQueryTermWeight, so a BM25Similarity or StableTflSimilarity k3 (query-term saturation) setting silently has no effect behind a per-field wrapper
rows.summary: You configure BM25Similarity with its opt-in k3 parameter (new BM25Similarity(1.2f, 0.75f, true, 7f)), whose javadoc promises that a term repeated in a query is weighted ((k3 + 1) * qtf) / (k3 + qtf) instead of linearly, and you install it through a PerFieldSimilarityWrapper, the documented way to use per-field similarities, even one whose get() returns that same instance for every field. You expect the query 'apple apple' to score as it does with the bare BM25Similarity, where BooleanQuery's duplicate-clause rewrite gives (body:apple)^1.7777778. Instead the rewrite asks the wrapper, which does not forward Similarity#computeQueryTermWeight and inherits its linear default, so the query becomes (body:apple)^2.0 and the document scores 0.63013375 instead of 0.5601189; StableTflSimilarity's k3 is ignored the same way.
rows.area: search / similarities (PerFieldSimilarityWrapper, Similarity#computeQueryTermWeight) and BooleanQuery duplicate-clause rewrite

rows.title: DOCS_AND_CUSTOM_FREQS fields (10.5.0+): the norm length counts terms but sumTotalTermFreq and totalTermFreq sum the custom frequencies, contradicting the FieldInfo#isTermDocField, IndexOptions and FieldStats javadocs and putting BM25's dl and avgdl in different units
rows.summary: You index two documents, 'a|5 b|5' and 'a|5 b|5 c|5 d|5', into a field with IndexOptions.DOCS_AND_CUSTOM_FREQS (DelimitedTermFrequencyTokenFilter, a TextField type with norms). Lucene stores their lengths as term counts, 2 and 4. FieldInfo#isTermDocField says such frequencies count as 1 'for statistical and scoring purposes', and FieldStats says sumTotalTermFreq 'is also the sum of each document's field length'. So you expect sumTotalTermFreq to be 6 and BM25's average length to be 3. Instead, sumTotalTermFreq and totalTermFreq sum the custom values (30), and BM25 explains dl=2.0 against avgdl=15.0. Each document's length is compared with an average inflated by the mean custom value, which quietly weakens length normalisation.
rows.area: core index / DOCS_AND_CUSTOM_FREQS (termdoc) field length vs term statistics; search similarities (BM25, SimilarityBase)

rows.title: AutomatonQuery.ramBytesUsed() is computed once at construction, so a query that runs on an NFA (WildcardQuery and RegexpQuery by default on main, opt-in NFA queries since 10.0.0) under-reports the DFA states it builds while searching, and an LRUQueryCache can hold far more heap than its RAM budget
rows.summary: You run a WildcardQuery or RegexpQuery whose automaton is not deterministic, for example '*a?????????' or 'a*b??????????', and expect its ramBytesUsed() to estimate the heap the query holds, which is what the Accountable javadoc says and what LRUQueryCache uses to stay within maxRamBytesUsed. On main such a query runs on an NFARunAutomaton that builds DFA states lazily during the search and keeps them on the query object, but AutomatonQuery stored ramBytesUsed() in a final field when it was constructed, so after one search the value is 36x to 310x too small (5,674 bytes reported vs 205,216 retained over 1,024 terms; 6,714 vs 2,081,152 on a 20,000-document field). An LRUQueryCache with a 1 MiB budget then keeps 4 such queries as keys that retain 2.7 to 7.4 MB while it accounts about 36 KB in total and evicts nothing; the matching documents are correct.
rows.area: search / AutomatonQuery RAM accounting (NFARunAutomaton lazily built DFA states; LRUQueryCache RAM budget)

rows.title: Geo3DPoint polygon and path queries report a constant 592-byte ramBytesUsed() regardless of shape size, because PointInGeo3DShapeQuery prices its GeoShape as a 256-byte unknown object, so LRUQueryCache can hold many times its maxRamBytesUsed (since 8.2.0)
rows.summary: You filter with a Geo3DPoint polygon or path query, for example newLargePolygonQuery with 2,000 edges or newPathQuery with 200 points, and expect its ramBytesUsed() to estimate the heap it holds, which is what Accountable promises and what LRUQueryCache charges against its maxRamBytesUsed budget. Instead PointInGeo3DShapeQuery.ramBytesUsed() passes the shape and its bounds to RamUsageEstimator.sizeOfObject, which prices every object that is not Accountable (no GeoShape is) at a fixed 256 bytes, so every such query reports 592 bytes whatever its size: 4.9x too low for an 8-edge polygon, 47x for 99 edges, about 2,300x for the 2,000-edge large polygon (1,360,960 bytes retained). An LRUQueryCache with a 1 MiB budget therefore keeps 8 such filters that retain 10.9 MB, accounts about 6 KB for them and evicts nothing; the hits are correct.

rows.title: PointInSetIncludingScoreQuery.ramBytesUsed() leaves out its per-value score list, so scoring numeric JoinUtil joins (ScoreMode Max, Min, Avg, Total) under-report their heap (1.5x-2.4x on 9.11.0 and later, 6.2x or more in 8.2.0-9.10.0) and LRUQueryCache under-charges them (since 8.2.0)
rows.summary: You build a numeric query-time join with JoinUtil.createJoinQuery(fromField, multipleValuesPerDocument, toField, numberType, fromQuery, fromSearcher, ScoreMode.Max) (or Min, Avg, Total) and expect its ramBytesUsed() to estimate the heap the query holds, which is what Accountable promises, what LRUQueryCache charges against maxRamBytesUsed, and what the string-field scoring join (TermsIncludingScoreQuery) and the ScoreMode.None numeric join (PointInSetQuery) do. Instead the PointInSetIncludingScoreQuery it returns adds up only its base object, field, from-query and packed join values, and leaves out aggregatedJoinScores, the FloatArrayList with one float per join value that its constructor fills: with 100,000 join values it reports 304,248 bytes while it retains 710,632 (2.3x; 1.5x-2.4x depending on how compactly the keys prefix-code), against 303,272 vs 304,544 for ScoreMode.None. A query cache holding such a join as a filter charges it the same low number (304,408 bytes charged, 710,632 retained), so the cache can hold up to about 2.5 times its budget in these keys; the matching documents are correct.

rows.title: IndexSearcher's cumulative maxClauseCount check never counts a query held by a values source (FunctionScoreQuery.boostByQuery's boost query, DoubleValuesSource.fromQuery, QueryValueSource): the function queries' visit() stops at the source and each embedded query is checked alone with a fresh budget, so the total number of executed clauses is unbounded
rows.summary: You search FunctionScoreQuery.boostByQuery(in, boostMatch, 2f), where in and boostMatch are each a 600-term disjunction (1,200 term clauses that all run), with the default maxClauseCount of 1024. You expect TooManyNestedClauses, which you do get for a BooleanQuery holding the same clauses (even when half of them are scoring-only SHOULD or MUST_NOT clauses), because the check counts 'total clauses cumulatively in all of its children' and LUCENE-8811 made it cumulative so that splitting clauses over sub-queries no longer bypasses it. Instead the search runs with correct hits: FunctionScoreQuery.visit visits only `in`, FunctionMatchQuery, FunctionRangeQuery and FunctionQuery.visit call visitLeaf(this), DoubleValuesSource and ValueSource have no visit hook, and the embedded query is rewritten later with searcher.rewrite, which checks it alone with a fresh count; FunctionScoreQuery(fromQuery), FunctionMatchQuery(fromQuery) and FunctionQuery/FunctionRangeQuery over QueryValueSource behave the same.
rows.area: queries / function queries (FunctionScoreQuery, FunctionMatchQuery, FunctionRangeQuery and FunctionQuery QueryVisitor traversal of DoubleValuesSource/ValueSource; consumer: IndexSearcher's cumulative clause limit)

rows.title: GroupingSearch.setCaching / setCachingInMB limit is applied per slice since #16247 (10.6.0 regression): with an IndexSearcher that has an executor, a query matching more documents than the limit is replayed from per-slice caches holding up to slices x limit instead of being purged and re-run (results unchanged)
rows.summary: You enable caching for a grouped search with GroupingSearch.setCaching(600, true) (or setCachingInMB) and search through an IndexSearcher that has an executor, and expect what the unchanged javadoc says and what 10.5.2 and a sequential searcher do: the cache holds at most the limit, and when the query matches more it is purged and the second pass re-runs the query. Instead, since #16247 GroupingSearch hands the limit to the new CachingCollectorManager, which applies it to each slice separately, so with 1000 matching documents over 2 slices each slice cache stays under 600, the caches hold all 1000 documents, and the second pass is replayed (the query runs once instead of twice). Results are the same; what breaks is the documented memory bound and the replay decision, and the cache can reach (number of slices) x limit.
rows.area: grouping / GroupingSearch two-pass caching x search / CachingCollectorManager (new in 10.6.0) under a concurrent IndexSearcher

rows.title: MemoryAccountingBitsetCollector sizes each collector's bitset to the doc-id span of its slice, so under concurrent search a slice whose segments are not adjacent in doc-id order allocates, and charges to the memory tracker, bits for the segments that other slices search
rows.summary: You search with MemoryAccountingBitsetCollectorManager and a CollectorMemoryTracker on an IndexSearcher built with an executor, and expect each slice's collector to allocate a bitset only for the segments it searches, as the manager's javadoc says ('each collector only allocates a bitset for the slices it processes'). Instead each collector sizes its bitset to the doc-id range from the first to the last segment of its slice, and the default slicing groups segments by size, not by doc-id order, so in an index whose segments are 10, 300,000, 10, 300,000 and 10 documents the slice of the three small segments allocates a bitset over 600,030 doc ids for its 30 documents. The search tracks 243,960 bytes against 159,480 for the same search without an executor, and a tracker limit of 161,528 bytes that the sequential search fits throws IllegalStateException 'Memory limit exceeded' with the executor; the matched documents are correct.

rows.title: LongRange/DoubleRange#getQuery(fastMatchQuery, ...) range queries report themselves as a leaf in visit() and never visit their fast-match query, so IndexSearcher's maxClauseCount check never counts the fast-match query
rows.summary: You build LongRange#getQuery(fastMatch, LongValuesSource) (or the DoubleRange or multi-valued overloads) with a fast-match query of 1,200 term clauses (two required 600-term disjunctions) and search it with the default maxClauseCount of 1024. You expect TooManyNestedClauses, which you do get when the same fast-match query is a sibling FILTER clause, because the check counts 'total clauses cumulatively in all of its children', Query#visit is documented to visit 'any child queries', and getQuery documents fastMatchQuery as 'a query to use as a filter'. Instead the search runs and returns the correct hits: ValueSourceQuery.visit and MultiValueSourceQuery.visit only call visitor.visitLeaf(this), so the fast-match query, which stays in the rewritten query and is executed as the approximation in createWeight, is seen by no clause check at all, and QueryVisitor.termCollector returns none of its terms.

rows.title: CompositeVerifyQuery.visit reports the whole query as a leaf and never visits the index query it rewrites and executes, so QueryVisitor term collection misses the index query's terms and IndexSearcher's cumulative maxClauseCount check does not count its clauses
rows.summary: You wrap your own index query, for example TermQuery(body:a) or a 20-clause DisjunctionMaxQuery, in new CompositeVerifyQuery(indexQuery, shapePredicate), then collect its terms with QueryVisitor.termCollector or search it after IndexSearcher.setMaxClauseCount(8). You expect [body:a] and an IndexSearcher.TooManyNestedClauses error, because Query#visit is documented to 'recurse through the query tree, visiting any child queries', the wrapper rewrites its index query and runs it as the approximation that every hit must match, and the same 20 clauses as a bare query or as a sibling FILTER clause are rejected. Instead CompositeVerifyQuery.visit only calls visitor.visitLeaf(this): termCollector returns [] and the clause check counts the whole query as one clause, so the over-limit query runs (its hits are correct).

rows.title: IndexSearcher's nested clause check accepts maxClauseCount + 1 clauses because it compares before incrementing (known: #10339 / LUCENE-9299) (released since 9.0)
rows.summary: You rewrite a query with two MUST disjunctions of 512 and 513 term clauses (1,025 leaves) under the default maxClauseCount of 1,024 and expect TooManyNestedClauses, because the limit is 'the maximum number of clauses permitted'. rows.title: SynonymQuery.Builder.addTerm stores a term before it checks the clause limit, so the term it rejects with TooManyClauses stays in the builder and build() returns a query over the limit that matches it (since 8.1.0)

Instead build() returns Synonym(f:a f:b f:c): addTerm stores the term (SynonymQuery.java:95) before it checks the limit (:96-98), and build() does not check again. rows.title: RandomSamplingFacetsCollector never samples the first hit of a segment that starts mid-bin: createSample does not handle randomIndex == counter at the end of a segment, so a sampling bin that crosses a segment boundary loses its sample (or samples at a stale offset)
rows.summary: You count facets with RandomSamplingFacetsCollector on a multi-segment index for a query with many more hits than sampleSize, and expect systematic sampling: one random hit out of every run of binSize consecutive hits, with a run that is cut by a segment boundary continued in the next segment, so every hit has about a 1/binSize chance to be sampled. Instead, when the hit picked for such a run is the first hit of the next segment, createSample leaves its carry-over state unset (it tests only randomIndex > counter and randomIndex < counter), so that run contributes no sample, or one at a stale offset, and the first hit of a segment that starts mid-bin is never sampled. Nothing fails; the sample and the amortized counts are just smaller than the reported sampling rate implies (4 hits in segments [1 | 3], sampleSize 2: half the seeds sample 1 hit instead of 2).

rows.title: CheckIndex -exorcise with more than one thread (threadCount > 1, the default on multi-core machines, or checkIndex(onlySegments, executor)) writes the surviving segments in ascending file-size order instead of commit order, so the repaired index's segment order and relative document order depend on the thread count

You expect the same repaired commit that a sequential run (-threadCount 1) writes: the documentation describes the thread count and the executor overload only as ways to speed up the check, and exorcise only as removing the broken segments. Instead the concurrent path collects the segment results in ascending file-size order (a sort added so that small segments print first) and exorciseIndex commits that list as it is, so the surviving segments, and with them the relative order of their documents, are permuted; an index written in insertion order comes back reversed, so Sort.INDEXORDER returns the newest documents first instead of the oldest.

rows.title: IndexWriter.hasUncommittedChanges() can return false for an acknowledged, uncommitted delete while another thread flushes or refreshes an NRT reader, because it reads changeCount before the in-RAM state (every release since 4.5.1)
rows.summary: You delete a committed document with deleteDocuments, do not commit, and call hasUncommittedChanges() while another thread calls flush() or refreshes an NRT reader; you expect true, because the delete was acknowledged and is not in the last commit, and the javadoc allows only false positives. Instead the method reads changeCount first (still equal to the last commit's) and the in-RAM state second, and if the flush applies the delete, increments changeCount and empties the delete buffers between those two reads, it returns false; the next call returns true. A caller that commits only when the method returns true skips that commit.

rows.title: FrozenBufferedUpdates narrows its packet RAM estimate to int and BufferedUpdatesStream subtracts it with an int negation, so a deletes/updates packet whose estimate is exactly 2^31 bytes (mod 2^32) leaves the stream's byte count at -2^32: for the rest of the writer's life NRT readers are never current while openIfChanged returns null, and hasUncommittedChanges() and hasDeletions() stay true
rows.summary: You buffer numeric doc-values updates in one IndexWriter (RAM-based flushing disabled, NoMergePolicy) so that the frozen packet's RAM estimate is exactly 2^31 bytes; the test gets there with 19 updates keyed by a term whose field name is 56,511,839 chars (about 60 MB of real heap), and the 19th update crosses main's 1945 MB delete-buffer limit, so the packet is frozen and applied. After commit() you expect a newly opened NRT reader to be current and hasUncommittedChanges() and hasDeletions() to be false. Instead isCurrent() is false while openIfChanged returns null, and both writer methods return true, for the writer's lifetime, because the packet is added to the stream's long counter as Integer.MIN_VALUE and subtracted as -Integer.MIN_VALUE, which in int arithmetic is Integer.MIN_VALUE again (main -ea and -da, 10.6.0, 10.5.2, 9.12.3).

rows.title: IndexWriter on main: a push of the buffered deletes that finds nothing left to freeze leaks one flush-ticket count, so for the rest of the writer's life every NRT reader reports isCurrent() == false, even right after commit(), while openIfChanged() returns null
rows.summary: Several threads add and delete documents on one IndexWriter; afterwards you commit and open an NRT reader without changing anything else, and you expect that reader's isCurrent() to be true, as it is on 10.5.2. Instead, if two threads pushed the buffered deletes at the same time and the second push found nothing left to freeze, DocumentsWriterFlushQueue.addTicket counted a ticket it never queued and never gives the count back (a regression of #15134). From then on DocumentsWriter.anyChanges() is always true, so every NRT reader of the writer, also ones opened after later commits, reports isCurrent() == false while openIfChanged() returns null.
rows.area: index / IndexWriter NRT (DocumentsWriterFlushQueue flush-ticket count, DocumentsWriter.anyChanges)

rows.title: LRUQueryCache's 16 hard partitions give a 0% hit rate with the class-javadoc configuration (main only)
rows.summary: On main, you build an LRUQueryCache with the configuration from its class javadoc (maxSize 256, 50 MB) and run one filter over more than 16 segments. You expect the filter to be cached. Instead maxSize and RAM are hard-split across 16 partitions routed by query, so it gets a 0% hit rate forever; maxSize < 16 caches nothing, and partition counts that are 0, negative or not a power of two crash or waste capacity.
rows.area: search / query cache

rows.title: On main, LRUQueryCache.clear() empties its partitions one at a time and then calls onClear() with no lock held, so an entry cached during clear() survives while a subclass that resets its statistics in onClear() drops it (it reports 0 entries for a cache holding 1, and -1 once that entry is evicted); regression from #15558, main only
rows.summary: You subclass LRUQueryCache to keep per-index statistics the way its class javadoc suggests (count in onCacheEntryInserted/onCacheEntryEvicted, reset in onClear()) and call clear() while searches are running. You expect the subclass's numbers to match getCacheSize() and ramBytesUsed() afterwards, as on 10.x, where clear() and onClear() run under the same lock every insertion takes; on main, clear() empties the partitions one at a time, each under its own lock, and then calls onClear() with no lock, so an entry that a search caches into an already emptied partition (or just before onClear()) stays in the cache while onClear() wipes its count. The subclass then reports 0 entries and 0 bytes for a cache that holds 1 entry of 336 bytes, -1 and -336 once that entry is evicted, and the error lasts until the next clear().
rows.area: search / query cache (LRUQueryCache.clear() and the onClear statistics callback)

rows.title: BpVectorReorderer never calls the Executor it is given; any non-null executor makes it fork its work onto ForkJoinPool.commonPool()
rows.summary: You reorder a segment with BpVectorReorderer and pass an Executor, for example the same-thread intra-merge executor that IndexWriter hands to BPReorderingMergePolicy under SerialMergeScheduler, or the pool the command line builds for --thread-count, and expect the work to run on the calling thread or on that executor, as it does for the sibling BPIndexReorderer. Instead the executor is never called: the tasks are RecursiveActions forked with ForkJoinTask.invokeAll from a thread outside any ForkJoinPool, so any non-null executor only switches forking on and the forked work runs on ForkJoinPool.commonPool(). With a run-on-caller executor and 4,096 two-dimensional vectors, vectors are read on a common-pool worker as well as on the caller; the resulting order is still correct.

rows.title: With an executor, grouped search breaks ties by slice number instead of doc ID, so tied groups and tied documents differ from sequential search
rows.summary: You run a grouped search (GroupingSearch, or the grouping collector managers) on an IndexSearcher that has an executor, and several groups or several documents tie on the sort, for example because every hit scores 1.0. You expect the tie to be broken by doc ID, as Sort's javadoc says and as the same search without an executor does, so the top group and the top documents are the same either way. Instead the per-slice results are combined with merges written for real shards, which break ties by shard index, here the slice number: the search returns doc 1 instead of doc 0, or group g1 instead of g0, and the choice changes whenever the slicing changes.

rows.title: With an executor, block grouping's TopGroups.maxScore includes groups that are not returned, so it changes with the index slicing (and with groupOffset > 0 it counts the skipped groups); regression in 10.5.0
rows.summary: You index each group as a document block and run block grouping (GroupingSearch(Query groupEndDocs)) with a field group sort on an IndexSearcher that has an executor. You expect TopGroups.maxScore to be the same number whether the search runs sequentially or concurrently: sequential block grouping and two-pass term grouping report the best score of the returned groups, and the javadoc says 'Highest score across all hits'. Since 10.5.0 the concurrent value is the maximum over every group that any slice kept, including groups that are not returned, so it changes with the slicing (sequential 1.0, concurrent 5.0 from an unreturned group, best hit 9.0 in the repro), while the returned groups and documents are correct.

rows.title: SynonymQuery adds up boosted term frequencies in float in heap order, so identical documents can score differently and explain() can differ from the hit score; with more than 2^24 occurrences in one field a score can exceed getMaxScore()
rows.summary: You run a SynonymQuery with three or more boosted terms, for example Synonym(a^0.2, b^0.2, c^0.3) over four identical documents 'a b c' with the default BM25, and expect identical documents to score the same and explain() to report the hit's score, because the query scores 'the sum of all term frequencies for the document'. SynonymScorer.freq() adds boost * freq in float, in the order of the disjunction's topList(), and that order depends on how the iterator reached the document, so the rounding differs: docs 0 and 3 score 0.038817033, docs 1 and 2 score 0.038817026, and explain(doc 1) reports 0.038817033. The same float sum can also round above the exact integer sum that the merged impacts use as the max-score bound once a field holds more than 2^24 occurrences of the terms: under ClassicSimilarity a document scores 1.032795 while getMaxScore() is 1.0327948, and a pruned top-1 search returns a different document than an exhaustive one.
rows.area: search / SynonymQuery scoring (SynonymScorer.freq float sum) and its merged-impacts max-score bound

rows.title: Document suggester: which equal-score copies of one suggestion are returned depends on n (top-2 [2, 1] is not a prefix of top-3 [2, 0, 1]), because NRTSuggesterBuilder numbers the copies in java.util.PriorityQueue heap order instead of doc-id order
rows.summary: You index three documents with the same suggestion 'c' and weights 1, 1 and 2 in one segment and call SuggestIndexSearcher.suggest(PrefixCompletionQuery 'c', n, skipDuplicates=false). For n=3 you get docs [2, 0, 1] (score, then the smaller doc id, as the collector's comparator orders them), so n=2 should return the first two, [2, 0]; it returns [2, 1]. NRTSuggesterBuilder.finishTerm numbers the copies of one analyzed form (its dedup bytes) by iterating a java.util.PriorityQueue, whose iterator returns heap-array order ([doc 2, doc 1, doc 0] here), and the per-segment TopNSearcher breaks score ties by those bytes and stops after n results, so for n=2 doc 0 never reaches the collector.

rows.title: Flexible StandardQueryParser: an exclusive int/long point bound at MAX/MIN wraps around, so the query matches every document with the field instead of none
rows.summary: You parse i:{2147483647 TO *], i>2147483647, l>9223372036854775807 or i<"-2147483648" with the flexible StandardQueryParser and a PointsConfig for the field. You expect no hits, because no int is larger than Integer.MAX_VALUE (or smaller than MIN_VALUE). Instead PointRangeQueryNodeBuilder adds or subtracts 1 for the exclusive bound without an overflow check, so MAX+1 wraps to MIN, the query becomes the full range and matches every document with the field (5 of 5 in the repro; {MAX TO MAX} matches all but one).

rows.summary: With the flexible StandardQueryParser and a Float/Double PointsConfig, you query x:[* TO 0} on an index that holds -0.0. You expect every document to match exactly one of x < 0 and x >= 0. Instead the parser uses Math.nextUp/nextDown for exclusive bounds, so x:[* TO 0} misses -0.0 documents and such a document matches neither x < 0 nor x >= 0.

rows.title: Flexible query parser: QueryNode#toQueryString prints field names without escaping, so nodes for escaped field names such as 'my field' or 'a:b' print strings that parse to a different query or do not parse
rows.summary: The standard flexible-parser grammar accepts escaped field names on purpose ('my\ field:x' is a query on the field 'my field', 'a\:b:x' on 'a:b'), and QueryNode#toQueryString is documented to return 'a query string understood by the query parser' that 'can be parsed back by the original text parser'. Every toQueryString that prints a field appends the name raw (only the term goes through the escaper), so the node of 'my\ field:x' prints 'my field:x', which parses as df:my OR field:x, and the node of 'a\:b:x' prints 'a:b:x', which is a syntax error. The same happens for phrase and fuzzy nodes, for range nodes on main (after the #7865 range fix), and for hand-built nodes such as new FieldQueryNode("my field", "x", 0, 0).
rows.area: queryparser / flexible parser node serialization (QueryNode#toQueryString of FieldQueryNode, QuotedFieldQueryNode, FuzzyQueryNode, AbstractRangeQueryNode and the other field-printing nodes)

rows.title: Flexible query parser: IntervalQueryNode#toQueryString prints some fn: interval functions in a form the parser rejects or reads as a different query (fn:fuzzyTerm(abc) prints as fn:fuzzyTerm(abc 2128))

A quoted literal with the ideographic space U+3000 prints unquoted and re-parses, with no error, as two separate literals.

rows.title: Flexible query parser: BoostQueryNode#toQueryString prints a boost below 0.001 (or above 2^63) in E-notation, e.g. ab^0.0009 prints ab^9.0E-4, which StandardSyntaxParser cannot parse back
rows.summary: You parse ab^0.0009 with the flexible StandardSyntaxParser, print the node tree with toQueryString, and expect text that parses back to the same boost, since QueryNode#toQueryString is documented as 'convert to a query string understood by the query parser' and the package documentation says the string 'can be parsed back by the original text parser'. Instead BoostQueryNode prints f:ab^9.0E-4, because its getValueString falls back to Float.toString, which uses E-notation below 0.001 and above 2^63 (ab^10000000000000000000 prints ab^1.0E19). The grammar's NUMBER token has no exponent, so re-parsing the printed text throws ParseException; the same happens to a per-field boost such as setFieldsBoost(Map.of("title", 0.0005f)) in the processed tree (title:lucene^5.0E-4).

rows.title: Flexible query parser: SlopQueryNode and PhraseSlopQueryNode print their int slop through a float, so toQueryString changes every slop above 2^24 (~16777217 prints ~16777216, ~2147483647 prints ~2147483648, which the parser rejects)

rows.title: DateRangePrefixTree prints a date range whose end is the last year of a thousand- or million-year block (a year X999, or 2 BC) with that end shown as the block's FIRST year, e.g. [1990 TO 1999] prints as "[1990 TO 1000]", so parseShape rejects the printed string ('Wrong order') or reads it as a much shorter range ([* TO 1999-12-31] prints as "[* TO 1000]")
rows.summary: You parse an ordinary date range such as [1990 TO 1999] with DateRangePrefixTree.parseShape and print it, expecting a string that parseShape reads back as the same range, as NRShape#toString promises ('The result should be parseable by parseShape(String)'). Instead it prints "[1990 TO 1000]", which parseShape rejects with IllegalArgumentException 'Wrong order', and [* TO 1999-12-31] prints as "[* TO 1000]" ([1990 TO 2999] as "[1990 TO 2000]"), which parses without error to a range that ends up to 999 years early. Range normalization turns an end of 1999 into the thousand-year cell 1000-1999 (an end of 2 BC into a million-year cell), and the per-cell printer writes a cell as its FIRST year, which is right for a range start but wrong for a range end; searches are unaffected, only the text is wrong.

rows.title: StandardTokenizer and UAX29URLEmailTokenizer with setMaxTokenLength(1) end the token stream at the first supplementary character (for example an emoji), so all later text of the field value is silently left out of the index
rows.summary: You set maxTokenLength to 1 on StandardTokenizer (or StandardAnalyzer, UAX29URLEmailTokenizer, or a factory with maxTokenLength=1) and tokenize text that contains a code point above U+FFFF, for example 'ab U+10400 cd' or 'hello U+1F600 world'. You expect what the setter documents, that too-long tokens are chopped and emitted as multiple tokens, so the words after that character are still tokenized and end() reports the input length as the final offset. Instead the 1-char scan buffer cannot hold the surrogate pair, the scanner's refill reports end of input at a token start, and the stream stops: [a, b] with final offset 3 of 8, [h, e, l, l, o], and nothing after the character is indexed.

rows.title: HTMLStripCharFilter leaves hexadecimal character references with six hex digits (􏿽 􀀀 the zero-padded &#x0000E9) undecoded, because its length check counts the leading 'x' and so lets only five hex digits through
rows.summary: You run HTML through HTMLStripCharFilter and expect every numeric character reference up to U+10FFFF to be decoded, as the scanner's own comment says ('10FFFF: max 6 hex chars') and as its decimal branch does for  and the zero-padded é. Instead a hex reference with six hex digits, such as 􏿽 􀀀 or é stays in the output as literal text: the length that is checked includes the leading 'x', so only five hex digits pass. rows.title: StandardTokenizerImpl.setBufferSize growing the buffer after yypushback to the buffer start loses a held-back high surrogate, so the next refill reads new input over it: a supplementary character silently disappears and the next offsets shift by one (UAX29URLEmailTokenizerImpl the same; since 4.10.0)

Instead it returns ab@0, cd@3: the first refill held the emoji's high surrogate back in the last slot of the 3-char buffer (zzFinalHighSurrogate), the growth keeps that hold-back, and because the pushback left the scan at buffer index 0 the next refill skips the shift that would fold the held char back in and reads new input over it, so the emoji is lost and the next offsets are one short (on longer input a later buffer shift folds in one stale NUL char, which is dropped but can split a word, and the offsets after it are right again).

rows.title: On main, LRUQueryCache.cleanUp() is synchronized on the cache object and takes partition locks while it holds that monitor, so a subclass whose statistics callbacks synchronize on the cache (synchronized methods or synchronized (this)) deadlocks the cleanup thread against a search, and every later search whose callback needs the monitor hangs too; regression from #15558, main only

rows.title: Monitor's ParallelMatcher starts blocking worker tasks in its constructor that only finish() releases: a Monitor#match that fails before finish() (an exception such as TooManyClauses from the presearcher, or a rejected submit) leaves its workers parked on the executor forever, and an executor that runs a worker on the calling thread (CallerRunsPolicy on a saturated pool) makes Monitor#match hang

rows.title: PrimaryNode.releaseCopyState leaks the pending-copy count when IndexWriter.decRefDeleter throws (for example after an I/O error closed the IndexWriter while a replica was copying), so PrimaryNode.close() then waits forever under the default remote-close timeout

rows.title: Classic QueryParser.parse (and its MultiFieldQueryParser, ComplexPhraseQueryParser and ExtendableQueryParser subclasses) throws StackOverflowError instead of the documented ParseException on deeply nested groups (about 2,650-3,700 levels, 5-7 KB of query text, on a 1 MB thread stack)
rows.summary: You parse a valid query with many nested groups, for example "(".repeat(d) + "a" + ")".repeat(d), with the classic QueryParser.parse(String), which documents '@throws ParseException if the parsing fails' and already turns the generated lexer's TokenMgrError (a java.lang.Error) and clause-limit hits into ParseException, and you expect the query (here just f:a) or a ParseException. Instead the generated recursive-descent grammar calls Query -> Clause -> Query once per '(' with no depth bound, the thread runs out of stack, and java.lang.StackOverflowError escapes parse. On a cold JVM about 2,650 levels (5,331 chars) are enough at -Xss1m and about 5,900 on the 2 MB aarch64 default stack, while the same 100,000-level input parses to f:a on a 256 MB stack.

rows.title: SimpleQueryParser.parse throws StackOverflowError on deeply nested parentheses, because parseSubQuery and consumeSubQuery recurse once per '(' with no depth bound, although the parser is meant to do its best with any human-entered text
rows.summary: You give SimpleQueryParser, the parser meant for raw human-entered text, a query with many balanced nested groups, for example "(".repeat(d) + "a" + ")".repeat(d), and expect a Query: its class javadoc says a person can type whatever they want and the parser will do its best to interpret it no matter how poorly composed, parse(String) declares no exception, and at small depths the same input parses to the plain TermQuery f:a. Instead parseSubQuery calls consumeSubQuery for every '(' and consumeSubQuery calls parseSubQuery again on the inner text, one frame pair per level with no depth bound, so a few thousand to about 25,000 levels (about 500 on a 256 KB stack), depending on stack size and JIT state, exhaust the thread stack and java.lang.StackOverflowError escapes parse. The clause limit does not help, because the nested groups collapse to a single clause.

rows.title: Automaton.Builder.addEpsilon(s, s) never returns and exhausts the heap when state s already has a transition, because its loop re-reads nextTransition while it appends copies that leave s again
rows.summary: You build an automaton with Automaton.Builder, give a state s one accepting self-loop arc (s -a-> s), and call addEpsilon(s, s). You expect it to return at once: its javadoc says it copies dest's arcs over to source, an epsilon from a state to itself adds nothing, and the sibling Automaton.addEpsilon returns on the same call. Instead the call never returns: its loop re-reads the growing transition count, every copy it appends again leaves s and is copied again, and it runs until OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space.

rows.title: BytesRefHash accepts initial capacity 1 but never grows the table, so add() or find() of any second distinct key spins forever; since 10.3.0 the same capacity also stores a key whose hashcode is -1 as an empty slot
rows.summary: You create new BytesRefHash(pool, 1, new BytesRefHash.DirectBytesStartArray(1)), which the constructor accepts because it rejects only capacities <= 0 and non-powers of two, add the key 'a', then add or look up 'b', expecting id 1 or -1 at once, as with capacity 2. Instead the call never returns: with one slot, hashHalfSize is 0, so add()'s rehash trigger 'count == hashHalfSize' never fires, the single slot stays full, and the linear probe in findHash loops forever looking for an empty slot. Since 10.3.0 (#14720) the same capacity also stores a key whose seeded murmur3 hashcode is exactly -1 as the EMPTY marker, so find() returns -1 for a key that was just added and adding it again gives it a second id.

rows.title: UsageTrackingQueryCachingPolicy(historySize) with historySize 715,827,883 to 1,431,655,767: FrequencyTrackingRingBuffer's IntBag sizes its hash table as maxSize * 3 / 2 in int, the product overflows to a 2-slot table, and the second distinct query recorded by onUse loops forever while holding the policy's monitor (larger sizes overflow too, to a table no larger than the history; assertions disabled; with -ea the constructor throws AssertionError instead) (since 5.0.0)
rows.summary: You create new UsageTrackingQueryCachingPolicy(715_827_883) (the same int overflow also breaks every larger size your heap can allocate) and install it on an IndexSearcher with a query cache, expecting it either to track that many recent queries or to reject the size up front with IllegalArgumentException, as FrequencyTrackingRingBuffer already does for sizes below 2. Instead the constructor succeeds (with assertions disabled), the first query is recorded, and the second distinct query loops forever inside onUse while holding the policy's lock, so that search hangs and every other search thread that uses the policy blocks. The cause is that FrequencyTrackingRingBuffer's internal IntBag computes its hash-table size as Math.max(2, maxSize * 3 / 2) in int: above 715,827,882 the product overflows, the table gets only 2 slots (the sentinel takes one, the first query hash the other), and IntBag.add's probe loop has no exit when every slot holds another key.

rows.title: TaskExecutor#invokeAll returns while a task is still running if the caller is interrupted
rows.summary: You run a concurrent search and the calling thread is interrupted. You expect invokeAll to wait for its tasks or to propagate their failures. Instead it returns while a task still runs: with assertions on an AssertionError fires, and with assertions off the task's exception is lost and the task may keep reading a reader the caller has released.

rows.title: DrillSideways with an ExecutorService reports every failure of its drill-down and drill-sideways searches as RuntimeException(ExecutionException(cause)), while sequential DrillSideways, and IndexSearcher with an executor since 9.8.0, throw the cause itself (for example IndexSearcher.TooManyClauses, ExitableDirectoryReader.ExitingReaderException or the declared IOException)
rows.summary: You construct DrillSideways with an ExecutorService so that its drill-down and drill-sideways searches run concurrently, and one of those searches fails, for example because the base query has more clauses than IndexSearcher's clause limit, an ExitableDirectoryReader timeout fires, or a query or collector throws IOException. You expect the exception the sequential DrillSideways throws for the same search: the class javadoc presents the two modes as alternative implementations that differ in speed and duplicate work, every search overload declares IOException, and IndexSearcher has rethrown task failures as-is since 9.8.0 (GITHUB#12516) precisely so that sequential and concurrent searches throw the same exceptions. Instead DrillSideways.searchConcurrently catches the ExecutionException from Future.get and throws new RuntimeException(e), so the caller receives RuntimeException -> ExecutionException -> the original exception, and catch blocks for TooManyClauses, ExitingReaderException or IOException do not fire.

rows.title: TaskExecutor.invokeAll, which runs concurrent IndexSearcher searches, throws IllegalArgumentException 'Self-suppression not permitted' instead of the tasks' exception, and can return while a started task is still running, when two tasks fail with the same exception object, because IOUtils.useOrSuppress calls addSuppressed without an identity check
rows.summary: You run a concurrent search (an IndexSearcher with an executor, or TaskExecutor.invokeAll directly) and two of its tasks fail with the same exception object, for example because the JVM reuses one preallocated NullPointerException at a hot code site. You expect what the invokeAll javadoc promises: it waits for all tasks to complete and throws the first failure, with later ones added as suppressed exceptions. Instead IOUtils.useOrSuppress calls exc.addSuppressed(exc), the JDK rejects that with IllegalArgumentException('Self-suppression not permitted'), and that exception escapes TaskExecutor.collectResults before the remaining tasks are awaited, so the caller gets the wrong exception type and invokeAll can return while another started task is still running.

rows.title: IOUtils.closeWhileSuppressingExceptions throws IllegalArgumentException 'Self-suppression not permitted' and skips the remaining closeables when a close() throws the very Throwable being handled (for example the JVM's shared OutOfMemoryError), because it calls ex.addSuppressed(e) without an identity check
rows.summary: After a failure, Lucene calls IOUtils.closeWhileSuppressingExceptions(ex, closeables...) to close what it had opened and attach any close failures to ex, for example when opening a DirectoryReader fails. If one close() throws the very object ex (the JVM reuses one OutOfMemoryError object once memory is exhausted), you expect what the method documents: every closeable is closed and, for an Error, that same Error is rethrown. Instead ex.addSuppressed(ex) throws IllegalArgumentException 'Self-suppression not permitted', which escapes the loop, so the remaining closeables are never closed and the caller sees the IllegalArgumentException instead of the original failure (kept only as its cause).

rows.title: OfflineSorter.verifyChecksum re-opens the file in its try-with-resources header, so when that re-open fails, the read failure it was called to annotate (an EOFException from a truncated entry, a read I/O error) is dropped and sort() throws only the unrelated open failure, with no cause and no suppressed exception (since 6.0.0)
rows.summary: You sort a file with OfflineSorter (directly, or through a suggester build or hunspell offline sorting), reading one of its entries fails (here a truncated entry gives EOFException), and the sorter's follow-up checksum check cannot re-open the same file (here the Directory's second openInput of that name throws IOException). You expect sort() to throw the read failure with the outcome of the checksum check attached, as verifyChecksum's own javadoc says and as CodecUtil.checkFooter(in, priorException) does on every path, even when the checksum cannot be computed. rows.title: A failed addIndexes(CodecReader...) leaves the incoming fields registered in the writer's field schema, so later valid documents that use those names differently are rejected until the writer is reopened
rows.summary: You import an index with IndexWriter.addIndexes(CodecReader...) and the call fails with an IOException (for example a full disk) while the merged segment is written; as its javadoc promises, no documents are added, and the writer stays open. You expect the writer to behave as if the call had never happened, so that a later document may use an imported field name with any schema, as it may on a fresh or reopened writer and after a validation-time failure of the same call. Instead the merge has already registered every incoming field in the writer-wide field schema before it failed, and nothing undoes that: a later document with NumericDocValuesField("f") is rejected ('cannot change field "f" from index options=DOCS to inconsistent index options=NONE') although no document with "f" was ever indexed into this writer, until the writer is reopened. No I/O error is needed: on a writer with an index sort, when the incoming indexes contain document blocks without a parent field, or with a merge policy that returns one merge per incoming reader, two incoming indexes that use a field differently make the call fail with IllegalArgumentException and leave the first index's schema registered in the same way, so a later document, or an import of only the second index, is rejected; before 9.9.0 every conflicting two-reader import did so.

rows.title: A failed addIndexes(CodecReader...) leaves its unstarted merges in the writer-wide addIndexes queue, so the next addIndexes call runs them on the earlier call's readers and fails with AlreadyClosedException if those readers were closed
rows.summary: You call addIndexes(CodecReader...) with a merge policy that turns the readers into several merges and with SerialMergeScheduler, and the first merge fails (for example disk full); the call throws, adds nothing, and the writer stays open and not tragic. You expect that failed call to be over, so you close its readers and later call addIndexes with other, valid readers, which should merge exactly those readers. Instead the failed call's unstarted merges are still in the writer's shared addIndexes queue, so the next call runs them first and throws AlreadyClosedException 'this IndexReader is closed', leaving its own merge queued in turn, so later calls keep failing this way until rollback() or close(); if you kept the old readers open, the next call silently runs the stale merge and writes a segment that is never used.

rows.title: With SerialMergeScheduler, a valid addIndexes(CodecReader...) call can run a concurrent call's queued merge on its own thread and fail with that merge's exception, discarding its own completed merge
rows.summary: Two threads call addIndexes(CodecReader...) on one IndexWriter configured with SerialMergeScheduler; call A's source is corrupt (or hits a read error) and call B's source is valid. You expect A to fail with its own exception and B to add its documents, as happens in either serial order and with the default ConcurrentMergeScheduler, because IndexWriter is documented as safe for concurrent calls to any method and each addIndexes call already rethrows the failures of its own merges. Instead B, which holds the scheduler, runs A's queued merge on its own thread after finishing its own, receives A's exception (for example CorruptIndexException 'checksum failed (hardware problem?)' naming A's source file), deletes its own completed merge and adds nothing, while A throws the same exception.

Instead, when the call reaches its entry check while deleteAll is waiting for the running merge to abort, it throws AlreadyClosedException 'this IndexWriter is closed. Cannot execute addIndexes(CodecReaders...) API' although the writer is open: isOpen() is true, deleteAll returns normally and the next addIndexes call on the same writer succeeds.

rows.title: TermInSetQuery.equals/hashCode ignore the rewrite method, so set queries that match different documents compare equal, and IndexWriter's delete-by-query buffer then applies only one of them
rows.summary: Since 9.6.0 TermInSetQuery is a MultiTermQuery whose rewrite method decides which documents it matches and how it scores, but its equals/hashCode still compare only the field and terms: new TermInSetQuery("f", [a]) equals SortedSetDocValuesField.newSlowSetQuery("f", [a]) although on a field with only doc values they match 0 and 1 documents, and on an ordinary field new TermInSetQuery("f", [a, b]) equals its TopTermsScoringBooleanQueryRewrite(1) variant although they match 2 and 1 documents. You expect queries that match different documents to be unequal, as PrefixQuery, AutomatonQuery, FuzzyQuery and TermRangeQuery are when only the rewrite method differs. Instead anything keyed on the un-rewritten query treats the two as one: IndexWriter.deleteDocuments with both queries in one flush window applies only the first, so a doc-values delete silently does not happen, or a document added in between is deleted although no call matched it.

rows.title: Numeric score joins (JoinUtil numeric overload, PointInSetIncludingScoreQuery) compare equal when only their per-value join scores differ, so DisjunctionMaxQuery keeps only one of two such joins and BooleanQuery merges them, returning wrong, clause-order-dependent scores
rows.summary: You build two numeric score joins with JoinUtil.createJoinQuery("fromId", false, "toId", Integer.class, fromQuery, searcher, ScoreMode.Max), one over from-index A and one over from-index B; both collect the join value 7 and score the to-document 0.3648 and 0.4311, and you expect DisjunctionMaxQuery([qa, qb], 0) to give the maximum 0.4311, as the string-key joins over the same data do. Instead qa.equals(qb) is true with equal hash codes, because PointInSetIncludingScoreQuery's equals/hashCode compare the score mode, to field, from query and collected join values but not the per-value scores (aggregatedJoinScores) or multipleValuesPerDocument, so DisjunctionMaxQuery keeps one of the two equal disjuncts (it rewrites to '(toId:{7} | toId:{7})') and scores 0.3648. rows.title: CharArrayMap.hashCode() and CharArraySet.hashCode() change on every call and differ for equal instances, because the inherited AbstractMap/AbstractSet hashCode sums identity hash codes of a fresh entry object and a fresh char[] key clone made on every iteration
