rows.title: MutableValue.compareTo orders values of different classes by subtracting the two classes' hash codes, so on a JVM whose identity hash codes can be negative (OpenJ9 by default) the int difference overflows and the order is not transitive; since 4.0.0-alpha
rows.summary: You compare MutableValues of different classes, for example a MutableValueBool, a MutableValueDouble and a MutableValueInt, with the public compareTo that MutableValue takes on by implementing Comparable<MutableValue>. You expect a consistent order: compareTo deliberately orders different classes (by class hash code, with a class-name tie-break), and Comparable requires that a < b and b < c imply a < c. On OpenJ9 with default settings, whose identity hash codes are negative or positive, the order can be cyclic instead (Bool < Double < Int, but Bool > Int), because 'c1.hashCode() - c2.hashCode()' overflows int (-1728369406 - 1684571406 = -3412940812 wraps to +882026484); on HotSpot identity hashes are non-negative 31-bit values, so it never fails there.

rows.title: Expressions: !, &&, || and ?: keep only the low 32 bits of a bitwise/shift result or hex/octal literal, so a non-zero value such as 1 << 32 or 0x100000000 counts as false
rows.summary: You compile a Lucene expression that tests a high bit of a long field, such as '(flags & 0x100000000) ? 10 : 1' over a NumericDocValuesField with flags = 2^32 + 1, and expect 10, because 'flags & 0x100000000' evaluates to 4294967296 and '(flags & 0x100000000) != 0' is 1. Instead you get 1: the compiler asks for the operand of !, &&, || and ?: as a 32-bit int and narrows a long-typed operand (the result of & | ^ ~ << >> >>>, or a hex/octal literal) by keeping only its low 32 bits, so every non-zero value whose low 32 bits are zero counts as false. The same number is true when written as the decimal literal 4294967296, as a variable or as '((1 << 32) + 0)', but false as '0x100000000' or '(1 << 32)'.

rows.title: AbstractKnnVectorQuery#mergeLeafResults is documented to return hits in any order, but rewrite() reads the k-th score from the last entry and DocAndScoreQuery the max score from the first, so an override that only reorders the hits changes the results
rows.summary: You subclass KnnFloatVectorQuery and override mergeLeafResults, whose javadoc says it returns 'index-level kNN results (no constraint on their ordering)' and is 'useful for reading and / or modifying the final results', so that it returns exactly the default merge's hits in another order (same documents, same scores). You expect the same search results as the stock query. Instead rewrite() takes the k-th score from the last entry and DocAndScoreQuery the max score from the first, so with doc-id order a top-1 search for the kNN query OR a 0.5-boosted term returns doc 0 (score 0.51) instead of the exact match, doc 200000 (score 1.0), and on a 10-segment index the k = 50 query re-enters no segment and returns farther documents (first differing doc 16000 instead of 19950).

rows.title: SpatialQuery's dense scorers decide 'no match' from a counter summed from bulk-iterator DocIdSetIterator#cost(), so LatLonPoint geometry queries and LatLonShape/XYShape queries with WITHIN or DISJOINT silently drop matching documents when a custom PointValues hands the bulk IntersectVisitor callbacks iterators with an upper-bound cost (latent: every in-tree PointValues reports exact costs; since 9.1.0)
rows.summary: A PointValues wrapper delegates everything to the default codec's points but hands each visited document to IntersectVisitor#visit(DocIdSetIterator, byte[]) as a one-document BitSetIterator whose cost() is maxDoc, an upper bound that the DocIdSetIterator#cost() javadoc explicitly allows ('generally an upper bound ... may be ... completely inaccurate'). Two documents, one with a single LatLonPoint inside a square and one with two LatLonPoint values outside it: LatLonPoint.newGeometryQuery(WITHIN, square) should count 1, as it does with the exact cost 1. Instead SpatialQuery's dense WITHIN scorer starts a counter at size() = 3 points, subtracts the reported cost 2 for each of the outside document's two points (3 -> 1 -> 0), reaches 0 and returns DocIdSetIterator.empty() although the inside document's bit is still set, so the query counts 0 with -da and trips the internal assert 'cost[0] > 0 || result.cardinality() == 0' (SpatialQuery.java:362) with -ea.

rows.title: IndexWriter#hasDeletions ignores committed soft deletes in segments the writer has not pooled, so a writer reopened on an index whose only deletions are soft deletes (or one that took such segments through addIndexes(Directory)) answers false, and true once an NRT reader is opened
rows.summary: You configure a soft-deletes field, soft-delete a document (softUpdateDocument, or updateDocValues on that field), commit, close, and open a new IndexWriter on the index; you expect hasDeletions() to return true, because its javadoc says 'Returns true if this index has deletions', IndexWriterConfig#setSoftDeletesField says a soft-deleted document 'is treated as if it has been hard-deleted through the IndexWriter API', and the same writer's getDocStats() counts the deleted document (maxDoc 2 and numDocs 1 in the repro). Instead it returns false, with -ea and -da, until DirectoryReader.open(writer) puts the segment into the reader pool; after that the same call on the unchanged index returns true. The loop over committed segments uses SegmentCommitInfo#hasDeletions() (delGen != -1, hard deletes only), while the buffered and pooled branches of the same method count soft deletes; the one-line fix is info.getDelCount(softDeletesEnabled) > 0.

rows.title: OpenStringBuilder.write(OpenStringBuilder arr) copies as many chars as this builder's own length instead of arr's length, so it appends nothing, appends chars from arr's buffer past arr's end (NULs or stale earlier content), or throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException
rows.summary: You append one OpenStringBuilder to another with dst.write(src) and expect dst to grow by src's contents, as it does with dst.append(src) and with every other write overload of the class. Instead the method copies dst's own length worth of chars out of src's buffer: an empty dst gets nothing (writing "lucene" gives ""), "hello" plus "ab" gives "helloab" followed by 3 NUL chars, a src that was reset and refilled with "q" leaks its earlier content ("1234" becomes "1234qECR"), and a dst longer than src's backing array throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException. The cause is one token: write(OpenStringBuilder arr) calls write(arr.buf, 0, len) (OpenStringBuilder.java:140), where len is the receiver's field, not arr.len.

rows.title: LatLonPoint, XYPointField and the range fields (IntRange, LongRange, FloatRange, DoubleRange, InetAddressRange) accept the inherited Field.setBytesValue, which IntPoint and the other numeric points reject, but their typed setters write from index 0 of the backing array, so after a BytesRef slice with a non-zero offset setLocationValue/setRangeValues silently leaves the old value indexed
rows.summary: You build a LatLonPoint at (10, 20), install the same encoded point as a slice of a larger buffer with field.setBytesValue(new BytesRef(buffer, 8, 8)), which the field accepts, then reuse the field with setLocationValue(-30, -40) and index it; you expect the document at (-30, -40), as the setter's javadoc 'Change the values of this field' says, or else an IllegalArgumentException from setBytesValue, which is what IntPoint, LongPoint, FloatPoint, DoublePoint and InetAddressPoint throw. Instead setLocationValue writes the new encoding into buffer[0, 8), outside the slice, while indexing reads the slice at its offset, so the document is indexed at (10, 20) and a box query around (-30, -40) finds nothing, with no error. XYPointField.setLocationValue and the setRangeValues of IntRange, LongRange, FloatRange, DoubleRange and InetAddressRange behave the same way, and after such a slice the ranges' getMin/getMax and toString read outside it too.

rows.title: Geo3dDistanceCalculator.within returns the opposite of 'distance <= limit' for every finite distance, so the default distance calculator of the Geo3d spatial context answers every within() call backwards
rows.summary: You create a spatial context with Geo3dSpatialContextFactory and ask its distance calculator whether the point (1, 0) is within 10 degrees of (0, 0), with ctx.getDistCalc().within(from, 1, 0, 10), and expect true: distance() returns 1.0 degree, and the spatial4j DistanceCalculator contract says within() is true when the distance is <= the limit. Instead it returns false, and within(from, 50, 0, 10) returns true although the distance is 50 degrees. The method body is 'return (distance < distance(from, toX, toY));', the exact negation of the contract, so every answer with a finite distance is inverted, including within(p, p, 0).

rows.title: geo3d NORMAL and NORMAL_SQUARED point distances are wrong on WGS84 and other ellipsoids because Vector.normalDistance assumes a unit-length vector, so the NORMAL distance from a point to itself is up to about 0.0045 planet units (0.00165, about 10.5 km, at latitude 0.3 rad) instead of 0
rows.summary: You build a geo3d circle or path on PlanetModel.WGS84 (or call Vector.normalDistance or DistanceStyle.NORMAL.computeDistance on two GeoPoints) and ask for the NORMAL or NORMAL_SQUARED distance, which Vector's javadoc defines as 'the normal (perpendicular) distance to a vector described by a vector taken from the origin', and expect 0 for a point and itself and about 7.85e-6 planet units for a point 50 m from a circle's centre. Instead both come out as 0.00165 (about 10.5 km) at latitude 0.3 rad, because Vector.normalDistanceSquared projects onto the receiver with t = dotProduct(v) and never divides by |this|^2, which is exact only for unit vectors, while WGS84 surface points have lengths between about 0.998 and 1.0011. The same offset enters every NORMAL and NORMAL_SQUARED circle and path distance on non-spherical planet models, with no error; on SPHERE the values are exact.

rows.title: GeoPath.computeDistance with DistanceStyle.LINEAR_SQUARED or NORMAL_SQUARED on a path of width > 0 (GeoStandardPath) returns the fourth power of the distance instead of its square for points inside a path segment, because the segment's result is converted back from aggregation form twice (regression since 9.5.0)
rows.summary: You build a path with GeoPathFactory.makeGeoPath and a width > 0 and call computeDistance with DistanceStyle.LINEAR_SQUARED (or NORMAL_SQUARED), expecting the square of the LINEAR (or NORMAL) path distance, which is what DistanceStyle's 'convert to aggregation form, aggregate, convert back' contract gives and what end-cap points, the zero-width path and Lucene 9.4.2 return. For a point inside a path segment you get the square of that value instead: 0.00803 rather than 0.0896 for a point whose LINEAR distance is 0.299, so the value jumps about 6x across a segment's end cutoff plane and can rank a farther point ahead of a nearer one. The cause is a leftover conversion from the 2022 path refactor: PathSegment.distance already converts its result back from aggregation form, and GeoStandardPath.distance converts the component tree's result back a second time.

rows.title: On a zero-width geo3d path (GeoDegeneratePath), computePathCenterDistance with DistanceStyle.LINEAR_SQUARED or NORMAL_SQUARED returns the unsquared distance and computeOutsideDistance returns the fourth power, instead of the squared distance, because the 2022 path refactor converted the path components to aggregation form but not the two places that combine them (regression since 9.5.0)
rows.summary: You build a zero-width path with GeoPathFactory.makeGeoPath(planetModel, 0, points) and call computePathCenterDistance or computeOutsideDistance with DistanceStyle.LINEAR_SQUARED (or NORMAL_SQUARED), expecting the square of the LINEAR (or NORMAL) distance, which is what DistanceStyle's 'convert to aggregation form, aggregate, convert back' contract gives, what the same path with width 1e-6 returns and what Lucene 9.4.2 returned. Instead, for a point 0.01 rad beside the path, computePathCenterDistance returns about 0.01 (the unsquared distance) and computeOutsideDistance returns about 1e-8 (the fourth power) where about 1e-4 is expected. The cause is an incomplete edit in the 2022 path refactor: GeoDegeneratePath's components now return the square root (the aggregation form of the squared styles), but computePathCenterDistance never squares the minimum back, and PathSegment.outsideDistance still returns the plain square, which outsideDistance then squares a second time.

rows.title: GraphTokenFilter.end(), the base of FixedShingleFilter, keeps only the final position increment and offset of its input's end state once its read-ahead has reached the end of the input, so any other end-of-stream attribute value set by the input's end() (a FlagsAttribute, TypeAttribute or custom attribute value) comes back as the attribute's default (latent: no shipped Lucene producer or consumer uses such a value; since 8.0.0)
rows.summary: You put a TokenFilter whose end() calls super.end() and then sets FlagsAttribute to 42 under FixedShingleFilter(.., 2) on a WhitespaceTokenizer over 'a b c', consume the stream and call end(). You expect the flags to read 42, as they do without the shingle filter or through the older ShingleFilter, because TokenFilter#end chains to the input and the TokenStream#end javadoc lets end() adjust other attributes whose end-of-stream value matters. Instead they read 0: GraphTokenFilter's read-ahead already called input.end() and recorded only the position increment and end offset, and its end() then resets every attribute (endAttributes()) and restores only those two.

rows.title: IndexWriter#tryUpdateDocValue does not validate the doc id: an id outside [0, maxDoc) returns success and silently updates or soft-deletes a different document, or commits a doc-values entry for a nonexistent document that a merge shifts onto other documents
rows.summary: You call IndexWriter#tryUpdateDocValue with an NRT reader and a doc id outside [0, reader.maxDoc()), for example 8 or 9 on an 8-document reader, 12 on a 10-document reader, or -1 on a 4-document leaf reader. You expect the call to be rejected, as the same reader rejects such an id ('docID must be >= 0 and < maxDoc', IllegalArgumentException), or at least to leave every other document alone. Instead, with assertions disabled (and for the negative leaf-reader id even with them enabled) it returns a sequence number > 0, which the javadoc says means the update succeeded, and writes the value to or soft-deletes a different live document (8 -> doc 0, 9 -> doc 1, -1 -> doc 3), or commits a doc-values entry for nonexistent doc 12 that CheckIndex accepts and that forceMerge turns into every document of the next segment carrying its predecessor's value (b0=777, b1=1000, ..., b9=1008; 1009 is lost).

rows.title: IndexWriter#addBatch does not validate tuple doc-ids on some doc-values column paths: a doc-values-only SORTED/SORTED_SET DictionaryColumn accepts a doc-id outside [0, numDocs) and writes the value onto a neighbouring document, and SORTED_NUMERIC/SORTED_SET columns check doc-id order only with a Java assert, so decreasing doc-ids close the writer (-ea) or are accepted and break later documents and commits (-da)
rows.summary: You add a batch with IndexWriter#addBatch whose doc-values-only DictionaryColumn (SORTED or SORTED_SET) has a tuple cursor that returns a batch doc-id equal to numDocs or -1, or whose SORTED_NUMERIC or SORTED_SET column returns doc-ids in decreasing order, for example (1, v) then (0, v'). You expect an IllegalArgumentException with the writer still open and no other document touched, which is what the same addBatch call does for LongColumn, BinaryColumn, vector and stored or indexed (row-pass) columns that break the same documented contract. Instead the out-of-range value is silently attached to the document indexed just before or just after the batch (it survives commit, and CheckIndex reports a clean index), and the out-of-order tuples either throw an AssertionError that closes the writer (-ea) or are accepted (-da), after which a later valid addDocument is rejected with 'Out of order doc ids: last=1, next=0', another later document reads a value from the batch, and the next commit can fail and close the writer.

rows.title: IndexWriter#addBatch does not reject a ColumnBatch whose numDocs() is negative (DocumentsWriterPerThread.reserveDocs only asserts n >= 0): with assertions off, the count is subtracted from the in-memory segment, so the next commit returns normally without documents added before the batch; with assertions on, the AssertionError closes the writer as a tragic event (since 10.5.0)

Instead, with assertions off, addBatch returns normally, the negative count is subtracted from the in-memory segment's document count, and the next commit returns normally with 0 documents instead of 1. With assertions on, the 'assert n >= 0' in DocumentsWriterPerThread.reserveDocs throws an AssertionError, which IndexWriter treats as a tragic event, so the writer closes.

rows.title: BinaryPoint.newRangeQuery(String, byte[][], byte[][]) does not throw the IllegalArgumentException its javadoc promises when lowerValue.length != upperValue.length if both bounds pack to the same number of bytes (for example 2 dimensions x 2 bytes against 1 x 4), and instead builds a query that reads the upper bound's bytes in the lower bound's dimension layout, because only the packed byte lengths are compared (since 6.0.0, LUCENE-7117/LUCENE-7118)
rows.summary: You call BinaryPoint.newRangeQuery("f", lower, upper) with a lower bound of two 2-byte dimensions and an upper bound of one 4-byte dimension, and expect the IllegalArgumentException its javadoc promises 'if lowerValue.length != upperValue.length'. Instead you get a query, printed as f:[binary(0 0) TO binary(1 1)],[binary(0 0) TO binary(1 1)]: the 4-byte upper bound was silently re-split into two 2-byte dimensions. newRangeQuery packs each bound on its own and passes only lowerValue.length as the dimension count, and the PointRangeQuery constructor compares only the packed byte lengths, so a dimension-count mismatch gets through whenever the byte totals agree.

rows.title: Sandbox PhraseWildcardQuery's Weight reports isCacheable true although its one expansion budget is spent across all of the reader's segments (smallest first), so after a reopen changes the segment set a query cache returns hits that differ from an uncached search on the same reader (since 8.4.0)
rows.summary: You build new PhraseWildcardQuery.Builder("f", 1).addMultiTerm(new PrefixQuery(new Term("f", "a"))).addTerm(new Term("f", "x")).build(), count it through an LRUQueryCache on a one-segment reader whose segment holds 'aa x' (count 1), then add a smaller segment holding 'ab x' and reopen. You expect the cached count on the reopened reader to equal the uncached count on that reader (1: the one allowed expansion is spent on the smaller new segment first, as documented), because a weight whose per-segment result depends on the other segments must not report itself cacheable (SegmentCacheable). Instead the query's Weight inherits PhraseWeight#isCacheable == true, the cache reuses the old segment's entry computed when it was the only segment, and the cached count is 2 (in the other direction a segment can also lose its hits).
rows.area: sandbox / search: PhraseWildcardQuery (PhraseWeight#isCacheable) and the query cache

rows.title: DynamicRangeUtil computes DynamicRangeInfo.centroid ('the average value in the range') from an unchecked long sum of the range's values, so when one range's values sum past Long.MAX_VALUE (for example six epoch-nanosecond timestamps of today) it silently returns a centroid outside [min, max], typically negative for positive values
rows.summary: You index six documents whose long doc-values field holds epoch-nanosecond timestamps one second apart (about 1.76e18 each) and ask DynamicRangeUtil.computeDynamicRanges for one range, or you pass three values of 4e18 to computeDynamicNumericRanges, and expect the range's centroid, documented as 'the average value in the range', to be about 1.7614800025e18 (or exactly 4e18). Instead you get -1.3129773431182584e18 (or -2.148914691236517e18), below the range's own min, with no error, because the method adds the range's values into a long valueSum that silently wraps once the true sum passes Long.MAX_VALUE and then divides the wrapped sum by the count. Count, weight, min and max are correct, and the weight sums in the same class are checked with Math.addExact and throw instead of wrapping.
rows.area: facet / dynamic range facets (DynamicRangeUtil.computeDynamicRanges and computeDynamicNumericRanges, DynamicRangeInfo.centroid)

rows.title: Flexible StandardQueryParser: the (...)@N min-should-match operator throws ClassCastException when the group does not build a BooleanQuery, e.g. (the fox)@1 with a stop-word analyzer or the boosted group (fox dog)^2@1
rows.summary: You parse (the fox)@1 ('at least one of the, fox') with the flexible StandardQueryParser and an analyzer that drops the stopword 'the', or the boosted group (fox dog)^2@1; the class javadoc documents @N for disjunction groups and boosts on grouped clauses, and parse() declares QueryNodeException for failures, so you expect a query (at least one of the remaining clauses, boosted as written). Instead parse() throws java.lang.ClassCastException ('TermQuery / BoostQuery cannot be cast to BooleanQuery') from MinShouldMatchNodeBuilder.build, which casts the group's query to BooleanQuery without a check: after the stopword is removed the one-clause group is collapsed to a TermQuery, and the grammar puts the boost inside the min-should-match node, so the group's query is a BoostQuery. Groups holding a single term, phrase, prefix or other non-Boolean query, such as (fox)@1 or ("quick fox")@1, fail the same way, while (fox dog)@1 works.

rows.title: Flexible query parser: EscapeQuerySyntaxImpl does not escape '@' after the first character of a term or a term that is exactly && or ||, so QueryNode#toQueryString output for such terms does not parse
rows.summary: Since 9.1 the standard flexible parser reads an '@' anywhere in a term as syntax (it must be escaped, as in user\@example.com), and && and || are its AND and OR operators, so QueryNode#toQueryString, documented to return 'a query string understood by the query parser', has to escape them. Its escaper EscapeQuerySyntaxImpl escapes '@' only when it is the first character of a term and lists AND, OR and NOT but not && or || as reserved words, so the node for 'user\@example.com' prints 'df:user@example.com' and the nodes for '\&&' and '\||' print 'df:&&' and 'df:||'. Parsing any of these strings again throws INVALID_SYNTAX_CANNOT_PARSE; with a small fix to the escaper's tables every printable-ASCII term of length 1-3 round-trips.
rows.area: queryparser / flexible parser term escaping (EscapeQuerySyntaxImpl, as used by QueryNode#toQueryString)

rows.title: JavascriptCompiler.compile lets the bytecode generator's method-size failure escape untranslated: a well-formed, shallowly nested expression that is too big for one JVM method throws ASM's MethodTooLargeException (or an ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException from ASM's frame computation) on 8.5.0 to 10.5.2 and the 10.6.0 release line, and the class-file API's IllegalArgumentException on main, instead of the documented ParseException / IllegalStateException
rows.summary: You compile a well-formed expression that is too big for one JVM method but nested far below the 1024 limit, for example a balanced sum of 10,000 terms or a depth-12 decision tree, with JavascriptCompiler.compile; the javadoc says it throws ParseException 'on failure to compile' and, since 10.6.0 (#16423), IllegalStateException 'if the resulting expression class fails to link (e.g., complexity)', and the author of #16423 said in its review that bytecode-limit refusals now become IllegalStateException. Instead the bytecode generator's own size-limit exception escapes untranslated, because it is thrown before the class is defined and outside every translating catch: org.objectweb.asm.MethodTooLargeException on the 10.6.0 release line and 8.5.0 to 10.5.2 (plus ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException 'Index -32768 out of bounds for length 40960' from ASM's frame computation when a 127-argument custom function is nested 130 or more deep), ASM's plain RuntimeException 'Method code too large!' on 4.6.0 to 8.4.1, and java.lang.IllegalArgumentException 'Code length N is outside the allowed range' from the JDK class-file API on main. Every expression that does compile evaluates correctly; only the exception type is wrong, and the main-only IllegalArgumentException leg is debatable (a JDK-documented type that maintainers may prefer to document rather than wrap).
rows.area: expressions / JavascriptCompiler code generation (compileExpression exception translation for class-file size limits)

rows.title: JavascriptCompiler.compile throws NumberFormatException instead of the documented ParseException for a hex or octal literal above Long.MAX_VALUE, such as 0x8000000000000000
rows.summary: You compile an expression such as '0x8000000000000000', '01000000000000000000000' or '1 + 0xffffffffffffffff' with JavascriptCompiler.compile, and you expect it either to compile (JavaScript reads 0x8000000000000000 as 2^63) or to fail with ParseException, because every compile overload documents '@throws ParseException on failure to compile' and the grammar accepts hex and octal literals of any length. Instead compile throws java.lang.NumberFormatException ('For input string: "8000000000000000" under radix 16'): visitNumeric parses hex and octal tokens with signed Long.parseLong, and compileExpression rethrows every RuntimeException that does not wrap a ParseException. The largest in-range literals, 0x7fffffffffffffff and 0777777777777777777777, compile and evaluate correctly, so the boundary is exactly Long.MAX_VALUE.
rows.area: expressions / JavascriptCompiler literal parsing (hex and octal literals in visitNumeric)

rows.title: JavascriptCompiler.compile(source, functions, Integer.MAX_VALUE) rejects every expression, even '1', because maxNestingDepth + 1 overflows to Integer.MIN_VALUE
rows.summary: You compile an expression with the new overload JavascriptCompiler.compile(source, functions, maxNestingDepth) and pass Integer.MAX_VALUE to ask for no practical nesting limit, and you expect it to accept at least everything that Integer.MAX_VALUE - 1 accepts, because the parameter is documented only as 'the maximum depth of nesting', with no bound. Instead every expression, even '1', fails with ParseException 'Nesting level too deep (>-2147483648)': the parse-time depth listener is created with maxNestingDepth + 1 to account for the root node, that int addition wraps to Integer.MIN_VALUE, and the depth check fails on the first parser rule. Integer.MAX_VALUE - 1 and the default limit of 1024 work, and the overload first shipped in 10.6.0 (released 2026-10-29).

rows.title: Word2VecSynonymFilterFactory accepts any positive maxSynonymsPerTerm, but Word2VecSynonymProvider sizes its HNSW search as maxSynonymsPerTerm + 1 with no clamp to the model size, so very large values (Integer.MAX_VALUE, where the + 1 overflows) make every in-model token throw IllegalArgumentException or OutOfMemoryError
rows.summary: You configure Word2VecSynonymFilterFactory with maxSynonymsPerTerm=2147483647 (Integer.MAX_VALUE), which its validation accepts ('must be a positive integer greater than 0'), to keep every synonym above minAcceptedSimilarity, and you expect those synonyms or a rejection at configuration time. The analyzer builds, but Word2VecSynonymProvider.getSynonyms passes maxSynonymsPerTerm + 1 (int arithmetic) as topK to HnswGraphSearcher.search, which wraps to Integer.MIN_VALUE, so the first token with a model vector throws IllegalArgumentException 'initialCapacity must be > 0 and < 2147483630; got: -2147483648' from TernaryLongHeap (on 9.7.0 to 10.3.2: 'maxSize must be > 0 ...' from LongHeap). Because the search size is never clamped to the model size and the search allocates its queues of topK entries up front, values close to Integer.MAX_VALUE fail the same way and values from roughly heap-bytes/16 up (1e8 at a 1 GiB heap) throw OutOfMemoryError, even for a 3-term model.

rows.title: PassageSelector.pickBest (MatchHighlighter) silently drops the highlight passages of permitted ranges that start after offset 0 when maxPassageWindow is Integer.MAX_VALUE: the int window shift 'to += range.from - from' wraps negative, so the second and later values of a multi-valued field lose their snippets (the residue of the LUCENE-10135 overflow fix)

rows.title: AnalyzingSuggester and FuzzySuggester compute the top-N queue depth num * maxAnalyzedPathsForOneInput in int, so with a synonym (token graph) analyzer a large num wraps it: lookup silently returns too few suggestions and skips higher-weighted ones, or throws NoSuchElementException, and with assertions on lookup(key, false, Integer.MAX_VALUE) typically fails 'assert completions.isComplete'
rows.summary: You build an AnalyzingSuggester (or FuzzySuggester) whose index-time analyzer expands one entry into several analyzed forms, for example a SynonymGraphFilter that also indexes 'lucene' as 'search' and 'find', and call lookup("luc", false, num) with a large num; num is documented as the 'maximum number of results to return', so you expect the 8 suggestions that num = 1000 returns. Instead the search's queue depth num * maxAnalyzedPathsForOneInput is computed in int (AnalyzingSuggester.java:786) and wraps: with 3 paths and num = 1431655766 it becomes 2, the top-N search prunes paths it still needs, and lookup returns [lucas, lucifer, lucid] with no error, skipping the higher-weighted luck, lucent and lucerne (FuzzySuggester: 5 of 8), and with 4 paths and num = 2^30 it becomes 0 and lookup throws NoSuchElementException. With assertions enabled, lookup(key, false, Integer.MAX_VALUE) on a suggester with 2 or more paths typically fails 'assert completions.isComplete' (:824), although the same call without assertions returns the right list.

rows.title: FSDirectory: a pending-delete retry running on one thread can delete a file that another thread has just re-created (createOutput) or renamed onto the same name, so a file that was written and closed successfully silently disappears
rows.summary: On a file system that refuses to delete open files (Windows, or a virus scanner), you delete a file that a reader still holds open, so FSDirectory keeps it as a pending delete; after the reader closes, one thread re-creates that name with createOutput (or renames another file onto it), writes and closes it, while another thread makes any mutating call on the same directory, for example sync() of an unrelated file. You expect the new file to stay, like any file that was created, closed and never deleted. Instead the other thread's pending-delete retry, which copied the pending set before the revive, deletes the new file: listAll() no longer lists it and openInput() fails (on main under the test framework's WindowsFS: 'x was created and closed successfully but is gone: [other]').

rows.title: NativeFSLockFactory tracks the write locks this JVM holds by real-path string instead of by file, so obtaining write.lock through a second path to the same file (a hard link, or a bind mount of the index directory) opens and closes a second channel on it, which silently drops the holder's OS lock while its ensureValid() keeps passing and lets an IndexWriter in another process open and commit to the same index
rows.summary: In one JVM you hold an index's write.lock (an open IndexWriter on directory A) and then, in the same JVM, open the same lock file through another real path: a bind mount of A at a second path, or a hard-link copy of A's files that includes write.lock, opened with IndexWriter, CheckIndex or addIndexes(Directory...). You expect that second open to fail with LockObtainFailedException while the first writer keeps its lock, so that a writer in another process on A is refused, as the IndexWriter javadoc promises. Instead the second open gets past NativeFSLockFactory's in-JVM check (LOCK_HELD compares toRealPath() strings, which differ), opens a second FileChannel, gets OverlappingFileLockException and closes that channel, which on Linux drops the process's lock on the file; the first lock still passes ensureValid(), a writer in another process then opens A and commits, and the first writer's next delete-only commit replaces that commit (on main: 'expected:<REFUSED> but was:<OBTAINED>' and 'the other process's acknowledged commit (doc 'child') was replaced by this writer's commit').
rows.area: store / NativeFSLockFactory (write.lock: in-JVM LOCK_HELD guard and cross-process mutual exclusion)

rows.title: HardlinkCopyDirectoryWrapper.copyFrom unwraps both directory chains to the innermost FSDirectory and hard-links there, so every FilterDirectory in between is skipped for the copied file: an inner TrackingDirectoryWrapper does not record it, an inner LockValidatingDirectoryWrapper does not check its lock, and a one-sided byte-transforming or namespace-owning layer is bypassed
rows.summary: You wrap an FSDirectory in TrackingDirectoryWrapper (or LockValidatingDirectoryWrapper, or your own FilterDirectory), wrap that in HardlinkCopyDirectoryWrapper, and copy a file in with copyFrom or IndexWriter.addIndexes(Directory...). You expect the copy to pass through the wrapped directory, as createOutput through the same wrapper does: on main Directory#copyFrom says 'Any per-file bookkeeping performed by createOutput must also cover copied files', and FilterDirectory#copyFrom names this class as one that delegates to in.copyFrom. Instead copyFrom unwraps both chains to the innermost FSDirectory and hard-links there, so no layer in between runs: getCreatedFiles() stays [], the copy succeeds after the inner write lock was released, and a byte-transforming layer on one side reads back the raw bytes (through addIndexes, a committed index that cannot be opened), with no error at copy time.

rows.title: NRTCachingDirectory.createOutput does not throw FileAlreadyExistsException when the name already exists in its other home (RAM cache vs wrapped directory), so the file ends up in both homes: deleteFile then leaves the other copy listed and readable, and close() fails and, with assertions disabled, loses the file

rows.title: ByteBuffersDirectory.rename ends with a leftover unconditional files.remove(source), so a file that another thread creates (createOutput) or renames onto the source name while the rename runs is silently deleted, although that thread's call returned normally
rows.summary: You share one ByteBuffersDirectory between two threads: one renames file 'a' to a new name while the other creates a new 'a' (createOutput, write, close) or renames a temp file onto 'a', and you expect the new 'a' to stay until someone deletes or renames it, as it does on FSDirectory. Instead, now and then the new file vanishes: rename has already moved its own entry with the checked files.remove(source, file) and then runs a leftover unconditional files.remove(source), which can only remove a different entry, the one the other thread has just put under 'a'. rows.title: IndexSplitter.split publishes a durable commit in the destination index without fsyncing the segment files it copied, so an OS crash or power loss soon after a split can leave a destination whose newest commit references empty files and cannot be opened
rows.summary: You copy segments into a new index with IndexSplitter (new IndexSplitter(src).split(dest, segments), or the command line 'IndexSplitter <src> <dest> <segments>'), and the machine crashes or loses power shortly after the call returns. You expect what every Lucene commit is built for (Directory.sync javadoc: Lucene syncs files 'to prevent a machine/OS crash from corrupting the index'; IndexWriter.commit syncs all referenced files first): the destination's commit only references files whose bytes are on stable storage. Instead split() copies the segment files with Files.copy and never fsyncs them, and SegmentInfos.commit then fsyncs only the new segments_N and the directory, so the commit and the copied file names can survive the crash while the copied .si, .cfs and .cfe data does not, and opening the destination fails (CorruptSegmentInfoException on _1.si on main, CorruptIndexException on 10.5.2 and 9.12.3, in the simulated post-crash state).
rows.area: misc / index tools (IndexSplitter.split, SegmentInfos.commit durability)

rows.title: After a commit, IndexFileDeleter deletes the old segments_N and then the files only it referenced with no directory fsync in between, so an OS crash that persists those unlinks out of order can leave a stale older commit that blocks IndexWriter
rows.summary: You index with IndexWriter on an FSDirectory with default settings and commit; after the new commit is fsynced, the default deletion policy removes the previous commit, first its segments_N and then the files only it used. You expect that an OS crash or power loss at that point leaves the old commit either complete or gone, which is what the FileDeleter comments and the LUCENE-6616 CHANGES entry ('the index is never left in a state where an expired segments_N references non-existing files') describe. Instead nothing fsyncs the directory between the two deletion passes, so on a file system that persists those unlinks out of order the old segments_N can survive while its _N.si or compound files are gone; DirectoryReader still opens the newest commit, but new IndexWriter fails (CorruptSegmentInfoException on main), listCommits throws and CheckIndex reports corruption (shown in crash states built in software from the real operation sequence; no physical crash was run).
rows.area: index / IndexFileDeleter and util/FileDeleter (deletion of expired commits, crash durability)

rows.title: PersistentSnapshotDeletionPolicy.snapshot() and release() return before the new save file's name is durable: persist() fsyncs snapshots_N but never calls Directory.syncMetaData(), so an OS crash or power loss can lose an acknowledged snapshot
rows.summary: You protect a commit with PersistentSnapshotDeletionPolicy.snapshot(), whose javadoc says that once the method returns the snapshot information is persisted in the directory. Instead persist() writes and fsyncs the new snapshots_N file but never fsyncs the directory (Directory.syncMetaData()), the step Lucene's own commit takes because a new file's name is not durable until then. After an OS crash or power loss the save file can be gone: the snapshot count comes back as 0 and, with the snapshots in a separate Directory, the reopened IndexWriter deletes the commit the snapshot was protecting (a lost release() instead brings a released snapshot back).

rows.title: Operations.complement and minus give a wrong, non-deterministic result for an automaton with an arc ending at Integer.MAX_VALUE, because totalize computes t.max + 1 in int and the wrap adds a dead-state arc that overlaps the real arc
rows.summary: You build Automata.makeCharRange('a', Integer.MAX_VALUE), which accepts every one-code-point word from "a" upward, and take its complement with Operations.complement; you expect a deterministic automaton (as the javadoc promises) that rejects "a". Instead the complement accepts "a" and is not deterministic, with no error: totalize, which complement uses to send every missing label to a dead state, computes t.max + 1 in int, the sum wraps to Integer.MIN_VALUE, so it also adds a dead-state arc over the whole code-point range on top of the real arc, and that dead state becomes accepting in the complement. Operations.minus, which subtracts through complement, likewise keeps words it should remove.
rows.area: util / automaton (Operations.totalize, used by Operations.complement and Operations.minus)

rows.title: RegExp numeric interval <n-m> accepts a leading '+' on a bound and counts it as a digit, so <+1-+9> matches 01..09 instead of 1..9 and <+100-999> loses its fixed width
rows.summary: You run a RegexpQuery, or a classic QueryParser query /<+1-+9>/, on a field with the terms 5 and 05. The RegExp javadoc says interval bounds are non-negative decimal integers and that bounds with the same number of digits fix the length of the matching strings, so you expect either an 'interval syntax error' (as for '-1', ' 1' or an overflowing bound) or the meaning of <1-9>, which matches 5. Instead the parser accepts the '+' and counts it as a digit, so <+1-+9> matches only 01 to 09 and returns 05; <+1-9> and <+100-999> lose their fixed width and accept any number of leading zeros, and <+100-+999> means 0100 to 0999.

rows.title: Automaton.copy while the receiver's current state is still open silently overwrites a copied state's transitions once that state is finished, because finishing it shrinks its block in place and moves the transition write position back into the copied block
rows.summary: You build an Automaton by hand: state 0 gets arcs 'a' and 'b' to state 1; while state 0 is still the state being built you append a small automaton x (0 -x-> 1, accepting) with copy, which becomes states 2 and 3, and then add state 1's arc 'c' to state 2, which by the class javadoc finishes state 0. You expect 0 -[a-b]-> 1 -c-> 2 -x-> 3, which accepts "acx", exactly what you get if you call finishState() before copy. Instead the automaton silently rejects "acx": finishing state 0 merges its two arcs into one in place and moves the transition write position back into the copied block, so state 1's new arc overwrites copied state 2's arc (state 2 now reads 2 -c-> 2 and state 3 is unreachable).
rows.area: util / automaton (Automaton.copy, finishState)

rows.title: Automaton.next(Transition, int) returns -1 for a label the state accepts when the Transition was positioned by initTransition, because initTransition stores an absolute transitions[] offset in Transition.transitionUpto and next() reads that field as an index among the state's own transitions (since 8.5.0)
rows.summary: You build the automaton 0 -a-> 1 -b-> 2, call initTransition(1, t) to position a Transition on state 1, and then call next(t, 'b'). You expect 2, the same as step(1, 'b'), because next() documents that it looks the label up starting from the Transition's source and transitionUpto, inclusive, and returns -1 only when no outgoing transition matches. Instead it returns -1 with no error: initTransition stores state 1's absolute offset into the transitions array (3) in transitionUpto, and next() reads that value as an index among state 1's own transitions (it has one), so its binary search never looks at the transition.

rows.title: RegExp(String, int, int) validates its two flag words with signed range comparisons instead of bit masks, so a syntax bit in match_flags next to a match bit (CASE_INSENSITIVE | INTERSECTION) or a negative flag word is accepted, and its stray bits take effect, instead of IllegalArgumentException (every release since 8.7.0)
rows.summary: You build new RegExp("a&b", RegExp.NONE, RegExp.CASE_INSENSITIVE | RegExp.INTERSECTION), with the syntax flag INTERSECTION put into the match-flags word by mistake. You expect IllegalArgumentException 'Illegal match flag', which the constructor throws for new RegExp("a&b", RegExp.NONE, RegExp.INTERSECTION), the same syntax bit alone. Instead no exception is thrown and '&' is parsed as intersection although syntax_flags is NONE, because the checks compare ranges ('match_flags > 0 && match_flags <= ALL', 'syntax_flags > ALL') instead of testing bits, so a match bit or the sign bit hides the stray bits, which then take effect through 'flags = syntax_flags | match_flags' (likewise new RegExp("a", -1) is accepted and matches "A").

rows.title: FSTCompiler.add passes the input's length where Arrays.mismatch expects an end index, so an IntsRef input with a non-zero offset gets a too-short shared prefix and the compiled FST silently lacks that key (unreleased regression on main from #13924)
rows.summary: You build an FST with FSTCompiler, add "ab" -> 1, then add "ac" -> 2 passed as an IntsRef slice that starts at offset 2 of a larger int[] (new IntsRef(new int[] {0, 0, 'a', 'c'}, 2, 2)), compile, and look up "ac"; IntsRef is documented as a slice (offset + length), add() only requires IntsRef#compareTo order, and 10.6.0 returns 2. On main, add() computes the shared prefix with Arrays.mismatch(lastInput.ints(), 0, lastInput.length(), input.ints, input.offset, input.length), whose last argument is an exclusive end index, so it compares an empty range, freezes the 'a' node of "ab" too early and gives the root a second arc labelled 'a'. With assertions off compile() returns normally and Util.get("ac") returns null ("ab" still answers 1); with -ea an assertion fires inside add().
rows.area: util / FST (FSTCompiler.add: the shared-prefix computation)

rows.title: IntsRefFSTEnum.seekCeil returns a term below the target (and seekFloor and seekExact answer wrongly) when a negative target int follows a prefix that is itself a term, because the seek compares it with the virtual end-of-term arc whose label is FST.END_LABEL = -1
rows.summary: You build a BYTE4 FST with [5] -> 1 and [5, 3] -> 2 and call seekCeil([5, Integer.MIN_VALUE]) on a fresh IntsRefFSTEnum; you expect [5, 3], the smallest term >= the target in IntsRef's signed order ([5] < [5, MIN_VALUE] < [5, 3]). Instead it returns [5], a term below the target, with or without assertions. IntsRefFSTEnum hands the raw target int to FSTEnum's arc scan, and the node after the final arc [5] starts with a virtual end-of-term arc labelled END_LABEL = -1, so a negative int either equals that label (-1) or sorts below it and the scan stops at [5]; seekFloor and seekExact go wrong the same way.
rows.area: util / FST (IntsRefFSTEnum seek targets vs. FSTEnum's virtual END_LABEL arc)

rows.title: Util.readCeilArc(FST.END_LABEL, ...) returns null on a non-final arc that has outgoing arcs, instead of its first outgoing arc, although the javadoc promises the first arc >= the label and every real label is greater than END_LABEL (-1); since 4.1.0
rows.summary: You build the FST {a, b} with the default FSTCompiler and call Util.readCeilArc(FST.END_LABEL, fst, start, new Arc, reader) on its start arc, which is not final because the empty string is not a key. You expect the arc 'a': the javadoc promises 'the first arc greater or equal than the given label', every real label is greater than END_LABEL (-1), the same call with label 0 or -2 returns 'a', and Lucene's own ceil seek (BytesRefFSTEnum.seekCeil) orders END_LABEL below every real label. Instead it returns null, because the method hands END_LABEL to FST.readEndArc, an exact 'is there an end arc?' lookup that returns null for a non-final arc without looking at its real arcs.

rows.title: Util.TopNSearcher computes TopResults.isComplete as rejectCount + topN <= maxQueueDepth in int, so with topN = Integer.MAX_VALUE, a bounded queue and one rejected result the sum wraps and isComplete is true although the queue dropped an accepted completion (every release since 4.8.0)
rows.summary: You subclass Util.TopNSearcher over the FST {a -> 1, b -> 2} with an acceptResult that rejects 'a', ask for every result (topN = Integer.MAX_VALUE) with a queue of depth 1, and call search(). You expect an empty result with isComplete false: the depth-1 queue dropped 'b', an accepted completion, and the flag's javadoc promises true only if the queue was large enough to find the complete list (topN = Integer.MAX_VALUE - 1 does give false). Instead isComplete is true, because search() computes rejectCount + topN <= maxQueueDepth in int and 1 + Integer.MAX_VALUE wraps to Integer.MIN_VALUE.

rows.title: FSTCompiler.Builder#directAddressingMaxOversizingFactor is documented so that any negative factor disables direct addressing, but a very negative one (Float.NEGATIVE_INFINITY, -Float.MAX_VALUE, or about -1e8 and below) saturates the int cost arithmetic in shouldExpandNodeWithDirectAddressing and turns direct addressing on, so five sparse BYTE4 keys give a 33.5 MB FST instead of 34 bytes (since 8.4.0)
rows.summary: You build an FST with FSTCompiler.Builder and set directAddressingMaxOversizingFactor(Float.NEGATIVE_INFINITY), because its javadoc says a negative value disables direct addressing and only binary-search nodes will be created. You expect the root node of five BYTE4 keys with labels 0, 1, 2, 3 and 2^28 to be a binary-search node and the FST to take 34 bytes, as it does with -1 or the default. Instead (int) (sizeForBinarySearch * factor) saturates to Integer.MIN_VALUE, the int subtraction for expansionCost wraps to a negative value, the node is written with direct addressing and the FST takes 33,554,447 bytes, almost all of them presence bits for the 2^28 label range; every key is still found.
rows.area: util / FST (FSTCompiler fixed-length node encoding: binary search vs direct addressing)

rows.title: An NRT DirectoryTaxonomyReader reopened during DirectoryTaxonomyWriter.replaceTaxonomy keeps the replaced taxonomy's ordinal/label caches and parent arrays, because the epoch is incremented only after the content change (wrong labels that persist, or ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException from openIfChanged)
rows.summary: You keep a near-real-time taxonomy reader open on a DirectoryTaxonomyWriter and refresh it with openIfChanged while the writer swaps in a rebuilt taxonomy with replaceTaxonomy, for example [a, b] replaced by [b, a]. You expect the refreshed reader to show either the old taxonomy or the new one, each with its own ordinals and labels, as the reader/writer concurrency contract and the reader's own 'was the taxonomy recreated?' check intend. Instead, a refresh that lands after the new content is visible but before replaceTaxonomy increments its epoch is treated as a plain append and reuses the replaced taxonomy's caches and parent arrays: it answers getOrdinal(a)=1 and getPath(1)=a, facet counts over the new index (three b documents, one a) come out labelled 'a (3), b (1)' instead of 'b (3), a (1)', and every later openIfChanged returns null, so the wrong reader stays current until the taxonomy changes again (with a smaller replacement the refresh throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException instead).
rows.area: facet / taxonomy NRT reopen (DirectoryTaxonomyWriter.replaceTaxonomy and deleteAll epoch vs DirectoryTaxonomyReader.doOpenIfChanged)

rows.title: An orphaned NRT reader can report isCurrent() true for different index content after a new writer session
rows.summary: You keep an NRT reader after its writer is rolled back or closed, then open a new writer on the same directory and change the index. You expect reader.isCurrent() to return false. Instead SegmentInfos.version restarts in each writer session and the closed-writer branch of isCurrent compares only versions, so the stale reader reports true for different content.

rows.title: IndexWriter opened from an older reader's IndexCommit takes SegmentInfos.version from that reader, not from the newest commit, so its commits can reuse the version of a newer commit and a reader still open on that commit reports isCurrent()=true and openIfChanged returns null
rows.summary: You keep an older commit (for example with NoDeletionPolicy or a snapshot), open a reader on it, and later go back to it by opening a new IndexWriter with setIndexCommit(thatReader.getIndexCommit()) and committing, while another reader is still open on a newer commit. You expect that reader to notice the new commits (isCurrent() false, openIfChanged returning the latest commit), as it does when the same commit is taken from DirectoryReader.listCommits. Instead the writer restarts SegmentInfos.version from the old reader instead of from the newest commit, so one of its commits can get exactly the newer commit's version (segments_3 holding [a, b, c] and segments_5 holding [a] are both version 10), and the stale reader reports isCurrent()=true, openIfChanged returns null and SearcherLifetimeManager.record throws IllegalArgumentException.

rows.title: Data race on SegmentInfos.version between newSegmentName and checkpoint
rows.summary: Several indexing threads allocate new segment names while the writer checkpoints. You expect every SegmentInfos.version increment to be kept, so the version check of a reader is reliable. Instead newSegmentName increments the version under synchronized(segmentInfos) while other increments hold the IndexWriter monitor, so an increment can be lost or go backwards and a stale reader can look current.

rows.title: IndexWriter.prepareCommit() re-reads the shared pendingSeqNo field after its post-commit maybeMerge, so if another thread finishes that commit and prepares the next one meanwhile, prepareCommit() returns the next commit's sequence number
rows.summary: The main thread adds a document and thread A calls IndexWriter.prepareCommit(); while A is still in the merge step that prepareCommit() runs after publishing its pending commit, the main thread calls commit() (which finishes A's commit and returns 3), adds another document (sequence number 4) and calls prepareCommit() again. You expect A's prepareCommit() to return 3, as its javadoc promises ('All sequence numbers <= this value will be reflected in the commit, and all others will not') and as commit() returned for the same commit. Instead it returns 6, the next commit's number, because prepareCommit() re-reads the shared pendingSeqNo field after its maybeMerge instead of returning its own result; the committed index itself is correct.

rows.title: addIndexes(CodecReader...) can register a merge and start a merge thread after a concurrent rollback() has returned, because AddIndexesMergeSource.registerMerge does not re-check that merges are enabled
rows.summary: You call addIndexes(CodecReader...) on one thread while another thread calls rollback() on the same writer (or the writer closes itself after a tragic error). You expect that once rollback() has returned the writer is closed and starts no more merges, so the addIndexes call just fails; Lucene's own TestAddIndexes rollback tests assert that no merge thread is left. Instead, if rollback() lands while addIndexes is asking the merge policy for its merges, the merge is registered after rollback has already aborted all merges, and ConcurrentMergeScheduler starts a new merge thread after rollback() and the scheduler's close() have returned; that thread throws an uncaught MergeException (AlreadyClosedException 'Lock instance already released' on 10.3.0 and later, 'this IndexWriter is closed' on 9.4.0-10.2.2) and addIndexes throws AlreadyClosedException.

rows.title: MergeObserver.await() and await(timeout) return true after a failed or aborted merge, although their javadoc says they return false on error
rows.summary: You call IndexWriter.forceMergeDeletes(false), which starts the merges in the background and returns a MergeObserver, and then call observer.await() to learn whether they worked; its javadoc says it returns true if all merges completed successfully and false on error. Instead it returns true even when the merge failed with an IOException or was aborted by rollback() or deleteAll(), because every merge's completion future is completed normally with a success flag that await() never reads. A caller that trusts the result believes the deleted documents were merged away although the merge never finished.

rows.title: A ReferenceManager refresh that throws is reported to its refresh listeners as afterRefresh(false), the same signal as 'nothing changed', so ControlledRealTimeReopenThread.waitForGeneration returns true for a change the current searcher does not contain and LiveFieldValues drops the values it buffered
rows.summary: You add, delete or update a document and wait for it with ControlledRealTimeReopenThread.waitForGeneration (or record its value in LiveFieldValues), and the next refresh of the SearcherManager throws, for example because a warm-up query in the SearcherFactory fails or an I/O error hits while the new segment is opened. You expect waitForGeneration to keep waiting or time out, and LiveFieldValues to keep the value, because the old searcher is still current and does not contain the change. Instead ReferenceManager.doMaybeRefresh calls every listener's afterRefresh(false) from a finally block, the same call a refresh that found nothing to do makes, so ControlledRealTimeReopenThread advances its searching generation and wakes the waiters with true, and LiveFieldValues throws away its buffered values.

rows.title: NRT PrimaryNode: one I/O error during flushAndRefresh leaves the new point unpublished to replicas, and the retry reports no changes
rows.summary: You run Lucene's NRT segment replication, index a document and call PrimaryNode.flushAndRefresh; it throws because opening one of the new files hits a transient I/O error, and once the error is gone you call flushAndRefresh again. You expect the retry to publish the new point to replicas, or the failed call to have left the previous point fully in place. Instead the failed call had already switched the primary's current point and released the previous point's files, but not the copy state that replicas are given, so the retry returns false ('no changes'), getCopyStateVersion() stays behind getCurrentSearchingVersion(), and replicas are not offered the new point until the index changes again.
rows.area: replicator / NRT segment replication (PrimaryNode.flushAndRefresh, setCurrentInfos: NRT point publication)

rows.title: An NRT replica's commit() can store in VERSION_KEY the version of a newer NRT point installed during its fsync, so the commit claims a version ahead of the SegmentInfos it holds
rows.summary: You run Lucene's NRT segment replication and call commit() on a replica while the primary keeps publishing NRT points, and during the commit's fsync the replica installs a newer point (version 5, documents [d1, d2]). You expect the commit's VERSION_KEY to name the version whose content it holds (version 3, [d1]), or at worst an older one, because the module uses that value as the place to resume replaying operations and PrimaryNode.commit accepts only a lagging value ('replaying more ops than necessary'). Instead commit() writes the SegmentInfos it captured before the fsync (version 3) but reads VERSION_KEY from the searcher that is current after it (5), so a primary started on that commit reports getLastCommitVersion()=5 while it holds only d1, and a replay from version 5 skips d2.

rows.title: An NRT replica acts on a late notification from an older primary generation: ReplicaNode.maybeNewPrimary deletes the current primary's pre-copied merged segment before its only check, an assert, so the replica's cut-over to the merged point fails or the segment is copied again (with or without assertions), and with assertions off lastPrimaryGen also moves back
rows.summary: You run Lucene's NRT segment replication and fail over cleanly: the old primary (generation 1) is closed, then replica A is promoted to primary (generation 2), and replica B follows A and pre-copies A's merged segment. A last notification from the old primary, delayed in transit, then reaches B; you expect B to ignore it, as it already ignores out-of-order older NRT versions, because the primary generation only ever grows. Instead ReplicaNode.maybeNewPrimary treats the older generation as a primary change and deletes A's pre-copied merged files before its only check (an assert), so B's cut-over to A's merged point fails with '_3.si cannot be read - it may be missing or corrupt' or B copies the merged segment again, and with assertions off B also sets lastPrimaryGen back to 1.

rows.title: An NRT replica's merge pre-copy callback (ReplicaNode.launchPreCopyMerge) synchronizes on itself instead of the ReplicaNode, so a primary change that lands while it installs the merged files leaves the old primary's pre-copied merged files pending and on disk
rows.summary: You run Lucene's NRT segment replication with merge pre-copy: the primary asks replica B to pre-copy a merged segment, and just as B has copied the bytes and is renaming the files into place, another node is promoted to primary and B receives its first NRT point (primaryGen 2). You expect B either to install the merged files and then discard them in the switch, or to notice the switch and cancel the pre-copy, because newNRTPoint says it discards the old primary's pre-copied merged segments and the callback itself checks whether the primary changed. Instead the callback's synchronized (this) locks the anonymous CopyJob.OnceDone, not the ReplicaNode, so the switch runs in the middle of it and B follows primaryGen 2 with the old primary's merged files [_2.cfe, _2.cfs, _2.si] still in pendingMergeFiles and on disk (with -ea, the new primary's later pre-copy of a same-named merged segment then fails with 'file "_2.si" is already being warmed!').

rows.title: ReplicaNode.newNRTPoint leaves curNRTCopy set to a cancelled, never-launched CopyJob when CopyJob.start() throws NodeCommunicationException, so isCopying() stays true although nothing is being copied (NRT replicator, every release since 6.0.0)

You expect newNRTPoint to give up on that point and go back to idle, so isCopying() returns false, as it does when the job cannot even be created. Instead newNRTPoint returns null and resets its state to idle, but curNRTCopy was already set to the job before start() and the catch block never clears it; the job is never launched, so its OnceDone (finishNRTCopy) never runs either, and isCopying() stays true until a later, newer NRT point replaces the job.

rows.title: SearcherLifetimeManager.prune orders searchers by the time each was first recorded instead of newest to oldest, so when an older searcher is first recorded after the current one, PruneByAge drops the current searcher (even right after record() returned a token for it) and keeps the older one
rows.summary: You use SearcherManager with SearcherLifetimeManager as the javadoc shows: request A acquires searcher S1, the manager refreshes to S2, request B acquires and records S2, and then A records S1. You expect prune to pass the searchers newest to oldest, as its javadoc says, so PruneByAge never drops S2, the current searcher. Instead prune sorts them by the time each was first recorded, so S1 goes first with age 0 and S2 is aged from S1's late record: 250 ms later, request C records S2 and gets a token, prune(new PruneByAge(0.1)) drops S2 anyway, acquire(token) returns null, and the older S1 is kept.

rows.title: ReferenceManager.maybeRefresh releases the new reference it has just made current when releasing the old one throws, so every later acquire() throws IllegalStateException (since 3.5.0)
rows.summary: You call maybeRefresh on a ReferenceManager (for example a SearcherManager), and releasing the old reference inside the swap throws an IOException, which decRef is documented to do; you expect maybeRefresh to throw it and the manager to stay usable, with acquire() returning the new current reference. Instead swapReference has already made the new reference current (ReferenceManager.java:56) before it releases the old one (:57), and doMaybeRefresh's cleanup finally, which exists for a new reference the swap never installed, releases it anyway (:174-178), so the manager drops its own count on its current reference and closes it. Every later acquire() then throws IllegalStateException 'The managed reference has already closed - this is likely a bug when the reference count is modified outside of the ReferenceManager', blaming the caller for a state the manager created itself.

rows.title: BayesianScoreQuery raises the minimum competitive score to at least 1e-7 before passing it to its inner query, so default top-k search silently drops the best hits when every competitive calibrated score is below 1e-7
rows.summary: You run an ordinary top-k search such as searcher.search(query, 10) with a BayesianScoreQuery whose calibrated scores (probabilities) are all below 1e-7, and more than 1,000 documents match. You expect the same top hits as an exhaustive search, because the scores are a monotone transform of the inner BM25 scores and explain() reports exactly those scores. Instead, once the collector starts pruning, BayesianScoreQuery rounds the requested minimum score up to 1e-7 before turning it into a BM25 threshold for the inner query, so the inner query skips documents that are still competitive and the search returns weaker hits (in the repros, in effect the first matches in doc-id order) with no error.
rows.area: search / top-k dynamic pruning (BayesianScoreQuery: BayesianScoreScorer#setMinCompetitiveScore)

rows.title: BayesianScoreQuery turns the minimum competitive probability into an inner-score threshold that lies inside the range of inner scores with exactly that probability, so default top-k search can skip a hit that is still competitive
rows.summary: You run an ordinary top-k search such as searcher.search(query, 10) with a BayesianScoreQuery, and more than 1,000 documents match. You expect the same top hits as an exhaustive search, because the probability is a monotone function of the inner score and pruning may skip only documents that score below the current k-th hit. Instead, when a later document's probability is exactly one float step above the k-th hit's (most often when probabilities are close to 1), BayesianScoreQuery turns that probability back into an inner-score threshold with a closed-form inverse that lands in the middle of the range of inner scores that all round to that probability, so the inner query skips the document and the search silently returns the weaker hit.
rows.area: search / top-k dynamic pruning (BayesianScoreQuery: BayesianScoreScorer#setMinCompetitiveScore)

rows.title: ScorerUtil.minRequiredScore returns NaN when the minimum competitive score is +Infinity, so block-max conjunctions and MaxScore disjunctions drop documents that score +Infinity
rows.summary: You run an ordinary top-k search, for example IndexSearcher#search(query, 1), with a two-clause conjunction or disjunction whose scores can overflow to +Infinity (two FeatureField linear queries over very large feature values, or two clauses with very large finite boosts). You expect the best documents first, +Infinity before Float.MAX_VALUE and ties by ascending doc id, as Lucene 10.2.2 returns them. Instead, once the minimum competitive score reaches +Infinity, ScorerUtil.minRequiredScore returns NaN and filterCompetitiveHits discards every remaining candidate, so the search silently returns doc 0 scoring Float.MAX_VALUE instead of doc 3000 scoring +Infinity (one thread, one segment), or docs 100, 101, 102 instead of the equally scored docs 0, 1, 2 (a concurrent search in which the slice with the higher doc ids finishes first).
rows.area: search / top-k dynamic pruning (block-max conjunction and MaxScore bulk scorers)

rows.title: WANDScorer mishandles a minimum competitive score of +Infinity: an assertion fails with -ea, and with -da it prunes documents that score +Infinity
rows.summary: You run a top-k search whose top-level disjunction runs on WANDScorer, for example three FeatureField linear SHOULD clauses with minimumNumberShouldMatch 2, over documents whose finite clause scores add up past Float.MAX_VALUE, so that they score +Infinity. You expect the same documents as an exhaustive (COMPLETE) search: hits tied at +Infinity stay competitive and are ordered by doc id (or by the next sort field). Instead, once the collector raises the minimum competitive score to +Infinity, WANDScorer.scaleMinScore fails its 'Float.isFinite(minScore)' assertion with -ea (even in a single-threaded search), and with -da it saturates the bound to Long.MAX_VALUE and prunes every remaining document, so a concurrent search with the default slicing returns docs 23, 24, 25 instead of 0, 1, 2, all scoring +Infinity.
rows.area: search / top-k dynamic pruning (WANDScorer)

rows.title: DisjunctionMaxQuery with tie-breaker 0 scores NaN instead of +Infinity when two matching disjuncts score +Infinity (Infinity + Infinity * 0), so COMPLETE-mode collection, some BooleanQuery nestings and explain() disagree with the default top-k search (since 1.9)
rows.summary: You index one document with two FeatureField features a = b = 1e38 and search DisjunctionMaxQuery([FeatureField.newLinearQuery(f, a, 64), newLinearQuery(f, b, 64)], tieBreakerMultiplier 0) with a collector that counts every hit (TopScoreDocCollectorManager(1, Integer.MAX_VALUE)). Each disjunct scores 64 * 1e38 = +Infinity, so with tie 0 you expect the maximum, +Infinity, which is what the default search(q, n) and DisjunctionMaxScorer.getMaxScore give. You get NaN, with no error: DisjunctionMaxScorer.score moves the first +Infinity into the sum of the other scores and returns Infinity + Infinity * 0 = NaN, and explain() and some BooleanQuery nestings give NaN too, so the same document's score and rank depend on how the query is executed.

rows.title: DisjunctionMaxQuery and LatLonPoint.newDistanceFeatureQuery accept a NaN tie-breaker or pivot distance (the pivot also +Infinity) because their range checks are false for NaN, so hits score NaN and a NaN query is not equal to itself
rows.summary: You build a DisjunctionMaxQuery with tieBreakerMultiplier NaN (for example a computed value, or the XML query parser text tieBreaker='NaN'), or a LatLonPoint.newDistanceFeatureQuery with pivotDistance NaN or +Infinity, and expect the IllegalArgumentException that both constructors already throw for every other out-of-range value ('tieBreakerMultiplier must be in [0, 1]', 'pivotDistance must be > 0'). Instead the value is accepted, because the checks are written as 'x < 0 || x > 1' and 'x <= 0', which are false for NaN (and '<= 0' is false for +Infinity): on main the hits come back with NaN scores, although the distance feature javadoc promises scores in [0, weight], and for a NaN value q.equals(q) is false because equals compares the field with ==. Older releases are worse: with a NaN tie-breaker, 8.0.0 and 8.11.4 return no top-k hits while count() finds them, and 9.12.3 with assertions off returns a sentinel ScoreDoc (doc 2147483647, score -Infinity) in place of a hit.

rows.title: XYDocValuesField.newDistanceSort accepts a NaN or infinite origin although its javadoc promises IllegalArgumentException for invalid coordinates (the LatLon twin and every other XY entry point reject such values); with a NaN origin, documents without a location sort first instead of last
rows.summary: You build a distance sort with XYDocValuesField.newDistanceSort("p", Float.NaN, 0f), or with an infinite x or y, and expect the IllegalArgumentException that its javadoc promises when the 'location has invalid coordinates', as LatLonDocValuesField.newDistanceSort throws for NaN and as the XYDocValuesField constructor, XYPointField.newDistanceQuery and XYCircle throw for the same values. Instead the sort is built and the search runs, because the XYPointSortField constructor checks only that the field name is not null. With a NaN origin every distance is NaN, which Double.compare orders after +Infinity, so a document without a location (distance +Infinity, documented as 'missing values sort last') is returned before the documents that have one; with an infinite origin all distances tie at +Infinity.

rows.title: SimpleRateLimiter.pause sleeps about 24.9 days for any remaining pause between about 2.5 and 24.9 days (up to 10x too long), because its int-overflow guard compares with 100000L * Integer.MAX_VALUE ns instead of 1000000L * Integer.MAX_VALUE ns (since 4.10.3)
rows.summary: You throttle IO with RateLimiter.SimpleRateLimiter and one call to pause needs, say, 3 days (259,200 bytes at 1 byte/s, or 3 days of bytes at 1 MB/s). You expect pause to sleep about 3 days, as it does for a 2-day pause and as it did up to 4.10.2. Instead the guard that is meant only to keep an int cast from overflowing fires at 100000L * Integer.MAX_VALUE ns (2.49 days) rather than at 1000000L * Integer.MAX_VALUE ns (24.86 days, where the cast really overflows), so pause asks Thread.sleep for Integer.MAX_VALUE ms and the thread sleeps 24.86 days, 8.3x the pause; every remaining pause between 2.49 and 24.86 days sleeps 24.86 days.

You expect StoredFields#document to return it, as it does for a string one character shorter. Instead every read throws java.lang.OutOfMemoryError 'UTF16 String size is 1073741823, should be less than 1073741823', whatever the heap, because DataInput.readString decodes with new String(bytes, 0, length, UTF_8), which on JDK 9 and later sizes its UTF-16 buffer by the byte count and refuses 2^30 - 1 or more units; merges that copy the document through a visitor, and flushes of an index-sorted writer, throw the same Error and close IndexWriter.

rows.title: BKDWriter does not cap its in-heap point buffer at the Java array limit, so with maxMBSortInHeap >= 2048 MB a points merge of more than 2^31 bytes throws NegativeArraySizeException and closes the IndexWriter
rows.summary: You give a points format a sort budget of 2048 MB or more, for example new Lucene90PointsWriter(state, 512, 2200.0) in a custom codec, and merge segments that hold more than 2 GiB of points of one multi-dimensional field (in the repro 8.4M points of 16 dims x 16 bytes). You expect the merge to succeed, because BKDWriter 'uses up to the specified maxMBSortInHeap heap space for writing', spills to disk beyond it, and its constructor accepts the value. Instead BKDWriter sizes its in-heap buffer as budget / bytesPerDoc points with no cap at the Java array limit, HeapPointWriter computes bytesPerDoc * size in int, the length wraps negative, and forceMerge(1) throws NegativeArraySizeException (-2110967296) and leaves the IndexWriter closed with that tragic exception.

rows.title: A single indexed token of 715,827,878 or more UTF-16 units closes IndexWriter and drops uncommitted documents instead of being rejected as an immense term
rows.summary: You index a document whose untokenized indexed field (or a TextField analyzed with KeywordAnalyzer) holds one value of 715,827,878 or more characters, for example 'a' repeated 715,827,883 times. You expect what Lucene does for any over-long term: addDocument throws the documented 'immense term' IllegalArgumentException, skips that document and keeps the IndexWriter open with the other buffered documents. Instead the UTF-16 to UTF-8 conversion sizes its buffer at 3 bytes per character before the length check, that size overflows int (ArithmeticException) or exceeds the maximum array length (IllegalArgumentException), and because the conversion runs inside the indexing chain's aborting try, IndexWriter closes itself and rolls back every document added since the last commit.

rows.title: During a commit or NRT refresh, deleteDocuments(Term...) and doc-values updates never wait on the delete-buffer stall added by #16867, so the shared delete buffer still grows past its hard limit and can overflow at 2 GiB (main and branch_11x only)
rows.summary: On Lucene main with #16867, one thread runs a commit or NRT refresh while another calls deleteDocuments(Term...) or a doc-values update (updateNumericDocValue, updateBinaryDocValue, updateDocValues). You expect these calls to be held at #16867's new 'hard limit' on the shared delete buffer, as document adds and updates (softUpdateDocument included) are, so that the buffer can no longer overflow. Instead only document adds and updates wait on the new stall: the delete and doc-values-update calls keep filling the buffer (to 8x a cap lowered to 256 KB in the repro), and at the real 1945 MB cap they still overflow it at 2 GiB with ArithmeticException 'integer overflow', after which the writer fails every flush and commit until rollback().

rows.title: ByteSliceReader's final-slice test (nextIndex + newSize >= endIndex) overflows int when a postings stream's last slice ends exactly at the 2^31-byte end of the in-RAM byte pool, so IndexWriter silently commits up to 3 wrong postings bytes that CheckIndex accepts
rows.summary: You add one very large document whose postings fill the indexing thread's in-RAM byte pool to its very last byte (global offset 2^31), and you expect the flushed segment to hold exactly the positions and payloads you indexed, or a loud failure such as the ArithmeticException Lucene has thrown since 9.8.0 once the pool would grow further. Instead, if one term's postings stream ends in the slice that occupies the pool's last bytes, ByteSliceReader.nextSlice computes nextIndex + newSize = 2^31 in int, which wraps negative, so it treats that final slice as non-final, reads its last 3 data bytes plus the level marker as a forwarding address, and returns the stream's last 1-3 bytes from an unrelated part of the pool. IndexWriter commits with no exception (with -ea and -da) and CheckIndex reports the segment clean; in the executed run the last 3 bytes of a 355-byte payload, 0x41 0x42 0x43, read back as 0x11.

rows.title: After one document overflows an in-memory segment's 2 GiB doc-values byte pool (a non-aborting ArithmeticException), the next document's new SORTED or SORTED_SET value is silently stored as another value, because ByteBlockPool.nextBuffer installs the new block before its overflow check throws
rows.summary: You index one document whose distinct SortedSetDocValuesField values (each up to 32766 bytes) add up to more than the in-memory segment's 2 GiB doc-values byte pool; addDocument throws ArithmeticException 'integer overflow', the document is deleted and the writer stays open, as for any non-aborting failure. You expect the next document, which has one SortedDocValuesField value "b", to be stored with "b" (or itself rejected). Instead its value is written into the pool's new block but recorded at the start of the previous block, so the segment is flushed with another value already in the pool (in the model run, the rejected document's last 32763-byte value) and no error, because ByteBlockPool.nextBuffer installs the new block, increments bufferUpto and resets byteUpto before its Math.addExact overflow check throws, leaving byteOffset one block behind.

rows.title: HNSW merge with graph reuse throws BufferAllocationException when the reused graph has more than 805,306,368 vectors
rows.summary: You merge an HNSW vector field in which one segment's graph has more than 805,306,368 vectors (Lucene writes such a segment without error, for example by merging smaller graphs) and expect the merge to reuse that graph as it does at any smaller size, because no HNSW vector-count limit is documented or enforced below IndexWriter.MAX_DOCS. Instead both mergers presize an IntIntHashMap to the graph size to map old to new ordinals, and that map's fixed 0.75 load factor and 2^30-slot table cap make its constructor throw BufferAllocationException ('Maximum array size exceeded for this load factor') before any other work. The merge fails again on every retry, so such a segment can never be merged with graph reuse; by code reading the IndexWriter is also closed as a tragic event.
