rows.title: ReqExclBulkScorer.WindowBits.applyMask adds offset + bitSet.length() in int, so FILTER/MUST + MUST_NOT queries silently drop every match in a 4096-doc window based at doc 2^31-4096 or above (up to the last 3,967 doc IDs of a segment near IndexWriter.MAX_DOCS)
rows.summary: You index one segment of IndexWriter.MAX_DOCS (2,147,483,519) documents with default settings, one of which has b:y, and count the matches of +*:* -b:y (MatchAllDocsQuery as FILTER plus a MUST_NOT term query) with a plain IndexSearcher; you expect 2,147,483,518. Instead you get 2,147,479,551: all 3,967 documents of the last window [2,147,479,552, MAX_DOCS) are silently missing, because ReqExclBulkScorer's WindowBits.applyMask computes Math.min(NO_MORE_DOCS, offset + bitSet.length()) in int, the sum wraps negative for a 4096-bit window based at 2^31-4096 or above, and the method then clears the whole window. Only segments with more than 2,147,479,552 documents and required clauses denser than 0.3% of maxDoc are affected, and only code since #16669 has the bug: 10.6.0 (released 2026-10-29), main and branch_10x.
rows.area: search / BooleanQuery MUST_NOT bulk scoring (ReqExclBulkScorer)

rows.title: Postings readers count skipped positions in an int, so once the skipped occurrences of one term within a postings block pass Integer.MAX_VALUE, nextPosition() returns an earlier document's positions and phrase queries silently miss matches
rows.summary: You index documents that each stay within Lucene's per-document limits but repeat one term about a billion times and run PhraseQuery f:"v t", which only C matches. You expect the postings reader to return C's own positions (101, 102, 103, ...) and the query to find C. Instead the reader adds up the frequencies of the documents whose positions it skipped in an int, the sum 2,147,483,696 wraps negative, the skip is not done, and nextPosition() returns the first skipped document's positions (1, 2, 3), so the query finds 0 hits with assertions off (with assertions on, an internal assertion fails instead).
rows.area: codecs / postings reader (Lucene104 BlockPostingsEnum position bookkeeping; also the Lucene101, Lucene103, Lucene99 and Lucene90 readers in backward-codecs)

rows.title: SweetSpotSimilarity.lengthNorm adds abs(x-min) + abs(x-max) in int, so a field of 1,073,741,848 or more terms (reachable with one custom term frequency) gets a NaN norm: the document is never collected, and default top-k search also skips competitive documents in the same postings block and skip range
rows.summary: You score with SweetSpotSimilarity (default factors) and index one document whose DOCS_AND_FREQS field has a length of at least 1,073,741,848, for example one token with custom term frequency 1.1e9 or about 1.07e9 ordinary tokens, expecting the documented lengthNorm 1/sqrt(x) (about 3.05e-5, the ClassicSimilarity value) and an ordinary, low-ranked hit. Instead lengthNorm's int sum |x-1| + |x-1| wraps negative, so the norm and the score are NaN and the document is never collected (exhaustive collection returns 5,999 of 6,000 matches); because the NaN also makes the postings block's maximum score NaN, default top-k search skips that block and the skip range above it, so search(q, 7) on a 10,000-document index misses three documents that score 1.0 and returns documents that score 0.5 instead. ClassicSimilarity on the same index is correct.
rows.area: misc / similarities (SweetSpotSimilarity lengthNorm; NaN effect on impacts-based top-k pruning in core search)

rows.title: FreeTextSuggester.decodeWeight casts n-gram counts to int, so a word or context seen more than Integer.MAX_VALUE times gets a negative or wrapped count: lookup returns scores outside the documented 0.0 to 1.0 range and can rank the most frequent word last
rows.summary: You build a FreeTextSuggester from text in which one word occurs more than Integer.MAX_VALUE (2,147,483,647) times and expect lookup to rank that word first with a score near 1.0, because the class javadoc says each result value is Long.MAX_VALUE times a score from 0.0 to 1.0 and build() counts n-grams as long. Instead decodeWeight returns (int) (Long.MAX_VALUE - output), so a count of 2,148,532,224 comes back as -2,146,435,072 and lookup('a', 2) returns [ab score 0.0, a score -0.999]: a negative score, with the most frequent word ranked below a word seen once. The same cast decodes context counts, so every prediction from a context seen that often is scored wrongly, and counts above 2^32 wrap to small positive numbers that stay inside the 0..1 range and are silently wrong.
rows.area: suggest / FreeTextSuggester (n-gram counts stored as long FST outputs; lookup-side decode)

rows.title: ByteBuffersDataOutput.copyBytes narrows its long length to a signed int, so a copy of 2 GiB or more (for example Directory.copyFrom into a ByteBuffersDirectory) silently copies nothing or only (int) numBytes bytes
rows.summary: You copy 2 GiB or more into an in-heap ByteBuffersDataOutput, for example with Directory.copyFrom or IndexWriter.addIndexes(Directory) into a ByteBuffersDirectory. You expect every byte to be copied, as DataOutput.copyBytes(DataInput, long numBytes) promises ('Copy numBytes bytes from input to ourself') and as Lucene 9.2.0 does. Instead the override stores the length in an int, copies max(0, (int) numBytes) bytes (nothing at all for any length from 2^31 to 2^32-1) and returns normally, so the destination file is empty or truncated with no exception; a copied index then fails to open with CorruptIndexException.

rows.title: Stored fields writer: the int slice loop in flush() wraps once a chunk is larger than 2,147,450,880 bytes, so a ~2 GiB document within the documented per-document limit closes IndexWriter when smaller documents are still buffered in its chunk
rows.summary: You index a small document and then, before the chunk fills, one document with about 2 GiB of stored content that is within the documented per-document limit, for example exactly 2^31 - 81,920 = 2,147,401,728 serialized bytes after a 49,153-byte document. You expect both to be indexed, as they are when the first document is one byte smaller. Instead flush() steps through the chunk with an int offset that wraps past Integer.MAX_VALUE, ByteBuffersDataInput.slice rejects the negative offset with IllegalArgumentException, and IndexWriter closes itself and drops every uncommitted document.

rows.title: Compressor.compress casts ByteBuffersDataInput.length() to int, so an input of 2^32 + k bytes is compressed as only its first k bytes and the call returns normally
rows.summary: You build a valid ByteBuffersDataInput of 2^32 + k bytes (here 4097 views of one 1 MiB buffer, so nothing is copied) and call CompressionMode.FAST.newCompressor().compress(in, out); you expect the whole input to be compressed, or an exception if it is too large. Instead compress returns normally after reading and compressing only the first k bytes (1 MiB of 4,296,015,872), leaving the input positioned at k, and the block it wrote decodes to just that prefix. All five core compressors start with 'final int len = (int) buffersInput.length()' (or length() - position() in the preset-dict modes), and for a length of 2^32 + k that cast yields k.
rows.area: codecs / compressing (Compressor.compress in CompressionMode FAST, FAST_DECOMPRESSION, HIGH_COMPRESSION and the Lucene90 preset-dict compressors)

rows.title: Lucene90StoredFieldsFormat (the default codec's stored fields) documents a per-document limit of 2^31 - 2^14 bytes, but the format it delegates to documents and enforces 2^31 - chunkSize (chunks of 81,920 / 491,520 bytes), so a document just below the stated limit can fail with ArithmeticException and close IndexWriter (documentation defect: the javadoc value has been stale since the chunks grew past 16 KiB)
rows.summary: You read the default codec's stored-fields documentation (Lucene90StoredFieldsFormat, 'Known limitations'), which says only individual documents larger than 2^31 - 2^14 = 2,147,467,264 bytes are unsupported, and you index a document of 2,147,403,644 serialized bytes, below that limit, right after a small document. addDocument fails with ArithmeticException ('integer overflow') and IndexWriter closes itself, while the same big document on its own is indexed. The writer does what the class it delegates to, Lucene90CompressingStoredFieldsFormat, documents (at most 2^31 - chunkSize bytes, with chunks of 81,920 or 491,520 bytes today); the outer javadoc's number was right only when chunks were 16 KiB and was never updated.

rows.title: addIndexes(CodecReader...) with the default config rejects inputs whose maxDoc() sum, deleted documents included, exceeds MAX_DOCS although only their live documents are added, because it always builds a merged view of the inputs for OneMerge#reorder (regression since 9.9.0)
rows.summary: You call IndexWriter.addIndexes(CodecReader...) with readers that have many deleted or filtered-out documents, so their live documents fit under IndexWriter.MAX_DOCS but their maxDoc() values (deleted documents included) add up to more. You expect the call to succeed, since addIndexes counts and reserves only live documents, its javadoc throws IllegalArgumentException only if the index would exceed MAX_DOCS, and 9.8.0 accepted the same call. Instead, with the default configuration it throws IllegalArgumentException 'Too many documents: composite IndexReaders cannot exceed ...' and adds nothing, because since 9.9.0 addIndexesReaderMerge always wraps the inputs in a SlowCompositeCodecReaderWrapper (a MultiReader over the uncompacted inputs) for OneMerge#reorder, whose default returns null and discards the view.

rows.title: MultiPassIndexSplitter's round-robin split loses or duplicates the last few documents of an index at about IndexWriter.MAX_DOCS for most part counts of 145 or more, because its int test (j + numParts - i) % numParts overflows
rows.summary: You split an index of IndexWriter.MAX_DOCS (2,147,483,519) documents with MultiPassIndexSplitter in round-robin mode, the command-line default, into 145 parts, and expect every document in exactly one part (part i gets the documents whose id j has j % numParts == i), as the split javadoc says: ids are 'assigned in a deterministic round-robin fashion to one of the output splits'. Instead the parts hold 2,147,483,527 documents in total: documents 2,147,483,511..518 belong to parts 16..23 but are also copied into parts 0..7, and with 149 parts documents 2,147,483,509..518 end up in no part at all; nothing reports an error. The cause is the keep test (j + numParts - i) % numParts == 0 at MultiPassIndexSplitter.java:103, computed in int: for the top doc ids j + numParts - i wraps negative and Java's % keeps the sign, while the equivalent j % numParts == i cannot overflow.
rows.area: misc / index tools (MultiPassIndexSplitter.split, round-robin mode)

rows.title: Index sorting by a STRING field with STRING_LAST: at merge, a document without a value gets the int key Integer.MAX_VALUE while documents with a value get long global ordinals, so when the inputs of one merge hold more than 2^31 - 1 distinct values (reachable through IndexWriter.addIndexes(CodecReader...)), the merged segment silently puts documents without a value ahead of documents with a value
rows.summary: You configure the index sort new SortField("s", SortField.Type.STRING, false, SortField.STRING_LAST) and merge, with IndexWriter.addIndexes(CodecReader...), sorted source indexes whose 's' dictionaries together hold more than 2^31 - 1 distinct values, expecting documents without a value to come after every document with one, as STRING_LAST and the in-segment comparator promise. At merge, IndexSorter.StringSorter gives a document with a value its long global ordinal (from an OrdinalMap over every input's full dictionary, deleted documents' values included) but gives a document without a value the int key Integer.MAX_VALUE, so every value whose global ordinal is above 2^31 - 1 sorts after the missing documents (a value at exactly 2^31 - 1 gets the same key as they do). The merged segment is written out of its declared sort with no error: in an end-to-end addIndexes(CodecReader...) test over two one-live-document segments whose dictionaries a FilterCodecReader enlarges to 2^30 + 1 terms each, the document without a value ends up at doc 0.

rows.title: addIndexes(CodecReader...) silently adds nothing when OneMerge#wrapForMerge brings the merged document count above Integer.MAX_VALUE, because MergeState sums the wrapped readers' numDocs() in an int with no MAX_DOCS check (index-sorted writers, since 9.9.0)
rows.summary: You open an index-sorted IndexWriter whose merge policy's findMerges(CodecReader...) returns a OneMerge whose wrapForMerge revives deleted documents (its javadoc allows a wrapper to 'add/remove fields or documents'), and call addIndexes(CodecReader...) with inputs whose live documents fit under MAX_DOCS but whose revived documents total more than Integer.MAX_VALUE; you expect the IllegalArgumentException that addIndexes documents for exceeding MAX_DOCS. Instead addIndexes returns normally and adds nothing: IndexWriter checked the limit only on the unwrapped readers, MergeState sums the wrapped readers' numDocs() in an int that wraps negative (-2,094,967,296 for 2 x 1.1 billion), SegmentMerger.shouldMerge() is then false, and addIndexesReaderMerge returns before writing a segment. Without an index sort, the merged view that IndexWriter builds first rejects the same total with IllegalArgumentException, so only index-sorted writers (and writers given block inputs without a parent field) get the silent no-op.

rows.title: Lucene90LiveDocsFormat.writeLiveDocs and CheckIndex.bitsCardinality step an int offset by 1024 that wraps to Integer.MIN_VALUE for segments of more than 2,147,482,624 documents, so a deletion in such a segment can never be committed (10.4.0+) and CheckIndex at level 2 or higher reports its valid live docs as an error (10.3.0+)
rows.summary: You index IndexWriter.MAX_DOCS (2,147,483,519) documents into one segment with the default IndexWriterConfig and codec, delete one of them by term and call commit(); you expect the deletion to be saved. Instead commit() throws 'ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException: Index -3 out of bounds for length 16' ('AssertionError: startIndex=-129, numBits=1024' with -ea) and close() throws it again, because Lucene90LiveDocsFormat.writeBits copies the live docs in 1024-bit batches with 'for (int offset = 0; offset < bits.length(); offset += copy.length())': after the batch at 2^31-1024 the offset wraps to Integer.MIN_VALUE, which is still below the length, so the next batch clears a negative range. CheckIndex.bitsCardinality has the same loop, so on 10.3.0 and later CheckIndex (level 2 or higher) also reports the valid live docs of such a segment as an error; only segments with more than 2,147,482,624 documents are affected.
rows.area: codecs / live docs (Lucene90LiveDocsFormat) and index / CheckIndex live-docs check

rows.title: Postings docIDRunEnd() returns Integer.MIN_VALUE for dense blocks after a term's last level-1 skip block when doc IDs are within 8,192 (4,096 before 10.4) of 2^31, so CheckIndex at level 2 or higher reports a healthy segment of about 2^31 documents as corrupt

You expect docIDRunEnd() to return a doc ID greater than the current one, as its javadoc promises, and CheckIndex to pass. Instead, in the dense blocks after the term's last full 8,192-doc level-1 skip block (4,096 docs in 10.2-10.3), the default postings reader returns Integer.MIN_VALUE and CheckIndex reports the healthy segment as corrupt ('Run end -2147483648 is <= doc ID 2147475456'); query results stay correct, and the repro writes the postings through the public codec API rather than indexing 2^31 documents with IndexWriter.

rows.title: SegmentInfos.readCommit compares delCount + softDelCount with maxDoc in int arithmetic, so for a segment of 2^30 or more documents an over-sized pair of deletion counts wraps negative and the commit is read without the CorruptIndexException ('invalid deletion count') that the same check gives for smaller segments (since 7.4.0)
rows.summary: You read a commit whose segment claims more deleted documents (hard deletes plus soft deletes) than it has; for a small segment SegmentInfos.readLatestCommit rejects it with CorruptIndexException 'invalid deletion count: 10 vs maxDoc=6'. For a segment of 2^30 documents with delCount = softDelCount = 2^30, each count is within maxDoc on its own, but their int sum wraps to Integer.MIN_VALUE, the check 'softDelCount + delCount > info.maxDoc()' passes, and the commit is returned with deletion counts that add up to twice the segment's size. The same method already keeps its total document count in a long; a (long) cast on the sum fixes it.
rows.area: core / index: SegmentInfos.readCommit (deletion-count consistency check of segments_N)

rows.title: FixedBitSet.ensureCapacity computes the grown length as int arr.length << 6, which wraps negative once the requested bit reaches about 1.91 billion, so DocsWithFieldSet iterates no documents and a flushed segment silently drops every value of its sparse doc-values and norms fields
rows.summary: You index into one segment until doc IDs pass about 1.91 billion (legal: IndexWriter.MAX_DOCS is 2^31-129) with a doc-values or norms field that only some documents have, then commit; you expect every indexed value to be in the segment. Instead, when the field's DocsWithFieldSet grows its FixedBitSet to the new doc ID, FixedBitSet.ensureCapacity computes the new length as arr.length << 6 in int arithmetic, which wraps negative once the backing array has 2^25 words, so the set's iterator returns no document although cardinality() counts them, and the flushed segment has no document with a value for that field (with -da; with -ea addDocument throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException for that document). The same call on a small set, ensureCapacity(new FixedBitSet(64), 2_000_000_000), returns a set with length() = -2,044,967,232; the twin LongBitSet.ensureCapacity had the identical overflow and was fixed in 2015 (LUCENE-6409), but FixedBitSet was not.

rows.title: Byte DOT_PRODUCT scores (VectorUtil.dotProductScore and the two Panama byte scorers) compute len * 2^15 in int, so from 65,536 dimensions every score is mirrored around 0.5 (closer vectors score lower) and at 131,072 dimensions scores become +/-Infinity or NaN
rows.summary: You score two byte vectors of 65,536 dimensions with VectorSimilarityFunction.DOT_PRODUCT (or VectorUtil.dotProductScore, or run a KnnByteVectorQuery on a byte DOT_PRODUCT field indexed through a format that raises getMaxDimensions) and expect the documented score 0.5 + dot / (len * 2^15): within [0, 1] and higher for more similar vectors. Instead the divisor len * (1 << 15) is multiplied in int before the cast to float, so from 65,536 dimensions it wraps to a negative number and every score is mirrored around 0.5: a vector identical to an all-ones query scores 0.49996948 and its opposite 0.5000305, and kNN returns the documents in exactly reverse order. At 131,072 dimensions the divisor wraps to 0 and the scores are +Infinity, -Infinity or NaN.
rows.area: util / VectorUtil byte DOT_PRODUCT score x internal/vectorization / Panama MemorySegment byte scorers

rows.title: Byte-vector similarity kernels wrap their int accumulators from 33,026 dimensions (squareDistance and the uint8 kernels) and from 131,072 dimensions (dotProduct, cosine), below the 2^18 / 2^16 no-overflow bounds their code comments state
rows.summary: You call VectorUtil.squareDistance, uint8SquareDistance or cosine on two equal-length byte vectors, or score them with VectorSimilarityFunction.EUCLIDEAN or COSINE, at a dimension below the 'will not overflow if dim < 2^18' bound (or 'dim < 2^16' for uint8) that the code comments in DefaultVectorUtilSupport state. You expect the exact sum of squared differences, cosine(v, v) = 1, and closer vectors to score higher. Instead every provider (scalar and Panama) adds up in a 32-bit int that wraps: from 33,026 dimensions the squared distance comes back negative (-2,147,451,646 instead of 2,147,515,650), from 131,072 dimensions cosine(v, v) is -1.0, and at 66,052 dimensions EUCLIDEAN scores the farthest possible vector above an adjacent one.

rows.title: The example native int8 dot product (lucene/misc/src/c/dotProduct.c, opt-in via -Dlucene.useNativeDotProduct=true) keeps its SVE loop index in int32, so VectorUtil.dotProduct(byte[], byte[]) on two arrays of at least 2^31 - 4*VL elements (2,147,483,520 at 256-bit SVE, 2,147,483,584 at 128-bit SVE) overflows the loop bound, reads past the end of both arrays and kills the JVM with SIGSEGV in vdot8s_sve
rows.summary: You enable Lucene's opt-in native dot product (-Dlucene.useNativeDotProduct=true plus a library built from the example lucene/misc/src/c/dotProduct.c) on an SVE machine and call VectorUtil.dotProduct(byte[], byte[]) on two legal arrays of 2,147,483,645 bytes whose exact dot product is 3, expecting 3 as the Panama and default providers return. Instead the SVE kernel vdot8s_sve keeps its loop index and vector length in int32_t, so its loop test 'i + 4 * vec_length <= limit' (dotProduct.c:66) overflows once i reaches 2^31 - 4*VL (VL = SVE vector length in bytes); in the compiled code the bound wraps negative while the load offset is a 64-bit register, so the loop keeps loading past the end of both arrays until it hits an unmapped page and the JVM dies with SIGSEGV in vdot8s_sve. Every length from 2^31 - 4*VL up to the JVM maximum crashes (2,147,483,520 at 256-bit SVE, 2,147,483,584 at 128-bit SVE), while one element less returns the exact result; a 64-bit loop index with svwhilelt_b8_s64 fixes it.
rows.area: core vectorization + misc native C / opt-in native int8 dot product (NativeVectorUtilSupport, lucene/misc/src/c/dotProduct.c vdot8s_sve)

rows.title: HNSW merge computes a graph's deleted percentage in int, so a graph with more than 21,474,836 deleted vectors (41-100% deleted) passes the 40% DELETE_PCT_THRESHOLD and is reused as the merge base; in 10.4.0-10.6.0 and branch_10x the opt-in concurrent merger then throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException for an all-deleted base (main since #16794, 11.0 only, rebuilds the graph instead)
rows.summary: You merge an HNSW vector segment that has had most of its vectors deleted and expect Lucene to rebuild the graph or reuse a cleaner one, because the DELETE_PCT_THRESHOLD javadoc says a graph with more than 40% of its vectors deleted is never selected as the merge base. Once more than 21,474,836 vectors of one graph are deleted, the percentage ((graphSize - live) * 100) / graphSize overflows int and goes negative (-59 for 25M deleted out of 30M), so the guard passes and a graph that is up to 100% deleted becomes the base, in either reader order and also when the segment is merged alone. The default merger still finishes, pruning and repairing the reused graph. rows.title: Bulk NumericDocValues#longValues (new in 10.5.0) throws on a valid dense segment for one exact request size per byte-aligned width, because its size guard checks the unpadded byte count against Integer.MAX_VALUE and then adds the padding bytes in int (40/48-bit: wraps to Integer.MIN_VALUE, 'read past EOF'; 16/24/56-bit: a byte[] above the JVM limit)

rows.title: IndexWriter.updateDocuments / softUpdateDocuments with an empty block leave about 33 KB of phantom RAM accounting at every refresh or commit that drops the empty per-thread writer, so ramBytesUsed grows without bound and, once it passes the RAM buffer, every later document is flushed into its own segment
rows.summary: You call IndexWriter.updateDocuments(term, List.of()), or softUpdateDocuments(term, List.of(), softField), to delete a key's documents and add nothing, then refresh or commit; you expect the delete to apply and nothing to stay buffered, so ramBytesUsed() returns to 0 as it does after deleteDocuments(term) or addDocuments(List.of()). Instead the call took a per-thread writer and charged its delete buffer (about 33 KB) to the flush control, and the next full flush throws that 0-document writer away without taking the charge back, so ramBytesUsed() climbs by about 33 KB per round and never comes down (20 rounds with a default config: 660,800 B). Once the phantom total passes the RAM buffer (about 510 rounds at the default 16 MB) the writer flushes after every document, so 200 small documents become 200 segments; with assertions enabled the writer closes itself with an AssertionError instead.
rows.area: index / IndexWriter flush-control RAM accounting (DocumentsWriterFlushControl.markForFullFlush drops a 0-document DocumentsWriterPerThread; reached through updateDocuments and softUpdateDocuments with an empty block)

rows.title: IndexWriter buffers the first doc-values update of each field twice in every buffered-updates packet (BufferedUpdates adds again the update that FieldUpdatesBuffer's constructor already recorded), so that update is RAM-accounted twice and, except on the all-same-value numeric path, applied twice to every matching document (since 7.7.0, LUCENE-8590)

Final values stay correct because the duplicate is identical and adjacent; Lucene 7.6.0 buffered the update once, and the double insert arrived with LUCENE-8590 in 7.7.0.

rows.title: SparseFixedBitSet.clear(int) and clear(int, int) drop a 4096-bit block's long[] when the block becomes empty but never subtract its bytes from ramBytesUsed, and a later set in that block adds a new array's bytes, so set/clear churn makes ramBytesUsed() grow without bound (24 bytes per set(0)/clear(0) cycle) while the real footprint stays constant (every release since 5.0.0)
rows.summary: You create a SparseFixedBitSet, set one bit and clear it again, so the 4096-bit block that held it becomes empty and the class drops that block's long[]. You expect ramBytesUsed() to return to the value of a fresh set: Accountable documents it as an estimate of the heap the object uses, and the class computes it exactly from its arrays in the constructor and in clear(). Instead the dropped array's 24 bytes stay counted (new SparseFixedBitSet(1) reports 88, and 112 after set(0) and clear(0)), and every later set in that block adds a new array's bytes, so repeating the cycle makes the estimate grow without bound while the set's real footprint stays the same.

rows.title: Merge-on-refresh never releases the file references of a merged segment that is dropped because all its documents were deleted during the merge, so IndexWriter leaves that segment's files on disk until the next writer opens the index
rows.summary: You keep an IndexWriter open, refresh near-real-time readers from it (DirectoryReader.openIfChanged) with merge-on-refresh on, which is the default since 9.3, and while a refresh-triggered merge of small segments runs, a commit or flush applies deletes that remove every document of that merge. You expect the merged segment, which IndexWriter drops as 100% deleted, to have its files deleted, as happens when the same segment is dropped by an ordinary merge. Instead the refresh has already taken a file reference on it and later closes its reader without releasing that reference, so the segment's files stay in the directory through deleteUnusedFiles(), commit(), close() and rollback(), until the next IndexWriter opens the index.
rows.area: index / IndexWriter NRT merge-on-refresh (getReader point-in-time merges) and IndexFileDeleter refcounts

rows.title: A Directory.deleteFile failure during a non-commit IndexFileDeleter checkpoint (for example while a flush drops a fully deleted segment) leaves one extra reference on every file of the writer's current segments, so the still-open IndexWriter never deletes those files once they become unused, not even in deleteUnusedFiles(), rollback() or close()
rows.summary: You index with an IndexWriter on a Directory whose deleteFile can throw an IOException (Directory.deleteFile declares it), and one delete fails while the writer checkpoints outside a commit, for example when flush() drops a newly flushed segment whose documents were all deleted; flush() throws, but the writer stays open and reports no tragic exception, so you keep indexing, merging and committing. You expect the writer to delete the files of segments that are merged away once no commit references them, as IndexFileDeleter's reference counting promises (LUCENE-5919 made its decRef exception-safe for this reason). Instead the checkpoint has already taken a reference on every current file and, because decRef threw, skips the line that records those files for release, so in the repro _0.cfe, _0.cfs and _0.si stay on disk after the merge, the next commit, deleteUnusedFiles() and close() (rollback), and only a new IndexWriter removes them.
rows.area: core / index IndexFileDeleter reference counting (non-commit checkpoint after a failed Directory.deleteFile; reached from IndexWriter flush, NRT flush and tryDeleteDocument)

rows.title: A failed addIndexes(CodecReader...) merge leaves its partially written segment files on disk while the writer stays open: commit(), deleteUnusedFiles(), later merges and a successful retry never delete them, only rollback(), close() or a new IndexWriter does (regression from LUCENE-6786, every release since 5.4.0)

rows.title: TieredMergePolicy forceMerge(n) with n > 1 can leave more than n segments, because segments too large to re-merge are not counted toward n
rows.summary: You call IndexWriter.forceMerge(2) (or any n > 1) with the default TieredMergePolicy on an index that holds one very large segment without deletes plus a few small segments, and expect at most n segments afterwards, as the forceMerge javadoc ('maximum number of segments left in the index after merging finishes') and TieredMergePolicy's 'maxNumSegments wins' note promise; merging only the small segments would get there without breaking any size limit. Instead findForcedMerges sets the large segment aside as too big to re-merge but never counts it against n, so it treats the small segments as already merged (or stops one merge early) and forceMerge returns with n + 1 or more segments. rows.title: TemporalMergePolicy.forceMergeDeletes never expunges deletes from a segment that is the only eligible one in its time window (or the odd one left after full batches)
rows.summary: You use TemporalMergePolicy and call IndexWriter.forceMergeDeletes() while some time window holds exactly one segment whose share of deleted documents is above forceMergeDeletesPctAllowed (default 10%), for example in a single-segment index, or after forceMerge(1), which leaves one segment per window. You expect that segment to be rewritten without its deleted documents, as the policy's setForceMergeDeletesPctAllowed javadoc and MergePolicy.findForcedDeletesMerges ('expunge all deletes') describe and as TieredMergePolicy and LogMergePolicy do. Instead the policy skips every window with fewer than two eligible segments (and drops the one left over after full batches of maxThreshold), so the call schedules no merge and returns at once: a 10-document segment with 5 deletes still has maxDoc 10, and calling it again changes nothing.
rows.area: index / merge policy (TemporalMergePolicy forced-deletes selection, IndexWriter.forceMergeDeletes)

rows.title: TemporalMergePolicy.forceMergeDeletes merges segments older than maxAgeSeconds, from different time windows, into one segment, because findForcedDeletesMerges does not skip the -1 'old data' bucket that findMerges and forceMerge skip (every release since 10.5.0)
rows.summary: You index time-series data with TemporalMergePolicy and setMaxAgeSeconds(30 days), so two segments whose newest timestamps are 2020-01-01 and 2021-01-01 are older than the limit and lie in different time windows, delete one of the four documents in each, and call IndexWriter.forceMergeDeletes(). You expect the two segments to stay apart: the class javadoc says segments older than setMaxAgeSeconds are not merged ('skipped during merge selection') and that segments from different time windows are never merged together, even during forceMerge, and forceMerge(1) and natural merges do skip them. Instead findForcedDeletesMerges treats the single -1 'old data' bucket, which holds every over-age segment whatever its window, as an ordinary window and merges the two segments into one (maxDoc 6, holding 2020 and 2021 data); without the age limit the same call keeps them apart, so turning on a setting meant to avoid cold-data I/O makes forceMergeDeletes rewrite and mix cold data.

rows.title: TemporalMergePolicy with setMaxThreshold(Integer.MAX_VALUE), a value the setter accepts, makes IndexWriter.forceMergeDeletes() throw OutOfMemoryError ('Requested array size exceeds VM limit') and merge nothing, because buildSequentialMerges pre-sizes its batch list to maxThreshold
rows.summary: You configure TemporalMergePolicy with setMaxThreshold(Integer.MAX_VALUE), which the setter accepts (it checks only maxThreshold >= minThreshold and says larger values merge more aggressively), and call IndexWriter.forceMergeDeletes() while one time window holds two segments whose share of deleted documents is above forceMergeDeletesPctAllowed, for example two 4-document segments with one deleted document each. You expect the two segments to be merged into one with no deleted documents left, as happens with the default maxThreshold of 8, and as natural merges and forceMerge do with the same setting. Instead buildSequentialMerges creates its batch list with new ArrayList<>(maxThreshold) before adding anything, so forceMergeDeletes() throws java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Requested array size exceeds VM limit at any heap size, no merge is registered and the deleted documents stay.

rows.title: FilterMergePolicy.getSizeUnit() returns BYTES instead of the wrapped policy's unit, so a wrapped LogDocMergePolicy makes compound-file decisions against the byte threshold and forceMerge(1) rewrites an already merged segment every time
rows.summary: You wrap a LogDocMergePolicy in a FilterMergePolicy (or in SoftDeletesRetentionMergePolicy, UpgradeIndexMergePolicy or OneMergeWrappingMergePolicy) and expect the wrapper to make the same compound-file choices as the policy it wraps, as it did in 10.x. Instead, on main FilterMergePolicy.size() still returns the wrapped policy's document count while getSizeUnit() says BYTES, so the compound-file check compares a document count with the 64 MiB byte threshold: forceMerge(1) of 70,000 small documents writes a compound segment where the plain policy writes a non-compound one, and every later forceMerge(1) rewrites that already merged segment again (3 of 3 calls).

rows.title: SoftDeletesRetentionMergePolicy's OneMerge wrapper forwards only wrapForMerge, so a reordering policy nested inside it (BPReorderingMergePolicy, or any OneMerge#reorder override) silently never reorders natural or forced merges, and BPReorderingMergePolicy's bp.reordered diagnostic is never written (since 9.9.0)
rows.summary: You configure IndexWriter with new SoftDeletesRetentionMergePolicy(field, query, new BPReorderingMergePolicy(base, reorderer)) to keep soft-deleted history and to reorder doc IDs on merge, then call forceMerge or let natural merges run. You expect the merged segments to be reordered, as BPReorderingMergePolicy documents for all forced merges and as the reverse nesting does on the same documents. Instead the retention policy replaces each merge with a new OneMerge that forwards only wrapForMerge, so IndexWriter's call to reorder() reaches the default that returns null: the merged segment silently keeps its original doc order and carries no bp.reordered diagnostic.
rows.area: index / merge policies (SoftDeletesRetentionMergePolicy OneMerge wrapping); misc / BP merge-time reordering (BPReorderingMergePolicy)

rows.title: MergePolicy.isMerged checks a segment read from disk against the codec instance it was loaded with (the shared Codec.forName instance, with default compound-file settings) instead of the writer's codec, so forceMerge(1) with a LogMergePolicy rewrites an already merged segment after every writer reopen
rows.summary: You give IndexWriter its own codec instance, for example new Lucene104Codec(Mode.BEST_COMPRESSION), turn compound files off on it as MIGRATE.md says (iwc.getCodec().compoundFormat().setShouldUseCompoundFile(false)), use a LogByteSizeMergePolicy and force-merge the index to one segment. You expect a later forceMerge(1) to leave that already merged segment alone, as it does in the same writer session and as 10.x does with the equivalent merge-policy settings. Instead, after the writer is closed and reopened, MergePolicy.isMerged asks the codec instance the segment was read with (the shared Codec.forName instance, whose settings are the defaults), decides the non-compound segment should have been compound, and forceMerge(1) rewrites it (_3 becomes _4); the merge itself uses the writer's codec and writes a non-compound segment again, so the same rewrite happens in every later writer session.
rows.area: index / merge policy compound-file check (MergePolicy.isMerged vs CompoundFormat settings)

rows.title: An NRT reader opened during a merge reuses the SegmentReaders the merge opened with a MERGE IOContext, so its searches read through merge-only inputs (direct I/O with DirectIODirectory, on-disk instead of RAM postings with DirectPostingsFormat, sequential read advice with ADVISE_BY_CONTEXT)
rows.summary: You let a merge start on segments that no NRT reader has opened yet (for example segments committed after the last refresh) and open an NRT reader with DirectoryReader.open(writer) while that merge runs. You expect that reader's searches to read the files through inputs opened for searching, as DirectIODirectory ('For all other cases (searching, writing) we delegate to the provided Directory instance') and DirectPostingsFormat ('at read time loads and stores all terms and postings directly in RAM') document. Instead the NRT reader gets the very SegmentReaders the merge opened with the MERGE IOContext, so with DirectIODirectory its searches read through the merge's direct-I/O inputs, with DirectPostingsFormat it searches the on-disk terms instead of the RAM postings, and with ADVISE_BY_CONTEXT its stored fields, vectors and HNSW graph are mapped with SEQUENTIAL advice; the hits stay correct.
rows.area: index / IndexWriter NRT reader pool (readers shared with merges)

rows.title: DirectIODirectory's inputs never override IndexInput#isEfficientFor, so the #16883/#16905 input sharing lets merges of NRT-open segments skip direct I/O and lets later sequential search reads go through the merge's direct-I/O input
rows.summary: You open an index with DirectIODirectory over the default MMapDirectory, keep an NRT reader open and let IndexWriter merge the segments that reader holds. You expect the merge to read their vector (.vec) and stored fields (.fdt) data with direct I/O while searches go through the delegate, as DirectIODirectory's javadoc says and as #16905 (which names this directory as the case it restores) intends. Instead the codec readers reuse the input the search already holds whenever that input says it is efficient for the merge, DirectIODirectory's inputs never answer that question (the default answer is yes), so the merge reads through the page cache, and with an advising delegate a sequential search read after the merge goes through the merge's direct-I/O input.

rows.title: HNSW addConnections descends from the worst upper-level candidate instead of the best
rows.summary: During merge-time HNSW graph repair and rebalancing, addConnections descends through the upper levels to find entry points. You expect it to descend from the best candidate, as its javadoc says. Instead it pops from a min-heap and descends from the worst; the naive fixes cut distance computations by 10-30% but lowered recall in 8 of 8 region-delete configurations.

In 10.2.x/10.3.x graph building goes through this scorer, so a forceMerge of a compress=true 4-bit field builds a different graph; searches are not affected.

rows.title: FlatBitVectorsScorer's RandomVectorScorerSupplier.copy() does not copy the vector values, so the copy's scorers read the original ByteVectorValues and the concurrent merge workers of HnswBitVectorsFormat (numMergeWorkers > 1) share one OffHeapByteVectorValues and its IndexInput (regression of #14181, since 10.2.0)
rows.summary: You index bit vectors with HnswBitVectorsFormat set up for concurrent merges (numMergeWorkers > 1 and an executor), and each merge worker gets scorerSupplier.copy(), which RandomVectorScorerSupplier documents as 'will copy the underlying vectorValues so the copy is safe to be used in other threads'. Instead, FlatBitVectorsScorer's supplier makes a copy of the values in its constructor (targetVectors) and never uses it: scorer() reads the original vectorValues and copy() wraps that same instance, so all workers read one shared, non-thread-safe OffHeapByteVectorValues and its IndexInput. The one-test repro shows it directly (a scorer from supplier.copy() makes 2 reads on the original values instead of 0, on main with -ea and -da and on 10.2.0 to 10.6.0, while 10.1.0 passes); in a concurrent merge the race gives occasionally wrong build-time scores.

rows.title: ScalarQuantizer.fromVectorsAutoInterval ignores the data and returns the first pair of its quantile search grid once one sampled vector's ten nearest-neighbour scores all tie (for example 11 identical vectors): that vector's correlation term is 0/0 = NaN, the NaN makes the mean NaN for every candidate pair, and the NaN-to-0.0 fallback then scores every pair 0.0 (every release from 9.11.0 through 10.6.0, and main)
rows.summary: You call ScalarQuantizer.fromVectorsAutoInterval (the dynamic confidence interval) on 20 random 8-dim vectors, and again on the same 20 plus 11 identical far-away vectors that change neither the candidate quantile grid nor any original vector's nearest neighbours. You expect the same best-correlated quantile pair both times, (-0.96047044, 0.957112) at 4 bits. Instead the second call returns (-0.9538363, 0.9618902), which is simply the first pair of the 16 x 16 search grid: each copy's ten neighbour scores tie, so its correlation term 1 - errors.var() / scoreVariance is 0/0 = NaN, the NaN makes the mean NaN, the fallback 'Double.isNaN(corr.mean) ? 0.0 : corr.mean' scores every candidate pair 0.0, and the first pair wins every comparison.

rows.title: ExitableDirectoryReader turns off filtered HNSW search on 9.x-format vector segments, so a filtered kNN query ignores the KnnSearchStrategy.Hnsw threshold even when the timeout never fires
rows.summary: On main you open an index whose vector segment was written by Lucene 9.8.0 (Lucene95 HNSW format), wrap the reader in ExitableDirectoryReader with a timeout that never fires, and run a KnnFloatVectorQuery (k=10) with a TermQuery filter that matches about 15% of the documents and the default search strategy. You expect the same graph walk and the same hits as on the unwrapped reader, because the wrapper only adds timeout checks and the documented threshold (60%; 0 never, 100 always) says the filtered HNSW search runs. Instead the wrapper hands the 9.x reader an anonymous Bits instead of the filter's BitSet, the reader therefore sizes the filter as 0 and never uses filtered search (even KnnSearchStrategy.Hnsw(100) returns exactly the Hnsw(0) hits), and 3 of the top 10 documents differ; every hit is still a valid, live filter match.

rows.title: LRUQueryCache.setSkipCacheFactor accepts NaN, 0, negative values and values below 1, which the constructor rejects with IllegalArgumentException, so a bad runtime setting is silently applied to query-cache admission (since 10.2.0)
rows.summary: You build an LRUQueryCache and later change its skip-cache factor at runtime with setSkipCacheFactor, passing NaN (for example from a failed parse), 0 or 0.5. You expect the IllegalArgumentException 'skipCacheFactor must be no less than 1' that the constructor throws for the same value (its check carries the comment '// NaN >= 1 evaluates false'). Instead the setter stores the value silently, and the cache's admission test 'cost / skipCacheFactor > leadCost' then runs with it: NaN or a negative value turns the skip heuristic off, 0 stops the caching of every clause that matches documents, and a value in (0, 1) can skip clauses that every valid factor caches; search hits stay correct.

rows.title: DisjunctionMaxQuery treats tie-breakers 0.0f and -0.0f as equal in equals() (IEEE ==) but hashes their raw bits in hashCode(), so two equal queries get different hash codes and the query cache, BooleanQuery clause sets and other hash-based structures treat them as different queries (since 1.9)
rows.summary: You build DisjunctionMaxQuery([f:x], 0.0f) and DisjunctionMaxQuery([f:x], -0.0f): equals returns true both ways (the constructor accepts -0.0f, and equalsTo compares the tie-breakers with ==, under which 0.0f == -0.0f), so by the Object#hashCode contract, which Query's javadoc requires so that QueryCache works, the two hash codes must be equal. Instead they differ by exactly 2^31, because hashCode adds Float.floatToIntBits(tieBreakerMultiplier), which is 0x00000000 for 0.0f and 0x80000000 for -0.0f. Hash-based structures therefore see two different queries: the query cache keeps a separate entry, a HashSet holds both and a BooleanQuery with both as FILTER clauses is not de-duplicated, while hits and scores stay the same.
rows.area: core / search: DisjunctionMaxQuery (equals and hashCode contract)

rows.title: spatial3d Vector (and so GeoPoint and the Geo3DPoint distance and box queries), Plane and the longitude-slice and degenerate latitude/longitude shapes compare doubles with == in equals() but hash Double.doubleToLongBits, so objects built with 0.0 and -0.0 are equal yet have different hash codes (since 5.2.0)
rows.summary: You build Geo3DPoint.newDistanceQuery("g", PlanetModel.WGS84, 0.0, 10.0, 1000.0) and the same query with latitude -0.0: equals() says they are equal, because the circle's centre GeoPoint is compared by Vector.equals, which uses ==, and under == the two centres (whose z is +0.0 and -0.0) are equal. By the Object#hashCode contract, which Query's javadoc asks subclasses to honour so that the query cache works, their hash codes must then be equal, but they differ by exactly 2^31, because Vector.hashCode hashes Double.doubleToLongBits(z), and those bits differ for the two zeros. Plane (its D) and the longitude-slice and degenerate latitude/longitude shapes have the same == versus doubleToLongBits pair, so box queries and the geom factories show it too, while hits and scores stay the same.

rows.title: Six function value sources (ConstValueSource, DoubleConstValueSource, LinearFloatFunction, ScaleFloatFunction, RangeMapFloatFunction, ReciprocalFloatFunction) and CommonTermsQuery's minimum-should-match fractions compare float/double parameters with == in equals() but hash their bits, so objects built with 0.0 and -0.0 are equal yet have different hash codes (since 4.0.0)

The same holds for DoubleConstValueSource, LinearFloatFunction, ScaleFloatFunction, RangeMapFloatFunction and ReciprocalFloatFunction and for the FunctionQuery and FunctionRangeQuery wrappers that hold them, so hash-based structures treat equal objects as different, while hits and scores stay the same.

rows.title: SimpleBindings rebuilds an Expression binding on every reference, so building the source of bindings that share sub-expressions creates one ExpressionValueSource per path (exponential in the depth of sharing)
rows.summary: You bind named expressions that use each other with SimpleBindings.add(String, Expression), which the class javadoc documents ('This can be used to reference expressions from other expressions'), and some of them share a sub-expression, for example X1 = L0 + R0 with L0 = X0 + 1 and R0 = X0 * 2, repeated in a chain. You expect getDoubleValuesSource to build each binding a bounded number of times, as building the same graph eagerly with add(String, DoubleValuesSource) does. Instead every reference re-applies expression::getDoubleValuesSource, so the shared graph is expanded into a tree with one ExpressionValueSource per path: 3*(2^d - 1) objects for a chain of d diamonds (196,605 for 49 bindings), and building the source of 70 or more such bindings exhausts a 1 GB heap before any document is read, while the computed values stay correct.
rows.area: expressions / SimpleBindings binding resolution (add(String, Expression), getDoubleValuesSource) and the ExpressionValueSource constructor

rows.title: SimpleBindings.validate() copies the whole binding path into a new set at every step and re-checks every binding once per origin, so validating a plain chain of 2000 expression bindings takes about 45 s instead of about 100 ms (cubic since 8.6.0, a regression from LUCENE-9338)
rows.summary: You build a chain of named expressions with SimpleBindings.add(String, Expression), each using the previous one (x1 = x0 + 1, x2 = x1 + 1, ..., x2000 = x1999 + 1), and call bindings.validate(), whose javadoc says it 'Traverses the graph of bindings, checking there are no cycles or missing references'. You expect a graph check that costs about as much as resolving every binding once, as on 8.5.2, where validate() of these 2000 bindings took about 100 ms. Instead, since 8.6.0 validate() starts a fresh walk from every binding, re-walks everything below it, and copies the whole current path into a new LinkedHashSet at every step, so its cost grows with the cube of the chain length: about 45 s for 2000 bindings and about 575 s for 4000 (at 1000 bindings it allocates 389.9 times the bytes of resolving every binding once), although the answer is still correct.
rows.area: expressions / SimpleBindings.validate() (cycle and missing-reference check, CycleDetectionBindings)

rows.title: Since #16857 (upstream main and branch_11x, unreleased), a segment that its index sort terminates early can still build an unused points-based competitive iterator when an earlier segment of the same field-sorted search crossed the hits threshold without early termination: NumericComparator keeps hitsThresholdReached on the comparator that all leaves share, so IndexSortedLeafFieldComparator's not forwarding setHitsThresholdReached() no longer stops the delegate's BKD work (512 point doc IDs read in the repro, up to about cost/7 per segment, where 10.6.0 reads 0; performance regression, results correct)
rows.summary: You search a MultiReader over two indexes for the top 10 by a long field f: the first index has no index sort and 2,000 hits, so the default 1,000-hit threshold is crossed there, and the second (4,096 documents) is sorted by f, so the search stops in it after a few documents. You expect that sorted segment to read no points: the new IndexSortedLeafFieldComparator says the comparator's skipping work, 'e.g. building iterators from points, is redundant work' there, and 10.6.0 reads 0. Instead, since #16857 the comparator still sees the threshold flag that the first segment set on the comparator shared by all segments, so it walks the sorted segment's BKD tree and builds a points iterator that nobody uses (512 point doc IDs here, up to about cost/7 per segment); the top 10 is still right, only the work is wasted.

rows.title: MMapDirectory applies a slice's read advice to the wrong bytes when the slice starts inside an mmap chunk and crosses into the next one (the #14109 prefetch fix missed this caller of advise())
rows.summary: You take a slice of an MMapDirectory file with IndexInput#slice(name, offset, length, IOContext) and a context that asks for RANDOM or SEQUENTIAL read advice, as the compound-file reader does for each inner file, and you expect the madvise hint to land on the slice's own pages. When the slice starts inside an mmap chunk and crosses into the next chunk, the hint is applied from the start of that chunk instead: in the repro, a slice of [512 KiB, 1.5 MiB) with 1 MiB chunks puts the RANDOM hint on [0, 1 MiB), so other inner files of a compound file get it, and a short slice that straddles a chunk boundary can get none of its own pages advised. Reads and query results stay correct; only the operating system's readahead and caching behaviour on those pages changes.
rows.area: store / MMapDirectory read advice (MemorySegmentIndexInput slices, compound files)

rows.title: BloomFilteringPostingsFormat's default filter silently stops filtering for segments of 226,279,579 docs or more: FuzzySet.createOptimalSet computes 2 * setSize in int, which wraps negative and yields a 64-bit filter with zero hash functions that answers MAYBE for every key (released since 9.6.0)
rows.summary: You index a primary key into a field that uses BloomFilteringPostingsFormat with the default filter factory, whose javadoc promises a filter targeting about 10% false positives sized from the segment's doc count, and you expect lookups of absent keys to be rejected quickly in every segment. For a segment of 226,279,579 docs or more, FuzzySet.createOptimalSet's int expression 2 * setSize wraps negative, the size lookup falls back to its smallest size (63) and the hash count rounds to 0, so the filter has 64 bits, never sets one and answers MAYBE for every key, and the saturation check meant to retire useless filters sees 0% saturation and saves it. Results stay correct, but every absent-key lookup on that segment goes to the terms dictionary: the repro's filter rejects 0 of 1,000 absent keys, while one doc fewer gives a 2^30-bit filter with 3 hash functions that rejected 2,000 of 2,000 in an independent test.
rows.area: codecs / bloom (BloomFilteringPostingsFormat, DefaultBloomFilterFactory, FuzzySet sizing)

rows.title: IndexedDISI returns its jump-table entry count as a signed short, so a sparse doc-values, norms or vector field whose last doc id is >= 2,147,352,576 stores a negative count and every reader ignores the jump table that was written (advance walks block by block; results stay correct)
rows.summary: You build a segment of more than 2,147,352,576 documents with the default codec, with a doc-values, norms or vector field that some documents lack and that a document near the end of the doc-id range has. You expect the field's index-time jump table (added in 8.0 'for O(1) advance') to be used, so that advance() to a far document jumps straight to its 65,536-doc block. Instead IndexedDISI.writeBitSet writes 32,768 or 32,769 table entries but returns their count as a short (-32,768 or -32,767), the codec stores that value, and every reader treats a negative count as 'no jump table', so advance() and advanceExact() walk the block headers one by one; the documents and values returned stay correct.
rows.area: codecs / IndexedDISI jump table (presence sets of sparse doc values, norms and vectors)

rows.title: Global-ordinals join explain() ignores toQuery, so documents that are not hits (from-side documents, or to-side documents a narrower toQuery excludes) are explained as matches
rows.summary: You build a global-ordinals join with JoinUtil.createJoinQuery(joinField, fromQuery, toQuery, searcher, scoreMode, ordinalMap), where 'from' and 'to' documents share one join field and fromQuery/toQuery tell them apart as the javadoc requires, and ask IndexSearcher.explain about a document the join does not return, for example a 'from' document whose join value was collected. You expect a non-match explanation, as upstream TestJoinUtil#testOrdinalsJoinExplainNoMatches asserts for other non-hits of this query and as CheckHits.checkNoMatchExplanations requires. Instead explain() checks only that the document's join value was collected and never consults toQuery, which the scorers do iterate, so it answers 'A match, join value X' in every ScoreMode; search results are unaffected, but BooleanQuery explanations built on it go wrong and BooleanWeight.explain can throw NullPointerException.
rows.area: join / JoinUtil global-ordinals join explain (GlobalOrdinalsQuery, GlobalOrdinalsWithScoreQuery)

rows.title: ExpressionRescorer.explain evaluates the expression with _score = 0 (the value of SortRescorer's placeholder explanation) instead of the first-pass score, so the explanation shows the wrong _score and expression values; the rescored ranking is correct
rows.summary: You rescore first-pass hits with an expression that reads _score, for example '_score * 100 + popularity' through Expression.getRescorer, and ask the rescorer to explain a hit. You expect what the ExpressionRescorer javadoc promises, an explanation 'showing the value of each variable': _score equal to the first-pass score the rescore used, and the expression value computed from it (107.0 for a first-pass score of 1.0 and popularity 7). Instead, since 7.0.0, ExpressionRescorer hands SortRescorer's explanation, whose value is always 0, to the expression as the score explanation, so the explanation reads '7.0 = _score * 100 + popularity' with a _score detail of 0.0, while the rescore itself (order, sort values, scores) is correct.
rows.area: expressions / ExpressionRescorer explain (Expression.getRescorer, ExpressionValueSource.explain over SortRescorer)

rows.title: AfterEffectB.explain shows the raw totalTermFreq and docFreq under children labelled 'F, ... + 1' and 'n, ... + 1' (and lists tfn twice), so its own formula (F + 1) / (n * (tfn + 1)) on the children it lists does not give the value it shows; the score itself is correct
rows.summary: You search with DFRSimilarity(basic model, new AfterEffectB(), normalization) and call IndexSearcher.explain on a hit. The AfterEffectB node says 'computed as (F + 1) / (n * (tfn + 1)) from:' and labels its children 'F, total number of occurrences of term across all documents + 1' and 'n, number of documents containing term + 1', so for a term with totalTermFreq 6 and docFreq 3 you expect F = 7 and n = 4. Instead the children show 6 and 3 (the raw statistics) and tfn is listed twice, so the formula on the listed children gives 0.71897 while the node correctly shows 0.61626 (I(n)B2); the score is right and only the explanation's operands are wrong.

rows.title: Normalization.NoNormalization.explain reports 1 instead of tf, so IBSimilarity explains its Distribution at tfn = 1 and that child disagrees with the score it explains
rows.summary: You score a field with IBSimilarity(distribution, lambda, new Normalization.NoNormalization()) and call IndexSearcher.explain on a document where the term occurs 3 times. You expect the explanation to add up: the IB node says it is 'computed as boost * distribution.score(stats, normalization.tfn(stats, freq, docLen), lambda.lambda(stats))', NoNormalization.tfn returns tf, and Normalization.explain is documented to return 'an explanation for the normalized term frequency', so the normalization child should show 3 and the Distribution child should equal the node at boost 1. Instead NoNormalization.explain returns the value 1, IBSimilarity feeds that 1 into distribution.explain as tfn, and the Distribution child shows 0.9162907 under a node of 1.7047480 (all four IB distribution/lambda pairs), while the score itself is right.
rows.area: core / search similarities (Normalization.NoNormalization explanation; IBSimilarity and DFRSimilarity explain trees)

rows.title: BBoxStrategy's overlap-ratio explanation (BBoxOverlapRatioValueSource) shows the target ratio under 'queryFactor' instead of the query ratio, so explain() misreports how the score was computed; the score itself is correct
rows.summary: You score documents with BBoxStrategy.makeOverlapRatioValueSource and call explain, and you expect the tree to show the terms of the documented formula, queryFactor = queryRatio * queryTargetProportion and targetFactor = targetRatio * (1 - queryTargetProportion). Instead the 'ratio' child of the 'queryFactor' node, printed next to 'area of <query box>', is targetRatio, the same number as under 'targetFactor': for the query box x[0,20] y[0,10] and the document box x[10,40] y[5,15] at proportion 0.3 it shows 0.16666667 (50/300) where queryRatio is 0.25 (50/200). The score (0.19166666) and the queryFactor value (0.075) are right; one token on line 255 is wrong, a slip from the 2015 LUCENE-6446 Explanation API rewrite, and 5.1.0 still showed queryRatio.

rows.title: ThaiRepeatFilter gives the repeated word the offsets of a deleted character or of the following markup instead of the Maiyamok's, when a CharFilter removed characters right after the Maiyamok (a zero-width space in the default ThaiAnalyzer, a closing tag with HTMLStripCharFilter)
rows.summary: You analyze 'บ่อยๆ' + U+200B + 'ครับ' (a word written with the repetition mark ๆ, then a zero-width space) with the stock ThaiAnalyzer and expect what happens without the zero-width space, and what the filter's CHANGES entry promises ('exact OffsetAttribute and highlighter compatibility'): the base token บ่อย covers the word [0,4) and the repeated token บ่อย covers the ๆ [4,5). Instead the base token gets [0,5), which includes the ๆ, and the repeated token gets [5,6), which is only the removed zero-width space: ThaiRepeatFilter assumes that the last characters of the token's offset span are its trailing ๆ, but the CharFilter's offset correction put the removed character at the end of that span. With HTMLStripCharFilter the repeated token points at the last character of the tag after the word instead, so a highlighter writes its markup inside the tag; terms and positions are correct and nothing fails.
rows.area: analysis / Thai (ThaiRepeatFilter offset split; ThaiAnalyzer with ThaiCharFilter, or a custom chain with HTMLStripCharFilter)

rows.title: KoreanTokenizer gives the parts of a decompounded word offsets counted back from the end of the word while their text is cut from the start of the word, so when the parts do not cover the whole word (a user-dictionary entry with a shorter segmentation such as '세종시 세종', or 7 compounds of the bundled dictionary such as 픽토그램) the offsets point at other characters (픽토 at [1,3) covers '토그')
rows.summary: You analyze text containing 픽토그램 ('pictogram') with the default KoreanAnalyzer, or 세종시 with the user dictionary entry '세종시 세종', and expect each decompounded part's offsets to cover the characters its text came from, as they do when the parts cover the whole word (가락지나물 gives 가락지[0,3) and 나물[3,5)). Instead nori cuts each part's text from the start of the word but counts its offsets back from the end of the word, so 픽토그램 gives 픽토[1,3), covering '토그', and 그[3,4), covering '램', and '세종시 세종' gives 세종[1,3), covering '종시'; highlighters mark the wrong characters. Lucene accepts both inputs without a check: UserDictionary rejects only a segmentation longer than the word, and 7 compounds in the bundled dictionary have parts that do not add up to the word.
rows.area: analysis / nori KoreanTokenizer (Viterbi decompound backtrace; UserDictionary and bundled-dictionary compounds)

rows.title: Monitor HighlightsMatch returns -1 offsets for a TextField document matched in a batch of two or more documents, but the real offsets when the same document is matched alone; the upstream batch test expects the offsets but cannot notice, because Hit.compareTo ignores offsets
rows.summary: You register a query with a Monitor and match a document whose text is in a plain TextField with HighlightsMatch.MATCHER; each hit carries its positions and character offsets (the phrase "cell biology" in 'the cell biology count' is positions 1-2, offsets 4-16). Match the same document in a batch of two or more documents with Monitor.match(Document[]) and the hits keep the right positions, but both offsets are -1, because a single document goes into a MemoryIndex that always stores offsets while a batch is indexed with the documents' own field types, and TextField indexes no offsets. The module's own test testHighlightBatches expects the real offsets in a batch (Hit(1, 4, 2, 16)) but cannot notice, because the hit set's contains() uses Hit.compareTo, which ignores offsets (the sibling bug LFV-915).
rows.area: monitor / HighlightsMatch on batches (DocumentBatch: MultiDocumentBatch keeps the caller's FieldType, SingletonDocumentBatch uses MemoryIndex with offsets)

rows.title: MappingCharFilter.reset() rewinds the input but keeps the offset corrections recorded on the first pass, so after a reset and re-read correctOffset() (and the token offsets a Tokenizer derives from it) are wrong, or BaseCharFilter's ordering assertion fires
rows.summary: You read a MappingCharFilter to the end, call reset() to rewind it (MappingCharFilter overrides reset() for this, and upstream TestMappingCharFilter.testReaderReset re-reads after it), read it again and expect correctOffset() to map the second pass's output back to the input exactly as on the first pass. Instead reset() rewinds the input and the filter's read state but not the offset-correction map it inherits from BaseCharFilter, so the second pass appends new corrections computed from the first pass's last cumulative diff: for the map a->xy over "a", correctOffset(2) returns 0 instead of 1, and a WhitespaceTokenizer over the re-read filter for "a b" gives xy[0,0] b[1,2] instead of xy[0,1] b[2,3]. For deleting or shrinking maps, with -ea the second read() trips BaseCharFilter's 'Offset ... is less than the last recorded offset' assertion, and with -da it returns offsets past the end of the input (b->'' over "ba": correctOffset(1) = 3 for a 2-character input).
rows.area: analysis / char filters (MappingCharFilter, BaseCharFilter offset correction)

rows.title: matchhighlight PassageFormatter closes crossing markers in opening order instead of innermost first, so per-marker end strings come out mis-nested (e.g. 'one two three' instead of 'one two three')
rows.summary: You format the passage 'one two three' with two crossing markers, [0,7) written as ... and [4,13) as ..., using PassageFormatter's Function constructor, or you highlight the crossing phrase queries 'one two' and 'two three' with MatchHighlighter.highlight(topDocs, q1, q2) and one tag per query. You expect well-nested output, 'one two three', because when a marker ends the formatter closes and re-opens the markers opened after it precisely to resolve the overlap into nested markup (Passage javadoc: markers 'can be overlapping or nested'). Instead it closes those markers in opening order rather than innermost first and returns 'one two three' (end to end 'one two three'), which an XML parser rejects.

rows.title: matchhighlight PassageSelector can cut a passage or a truncated match between the two halves of a supplementary character, so FieldValueHighlighters.maxLeadingCharacters and highlighted return a snippet with an unpaired surrogate
rows.summary: You highlight a stored value with matchhighlight's FieldValueHighlighters, for example maxLeadingCharacters(5, '...', fields) on a value that starts with the word BOLD written in mathematical bold capitals (U+1D401 U+1D40E U+1D40B U+1D403, two UTF-16 units each), or highlighted(5, ...) with a term query that matches that word. You expect a snippet of whole characters within the 5-unit budget, for example the first two letters and '...', just as the ASCII value 'boldtext' is cut inside the word but between characters ('boldt...'). Instead the snippet ends with the first half of the third letter ('\uD835\uDC01\uD835\uDC0E\uD835...' and '>\uD835\uDC01\uD835\uDC0E\uD835<...'), because PassageSelector cuts windows and long matches at a raw UTF-16 offset and BreakIteratorShrinkingAdjuster keeps that raw edge when no word boundary fits in the window.

rows.title: matchhighlight's default BreakIteratorShrinkingAdjuster moves the end of a marker-less default passage back past the passage start when no word ends inside the passage and returns an empty range before it, so PassageSelector.pickBest fails its own 'Adjusters must not expand the passage's range' assertion with -ea and silently drops that value's default passage with -da (values '01234' and '56789' at window 4 give one passage, not two); since 9.0.0
rows.summary: You ask matchhighlight's default passage selector for up to two passages of a two-valued field without matches, FieldValueHighlighters.defaultPassageSelector().pickBest("01234 56789", List.of(), 4, 2, [0,5), [6,11)) (the values '01234' and '56789' joined with a one-character gap, as MatchHighlighter joins them), and expect one truncated default passage per value, [0,4) and [6,10), just as the first value keeps its truncated passage. Instead BreakIteratorShrinkingAdjuster walks the end of the second passage [6,10) back to the last word end before it, offset 5, and returns the empty range [5,5), which lies before the passage: with -ea pickBest throws 'AssertionError: Adjusters must not expand the passage's range: was [[from=6, to=10], markers=[]] => changed to [from=5, to=5]', and with -da it returns only [0,4), so the second value gets no snippet.

rows.title: AttributeSource.removeAllAttributes() leaves the cached State chain in place, so until the next addAttribute() captureState/restoreState, copyTo, hashCode, the impls iterator, reflection and clearAttributes/endAttributes still act on the removed attributes
rows.summary: You call removeAllAttributes() on an AttributeSource (for example a token stream you reuse with a different set of attributes) after it has been used, for example by clearAttributes(), which every Tokenizer calls for each token. You expect it to behave like a new, empty source until you add attributes again, as hasAttributes() (false) and equals() (equal to a new AttributeSource) already say. Instead the method clears its two maps but not the cached chain of attribute instances that captureState(), copyTo(), hashCode(), the impls iterator, reflection and clearAttributes()/endAttributes() walk, so until the next addAttribute() they still see the removed attributes: restoreState(captureState()) on the same source throws IllegalArgumentException, hashCode() differs from that of an equal empty source, and reflectAsString() still prints 'term=foo,...'.
rows.area: core / util AttributeSource (removeAllAttributes and the cached State chain, getCurrentState / currentState[0])

rows.title: Flexible query parser: AbstractRangeQueryNode.toQueryString does not keep the 11.0 'can be parsed back' promise for quoted bounds that contain a space, ']' or '}' or for open bounds in processed trees, and an open point bound makes it throw IllegalArgumentException, which escapes StandardQueryParser.parse at the clause limit
rows.summary: You parse a range such as f:["a b" TO c] or f:[a TO *] with the flexible StandardQueryParser, call toQueryString on the range node and parse the result again, as the 11.0 CHANGES entry for #7865 says you can. Instead a bound with a space, ']' or '}' prints backslash-escaped (f:[a\ b TO c]), which the range lexer rejects even for the syntax parser's own node; a processed open term bound prints as nothing (f:[a TO ]); and a processed open point bound (i:[1 TO *] with a PointsConfig) makes toQueryString and toString throw IllegalArgumentException 'Cannot format given Object as a Number'. Because BooleanQueryNodeBuilder builds its too-many-clauses message with toQueryString, a query over the clause limit that contains such an open point range makes StandardQueryParser.parse throw that IllegalArgumentException instead of the documented QueryNodeException, in every release since 4.0.

rows.title: ComplexPhraseQueryParser skips its same-field check for prefix and regular-expression clauses: "jo* id:2*" parses and then fails at search time with IllegalArgumentException, and name:"id:2*" searches field id
rows.summary: You parse a quoted phrase such as "jo* id:2*" or "jo* id:/2/" with ComplexPhraseQueryParser on the default field name; its class javadoc says the second pass checks that all embedded clauses refer to the same field, and it rejects "jo* id:2", "jo* id:2?", "jo* id:2~1" and "jo* id:[1 TO 2]" at parse time, so you expect a parse error. Instead parse() succeeds, because the check is wired into newTermQuery, getWildcardQuery, getRangeQuery and getFuzzyQuery but the class never overrides getPrefixQuery or getRegexpQuery, and the search then throws IllegalArgumentException 'Clauses must have same field.'. A one-clause phrase such as name:"id:2*" also parses, and because rewrite returns a lone multi-term query unchanged, it searches field id and returns the document whose id is 2.

rows.title: QueryBuilder hands a token boost (BoostAttribute) above 1 or equal to 0 on a word that shares its position with a synonym straight to SynonymQuery, which throws IllegalArgumentException, so every query containing that word fails, while the same weight on a word without a synonym works
rows.summary: You configure weighted synonyms ('leopard, panthera|1.5') or let users type boosts ('leopard|2'), and expect QueryBuilder to apply the weight, as it does for a word without a synonym: 'lion => simba|1.5' gives (body:simba)^1.5 and 'tiger|2' gives (body:tiger)^2.0. But when the boosted token shares its position with another token, QueryBuilder.newSynonymQuery passes the raw boost to SynonymQuery.Builder.addTerm, which accepts only (0, 1], so building the query throws IllegalArgumentException 'boost must be a positive float between 0 (exclusive) and 1 (inclusive)' and QueryParser.parse('spotted leopard') fails with it instead of returning a query or a ParseException. Weights in (0, 1] work on both paths; whether 1.5 or 0 works depends only on whether the analyzer stacked the token.

rows.title: SolrSynonymParser rejects a whole synonyms file because one line holds only spaces or tabs, although its javadoc says blank lines are comments (ParseException 'Invalid synonym rule at line N', every release since 3.4.0)

A truly empty line parses fine, and so did whitespace-only lines in the Solr loader this format came from before 3.4.

rows.title: MappingCharFilterFactory throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException ('Index 256 out of bounds for length 256') when a mapping rule's source or target is longer than 256 characters, because it unescapes every rule string into a fixed char[256] buffer, so the analyzer cannot be built
rows.summary: You configure the mapping char filter with a mapping file that contains one rule whose source or target is longer than 256 characters, for example "abc" => "<257 x>" or a long boilerplate phrase mapped to "", and expect the factory to build the map (NormalizeCharMap.Builder accepts such strings when called directly, and no limit is documented) or to reject the rule with an IllegalArgumentException that names it, as it does for other bad rules. Instead MappingCharFilterFactory.inform() throws java.lang.ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException: Index 256 out of bounds for length 256 from parseString, which copies each unescaped rule string into a fixed 256-character instance buffer without a bounds check. A 256-character string still works, and the limit counts characters after unescaping (256 \uNNNN escapes, 1536 raw characters, pass).

rows.title: HyphenationCompoundWordTokenFilterFactory passes the raw 'hyphenator' file name to the XML parser as the base system id (a URI), so with the JDK's built-in parser a valid hyphenation grammar named e.g. hyph_ø.xml, or with '%', '[', '{' or '\' in its name, fails to load with MalformedURIException
rows.summary: You configure HyphenationCompoundWordTokenFilterFactory with hyphenator=hyph_ø.xml, a valid FOP grammar with the standard DOCTYPE, and expect the analyzer to build, as it does when the same file is named hyph_o.xml. Instead, with the JDK's built-in XML parser, the build throws URI$MalformedURIException 'Path contains invalid character: ø': the factory hands the raw resource name to the parser as the base system id, which must be a URI, and the parser fails while resolving the DOCTYPE's relative 'hyphenation.dtd' against it, before Lucene's entity resolver gets the chance to supply the bundled DTD. The public getHyphenationTree(String) and PatternParser.parse(String), documented to take a file name, pass it as a URI the same way.

rows.title: Hunspell Dictionary throws NullPointerException instead of a parse error when a REP, MAP, ICONV/OCONV, COMPOUNDRULE, BREAK or CHECKCOMPOUNDPATTERN table at the end of the .aff file has fewer lines than its count

rows.title: Hunspell Dictionary throws a raw ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException (or NullPointerException) instead of a descriptive error when a .dic entry uses an AM morphological alias number that the .aff file does not define, although the same mistake in the AF flag-alias table gets 'Bad flag alias number'

You expect a descriptive error, as for the same mistake in the flag-alias (AF) table, which gives IllegalArgumentException 'Bad flag alias number:2' (C Hunspell's source, the reference implementation, range-checks the index and keeps the word without morphological data; its 'bad morph. alias index' warning prints only in builds with HUNSPELL_WARNING_ON). Instead every Dictionary constructor fails with java.lang.ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException 'Index 1 out of bounds for length 1' (or NullPointerException 'Cannot invoke "String.isBlank()" because "morphData" is null') from Dictionary.splitMorphData, which reads morphAliases[alias - 1] with no range check, and has done so since AM aliases were added in 4.10.0 (LUCENE-5778).

rows.title: Sorter.heapChild overflows int, so IntroSorter's heap-sort fallback compares a negative slot outside [from, to) when 2*to - from > 2^31 (ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException from ArrayUtil.introSort on a legal array slice)
rows.summary: You sort a legal slice with IntroSorter, for example ArrayUtil.introSort on the last 1,000 elements of an array of length ArrayUtil.MAX_ARRAY_LENGTH (or a slice of more than 2^30 elements starting at 0), and the element order makes IntroSorter give up on quicksort and fall back to heap sort. You expect the slice [from, to) to be sorted using only slots inside it. Instead Sorter.heapChild computes 2*(i - from) + 1 + from in int, which wraps to a negative number for a node that has no child, siftDown's 'leftChild < to' check lets it through, and compare is called with a negative slot, so the array-backed sort throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException ('Index -2147482757 out of bounds for length 2147483631').

Instead the constructor throws IllegalArgumentException 'No enum constant ...JapaneseCompletionFilter.Mode.query': the toUpperCase is applied to the default name "INDEX", which is already upper case, so the configured value reaches the case-sensitive Enum.valueOf unchanged and only the exact names INDEX and QUERY work.

rows.title: AbstractAnalysisFactory.requireChar silently cuts a mandatory char parameter longer than one char to its first char (and throws StringIndexOutOfBoundsException for an empty value) instead of rejecting it with IllegalArgumentException, as its optional twin getChar does

Instead requireChar returns 'a' with no error, because its body is just require(args, name).charAt(0); and since require() has already removed the key, the factory's usual 'Unknown parameters' check cannot catch the bad value either. The same missing check makes an empty value throw StringIndexOutOfBoundsException rather than IllegalArgumentException, and turns a supplementary character into a lone high surrogate.
