rows.title: AbstractAnalysisFactory.splitAt puts its separator into a regex character class without quoting it, so a factory that splits on '^' or '[' (or backslash) gets a PatternSyntaxException for every non-null list instead of the split items (every release since 7.4.0)
rows.summary: You write a custom analysis factory that splits a setting on '^' with the inherited helper, splitAt('^', "a^b"), and expect [a, b], as you get for ',', '.', '|', '*' or ']'. Instead every call with a non-null list throws java.util.regex.PatternSyntaxException 'Unclosed character class', because splitAt pastes the separator unquoted into a regex character class (list.split("(?<!\\\\)[" + separator + "]")), and '^' right after '[' means 'not', so the ']' after it is read as a literal and the class is never closed. '[' (which opens a nested class) and backslash (which escapes the closing ']') fail the same way; the other 65,533 char separators work.
rows.area: core / analysis: AbstractAnalysisFactory list-splitting helper (splitAt, used for factory arguments)

Explicit should, must, mustNot and filter values work as before, and writing occurs="should" is a workaround.

rows.title: SimpleWKTShapeParser rejects a MULTIPOINT whose points each sit in their own parentheses, e.g. MULTIPOINT ((1 2), (3 4)), with ParseException "expected ) but found: ','", although it accepts MULTIPOINT ((1 2)) and MULTIPOINT (1 2, 3 4) (every release since 7.6.0)
rows.summary: You call SimpleWKTShapeParser.parse("MULTIPOINT ((1 2), (3 4))"), the Simple Features WKT form in which each point of a multipoint sits in its own parentheses, and expect double[][] {{1, 2}, {3, 4}}, because the class says it parses WKT in compliance with ISO/IEC 13249-3:2016 and it already accepts MULTIPOINT ((1 2)) and the bare legacy form MULTIPOINT (1 2, 3 4). Instead it throws java.text.ParseException "expected ) but found: ','", also inside a GEOMETRYCOLLECTION and with 3D points. The cause is in parseCoordinates: when the first point starts with '(' the code before the loop does not read that point's ')', so the loop takes that ')' as the end of the whole list and the check after the loop then finds the ',' where it wants the missing ')'; whether a parenthesized point is accepted therefore depends on where it sits (MULTIPOINT (1 2, (3 4), 5 6) parses, while MULTIPOINT (1 2, (3 4)) fails with 'expected word but found: END-OF-STREAM').

rows.title: SimpleWKTShapeParser.parseExpectedType(wkt, ShapeType.GEOMETRYCOLLECTION) does no type check, because GEOMETRYCOLLECTION is also the parser's internal 'skip the check' marker for the first member of a collection: POINT (1 2) is returned as a double[] instead of the ParseException 'Expected geometry type: [GEOMETRYCOLLECTION], but found: [POINT]' that every other expected type gets (every release since 7.6.0)

Instead it returns double[]{1.0, 2.0}, and LINESTRING, POLYGON or MULTIPOINT text likewise comes back as its own type, never as the Object[] a collection parses to. The cause is that GEOMETRYCOLLECTION doubles as an internal marker: parseGeometryCollection parses a collection's first member with ShapeType.GEOMETRYCOLLECTION to mean 'no check' (later members get null for the same purpose), so parseGeometry checks the type only when shapeType != null && shapeType != GEOMETRYCOLLECTION, and a public caller who asks for a collection hits the marker.

rows.title: Polygon.fromGeoJSON garbles every \uXXXX string escape (it appends the code point as decimal digits and then reads the four hex digits again), so valid GeoJSON with an escaped letter in a key or type value is rejected with ParseException, and a malformed escape throws NumberFormatException (every release since 6.2.0)
rows.summary: You call Polygon.fromGeoJSON on valid GeoJSON in which one character of a key or of the type value is written as a JSON \uXXXX escape, for example {"type": "\u0050olygon", "coordinates": ...}, and expect the same polygon as for {"type": "Polygon", ...}, because JSON (RFC 8259 section 7) lets any string character be escaped and the parser has a branch commented '4 hex digit unicode BMP escape'. Instead that branch appends the code point with StringBuilder.append(int), that is as decimal digits, and does not skip the four hex digits, so "\u0050olygon" becomes "800050olygon" and the call throws ParseException 'can only handle type ... but got 800050olygon' (an escaped key such as "\u0074ype" gives 'did not see type: Polygon or MultiPolygon'). A malformed escape such as \uZZZZ throws an unchecked NumberFormatException instead of ParseException, and because a garbled key no longer matches, a non-CRS84 crs whose 'name' key is escaped, or a second feature whose 'coordinates' key is escaped, is silently accepted instead of rejected.

rows.title: Tessellator's self-intersection check divides by a determinant that can round to 0.0 when two nearly parallel edges are flagged as crossing: an invalid polygon is rejected with 'Polygon self-intersection at lat=Infinity lon=Infinity' (-da) or with a bare AssertionError from 'assert determinant != 0' (-ea) instead of an IllegalArgumentException naming a real location
rows.summary: You index a polygon with LatLonShape.createIndexableFields(name, polygon, true), asking Lucene to check it for self-intersections, and the polygon is invalid because one edge runs back over part of an earlier edge (lats {0, 7, 4, 3.85, 1.4, 2, 0}, lons {0, 1, 8, 0.55, 0.2, -7, 0}). You expect the IllegalArgumentException 'Polygon self-intersection at lat=.. lon=..' naming where the ring crosses itself, as other invalid polygons get. Instead the check flags two nearly parallel edges whose determinant rounds to exactly 0.0 and divides by it: without assertions (production) the message reads 'Polygon self-intersection at lat=Infinity lon=Infinity', and with -ea the internal 'assert determinant != 0' throws a bare java.lang.AssertionError out of the indexing call.

rows.title: Tessellator.tessellate(XYPolygon, boolean, Monitor) hands every Cartesian vertex to the Monitor as a geographic Point(y, x), so attaching a Monitor to an XY polygon with a vertex at |x| > 180 or |y| > 90 throws 'invalid longitude/latitude', although the same polygon tessellates without one (every release since 9.3.0)
rows.summary: You tessellate a Cartesian XYPolygon, for example the square (0,0) (500,0) (500,50) (0,50), with Tessellator.tessellate(polygon, false, monitor) and a no-op Tessellator.Monitor to watch the algorithm, and expect the same 2 triangles that tessellate(polygon, false) returns, since the Monitor is documented as an observer that 'will receive calls with internal data at each step of the triangulation algorithm'. Instead the call throws IllegalArgumentException 'invalid longitude 500.0; must be between -180.0 and 180.0': getPoints, which builds the point lists passed to the callbacks, wraps every node as a geographic new Point(node.getY(), node.getX()), and the Point constructor range-checks latitude and longitude. Any XY vertex with |x| > 180 or |y| > 90 fails this way, so the XY overload with a monitor works only when the Cartesian coordinates happen to lie inside the latitude/longitude ranges.

rows.title: IndexMergeTool's '--' end-of-options branch compares Strings with ==, so a command-line '--' is rejected as an unrecognized option, and if the branch ever fires it leaves '--' as the target path
rows.summary: You run the IndexMergeTool command line with '--' before the paths, for example 'IndexMergeTool -- -merged src1 src2', and expect the parser's dedicated '--' branch (IndexMergeTool.java:61) to end option parsing, as the usual command-line convention says, so that '-merged' is taken as the target directory. Instead the branch compares the argument with == against the literal "--", which is never true for a command-line argument, so '--' falls through to the option switch and the tool stops with "unrecognized option: '--'" and exit code 2 without merging anything. The branch is also wrong when it does fire (only when Java code passes the literal "--" to main()): it stops without skipping the '--', so '--' becomes the merged-index path and the intended target is read as the first source index.

rows.title: Luke: Search.nextPage() after a full last page returns an empty page with offset 0 instead of Optional.empty() when the hit total is a lower bound, so with default settings and more than 1,000 hits the Search tab ends on an empty page with 'previous' disabled
rows.summary: You open an index in Luke, run a search that matches more than 1,000 documents with the default settings and click 'next' up to the last page; when that page is full (for example 2,000 hits), the shown total is a lower bound ('2000+'), so 'next' stays enabled, and you expect one more click to do nothing, as Search.nextPage's javadoc says ('search results, or empty if there are no more results'). Instead nextPage() returns a page with no hits whose offset is 0: the results table empties, the range reads '1 ~ 0' and 'previous' is disabled, so the earlier pages can only be reached by running the search again. The cause is that nextPage moves its page counter before it knows the page exists and checks for the end only when the total is exact, and SearchResults.of sets the offset only inside its loop over the hits.

rows.title: Luke: a sorted search ignores exactHitsCount, so a sorted Search-tab query with more than 1,000 hits shows a lower-bound total ('1001+ hits') although the Sort tab forces 'exact hits count' on
rows.summary: You open an index in Luke, pick a sort field in the Sort tab (Luke then ticks and greys out 'exact hits count') and run a search that matches more than 1,000 documents; you expect the exact total, as the javadoc of the Sort overload of Search.search promises ('if set to true, the exact total hits count is returned'). Instead Luke shows a lower bound such as '1001+ hits', and there is no way to get the exact count of a sorted search. The cause is that SearchImpl.search() passes exactHitsCount only to the unsorted collector; the sorted branch calls IndexSearcher.searchAfter(after, query, pageSize, sort), which counts exactly only up to 1,000 hits.

rows.title: SearcherTaxonomyManager refresh calls t2.addSuppressed(t2), so when the taxonomy reopen fails and closing the just-reopened index reader also fails, maybeRefresh throws IllegalArgumentException ('Self-suppression not permitted') and the taxonomy failure is lost
rows.summary: You use SearcherTaxonomyManager, and one refresh hits two I/O failures at once: reopening the taxonomy fails, and closing the index reader that was just reopened also fails. You expect maybeRefresh() to throw the taxonomy failure as an IOException, its documented contract, with the close failure attached as a suppressed exception. Instead it throws IllegalArgumentException('Self-suppression not permitted'), because the cleanup code calls t2.addSuppressed(t2) where t1.addSuppressed(t2) was meant, so the taxonomy failure is lost entirely and callers that catch IOException do not see it.

rows.title: SpellChecker.indexDictionary never closes or rolls back its IndexWriter when the build throws, so the spell index stays write-locked and every later indexDictionary, clearIndex or IndexWriter on it in the same JVM fails with LockObtainFailedException until the JVM restarts
rows.summary: You build a spell index with SpellChecker.indexDictionary and the build throws, for example because the word-list file is not valid UTF-8, has a line longer than 32766 bytes, or its reader hits an I/O error; you fix the input and call indexDictionary or clearIndex again. You expect the retry to work, because the failed call should close or roll back the IndexWriter it opened. Instead indexDictionary closes its writer only on the success path, so the writer, which the caller cannot reach, keeps the spell index's write lock, and every later write to that index in the same JVM throws LockObtainFailedException 'Lock held by this virtual machine' until the JVM restarts.

rows.title: When opening a persistent Monitor fails after its query index has built the IndexWriter (stored queries the serializer cannot parse, no serializer for a non-empty index, an I/O error, or a purge frequency of 0), the writer and its write lock are never released, so the same index cannot be opened for writing again in that JVM

You expect the failed constructor to release what it acquired, as IndexWriter's own constructor does for its write lock, so that you can fix the parser or the configuration and open the index again. Instead the IndexWriter, its SearcherManager and the write lock stay open with no object left to close them, so every later writable Monitor on that path in the same JVM fails with LockObtainFailedException 'Lock held by this virtual machine', even with a correct serializer, until the JVM restarts.

rows.title: DirectoryTaxonomyWriter.close() skips its own cleanup when its commit fails: after an I/O error that closes the internal IndexWriter every close() throws and the writer's near-real-time reader keeps its segment files open, and after an fsync error inside close() the IndexWriter and the taxonomy write lock stay held until close() is retried or rollback() is called (every release since 5.0.0)
rows.summary: You add categories to a DirectoryTaxonomyWriter, a commit fails with an I/O error (for example a full disk while the new segment is written), and you then call close(), whose javadoc says it 'Frees used resources as well as closes the underlying IndexWriter'. You expect close() to release the writer's resources even when it throws, as IndexWriter.close() has done since LUCENE-4246. Instead close() is 'commit(); indexWriter.close(); doClose();' with no try/finally, so it throws AlreadyClosedException from its own commit() on every call and never closes its internal near-real-time reader, whose segment file stays open; when the error is an fsync inside close(), the internal IndexWriter and the taxonomy's write lock also stay held until close() is retried or rollback() is called.

rows.title: ReplicaNode.close() throws NullPointerException and never releases the index write lock when start() failed or was never called, so the index stays write-locked for the rest of the JVM (since 6.0.0)
rows.summary: You subclass ReplicaNode (as the module's SimpleReplicaNode does), call start() and, when it fails with an IOException (in the minimal repro sendNewReplica() throws its declared IOException; in an earlier test the replica Directory's first listAll() throws), close the node, then open a new IndexWriter on the same FSDirectory path. Instead close() throws NullPointerException ('Cannot invoke ReferenceManager.close() because this.mgr is null') at its first step, because the SearcherManager is created only near the end of start(), so it never reaches IOUtils.close(writeFileLock, dir), and once that exception is caught a new IndexWriter on the path fails with LockObtainFailedException 'Lock held by this virtual machine'; a node that is closed without ever calling start() hits the same NullPointerException and held lock.

rows.title: After one failed fsync of its save file, PersistentSnapshotDeletionPolicy's next fault-free snapshot() or release() fails with FileAlreadyExistsException on its own leftover file: persist() leaves the complete snapshots_N behind when Directory.sync throws and does not advance its generation, while snapshot() and release() undo their change in memory
rows.summary: You call PersistentSnapshotDeletionPolicy.snapshot() (or release()), fsync of the new save file snapshots_N fails once, the call throws and the policy undoes the change in memory; you expect the next call, with no fault, to work. Instead persist() has left the complete snapshots_N in the directory (its delete-on-failure block covers only creating and writing the file, not the sync) and has not advanced its generation, so the next snapshot() or release() writes the same name and fails with FileAlreadyExistsException; that call's cleanup deletes the leftover, and the call after it works. Secondary, contract open: a policy re-opened before that next call adopts the leftover, so a snapshot() that threw is in effect and a release() that threw has taken effect.

rows.title: When a merge fails to open the refreshed reader of a segment with doc-values updates, IndexWriter never releases its reference on the pooled segment reader, so the segment's files stay open after IndexWriter.close
rows.summary: You update a doc-values field (or use soft deletes) and open NRT readers from your IndexWriter, then delete a document, and a merge (a merge-on-commit, a merge-on-refresh, or an ordinary or forced merge) has to open a fresh copy of that segment's pooled reader with the new deletions, and opening it fails with an IOException. You expect the merge to fail cleanly and IndexWriter to give back every reader reference it took, so that once the writer is closed no file of the index is still open. Instead ReadersAndUpdates.getReaderForMerge never releases the reference it took on the pooled reader, so that segment's compound file and doc-values update files stay open after IndexWriter.close, even when the failure was not tragic and the writer went on to commit and close normally.
rows.area: index / IndexWriter merge-reader acquisition (ReadersAndUpdates.getReaderForMerge)

rows.title: If aborting one in-memory segment throws during IndexWriter.rollback() or the tragic self-close, DocumentsWriter.abort() stops: the other buffered segments are never aborted, stay locked, and keep their stored-fields outputs open (a permanent leak since 4.7.1)
rows.summary: Two threads add documents to one IndexWriter, so it buffers two in-memory segments, and then you call rollback(); while the first segment is being aborted an exception is thrown (here by the writer's InfoStream). You expect rollback() to pass that exception on but still release everything, which is what Lucene's own TestIndexWriterExceptions#testExceptionDuringRollback requires ('we are closed, no locks or files held'). Instead DocumentsWriter.abort() stops at the failing segment: the other segment is never aborted, stays locked by the thread that called rollback() and keeps its four stored-fields outputs open, and because the writer is now closed nothing can release them.

rows.title: Opening a segment whose stored-fields (.fdm) or term-vectors (.tvm) meta file has a damaged slice pointer reports CorruptIndexException but leaves the .fdx (.tvx) file open, because FieldsIndexReader's constructor closes its input only when the header or checksum step fails
rows.summary: You open an index with DirectoryReader.open, and one segment's stored-fields meta file (.fdm), or term-vectors meta file (.tvm), has a damaged byte in one of the pointers that say where the index data sits in the .fdx (.tvx) file, as a disk or copy error can leave it. You expect what Lucene does for other damaged files: the open fails with CorruptIndexException and every file it opened is closed again. rows.title: When DirectoryReader.openIfChanged on a FilterDirectoryReader (for example SoftDeletesDirectoryReaderWrapper) fails while wrapping the reopened reader, the newly opened inner reader is never closed, so the segment readers it shares with the old reader, and its files, leak

You expect the failed call to release what it opened, so that closing your old reader, the only one you hold ('The provided reader is not closed (you are responsible for doing so); if a new reader is returned you also must eventually close it'), frees every segment reader and file. Instead FilterDirectoryReader.wrapDirectoryReader neither returns nor closes the inner reader it was just given, so that reader keeps an extra reference on every shared segment (refCount 2 after the failure, still 1 after you close the old reader) and the new segments' files stay open.

rows.title: DirectoryReader.open and openIfChanged with an ExecutorService never close the segment readers of tasks the executor already accepted when a later submit is rejected (or when the opening thread is interrupted while it waits), so those segments' files stay open

rows.title: If MergePolicy.keepFullyDeletedSegment throws while IndexWriter opens an NRT reader (for example a read error while SoftDeletesRetentionMergePolicy runs its retention query), StandardDirectoryReader.open never releases the SegmentReader it obtained just before the check, so that segment's core and files stay open after IndexWriter.close()

rows.title: MultiReader.close() leaves later sub-readers open when closing an earlier sub-reader throws an unchecked exception: doClose catches only IOException (every release since 1.4)
rows.summary: You wrap two DirectoryReaders in a MultiReader (the one-argument constructor closes its sub-readers on close) and the first reader has a reader-closed listener that throws an unchecked exception such as IllegalStateException. You expect MultiReader.close() to close both sub-readers and rethrow the first failure, which is what it does when the failure is an IOException and what IndexReader's own close does under unchecked exceptions. Instead doClose catches only IOException, so the loop stops after the first reader: the second reader is never closed (its refCount stays 1), and because the MultiReader already counts as closed, it can no longer be closed through the MultiReader.

rows.title: With an index sort, a failure while creating the sorted stored-fields or term-vectors writer during flush leaves the reader on the temporary .fdt/.fdx (.tvd/.tvx) files open after IndexWriter closes itself
rows.summary: You configure an index sort, and while a flush is creating the final sorted stored-fields (or term-vectors) files, creating or opening a file fails with an IOException, for example because the process has too many open files. You expect IndexWriter to close itself, as it does after any failed flush, and to release every file it opened. Instead the reader that the flush had just opened on the temporary .fdt/.fdx (or .tvd/.tvx) files is never closed, because it is opened one statement before the try whose finally closes it, so two inputs on already-deleted temporary files stay open (on MMapDirectory, mapped) after IndexWriter and the Directory are closed.

rows.title: A commit that fails before startCommit (merge-on-commit setup, doAfterFlush, the merge scheduler or the event listener) keeps references on all of its files, so the still-open writer never deletes them, not even on rollback() or close()
rows.summary: You call commit() and it throws a non-tragic exception early, for example an IOException while Lucene opens the small segments it merges as part of the commit (on by default), or from your MergePolicy.findFullFlushMerges or doAfterFlush override; the writer stays open, as Lucene intends. You expect the writer to delete the files of that failed commit once they are no longer needed: after later merges and commits, on deleteUnusedFiles(), on rollback() (whose javadoc says it removes any temporary files) or on close(). Instead prepareCommit has already taken a reference on every file of the commit and releases it only if startCommit fails, so these files keep a positive reference count and stay on disk until a new IndexWriter opens the directory.

rows.title: With reader pooling off, an IOException while IndexWriter opens a segment reader to apply buffered deletes leaks the reader-pool reference that IndexWriter.openSegmentStates took for it, so the segment's ReadersAndUpdates, and the SegmentReader and open files a later apply opens for it, stay in the pool until the segment is merged away or the writer closes (every release since 4.0.0)
rows.summary: You turn reader pooling off (IndexWriterConfig.setReaderPooling(false)) and delete a document; while one flush() applies that delete, opening the segment's reader fails with an IOException, so that flush throws, the writer stays open, and another flush or commit applies the delete successfully. You expect the writer to give back every reader-pool reference it took, so that, as without the I/O error, the segment is no longer pooled once the delete is applied and committed. Instead IndexWriter.openSegmentStates never releases the reference it took for the SegmentState whose constructor threw: the segment stays in the pool with refCount 2, and the SegmentReader (with its open files) that the next apply opens is kept until the segment is merged away or the writer closes.

rows.title: ReferenceManager.close() skips the afterClose() cleanup hook when releasing the current reference throws, and every later close() does nothing, so a subclass's afterClose() never runs (since 3.6.0)
rows.summary: You write a ReferenceManager subclass that frees its own resources in afterClose(), which the javadoc describes as 'Called after close(), so subclass can free any resources', and you close it while the final release of the current reference throws an IOException (for example a reader's ClosedListener fails). You expect close() to report the IOException and still run afterClose(), or at least to let a second close() run it. Instead close() throws without calling afterClose(), and because it has already set the current reference to null, every later close() returns at once, so the hook never runs and its resources are never freed.

rows.title: OfflineSorter.sort with an ExecutorService runs its failure cleanup before the partition-sort and merge tasks it already submitted have finished, so each task still queued or running leaves a temp file (prefix_sort_N.tmp) behind that nothing deletes (released since 6.6.0)
rows.summary: You give OfflineSorter your own ExecutorService so it sorts partitions in parallel, and when sort() fails (an I/O error, a truncated input file, or an interrupt of the sorting thread) you expect it to delete every temp file it created, as it does without an executor and as its own code comment says ('So we can remove any partially written temp files on exception'). Instead sort() deletes only the temp files that exist at that moment and rethrows, without waiting for or cancelling the partition-sort and merge tasks it already handed to the executor. Those tasks then run and each writes a new prefix_sort_N.tmp file that nothing ever deletes (executed: the directory holds no sorter file right after sort() throws, and foo_sort_1.tmp once the queued task has run; with exec == null the same failure leaves nothing).

rows.title: IndexRearranger.execute() shuts down its own thread pool only when the run succeeds, so a run that fails after starting work leaves non-daemon 'rearranger' worker threads alive forever and keeps the JVM from exiting
rows.summary: You run IndexRearranger.execute() and it fails after it has started its work, for example because one of your DocumentSelectors throws an IOException. You expect execute() to throw that error and to release the thread pool it created for the run, as it does when the run succeeds. Instead executor.shutdown() is only the last statement of execute(), not in a finally, so on the failure path the pool's worker threads, which are non-daemon and never time out, stay alive forever: a program whose rearrange failed does not exit, and every failed call leaves more idle threads.

rows.title: LockVerifyServer: when its 30-second accept timeout fires after some but not all clients have connected, run() throws SocketTimeoutException but the threads it started for the connected clients wait forever on the start latch, so the standalone server process never exits (every release since 4.8.0)
rows.summary: You start LockVerifyServer for two clients (the documented way to test a lock factory with LockStressTest), one client connects and the other never starts. You expect the server to end once its 30-second accept timeout fires, which is why the timeout exists: the code comment says 'give clients at most 30 secs to connect and send bytes', and a maintainer kept it in #12535 so 'the server ends if one of the clients does not start'. Instead run() throws SocketTimeoutException, but the thread it already started for the connected client stays parked forever on the start latch, which is counted down only after every client has connected, so the server JVM never exits and has to be killed.

rows.title: SortedInputIterator leaves its temp input file (and, when reopening the sorted file fails, the sorted file too) in the temp Directory when its constructor fails, so every WFSTCompletionLookup or TSTLookup build that fails while reading or sorting its input leaks a temp file (regression since 6.0.0)

Instead SortedInputIterator, which both suggesters use to sort their input, leaves its temp input file behind: its constructor copies and sorts the input in sort() without any cleanup on failure and throws before the caller has an object it could close, so three failed builds leave suggest_input_0.tmp, suggest_input_1.tmp and suggest_input_2.tmp. This is a regression from LUCENE-7113 (6.0.0), which rewrote sort() and dropped the failure cleanup that 5.5.x still had.

rows.title: IntObjectHashMap, LongObjectHashMap and CharObjectHashMap clear() reset the keys but never null the values array, so every former value stays strongly reachable; the default codec's Lucene103BlockTreeTermsReader.close() and Lucene90PointsReader.close(), which call clear() so that a closed reader's per-field objects can be garbage collected, therefore release nothing (since 9.11.0)
rows.summary: You put a value into an IntObjectHashMap (or a LongObjectHashMap or CharObjectHashMap) and call clear(). You expect the map to drop its reference to the value, as java.util.HashMap.clear() and the HPPC code these classes were forked from do, and as the default codec's Lucene103BlockTreeTermsReader.close() ('Clear so refs to terms index is GCable even if app hangs onto us') and Lucene90PointsReader.close() ('Free up heap') rely on. Instead clear() resets only the keys (where HPPC fills the values with null there is an empty '/* */' comment), so size() is 0 but the values array still holds the object, and an application that keeps a closed DirectoryReader keeps every field's FieldReader and BKDReader reachable.

rows.title: LRUQueryCache registers another core-closed listener each time a still-open segment core is cleared with clearCoreCacheKey and then cached again (on 10.x also after clear()), so a long-lived segment core collects one duplicate listener per clear-and-recache cycle
rows.summary: You cache a query for a segment, call LRUQueryCache.clearCoreCacheKey with that segment's core key while the reader stays open (then cleanUp()), and search again so the query is cached for the same core once more. You expect the cache to keep its single close listener on that core, because the code registers one listener per core (the registeredClosedListeners map that #15558 added), so closing the reader should notify the cache once. Instead clearCoreCacheKey also forgets that the listener was registered, the next caching registers a second one, and closing the reader runs the cache's listener twice; every further clear-and-recache cycle adds one more, and on 10.x the same happens after clear().

rows.title: GetTermInfo.getTermInfo opens a DirectoryReader on the caller's Directory and never closes it, so every call leaks that reader's open index files (file descriptors or memory mappings)
rows.summary: You call GetTermInfo.getTermInfo(dir, term) from Java to print a term's document frequency and total term frequency, and expect it to release the index files it opened, as its sibling HighFreqTerms.main does for its reader. Instead it opens a DirectoryReader, prints the two numbers and returns without closing the reader, which the caller never sees and so cannot close. rows.title: ICUTokenizerFactory leaves a custom per-script rule file (rulefiles) open when reading or decoding it fails: parseRules closes its reader only after a successful read loop, so a rule file that is not valid UTF-8, or an I/O error while reading it, leaves the stream the ResourceLoader opened unclosed until garbage collection (every release since 4.1.0)

Instead parseRules calls reader.close() only after its read loop has finished normally, so the exception skips the close and the InputStream returned by the ResourceLoader stays open: a tracking loader still holds it after inform() threw, and with a real file read through FilesystemResourceLoader the test framework's LeakFS reports 'file handle leaks: [InputStream(.../latin-rules.rbbi)]'. The descriptor is released only when the stream is garbage collected; a rule file that decodes but does not compile is closed before compiling and does not leak.

rows.title: Analyzer.normalize(String, String) closes only the StringReader it creates and never the Reader or CharFilter returned by initReaderForNormalization, so a normalization CharFilter is closed when the same chain analyzes text (Tokenizer.close()) but never when a query parser normalizes a multi-term query term (latent: no shipped CharFilter releases anything of its own in close(); since 6.2.0)

rows.title: WordBreakSpellChecker.suggestWordCombinations does not honour maxEvaluations: the counter is compared with == and the break leaves only the inner loop, so every later left term is still evaluated and a limit of 0 or less is ignored (the #12077 fix in 9.5.0 covered only suggestWordBreaks)
rows.summary: You call WordBreakSpellChecker.setMaxEvaluations(n), documented as 'the maximum number of word combinations to evaluate', and then suggestWordCombinations, and you expect at most n combined-term lookups and so at most n suggestions. Instead the limit cuts off only the rest of the one left term at which the counter first equals n, and every later left term is evaluated in full: with every 2-6 letter run of 'abcdef' indexed, the query [a, b, c, d, e, f], maxChanges=5 and maxEvaluations=1, 11 of the 15 combinations are evaluated and returned, and maxEvaluations=0 evaluates all 15. Nothing is thrown and the work stays bounded by the number of terms times maxChanges; only the configured cap is not applied.

rows.title: ParallelLeafReader stored fields ignore StoredFieldVisitor.Status.STOP: the later parallel readers still offer and deliver fields after the visitor answered STOP
rows.summary: You split a document over two lockstep indexes (title in index A, price in index B), open them as a ParallelLeafReader, and load the document with a StoredFieldVisitor that answers STOP at title and YES otherwise, expecting the visit to end at title, as STOP promises ('stop processing any other fields for this document') and as a single index holding the same document does. Instead the second parallel reader still asks needsField(price) and delivers price=42 after the STOP, because ParallelLeafReader.storedFields().document() hands the visitor to each parallel reader in turn and never checks its answer. rows.title: SpanMultiTermQueryWrapper's top-N span rewrites (TopTermsSpanBooleanQueryRewrite, FrequentTermsSpanBooleanQueryRewrite) do not cap their size at IndexSearcher#getMaxClauseCount, so a span-wrapped FuzzyQuery that works unwrapped throws TooManyNestedClauses

rows.title: SpanMultiTermQueryWrapper.FrequentTermsSpanBooleanQueryRewrite (new in 10.6.0) sizes its priority queue from maxSize before collecting any term, so maxSize >= 2147483631 (for example Integer.MAX_VALUE as 'no limit') makes every rewrite throw IllegalArgumentException, and a large maxSize allocates a (maxSize + 1)-slot array on every rewrite
rows.summary: You wrap a PrefixQuery in SpanMultiTermQueryWrapper, call setRewriteMethod(new FrequentTermsSpanBooleanQueryRewrite(Integer.MAX_VALUE)), whose javadoc promises only that it 'keeps at most maxSize terms' (ranked by document frequency instead of boost, unlike TopTermsSpanBooleanQueryRewrite), and expect it to keep all 3 matching terms, as TopTermsSpanBooleanQueryRewrite(Integer.MAX_VALUE) does on the same index. Instead the constructor accepts the value and every search then throws IllegalArgumentException 'maxSize must be >= 0 and < 2147483631; got: 2147483647', because getTopLevelBuilder() returns PriorityQueue.usingComparator(maxSize, order) and ScoringRewrite.rewrite calls it before it collects any term, so the internal queue pre-allocates maxSize + 1 slots (or rejects a size it cannot allocate) instead of being sized by the terms actually found; for the same reason a large legal cap such as 2^26 allocates about 268 MB per rewrite for 3 terms. Sizing the queue lazily, by min(maxSize, collected terms), as the sibling TopTermsRewrite does with a growing queue, fixes both and leaves every result unchanged.

rows.title: BytesRefArray.iterator(Comparator) throws NullPointerException for a null comparator once the array holds 2 or more values, instead of iterating in append order as its javadoc says (regression since 8.5.0, LUCENE-9228)
rows.summary: You append two or more values (for example c, a, b) to a BytesRefArray and call iterator((Comparator<BytesRef>) null), expecting the values back in append order, as the method's javadoc promises ('Otherwise the order is the same as the values were appended') and as Lucene 8.4.1 and earlier do. Instead the call throws NullPointerException ('Cannot invoke Comparator.compare ... because this.val$cmp is null', from StringSorter$1.compare via BytesRefArray.sort), because the method now always sorts with the given comparator; with 0 or 1 values, or with the no-arg iterator(), append order still comes back. The one-line fix restores the pre-8.5 null check ('return iterator(comp == null ? null : sort(comp, false));'); a maintainer may instead prefer to correct the javadoc.

rows.title: XYPolygon evaluates its winding sum in float, so valid polygons with large finite coordinates (differences of about 1.8e19 or more) can get the wrong winding order, and XYShape rejects them as 'Unable to Tessellate shape'
rows.summary: You build an XYPolygon with large but finite float coordinates, which the constructor accepts (any finite float), for example the triangle (0,0), (2^66,2^66), (2^67,2^66), and index it with XYShape.createIndexableFields; you expect it to index exactly like the same triangle at scale 1, because multiplying every coordinate by a power of two is exact and changes neither the shape nor its orientation. The constructor computes the winding sum with float products, which overflow to Infinity once coordinate differences reach about 1.8e19; Infinity minus Infinity is NaN, and a NaN sum is labelled CW. The Tessellator then links the ring the wrong way round, finds no ear to cut, and rejects the valid polygon with 'Unable to Tessellate shape. Possible malformed shape detected.'
rows.area: geo / XY shapes (XYPolygon winding order, Tessellator.tessellate(XYPolygon), XYShape.createIndexableFields and createDocValueField)

rows.title: Rectangle.fromPointDistance throws 'invalid longitude NaN' for some legal circles whose edge stops just short of a pole, so LatLon distance queries on them fail with IllegalArgumentException
rows.summary: You run LatLonPoint.newDistanceQuery("p", 0.43945312499999994, 0, 9958692.080819247), a valid centre and a finite, non-negative radius whose circle stops about 7 cm short of the north pole, and expect it to match the two indexed points inside the circle. Instead IndexSearcher.count throws IllegalArgumentException 'invalid longitude NaN; must be between -180.0 and 180.0' from Rectangle.fromPointDistance, and LatLonDocValuesField.newSlowDistanceQuery throws the same when it is built. The bounding box computes asin(sin(r) / cos(lat)) without a clamp, and SloppyMath.cos, which is not monotone across its lookup-table switches, makes the quotient 1.0000000000000002 although its exact value is below 1, so asin returns NaN.

rows.title: geo3d path distance methods (GeoStandardPath, GeoDegeneratePath) and Geo3DDocValuesField.newPathSort throw RuntimeException "Can't find world intersection" for a point inside the path that sits at the edge of the 1e-12 tolerance band of a segment's cutoff plane

Instead, when the point sits at the very edge of the 1e-12 tolerance band of a segment's cutoff plane, the call throws RuntimeException("Can't find world intersection ..."): on the unit sphere a point 3.4e-6 rad beside a path of width 1e-4 and 1e-12 rad past its middle point throws instead of returning about 0.1000034, the same happens for a zero-width path's nearest and centre distance, and a 500 km path sort whose middle point sits at a stored document's decoded longitude makes IndexSearcher.search throw. The cause: the segment's tolerant section test accepts the point, then the same tolerant test rejects both rounded perpendicular feet of the point on the path, and the code throws instead of picking one.

rows.title: Automata.makeBinaryInterval (TermRangeQuery.toAutomaton) stores an empty arc [256, 255] for an open-ended range whose lower term starts with byte 0xFF, so determinizing a union of such automata, or searching one with an AutomatonQuery, throws in StateSet.decr (since 5.2.0)

You expect a DFA that accepts every term from {0xFF, 'a'} up, such as {0xFF, 'c'}, as you get when the lower terms start with 0xFE. Instead Operations.determinize throws AssertionError (-ea) or ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException 'Index -7 out of bounds for length 9' (-da) in StateSet.decr, and an AutomatonQuery search over the union fails the same way, because makeBinaryInterval's open-upper branch adds the transition [minLabel + 1, 0xFF], here the empty range [256, 255], without the 'minLabel < 255' guard its sibling branch has.

rows.title: Operations.determinize throws (AssertionError with -ea, ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException with -da) for a valid automaton with an arc ending at Integer.MAX_VALUE, because its sweep sorts points with 'point - other.point' and the arc's end point 1 + max wraps to Integer.MIN_VALUE
rows.summary: You build the union of {0}[11, Integer.MAX_VALUE] and {0}[0, 10] (a 0 followed by any one label) with Automata.makeChar, makeCharRange, Operations.concatenate and union, and call Operations.determinize; you expect a deterministic automaton for the same language. Instead it throws AssertionError in StateSet.decr with -ea, and ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException 'Index -5 out of bounds for length 9' with -da. The sweep files the end of the [11, MAX] arc under 1 + MAX, which wraps to Integer.MIN_VALUE, and sorts its points with the subtraction point - other.point, which is no consistent order for MIN and 0, so it closes the [0, 10] arc before opening it and decrements a state it never added.

rows.title: Automaton.finishState leaves same-destination arcs unmerged after an arc ending at Integer.MAX_VALUE (max + 1 wraps in int), so the state is flagged non-deterministic and determinize hands back a one-state automaton that CharacterRunAutomaton rejects
rows.summary: You build the automaton ([0, Integer.MAX_VALUE] | [5, 10])* with Automata.makeCharRange, Operations.union and Operations.repeat, determinize it and run it with CharacterRunAutomaton; you expect it to accept "abc", because a finished state merges same-destination ranges that touch or overlap into one arc, as the Automaton javadoc promises. Instead the CharacterRunAutomaton constructor throws IllegalArgumentException 'Automaton must be deterministic': finishState merges a range only while min <= max + 1, and once max is Integer.MAX_VALUE that sum wraps to Integer.MIN_VALUE, so [5, 10] stays a second, overlapping arc, the state is flagged non-deterministic, and determinize returns the one-state automaton unchanged. The accepted language is right; only the reduced form and the determinism flag are wrong.

rows.title: InputStreamDataInput.skipBytes calls InputStream.skip once and throws EOFException whenever it skips fewer bytes than asked, but InputStream.skip may legally skip fewer bytes before the end (BufferedInputStream.skip skips only what it has buffered), so skipBytes(n) fails with data left in the stream and the bytes it did skip are lost (since 9.0.0)
rows.summary: You wrap a BufferedInputStream in an InputStreamDataInput, read a byte (which fills the stream's 8 KiB buffer) and call skipBytes(10,000) with 99,999 bytes left. You expect the skip to succeed, as DataInput.skipBytes ('Skip over numBytes bytes') promises and as Lucene 8.x did, and the next readByte() to return byte 10,001. Instead skipBytes calls InputStream.skip once, gets back only the 8,191 buffered bytes (a short count the JDK contract allows before the end of the stream), treats that as end of input and throws EOFException, after those 8,191 bytes have already been consumed; no Lucene code makes this call, so only applications that skip on this public class are affected.

rows.title: ByteBuffersDataInput readShort/readInt/readLong throw IndexOutOfBoundsException instead of EOFException on a read past the end of input longer than one block (ByteBuffersDirectory files over 1 KiB)
rows.summary: You write a file of more than 1 KiB to a ByteBuffersDirectory (say 1,030 bytes), seek to 2 bytes before the end and call readInt(), and expect an EOFException: readByte() and readBytes() of the same input throw it, NIOFSDirectory and MMapDirectory throw it for the same bytes, and BaseDirectoryTestCase#testIntsUnderflow requires it of every Directory. The cause is the fast path added in 9.0.0 (LUCENE-10149): it checks the read against the block size (blockOffset + width <= blockMask), not against the end of the data in the last block, and reads with an absolute ByteBuffer get whose exception nothing translates.

rows.title: Slicing an MMapDirectory clone with read advice after its original is closed throws AssertionError instead of AlreadyClosedException (PosixNativeAccess.madvise wraps the closed-arena IllegalStateException in an Error)

Instead the slice call throws java.lang.AssertionError: java.lang.IllegalStateException: Already closed, because PosixNativeAccess.madvise wraps every Throwable of the native posix_madvise call in an AssertionError before MemorySegmentIndexInput.advise() can turn the closed-arena IllegalStateException into AlreadyClosedException. It is an explicit throw, not an assert, so it happens with assertions disabled too; no data is read or written wrongly.

rows.title: ByteBuffersIndexOutput.getChecksum returns 0 for an empty output without asking the supplied Checksum (Adler32 of no bytes is 1), because its size-keyed cache starts out as 'size 0, value 0'
rows.summary: You create a ByteBuffersIndexOutput with the public constructor that takes your own java.util.zip.Checksum, for example new Adler32(), and call getChecksum() before writing anything; you expect Adler32's value for no bytes, which is 1, because IndexOutput.getChecksum returns 'the current checksum of bytes written so far'. Instead you get 0: getChecksum caches its last result by output size, and that cache starts as 'size 0, value 0', so for an empty output it never asks the Checksum. With CRC32, the only Checksum Lucene itself uses, the checksum of no bytes is 0, so the shortcut happens to be right there, and once a byte is written Adler32 values are correct too.
rows.area: store / ByteBuffersIndexOutput (getChecksum with a caller-supplied java.util.zip.Checksum)

rows.title: (Latent) PagedBytesDataInput.clone(), setPosition(getPosition()) and a skipBytes that lands on the end look up the block after the last one when the data ends exactly on a block border, so with 16 full blocks (for example 64 KiB at blockBits 12) they throw ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException, and with other block counts they leave a null current block (since 3.5.0)
rows.summary: You write data into a PagedBytes whose length is an exact multiple of its block size (here 16 blocks of 4 KiB), freeze it, read a PagedBytesDataInput from getDataInput() to the end, and then clone it, call setPosition(getPosition()), or skip the last bytes so that the position lands exactly on the end. You expect an input positioned at the end, as setPosition's javadoc ('Seek to a position previously obtained from getPosition') and DataInput.clone's ('positioned at the same point as the stream they were cloned from') promise, and as happens when the data ends inside a block or is empty. Instead setPosition looks up the block after the last one, because it resolves the block eagerly while the reads move to the next block only when they need more bytes, and throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException 'Index 16 out of bounds for length 16' (or, for other block counts, leaves a null block that the next zero-length read trips over); no Lucene code makes these calls, so only code that uses the internal class directly is affected.
rows.area: core / util: PagedBytes (PagedBytes.PagedBytesDataInput setPosition, clone, skipBytes; @lucene.internal)

rows.title: ByteBuffersDataOutput's documented largest block size LIMIT_MAX_BITS_PER_BLOCK = 31 is off by one: the expert constructor (and FSTCompiler.getOnHeapReaderWriter(31)) accepts 31 block bits, but 1 << 31 is Integer.MIN_VALUE, so the output cannot hold a single byte and its first write throws IllegalArgumentException 'capacity < 0'
rows.summary: You build a ByteBuffersDataOutput with the expert constructor and 31 block bits, the value of the public constant LIMIT_MAX_BITS_PER_BLOCK, documented as the 'Largest maxBitsPerBlock allowed' (the constructor rejects 32 with 'too large, must not exceed 31' and accepts 31), or you call FSTCompiler.getOnHeapReaderWriter(31), and expect either a usable output or the same IllegalArgumentException at construction that 32 gets. Instead the output is created, and its first writeByte throws IllegalArgumentException 'capacity < 0: (-2147483648 < 0)' from ByteBuffer.allocate, because appendBlock computes the block size as 1 << 31 in int, which is Integer.MIN_VALUE. No Java ByteBuffer can hold 2^31 bytes, so 31 is never a usable block size, and Lucene's own FST read side caps the same value at 30.
rows.area: core / store (ByteBuffersDataOutput block-size limit; also util/fst FSTCompiler.getOnHeapReaderWriter)

rows.title: IndexWriter accepts doc-values updates of the reserved parent field; with index sorting and document blocks this leaves a segment that fails CheckIndex, or an index whose merges fail
rows.summary: You use index sorting with a parent field (IndexWriterConfig#setParentField) and document blocks, and call IndexWriter#updateNumericDocValue or #updateDocValues on that parent field, for example to give a child document a parent mark or to set a parent's mark to null. You expect the call to be rejected with IllegalArgumentException, as IndexWriter rejects doc-values updates of index-sort fields and any document that contains the parent field ('is a reserved field'), or else the index to stay valid. Instead the update is accepted: a child given a mark can put the segment out of index-sort order, so CheckIndex fails ('segment has indexSort=<long: "sort"> but docID=1 sorts after docID=2') as soon as the update is committed, and a removed mark makes the next merge throw EOFException in MultiSorter and close the writer when the unmarked block was the last of its segment and every document there has a sort value, and otherwise silently moves the orphaned documents into the next block.
rows.area: index / IndexWriter doc-values updates

rows.title: If merge setup throws, the vectors merge instances obtained so far never get finishMerge (MergeState constructor and PerFieldKnnVectorsFormat merge copy constructor)
rows.summary: You merge segments that have vectors (forceMerge, a background merge or addIndexes(CodecReader...)) and the merge fails while it is being set up, after it already took a vectors merge instance from one source segment or one vector field, for example because re-opening a data file for sequential reads throws an IOException. You expect every merge instance obtained with KnnVectorsReader#getMergeInstance to get its finishMerge call on this failure too, as #14977 ('always called regardless of merge outcome'), the 10.6.0 CHANGES entry for GITHUB#14930 ('including exceptional exits') and the test framework's AssertingKnnVectorsReader close check (mergeInstanceCount == finishMergeCount) say. Instead the failure happens inside new SegmentMerger(...) (the MergeState constructor) or inside the PerFieldKnnVectorsFormat merge copy constructor, before IndexWriter enters the try/finally that calls cleanupMerge, so the instances already obtained never get finishMerge (obtained=1, finished=0); stock formats on main see no effect because their finishMerge does nothing.
rows.area: index / merge setup (MergeState merge instances, KnnVectorsReader finishMerge lifecycle)

rows.title: IndexWriter's merge-on-commit / merge-on-getReader wrapper forwards mergeFinished to the merge policy's OneMerge but never calls its mergeInit, so a merge that ran and committed reaches the policy's OneMerge as mergeFinished(success=true) with no mergeInit before it (since 8.6.0)

You expect that OneMerge to get mergeInit when the merge starts and mergeFinished when it ends, as the same OneMerge does when it comes from findMerges or forceMerge. Instead IndexWriter wraps the policy's merge in its own OneMerge that forwards mergeFinished and the other hooks but not mergeInit, so the policy's OneMerge sees mergeFinished(success=true) for a merge that ran and committed and never sees mergeInit (in the repro: mergeInit=0, mergeFinished=1 for the merge on commit and on getReader; 1 and 1 for forceMerge).

rows.title: FLOAT16 vectors read back from a quantized index whose raw vectors were dropped can contain +-Infinity, so full-precision rescoring ranks an exact match last
rows.summary: You index finite FLOAT16 vectors with large components (for example 60000) in the Lucene104 scalar-quantized format, then drop the raw vectors the way the format's own tests do (simulateEmptyRawVectors), so reads go through the dequantized fp16 view. You expect getFloat16VectorValues().vectorValue() to return an approximation of each stored vector, and full-precision rescoring with a document's own vector to rank that document first. Instead OptimizedScalarQuantizer.deQuantize(byte[], short[], ...) narrows a slightly out-of-range float reconstruction to fp16 without saturating, so 60000 comes back as Infinity, and rescoring gives the exact match the score 0.0 and ranks it last (with -ea, an AssertionError in VectorUtil.squareDistance).

rows.title: With assertions enabled, the first document fails an internal assertion (and since 10.0.0 IndexWriter then closes itself) when setRAMBufferSizeMB is given a huge value such as Double.MAX_VALUE or +Infinity, because DocumentsWriterFlushControl.assertMemory doubles the RAM buffer in long arithmetic and its upper bound wraps negative (-ea only; every release since 4.0.0)

rows.title: An interrupted wait in IndexWriter's flush stall skips the waiter deregistration (DocumentsWriterStallControl.waitIfStalled), so with assertions enabled the same thread's next addDocument during a stall of the same writer fails an internal assert and IndexWriter closes itself as a tragic event, losing its uncommitted documents (tragic close since 10.0.0; the skipped deregistration since 4.0)
rows.summary: With assertions enabled, you interrupt a thread that is blocked in addDocument because IndexWriter has stalled indexing to let its flushes catch up; as the IndexWriter javadoc documents, the call throws ThreadInterruptedException and the writer stays open. You expect that thread's later calls in a stall to leave the writer open too, interrupted or not. Instead the first interrupt skipped the step that removes the thread from the stall control's waiter list, so the thread's next wait in a stall of the same writer fails the 'registered only once' assert, and IndexWriter treats that AssertionError as a tragic event and closes, discarding the uncommitted documents (since 10.0.0; without assertions nothing visible happens).

rows.title: With assertions enabled, re-sorting an index with document blocks through SortingCodecReader and addIndexes fails SortingCodecReader's cache assertion for the parent field

You expect the re-sort to succeed, as it does with assertions disabled (the result is then correctly sorted with every block intact) and as it does for an index without blocks. Instead, with Java assertions enabled (-ea), addIndexes throws AssertionError 'only sort fields should be cached twice but [_parent] is not a sort field' and the destination writer closes, because MultiSorter reads the parent field's doc values once to find the blocks and the doc-values merge reads them again, while SortingCodecReader's internal check allows a second read only for sort fields.

rows.title: With assertions enabled, calling Scorable.getChildren() from LeafCollector.setScorer on a TOP_SCORES BooleanQuery with minimumNumberShouldMatch >= 2 throws AssertionError from WANDScorer.ensureConsistent, which calls score() on sub-scorers that are not positioned yet (clauses such as ConstantScoreQuery, PrefixQuery or a TermQuery on a docs-only field; 10.1.0 through 10.6.0 and main)
rows.summary: You search a BooleanQuery with three SHOULD clauses and minimumNumberShouldMatch 2 with a collector whose scoreMode is TOP_SCORES and whose setScorer walks the scorer tree with Scorable.getChildren(), a pattern Lucene's own TestBooleanQueryVisitSubscorers uses. You expect getChildren() to return the three clause scorers, as it does with assertions disabled. Instead, with -ea, WANDScorer.getChildren() runs its internal consistency check before any document has been read: the check calls score() on the not-yet-positioned clause scorers and asserts that their sum equals the lead score, which is still 0, so the search fails with AssertionError at WANDScorer.java:238 whenever a clause scores non-zero while unpositioned (for example ConstantScoreQuery clauses).
rows.area: core / search: WANDScorer (Scorable.getChildren before the first document, TOP_SCORES minimum-should-match disjunctions)

rows.title: LazyDocument.fetchRealValues checks its value-count assertion in the wrong direction: with assertions enabled, reading a lazy value of a multi-valued field before that field's last getField call throws AssertionError ('More lazy values then real values'), while the over-request case the message names is not caught and fails with ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException
rows.summary: For a document whose stored field f has the values v0 and v1, you call LazyDocument.getField(f), read the returned field, then call getField(f) again and read the second one; getField's own comment says the document is re-fetched when more lazy fields are requested after others were loaded, so you expect v0 and then v1. With assertions enabled the first read instead throws AssertionError 'More lazy values then real values for field: f', because fetchRealValues asserts realValues.length <= lazyValues.size() (LazyDocument.java:113-114), the reverse of what its message and the loop right after it (:116-121, which reads realValues[i] once per lazy value) need. With -da the same calls return v0 and v1, and the case the message describes (more getField calls than stored values) passes the assertion and fails with ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException in both modes.
rows.area: misc / document: LazyDocument (lazy loading of stored fields, multi-valued fields)

rows.title: Default points format: after a PointTree visits a leaf and moves back to its parent, the next visitDocIDs, visitDocValues or moveToChild there fails an assertion in BKDReader (only with -ea; results are correct with -da)
rows.summary: You index points with the default codec, take a PointTree from PointValues.getPointTree(), go down to a leaf, visit its documents (visitDocIDs or visitDocValues), call moveToParent() and then visit the parent or call moveToChild() again, which the API has allowed since LUCENE-10262 (Lucene 9.1, 'This change allows random navigation of a PointValues#PointTree'), and expect the parent's documents or its first child. Instead, with assertions enabled, that next call throws AssertionError in BKDReader.BKDPointTree.resetNodeDataPosition (BKDReader.java:401): the leaf visit had reset the reader's inner-node input to a saved position that readNodeData writes only for inner nodes, so for a leaf it is stale (0 on a fresh tree), and the parent then finds the input behind its own saved position. With assertions disabled every later read seeks to an absolute position first, so all results are correct and only -ea test runs fail.
rows.area: util / BKD points (BKDReader.BKDPointTree navigation: visitDocIDs/visitDocValues on a leaf reset the inner-node input; default points format)

rows.title: Hunspell spell() and suggest() throw AssertionError under -ea when a word ends with a CHECKCOMPOUNDPATTERN replacement whose beginchars are empty, because the compound check looks up a zero-length second part
rows.summary: You load a Hunspell dictionary with a compound rule such as 'CHECKCOMPOUNDPATTERN o /X z' (a simplified compound form whose second part may begin with anything: hunspell(5) allows empty beginchars with a flag and an optional replacement) and call Hunspell.spell("foz"), and expect true or false; C Hunspell 1.3.2 and 1.7.2 both say false. Instead, with assertions enabled, spell() and suggest() throw java.lang.AssertionError from WordStorage.lookupWord ('assert length > 0'). The cause: checkCompoundPatternReplacements expands the final 'z' to 'o' plus empty beginchars and puts the break right after 'foo', but never checks that a second part remains, so checkCompoundsAfter looks up a second part of length 0; with -da that lookup finds nothing and spell() returns false for the repro.
rows.area: analysis / hunspell (Hunspell.spell and suggest compound checking, CHECKCOMPOUNDPATTERN replacements)

rows.title: BpVectorReorderer scales a zero DOT_PRODUCT/COSINE centroid by 1/sqrt(0), so a split whose vectors cancel out gets a NaN centroid: with assertions on, reordering fails and a reordering merge closes the IndexWriter; with assertions off, that split is silently not refined
rows.summary: You index DOT_PRODUCT or COSINE float vectors and reorder them with BpVectorReorderer, by calling computeDocMap or by merging through BPReorderingMergePolicy, for example 64 legal unit vectors where docs 0..31 alternate (1,0) and (-1,0) and docs 32..63 are (0,1); you expect a valid reordering, as for any other legal vectors. Instead the half whose vectors cancel out sums to the zero vector, computeCentroid normalizes it by 1/sqrt(0) = Infinity and the centroid becomes NaN. With assertions on, VectorUtil.dotProduct then fails with 'AssertionError: not finite: NaN from <[1.0, 0.0],[NaN, NaN]>' and the merge path closes the IndexWriter; with assertions off nothing throws, but the NaN biases leave that split in doc-ID order.
rows.area: misc / BP merge-time reordering (BpVectorReorderer centroid arithmetic)

rows.title: TopDocs.merge with a custom tie breaker fails an assertion (only with -ea) when the tie breaker returns 0 for tied hits from two different shards at the same rank
rows.summary: You merge per-shard results with TopDocs.merge(start, topN, shardHits, tieBreaker), or the Sort overload, and pass a valid Comparator<ScoreDoc> tie breaker that ignores the shard, for example one that compares doc ids only; two shards each have a hit with the same score (or sort value) at the same rank and the same local doc id. You expect both hits back, since the method accepts any custom tie breaker and its helper documents that a 0 from the tie breaker falls back to hit indices. Instead, with assertions enabled, the merge throws AssertionError at TopDocs.java:88 ('assert first.hitIndex != second.hitIndex'), because that check assumes a tie can only come from the same shard while the merge queue only ever compares hits of different shards; with -da both hits are returned.

rows.title: FixedBitSet.ensureCapacityAndClear returns the old set bits instead of a cleared set when it grows a set whose backing array is larger than needed: the array-reuse branch wraps the old array without clearing it (since 10.4.0)
rows.summary: You wrap a two-word long[] in a 64-bit FixedBitSet (the FixedBitSet(long[], int) constructor says the array 'may be larger' as long as the extra bits are clear), set bit 0, and call FixedBitSet.ensureCapacityAndClear(bits, 64) to make room for bit 64. You expect an empty set, because the javadoc says the method will 'Clear the given bits and ensure it can store a value at desiredBit index', and the two-step code it replaced (ensureCapacity, then clear()) returns one. Instead the method sees that the existing array is already big enough, wraps that same array in a new 128-bit set without zeroing it, and returns a set in which bit 0 is still set (cardinality 1 instead of 0).

rows.title: FixedBitSet.xor with a longer set that fits in the same number of 64-bit words copies that set's bits at or above length() into the ghost bits, so cardinality, nextSetBit, equals and hashCode report bits the set cannot hold (since 4.7.0)
rows.summary: You make a 10-bit FixedBitSet a and a 20-bit FixedBitSet b with only bit 15 set, and call a.xor(b). You expect a to stay empty, because none of its bits 0..9 changed and the class keeps the bits past length() (its 'ghost bits') clear, as cardinality, nextSetBit, equals and hashCode rely on. Instead xor XORs whole 64-bit words and checks only that b has no more words than a (both have one), so bit 15 lands in a's word: a.cardinality() returns 1 and a.nextSetBit(0) returns 15 for a set of length 10, and a no longer equals an empty 10-bit set.

Instead or/xor combine whole 64-bit words and check only that other has no more words (both have one, and the check is an assert), so bit 20 lands in the set's word: cardinality() returns 1 and nextSetBit(0) returns 20 for a set of length 10, with no error.

rows.title: IntObjectHashMap, LongObjectHashMap and CharObjectHashMap ramBytesUsed() size the reused values() cursor instead of each value, so every entry is charged a flat 256 bytes whatever its value: a map holding an 8 MiB long[] reports 416 bytes, and a null value adds 256 (since 9.11.0)
rows.summary: You put a value into an IntObjectHashMap (or a LongObjectHashMap or CharObjectHashMap) and call ramBytesUsed(). You expect the estimate to include that value, which is what the method's own sizeOfValues() loop is for: it walks values() and calls RamUsageEstimator.sizeOfObject once per entry. Instead the loop passes the iterator's reused ObjectCursor rather than cursor.value, sizeOfObject does not know that type and returns its 256-byte default, so every entry adds exactly 256 bytes: a map holding an 8 MiB long[] reports 416 bytes, and putting a null value into an empty map raises the estimate from 160 to 416 bytes.

rows.title: PriorityQueue.downHeap computes the child index i << 1 in int, so a queue holding 2^30 or more elements can throw ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException (when a sift-down reaches node 2^30) from updateTop, pop or insertWithOverflow and is left with one element lost and another duplicated
rows.summary: You fill a Lucene PriorityQueue with 2^30 + 1 elements, a size its constructor accepts (any maxSize below ArrayUtil.MAX_ARRAY_LENGTH), and call updateTop, pop or insertWithOverflow; you expect the usual log(size) sift-down and the new least element back. Instead, when the sift-down reaches node 2^30, the child index i << 1 wraps to Integer.MIN_VALUE, the negative index -2147483647 passes the 'k <= size' check, and the call throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException after children were already moved up, so the queue has lost the element being sifted and holds a second copy of another. A queue of 2^30 - 1 elements works; exactly 2^30 already fails for updateTop.

rows.title: (Latent) FixedBitSet.approximateCardinality returns a negative value for bit sets of 2^31-63 bits or more, because its scale factor 64 * numWords overflows int
rows.summary: You create a FixedBitSet of 2^31-63 to 2^31-1 bits (for example new FixedBitSet(Integer.MAX_VALUE), a legal length: the class javadoc points to LongBitSet only for more than 2.1B bits), set some bits and call approximateCardinality(); you expect a non-negative estimate of the number of set bits, as BitSet documents ('an approximation of the cardinality of this set'). Instead it returns a negative number (-2147418112 with all 2^31-1 bits set, -64 with a single set bit), because the scale factor (interval / rangeLength) * numWords / maxWord is computed in int and its product 64 * numWords wraps to Integer.MIN_VALUE once the set has 2^25 words; new BitDocIdSet(bits) then throws IllegalArgumentException 'cost must be >= 0'. No Lucene code path builds a bit set that long (doc-ID sets stop at IndexWriter.MAX_DOCS = 2^31-129 bits), so only external code that uses FixedBitSet directly over another int domain is affected.

Instead the method adds the array header and the per-element references in int arithmetic, which wraps, so it returns -2,147,483,616; in general the estimate is too low by a multiple of 2^32 bytes from 536,870,908 elements on (268,435,453 with 8-byte references), and it is negative only when the elements' own sizes add little.

rows.title: (Latent) MonotonicBlockPackedWriter writes a block whose values end close to Long.MAX_VALUE with too few bits, so MonotonicBlockPackedReader returns wrong values: min + (long) (avg * i) overflows in flush()

rows.title: PackedInts' int[] -> byte[] encoder writes wrong bytes at 33 to 64 bits per value, because BulkOperationPacked.encode(int[], .., byte[], ..) shifts an int and Java takes an int shift count mod 32: the value 1 at 64 bits is written as 0x0000000100000001; latent, no Lucene code encodes int[] this way (since 4.2.0)
rows.summary: You get the PACKED encoder for 64 bits per value from PackedInts.getEncoder and encode the int[] {1} into a byte[] of one block. You expect the 64-bit big-endian block of 1, {0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 1}, which is what the same encoder writes for the long[] {1L} and what its int[] -> long[] overload produces. Instead it writes {0, 0, 0, 1, 0, 0, 0, 1}, which decodes as 4294967297: the int[] -> byte[] loop (BulkOperationPacked.java:243-269) holds the value in an int and shifts it right by 56, 48, 40, 32, ... bits, and Java takes an int shift count mod 32, so the high bytes get copies of the low bytes (the same happens at every width from 33 to 64).
rows.area: util / packed (PackedInts bulk encoders: BulkOperationPacked.encode(int[] -> byte[]))

rows.title: PackedInts' int[] -> long[] encoder sign-extends the low part of a value that crosses a 64-bit block, so at 35, 37-39, 41-47 or 49-63 bits per value an int with its top bit set (for example -1, which the encoder reads as 4294967295 everywhere else) gets extra high bits and decodes too large; latent, no Lucene code encodes int[] this way (since 4.0.0)
rows.summary: You get the PACKED encoder for 35 bits per value from PackedInts.getEncoder, encode one iteration of 64 ints that are all 0 except values[53] = -1 into long blocks, and decode the blocks back to long[]. You expect value 53 to come back as 4294967295, because the int[] encoder reads each int as its unsigned 32-bit value (it does so on its other branches, and the upstream TestPackedInts oracle defines an int that way), and that is what you get at any position that does not straddle two blocks and at 33, 34, 36, 40, 48 or 64 bits per value. Instead it comes back as 17179869183 (2^34 - 1): value 53 straddles blocks 28 and 29, and BulkOperationPacked.java:209 masks its 34-bit low part out of the sign-extended int instead of the zero-extended one, so two extra bits are set.
rows.area: util / packed (PackedInts bulk encoders: BulkOperationPacked.encode(int[] -> long[]))

rows.title: PackedInts.getWriterNoHeader's documented unknown-count mode (valueCount -1) throws on the first add, or already in the factory, whenever mem is at least byteBlockCount + 8 * byteValueCount (for PACKED every width from 127 bytes, PackedInts.DEFAULT_BUFFER_SIZE included), because BulkOperation.computeIterations treats -1 as a real count and sizes the write buffers for 0 (or -1) values; latent, no Lucene code uses the -1 mode (since 4.0.0-BETA)
rows.summary: You create a headerless packed-ints writer with PackedInts.getWriterNoHeader(out, PACKED, -1, 7, PackedInts.DEFAULT_BUFFER_SIZE), which the javadoc allows ('just pass -1 as valueCount' to start writing without knowing how many values will follow), add the value 5 and call finish(), and you expect to read 5 back, as you can with mem 0 or with a known count. Instead the first add throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException 'Index 0 out of bounds for length 0' at PackedWriter.add, with -ea and -da: BulkOperation.computeIterations applies a cap meant for a known count ('don't allocate for more than the size of the reader'), which for -1 returns 0 iterations (or -1 at 8, 16, ..., 64 bits per value, where the factory throws NegativeArraySizeException), so the writer gets empty buffers. Every PACKED width fails once mem is 127 bytes or more; no Lucene code uses the -1 mode, so only code that calls this internal writer API itself hits it.
rows.area: util / packed ints (PackedInts.getWriterNoHeader, PackedWriter, BulkOperation.computeIterations)

rows.title: The default SortedSetDocValues terms enum casts the ordinal to int in seekExact(long) and seekExact(term, TermState): on a view with more than 2^31 values a seek by ordinal throws, and from 2^32 values on it can silently land on the wrong term
rows.summary: You take the terms enum of a sorted-set doc-values view with more than 2^31 distinct values (for example MultiDocValues.getSortedSetValues over a very large multi-segment index), position it on a term with seekCeil, keep ord() or termState(), and later return with seekExact(ord) or seekExact(term, state); you expect to land on that term again, because sorted-set ordinals are longs and termsEnum() is documented to support ord() and seekExact(long). Instead seekExact(long) stores '(int) ord' (SortedSetDocValuesTermsEnum.java:69), so for ordinals from 2^31 to 2^32-1 it asks the values for a negative ordinal and throws, and for 2^32+5 it silently positions on ordinal 5 and returns that term, with -ea and -da. seekCeil, seekExact(BytesRef), next() and ord() use long arithmetic and are correct; the fix is to drop the cast.
rows.area: index / sorted-set doc values terms enum (SortedSetDocValuesTermsEnum, the default SortedSetDocValues#termsEnum())

rows.title: BufferingKnnVectorsWriter hands writeField vector values whose ordToDoc(ord) returns ord, which is wrong for sparse fields and, with an index sort, for every field (latent: no shipped writer calls it)
rows.summary: You build a vector codec on BufferingKnnVectorsWriter and, in writeField, ask the flush-time vector values which document a vector ordinal belongs to (ordToDoc, or getAcceptOrds, which is built on it), expecting what the javadoc promises, 'the docid of the document indexed with the given vector ordinal'. Instead the buffered values answer ordToDoc(ord) = ord, which is right only when every document has a vector and there is no index sort: for a field that documents 0, 2 and 3 have, ordinals 1 and 2 map to documents 1 and 2 instead of 2 and 3, so a getAcceptOrds filter that accepts only document 2 accepts document 3's vector and one that accepts only document 3 accepts none; under a reversing index sort even a dense field's ordinals map to themselves instead of to their documents' sorted positions. Iteration (nextDoc, index, vectorValue) stays correct, nothing throws, and FLOAT32, BYTE and FLOAT16 behave the same.
rows.area: codecs / BufferingKnnVectorsWriter flush-time vector values (KnnVectorValues.ordToDoc and getAcceptOrds)

rows.title: HnswGraph.DenseNodesIterator.consume() (the level-0 node iterator of every HNSW graph) does not advance its cursor, so draining level 0 in chunks with consume() returns the first chunk forever and a nextInt() after consume() starts again at node 0 (latent: Lucene itself never calls consume() on level 0)
rows.summary: You take the level-0 node iterator of an HNSW graph (getNodesOnLevel(0), a DenseNodesIterator over the node ids [0, size)) and read it in chunks with consume(buf), expecting each call to hand out the next block of ids, as the javadoc ('Consume integers from the iterator') and the two sibling iterator classes do. Instead DenseNodesIterator.consume copies the block but never moves its cursor, so every call returns the same first block, hasNext() stays true and the loop never ends; a nextInt() after consume() also starts again at 0. Lucene's own code never calls consume() on level 0, so indexes and search results are not affected.

rows.title: With an index sort, the flush-time iterator that IndexWriter hands to a doc-values or norms consumer for a numeric field that every document has ends intoBitSet(upTo >= maxDoc) on docID() == maxDoc instead of NO_MORE_DOCS, so a custom consumer that bulk-loads it and loops until NO_MORE_DOCS never finishes (latent: Lucene's own consumers skip the bulk load for such fields)
rows.summary: You sort an index at flush and every document in the segment has a given numeric doc-values field (or norms, or a single-valued SortedNumericDocValuesField); a custom DocValuesFormat or NormsFormat consumer bulk-loads the iterator it gets at flush with intoBitSet(maxDoc) or intoBitSet(NO_MORE_DOCS) and expects it to end on NO_MORE_DOCS, as the reference loop in the intoBitSet javadoc does. Instead NumericDocValuesWriter.SortingNumericDocValues sets the right bits but leaves docID() at maxDoc, a position the docID() contract never allows, so a consumer that loops until NO_MORE_DOCS never ends; fed to IndexedDISI.writeBitSet it fails the flush with an AssertionError (-ea) or keeps writing empty-block headers until the output fails (-da). Lucene's own consumers never bulk-load a field that every document has, so stock indexes and search results are not affected.
rows.area: index / doc values and norms flush with index sorting (NumericDocValuesWriter.SortingNumericDocValues)

rows.title: The flush-time doc-values iterators that IndexWriter hands to a DocValuesConsumer move only their doc-ID cursor in intoBitSet(), so values read afterwards belong to earlier documents (NUMERIC, BINARY, SORTED, SORTED_NUMERIC, SORTED_SET; latent: Lucene's own consumers never read values after intoBitSet on the same iterator)
rows.summary: A custom doc-values codec receives, at flush, the iterator over a field's buffered values; it calls nextDoc(), bulk-loads the next documents into a bit set with intoBitSet(), and then reads the value of the current document, expecting what the documented nextDoc() loop gives. Instead the five flush-time iterators (one per doc-values type) move only their doc-ID cursor in intoBitSet(), so the value read belongs to an earlier document, and every later value of the field in that segment stays shifted by the same number of documents (doc 2 reports doc 0's value, doc 3 reports doc 1's). Lucene's own doc-values consumer never reads values after intoBitSet() on the same iterator, so indexes written by stock Lucene are correct.
rows.area: index / doc values flush (DocValuesWriter Buffered*DocValues iterators handed to DocValuesConsumer)
