rows.title: The merge-time postings enum that the default FieldsConsumer.merge hands to a postings format's write() (MappingMultiPostingsEnum) returns -1 from docID() after nextDoc() has returned NO_MORE_DOCS, and, when it is reused after a partly read term, that term's document before the first nextDoc() (latent: Lucene's own postings writers use nextDoc()'s return value)
rows.summary: A custom postings format that keeps the default merge receives, in FieldsConsumer.write, a merged view of the segments' postings; it walks a term's documents with nextDoc() until NO_MORE_DOCS and then reads docID(), expecting NO_MORE_DOCS as DocIdSetIterator documents. Instead the merge-time enum (MappingMultiPostingsEnum) returns -1, the 'not started yet' value, because docID() is derived from its current sub-enum, which is null once the merge of that term is exhausted; when the enum is reused for the next term after a partly read one, docID() also reports the old term's document instead of -1 until the first nextDoc(). Lucene's own postings writers use nextDoc()'s return value and are not affected; helpers that start from docID(), such as FixedBitSet.or, throw at merge on a term whose documents are all deleted.
rows.area: index / postings merge (MappedMultiFields / MappingMultiPostingsEnum handed to FieldsConsumer.write)

rows.title: The merge-time FieldInfos view given to per-field doc-values and postings delegates (PerFieldMergeState.FilterFieldInfos) throws NullPointerException from fieldInfo(int) for a field number the wrapped segment does not have, where FieldInfos#fieldInfo(int) documents a null result (every release since 6.3.0)
rows.summary: You plug a custom doc-values (or postings) format into the codec as a per-field delegate, and its merge looks up, in a source segment's FieldInfos (mergeState.fieldInfos[i]), the number of a merged field that this segment does not have, for example field 'b' when the first segment was committed before any document had 'b'. FieldInfos#fieldInfo(int) documents 'the FieldInfo object or null when the given fieldNumber doesn't exist', and the same view's fieldInfo(String) returns null for 'b', so you expect null. Instead the per-field merge view reads res.name on the null result and throws NullPointerException ('Cannot read field "name" because "res" is null'), which fails the merge unless your format catches it.

rows.title: Postings read through SortingCodecReader return endOffset() 0 instead of the documented -1 for a field indexed with positions but without offsets, while startOffset() correctly returns -1 (the sorted postings enum's nextDoc() resets endOffset to 0 whether or not offsets are stored; every release since 4.3.0)
rows.summary: You index a plain TextField (positions, no offsets), wrap the segment with SortingCodecReader.wrap(leaf, sort) using a sort that reorders the documents, and read a term's postings with PostingsEnum.ALL (or OFFSETS), calling nextDoc() and nextPosition(). You expect startOffset() and endOffset() to both return -1, as PostingsEnum documents ('or -1 if offsets were not indexed') and as the unwrapped segment reader does. Instead startOffset() returns -1 but endOffset() returns 0, because the sorted enum's nextDoc() always sets endOffset = 0 as the base for decoding delta-coded offsets, and nextPosition() overwrites it only when the field stores offsets.

rows.title: PerFieldMergeState.FilterFieldInfos, the FieldInfos view that per-field doc-values and postings delegates get at merge time, restricts every has* flag, size(), iteration and fieldInfo(..) to the delegate's fields except hasVectorValues(), which still reports the whole segment, so it returns true when none of the view's fields has vectors (every release since 9.0.0)
rows.summary: You give the codec a custom doc-values format through getDocValuesFormatForField whose merge looks at mergeState.mergeFieldInfos, index two documents (one commit each) that each have a numeric doc-values field 'd' and a float vector field 'v', and call forceMerge(1). The view your format gets contains only 'd' (size() is 1, iteration and fieldInfo(..) see only 'd', and the nine other has* flags are recomputed over 'd' alone), so you expect hasVectorValues(), documented as 'Returns true if any fields have vector values', to be false. Instead it returns true, inherited from the segment's field 'v', because FilterFieldInfos computes its base flags over every field of the segment and overrides every has* method except hasVectorValues(), which FieldInfos gained in 9.0.0 after the view was written; a postings delegate under a PerFieldPostingsFormat sees the same.

rows.title: The merge-time postings view (MappedMultiFields) accepts a PostingsEnum built for an earlier merge as the reuse hint, because MappedMultiTermsEnum.postings(reuse, flags) compares only the field name and not the MergeState; the reused MappingMultiPostingsEnum keeps the earlier merge's per-segment doc maps, so a postings format that passes such an enum back gets wrong doc ids ([0, 1, 2, 3, 1] instead of [0, 1, 2, 3, 4]) or an ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException (every release since 5.0.0)
rows.summary: You write a postings format whose FieldsConsumer.write pulls postings from the Fields that a merge hands it, keep the PostingsEnum it returned, and pass that enum back as the reuse hint in a later merge. You expect the result to list the same documents as a fresh enum, since TermsEnum.postings documents reuse only as a hint ('pass a prior PostingsEnum for possible reuse'). Instead MappedMultiFields accepts the old enum because only the field name matches, resets it against the earlier merge's per-segment doc maps and returns wrong doc ids ([0, 1, 2, 3, 1] instead of [0, 1, 2, 3, 4] in the repro), or throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException when the new merge has more segments; no Lucene codec passes an enum from one merge into another, so only such custom codec code is affected.

rows.title: A PostingsEnum reused through SortingCodecReader from a field with payloads onto a field without positions returns the previous field's payload from getPayload() instead of null (SortingPostingsEnum.reset() does not clear the payload buffer; since 9.6.0)
rows.summary: You index two documents with a text field p whose token carries the payload 'xyz' and a field q indexed with DOCS_AND_FREQS, wrap the segment with SortingCodecReader.wrap(leaf, sort) using a sort that reorders the documents, read p's postings with PostingsEnum.ALL (getPayload() is 'xyz'), and then pass that enum back as the reuse argument for q's postings with ALL. You expect nextPosition() to return -1 and getPayload() to return null, as PostingsEnum documents ('or null if no payload was indexed') and as the unwrapped segment reader does for the same calls. Instead getPayload() returns 'xyz', because the sorted enum's reset() re-initialises the document and offset state but not its payload buffer, and nextPosition() returns -1 for a field without positions before it reaches the only code that sets or clears that buffer.

rows.title: During a doc-values update rewrite, the iterator IndexWriter hands to a DocValuesConsumer (ReadersAndUpdates.MergedDocValues) throws from intoBitSet when the destination bit set covers every returned doc but ends before upTo, because it bulk-loads on-disk docs whose values the update removed, contrary to the DocIdSetIterator#intoBitSet contract (latent: Lucene's own consumer always passes a full 65536-doc window; since 10.3.0, #14552)
rows.summary: A custom doc-values codec, while IndexWriter rewrites a numeric column after a doc-values update, positions the iterator it is given on its first doc and calls intoBitSet(NO_MORE_DOCS, bits, 0) with a bit set just large enough for the docs that iterator returns; in the repro a 65-doc segment has values in docs 0 and 64 and the update removes doc 64's value, so the iterator returns only doc 0 and a 1-bit destination should get bit 0, because the javadoc says intoBitSet must behave exactly like the loop 'for (doc = docID(); doc < upTo; doc = nextDoc()) bitSet.set(doc - offset)'. Instead ReadersAndUpdates.MergedDocValues.intoBitSet first bulk-loads every on-disk doc below upTo, including the removed doc 64, into a scratch bit set of the destination's size, so FixedBitSet.set(64) fails (AssertionError 'index=64, numBits=1' with -ea, ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException 'Index 1 out of bounds for length 1' with -da) and IndexWriter.commit() throws. Upstream declared this call shape legal when it fixed the same failure in BitSetIterator (#14142) and IndexedDISI (#14922); Lucene's own consumer always passes a full window, so only custom codecs hit it.

rows.title: The default postings enum's intoBitSet throws IndexOutOfBoundsException when the destination bit set ends before upTo inside a dense (bit-set-encoded) postings block, although every matching doc below upTo fits, contrary to the DocIdSetIterator#intoBitSet contract (latent: no Lucene caller passes such a window; since 10.2.0, #14133)
rows.summary: You index 512 documents with a StringField term t in every other one (docs 0, 2, ..., 510), so its first full postings block is stored as a bit set, position t's PostingsEnum on doc 0 and call intoBitSet(400, new FixedBitSet(399), 0); every matching doc below 400 (0, 2, ..., 398) fits in 399 bits, and the javadoc says the call must behave exactly like the loop 'for (doc = docID(); doc < upTo; doc = nextDoc()) bitSet.set(doc - offset)', so you expect bits 0, 2, ..., 398 and docID() 400. Instead it throws IndexOutOfBoundsException 'Range [1, 1 + 399) out of bounds for length 399' from FixedBitSet.orRange, with -ea and -da: the bit-set branch copies the whole slice [current doc + 1, min(upTo, last doc of the block + 1)) with one orRange, which bound-checks the full length against the destination whether the bits are set or not. Upstream declared this call shape legal when it fixed the same failure in BitSetIterator (#14142) and IndexedDISI (#14922), but the postings reader was never changed; no Lucene caller passes such a window, so only direct callers hit it.

rows.title: SimpleText points: PointTree.clone() shares a saved split-value array with the tree it was cloned from, so moving one tree corrupts the node bounds the other reports
rows.summary: You index points with the SimpleText codec, take a PointTree from PointValues.getPointTree(), clone it and keep moving both the clone and the original, and expect each tree to report the bounds of its own current node, as PointTree#clone promises ('the current node becomes the root of the new tree') and as the default points format does. Instead SimpleTextPointTree.clone() copies the reference to the original's saved split-value array for the current level, so a move of one tree overwrites the bound that the other tree restores when it moves back up: after tree.moveToChild(), tree.moveToParent(), clone = tree.clone(), clone.moveToChild(), tree.moveToChild(), tree.moveToSibling(), clone.moveToParent(), the clone at its root reports max 0 instead of 2047 for the values 0..2047. Any traversal that prunes on those bounds can then miss or wrongly include cells; no in-tree query moves trees this way.
rows.area: codecs / SimpleText points format (SimpleTextBKDReader.SimpleTextPointTree#clone)

rows.title: AxiomaticF2LOG and AxiomaticF2EXP scores drop by 1 ulp as term frequency crosses a power of two
rows.summary: You score with AxiomaticF2LOG or AxiomaticF2EXP at default parameters and no boost. You expect the score never to decrease as term frequency rises, which impacts-based pruning relies on. Instead it drops by 1 ulp when the frequency crosses a power of two, so a pruned search can return a different top hit than exhaustive search.

rows.title: Lucene103 block tree never sets Stats.indexNumBytes, so Terms.getStats() and CheckIndex -verbose print 'index trie: 0 bytes' for every field
rows.summary: You run CheckIndex -verbose at level 2 or more (or call Terms.getStats()) on an index written with the default codec and expect each field's block-tree statistics to say how many bytes its terms index takes, as the field's javadoc 'Byte size of the index' and the printed label 'index trie: N bytes' promise. Since 10.3.0 the Lucene103 block tree never assigns Stats.indexNumBytes, so every field prints 'index trie: 0 bytes', even a 20,000-term field with 607 blocks in a segment whose .tip file is 2,473 bytes. Nothing else reads the number, so search and indexing are unaffected, and the older Lucene90 block tree had already stopped reporting the real size (a constant such as 56 bytes since 8.6.0), so this is a small diagnostic defect, not a regression of a working metric.
rows.area: codecs / block-tree terms dictionary (Lucene103 Stats, CheckIndex verbose statistics)

rows.title: Block tree Stats.toString prints the compressed suffix bytes per block as the average on the 'term suffix bytes before compression' line (Terms.getStats(), CheckIndex -verbose)
rows.summary: You call Terms.getStats() (or run CheckIndex -verbose at -level 2 or more) on a default-codec index and read the block tree line 'N term suffix bytes before compression (A suffix-bytes/block)', expecting A to be N divided by the block count, as every other average in that output divides its own line's total. Since 8.5.0, A is the compressed (on-disk) suffix bytes divided by the block count, the figure that belongs to the next line: a 2,000-term field with 80 blocks prints '34376 term suffix bytes before compression (128.9 suffix-bytes/block)', where 34376 / 80 = 429.7 and 128.9 = 10314 compressed bytes / 80. Only this one diagnostic figure is wrong; the totals, the compression ratio, the public Stats fields, indexing and search are unaffected.

rows.title: IndexWriter's 'BD' InfoStream over-reports the deletes and updates of a buffered-updates packet that is resolved again after a concurrent merge commits, because FrozenBufferedUpdates.apply returns the packet's running total instead of this call's count (8 reported for 4 deleted documents)

You expect the 'BD' log to report the documents the packet newly deleted, 4 in the test, and the second pass's own phase line does report '0 new deletions'. Instead the second pass's 'done inner apply' line repeats the first pass's 4 and the final 'done apply del packet ... N new deletes/updates' line reports 8, because FrozenBufferedUpdates.apply returns the packet's running total and IndexWriter.forceApply adds the returned values up; the index itself is correct (4 documents deleted), only the logged counts are wrong.

rows.title: CharArraySet.toString leaves out the ", " after an empty-string element that is iterated first, so the two-element set {"", "a"} prints as [a], the same text as the one-element set {"a"} (every release since 3.1.0)
rows.summary: You build a CharArraySet that holds the empty string and one other word, for example new CharArraySet(2, false) with add("") and add("a") (or StopFilter.makeStopSet("", "the")), and print it. You expect "[, a]": CharArraySet extends AbstractSet, its toString keeps AbstractCollection.toString's documented format (elements in iterator order, in brackets, adjacent ones separated by ", "), and Lucene's TestCharArraySet.testToString pins that format. Instead it prints "[a]", the same text as the one-element set {"a"}, because toString writes the separator only when the builder is longer than "[" (sb.length() > 1), and an empty first element leaves the builder at "[".

rows.title: RunAutomaton.toString prints the exclusive alphabetSize as the inclusive end of the last character class, so new CharacterRunAutomaton(Automata.makeAnyChar()).toString() shows the range \\U00000000-\\U00110000, one past Character.MAX_CODE_POINT (every release since 6.5.0)
rows.summary: You build a run automaton for any single code point, new CharacterRunAutomaton(Automata.makeAnyChar()), and print it. rows.title: AutomatonToTokenStream.toTokenStream silently requires every state to be reachable from state 0, which its javadoc does not say, and rejects an acyclic automaton with an unreachable state with a false 'Cycle found in automaton' / 'Start node has incoming edges, creating cycle' message (documentation and error-message defect; the restriction itself was stated at design time)

rows.title: FloatArrayList.equals treats [0.0f] and [-0.0f] as equal (primitive ==), but hashCode hashes the raw float bits, so two equal lists get different hash codes (31 vs 1832674751); a latent Object#hashCode contract break in the @lucene.internal hppc list, with no in-tree caller of either method, since 9.11.0
rows.summary: You build FloatArrayList.from(0.0f) and FloatArrayList.from(-0.0f) and compare them: equals returns true (both ways), so by the Object#hashCode contract the two hash codes must be equal. Instead hashCode returns 31 for one list and 1832674751 for the other, because equals compares elements with primitive == (under which 0.0f == -0.0f) while hashCode mixes Float.floatToIntBits, which differs for the two zeros. A HashSet holding one list therefore does not find the other, and can hold both.

rows.title: Test-framework ForceMergePolicy, documented as 'only returns forced merges', still lets the wrapped policy's natural merges run on commit() and NRT reopen, because it inherits FilterMergePolicy's forwarding of findFullFlushMerges (regression since 9.3.0)
rows.summary: You wrap a merge policy in the test framework's ForceMergePolicy, documented as 'A MergePolicy that only returns forced merges' for when you 'wish to disallow background merges', keep the rest of IndexWriterConfig at its defaults, and commit or open an NRT reader after each of several small flushes. You expect every flushed segment to stay until you call forceMerge, as with NoMergePolicy. Instead ForceMergePolicy only nulls findMerges and inherits FilterMergePolicy's forward of findFullFlushMerges, whose MergePolicy default runs the wrapped policy's own natural merges of small segments, so with the default 500 ms merge-on-commit wait 25 one-document commits leave 1 segment instead of 25 (and an NRT reader after 25 flushes has 1 leaf).

rows.title: IndexWriter.deleteDocuments(Query...) and updateDocuments(Query, ...) do not document that the query runs only when the buffered delete is applied later, or that an exception it throws then (for example a PhraseQuery or FieldExistsQuery on a StringField, or TooManyClauses from an interval prefix once more than 128 terms match) closes the IndexWriter and discards every change since the last commit (documentation defect; the close itself is an intended fail-safe)
rows.summary: You index 10 documents with a StringField id, commit 6 of them, and call deleteDocuments(new PhraseQuery("id", "d1", "d2")), which returns a sequence number; nothing in its javadoc says the query runs later or what happens if it fails then. The query actually runs only when the buffered delete is applied, and because a StringField has no positions the PhraseQuery throws IllegalStateException at that point: the exception comes out of the next commit (or flush, NRT open, merge, close, or an unrelated addDocument), the IndexWriter closes itself and the 4 uncommitted documents are gone. The close is a deliberate fail-safe (the same documents are lost without it); what is missing is a warning on deleteDocuments(Query...) and both updateDocuments(Query, ...) overloads, and in the class NOTE on when the writer closes itself.
rows.area: index / IndexWriter delete-by-query (deleteDocuments(Query...) and updateDocuments(Query, ...) javadoc and class NOTE vs deferred application in FrozenBufferedUpdates and the applyUpdatesPacket tragic close)

rows.title: Classic QueryParser and flexible StandardQueryParser: the query syntax docs never say that only space, TAB, LF, CR and U+3000 separate clauses, so AND, OR or '-' written next to any other Unicode space (EN, EM or THIN space, U+205F, NBSP, ...) silently becomes part of a search term and a field prefix spreads to the following words: 'title:foo<EM SPACE>AND<EM SPACE>-bar' parses as 'title:foo title:and title:bar'
rows.summary: You parse 'title:foo AND -bar' with the classic or the flexible query parser, but the spaces are EM SPACEs (U+2003), as in text pasted from a formatted document; nothing in the query syntax docs says which characters separate clauses, so you expect the same query as with ordinary spaces, '+title:foo -body:bar'. Instead both grammars separate clauses only on space, TAB, LF, CR and U+3000, so 'foo<EM>AND<EM>-bar' is one term that the analyzer splits under the first field: the result is 'title:foo title:and title:bar', AND became the search word 'and', the '-' exclusion is gone and a document whose body contains bar now matches (2 hits instead of 1). The closed separator set is very likely intended, so the defect is the missing documentation; when the next clause has its own field prefix ('-body:bar') both parsers throw ParseException instead.
rows.area: queryparser / classic and flexible standard grammars (_WHITESPACE, _TERM_START_CHAR) and the query syntax documentation

rows.title: Bundled commons-codec upgrades changed phonetic filter tokens (RefinedSoundex in 10.2.0; Metaphone, ColognePhonetic and Daitch-Mokotoff on main), and neither CHANGES.txt nor MIGRATE.md mentions it or asks for re-indexing (documentation defect)
rows.summary: You index a field with a phonetic filter, for example PhoneticFilter with ColognePhonetic, upgrade Lucene and keep searching the same index; you expect the same tokens or a CHANGES/MIGRATE note telling you to re-index, as Lucene gave in 2014 for the Beider-Morse change of the commons-codec 1.10 upgrade (LUCENE-6058) and gives on main for the Snowball upgrade (GITHUB#15505). Instead the bundled commons-codec moved from 1.13 (up to 10.1.0) to 1.17.2 (10.2.0 to 10.6.0) and to 1.23.0 (main) with no note anywhere, and its encoder fixes change the tokens: 'Köln' gets the RefinedSoundex code K378 from 10.2.0 (10.1.0 kept only the word), and on main 'chantaient' becomes XNTN instead of KNTN (Metaphone), 'quick' 4 instead of 44 (ColognePhonetic) and "it's" 040000 instead of 034000 (Daitch-Mokotoff). An index written by the older version and searched by the newer one silently misses or changes matches in that field until it is re-indexed (executed: ColognePhonetic with inject=false, the query 'quick' finds no document in a 10.5.2 index searched by main, against 2 in a fresh index).

rows.title: Word2VecSynonymFilter documents minAcceptedSimilarity as a cosine similarity, but Word2VecSynonymProvider compares it with the normalised score (1 + cosine) / 2, so the effective cosine cutoff is 2m - 1 (the default 0.8 accepts cosine 0.6, 0.5 accepts orthogonal terms, values below 0.5 accept negatively correlated terms); documentation defect, the javadoc fix is the default proposal
rows.summary: You build Word2VecSynonymFilter with minAcceptedSimilarity 0.8 (the factory default), whose only documentation says it is the 'minimal value of cosine similarity between the searched vector and the retrieved ones', so you expect only model terms at cosine 0.8 or more as synonyms. Word2VecSynonymProvider compares the threshold with the DOT_PRODUCT score of the unit-length model vectors, which is (1 + cosine) / 2, so the real cosine cutoff is 2m - 1: at 0.8 a term at cosine 0.65 is emitted, at 0.5 an orthogonal term (cosine 0) is emitted, and at 0.2 a term at cosine -0.5 is emitted. The authors' intent points to the score scale (the factory accepts only (0, 1]), so the fix is a javadoc clarification, not a code change.
rows.area: analysis-common / synonym.word2vec (Word2VecSynonymFilter minAcceptedSimilarity javadoc vs Word2VecSynonymProvider threshold test)

rows.title: FacetSets.adoc says MatchingFacetSetsCounts counts the documents each FacetSetMatcher matches, but it counts matching facet sets, so one document can add more than 1 to a matcher (documentation defect; the per-set code is intended and pinned by upstream tests)
rows.summary: You index documents that each hold several facet sets (the adoc's own example: one (genre, year) set per movie of an actor) and count them with MatchingFacetSetsCounts, which the user guide FacetSets.adoc says 'counts how many documents are matched by each of a list of FacetSetMatcher'. You expect each matcher's value to be a number of documents, never larger than FacetResult.value. Instead the code adds 1 for every matching facet set, so one document with the sets (Thriller, 2020) and (Thriller, 2021) gives 2 for a 'Thriller 2020-2022' range matcher while FacetResult.value is 1; upstream tests pin this per-set count, so the conservative fix is to correct the documentation, although maintainers could instead choose per-document counts.

rows.title: Lucene90StoredFieldsFormat's class javadoc says the BEST_SPEED / BEST_COMPRESSION stored-fields modes 'can be configured like this' with indexWriterConfig.setCodec(new Lucene100Codec(Mode...)), but since 10.1.0 Lucene100Codec is a read-only codec in lucene-backward-codecs: the example does not compile against lucene-core, and with backward-codecs on the classpath the first commit of a document with an indexed field throws UnsupportedOperationException and closes the IndexWriter (documentation defect)
rows.summary: The Lucene90StoredFieldsFormat javadoc says you can switch stored fields to the smaller BEST_COMPRESSION mode 'like this': indexWriterConfig.setCodec(new Lucene100Codec(Mode.BEST_COMPRESSION)). Since Lucene 10.1.0, Lucene100Codec is no longer the current codec but a read-only one in lucene-backward-codecs, so the example does not compile against lucene-core, and with backward-codecs on the classpath the first commit of a document with an indexed field throws UnsupportedOperationException ('This postings format may not be used for writing, use the current postings format') and closes the IndexWriter. The same steps with the current codec, new Lucene104Codec(Lucene104Codec.Mode.BEST_COMPRESSION), work, so only the javadoc is wrong.

rows.title: LMSimilarity.DefaultCollectionModel's javadoc gives p(w|C) as ttf / (T + 1) (and the LMSimilarity class javadoc as ttf / T), but computeProbability returns (ttf + 1) / (T + 1), so a user who computes p(w|C) from the docs is off by a factor (ttf + 1) / ttf (2x for a term that occurs once); Lucene's scores are correct (documentation defect)
rows.summary: You use LMDirichletSimilarity or LMJelinekMercerSimilarity with the default collection model and read the javadoc to work out p(w|C), the collection probability that both scores divide by. The DefaultCollectionModel javadoc says it is the term's number of occurrences in the collection divided by the total number of tokens + 1 (the LMSimilarity class javadoc says divided by the total number of tokens), so for a term that occurs once in a field of 9 tokens you expect 1/10. The code returns (ttf + 1) / (T + 1) = 2/10, on purpose since LUCENE-3430 (2011), so Lucene's scores are right and only the two javadoc sentences are stale.
rows.area: core / search similarities (LMSimilarity.DefaultCollectionModel javadoc, language-model similarities)

rows.title: Intervals.within and notWithin are documented as opposites, but a multi-position source interval only partly inside the n-position window around the reference matches neither (documentation / API-contract defect)
rows.summary: You index 'the new york times' and run within(phrase(new, york), 1, times) and notWithin(phrase(new, york), 1, times), and you expect exactly one of them to match, because the javadoc says within returns source intervals that 'appear within a set number of positions' of the reference and notWithin those that 'do not appear within' it, and the fn:within / fn:notWithin docs give both the same 'maximum positions' parameter. Instead neither matches: within keeps an interval only if all of it lies inside the window [r.start-n, r.end+n] (here [2,4]), while notWithin drops it if any part touches that window, so 'new york' at [1,2], which touches the window without lying inside it, is in neither result (within needs n = 2 for a phrase directly next to the reference). In the same way, on 'new york' both within(phrase(new, york), 0, york) and notWithin(phrase(new, york), 0, york) return nothing, and no doc says that a partly-near interval matches neither.
rows.area: queries / intervals (Intervals.within / Intervals.notWithin and their javadoc; queryparser fn:within / fn:notWithin docs)

rows.title: MultiTermQuery.getTermsEnum's javadoc says the returned TermsEnum is already positioned on the first matching term, but it is unpositioned and every Lucene consumer calls next() first, so a MultiTermQuery subclass that positions its enum as documented silently loses its first matching term in each segment, and a caller who reads term() first gets the empty term (javadoc only; the code is correct); since 4.0.0
rows.summary: You write a MultiTermQuery subclass whose getTermsEnum(Terms, AttributeSource) returns a prefix FilteredTermsEnum that you have already advanced with next(), because that method's javadoc says 'The TermsEnum must already be positioned to the first matching term', and you index apple, banana and blueberry. You expect your query for prefix b to count 2 documents, like PrefixQuery f:b*, but it counts 1: Lucene's rewrites call next() before they read the first term, so the term you positioned on (banana) is skipped; in the same way, reading term() first on the public getTermsEnum(Terms), whose javadoc says the enum 'is positioned to the first matching term', gives the empty term instead of banana. The unpositioned enum is the intended design (TermsEnum's class contract, LUCENE-2110), so only the two sentences, left over from the pre-4.0 FilteredTermEnum API, are wrong.
rows.area: search / MultiTermQuery term expansion (getTermsEnum javadoc; TermCollectingRewrite and AbstractMultiTermQueryConstantScoreWrapper call next() before the first term)

rows.title: ConjunctionUtils.createConjunction's javadoc does not say that every TwoPhaseIterator's approximation must also be in allIterators, so a caller who passes a DocIdSetIterator and a TwoPhaseIterator as the two lists 'to combine' silently gets wrong documents, extra or missing (javadoc only; the code works as designed; since 9.0.0)
rows.summary: You call the public ConjunctionUtils.createConjunction(allIterators, twoPhaseIterators) with DocIdSetIterator.all(10) in the first list and, in the second, a TwoPhaseIterator whose approximation is DocIdSetIterator.range(4, 7) and whose matches() always returns true. The javadoc describes both arguments only as lists 'to combine', and a TwoPhaseIterator stands for the documents of its approximation that matches() confirms, so you expect [4, 5, 6], which is what intersectIterators with TwoPhaseIterator.asDocIdSetIterator, or lists built with addIterator/addTwoPhaseIterator, return. Instead you get all ten documents with no error: the factory leads the iteration with allIterators only and uses the two-phase list only as per-document checks, so an approximation that is not also in allIterators is never advanced and matches() runs while it is still at -1 (with a matches() that reads its approximation, true hits are dropped instead).

rows.title: SingleTermsEnum's constructor javadoc says the new enum already points to the term, but it stays unpositioned until the first next(), so a caller who follows it reads an empty term, docFreq 0 and empty postings (javadoc only; the code is correct); since 4.0.0-alpha
rows.summary: You index the term b in field f, open the reader and call new SingleTermsEnum(terms.iterator(), new BytesRef("b")). You expect what the constructor javadoc says, 'After calling the constructor the enumeration is already pointing to the term, if it exists', so term() should return b and docFreq() and postings() should describe it. Instead the enum is unpositioned until the first next(), like every TermsEnum: the constructor only records the seek term (setInitialSeekTerm) and FilteredTermsEnum seeks lazily inside next(), so term() returns an empty BytesRef and, with -da, docFreq() is 0 and postings() are empty; the lazy code is the intended design (LUCENE-2110) and the sentence is a leftover from the pre-4.0 SingleTermEnum, which did position itself in its constructor.

rows.title: MultiSimilarity does not document that only sims[0] computes the field norm, so the other sub-similarities' index-time norm settings (discountOverlaps, a computeNorm override) are silently ignored and the array order decides the stored norm, and its inherited getDiscountOverlaps() always returns true (documentation defect; on one index the score is an exact sum in either order)
rows.summary: You combine two sub-similarities in a MultiSimilarity, for example BM25 with discountOverlaps=true and BM25 with discountOverlaps=false, and use it for indexing and searching; the javadoc says only that it 'will sum the scores of the provided sims' (CombSUM), so you expect both sub-similarities' settings to count. In fact computeNorm returns sims[0].computeNorm(state), so only the first sub-similarity writes the field's single norm and every sub-scorer decodes that norm: the second one's discountOverlaps (or its own computeNorm encoding) is silently ignored, swapping the array order changes the stored norms and therefore the scores (0.7534208 for [discount, noDiscount] vs 0.6862843 for [noDiscount, discount] in an independent repro), and the inherited getDiscountOverlaps() returns true even when sims[0] counts overlap tokens. The single norm is the intended one-norm-per-field design and on any one index the score is an exact sum in either order; what is missing is the documentation (and a correct getter), so the fix is a javadoc sentence, optionally plus passing sims[0].getDiscountOverlaps() to the super constructor.
rows.area: core / search similarities (MultiSimilarity: undocumented norm ownership, inherited getDiscountOverlaps)

rows.title: TaxonomyFacetLabels javadoc offers it as a replacement for stored fields, but for dimensions configured multi-valued plus hierarchical (or multi-valued plus requireDimCount) it also returns the ancestor paths and the bare dimension that FacetsConfig indexes only for counting (documentation/contract defect; every release since 8.7.0)
rows.summary: You add FacetField("Author", "Bob") and FacetField("Publish Date", "2010", "10", "15") to a document and read its labels back with TaxonomyFacetLabels, whose javadoc offers it as a way to skip stored fields for these values, so you expect [Author/Bob, Publish Date/2010/10/15]; that is what you get when both dimensions are single-valued. With Publish Date configured multi-valued and hierarchical you get [Author/Bob, Publish Date/2010, Publish Date/2010/10, Publish Date/2010/10/15], and with Author configured multi-valued with requireDimCount you get [Author, Author/Bob, Publish Date/2010/10/15]. FacetsConfig deliberately indexes those ancestor (and dimension) ordinals so that multi-valued counts are right, and the reader turns every indexed ordinal back into a label; the javadoc never says so.

rows.title: ConcatenateGraphFilter, its factory and CompletionAnalyzer misdocument maxGraphExpansions: the javadoc promises a TooComplexToDeterminizeException when the token graph has more than maxGraphExpansions paths (and 'no limit on graph expansions' for CompletionAnalyzer's 1- and 3-argument constructors), but the code silently keeps the first maxGraphExpansions paths (default 10000) and also uses the same value as the determinize work limit, so it can throw for a graph with fewer paths than the limit (documentation defect; the truncation is intended)
rows.summary: You set maxGraphExpansions on ConcatenateGraphFilter (or its factory), or use CompletionAnalyzer's 1- or 3-argument constructor, and expect what the javadoc says: a TooComplexToDeterminizeException when the token graph has more than that many paths, and, for CompletionAnalyzer, no limit at all. Instead the filter silently emits only the first maxGraphExpansions paths (a 4-path synonym graph at limit 3 gives 3 tokens and no error; CompletionAnalyzer keeps 10000 of 16384 paths), and because the same number is also passed to determinize as its work limit, a 2-path graph at limit 3 throws. Silent truncation is the suggester's deliberate design (LUCENE-4971), so the fix is to correct the javadoc, not the code.

rows.title: QuantizedByteVectorValues.getCorrectiveTerms' javadoc calls the third EUCLIDEAN corrective term 'the l2norm of the centered vector', but OptimizedScalarQuantizer stores, and Lucene104ScalarQuantizedVectorScorer requires, the squared l2norm, so an implementer who supplies the documented value gets wrong EUCLIDEAN scores from Lucene's public scorer (1/6 instead of 1/26 for a centered vector (3, 4)); javadoc only, the code is intended; since 10.4.0
rows.summary: You implement the public abstract QuantizedByteVectorValues for a EUCLIDEAN field and, as getCorrectiveTerms' javadoc says, return 'the l2norm of the centered vector' as the third corrective term: 5 for the vector (4, 5) with centroid (1, 1). Lucene's public Lucene104ScalarQuantizedVectorScorer then scores the query (7, 9), whose true squared distance to (4, 5) is 25, as 0.16666667 (1/6) instead of 0.03846154 (1/26), because it computes the squared distance as queryCorrection + indexCorrection - 2 * dot and needs the squared norm 25 there; Lucene's own quantizer indeed stores the squared norm (13.0, not sqrt(13) = 3.6055512, for a centered vector (2, 3)). The code is intended and correct; only the javadoc, which omits the word 'squared', is wrong.
rows.area: core / vector quantization (util.quantization QuantizedByteVectorValues.getCorrectiveTerms javadoc vs OptimizedScalarQuantizer and Lucene104ScalarQuantizedVectorScorer)

rows.title: CachingCollectorManager (new in 10.6.0) does not document that it is single-use: reused for a second search, replay() replays the hits of both searches and one earlier overflow keeps isCached() false
rows.summary: You wrap a reusable CollectorManager in a CachingCollectorManager, run a search with it, then run a second search with the same instance and call isCached() and replay(secondPassManager), the workflow the class javadoc shows for one search. Nothing in its javadoc says an instance serves only one search, unlike TopScoreDocCollectorManager and TopFieldCollectorManager, which say 'a new collectorManager should be created for each search due to its internal states', while Lucene's stated norm (TotalHitCountCollectorManager) is that managers are generally reusable. Instead the manager keeps the per-slice caches of every search in one list that is never cleared, so replay() returns the hits of both searches (the repro: [0..9] instead of the second search's [3..9]) and one earlier overflow makes isCached() false for every later search, with no error.

rows.title: MIGRATE.md's 11.0 'Upgrade Example' says forceMerge(1) 'Rewrites all segments to latest format', but with the default merge policy it leaves an index that already has one segment and no deletions unchanged in its 9.x or 10.x format (documentation defect, unreleased; the code is correct)
rows.summary: Lucene main's MIGRATE.md tells users who open a Lucene 9.x or 10.x index to upgrade its segments by opening an IndexWriter and calling forceMerge(1), with the comment 'Rewrites all segments to latest format' (line 179), and line 153 offers forceMerge() as a way 'to upgrade segment formats immediately'. With the default merge policy, forceMerge(1) does nothing on an index that already has one segment and no deletions: TieredMergePolicy reports it as already merged, so on Lucene's own single-segment 9.0.0 test index the segment is still version 9.0.0 with codec Lucene90 afterwards. The code behaves as designed (forceMerge only promises a segment count, and UpgradeIndexMergePolicy and IndexUpgrader exist for exactly this case); the guide should wrap the merge policy in UpgradeIndexMergePolicy or point to IndexUpgrader.

rows.title: On main, the javadocs of LRUQueryCache.clearQuery and clearCoreCacheKey still say 'Remove all cache entries', but since #15558 both methods only mark the entries for the next cleanUp(), so the entries stay counted and keep producing cache hits until then; MIGRATE.md does not mention the deferred removal or the new cleanUp() duty (documentation defect, main only)
rows.summary: On main you install an LRUQueryCache, run a query so that it is cached, and call clearQuery(query) or clearCoreCacheKey(key), whose javadocs say 'Remove all cache entries for the given query' and '... for the given core cache key'. You expect the entries to be gone when the call returns, as on 10.x; instead #15558 made both methods only add the query or key to a pending set, so getCacheSize() still counts the entry and the next search is a cache hit (with correct documents) until cleanUp() runs. The deferral is deliberate and the class javadoc describes it, but the two method javadocs were left unchanged, and MIGRATE.md, whose 11.0 recipe builds a cache with no cleanup, never mentions the new cleanUp() or CacheCleanUpParameters duty.

rows.title: On main, LRUQueryCache's class javadoc still says its statistics callbacks are 'called synchronously and under a lock', but since #15558 the callbacks of different partitions run at the same time and onClear() runs under no lock, and neither the javadoc nor MIGRATE.md tells subclasses that their statistics must now be thread-safe (documentation defect, main only)
rows.summary: You subclass LRUQueryCache to keep per-index statistics in its callbacks, as the class javadoc suggests, and trust its sentence that the callbacks 'are called synchronously and under a lock', which on 10.x meant one cache-wide write lock around every insertion, eviction and clear callback, so plain fields were safe. On main, #15558 gave each partition (16 by default) its own lock, so insertion and eviction callbacks of different partitions run at the same time (2 at once in a deterministic JUnit, up to 3 in a stress where a plain counter loses updates), and clear() calls onClear() with no lock held. The partitioning itself is intended.

rows.title: A PersistentSnapshotDeletionPolicy re-opened over its save file counts the persisted snapshots, but getSnapshots() is empty and getIndexCommit(gen) returns null until an IndexWriter has opened with it, and no javadoc states this precondition (documentation gap; the behaviour is by design)

You expect getSnapshots() and getIndexCommit(gen) to show the persisted snapshot that getSnapshotCount() counts, or the javadoc to say that the policy must first be passed to an IndexWriter. Instead getSnapshotCount() is 1 while getSnapshots() is empty and getIndexCommit(gen) returns null, which its javadoc says means 'not currently snapshotted'; this is by design (the IndexCommit objects come from the writer's onInit call), but no javadoc states the precondition.

rows.title: On main, LRUQueryCache's onCacheEntryInserted/onCacheEntryEvicted javadoc still calls ramBytesUsed 'the total RAM cost of this entry', but since #16657 a query's shared RAM is reported only with its first inserted entry and its last removed entry, so one entry is inserted and evicted with different amounts and per-segment or per-index RAM kept through these callbacks drifts (one index stays positive, another goes negative) (documentation defect, main only)
rows.summary: You subclass LRUQueryCache to keep per-index RAM statistics in onCacheEntryInserted/onCacheEntryEvicted, whose javadoc says ramBytesUsed is 'the total RAM cost of this entry' (and of the evicted entry), so you expect each entry to give back at eviction what it added at insertion and an index's total to return to 0 once its entries are gone. Since #16657 the cache deliberately counts a query's own RAM once per distinct query and reports it only with the query's first inserted entry and with the entry that drops its last reference, usually entries of different segments or indices: in a two-segment index one entry is inserted with 344 bytes and evicted with 160, and with two indices sharing one cache index A keeps +184 bytes after it is closed while index B ends at -184. The dedup and the cache's own accounting are correct.

rows.title: BinaryRangeDocValues' public constructor javadoc says numBytesPerDimension is the 'size of each dimension (2 * encoded value size)', but the class already doubles the value and needs the encoded value size itself (what every in-tree caller passes), so code that follows the javadoc gets ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException on the first document; documentation defect, javadoc-only fix; since 9.5.0
rows.summary: You index a LongRangeDocValuesField and wrap the field's BinaryDocValues in new BinaryRangeDocValues(values, 1, 2 * Long.BYTES), because the constructor's javadoc says numBytesPerDimension is the 'size of each dimension (2 * encoded value size)'. You expect nextDoc() to return the document and getPackedValue() to hold its 16-byte encoded range. Instead nextDoc() throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException ('arraycopy: last source index 32 out of bounds for byte[16]'): the class already multiplies by 2 (one min and one max per dimension) and needs the size of one encoded value (Long.BYTES), which is what Lucene's own callers pass, so the javadoc doubles the width a second time.

rows.title: XYPointField.newDistanceQuery and XYDocValuesField.newSlowDistanceQuery document the radius as 'must be non-negative and finite', but a radius of 0 throws IllegalArgumentException ('radius must be bigger than 0, got 0.0') because XYCircle requires radius > 0; documentation defect (the rejection is intended), since 8.5.0
rows.summary: You call XYPointField.newDistanceQuery("p", 1f, 2f, 0f), or XYDocValuesField.newSlowDistanceQuery with the same arguments, to find the points exactly at (1, 2), because both javadocs say the radius 'must be non-negative and finite' and promise IllegalArgumentException only if the radius 'is invalid'. Instead both throw IllegalArgumentException 'radius must be bigger than 0, got 0.0' at query construction: they pass the radius to XYCircle, whose constructor rejects radius <= 0, while the lat/lon twins with the same wording (LatLonPoint.newDistanceQuery, LatLonDocValuesField.newSlowDistanceQuery) accept 0 and match the point at the centre. The rejection is deliberate (the maintainers have called radius 0 'not allowed' and changed Lucene's own random tests to avoid it), so the defect is the javadoc, whose likely fix is 'must be positive and finite'.

rows.title: MMapDirectory(Path, LockFactory, long) and the protected FSDirectory(Path, LockFactory) constructor document 'lockFactory ... or null for the default (NativeFSLockFactory)', but a null lockFactory throws NullPointerException 'LockFactory must not be null, use an explicit instance!' from BaseDirectory (javadoc only: rejecting null is intended since 5.0.0, LUCENE-5953)
rows.summary: You open an index directory with new MMapDirectory(path, null, MMapDirectory.DEFAULT_MAX_CHUNK_SIZE), or write an FSDirectory subclass whose constructor calls super(path, null), because both javadocs say '@param lockFactory the lock factory to use, or null for the default (NativeFSLockFactory)'. You expect a directory that locks with NativeFSLockFactory; instead the constructor throws NullPointerException 'LockFactory must not be null, use an explicit instance!' from BaseDirectory and no directory is returned. rows.title: JaroWinklerDistance.setThreshold javadoc says 'Set to a negative value to get the Jaro distance', but a negative threshold adds the Winkler bonus to every pair (the same as threshold 0); only a threshold of 1 or more gives plain Jaro; documentation defect, the javadoc fix is the default proposal
rows.summary: You want the plain Jaro similarity from JaroWinklerDistance, so, as the setThreshold javadoc says ('Set to a negative value to get the Jaro distance'), you call setThreshold(-1) and expect getDistance("martha", "marhta") to return the Jaro value 0.9444. Instead it returns 0.9611, the Jaro-Winkler value: getDistance skips the Winkler bonus only when the Jaro value is below the threshold, which never happens for a negative threshold, so every pair gets the bonus, exactly as with threshold 0. Only a threshold of 1 or more gives plain Jaro; the sentence has been false since the class was added in 2008, so the javadoc is the side to fix by default.

rows.title: ImpactsSource#advanceShallow javadoc does not say that the current document's freq(), positions and docIDRunEnd() become invalid after a shallow advance past its block: the default codec then returns another block's data, and a lazy freq() breaks the next legal advance() (javadoc and assertion gap; the codec behaviour is intended)

Lucene's own callers always advance before reading, so the codec behaviour is intended; what is missing is this precondition in the ImpactsSource javadoc and a check for it in the test framework's AssertingImpactsEnum.

rows.title: CodecUtil's codec header and footer javadoc gives Magic, Version, AlgorithmID and Checksum as the little-endian DataOutput#writeInt/#writeLong, but CodecUtil writes these fields big-endian, so a header or footer read or written as documented comes out byte-swapped or is rejected (documentation defect; the writer and reader agree)
rows.summary: You write a file with CodecUtil.writeHeader(out, "Foo", 1) and CodecUtil.writeFooter(out) and decode it as the CodecHeader and CodecFooter grammars in CodecUtil's javadoc say: they link Magic, Version and AlgorithmID to DataOutput#writeInt and Checksum to DataOutput#writeLong, which are little-endian since 9.0, so you read them with readInt/readLong and expect Magic 0x3fd76c17 (the javadoc says 'It is always' CODEC_MAGIC), Version 1, footer Magic 0xc02893e8 and the file's CRC. Instead you get Magic 0x176cd73f, Version 16777216, footer Magic 0xe89328c0 and Checksum 0x62233eeb00000000, each byte-swapped, because CodecUtil writes these fields big-endian (writeBEInt/writeBELong); the other way round, a header or footer written with writeInt/writeLong as documented is rejected by checkHeader/checkFooter with CorruptIndexException. Lucene's own reader matches its writer, so indexing and search are unaffected; only the five javadoc links, left unchanged when LUCENE-9047 made DataOutput little-endian in 9.0.0, are wrong.

rows.title: The file-format javadoc of the default field infos format (Lucene94FieldInfosFormat) gives a wrong .fnm grammar: the per-field sequence leaves out IndexOptions, the doc-values skip-index byte, PointIndexDimensionCount and the three vector elements, and the value tables miss written values (doc-values codes 4 and 5, FieldBits 0x8 and 0x10, IndexOptions 5 since 10.5.0, VectorEncoding 2 on main) (documentation defect; the writer and reader agree)

rows.title: The file-format javadoc of the default doc-values format (Lucene90DocValuesFormat) says terms dictionaries are 'written in chunks of 16, with the first value written completely', but since 9.0 they are written in blocks of 64 terms whose other 63 terms are prefix-coded and then LZ4-compressed; it also says table compression is used for fewer than 256 unique values, while exactly 256 are table-compressed (documentation defect; the writer and reader agree)

Since Lucene 9.0 the writer instead uses blocks of 64 terms: only the first term of each block is stored in full, and the other 63 are prefix-coded and then compressed with LZ4, a step the javadoc never mentions, so in the .dvd file only terms 0, 64, 128, ... appear in clear, not 0, 16, 32, .... The same javadoc says a lookup table is used for numeric fields with fewer than 256 unique values, but a field with exactly 256 is also table-compressed; Lucene's own reader matches the writer, so nothing breaks at runtime, only the documentation is wrong.

rows.title: The file-format javadoc of the default compound format (Lucene90CompoundFormat) gives an incomplete .cfe entry-table grammar: it leaves out the codec footer the writer appends (the .cfs line beside it lists one), and it says each entry holds the file's name although the writer stores the name with the segment name stripped (documentation defect; the writer and reader agree)
rows.summary: You decode the compound entry table (.cfe) of a default-codec segment by following the Lucene90CompoundFormat javadoc, which says the file is Header, FileCount and then FileCount entries of FileName, DataOffset, DataLength, each holding 'a String with that file's name'. The writer also appends a 16-byte codec footer (the .cfs line just above lists its Footer, the .cfe line does not) and stores each name with the segment name stripped, for example '.nvd' for _0.nvd, so a parser built from the text ends 16 bytes early (byte 134 of 150 in the minimal repro, byte 502 of 518 in the hunt's 20-document test) and cannot find the sub-files by the names it read. Lucene's own reader checks the footer and puts the segment name back, so nothing breaks at runtime; only the documentation is wrong (the type line also lists an unused 'Checksum', which belongs to the linked CodecFooter grammar, so dropping it is cleanup).

rows.title: The file-format javadocs of the default vector formats (Lucene99FlatVectorsFormat and Lucene99HnswVectorsFormat) give a wrong .vemf/.vem/.vex grammar: both metadata lists leave out the int32 vector encoding that is written right after the field number, so every later element is misread, and since 10.3 the .vex list still calls the HNSW neighbour deltas vints although they are group-varint encoded (documentation defect; the writers and readers agree)
rows.summary: You decode the vector metadata (.vemf, .vem) or the HNSW graph (.vex) files of the default codec by following the Lucene99FlatVectorsFormat and Lucene99HnswVectorsFormat javadocs, which list each field as '[int32] field number, [int32] vector similarity function ordinal, [vlong] offset, ...' and each neighbour list as '[vint] count, array[vint] delta-encoded ordinals'. Both writers instead store an extra int32, the vector encoding (BYTE or FLOAT32), between the field number and the similarity, and since 10.3 they write the neighbour deltas with group-varint, so a parser built from the text reads the encoding as the similarity (a COSINE float field comes out as DOT_PRODUCT), gets the offset, length, dimension and count wrong, and decodes wrong neighbours from the first list of 4 or more neighbours on. Lucene's own readers match the writers, so nothing breaks at runtime; only the documentation is wrong, the metadata part since 9.4.0 and the .vex part since 10.3.0.

rows.title: The file-format javadoc of the default term-vectors format (Lucene90TermVectorsFormat) contradicts the .tvd bytes in three places: the Flags bit meaning is inverted, FieldNums are called delta-encoded but are the plain field numbers, and AvgCharsPerTerm is called absent without positions but is written whenever a field has offsets (documentation defect; the writer and reader agree)
rows.summary: You decode a .tvd chunk of the default term-vectors format by following its javadoc, which says the Flags Bit is 1 when all fields of the chunk have the same options, that FieldNums is a delta-encoded list, and that AvgCharsPerTerm is absent unless some field has both positions and offsets. The writer does the opposite on all three: it writes 0 for 'same options' (then one flag per distinct field) and 1 otherwise, it stores the plain sorted field numbers (fields 1, 3, 6 are stored as 1, 3, 6, which summed as deltas give 1, 4, 10), and it writes one AvgCharsPerTerm value per distinct field whenever any field has offsets, so a parser built from the text misreads the chunk. Lucene's own reader matches the writer, so nothing breaks at runtime; only the documentation is wrong, and it has been since it was written in 2013.

rows.summary: You read the Lucene 10.6.0 release notes (CHANGES.txt or the generated Changes.html of RC1) and follow the issue link of the entry 'CheckIndex now reports which segment's .si file could not be read'. You expect it to lead to GITHUB#7820, the issue the feature commit, CheckIndex.java and main's copy of the entry all name; instead the entry says GITHUB#17820 and its GitHub issue link (number 17820) returns 404. The extra digit was added when #16788 was backported to branch_10x and branch_10_6 (main's commit of the same PR kept 7820), and it ships in the RC1 source release.

rows.title: The documentation front page's 'API Javadocs' list links benchmark-jmh/index.html, a page no build renders: the Java port of the documentation build (#15350, backported by #16592) lists every module that has a renderSiteJavadoc task, while the Groovy build it replaced listed only modules whose task is enabled (dead link in the released 10.6.0 docs and in documentation builds of main, branch_11x and branch_10_6; documentation defect)
rows.summary: You open the front page of the Lucene 10.6.0 documentation (docs/index.html in the binary release, or a documentation build of main) and click benchmark-jmh in its 'API Javadocs' list. You expect that module's javadocs, as for the other 31 entries; instead the page does not exist, because benchmark-jmh's build disables its site javadocs ('No special javadocs for JMH benchmarks') and the Java port of the documentation build lists every module that has a renderSiteJavadoc task without checking that the task is enabled, which the Groovy build up to 10.5.2 did. Adding '&& t.getEnabled()' to that filter removes exactly this entry and nothing else.

rows.title: The 10.6.0 documentation front page says the Migration Guide covers migrating 'from Lucene 0.x' (main builds: 'Lucene 12; ... from Lucene 2.x'), because the build binds majorVersion as a String and the template's ${project.majorVersion-1} then deletes the first '1' character instead of subtracting (documentation build defect)
rows.summary: You open the documentation front page of Lucene 10.6.0 (docs/index.html) and read the Migration Guide entry. You expect 'What changed in Lucene 10; how to migrate code from Lucene 9.x.', as 10.5.2 says, because the template computes the previous major as ${project.majorVersion-1}; instead it says 'how to migrate code from Lucene 0.x.' (a main build says 'Lucene 12; ... from Lucene 2.x.'). Since the build's version globals became Java (#14862 on main, backported to 10.x in #16592), the template gets majorVersion as the String '10', and Groovy's String minus 1 deletes the first '1' character instead of subtracting; binding the value as an int restores 'from Lucene 9.x' (main: '11.x').

rows.title: PersistentSnapshotDeletionPolicy.getLastSaveFile reads nextWriteGen without synchronization (benign data race)
rows.summary: You call getLastSaveFile while other threads snapshot or release commits. You expect the latest save file. Instead it reads nextWriteGen without synchronization and can see a stale value; persistence itself is unaffected.
